diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['          sample_traits,', '        channel=GetPixelChannelChannel(image,i);', '        traits=GetPixelChannelTraits(image,channel);', '        sample_traits=GetPixelChannelTraits(sample_image,channel);', '            (sample_traits == UndefinedPixelTrait))'], 'added_lines': ['          image_traits,', '        channel=GetPixelChannelChannel(sample_image,i);', '        traits=GetPixelChannelTraits(sample_image,channel);', '        image_traits=GetPixelChannelTraits(image,channel);', '            (image_traits == UndefinedPixelTrait))']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read in SampleImage() in MagickCore/resize.c in ImageMagick 7.0.6-8 Q16 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The inner loop iterates i from 0 to GetPixelChannels(sample_image) (line 102), but indexes channel traits and channels using image (lines 109-110) while the sample image may have a different number of channels. The read p[x_offset[x]*GetPixelChannels(image)+i] (lines 115-116) combines the sample image's channel count i with the image's channel stride, and the offset x_offset[x] can point at the last column of image, so the final index can exceed the row buffer returned by GetCacheViewVirtualPixels.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads pixel data beyond the allocated row buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing bound check on the computed p index, not a write, distinguishes it from CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the channel loop bound is taken from sample_image while p is indexed using GetPixelChannels(image) and i, and x_offset[x] can equal image->columns-1. Trigger: a crafted image whose channel layout or dimensions cause x_offset[x]*GetPixelChannels(image)+i to reach past the virtual pixel row. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read of pixel data, leading to denial of service (crash).

commit_msg:
The current CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting scheme for the DOI
definitions is a bit flawed in that we:

1. Don't correctly match gets/puts in netlbl_cipsov4_list().
2. Decrement the refcount on each attempt to remove the DOI from the
   DOI list, only removing it from the list once the refcount drops
   to zero.

This patch fixes these problems by adding the missing "puts" to
netlbl_cipsov4_list() and introduces a more conventional, i.e.
not-buggy, refcounting mechanism to the DOI definitions.  Upon the
addition of a DOI to the DOI list, it is initialized with a refcount
of one, removing a DOI from the list removes it from the list and
drops the refcount by one; "gets" and "puts" behave as expected with
respect to refcounts, increasing and decreasing the DOI's refcount by
one.

Fixes: b1edeb102397 ("netlabel: Replace protocol/NetLabel linking with refrerence counts")
Fixes: d7cce01504a0 ("netlabel: Add support for removing a CALIPSO DOI.")
Reported-by: syzbot+9ec037722d2603a9f52e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul@paul-moore.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tspin_lock(&cipso_v4_doi_list_lock);', '\tlist_del_rcu(&doi_def->list);', '\tspin_unlock(&cipso_v4_doi_list_lock);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The Linux kernel before 5.11.14 has a use-after-free in cipso_v4_genopt in net/ipv4/cipso_ipv4.c because the CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting for the DOI definitions is mishandled, aka CID-ad5d07f4a9cd. This leads to writing an arbitrary value.

code_evidence: The putdef path drops the DOI refcount and only proceeds to teardown when refcount_dec_and_test reaches zero, so removal from the list and freeing occur at the final put.
In the before state, list_del_rcu(&doi_def->list) is executed here under the list lock; the patch removes it, changing when the DOI leaves the global list relative to its refcount.
After the list deletion, the function invalidates the cache and schedules call_rcu to free the DOI via cipso_v4_doi_free_rcu, so the object is freed asynchronously.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the release side of the DOI lifetime: it frees the DOI through call_rcu once the refcount hits zero. Because the surrounding refcounting scheme permits later access through a stale reference, the supported weakness is memory reuse after free, matching CWE-416; it is not merely an integer refcount error but the resulting dangling-pointer use.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!refcount_dec_and_test(&doi_def->refcount))
return;

cipso_v4_cache_invalidate();
call_rcu(&doi_def->rcu, cipso_v4_doi_free_rcu);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The flawed get/put accounting on DOI definitions allows the refcount to reach zero and schedule cipso_v4_doi_free_rcu while another path can still obtain or retain a reference to the same DOI. A subsequent lookup or use, such as in CIPSO option generation, dereferences the freed DOI, yielding a use-after-free that can lead to arbitrary writes.

description: ZmartZone IAM mod_auth_openidc 2.3.10.1 and earlier is affected by: Cross Site Scripting (XSS). The impact is: Redirecting the user to a phishing page or interacting with the application on behalf of the user. The component is: File: src/mod_auth_openidc.c, Line: 3109. The fixed version is: 2.3.10.2.

code_evidence: Line 19 embeds the poll interval into generated JavaScript via the %s format specifier inside the setInterval call, so the value is inserted as raw text into the served page.
Lines 53-56 read the user-controlled 'poll' request parameter and only substitute the default "3000" when it is NULL; any non-NULL value is accepted without validation and kept as a string.
Lines 58-60 pass s_poll_interval into apr_psprintf, placing the unvalidated value into the HTML/JS response sent to the client.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: User-controllable input is placed into a generated web page without neutralization, matching CWE-79. The fix uses %d and range-checks the integer, confirming the intended numeric constraint; this is improper output neutralization rather than e.g. open redirect, since arbitrary script executes.

evidence_lines.code: "        timerID = setInterval('checkSession()', %s);\n"

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 'poll' parameter is copied verbatim into an inline script without numeric validation or escaping. Trigger: a crafted poll value containing script syntax breaks out of the setInterval argument. Consequence: the browser executes attacker-supplied JavaScript in the RP iframe's origin, enabling redirect to a phishing page or acting on the user's behalf.

description: MagickCore/memory.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds write) via a crafted PDB file.

code_evidence: At [103,104,105] the runlength buffer is sized from packets (bits_per_pixel*image->columns+7)/8 multiplied by image->rows; before the fix only 2*packets bytes per row were allocated.

At [124,163,164,165,171,172,173,177] q advances through runlength via EncodeRLE and buffer literals are copied into buffer, with the RLE stream written to q; the per-row allocation bound is the only limit on how far q can advance.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because EncodeRLE writes through q beyond the bounds of the under-sized runlength allocation. This is a buffer-size miscalculation leading to out-of-bounds write, not an out-of-bounds read or integer overflow alone.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation in [104,105] under-provisions the runlength buffer relative to the encoded RLE output produced by EncodeRLE calls at [152,163,171,185], so q can advance past the end of the allocated region and EncodeRLE writes out of bounds. Trigger is encoding a crafted PDB image with many literal runs; consequence is memory corruption/denial of service.

commit_msg:
Currently, locking of ->session is very inconsistent; most places
protect it using the legacy tty mutex, but disassociate_ctty(),
__do_SAK(), tiocspgrp() and tiocgsid() don't.
Two of the writers hold the ctrl_lock (because they already need it for
->pgrp), but __proc_set_tty() doesn't do that yet.

On a PREEMPT=y system, an unprivileged user can theoretically abuse
this broken locking to read 4 bytes of freed memory via TIOCGSID if
tiocgsid() is preempted long enough at the right point. (Other things
might also go wrong, especially if root-only ioctls are involved; I'm
not sure about that.)

Change the locking on ->session such that:

 - tty_lock() is held by all writers: By making disassociate_ctty()
   hold it. This should be fine because the same lock can already be
   taken through the call to tty_vhangup_session().
   The tricky part is that we need to shorten the area covered by
   siglock to be able to take tty_lock() without ugly retry logic; as
   far as I can tell, this should be fine, since nothing in the
   signal_struct is touched in the `if (tty)` branch.
 - ctrl_lock is held by all writers: By changing __proc_set_tty() to
   hold the lock a little longer.
 - All readers that aren't holding tty_lock() hold ctrl_lock: By
   adding locking to tiocgsid() and __do_SAK(), and expanding the area
   covered by ctrl_lock in tiocspgrp().

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jiri Slaby <jirislaby@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn -ENOTTY;', '\treturn put_user(pid_vnr(real_tty->session), p);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long flags;', '\tpid_t sid;', '', '', '\tspin_lock_irqsave(&real_tty->ctrl_lock, flags);', '\t\tgoto err;', '\tsid = pid_vnr(real_tty->session);', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&real_tty->ctrl_lock, flags);', '', '\treturn put_user(sid, p);', '', 'err:', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&real_tty->ctrl_lock, flags);', '\treturn -ENOTTY;']}
description: A locking inconsistency issue was discovered in the tty subsystem of the Linux kernel through 5.9.13. drivers/tty/tty_io.c and drivers/tty/tty_jobctrl.c may allow a read-after-free attack against TIOCGSID, aka CID-c8bcd9c5be24.

code_evidence: The function reads real_tty->session at line 5 for the NULL check and again at line 7 inside put_user(pid_vnr(real_tty->session), p), without acquiring real_tty->ctrl_lock or any lock protecting ->session. The session pointer is dereferenced twice across a window that is not serialized against concurrent writers such as disassociate_ctty() or __proc_set_tty(), so the value can change between the check and the use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 covers improper locking of a shared resource. Here the shared real_tty->session is read without the ctrl_lock that writers hold, an inconsistent locking discipline enabling a race and use-after-free. It is not merely a generic race but a missing lock acquisition on a specific shared field.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: readers of real_tty->session take no lock, while writers modify it under ctrl_lock/tty_lock. Trigger: an unprivileged TIOCGSID caller is preempted after the NULL check at line 5 but before the dereference at line 7, while another path frees or replaces the session. Consequence: pid_vnr() reads a freed session object (read-after-free), leaking 4 bytes of freed memory or causing corruption/DoS. The fix adds ctrl_lock around the check and the dereference, copying the pid into a local sid before put_user().

commit_msg:
socket: close race condition between sock_close() and sockfs_setattr()

fchownat() doesn't even hold refcnt of fd until it figures out
fd is really needed (otherwise is ignored) and releases it after
it resolves the path. This means sock_close() could race with
sockfs_setattr(), which leads to a NULL pointer dereference
since typically we set sock->sk to NULL in ->release().

As pointed out by Al, this is unique to sockfs. So we can fix this
in socket layer by acquiring inode_lock in sock_close() and
checking against NULL in sockfs_setattr().

sock_release() is called in many places, only the sock_close()
path matters here. And fortunately, this should not affect normal
sock_close() as it is only called when the last fd refcnt is gone.
It only affects sock_close() with a parallel sockfs_setattr() in
progress, which is not common.

Fixes: 86741ec25462 ("net: core: Add a UID field to struct sock.")
Reported-by: shankarapailoor <shankarapailoor@gmail.com>
Cc: Tetsuo Handa <penguin-kernel@i-love.sakura.ne.jp>
Cc: Lorenzo Colitti <lorenzo@google.com>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsock_release(SOCKET_I(inode));'], 'added_lines': ['\t__sock_release(SOCKET_I(inode), inode);']}
description: In net/socket.c in the Linux kernel through 4.17.1, there is a race condition between fchownat and close in cases where they target the same socket file descriptor, related to the sock_close and sockfs_setattr functions. fchownat does not increment the file descriptor reference count, which allows close to set the socket to NULL during fchownat's execution, leading to a NULL pointer dereference and system crash.

code_evidence: sock_close() calls sock_release(SOCKET_I(inode)) without any lock protecting the socket/inode state; the release path sets sock->sk to NULL while a concurrent sockfs_setattr() (reached via fchownat) may still dereference it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function participates in a concurrent code sequence lacking exclusive access to the shared socket resource, matching CWE-362's race-condition definition; the fix serializes via inode_lock and a NULL check, confirming the synchronization gap rather than a different weakness.

evidence_lines.code: sock_release(SOCKET_I(inode));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sock_close() releases the socket without synchronizing against sockfs_setattr(), so the setattr path can observe sock->sk after the release path has nulled it. Trigger: fchownat() and close() target the same socket fd concurrently, since fchownat does not hold an fd reference. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and crash (availability DoS).

commit_msg:
Close connection if we derive an extra 1-rtt write cipher

Summary: Fixes CVE-2021-24029

Reviewed By: mjoras, lnicco

Differential Revision: D26613890

fbshipit-source-id: 19bb2be2c731808144e1a074ece313fba11f1945
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    CHECK(!conn.oneRttWriteCipher.get());'], 'added_lines': ['    if (conn.oneRttWriteCipher) {', '      throw QuicTransportException(', '          "Duplicate 1-rtt write cipher", TransportErrorCode::CRYPTO_ERROR);', '    }']}
description: A packet of death scenario is possible in mvfst via a specially crafted message during a QUIC session, which causes a crash via a failed assertion. Per QUIC specification, this particular message should be treated as a connection error. This issue affects mvfst versions prior to commit a67083ff4b8dcbb7ee2839da6338032030d712b0 and proxygen versions prior to v2021.03.15.00.

code_evidence: When a 1-rtt write cipher is derived (line 25), the code logs and traces it (lines 26-29), then asserts the connection has no existing 1-rtt write cipher via CHECK(!conn.oneRttWriteCipher.get()) at line 30 before assigning it at line 31. The assert fires if a duplicate cipher is derived, which a crafted QUIC message can cause.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a reachable assertion (CHECK at line 30) that an attacker can trigger through crafted QUIC input, causing a crash rather than a handled connection error, matching CWE-617. This is distinct from a general null-pointer or logic error because the security impact stems from the fatal assertion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a reachable CHECK assertion guards the assignment of the 1-rtt write cipher instead of handling the duplicate-derivation condition as a protocol error. Trigger: a specially crafted message during a QUIC session causes the handshake layer to derive a second 1-rtt write cipher while one is already set. Consequence: the assertion fails and the process crashes (denial of service).

Nearly all TrueType fonts have this bit */', "    /* set, as hinting won't work really well otherwise.             */", '    /*                                                               */', '    if ( face->header.Flags & 8 )', '    {', '      /* the TT spec always asks for ROUND, not FLOOR or CEIL */', '      size_metrics->ascender = FT_PIX_ROUND(', '                                 FT_MulFix( face->root.ascender,', '                                            size_metrics->y_scale ) );', '      size_metrics->descender = FT_PIX_ROUND(', '                                 FT_MulFix( face->root.descender,', '                                            size_metrics->y_scale ) );', '      size_metrics->height = FT_PIX_ROUND(', '                               FT_MulFix( face->root.height,', '                                          size_metrics->y_scale ) );', '    }', '', '    size->ttmetrics.valid = TRUE;', '', '    if ( only_height )', '    {', '      /* we must not recompute the scaling values here since       */', "      /* `tt_size_reset' was already called (with only_height = 0) */", '      return FT_Err_Ok;', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['  tt_size_reset( TT_Size  size )', '    FT_Error          error;', '    TT_Face           face         = (TT_Face)size->root.face;', '    FT_Size_Metrics*  size_metrics = &size->hinted_metrics;', '    error = tt_size_reset_height( (FT_Size)size );', '    if ( error )', '      return error;']}
description: In multiple locations, there is a possible code execution due to type confusion. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: `face` is obtained by casting `size->root.face` to `TT_Face` and then dereferenced as `face->is_cff2` without verifying the object is actually a TrueType face; a CFF/CFF2 or otherwise mismatched size object would be interpreted through the wrong structure layout.
`size_metrics` is derived from `size->hinted_metrics` and overwritten from `size->root.metrics`; the ppem check only guards the copied values, not the validity of the size/face pairing.
When `only_height` is set the function returns early after setting `ttmetrics.valid`, so later callers may rely on reset state that was computed against an incompatible face type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses resources (`size->root.face`, `size->hinted_metrics`) through types incompatible with their actual allocation, matching CWE-843's definition of type confusion. It is not merely a null/invalid-pointer issue: the weakness is interpreting one object layout as another.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `tt_size_reset` casts and dereferences the face and size objects via TrueType-specific types (`TT_Face`, `TT_Size`) without confirming the underlying object's actual type. Trigger: a size/face whose real type is not the expected TrueType type reaches this function (e.g. CFF2 handling removed/misrouted). The incompatible layout access can yield logical corruption and, in memory-unsafe contexts, out-of-bounds access leading to code execution.

commit_msg:
nla: invalidate sec handle after creation

If sec pointer isn't invalidated after creation it is not possible
to check if the upper and lower pointers are valid.

This fixes a segfault in the server part if the client disconnects before
the authentication was finished.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tSecInvalidateHandle(&credssp->context);']}
description: FreeRDP before 1.1.0-beta+2013071101 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) by disconnecting before authentication has finished.

code_evidence: credssp is allocated with malloc then immediately passed to ZeroMemory before any NULL check; if malloc returns NULL, ZeroMemory dereferences a NULL pointer.

The function zero-initializes embedded SecBuffer fields but, before the fix, does not invalidate credssp->context; the added SecInvalidateHandle(&credssp->context) marks the security handle invalid so later validity checks can reject an unfinished/aborted authentication.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid without first confirming it is non-NULL, matching CWE-476. This is a direct NULL dereference rather than a use-after-free, since the defect is the missing NULL constraint on the freshly allocated pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked malloc result: ZeroMemory(credssp, ...) at line 5 dereferences credssp before the NULL test at line 6. Trigger is allocation failure (or, per the commit, a client disconnect before authentication completes where an un-invalidated context handle is later treated as valid); supported consequence is a NULL/invalid pointer dereference causing a server crash (DoS).

description: Memcached 1.6.x before 1.6.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (daemon crash) via a crafted binary protocol header to try_read_command_binary in memcached.c.

code_evidence: Line 31 reads extlen as an attacker-controlled uint8_t from the binary header (up to 255), and line 32 reads keylen; the length check on line 33 only confirms enough bytes exist, not that extlen fits the destination.

Line 45 allocates extbuf sized for binary_header plus BIN_MAX_EXTLEN, but line 46 memcpy's extlen bytes into extbuf + sizeof(c->binary_header) with no clamp, so extlen exceeding BIN_MAX_EXTLEN writes past the stack buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because this is a buffer copy (memcpy) whose input size is not validated against the destination size, producing a write past the end of extbuf. The later patch clamps the copy length to BIN_MAX_EXTLEN, confirming the missing size check rather than an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
char extbuf[sizeof(c->binary_header) + BIN_MAX_EXTLEN];
memcpy(extbuf + sizeof(c->binary_header), c->rcurr + sizeof(c->binary_header), extlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the memcpy length extlen is taken directly from the request header without bounding it to BIN_MAX_EXTLEN, the destination's extension capacity. Trigger: a crafted binary protocol header declaring extlen larger than BIN_MAX_EXTLEN with sufficient rbytes. Consequence: stack buffer overflow corrupting adjacent stack memory, supporting daemon crash (DoS) and potential memory modification/control-flow impact.

commit_msg:
FuzzUSB (a variant of syzkaller) found an illegal array access
using an incorrect index while binding a gadget with UDC.

Reference: https://www.spinics.net/lists/linux-usb/msg194331.html

This bug occurs when a size variable used for a buffer
is misused to access its strcpy-ed buffer.
Given a buffer along with its size variable (taken from user input),
from which, a new buffer is created using kstrdup().
Due to the original buffer containing 0 value in the middle,
the size of the kstrdup-ed buffer becomes smaller than that of the original.
So accessing the kstrdup-ed buffer with the same size variable
triggers memory access violation.

The fix makes sure no zero value in the buffer,
by comparing the strlen() of the orignal buffer with the size variable,
so that the access to the kstrdup-ed buffer is safe.

description: gadget_dev_desc_UDC_store in drivers/usb/gadget/configfs.c in the Linux kernel 3.16 through 5.6.13 relies on kstrdup without considering the possibility of an internal '\0' value, which allows attackers to trigger an out-of-bounds read, aka CID-15753588bcd4.

commit_msg:
A BPF program might try to reserve a buffer larger than the ringbuf size.
If the consumer pointer is way ahead of the producer, that would be
successfully reserved, allowing the BPF program to read or write out of
the ringbuf allocated area.

Reported-by: Ryota Shiga (Flatt Security)
Fixes: 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it")
Signed-off-by: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo <cascardo@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (len > rb->mask + 1)', '\t\treturn NULL;', '']}
description: The eBPF RINGBUF bpf_ringbuf_reserve() function in the Linux kernel did not check that the allocated size was smaller than the ringbuf size, allowing an attacker to perform out-of-bounds writes within the kernel and therefore, arbitrary code execution. This issue was fixed via commit 4b81ccebaeee ("bpf, ringbuf: Deny reserve of buffers larger than ringbuf") (v5.13-rc4) and backported to the stable kernels in v5.12.4, v5.11.21, and v5.10.37. It was introduced via 457f44363a88 ("bpf: Implement BPF ring buffer and verifier support for it") (v5.8-rc1).

code_evidence: len is computed as round_up(size + header, 8) with no comparison against the ringbuf capacity; the only bound check before the fix is size > RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ.
The reservation check compares new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask, a relative distance, so a large len can pass when cons_pos lags far behind prod_pos.
hdr is placed at rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask) and the record length stored; returning hdr + header hands the BPF program a region that may extend past rb->data's allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns a writable pointer whose extent exceeds the allocated ringbuf buffer, so BPF writes land past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an integer overflow: the missing capacity constraint on len is the direct cause of the out-of-bounds region.

evidence_lines.code: len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reserve path validates only the relative producer-consumer distance, not that the rounded record length fits the ring buffer. Trigger: a BPF program requests a size larger than the ringbuf while the consumer pointer is far behind the producer, so the distance check passes. Consequence: the returned pointer plus size reaches beyond the ringbuf data area, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes in kernel memory.

commit_msg:
Fix for issue #282

The fix limits recursion depths when parsing arrays and objects.
The limit is configurable via the `JSON_PARSER_MAX_DEPTH` setting
within `jansson_config.h` and is set by default to 2048.

Update the RFC conformance document to note the limit; the RFC
allows limits to be set by the implementation so nothing has
actually changed w.r.t. conformance state.

Reported by Gustavo Grieco.

description: The dissect_sdp function in epan/dissectors/packet-sdp.c in the SDP dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 does not prevent use of a negative media count, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted packet.

commit_msg:
Jann Horn points out that our TLB flushing was subtly wrong for the
mremap() case.  What makes mremap() special is that we don't follow the
usual "add page to list of pages to be freed, then flush tlb, and then
free pages".  No, mremap() obviously just _moves_ the page from one page
table location to another.

That matters, because mremap() thus doesn't directly control the
lifetime of the moved page with a freelist: instead, the lifetime of the
page is controlled by the page table locking, that serializes access to
the entry.

As a result, we need to flush the TLB not just before releasing the lock
for the source location (to avoid any concurrent accesses to the entry),
but also before we release the destination page table lock (to avoid the
TLB being flushed after somebody else has already done something to that
page).

This also makes the whole "need_flush" logic unnecessary, since we now
always end up flushing the TLB for every valid entry.

Reported-and-tested-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Will Deacon <will.deacon@arm.com>
Tested-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
Acked-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t  pmd_t *old_pmd, pmd_t *new_pmd, bool *need_flush)', '\t\tif (pmd_present(pmd) && pmd_dirty(pmd))', '\t\tif (force_flush)', '\t\t\tflush_tlb_range(vma, old_addr, old_addr + PMD_SIZE);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\t*need_flush = true;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t  pmd_t *old_pmd, pmd_t *new_pmd)', '\t\tif (pmd_present(pmd))', '\t\tif (force_flush)', '\t\t\tflush_tlb_range(vma, old_addr, old_addr + PMD_SIZE);']}
description: Since Linux kernel version 3.2, the mremap() syscall performs TLB flushes after dropping pagetable locks. If a syscall such as ftruncate() removes entries from the pagetables of a task that is in the middle of mremap(), a stale TLB entry can remain for a short time that permits access to a physical page after it has been released back to the page allocator and reused. This is fixed in the following kernel versions: 4.9.135, 4.14.78, 4.18.16, 4.19.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's TLB flush ordering issue reflects a stale TLB entry / use-after-free window (CWE-416-like), not incomplete cleanup of temporary resources; the code contains no resource cleanup omission matching CWE-459.

commit_msg:
By validating length fields from server responses, out of boundary
accesses and endless loops can be mitigated.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    size_t size;', '            size += SizeClassInfo(&any, (int)list->num_classes);', '\tNptr = ((unsigned char *)list) + rlen + 1;', '\t    if (nptr > Nptr)', '\t\tgoto out;'], 'added_lines': ['    size_t s, size;', '    char *end = NULL;', '\tend = (char *)list + rlen;', '            s = SizeClassInfo(&any, end - (char *)any, (int)list->num_classes);', '            if (!s)', '                goto out;', '            size += s;', '\tNptr = ((unsigned char *)list) + rlen;', '\t    if (nptr >= Nptr)', '\t\tgoto out;']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in X.org libXi before 1.7.7 allow remote X servers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds memory access or infinite loop) via vectors involving length fields.

code_evidence: Line 30 computes size = *ndevices * sizeof(XDeviceInfo) using the server-supplied ndevices count with no overflow check; rlen is bounded but size is not.

Line 42 derives the class-info pointer from *ndevices * sizeof(xDeviceInfo), and the loop at 44-46 accumulates SizeClassInfo results into size without validating the per-device class count against the reply buffer.

Lines 47-51 walk the name data using *nptr + 1 increments, accumulating into size and only checking nptr against Nptr after the pointer arithmetic, so a large length byte can make nptr skip past the buffer before the check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operations are integer multiplications and additions whose results are assumed to remain valid sizes/offsets; wraparound yields an undersized allocation or corrupted pointer arithmetic. This is the size-calculation flaw, distinct from a pure out-of-bounds read that would follow once the wrapped value is used.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is unchecked arithmetic on attacker-controlled length and count fields from the X server reply: the device-count multiplication and the accumulated size/name-length additions can wrap, producing a small allocation or letting the name pointer advance past the buffer. The trigger is a crafted ListInputDevices reply; the supported consequence is out-of-bounds access or an infinite loop, matching the described DoS.

commit_msg:
x86/traps: Use an Interrupt Stack Table for #DB

PV guests can use architectural corner cases to cause #DB to be raised after
transitioning into supervisor mode.

Use an interrupt stack table for #DB to prevent the exception being taken with
a guest controlled stack pointer.

This is part of XSA-260 / CVE-2018-8897

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -2,11 +2,11 @@
 {
     switch ( get_stack_page(sp) )
     {
-    case 0 ... 2:
+    case 0 ... 3:
         return ROUNDUP(sp, PAGE_SIZE) - sizeof(unsigned long);
 
 #ifndef MEMORY_GUARD
-    case 3 ... 5:
+    case 4 ... 5:
 #endif
     case 6 ... 7:
         return ROUNDUP(sp, STACK_SIZE) - sizeof(unsigned long);
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    case 0 ... 2:', '    case 3 ... 5:'], 'added_lines': ['    case 0 ... 3:', '    case 4 ... 5:']}
description: A statement in the System Programming Guide of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual (SDM) was mishandled in the development of some or all operating-system kernels, resulting in unexpected behavior for #DB exceptions that are deferred by MOV SS or POP SS, as demonstrated by (for example) privilege escalation in Windows, macOS, some Xen configurations, or FreeBSD, or a Linux kernel crash. The MOV to SS and POP SS instructions inhibit interrupts (including NMIs), data breakpoints, and single step trap exceptions until the instruction boundary following the next instruction (SDM Vol. 3A; section 6.8.3). (The inhibited data breakpoints are those on memory accessed by the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction itself.) Note that debug exceptions are not inhibited by the interrupt enable (EFLAGS.IF) system flag (SDM Vol. 3A; section 2.3). If the instruction following the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction is an instruction like SYSCALL, SYSENTER, INT 3, etc. that transfers control to the operating system at CPL < 3, the debug exception is delivered after the transfer to CPL < 3 is complete. OS kernels may not expect this order of events and may therefore experience unexpected behavior when it occurs.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only classifies a stack pointer into page ranges and returns a rounded dump bottom; it contains no shared-resource access, synchronization, or concurrent code sequence, so it does not support a race-condition classification.

description: Nokogiri is an open source XML and HTML library for the Ruby programming language. Nokogiri `1.13.8` and `1.13.9` fail to check the return value from `xmlTextReaderExpand` in the method `Nokogiri::XML::Reader#attribute_hash`. This can lead to a null pointer exception when invalid markup is being parsed. For applications using `XML::Reader` to parse untrusted inputs, this may potentially be a vector for a denial of service attack. Users are advised to upgrade to Nokogiri `>= 1.13.10`. Users may be able to search their code for calls to either `XML::Reader#attributes` or `XML::Reader#attribute_hash` to determine if they are affected.

c_node = xmlTextReaderExpand(c_reader);
c_property = c_node->properties;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of xmlTextReaderExpand is not validated. Trigger: invalid or malicious markup causes expansion to fail and return NULL. Consequence: c_node->properties dereferences NULL, crashing the process and enabling denial of service.

description: In radare2 before 2.9.0, a heap overflow vulnerability exists in the read_module_referenced_functions function in libr/anal/flirt.c via a crafted flirt signature file.

code_evidence: Only a negative length is rejected; the upper bound of ref_function_name_length is not constrained before the copy loop.
The loop iterates j from 0 to ref_function_name_length-1 and writes each byte into ref_function->name[j], so a length exceeding the fixed RFlirtName buffer overflows it.
The terminating write at index ref_function_name_length also writes one byte past the intended name buffer when the length is at or beyond its capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-sized data past the end of a fixed-size heap buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an integer issue: the missing upper-bound check directly permits the overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ref_function_name_length is attacker-controlled from the flirt signature file and only checked for negativity, not against R_FLIRT_NAME_MAX. Trigger: a crafted file supplies a large length, causing the copy loop and null terminator to write past the fixed name buffer. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write, memory corruption and potential crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
userfaultfd: shmem/hugetlbfs: only allow to register VM_MAYWRITE vmas

After the VMA to register the uffd onto is found, check that it has
VM_MAYWRITE set before allowing registration.  This way we inherit all
common code checks before allowing to fill file holes in shmem and
hugetlbfs with UFFDIO_COPY.

The userfaultfd memory model is not applicable for readonly files unless
it's a MAP_PRIVATE.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20181126173452.26955-4-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: ff62a3421044 ("hugetlb: implement memfd sealing")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>

Reviewed-by: Hugh Dickins <hughd@google.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Fixes: 4c27fe4c4c84 ("userfaultfd: shmem: add shmem_mcopy_atomic_pte for userfaultfd support")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>

Cc: Mike Kravetz <mike.kravetz@oracle.com>
Cc: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * UFFDIO_COPY will fill file holes even without', '\t\t * PROT_WRITE. This check enforces that if this is a', '\t\t * MAP_SHARED, the process has write permission to the backing', '\t\t * file. If VM_MAYWRITE is set it also enforces that on a', '\t\t * MAP_SHARED vma: there is no F_WRITE_SEAL and no further', '\t\t * F_WRITE_SEAL can be taken until the vma is destroyed.', '\t\t */', '\t\tret = -EPERM;', '\t\tif (unlikely(!(cur->vm_flags & VM_MAYWRITE)))', '\t\t\tgoto out_unlock;', '', '\t\tWARN_ON(!(vma->vm_flags & VM_MAYWRITE));']}
description: The userfaultfd implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.19.7 mishandles access control for certain UFFDIO_ ioctl calls, as demonstrated by allowing local users to write data into holes in a tmpfs file (if the user has read-only access to that file, and that file contains holes), related to fs/userfaultfd.c and mm/userfaultfd.c.

code_evidence: Loop over VMAs in the requested range; vma_can_userfault(cur) is the only eligibility gate before registration, and it does not test VM_MAYWRITE.
Checks whether the VMA is already registered to another context, but no write-permission check on the backing file/VMA is performed.
The skip label and flag comparison only test whether the requested UFFD flags are already set, not whether the VMA is writable.
Registration writes new_flags and assigns ctx to the VMA, marking it userfaultfd-managed and enabling UFFDIO_COPY into it later.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an authorization check (vma_can_userfault and context checks) but omits the required write-permission constraint, so a user lacking write access can gain write-like capability via UFFDIO_COPY. This is incorrect authorization (CWE-863), not merely a missing input validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: userfaultfd_register accepts a MAP_SHARED VMA backed by a file the caller can only read, because it never verifies VM_MAYWRITE. Once registered, UFFDIO_COPY can fill file holes even without PROT_WRITE, letting a read-only user modify file contents.

commit_msg:
Prevent unitialized memory access in `GraphConstructor::MakeEdge`

The `MakeEdge` implementation assumes that there exists an output at `output_index` of `src` node and an input at `input_index` of `dst` node. However, if this is not the case this results in accessing data out of bounds. Because we are accessing an array that is a private member of a class and only in read only mode, this usually results only in unitialized memory access. However, it is reasonable to think that malicious users could manipulate these indexes to actually read data outside the class, thus resulting in information leakage and further exploits.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 346343288
Change-Id: I2127da27c2023d27f26efd39afa6c853385cab6f
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (output_index >= src->num_outputs()) {', '    return errors::InvalidArgument(', '        "Output ", output_index, " of node ", src->name(),', '        " does not exist. Node only has ", src->num_outputs(), " outputs.");', '  }', '  if (input_index >= dst->num_inputs()) {', '    return errors::InvalidArgument(', '        "Input ", input_index, " of node ", dst->name(),', '        " does not exist. Node only has ", dst->num_inputs(), " inputs.");', '  }', '']}
description: In affected versions of TensorFlow under certain cases, loading a saved model can result in accessing uninitialized memory while building the computation graph. The MakeEdge function creates an edge between one output tensor of the src node (given by output_index) and the input slot of the dst node (given by input_index). This is only possible if the types of the tensors on both sides coincide, so the function begins by obtaining the corresponding DataType values and comparing these for equality. However, there is no check that the indices point to inside of the arrays they index into. Thus, this can result in accessing data out of bounds of the corresponding heap allocated arrays. In most scenarios, this can manifest as unitialized data access, but if the index points far away from the boundaries of the arrays this can be used to leak addresses from the library. This is fixed in versions 1.15.5, 2.0.4, 2.1.3, 2.2.2, 2.3.2, and 2.4.0.

code_evidence: MakeEdge calls src->output_type(output_index) and dst->input_type(input_index) without checking that output_index < src->num_outputs() or input_index < dst->num_inputs(). The caller-supplied indices are used directly to index into per-node type arrays.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked index causes the function to read memory that was never initialized for that slot, matching CWE-908 (use of uninitialized resource) with read-memory confidentiality impact. It is not merely CWE-125 because the primary described effect is consuming uninitialized slot data, though the underlying cause is the absent bounds check.

evidence_lines.code:
DataType src_out = src->output_type(output_index);
DataType dst_in = dst->input_type(input_index);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing bounds validation on output_index and input_index before array access. Trigger: a saved model whose edge references an output/input slot that does not exist. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the type arrays, yielding uninitialized or adjacent memory (potential address leakage) rather than a valid DataType.

description: A vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel, where accessing a deallocated instance in printer_ioctl() printer_ioctl() tries to access of a printer_dev instance. However, use-after-free arises because it had been freed by gprinter_free().

code_evidence: printer_close obtains the device pointer from fd->private_data (line 4), clears dev->printer_cdev_open and fd->private_data under the lock (lines 7-8), then unlocks (line 10) and only logs/returns (line 11). The function never releases the kref reference that the open path took, so the printer_dev object's lifetime is not tied to the file's open/close lifecycle.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a lifetime/refcount imbalance that permits a freed printer_dev to be referenced afterward by an ioctl, which is exactly CWE-416 use after free rather than a mere null dereference or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: printer_close fails to drop the reference obtained at open, leaving the object freeable while a file descriptor still holds it. Trigger: configfs unlink invokes gprinter_free/usb_put_function, freeing the printer_dev while a concurrent printer_ioctl still uses fd->private_data. Supported consequence: use-after-free read/spin_lock on freed memory, as in the reported KASAN __lock_acquire report.

commit_msg:
ahci: Update byte count after DMA completion

Currently, DMA read/write operations neglect to update
the byte count after a successful transfer like ATAPI
DMA read or PIO read/write operations do.

We correct this oversight by adding another callback into
the IDEDMAOps structure. The commit callback is called
whenever we are cleaning up a scatter-gather list.
AHCI can register this callback in order to update post-
transfer information such as byte count updates.

We use this callback in AHCI to consolidate where we delete
the SGlist as generated from the PRDT, as well as update the
byte count after the transfer is complete.

The QEMUSGList structure has an init flag added to it in order
to make qemu_sglist_destroy a nop if it is called when
there is no sglist, which simplifies cleanup and error paths.

This patch fixes several AHCI problems, notably Non-NCQ modes
of operation for Windows 7 as well as Hibernate support for Windows 7.

commit_msg:
jp3d/jpwl convert: fix write stack buffer overflow

Missing buffer length formatter in fscanf call might lead to write
stack buffer overflow.

fixes #1044 (CVE-2017-17480)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        fscanf(f, "PG%[ \\t]%c%c%[ \\t+-]%d%[ \\t]%d%[ \\t]%d", temp, &endian1, &endian2,', '               signtmp, &prec, temp, &w, temp, &h);'], 'added_lines': ['        fscanf(f, "PG%31[ \\t]%c%c%31[ \\t+-]%d%31[ \\t]%d%31[ \\t]%d", temp, &endian1,', '               &endian2, signtmp, &prec, temp, &w, temp, &h);']}
description: In OpenJPEG 2.3.0, a stack-based buffer overflow was discovered in the pgxtoimage function in jpwl/convert.c. The vulnerability causes an out-of-bounds write, which may lead to remote denial of service or possibly remote code execution.

code_evidence: signtmp and temp are fixed 32-byte stack arrays. The fscanf format at lines 107-108 uses unbounded %[ \t+-] and %[ \t] conversions writing into signtmp and temp, with no field-width limit. Header data from the opened PGX file (fopen at line 100) directly feeds these conversions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing past a fixed-size stack buffer via unchecked input length is an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787. It differs from CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read) because the overflow is on the write side into temp/signtmp.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded scanset conversions copy an arbitrarily long run of whitespace/sign characters from the file header into 32-byte stack buffers. Trigger: a crafted .pgx header containing a long whitespace/sign run. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, an out-of-bounds write that can crash the process or potentially enable code execution.

commit_msg:
In vrend clear dispatch function, the 'buffers' is read from
guest. A malicious guest can specify a bad 'buffers' to make
a the function call util_format_is_pure_uint() even the
'ctx->sub->surf[i]' is NULL. This can cause a NULL pointer deref.
Make a sanity check to avoid this.

[airlied: use a define]

Signed-off-by: Li Qiang <liq3ea@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 void vrend_set_framebuffer_state(struct vrend_context *ctx,
-                                 uint32_t nr_cbufs, uint32_t surf_handle[8],
+                                 uint32_t nr_cbufs, uint32_t surf_handle[PIPE_MAX_COLOR_BUFS],
                                  uint32_t zsurf_handle)
 {
    struct vrend_surface *surf, *zsurf;
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                 uint32_t nr_cbufs, uint32_t surf_handle[8],'], 'added_lines': ['                                 uint32_t nr_cbufs, uint32_t surf_handle[PIPE_MAX_COLOR_BUFS],']}
description: The util_format_is_pure_uint function in vrend_renderer.c in Virgil 3d project (aka virglrenderer) 0.6.0 and earlier allows local guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted VIRGL_CCMD_CLEAR command.

code_evidence: The loop indexes ctx->sub->surf[i] for i < nr_cbufs, which is guest-controlled; when surf_handle[i] is 0, surf is set to NULL and vrend_surface_reference stores NULL into ctx->sub->surf[i].

Later, if nr_cbufs > 0 but all entries are NULL, the scan loop finds surf == NULL and returns early; however the clear path may still call util_format_is_pure_uint on a NULL ctx->sub->surf[i] because the loop above permits NULL slots to remain.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the code stores NULL into ctx->sub->surf[i] and later code dereferences it without a validity check. This is not an out-of-bounds issue, since the array bound is fixed; the defect is the missing non-NULL constraint on the dereferenced surface pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nr_cbufs and the per-slot handles come from the guest, and the function does not enforce that any non-NULL color surface exists before later clear code dereferences ctx->sub->surf[i]. Trigger: a VIRGL_CCMD_CLEAR with a bad buffer selection leaves a NULL surface slot. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and guest-triggered host DoS.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12997/LLDP: Don't use an 8-bit loop counter.

If you have a

	for (i = 0; i < N; i++)

loop, you'd better make sure that i is big enough to hold N - not N-1,
N.

The TLV length here is 9 bits long, not 8 bits long, so an 8-bit loop
counter will overflow and you can loop infinitely.

This fixes an infinite loop discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add tests using the capture files supplied by the reporter(s).

Clean up the output a bit while we're at it.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint8_t i;', '        \tND_PRINT((ndo, "\\n\\t      Priority: %d, RES: %d, Sel: %d",', '        \t\t tval >> 5, (tval >> 3) & 0x03, (tval & 0x07)));', '        \tND_PRINT((ndo, "Protocol ID: %d", EXTRACT_16BITS(tptr + i + 5)));'], 'added_lines': ['    u_int i;', '        \tND_PRINT((ndo, "\\n\\t      Priority: %u, RES: %u, Sel: %u, Protocol ID: %u",', '        \t\t tval >> 5, (tval >> 3) & 0x03, (tval & 0x07),', '        \t\t EXTRACT_16BITS(tptr + i + 5)));']}
description: The LLDP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 could enter an infinite loop due to a bug in print-lldp.c:lldp_private_8021_print().

code_evidence: The loop counter i is declared as uint8_t, an 8-bit unsigned type.

In the APPLICATION_PRIORITY case, sublen=tlv_len-5 is derived from the 9-bit TLV length; the loop while(i<sublen) increments i by 3 each iteration. When sublen exceeds 255, the 8-bit i wraps around after 255 and can never satisfy i<sublen, so the loop never exits.
The CDCP case uses the same 8-bit i with sublen=tlv_len-8 and the while(i<sublen) loop, giving the same wrap-around infinite-loop behavior.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's loop exit condition i<sublen is unreachable because i wraps around as a uint8_t, matching CWE-835's infinite loop with unreachable exit condition. This is a loop-counter overflow, not a buffer overread.

evidence_lines.code: uint8_t i;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an 8-bit loop counter compares against a sublen derived from a multi-bit TLV length that can exceed 255. Trigger: a crafted LLDP frame whose TLV length makes sublen large enough that i, incremented by 3, wraps modulo 256 before reaching sublen. Consequence: the while loop never terminates, causing CPU consumption/DoS in the parser.

commit_msg:
Fix a couple buffer overflows

https://hackerone.com/reports/502816
https://hackerone.com/reports/507858

https://github.com/videolan/vlc/blob/master/contrib/src/faad2/faad2-fix-overflows.patch
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ld->bytes_left = ld->buffer_size - words*4;'], 'added_lines': ['    if (ld->buffer_size < words * 4)', '        ld->bytes_left = 0;', '    else', '        ld->bytes_left = ld->buffer_size - words*4;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Freeware Advanced Audio Decoder 2 (FAAD2) 2.8.8. The faad_resetbits function in libfaad/bits.c is affected by a buffer overflow vulnerability. The number of bits to be read is determined by ld->buffer_size - words*4, cast to uint32. If ld->buffer_size - words*4 is negative, a buffer overflow is later performed via getdword_n(&ld->start[words], ld->bytes_left).

code_evidence: Line 4 derives `words = bits >> 5` from the caller-supplied `bits`; line 5 derives `remainder`; line 6 computes `ld->bytes_left = ld->buffer_size - words*4` with no check that `words*4` does not exceed `buffer_size`.
Because `bytes_left` is a uint32, a negative difference wraps to a huge value, so the `bytes_left >= 4` branch is taken and `getdword(&ld->start[words])` reads at `words` past the buffer.
Line 26 then sets `ld->tail = &ld->start[words+2]`, another out-of-bounds pointer derived from the unchecked `words`.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs memory reads and pointer arithmetic outside the intended buffer bounds due to the missing size constraint on `words`. This is a direct out-of-bounds buffer operation, not merely an integer issue, though the unsigned wrap is the enabling mechanism.

evidence_lines.code: ld->tail = &ld->start[words+2];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the subtraction in line 6 is performed without validating that `bits >> 5` scaled by 4 stays within `ld->buffer_size`. Trigger: a caller passes a `bits` value whose word offset exceeds the buffer. The wrapped `bytes_left` and unchecked `words` cause reads at `ld->start[words]` and `start[words+1]`, an out-of-bounds read that can crash or disclose memory.

commit_msg:
[tf.data] Set limit on number of threads used in threadpool_dataset.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 410922677
Change-Id: Ib25814a99043ab10805b5d2d7088ae0e0b7b04fd
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  OP_REQUIRES(ctx, num_threads >= 0,', '              errors::InvalidArgument("`num_threads` must be >= 0"));'], 'added_lines': ['  OP_REQUIRES_OK(ctx, ValidateNumThreads(num_threads));']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `ThreadPoolHandle` can be used to trigger a denial of service attack by allocating too much memory. This is because the `num_threads` argument is only checked to not be negative, but there is no upper bound on its value. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: `num_threads` is parsed from the op attribute into an int64_t [4,5,6]. The only validation is the lower bound `num_threads >= 0` [7,8]; no upper bound or maximum is enforced before the value is passed to `new Dataset(ctx, input, num_threads)` [9], which constructs the thread pool with that many threads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates a reusable resource (threads) on behalf of an actor while imposing only a lower bound and no upper limit or throttling. The missing upper-bound constraint is the direct cause; the resource exhaustion is the consequence, not a separate weakness such as integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser accepts any non-negative `num_threads` and constructs a Dataset/thread pool sized by it, with no cap on the count. Trigger: an attacker supplies a very large `num_threads` value. Consequence: the thread pool allocates excessive threads/memory, exhausting resources and causing denial of service (availability impact).

description: coders/dds.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted DDS file.

code_evidence: The covariance array elements are copied directly into row0, row1 and row2 without any check of their magnitude or finiteness; these floats originate from a crafted DDS file's pixel data.
The normalized vector is computed by dividing each component by MaxF(w.x,MaxF(w.y,w.z)). No guard ensures this maximum is nonzero or finite before division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts file-derived float data and performs arithmetic without validating that values are finite or that the divisor is nonzero, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input properties required for safe processing. This is a missing input-property constraint rather than a bounds/index defect, so CWE-20 is the appropriate label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled covariance values flow unvalidated into the normalization divisor. If the crafted DDS data yields a zero or non-finite maximum, the division at line 42 produces inf/NaN, which propagates into the principle vector and later computations, causing a crash or denial of service. The trigger is a crafted DDS file; the supported consequence is availability impact (DoS).

This can avoid memory leak when hotunplug the ahci device.

description: Memory leak in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator), when built with IDE AHCI Emulation support, allows local guest OS privileged users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by repeatedly hot-unplugging the AHCI device.

code_evidence: ahci_uninit only frees the s->dev array via g_free; it never iterates over the per-port IDEState objects (ad->port.ifs[j]) to release resources associated with each AHCIDevice before freeing the container array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to release allocated memory whose lifetime has ended during device teardown, matching CWE-401 (Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime). It is not a double-free or use-after-free, since the issue is the absence of release, not incorrect ordering of frees.

commit_msg:
The functions that were used in the emulation of fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt and
sidt were originally meant for task switching, and as such they did not
check privilege levels.  This is very bad when the same functions are used
in the emulation of unprivileged instructions.  This is CVE-2018-10853.

The obvious fix is to add a new argument to ops->read_std and ops->write_std,
which decides whether the access is a "system" access or should use the
processor's CPL.

Fixes: 129a72a0d3c8 ("KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std", 2017-01-12)
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tr = ops->read_std(ctxt, base + 102, &io_bitmap_ptr, 2, NULL);', '\tr = ops->read_std(ctxt, base + io_bitmap_ptr + port/8, &perm, 2, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tr = ops->read_std(ctxt, base + 102, &io_bitmap_ptr, 2, NULL, true);', '\tr = ops->read_std(ctxt, base + io_bitmap_ptr + port/8, &perm, 2, NULL, true);']}
description: A flaw was found in the way Linux kernel KVM hypervisor before 4.18 emulated instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor. It did not check current privilege(CPL) level while emulating unprivileged instructions. An unprivileged guest user/process could use this flaw to potentially escalate privileges inside guest.

code_evidence: emulator_io_port_access_allowed reads the TSS I/O bitmap pointer via ops->read_std without a privilege/system flag at line 23, so the access is performed with the processor's CPL rather than as a system access.

The second read_std at line 28 fetches the permission bits for the queried port with the same CPL-based access, so the permission check itself can be subverted when emulating unprivileged instructions.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an access-control decision but fails to enforce the required privilege level on the memory reads underlying that decision, matching improper privilege management (CWE-269). The missing system-access flag is the root cause; the resulting privilege escalation is the impact, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the I/O bitmap reads use ops->read_std without constraining the access to a system-level operation, so a guest at CPL>0 can influence the bitmap/perm values used by the access check. Trigger: an unprivileged guest process executes an I/O instruction emulated through this path. Consequence: the allowed/denied decision is computed from attacker-influenced data, enabling privilege escalation inside the guest.

commit_msg:
shared/gatt-server: Fix heap overflow when appending prepare writes

The code shall check if the prepare writes would append more the
allowed maximum attribute length.

Fixes https://github.com/bluez/bluez/security/advisories/GHSA-479m-xcq5-9g2q
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tecode = check_length(length, 0);', '\tif (ecode)', '\t\tgoto error;', '']}
description: A heap overflow vulnerability was found in bluez in versions prior to 5.63. An attacker with local network access could pass specially crafted files causing an application to halt or crash, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: The function validates only that length >= 2 before use; there is no upper bound check on length.
The attacker-supplied length is passed to gatt_db_attribute_write as length - 2, which is used as the write payload size for the attribute.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds a check_length(length, 0) call before permissions, showing the missing constraint is on the size value used by downstream allocation/copy. This is an integer/length validation weakness whose unchecked value drives a memory overrun, consistent with CWE-190. It is not merely a permissions issue (CWE-862), since no authorization check would bound the length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write handler trusts the PDU length without verifying it against the attribute's maximum allowed length, so an oversized prepare-write payload reaches the attribute write path. Trigger: a crafted ATT write PDU whose length exceeds the attribute limit. The appended data overruns the attribute buffer, producing a heap overflow that can crash the service (DoS) or corrupt memory.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5, the CQL dissector could go into an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-cql.c by checking for a nonzero number of columns.

code_evidence: After reading result_rows_row_count, the code adds a Rows subtree and then enters a loop over j < result_rows_row_count. Inside, when offset_row_metadata is zero it loops over k < result_rows_columns_count, reading a 4-byte length and bytes_length bytes then advancing offset. If result_rows_columns_count is zero, neither inner loop body nor parse_row path consumes any bytes, so offset never changes across the outer iterations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop over result_rows_row_count lacks a reachable progress/exit condition when result_rows_columns_count is zero, so it iterates without advancing offset; this matches CWE-835 (loop with unreachable exit condition). It is not a simple off-by-one bounds issue, since no byte is consumed at all.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the outer row loop is not guarded by a nonzero column count, and with zero columns the inner column loop body executes zero times, leaving offset unchanged. Trigger: a RESULT/ROWS response with zero columns but a positive row count. Consequence: the outer loop re-iterates at the same offset, spinning indefinitely on the dissector thread and consuming CPU (DoS).

commit_msg:
IB/security: Restrict use of the write() interface

The drivers/infiniband stack uses write() as a replacement for
bi-directional ioctl().  This is not safe. There are ways to
trigger write calls that result in the return structure that
is normally written to user space being shunted off to user
specified kernel memory instead.

For the immediate repair, detect and deny suspicious accesses to
the write API.

For long term, update the user space libraries and the kernel API
to something that doesn't present the same security vulnerabilities
(likely a structured ioctl() interface).

The impacted uAPI interfaces are generally only available if
hardware from drivers/infiniband is installed in the system.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jann@thejh.net>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgunthorpe@obsidianresearch.com>
[ Expanded check to all known write() entry points ]
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Doug Ledford <dledford@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(!ib_safe_file_access(fp)))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;', '']}
description: The InfiniBand (aka IB) stack in the Linux kernel before 4.5.3 incorrectly relies on the write system call, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (kernel memory write operation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a uAPI interface.

code_evidence: qib_write is a file_operations write handler, so it is directly reachable by local users through write() on the qib device node; the pre-patch function has no caller-identity or access check at entry.

The function takes user-controlled data (ucmd from the __user pointer) and dispatches on cmd.type to privileged operations; ctxt_fp(fp) only resolves the context, and the check at 96 rejects a missing context but does not verify the caller's privileges.

Several command paths write kernel-derived results back to user-supplied addresses cast from cmd fields (spu_base_info, ctxt_info, sdma_inflight, sdma_complete), so a caller controlling those fields can redirect kernel writes to arbitrary kernel memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and access-control management; the function exposes privileged operations to unprivileged callers because it lacks a caller-access check, which is exactly the access-control failure described. A generic memory-safety label would miss the missing-permission root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write() entry point performs privileged InfiniBand operations and copies results to user-controlled pointers without any access-control gate on the calling process. Trigger: a local user opens the device and issues write commands whose structures carry attacker-chosen destination addresses. Consequence: kernel memory can be overwritten, causing denial of service or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
UDP IPv6 packets auto flowlabels are using a 32bit secret
(static u32 hashrnd in net/core/flow_dissector.c) and
apply jhash() over fields known by the receivers.

Attackers can easily infer the 32bit secret and use this information
to identify a device and/or user, since this 32bit secret is only
set at boot time.

Really, using jhash() to generate cookies sent on the wire
is a serious security concern.

Trying to change the rol32(hash, 16) in ip6_make_flowlabel() would be
a dead end. Trying to periodically change the secret (like in sch_sfq.c)
could change paths taken in the network for long lived flows.

Let's switch to siphash, as we did in commit df453700e8d8
("inet: switch IP ID generator to siphash")

Using a cryptographically strong pseudo random function will solve this
privacy issue and more generally remove other weak points in the stack.

Packet schedulers using skb_get_hash_perturb() benefit from this change.

Fixes: b56774163f99 ("ipv6: Enable auto flow labels by default")
Fixes: 42240901f7c4 ("ipv6: Implement different admin modes for automatic flow labels")
Fixes: 67800f9b1f4e ("ipv6: Call skb_get_hash_flowi6 to get skb->hash in ip6_make_flowlabel")
Fixes: cb1ce2ef387b ("ipv6: Implement automatic flow label generation on transmit")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Berger <jonathann1@walla.com>
Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Benny Pinkas <benny@pinkas.net>
Cc: Tom Herbert <tom@herbertland.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static inline u32 __flow_hash_from_keys(struct flow_keys *keys, u32 keyval)', '\thash = __flow_hash_words(flow_keys_hash_start(keys),', '\t\t\t\t flow_keys_hash_length(keys), keyval);'], 'added_lines': ['static inline u32 __flow_hash_from_keys(struct flow_keys *keys,', '\t\t\t\t\tconst siphash_key_t *keyval)', '\thash = siphash(flow_keys_hash_start(keys),', '\t\t       flow_keys_hash_length(keys), keyval);']}
description: The flow_dissector feature in the Linux kernel 4.3 through 5.x before 5.3.10 has a device tracking vulnerability, aka CID-55667441c84f. This occurs because the auto flowlabel of a UDP IPv6 packet relies on a 32-bit hashrnd value as a secret, and because jhash (instead of siphash) is used. The hashrnd value remains the same starting from boot time, and can be inferred by an attacker. This affects net/core/flow_dissector.c and related code.

code_evidence: __flow_hash_from_keys derives the flow hash from flow_keys fields via __flow_hash_words using a caller-supplied 32-bit keyval; the hash is computed and returned directly (with a zero-substitution) as the value used for flow labels.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The secret-dependent hash relies on an insufficiently random 32-bit key rather than a cryptographically strong PRF, matching CWE-330. It is a weak-randomness/secret issue, not the broader information exposure itself.

evidence_lines.code:
hash = __flow_hash_words(flow_keys_hash_start(keys),
flow_keys_hash_length(keys), keyval);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the hash is produced with a 32-bit jhash-style key over receiver-known packet fields, so the secret is small and inferable. Trigger: an attacker observes generated flow labels/hashes for known flows. Supported consequence: the key is recovered, allowing device/user tracking via predictable flow labels.

commit_msg:
tls: clear data after a starttls acknowledgement

After a starttls acknowledgement message, clear the buffers of any
incoming data / commands.  This will ensure that all future data is
handled securely.

Co-authored-by: Pietro Cerutti <gahr@gahr.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        enum ImapExecResult rc = imap_exec(adata, "STARTTLS", IMAP_CMD_NO_FLAGS);'], 'added_lines': ['        enum ImapExecResult rc = imap_exec(adata, "STARTTLS", IMAP_CMD_SINGLE);', '        // Clear any data after the STARTTLS acknowledgement', '        mutt_socket_empty(adata->conn);', '']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: After issuing STARTTLS with imap_exec, the code proceeds to mutt_ssl_starttls and then a CAPABILITY command based only on the exec result; it does not discard data already buffered on adata->conn. Any bytes a server (or MITM) appended after the STARTTLS acknowledgement remain in the connection buffer and are later parsed in the TLS context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function lets externally supplied elements (bytes after the STARTTLS reply) be parsed by the downstream IMAP/TLS handling without neutralizing the boundary, which matches CWE-74 injection into a downstream component. The fix (IMAP_CMD_SINGLE plus mutt_socket_empty) confirms the missing buffer-clearing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the STARTTLS acknowledgement is not treated as a boundary, so residual unread data in the socket/buffer is carried into the post-TLS session. Trigger: a malicious server or on-path attacker sends extra, crafted data after the STARTTLS response. Consequence: injected commands are interpreted as TLS-protected traffic, enabling response injection and bypassing the intended protection.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t//safety check, should never happen', '\t\t\tif (!a) return GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE;']}
description: GPAC 2.1-DEV-rev87-g053aae8-master. has a Null Pointer Dereference vulnerability in gf_isom_parse_movie_boxes_internal due to improper return value handling of GF_SKIP_BOX, which causes a Denial of Service. This vulnerability was fixed in commit 37592ad.

code_evidence: gf_isom_parse_root_box writes the parsed box into local pointer 'a' and returns an error code. On the GF_ISOM_INCOMPLETE_FILE path (line 25) the function returns e at line 34, and on other negative codes it returns at line 36, so 'a' may never be assigned. When e >= 0 at line 24 the error is treated as success and control falls to line 38, which dereferences a->type without any NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences pointer 'a' expecting it to be valid, but the success path does not guarantee assignment, directly matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). This is not a missing bounds check or use-after-free; the flaw is the unchecked NULL pointer used in the switch expression.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of gf_isom_parse_root_box is interpreted as success (e >= 0) while the output box pointer 'a' may be left unset/NULL, and no null check precedes the a->type switch. Trigger: a crafted file causing the box parser to report a non-negative result without producing a box (the GF_SKIP_BOX handling noted in the commit). Consequence: NULL pointer dereference at line 38, crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/fpu/xsaves: Fix improper uses of __ex_table

Commit:

  f31a9f7c7169 ("x86/xsaves: Use xsaves/xrstors to save and restore xsave area")

introduced alternative instructions for XSAVES/XRSTORS and commit:

  adb9d526e982 ("x86/xsaves: Add xsaves and xrstors support for booting time")

added support for the XSAVES/XRSTORS instructions at boot time.

Unfortunately both failed to properly protect them against faulting:

The 'xstate_fault' macro will use the closest label named '1'
backward and that ends up in the .altinstr_replacement section
rather than in .text. This means that the kernel will never find
in the __ex_table the .text address where this instruction might
fault, leading to serious problems if userspace manages to
trigger the fault.

description: coders/xcf.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a crafted XCF file.

code_evidence: The buffer xcfdata is allocated with only data_length elements, derived from the file-supplied tile data size.

The loops iterate over tile_image->rows and tile_image->columns, independent of data_length, so the number of pixel reads is governed by image dimensions.
In the RGB branch each iteration dereferences xcfdata->red/green/blue/alpha and then increments xcfdata, consuming one XCFPixelInfo per pixel without bounding against data_length.

evidence_lines.code: xcfdata=(XCFPixelInfo *) AcquireQuantumMemory(data_length,sizeof(*xcfdata));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: allocation size (data_length) is decoupled from the iteration count (rows*columns). Trigger: a crafted XCF file declaring image dimensions whose pixel count exceeds the supplied tile data. Consequence: the loops dereference xcfdata past the allocated buffer, an out-of-bounds read.
