commit_msg:
Fixing HPACK header table resize issue

Summary: On resizing the header table down and then up again, a resize can be called against the underlying vector that actually sizes it down.  This causes a lot of things to break as the code that does the resizing assumes the underlying vector is only ever resized up.

Reviewed By: afrind

Differential Revision: D4613681

fbshipit-source-id: 35b61cab53d5bc097424d6c779f90b7fdea42002
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (capacity_ <= oldCapacity) {', '    auto oldTail = tail();', '    auto oldLength = table_.size();', '    table_.resize(newLength);', '    if (size_ > 0 && oldTail > head_) {', '      // the list wrapped around, need to move oldTail..oldLength to the end of', '      // the now-larger table_', '      std::copy(table_.begin() + oldTail, table_.begin() + oldLength,', '                table_.begin() + newLength - (oldLength - oldTail));', '      // Update the names indecies that pointed to the old range', '      for (auto& names_it: names_) {', '        for (auto& idx: names_it.second) {', '          if (idx >= oldTail) {', '            DCHECK_LT(idx + (table_.size() - oldLength), table_.size());', '            idx += (table_.size() - oldLength);', '          } else {', '            // remaining indecies in the list were smaller than oldTail, so', '            // should be indexed from 0', '            break;'], 'added_lines': ['  // TODO: ddmello - the below is a little dangerous as we update the', '  // capacity right away.  Some properties of the class utilize that variable', '  // and so might be better to refactor and update capacity at the end of the', '  // method (and update other methods)', '  if (capacity_ == oldCapacity) {', '    return;', '  } else if (capacity_ < oldCapacity) {', '    // NOTE: currently no actual resizing is performed...', '    // NOTE: due to the above lack of resizing, we must determine whether a', '    // resize is actually appropriate (to handle cases where the underlying', '    // vector is still >= to the size related to the new capacity requested)', '    if (newLength > table_.size()) {', '      auto oldTail = tail();', '      auto oldLength = table_.size();', '      table_.resize(newLength);', '      if (size_ > 0 && oldTail > head_) {', '        // the list wrapped around, need to move oldTail..oldLength to the end', '        // of the now-larger table_', '        std::copy(table_.begin() + oldTail, table_.begin() + oldLength,', '                  table_.begin() + newLength - (oldLength - oldTail));', '        // Update the names indecies that pointed to the old range', '        for (auto& names_it: names_) {', '          for (auto& idx: names_it.second) {', '            if (idx >= oldTail) {', '              DCHECK_LT(idx + (table_.size() - oldLength), table_.size());', '              idx += (table_.size() - oldLength);', '            } else {', '              // remaining indecies in the list were smaller than oldTail, so', '              // should be indexed from 0', '              break;', '            }']}
description: In the course of decompressing HPACK inside the HTTP2 protocol, an unexpected sequence of header table resize operations can place the header table into a corrupted state, leading to a use-after-free condition and undefined behavior. This issue affects Proxygen from v0.29.0 until v2017.04.03.00.

code_evidence: The shrink branch (capacity_ <= oldCapacity) only calls evict(0) and does not resize table_ down, so the underlying vector keeps its old size while capacity_ is updated.

The grow branch unconditionally records oldTail/oldLength and calls table_.resize(newLength); when a prior shrink left table_ larger, this can actually shrink the vector (the commit message confirms this).

std::copy then reads from table_.begin()+oldTail through table_.begin()+oldLength and writes to table_.begin()+newLength-(oldLength-oldTail), using bounds derived from the pre-resize size that no longer match the shrunk vector.
The names_ index adjustment adds (table_.size() - oldLength); after an unexpected shrink this is a negative offset, producing stale indices into the vector.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale offsets and indices reference elements of a vector whose storage changed size, so later accesses use memory no longer valid for the original layout, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the corruption persists and is reused after the underlying allocation is altered.

evidence_lines.code:
if (capacity_ <= oldCapacity) {
evict(0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the resize path assumes table_ only ever grows, so a shrink-then-grow sequence calls resize with a smaller newLength, invalidating oldTail/oldLength-derived bounds. The subsequent std::copy and index adjustment operate on the resized vector using stale offsets, corrupting the table state and yielding use-after-free/undefined behavior on later header lookups.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow (CVE-2021-21309). (#8522)

On 32-bit systems, setting the proto-max-bulk-len config parameter to a high value may result with integer overflow and a subsequent heap overflow when parsing an input bulk (CVE-2021-21309).

This fix has two parts:

Set a reasonable limit to the config parameter.
Add additional checks to prevent the problem in other potential but unknown code paths.

(cherry picked from commit d32f2e9999ce003bad0bd2c3bca29f64dcce4433)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    ASSERT_NO_SIZE_OVERFLOW(size);']}
description: Redis is an open-source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions of Redis an integer overflow bug in 32-bit Redis version 4.0 or newer could be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially result with remote code execution. Redis 4.0 or newer uses a configurable limit for the maximum supported bulk input size. By default, it is 512MB which is a safe value for all platforms. If the limit is significantly increased, receiving a large request from a client may trigger several integer overflow scenarios, which would result with buffer overflow and heap corruption. We believe this could in certain conditions be exploited for remote code execution. By default, authenticated Redis users have access to all configuration parameters and can therefore use the “CONFIG SET proto-max-bulk-len” to change the safe default, making the system vulnerable. **This problem only affects 32-bit Redis (on a 32-bit system, or as a 32-bit executable running on a 64-bit system).** The problem is fixed in version 6.2, and the fix is back ported to 6.0.11 and 5.0.11. Make sure you use one of these versions if you are running 32-bit Redis. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent clients from directly executing `CONFIG SET`: Using Redis 6.0 or newer, ACL configuration can be used to block the command. Using older versions, the `rename-command` configuration directive can be used to rename the command to a random string unknown to users, rendering it inaccessible. Please note that this workaround may have an additional impact on users or operational systems that expect `CONFIG SET` to behave in certain ways.

code_evidence: Line 11 forwards the caller-supplied size directly to zmalloc(size) without any bound check on the value.

Lines 22 and 24-26 compute size+PREFIX_SIZE and store size as the allocation size; on a 32-bit build a near-SIZE_MAX size wraps the addition, so the prefix bookkeeping and the realloc request disagree with the requested size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is arithmetic on an allocation size that can wrap, producing an undersized buffer and heap overflow — the definition of CWE-190 in a memory-allocation context. The fix's ASSERT_NO_SIZE_OVERFLOW(size) guard confirms the intended constraint; this is integer overflow, not merely a generic buffer overflow, because the wrap in size+PREFIX_SIZE is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: if (ptr == NULL) return zmalloc(size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: zrealloc performs size+PREFIX_SIZE arithmetic (and passes size through to zmalloc/realloc) with no guard against wraparound on 32-bit platforms. Trigger: a caller supplies a size near SIZE_MAX, derived from a configurable bulk-length limit. The addition wraps to a small value, so a small buffer is allocated while the caller believes it is large, and subsequent writes based on the original size corrupt the heap.

commit_msg:
ext4: fix slab-use-after-free in ext4_es_insert_extent()

Yikebaer reported an issue:
==================================================================
BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in ext4_es_insert_extent+0xc68/0xcb0
fs/ext4/extents_status.c:894
Read of size 4 at addr ffff888112ecc1a4 by task syz-executor/8438

CPU: 1 PID: 8438 Comm: syz-executor Not tainted 6.5.0-rc5 #1
Call Trace:
 [...]
 kasan_report+0xba/0xf0 mm/kasan/report.c:588
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0xc68/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:894
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]

Allocated by task 8438:
 [...]
 kmem_cache_zalloc include/linux/slab.h:693 [inline]
 __es_alloc_extent fs/ext4/extents_status.c:469 [inline]
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0x672/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:873
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]

Freed by task 8438:
 [...]
 kmem_cache_free+0xec/0x490 mm/slub.c:3823
 ext4_es_try_to_merge_right fs/ext4/extents_status.c:593 [inline]
 __es_insert_extent+0x9f4/0x1440 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:802
 ext4_es_insert_extent+0x2ca/0xcb0 fs/ext4/extents_status.c:882
 ext4_map_blocks+0x92a/0x16f0 fs/ext4/inode.c:680
 ext4_alloc_file_blocks.isra.0+0x2df/0xb70 fs/ext4/extents.c:4462
 ext4_zero_range fs/ext4/extents.c:4622 [inline]
 ext4_fallocate+0x251c/0x3ce0 fs/ext4/extents.c:4721
 [...]
==================================================================

The flow of issue triggering is as follows:
1. remove es
      raw es               es  removed  es1
|-------------------| -> |----|.......|------|

2. insert es
  es   insert   es1      merge with es  es1     merge with es and free es1
|----|.......|------| -> |------------|------| -> |-------------------|

es merges with newes, then merges with es1, frees es1, then determines
if es1->es_len is 0 and triggers a UAF.

The code flow is as follows:
ext4_es_insert_extent
  es1 = __es_alloc_extent(true);
  es2 = __es_alloc_extent(true);
  __es_remove_extent(inode, lblk, end, NULL, es1)
    __es_insert_extent(inode, &newes, es1) ---> insert es1 to es tree
  __es_insert_extent(inode, &newes, es2)
    ext4_es_try_to_merge_right
      ext4_es_free_extent(inode, es1) --->  es1 is freed
  if (es1 && !es1->es_len)
    // Trigger UAF by determining if es1 is used.

We determine whether es1 or es2 is used immediately after calling
__es_remove_extent() or __es_insert_extent() to avoid triggering a
UAF if es1 or es2 is freed.

Reported-by: Yikebaer Aizezi <yikebaer61@gmail.com>
Closes: https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/CALcu4raD4h9coiyEBL4Bm0zjDwxC2CyPiTwsP3zFuhot6y9Beg@mail.gmail.com
Fixes: 2a69c450083d ("ext4: using nofail preallocation in ext4_es_insert_extent()")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Baokun Li <libaokun1@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230815070808.3377171-1-libaokun1@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (es && !es->es_len)', '\t\t__es_free_extent(es);'], 'added_lines': ["\t/* Free preallocated extent if it didn't get used. */", '\tif (es) {', '\t\tif (!es->es_len)', '\t\t\t__es_free_extent(es);', '\t\tes = NULL;', '\t}']}
description: The Linux kernel before 6.5.4 has an es1 use-after-free in fs/ext4/extents_status.c, related to ext4_es_insert_extent.

code_evidence: Under write_lock, __es_remove_extent() is called with preallocated es; the subsequent `if (es && !es->es_len)` reads es->es_len and may free es, but es is not cleared afterward, so later retry iterations (line 18) can reuse the stale es pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads and potentially frees a pointer (es) after the object may have been freed by the merge logic, which is exactly reuse of freed memory (CWE-416), not a mere NULL-check bug or double-free-only pattern.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: after __es_remove_extent() may merge and free the preallocated es extent, the code dereferences es->es_len and leaves es set. Trigger: an err path causing goto retry re-enters with a freed es, or the merge frees es before the check. Consequence: slab use-after-free read of es->es_len and possible double free.

An privileged attacker can cause a crash by mounting a crafted ext4
image which triggers a out-of-bounds read in the function
ext4_valid_block_bitmap() in fs/ext4/balloc.c.

This issue has been assigned CVE-2018-1093.

BugLink: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199181
BugLink: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1560782
Reported-by: Wen Xu <wen.xu@gatech.edu>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct ext4_sb_info *sbi = EXT4_SB(sb);', '\tif ((bitmap_blk <= le32_to_cpu(sbi->s_es->s_first_data_block)) ||', '\t    (bitmap_blk >= ext4_blocks_count(sbi->s_es))) {', '\t\text4_error(sb, "Invalid inode bitmap blk %llu in "', '\t\t\t   "block_group %u", bitmap_blk, block_group);', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(-EFSCORRUPTED);', '\t}']}
description: The ext4_valid_block_bitmap function in fs/ext4/balloc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.15.15 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) via a crafted ext4 image because balloc.c and ialloc.c do not validate bitmap block numbers.

code_evidence: Line 11 reads the inode bitmap block number directly from the on-disk group descriptor via ext4_inode_bitmap, with no validation of the value before use.
Line 12 passes this unvalidated bitmap_blk to sb_getblk, and lines 44-48 submit a read for that block and wait on it, so a crafted image can direct I/O at an arbitrary block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked bitmap_blk drives a read of memory/block data at an attacker-chosen location, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. It is not merely a missing bounds check on an index; the concrete effect is reading past the intended buffer region.

evidence_lines.code:
bitmap_blk = ext4_inode_bitmap(sb, desc);
bh = sb_getblk(sb, bitmap_blk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bitmap block number from the untrusted ext4 image is used without checking it lies within the filesystem's block range. description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions all TFLite operations that use quantization can be made to use unitialized values. [For example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/depthwise_conv.cc#L198-L200). The issue stems from the fact that `quantization.params` is only valid if `quantization.type` is different that `kTfLiteNoQuantization`. However, these checks are missing in large parts of the code. We have patched the issue in GitHub commits 537bc7c723439b9194a358f64d871dd326c18887, 4a91f2069f7145aab6ba2d8cfe41be8a110c18a5 and 8933b8a21280696ab119b63263babdb54c298538. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

Trigger: a full-integer SVDF model whose tensors carry kTfLiteNoQuantization, leaving params uninitialized. Consequence: dereferencing an uninitialized params pointer reads uninitialized/attacker-influenced data or crashes.

commit_msg:
The ptrace PEEKUSR/POKEUSR (aka PEEKUSER/POKEUSER) API allows a process
to read/write registers of another process.

To get/set a register, the API takes an index into an imaginary address
space called the "USER area", where the registers of the process are
laid out in some fashion.

The kernel then maps that index to a particular register in its own data
structures and gets/sets the value.

The API only allows a single machine-word to be read/written at a time.
So 4 bytes on 32-bit kernels and 8 bytes on 64-bit kernels.

The way floating point registers (FPRs) are addressed is somewhat
complicated, because double precision float values are 64-bit even on
32-bit CPUs. That means on 32-bit kernels each FPR occupies two
word-sized locations in the USER area. On 64-bit kernels each FPR
occupies one word-sized location in the USER area.

Internally the kernel stores the FPRs in an array of u64s, or if VSX is
enabled, an array of pairs of u64s where one half of each pair stores
the FPR. Which half of the pair stores the FPR depends on the kernel's
endianness.

To handle the different layouts of the FPRs depending on VSX/no-VSX and
big/little endian, the TS_FPR() macro was introduced.

Unfortunately the TS_FPR() macro does not take into account the fact
that the addressing of each FPR differs between 32-bit and 64-bit
kernels. It just takes the index into the "USER area" passed from
userspace and indexes into the fp_state.fpr array.

On 32-bit there are 64 indexes that address FPRs, but only 32 entries in
the fp_state.fpr array, meaning the user can read/write 256 bytes past
the end of the array. Because the fp_state sits in the middle of the
thread_struct there are various fields than can be overwritten,
including some pointers. As such it may be exploitable.

It has also been observed to cause systems to hang or otherwise
misbehave when using gdbserver, and is probably the root cause of this
report which could not be easily reproduced:
  https://lore.kernel.org/linuxppc-dev/dc38afe9-6b78-f3f5-666b-986939e40fc6@keymile.com/

Rather than trying to make the TS_FPR() macro even more complicated to
fix the bug, or add more macros, instead add a special-case for 32-bit
kernels. This is more obvious and hopefully avoids a similar bug
happening again in future.

Note that because 32-bit kernels never have VSX enabled the code doesn't
need to consider TS_FPRWIDTH/OFFSET at all. Add a BUILD_BUG_ON() to
ensure that 32-bit && VSX is never enabled.

Fixes: 87fec0514f61 ("powerpc: PTRACE_PEEKUSR/PTRACE_POKEUSER of FPR registers in little endian builds")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v3.13+
Reported-by: Ariel Miculas <ariel.miculas@belden.com>
Tested-by: Christophe Leroy <christophe.leroy@csgroup.eu>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220609133245.573565-1-mpe@ellerman.id.au
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (fpidx < (PT_FPSCR - PT_FPR0))', '\t\tmemcpy(data, &child->thread.TS_FPR(fpidx), sizeof(long));', '\telse'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fpidx < (PT_FPSCR - PT_FPR0)) {', '\t\tif (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PPC32))', '\t\t\t// On 32-bit the index we are passed refers to 32-bit words', '\t\t\t*data = ((u32 *)child->thread.fp_state.fpr)[fpidx];', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tmemcpy(data, &child->thread.TS_FPR(fpidx), sizeof(long));', '\t} else']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.18.3 on powerpc 32-bit platforms. There is a buffer overflow in ptrace PEEKUSER and POKEUSER (aka PEEKUSR and POKEUSR) when accessing floating point registers.

code_evidence: fpidx is derived from the user-controlled index (index - PT_FPR0); the only bound check is index > PT_FPSCR, so any index up to PT_FPSCR yields an fpidx in [0, PT_FPSCR-PT_FPR0).

The branch condition fpidx < (PT_FPSCR - PT_FPR0) admits fpidx values up to 63, but TS_FPR(fpidx) indexes fp_state.fpr, which has only 32 u64 entries on 32-bit kernels, so memcpy reads past the array end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because memcpy copies from the FPR array into the caller's data without validating that the computed fpidx stays within the array's 32 entries, producing an out-of-bounds copy. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read since the paired POKEUSER path writes past the same bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
if (fpidx < (PT_FPSCR - PT_FPR0))
memcpy(data, &child->thread.TS_FPR(fpidx), sizeof(long));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the USER-area index is not translated to the narrower 32-bit FPR array layout before indexing. Trigger: a ptrace PEEKUSR request with an FPR index in the upper half of the USER area on 32-bit powerpc. Consequence: memcpy copies sizeof(long) bytes from beyond fp_state.fpr, disclosing adjacent thread_struct memory (and the symmetric poke path writes it).

description: epan/dissectors/packet-pktap.c in the Ethernet dissector in Wireshark 2.x before 2.0.4 mishandles the packet-header data type, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: The PPI header fields version, flags, tot_len and dlt are read directly from the packet via tvb_get_* with no validation of tot_len, data_len or dlt.

The while loop subtracts the attacker-controlled data_len from tot_len and advances offset by data_len; data_len is derived from two 16-bit packet fields plus 4 and is never checked against the remaining length or tot_len, so offset can exceed the buffer.

The crash is the consequence of this missing validation, not a separate weakness class.

commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

commit_msg:
posix-timers: Sanitize overrun handling

The posix timer overrun handling is broken because the forwarding functions
can return a huge number of overruns which does not fit in an int. As a
consequence timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun can turn into
random number generators.

The k_clock::timer_forward() callbacks return a 64 bit value now. Make
k_itimer::ti_overrun[_last] 64bit as well, so the kernel internal
accounting is correct. 3Remove the temporary (int) casts.

Add a helper function which clamps the overrun value returned to user space
via timer_getoverrun(2) or siginfo::si_overrun limited to a positive value
between 0 and INT_MAX. INT_MAX is an indicator for user space that the
overrun value has been clamped.

Reported-by: Team OWL337 <icytxw@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Acked-by: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Michael Kerrisk <mtk.manpages@gmail.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180626132705.018623573@linutronix.de
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\ttimr->it_overrun += (unsigned int)', '\t\t\t\thrtimer_forward(timer, now,', '\t\t\t\t\t\ttimr->it_interval);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\ttimr->it_overrun += hrtimer_forward(timer, now,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t\t    timr->it_interval);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. An Integer Overflow in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the POSIX timer code is caused by the way the overrun accounting works. Depending on interval and expiry time values, the overrun can be larger than INT_MAX, but the accounting is int based. This basically makes the accounting values, which are visible to user space via timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun, random. For example, a local user can cause a denial of service (signed integer overflow) via crafted mmap, futex, timer_create, and timer_settime system calls.

code_evidence: The overrun accumulator is updated as `timr->it_overrun += (unsigned int) hrtimer_forward(...)`. The return value of hrtimer_forward is cast to unsigned int before being added to it_overrun, so a 64-bit forward count is truncated to 32 bits and accumulated into a narrower field without any bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code performs an increment/accumulation that can exceed the representable range of the integer field, and the logic assumes the accumulated value remains valid. This is an integer overflow/wraparound in the overrun accounting, distinct from a mere format or type-punning issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the hrtimer_forward result is truncated to unsigned int and accumulated into ti_overrun without clamping, so with crafted interval/expiry values the accounting wraps and the value later exposed via timer_getoverrun(2)/si_overrun becomes an arbitrary or negative value. Trigger: a local user creates and arms a POSIX timer whose forward count exceeds the int range. Consequence: incorrect overrun accounting visible to user space, supporting a signed-overflow DoS and misleading results.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. A denial-of-service vulnerability affects applications on a 32-bit systems that use PJSIP versions 2.12 and prior to play/read invalid WAV files. The vulnerability occurs when reading WAV file data chunks with length greater than 31-bit integers. The vulnerability does not affect 64-bit apps and should not affect apps that only plays trusted WAV files. A patch is available on the `master` branch of the `pjsip/project` GitHub repository. As a workaround, apps can reject a WAV file received from an unknown source or validate the file first.

code_evidence: The unbounded for(;;) loop reads 8-byte subchunks until a DATA_TAG is found; on any non-data subchunk it seeks forward by size_to_read = subchunk.len and repeats. The loop's only termination is break at line 153 when subchunk.id == PJMEDIA_DATA_TAG; there is no iteration cap or position-progress guard, so the exit condition depends entirely on eventually reading a data chunk.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains an iteration whose exit condition cannot be reached for malformed input, matching CWE-835's infinite loop with unreachable exit condition. The patch's added overflow checks on subchunk.len and fmt_hdr.len confirm the loop-termination dependency on chunk lengths; this is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's exit condition is reachable only if a DATA_TAG subchunk is encountered; a crafted WAV whose subchunk.len is negative (or otherwise causes backward/zero seek) keeps the file position from advancing toward a data chunk. Trigger: parsing an invalid WAV file from an untrusted source. Consequence: repeated reads/seeks without termination, causing CPU resource exhaustion (denial of service).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can cause a heap buffer overflow in `QuantizedReshape` by passing in invalid thresholds for the quantization. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/a324ac84e573fba362a5e53d4e74d5de6729933e/tensorflow/core/kernels/quantized_reshape_op.cc#L38-L55) assumes that the 2 arguments are always valid scalars and tries to access the numeric value directly. However, if any of these tensors is empty, then `.flat<T>()` is an empty buffer and accessing the element at position 0 results in overflow. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: input tensors 2 and 3 are assumed to contain at least one element. Trigger: an attacker supplies empty or non-scalar threshold tensors; flat<float>() yields an empty buffer, and accessing index 0 reads/writes out of bounds. Supported consequence: memory corruption (heap buffer overflow) potentially leading to crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix infinite loop in xmlStringLenDecodeEntities

When ctxt->instate == XML_PARSER_EOF,xmlParseStringEntityRef
return NULL which cause a infinite loop in xmlStringLenDecodeEntities

Found with libFuzzer.

Signed-off-by: Zhipeng Xie <xiezhipeng1@huawei.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t   (c != end2) && (c != end3)) {'], 'added_lines': ['           (c != end2) && (c != end3) &&', '           (ctxt->instate != XML_PARSER_EOF)) {']}
description: xmlStringLenDecodeEntities in parser.c in libxml2 2.9.10 has an infinite loop in a certain end-of-file situation.

code_evidence: Lines 28-30: the main while loop continues only while c is nonzero and not an end delimiter; the loop body does not advance str in the entity-reference branches.

Lines 44-88: when str[1]=='#' or an entity reference is parsed, xmlParseStringEntityRef is called on &str. If it returns NULL (as at EOF) or handles a predefined/other entity, str is not advanced, so c is unchanged on the next iteration.
Lines 134-138: c is only recomputed from CUR_SCHAR(str,l) when str<last; otherwise c=0, but when the entity branch fails to advance str and str<last, the loop re-enters with the same c and same str.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the loop's exit condition (c==0 or delimiter) cannot be reached when the entity branch fails to advance str, producing a non-input-consuming infinite loop. This is a reachable-exit-condition defect, not merely resource exhaustion from deep recursion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop's exit condition depends on c and str, but the entity-reference branch can leave both unchanged when xmlParseStringEntityRef returns NULL at XML_PARSER_EOF. Trigger: input ending in an entity reference that causes the parser to enter EOF state. Consequence: the while loop at lines 28-30 iterates forever without consuming input, causing CPU denial of service.

commit_msg:
The current CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting scheme for the DOI
definitions is a bit flawed in that we:

1. Don't correctly match gets/puts in netlbl_cipsov4_list().
2. Decrement the refcount on each attempt to remove the DOI from the
   DOI list, only removing it from the list once the refcount drops
   to zero.

This patch fixes these problems by adding the missing "puts" to
netlbl_cipsov4_list() and introduces a more conventional, i.e.
not-buggy, refcounting mechanism to the DOI definitions.  Upon the
addition of a DOI to the DOI list, it is initialized with a refcount
of one, removing a DOI from the list removes it from the list and
drops the refcount by one; "gets" and "puts" behave as expected with
respect to refcounts, increasing and decreasing the DOI's refcount by
one.

Fixes: b1edeb102397 ("netlabel: Replace protocol/NetLabel linking with refrerence counts")
Fixes: d7cce01504a0 ("netlabel: Add support for removing a CALIPSO DOI.")
Reported-by: syzbot+9ec037722d2603a9f52e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Paul Moore <paul@paul-moore.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tspin_lock(&calipso_doi_list_lock);', '\tlist_del_rcu(&doi_def->list);', '\tspin_unlock(&calipso_doi_list_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tcalipso_cache_invalidate();']}
description: The Linux kernel before 5.11.14 has a use-after-free in cipso_v4_genopt in net/ipv4/cipso_ipv4.c because the CIPSO and CALIPSO refcounting for the DOI definitions is mishandled, aka CID-ad5d07f4a9cd. This leads to writing an arbitrary value.

code_evidence: calipso_doi_putdef decrements the DOI refcount and returns early unless it reaches zero (lines 5-6). When it does reach zero, it removes the DOI from calipso_doi_list under the lock (lines 7-9) and then schedules calipso_doi_free_rcu via call_rcu (line 10), which eventually frees doi_def.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the DOI definition after refcount reaches zero, and the buggy refcounting scheme lets subsequent code dereference the freed structure, matching CWE-416 (reusing memory after it is freed).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the refcount-based free path removes and frees the DOI definition while other holders may still reference it, because gets/puts and list handling are mismatched. Trigger: a caller that obtains a DOI reference without a matching get, or concurrent access to a DOI whose refcount hit zero. Consequence: use-after-free of doi_def, leading to arbitrary memory write.

commit_msg:
[MJ2] Avoid index out of bounds access to pi->include[]

Signed-off-by: Young_X <YangX92@hotmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    /* Avoids index out of bounds access with include*/', '                    if (index >= pi->include_size) {', '                        opj_pi_emit_error(pi, "Invalid access to pi->include");', '                        return OPJ_FALSE;', '                    }']}
description: Out-of-bounds accesses in the functions pi_next_lrcp, pi_next_rlcp, pi_next_rpcl, pi_next_pcrl, pi_next_rpcl, and pi_next_cprl in openmj2/pi.c in OpenJPEG through 2.3.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash).

code_evidence: The nested loops derive pi->precno from poc.precno0/precno1 (line 23 sets precno1 from res->pw*res->ph when tp_on is false), and index is computed at lines 26-27 as a combination of layno, resno, compno and precno scaled by step values. Line 28 then reads pi->include[index] and line 29 writes it without any check that index is within the allocated include array. The patch adds exactly this missing bound check before the access, confirming the pre-patch code indexes include[] with an unvalidated derived position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the function processes derived index/position metadata from the input codestream without validating that it lies within the include[] bounds, then uses it unsafely. This is improper validation of a derived index; the out-of-bounds access is the consequence, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the packet/iteration coordinates (layno, resno, compno, precno) are attacker-influenced via the codestream POC/resolution data and are combined into index without verifying index < pi->include_size. Trigger: crafted precinct/packet geometry causes index to exceed the include buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write on pi->include, leading to a crash (DoS) and potentially memory corruption.

description: Integer overflow in the jpc_dec_tiledecode function in jpc_dec.c in JasPer before 1.900.12 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted image file, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Negative dimensions are rejected, but there is no upper-bound check on numrows or numcols, so both can be large positive ints.
matrix->datasize_ is computed as numrows * numcols in int arithmetic; the product can exceed INT_MAX and wrap to a small or negative value.
The wrapped datasize_ is then passed to jas_alloc2 as the allocation element count, so the buffer is sized from the overflowed product while later indexing uses numcols.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the allocation size derives from an int multiplication that can wrap before being used as a size. This is not merely an allocation failure; the overflowed value is the size used for memory allocation, making the wraparound directly security-relevant.

evidence_lines.code:
if (numrows < 0 || numcols < 0) {
return 0;
matrix->datasize_ = numrows * numcols;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the element count is computed with an unchecked int multiplication (line 17) instead of a checked size computation. A crafted image yielding large numrows/numcols triggers integer wraparound, producing an undersized heap allocation at line 26; subsequent row-pointer and zeroing loops index using the true dimensions, causing a heap-based buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
Backporting recursive handling of DefaultRoot path, when AllowChrootSymlinks
is off, to 1.3.5 branch.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        struct stat st;', '        pr_fs_clear_cache();', '        res = pr_fsio_lstat(path, &st);', '          xerrno = errno;', '          pr_log_pri(PR_LOG_WARNING, "error: unable to check %s: %s", path,', '            strerror(xerrno));', '', '          errno = xerrno;', '          return -1;', '        }', '', '        if (S_ISLNK(st.st_mode)) {', '          pr_log_pri(PR_LOG_WARNING,', '            "error: DefaultRoot %s is a symlink (denied by AllowChrootSymlinks "', '            "config)", path);'], 'added_lines': ['        res = is_symlink_path(p, path, pathlen);', '          if (errno == EPERM) {', '            pr_log_pri(PR_LOG_WARNING, "error: DefaultRoot %s is a symlink "', '              "(denied by AllowChrootSymlinks config)", path);', '          }']}
description: ProFTPD before 1.3.5e and 1.3.6 before 1.3.6rc5 controls whether the home directory of a user could contain a symbolic link through the AllowChrootSymlinks configuration option, but checks only the last path component when enforcing AllowChrootSymlinks. Attackers with local access could bypass the AllowChrootSymlinks control by replacing a path component (other than the last one) with a symbolic link. The threat model includes an attacker who is not granted full filesystem access by a hosting provider, but can reconfigure the home directory of an FTP user.

code_evidence: When allow_symlinks is FALSE, the code prepares a single path buffer and a single struct stat for a symlink check of the DefaultRoot directory.
The path is stripped of a trailing slash and pathlen computed, but only this final component is normalized; intermediate components are not examined.
pr_fsio_lstat(path, &st) inspects only the final path component, so a symlink earlier in the path is not detected.
If the lstat result is a symlink the code rejects it with EPERM, but this check is limited to the last component.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a path while failing to prevent a link in that path from resolving to an unintended resource; the incomplete last-component-only check is the improper link resolution. This is not merely a TOCTOU race (CWE-367) since the flaw is the missing detection of intermediate symlinks, not a time-of-check gap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AllowChrootSymlinks enforcement uses lstat on the whole path string, which only reports the final path component's type, so intermediate directory components that are symbolic links are not detected. Trigger: a local attacker able to reconfigure an FTP user's home directory places a symlink in a non-final path component. Consequence: the chroot restriction is bypassed, allowing access outside the intended directory.

are not cleared. This can later cause a NULL pointer dereference in

[...]

To fix the issue, set file alloc range and alloc_hint to zero after

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 4278a0deb1f6 ("io_uring: defer alloc_hint update to io_file_bitmap_set()")
Signed-off-by: Savino Dicanosa <sd7.dev@pm.me>

description: A NULL pointer dereference was found in io_file_bitmap_get in io_uring/filetable.c in the io_uring sub-component in the Linux Kernel. When fixed files are unregistered, some context information (file_alloc_{start,end} and alloc_hint) is not cleared. A subsequent request that has auto index selection enabled via IORING_FILE_INDEX_ALLOC can cause a NULL pointer dereference. An unprivileged user can use the flaw to cause a system crash.

code_evidence: After freeing the file tables at line 19, the function only clears file_data and nr_user_files; it never resets the file_alloc_start/file_alloc_end range or alloc_hint stored in ctx. The added fix line io_file_table_set_alloc_range(ctx, 0, 0) is absent, leaving stale allocation-range state that references the freed bitmap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The resulting fault is a dereference of a NULL bitmap pointer reached via stale alloc-range state, matching CWE-476. It is not a use-after-free: the pointer is NULL, not a dangling freed address.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Unregistering fixed files frees the bitmap via io_free_file_tables but leaves file_alloc_end/alloc_hint non-zero. A later IORING_FILE_INDEX_ALLOC request enters io_file_bitmap_get with stale range state and dereferences the now-NULL bitmap, causing a kernel NULL pointer dereference and crash. Root cause is missing state reset after free; the NULL deref is the consequence.

commit_msg:
ocfs2: subsystem.su_mutex is required while accessing the item->ci_parent

The subsystem.su_mutex is required while accessing the item->ci_parent,
otherwise, NULL pointer dereference to the item->ci_parent will be
triggered in the following situation:

add node                     delete node
sys_write
 vfs_write
  configfs_write_file
   o2nm_node_store
    o2nm_node_local_write
                             do_rmdir
                              vfs_rmdir
                               configfs_rmdir
                                mutex_lock(&subsys->su_mutex);
                                unlink_obj

                                 item->ci_parent = NULL;
	 to_o2nm_cluster_from_node
	  node->nd_item.ci_parent->ci_parent
	  BUG since of NULL pointer dereference to nd_item.ci_parent

Moreover, the o2nm_cluster also should be protected by the

description: In fs/ocfs2/cluster/nodemanager.c in the Linux kernel before 4.15, local users can cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and BUG) because a required mutex is not used.

code_evidence: Line 5 dereferences the node's parent chain via to_o2nm_cluster_from_node(node) to obtain cluster before any subsystem lock is held, and the resulting pointer is used unconditionally.
Lines 17-18 and 28 use cluster->cl_nodes_lock and cluster->cl_nodes[tmp] without validating that cluster is non-NULL.

PR25822, Invalid read in process_symbol_table

description: A Denial of Service vulnerability exists in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) in GNU Binutils 2.35 due to an invalid read in process_symbol_table, as demonstrated in readeif.

commit_msg:
asymcute: don't make the assumption that req->arg is non-NULL

This fixes a denial of service where an attacker would be able to cause
a NULL pointer dereference by sending a spoofed packet. This attack only
requires knowledge about pending message ids.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (sub == NULL) {', '            return;', '        }', '']}
description: RIOT 2019.07 contains a NULL pointer dereference in the MQTT-SN implementation (asymcute), potentially allowing an attacker to crash a network node running RIOT. This requires spoofing an MQTT server response. To do so, the attacker needs to know the MQTT MsgID of a pending MQTT protocol message and the ephemeral port used by RIOT's MQTT implementation. Additionally, the server IP address is required for spoofing the packet.

code_evidence: Line 11 checks data[7] for MQTTSN_ACCEPTED; line 12 casts req->arg to asymcute_sub_t * and assigns it to sub without any NULL check.
Lines 13-16 immediately dereference sub->topic->id, sub->topic->con, and then sub->next and con->subscriptions, all through the unvalidated sub pointer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes req->arg is non-NULL and stores it in sub, then dereferences sub->topic and sub->next. Trigger: a spoofed SUBACK packet matching a pending message id whose request has a NULL arg. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference crashes the node (denial of service).

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix race among timer ioctls

ALSA timer ioctls have an open race and this may lead to a
use-after-free of timer instance object.  A simplistic fix is to make
each ioctl exclusive.  We have already tread_sem for controlling the
tread, and extend this as a global mutex to be applied to each ioctl.

The downside is, of course, the worse concurrency.  But these ioctls
aren't to be parallel accessible, in anyway, so it should be fine to
serialize there.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tmutex_init(&tu->tread_sem);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_init(&tu->ioctl_lock);']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 uses an incorrect type of mutex, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition, use-after-free, and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: The open handler allocates a per-file snd_timer_user object with kzalloc, initializes its spinlock and waitqueue, and initializes the tread_sem mutex at line 13; the object is then published via file->private_data at line 22. The initialization here only creates the mutex; the actual serialization of concurrent ioctl paths is implemented elsewhere, so this function alone does not enforce exclusivity over the timer instance.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent-access synchronization flaw over a shared resource (the timer instance), matching CWE-362; the commit explicitly fixes a race among ioctls leading to use-after-free. It is not merely a type error, since the mutex's role is to serialize concurrent ioctl sequences.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timer instance is created and published to file->private_data without the ioctl paths being serialized against each other. Trigger: a local user issues concurrent ALSA timer ioctl calls on the same timer instance. Consequence: the shared timer object can be freed or modified by one ioctl while another is still using it, yielding a race and use-after-free crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

code_evidence: The SVM fast-path guard decides whether to load FS/GS via svm_load_segs based on !cpu_has_fsgsbase and the guest's fs/gs selectors and saved base values; it never checks whether %cr4.fsgsbase is actually active in hardware.

When the fast path is skipped, the fallback writes guest bases with wrfsbase/wrgsbase/wrgsshadow using the guest's stored values without confirming the hardware FSGSBASE state matches the guest kernel's chosen %cr4 setting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate that the hardware FSGSBASE state conforms to the guest-declared %cr4 before using it to select FS/GS base loading paths, i.e. missing a required consistency check on state used for safe processing. !((uregs->fs | uregs->gs) & ~3) &&
(n->arch.pv.fs_base | n->arch.pv.gs_base_user | n->arch.pv.ldt_ents) )

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code uses the guest's virtualised FSGSBASE state (cpu_has_fsgsbase / stored bases) to choose how to load FS/GS bases instead of validating the actual hardware %cr4.fsgsbase. Trigger: a 64-bit PV guest clears FSGSBASE in its virtual %cr4 while hardware keeps the bit set. Consequence: the guest can still execute RD/WR{FS,GS}BASE, violating its kernel's assumption, enabling DoS or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
CHANGES: snmpd: Stop reading and writing the mib_indexes/* files

Caching directory contents is something the operating system should do
and is not something Net-SNMP should do. Instead of storing a copy of
the directory contents in ${tmp_dir}/mib_indexes/${n}, always scan a
MIB directory.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['add_mibfile(const char* tmpstr, const char* d_name, FILE *ip )', '        if (ip)', '            fprintf(ip, "%s %s\\n", token, d_name);'], 'added_lines': ['add_mibfile(const char* tmpstr, const char* d_name)']}
description: Net-SNMP through 5.7.3 allows Escalation of Privileges because of UNIX symbolic link (symlink) following.

code_evidence: add_mibfile receives a caller-supplied path in tmpstr and a d_name string; it does not validate either against symbolic links or path traversal before use.
The function calls fopen(tmpstr, "r") directly on the supplied path, following any symlink that tmpstr resolves to and reading the target file's contents.
On a valid MIB header, the module name and d_name are written via fprintf(ip, ...) to the caller's FILE, propagating attacker-influenced directory entries into the index cache.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file by name and fails to prevent that name from resolving through a symbolic link to an unintended resource. It is not merely path traversal (CWE-22); the core issue is link resolution before access.

evidence_lines.code: add_mibfile(const char* tmpstr, const char* d_name, FILE *ip )

if (ip)
fprintf(ip, "%s %s\n", token, d_name);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fopen(tmpstr, "r") opens an attacker-controlled path without O_NOFOLLOW or link/traversal checks, so a symlink planted in a MIB directory is followed and its target is read. Trigger: an unprivileged user places a symlink in a scanned directory; when a privileged SNMP daemon scans it, the linked file is opened and its parsed content plus d_name are consumed. Consequence is unauthorized read of files reachable by the daemon's privileges.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.13, epan/dissectors/packet-lapd.c has a memory leak.

code_evidence: convo_data is allocated with wmem_new(wmem_file_scope()) and stored via conversation_add_proto_data. Its addr_a and addr_b are then populated with copy_address, which allocates address data using the default (packet-scope) allocator rather than file scope.

This is a resource-lifetime leak, not a use-after-free or buffer overflow.

Trigger: every new conversation processed by this dissector path. Consequence: the address allocations are never released with their owning conversation data, producing a memory leak (resource exhaustion).

commit_msg: Fixed asan heap buffer overflow when not enough space to write compressed block size.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                   int32_t leftoverblock, int32_t ntbytes, int32_t maxbytes,', '    if (ntbytes + maxout > maxbytes) {', '      maxout = (int64_t)maxbytes - (int64_t)ntbytes;', '        if ((ntbytes + neblock) > maxbytes) {'], 'added_lines': ['                   int32_t leftoverblock, int32_t ntbytes, int32_t destsize,', '      if (ntbytes > destsize) {', '        /* Not enough space to write out compressed block size */', '        return -1;', '      }', '    if (ntbytes + maxout > destsize) {', '      maxout = (int64_t)destsize - (int64_t)ntbytes;', '        if ((ntbytes + neblock) > destsize) {']}
description: blosc2.c in Blosc C-Blosc2 through 2.0.0.beta.5 has a heap-based buffer overflow when there is a lack of space to write compressed data.

code_evidence: In the run branch, dest is advanced by 4 bytes (line 44) and ntbytes increased (line 45) before _sw32(dest - 4, -value) writes the encoded run length; no check compares ntbytes against the destination capacity before this write.
The non-run path guards with ntbytes + maxout > maxbytes, clamping maxout to maxbytes - ntbytes; if this residual is <= 0 it returns 0, otherwise the compressor writes up to maxout bytes at dest.
The incompressible fallback checks (ntbytes + neblock) > maxbytes before memcpy(dest, _src + j*neblock, neblock), then writes the block size via _sw32(dest - 4, cbytes).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memory write through _sw32(dest - 4, -value) with no capacity check in the run path, directly writing beyond the intended destination buffer. This is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), distinct from CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read), since the defect is a write past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the run-length branch writes the 4-byte split header at dest - 4 without verifying that ntbytes (already incremented by 4) still fits within maxbytes. Trigger: a run-heavy input with a small destination buffer where ntbytes reaches or exceeds the capacity. Consequence: a heap-based out-of-bounds write of the encoded run value past the destination buffer, corrupting adjacent heap memory.

commit_msg:
This is a complement to commit aa6dd211e4b1 ("inet: use bigger hash
table for IP ID generation"), but focusing on some specific aspects
of IPv6.

Contary to IPv4, IPv6 only uses packet IDs with fragments, and with a
minimum MTU of 1280, it's much less easy to force a remote peer to
produce many fragments to explore its ID sequence. In addition packet
IDs are 32-bit in IPv6, which further complicates their analysis. On
the other hand, it is often easier to choose among plenty of possible
source addresses and partially work around the bigger hash table the
commit above permits, which leaves IPv6 partially exposed to some
possibilities of remote analysis at the risk of weakening some
protocols like DNS if some IDs can be predicted with a good enough
probability.

Given the wide range of permitted IDs, the risk of collision is extremely
low so there's no need to rely on the positive increment algorithm that
is shared with the IPv4 code via ip_idents_reserve(). We have a fast
PRNG, so let's simply call prandom_u32() and be done with it.

Performance measurements at 10 Gbps couldn't show any difference with
the previous code, even when using a single core, because due to the
large fragments, we're limited to only ~930 kpps at 10 Gbps and the cost
of the random generation is completely offset by other operations and by
the network transfer time. In addition, this change removes the need to
update a shared entry in the idents table so it may even end up being
slightly faster on large scale systems where this matters.

The risk of at least one collision here is about 1/80 million among
10 IDs, 1/850k among 100 IDs, and still only 1/8.5k among 1000 IDs,
which remains very low compared to IPv4 where all IDs are reused
every 4 to 80ms on a 10 Gbps flow depending on packet sizes.

Reported-by: Amit Klein <aksecurity@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Reviewed-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210529110746.6796-1-w@1wt.eu
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tconst struct {', '\t\tstruct in6_addr dst;', '\t\tstruct in6_addr src;', '\t} __aligned(SIPHASH_ALIGNMENT) combined = {', '\t\t.dst = *dst,', '\t\t.src = *src,', '\t};', '\tu32 hash, id;', '\t/* Note the following code is not safe, but this is okay. */', '\tif (unlikely(siphash_key_is_zero(&net->ipv4.ip_id_key)))', '\t\tget_random_bytes(&net->ipv4.ip_id_key,', '\t\t\t\t sizeof(net->ipv4.ip_id_key));', '', '\thash = siphash(&combined, sizeof(combined), &net->ipv4.ip_id_key);', '', '\t/* Treat id of 0 as unset and if we get 0 back from ip_idents_reserve,', '\t * set the hight order instead thus minimizing possible future', '\t * collisions.', '\t */', '\tid = ip_idents_reserve(hash, 1);', '\tif (unlikely(!id))', '\t\tid = 1 << 31;'], 'added_lines': ['\tu32 id;', '\tdo {', '\t\tid = prandom_u32();', '\t} while (!id);']}
description: In the IPv6 implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.13.3, net/ipv6/output_core.c has an information leak because of certain use of a hash table which, although big, doesn't properly consider that IPv6-based attackers can typically choose among many IPv6 source addresses.

code_evidence: The function builds a combined structure from the caller-supplied dst and src IPv6 addresses and hashes it with siphash under net->ipv4.ip_id_key to derive the fragment ID.
The key is obtained from net->ipv4.ip_id_key and only regenerated if siphash_key_is_zero; there is no per-source-address keying or rekeying.
The siphash output is passed to ip_idents_reserve(hash, 1), so the resulting ID is a deterministic function of (dst, src, key), and the key is shared across all IPv6 flows.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reliance on a risky, insufficiently randomized ID-generation scheme (shared key, deterministic hash of attacker-chosen addresses), matching CWE-327's use of a risky cryptographic algorithm/mechanism for a security-sensitive value. It is not CWE-330 (insufficient randomness) because the code does invoke siphash; the flaw is the design of the ID derivation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ID is derived deterministically from attacker-influenced src/dst using a single shared, long-lived key. Trigger: an attacker choosing many IPv6 source addresses observes the resulting fragment IDs and learns the hash/key behavior. Supported consequence: predictable IP fragment IDs, enabling remote inference/analysis of the ID sequence (information leak), not a cryptographic break of siphash itself.

commit_msg: gnrc_tcp: abort on unknown option

description: In the TCP implementation (gnrc_tcp) in RIOT through 2019.07, the parser for TCP options does not terminate on all inputs, allowing a denial-of-service, because sys/net/gnrc/transport_layer/tcp/gnrc_tcp_option.c has an infinite loop for an unknown zero-length option.

code_evidence: The while loop at [9] is bounded by opt_left, which is decremented only by option->length at [38]. For an unknown option kind [29-32], the default branch has no return, so control falls through to the length check [33] and pointer/length advance [37-38]. If option->length is zero, opt_ptr and opt_left are unchanged, so the loop re-reads the same option forever. The added return -1 in the default branch terminates on unknown options.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loop's exit condition (opt_left > 0) is unreachable for a zero-length unknown option because no state changes, matching CWE-835's infinite loop with availability impact; the added return in the default case removes the unhandled path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the default branch for unknown option kinds lacks a terminating return, and a zero-length option causes opt_left to never decrease. Trigger: a peer sends a TCP header containing an unknown option with length 0. Consequence: the parser spins indefinitely in the while loop, consuming CPU and causing denial of service.

commit_msg:
Prevent undefined behavior

Fix #2068 in main branch.

Signed-off-by: Steven Bellock <sbellock@nvidia.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (spdm_response->ct_exponent > LIBSPDM_MAX_CT_EXPONENT) {', '        status = LIBSPDM_STATUS_INVALID_MSG_FIELD;', '        goto receive_done;', '    }', '']}
description:
libspdm is a sample implementation that follows the DMTF SPDM specifications. Prior to versions 2.3.3 and 3.0, following a successful CAPABILITIES response, a libspdm Requester stores the Responder's CTExponent into its context without validation. If the Requester sends a request message that requires a cryptography operation by the Responder, such as CHALLENGE, libspdm will calculate the timeout value using the Responder's unvalidated CTExponent.

A patch is available in version 2.3.3. A workaround is also available. After completion of VCA, the Requester can check the value of the Responder's CTExponent. If it greater than or equal to 64, then the Requester can stop communication with the Responder.

code_evidence: The CAPABILITIES response field ct_exponent is copied directly from the untrusted responder message into spdm_context->connection_info.capability.ct_exponent with no range check on this path; the patch adds a check for spdm_response->ct_exponent > LIBSPDM_MAX_CT_EXPONENT before this assignment.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a remotely supplied metadata field and stores it without checking that it falls within the required domain (<= LIBSPDM_MAX_CT_EXPONENT), which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The defect is a missing validation constraint on received data, not a transformation or encoding issue.

evidence_lines.code:
spdm_context->connection_info.capability.ct_exponent = spdm_response->ct_exponent;
spdm_context->connection_info.capability.flags = spdm_response->flags;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Requester trusts the Responder's ct_exponent without validating it against LIBSPDM_MAX_CT_EXPONENT. Trigger: a malicious/compromised Responder returns an out-of-range ct_exponent in its CAPABILITIES response. Supported consequence: the stored value is later used to compute timeout values, leading to undefined behavior (per commit) during cryptographic operations such as CHALLENGE.

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. When `mlir::tfg::ConvertGenericFunctionToFunctionDef` is given empty function attributes, it gives a null dereference. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit aed36912609fc07229b4d0a7b44f3f48efc00fd0. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

The success path at line 61 calls nfc_llcp_send_snl_sdreq(local, ...) and then falls into exit at lines 62-65, which only unlocks the device and drops the device reference; no nfc_llcp_local_put(local) is performed, so the local object's reference obtained via find_local is leaked on every path.

commit_msg:
Fix bug in PngChunk::readRawProfile

- Now it takes into account text.size_ when searching for a newline
char.

description: In Exiv2 0.26 and previous versions, PngChunk::readRawProfile in pngchunk_int.cpp may cause a denial of service (application crash due to a heap-based buffer over-read) via a crafted PNG file.

code_evidence: sp is set to text.pData_+1 and the newline scan `while (*sp != '\n') sp++;` has no bound check against text.size_, so a crafted text buffer lacking a newline walks past the allocation.
After the newline scan, `sp` is advanced again over '\0', ' ' and '\n' without checking text.size_; atol then parses from possibly out-of-bounds memory.
The hex decode loop reads `*sp` in the inner while and on each nibble fetch; the only guard is `*sp == '\0'`, which does not stop at text.size_, so decoding can read past the buffer end.

commit_msg:
Fix wild free.

`huffdata` is initially allocated using `aligned_dealloc` but can be
replaced with `data2` which is allocated using `custom_calloc`.
This can cause a wild free when `aligned_dealloc(huffdata)` is called.
Fix by replacing allocation sites with aligned_alloc.

Noticed and fixed a similar problem with `hdrdata`.

Lines 20-21 zero the region beyond dsize and copy dsize bytes into tmp, then line 22 frees data2.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs bounded writes via memset and memcpy whose extent depends on dsize/adds; an incorrect size relationship permits writing past the allocated buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. The allocator mismatch described in the commit is a related free issue, not the write itself.

unsigned char * tmp = (unsigned char*)custom_malloc(new_size);

If dsize or adds is inconsistent with the actual allocated buffer, the memset/memcpy at lines 20-21 write past the intended buffer boundary.

commit_msg:
Fix `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor` failing CHECK.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 368706628
Change-Id: I5c9ea4833f38835ee183ca50d63251dc89c9f3bc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      const RowPartitionTensor& value_rowids,', '    DCHECK_EQ(result->size(), value_rowids.size());'], 'added_lines': ['      OpKernelContext* context, const RowPartitionTensor& value_rowids,', '    OP_REQUIRES(context, result->size() == value_rowids.size(),', '                errors::InvalidArgument("Invalid row ids."));']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor`, an attacker can exploit an undefined behavior if input arguments are empty. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L356-L360) only checks that one of the tensors is not empty, but does not check for the other ones. There are multiple `DCHECK` validations to prevent heap OOB, but these are no-op in release builds, hence they don't prevent anything. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function reserves result based on value_rowids.size() and returns early only when index_size==0, so the output vector size is assumed to equal the input row-id count.
The first element is read via value_rowids(0) and used to index parent_output_index[current_value_rowid]; the only guard is DCHECK_LT, which is a no-op in release builds.
In the loop, each new value_rowid is used to index parent_output_index[next_value_rowid] with only a DCHECK_LT guard; the final DCHECK_EQ merely asserts result size equals input size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-131 fits because the code fails to correctly validate/calculate the size relationship between value_rowids and parent_output_index before indexing and building the result vector, producing an incorrect effective size and OOB access; this is not merely a numeric overflow (CWE-190) since the defect is a missing size-consistency check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size/length relationship between value_rowids and parent_output_index is only checked by DCHECKs that vanish in release builds, so an out-of-range row id indexes parent_output_index out of bounds. Trigger: crafted value_rowids containing an id >= parent_output_index.size(). Consequence: heap out-of-bounds read and a size mismatch in result, leading to undefined behavior/crash.

description: An issue was discovered in Tcpreplay 4.3.0 beta1. A heap-based buffer over-read was triggered in the function dlt_en10mb_encode() of the file plugins/dlt_en10mb/en10mb.c, due to inappropriate values in the function memmove(). The length (pktlen + ctx -> l2len) can be larger than source value (packet + ctx->l2len) because the function fails to ensure the length of a packet is valid. This leads to Denial of Service.

code_evidence: When newl2len != ctx->l2len, the code reallocs only when newl2len > ctx->l2len, then unconditionally calls memmove(packet + newl2len, packet + ctx->l2len, pktlen - ctx->l2len). The source read offset is packet + ctx->l2len and the read length is pktlen - ctx->l2len; the prior checks only ensure pktlen >= newl2len and pktlen >= ctx->l2len, not that the source range fits the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The memmove reads pktlen - ctx->l2len bytes from packet + ctx->l2len without ensuring that range is within the buffer, which is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing size constraint causes the read past the buffer end, matching the target weakness rather than a write overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no validation that pktlen and ctx->l2len describe a valid source buffer before memmove. Trigger: crafted packet with an l2len such that pktlen - ctx->l2len reads past the allocated packet buffer (e.g., when newl2len <= ctx->l2len and no realloc occurs). Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read leading to crash/DoS.

description: The dissect_nhdr_extopt function in epan/dissectors/packet-lbmc.c in the LBMC dissector in Wireshark 2.0.x before 2.0.2 does not validate length values, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer overflow and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: fragment_offset is read from the packet (line 24) and data_len is derived from the packet-controlled hdrlen (line 34); both feed data_offset and len_dissected without any bound check.

In the reassembly-complete branch, tvb_memcpy writes data_len bytes to reassembly->data + fragment_offset (line 44), then reassembly->len is incremented by data_len (line 45); neither fragment_offset nor the combined length is validated against the destination buffer size.

The more-fragments in-progress branch performs the same unchecked write at line 90 and increments reassembly->len at line 91, so a crafted packet with a large fragment_offset or data_len can write past the fixed reassembly->data buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts length and offset metadata from the packet but does not validate that they are within safe bounds before using them in a memory copy, which is a missing input-validation constraint (CWE-20). The lower-level buffer overflow is the consequence of this unvalidated input, not the input-validation defect itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: packet-supplied fragment_offset and hdrlen-derived data_len are used to compute a destination offset and copy length without validating them against the reassembly buffer capacity. Trigger: a crafted LBMC EXTOPT packet with a large fragment offset or data length. Consequence: stack-based buffer overflow in reassembly->data, causing a crash (DoS) and potentially memory corruption.

commit_msg:
sctp: Prevent soft lockup when sctp_accept() is called during a timeout event

A case can occur when sctp_accept() is called by the user during
a heartbeat timeout event after the 4-way handshake.  Since
sctp_assoc_migrate() changes both assoc->base.sk and assoc->ep, the
bh_sock_lock in sctp_generate_heartbeat_event() will be taken with
the listening socket but released with the new association socket.
The result is a deadlock on any future attempts to take the listening
socket lock.

Note that this race can occur with other SCTP timeouts that take
the bh_lock_sock() in the event sctp_accept() is called.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct net *net = sock_net(asoc->base.sk);', '\tbh_lock_sock(asoc->base.sk);', '\tif (sock_owned_by_user(asoc->base.sk)) {', '\t\tasoc->base.sk->sk_err = -error;', '\tbh_unlock_sock(asoc->base.sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct sock *sk = asoc->base.sk;', '\tstruct net *net = sock_net(sk);', '\tbh_lock_sock(sk);', '\tif (sock_owned_by_user(sk)) {', '\t\tsk->sk_err = -error;', '\tbh_unlock_sock(sk);']}
description: net/sctp/sm_sideeffect.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3 does not properly manage the relationship between a lock and a socket, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via a crafted sctp_accept call.

code_evidence: The socket used for locking is re-read from asoc->base.sk at each step: net is derived from asoc->base.sk, bh_lock_sock locks asoc->base.sk, and sock_owned_by_user tests asoc->base.sk.
The error path writes asoc->base.sk->sk_err and out_unlock releases asoc->base.sk, again re-reading the association's socket rather than using a saved reference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a concurrent code sequence (timeout handler vs. accept/migrate) shares the association socket without atomic lock/unlock pairing, violating exclusivity and atomicity. The result is a deadlock DoS, not a mere logic error, because the lock is held on a different socket than the one released.

evidence_lines.code:
asoc->base.sk->sk_err = -error;
bh_unlock_sock(asoc->base.sk);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timeout handler does not capture the socket reference once; it dereferences asoc->base.sk repeatedly, so a concurrent sctp_accept()/sctp_assoc_migrate() can change asoc->base.sk between the lock and unlock. The handler then locks the listening socket but unlocks the migrated association socket, leaving the listening socket lock held and causing a deadlock/soft lockup that denies service.

description: Race conditions in opa-fm before 10.4.0.0.196 and opa-ff before 10.4.0.0.197.
