commit_msg:
FLACExtractor: copy protect mWriteBuffer

Bug: 30895578
Change-Id: I4cba36bbe3502678210e5925181683df9726b431
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        mWriteBuffer = buffer;'], 'added_lines': ['        memmove(mWriteBuffer, buffer, sizeof(const FLAC__int32 * const) * getChannels());']}
description: A remote code execution vulnerability in FLACExtractor.cpp in libstagefright in Mediaserver could enable an attacker using a specially crafted file to cause memory corruption during media file and data processing. This issue is rated as Critical due to the possibility of remote code execution within the context of the Mediaserver process. Product: Android. Versions: 4.4.4, 5.0.2, 5.1.1, 6.0, 6.0.1, 7.0, 7.1.1, 7.1.2. Android ID: A-34970788.

code_evidence: The callback receives per-channel pointers as buffer[] (line 2) and stores the frame header (line 6). Line 7 assigns the caller-owned pointer array mWriteBuffer = buffer, retaining a reference without copying the pointed-to channel data; line 8 then signals mWriteCompleted so the stored pointer is consumed later. Because the FLAC parser only guarantees the buffer until the next frame or finish, later use of mWriteBuffer dereferences memory whose lifetime/contents are no longer controlled, outside the intended per-frame buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale alias causes downstream operations to access memory outside the intended buffer boundaries, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within memory bounds. The fix (memmove of getChannels() pointers) confirms the missing bounded copy; a lifetime-specific CWE would be a narrower root cause, but CWE-119 is the supplied target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder-provided buffer pointer is aliased into mWriteBuffer instead of copying the channel pointers, so the consumer reads through a dangling/stale pointer array after the decoder reuses or frees it. Trigger: a crafted FLAC file whose frame triggers the write callback followed by decoder buffer reuse. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read/write on memory outside the intended frame buffer, enabling memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Commit a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars") is
checking whether maps are read-only both from BPF program side and user space
side, and then, given their content is constant, reading out their data via
map->ops->map_direct_value_addr() which is then subsequently used as known
scalar value for the register, that is, it is marked as __mark_reg_known()
with the read value at verification time. Before a23740ec43ba, the register
content was marked as an unknown scalar so the verifier could not make any
assumptions about the map content.

The current implementation however is prone to a TOCTOU race, meaning, the
value read as known scalar for the register is not guaranteed to be exactly
the same at a later point when the program is executed, and as such, the
prior made assumptions of the verifier with regards to the program will be
invalid which can cause issues such as OOB access, etc.

While the BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG map flag is always fixed and required to be
specified at map creation time, the map->frozen property is initially set to
false for the map given the map value needs to be populated, e.g. for global
data sections. Once complete, the loader "freezes" the map from user space
such that no subsequent updates/deletes are possible anymore. For the rest
of the lifetime of the map, this freeze one-time trigger cannot be undone
anymore after a successful BPF_MAP_FREEZE cmd return. Meaning, any new BPF_*
cmd calls which would update/delete map entries will be rejected with -EPERM
since map_get_sys_perms() removes the FMODE_CAN_WRITE permission. This also
means that pending update/delete map entries must still complete before this
guarantee is given. This corner case is not an issue for loaders since they
create and prepare such program private map in successive steps.

However, a malicious user is able to trigger this TOCTOU race in two different
ways: i) via userfaultfd, and ii) via batched updates. For i) userfaultfd is
used to expand the competition interval, so that map_update_elem() can modify
the contents of the map after map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load() were executed.
This works, because userfaultfd halts the parallel thread which triggered a
map_update_elem() at the time where we copy key/value from the user buffer and
this already passed the FMODE_CAN_WRITE capability test given at that time the
map was not "frozen". Then, the main thread performs the map_freeze() and
bpf_prog_load(), and once that had completed successfully, the other thread
is woken up to complete the pending map_update_elem() which then changes the
map content. For ii) the idea of the batched update is similar, meaning, when
there are a large number of updates to be processed, it can increase the
competition interval between the two. It is therefore possible in practice to
modify the contents of the map after executing map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load().

One way to fix both i) and ii) at the same time is to expand the use of the
map's map->writecnt. The latter was introduced in fc9702273e2e ("bpf: Add mmap()
support for BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY") and further refined in 1f6cb19be2e2 ("bpf:
Prevent re-mmap()'ing BPF map as writable for initially r/o mapping") with
the rationale to make a writable mmap()'ing of a map mutually exclusive with
read-only freezing. The counter indicates writable mmap() mappings and then
prevents/fails the freeze operation. Its semantics can be expanded beyond
just mmap() by generally indicating ongoing write phases. This would essentially
span any parallel regular and batched flavor of update/delete operation and
then also have map_freeze() fail with -EBUSY. For the check_mem_access() in
the verifier we expand upon the bpf_map_is_rdonly() check ensuring that all
last pending writes have completed via bpf_map_write_active() test. Once the
map->frozen is set and bpf_map_write_active() indicates a map->writecnt of 0
only then we are really guaranteed to use the map's data as known constants.
For map->frozen being set and pending writes in process of still being completed
we fall back to marking that register as unknown scalar so we don't end up
making assumptions about it. With this, both TOCTOU reproducers from i) and
ii) are fixed.

Note that the map->writecnt has been converted into a atomic64 in the fix in
order to avoid a double freeze_mutex mutex_{un,}lock() pair when updating
map->writecnt in the various map update/delete BPF_* cmd flavors. Spanning
the freeze_mutex over entire map update/delete operations in syscall side
would not be possible due to then causing everything to be serialized.
Similarly, something like synchronize_rcu() after setting map->frozen to wait
for update/deletes to complete is not possible either since it would also
have to span the user copy which can sleep. On the libbpf side, this won't
break d66562fba1ce ("libbpf: Add BPF object skeleton support") as the
anonymous mmap()-ed "map initialization image" is remapped as a BPF map-backed
mmap()-ed memory where for .rodata it's non-writable.

Fixes: a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars")
Reported-by: w1tcher.bupt@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -1,4 +1,19 @@
 static bool bpf_map_is_rdonly(const struct bpf_map *map)
 {
-	return (map->map_flags & BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG) && map->frozen;
+	/* A map is considered read-only if the following condition are true:
+	 *
+	 * 1) BPF program side cannot change any of the map content. The
+	 *    BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG flag is throughout the lifetime of a map
+	 *    and was set at map creation time.
+	 * 2) The map value(s) have been initialized from user space by a
+	 *    loader and then "frozen", such that no new map update/delete
+	 *    operations from syscall side are possible for the rest of
+	 *    the map's lifetime from that point onwards.
+	 * 3) Any parallel/pending map update/delete operations from syscall
+	 *    side have been completed. Only after that point, it's safe to
+	 *    assume that map value(s) are immutable.
+	 */
+	return (map->map_flags & BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG) &&
+	       READ_ONCE(map->frozen) &&
+	       !bpf_map_write_active(map);
 }

The', '\t *    BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG flag is throughout the lifetime of a map', '\t *    and was set at map creation time.', '\t * 2) The map value(s) have been initialized from user space by a', '\t *    loader and then "frozen", such that no new map update/delete', '\t *    operations from syscall side are possible for the rest of', "\t *    the map's lifetime from that point onwards.", '\t * 3) Any parallel/pending map update/delete operations from syscall', "\t *    side have been completed. Only after that point, it's safe to", '\t *    assume that map value(s) are immutable.', '\t */', '\treturn (map->map_flags & BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG) &&', '\t       READ_ONCE(map->frozen) &&', '\t       !bpf_map_write_active(map);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's ebpf verifier between bpf_map_update_elem and bpf_map_freeze due to a missing lock in kernel/bpf/syscall.c. In this flaw, a local user with a special privilege (cap_sys_admin or cap_bpf) can modify the frozen mapped address space. This flaw affects kernel versions prior to 5.16 rc2.

code_evidence: bpf_map_is_rdonly() returns true based solely on map->map_flags & BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG and map->frozen, with no check that in-flight map update/delete operations have completed. The verifier then treats the map contents as known scalars, making assumptions about values that a concurrent syscall-side write can still change after the freeze check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits because the function's check of the resource state (frozen) can be invalidated before the checked state is used as a constant by the verifier. The missing constraint on pending writes is the check/use gap; a plain data race would not capture the verifier's assumption about immutable contents.

evidence_lines.code: return (map->map_flags & BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG) && map->frozen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the read-only decision checks map->frozen but not map->writecnt, so a pending update that passed the writability check before freeze can complete afterward. Trigger: userfaultfd or batched updates widen the window between freeze/prog-load and the pending write. Consequence: verifier assumptions about constant map data become invalid, enabling OOB access.

commit_msg: fix issue #13, by dividing zero without sanity check in jfif.c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!sfh_max) sfh_max = 1;', '    if (!sfv_max) sfv_max = 1;']}
description: jfif_decode in jfif.c in ffjpeg through 2019-08-21 has a divide-by-zero error.

code_evidence: sfh_max and sfv_max are initialized to 0 at lines 9-10 and only updated from jfif->comp_info[c].samp_factor_h/v for c < jfif->comp_num (lines 33-40). If comp_num is 0 or all sampling factors are 0, both maxima remain 0. Lines 41-42 compute mcuw/mcuh = 0, then lines 43-46 use them as divisors: ALIGN(width, mcuw), ALIGN(height, mcuh), and jw/mcuw, jh/mcuh.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs integer division and modulo operations where the divisor derives directly from unvalidated input fields, matching CWE-369 Divide By Zero. This is not merely an out-of-bounds issue; the immediate defect is a zero divisor causing a crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sampling-factor maxima are not validated to be nonzero before being used as divisors. Trigger: a crafted JFIF with zero components or zero sampling factors leaves sfh_max/sfv_max at 0. Consequence: division by zero at the ALIGN macro or jw/mcuw and jh/mcuh, causing a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg: Fix #8731 - Crash in ELF parser with negative 32bit number
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tvstart += entry->vn_aux;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tst32 vnaux = entry->vn_aux;', '\t\tif (vnaux < 1) {', '\t\t\tgoto beach;', '\t\t}', '\t\tvstart += vnaux;']}
description: In radare2 2.0.1, an integer exception (negative number leading to an invalid memory access) exists in store_versioninfo_gnu_verneed() in libr/bin/format/elf/elf.c via crafted ELF files on 32bit systems.

code_evidence: vstart = need + i is a raw pointer into the calloc'd buffer; only sizeof(Elf_(Verneed)) is checked against end before vstart is advanced by the attacker-controlled 32-bit vn_aux.

The inner loop reads Vernaux fields via READ32/READ16 at vstart, but the bound check vstart + sizeof(Elf_(Vernaux)) <= end uses pointer arithmetic on vstart that was already offset by vn_aux; a negative/large vn_aux can push vstart outside need..end, so the READ macros dereference out-of-bounds memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads Vernaux fields through vstart beyond the intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The crash is the consequence of the OOB access, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
for (j = 0, isum = i + entry->vn_aux; j < entry->vn_cnt && vstart + sizeof (Elf_(Vernaux)) <= end; ++j) {
vaux.vna_hash = READ32 (vstart, k)
vaux.vna_flags = READ16 (vstart, k)
vaux.vna_other = READ16 (vstart, k)
vaux.vna_name = READ32 (vstart, k)
vaux.vna_next = READ32 (vstart, k)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is missing validation of entry->vn_aux before it is added to vstart; a crafted ELF with a negative 32-bit vn_aux moves vstart before the allocated buffer while the loop condition still passes. The READ32/READ16 macros then read out-of-bounds, causing the described integer exception/crash on 32-bit systems.

commit_msg:
Doing a "get_user_pages()" on a copy-on-write page for reading can be
ambiguous: the page can be COW'ed at any time afterwards, and the
direction of a COW event isn't defined.

Yes, whoever writes to it will generally do the COW, but if the thread
that did the get_user_pages() unmapped the page before the write (and
that could happen due to memory pressure in addition to any outright
action), the writer could also just take over the old page instead.

End result: the get_user_pages() call might result in a page pointer
that is no longer associated with the original VM, and is associated
with - and controlled by - another VM having taken it over instead.

So when doing a get_user_pages() on a COW mapping, the only really safe
thing to do would be to break the COW when getting the page, even when
only getting it for reading.

At the same time, some users simply don't even care.

For example, the perf code wants to look up the page not because it
cares about the page, but because the code simply wants to look up the
physical address of the access for informational purposes, and doesn't
really care about races when a page might be unmapped and remapped
elsewhere.

This adds logic to force a COW event by setting FOLL_WRITE on any
copy-on-write mapping when FOLL_GET (or FOLL_PIN) is used to get a page
pointer as a result.

The current semantics end up being:

 - __get_user_pages_fast(): no change. If you don't ask for a write,
   you won't break COW. You'd better know what you're doing.

 - get_user_pages_fast(): the fast-case "look it up in the page tables
   without anything getting mmap_sem" now refuses to follow a read-only
   page, since it might need COW breaking.  Which happens in the slow
   path - the fast path doesn't know if the memory might be COW or not.

 - get_user_pages() (including the slow-path fallback for gup_fast()):
   for a COW mapping, turn on FOLL_WRITE for FOLL_GET/FOLL_PIN, with
   very similar semantics to FOLL_FORCE.

If it turns out that we want finer granularity (ie "only break COW when
it might actually matter" - things like the zero page are special and
don't need to be broken) we might need to push these semantics deeper
into the lookup fault path.  So if people care enough, it's possible
that we might end up adding a new internal FOLL_BREAK_COW flag to go
with the internal FOLL_COW flag we already have for tracking "I had a
COW".

Alternatively, if it turns out that different callers might want to
explicitly control the forced COW break behavior, we might even want to
make such a flag visible to the users of get_user_pages() instead of
using the above default semantics.

But for now, this is mostly commentary on the issue (this commit message
being a lot bigger than the patch, and that patch in turn is almost all
comments), with that minimal "enable COW breaking early" logic using the
existing FOLL_WRITE behavior.

[ It might be worth noting that we've always had this ambiguity, and it
  could arguably be seen as a user-space issue.

  You only get private COW mappings that could break either way in
  situations where user space is doing cooperative things (ie fork()
  before an execve() etc), but it _is_ surprising and very subtle, and
  fork() is supposed to give you independent address spaces.

  So let's treat this as a kernel issue and make the semantics of
  get_user_pages() easier to understand. Note that obviously a true
  shared mapping will still get a page that can change under us, so this
  does _not_ mean that get_user_pages() somehow returns any "stable"
  page ]

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Tested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Kirill Shutemov <kirill@shutemov.name>
Acked-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Cc: Matthew Wilcox <willy@infradead.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn pmd_write(pmd) ||', '\t       ((flags & FOLL_FORCE) && (flags & FOLL_COW) && pmd_dirty(pmd));'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn pmd_write(pmd) || ((flags & FOLL_COW) && pmd_dirty(pmd));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7.3, related to mm/gup.c and mm/huge_memory.c. The get_user_pages (aka gup) implementation, when used for a copy-on-write page, does not properly consider the semantics of read operations and therefore can grant unintended write access, aka CID-17839856fd58.

code_evidence: can_follow_write_pmd decides whether a PMD may be followed for writing based on pmd_write(pmd) or the FOLL_FORCE/FOLL_COW/dirty combination. The condition is evaluated against a page-table entry that can be changed concurrently by another thread (COW break, unmap, or takeover), so the decision and subsequent use are not atomic with respect to that modification.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the weakness is a timing window in a concurrent sequence: shared page-table state is inspected and then acted upon without exclusivity, allowing an interfering COW/unmap sequence to modify it. The defect is the non-atomic check/use of shared mapping state, not a simple missing bounds or type check.

evidence_lines.code:
return pmd_write(pmd) ||
((flags & FOLL_FORCE) && (flags & FOLL_COW) && pmd_dirty(pmd));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the check of PMD writability/COW state is a snapshot taken without holding exclusive control over the mapping, so a concurrent COW or unmap can change the entry between the check and its use. Trigger: another thread faults or unmaps the copy-on-write page while get_user_pages follows it. Consequence: the caller may follow a page whose ownership/VM association changed, granting unintended write access or returning a page controlled by another VM.

commit_msg:
keyfile settings: Use tighter permissions

When creating directories, create them with 700 permissions,
instead of 777.

Closes: #1658
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  g_file_make_directory_with_parents (kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['  g_mkdir_with_parents (g_file_peek_path (kfsb->dir), 0700);']}
description: The keyfile settings backend in GNOME GLib (aka glib2.0) before 2.60.0 creates directories using g_file_make_directory_with_parents (kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL) and files using g_file_replace_contents (kfsb->file, contents, length, NULL, FALSE, G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION, NULL, NULL, NULL). Consequently, it does not properly restrict directory (and file) permissions. Instead, for directories, 0777 permissions are used; for files, default file permissions are used. This is similar to CVE-2019-12450.

code_evidence: kfsb->dir is derived from the keyfile path under the user config directory (lines 7-10), so it is a security-critical configuration location. Line 21 calls g_file_make_directory_with_parents (kfsb->dir, NULL, NULL), passing NULL for both GMountOperation and GError, and no mode is supplied, so the created directory receives the default (0777) permissions rather than restrictive ones.

patch 9.0.0025: accessing beyond allocated memory with the cmdline window

Problem:    Accessing beyond allocated memory when using the cmdline window in
            Ex mode.
Solution:   Use "*" instead of "'<,'>" for Visual mode.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t//  "\'<,\'>mods" -> "mods\'<,\'>+', '\t\tSTRCPY(orig_cmd + len, "\'<,\'>+");'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t//  "\'<,\'>mods" -> "mods *+', '\t\t//  Use "*" instead of "\'<,\'>" to avoid the command getting', '\t\t//  longer, in case is was allocated.', '\t\tSTRCPY(orig_cmd + len, " *+");']}

The destination is orig_cmd, the caller-provided command buffer, and the appended literal is longer than the 5-byte "'<,'>" prefix that was stripped at line 16-18, so the write at orig_cmd+len can exceed the allocation.

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    check_free_port(d, port);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The function takes d->event_lock, obtains a free port via get_free_port(d), and on failure exits through ERROR_EXIT_DOM while still holding the lock.

On success it records alloc->port = port and reaches out: where it unlocks event_lock and releases the domain; the added check_free_port(d, port) runs at out: only after the port has been allocated and while the lock is still held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the added check coordinates port allocation with concurrent evtchn_reset() under the shared event_lock, addressing a timing window over shared event-channel state; the function itself serializes its critical section with the lock, so the weakness is the concurrent-reset interaction rather than unsynchronized access within evtchn_alloc_unbound itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the port-allocation path must account for concurrent evtchn_reset() activity; the fix adds check_free_port() at the out label so newly opened ports are counted under d->event_lock before the lock is dropped. The trigger is a racing reset/bind sequence that could otherwise leave the active-port count inconsistent with the internal limit; the supported consequence is violation of internal port-validity assumptions (out-of-bounds access or bug checks), not a new race introduced by this function.

commit_msg:
x86/vpt: fix race when migrating timers between vCPUs

The current vPT code will migrate the emulated timers between vCPUs
(change the pt->vcpu field) while just holding the destination lock,
either from create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target if
the global target is adjusted. Changing the periodic_timer vCPU field
in this way creates a race where a third party could grab the lock in
the unlocked region of pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target (or before
create_periodic_time performs the vcpu change) and then release the
lock from a different vCPU, creating a locking imbalance.

Introduce a per-domain rwlock in order to protect periodic_time
migration between vCPU lists. Taking the lock in read mode prevents
any timer from being migrated to a different vCPU, while taking it in
write mode allows performing migration of timers across vCPUs. The
per-vcpu locks are still used to protect all the other fields from the
periodic_timer struct.

Note that such migration shouldn't happen frequently, and hence
there's no performance drop as a result of such locking.

This is XSA-336.

Reported-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Tested-by: Igor Druzhinin <igor.druzhinin@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);', '    spin_unlock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    pt_vcpu_lock(v);', '    pt_vcpu_unlock(v);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There is a race condition when migrating timers between x86 HVM vCPUs. When migrating timers of x86 HVM guests between its vCPUs, the locking model used allows for a second vCPU of the same guest (also operating on the timers) to release a lock that it didn't acquire. The most likely effect of the issue is a hang or crash of the hypervisor, i.e., a Denial of Service (DoS). All versions of Xen are affected. Only x86 systems are vulnerable. Arm systems are not vulnerable. Only x86 HVM guests can leverage the vulnerability. x86 PV and PVH cannot leverage the vulnerability. Only guests with more than one vCPU can exploit the vulnerability.

code_evidence: pt_save_timer acquires only v->arch.hvm.tm_lock, the per-vCPU lock.
While holding that lock it iterates the vCPU's tm_list and stops each periodic timer whose do_not_freeze flag is clear.
It then calls pt_freeze_time(v) and releases the same per-vCPU lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function synchronizes access to a shared resource (the timer list and its lock) with a per-vCPU lock that does not exclude cross-vCPU migration, creating a timing window for concurrent interference. This matches CWE-362; it is not merely a missing-lock bug, since a lock is taken but does not provide exclusivity over the migrated resource.

evidence_lines.code: spin_lock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);

pt_freeze_time(v);
spin_unlock(&v->arch.hvm.tm_lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The periodic timers in tm_list can be migrated between vCPUs by another path (create_periodic_time or pt_adjust_global_vcpu_target) while only the destination lock is held. This function takes just the per-vCPU lock, so a concurrent migration can move entries out of the list during iteration, and the lock acquired here may be released by a different vCPU, producing a locking imbalance that can hang or crash the hypervisor.

KVM: x86: drop error recovery in em_jmp_far and em_ret_far

em_jmp_far and em_ret_far assumed that setting IP can only fail in 64
bit mode, but syzkaller proved otherwise (and SDM agrees).
Code segment was restored upon failure, but it was left uninitialized
outside of long mode, which could lead to a leak of host kernel stack.
We could have fixed that by always saving and restoring the CS, but we

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tunsigned short sel, old_sel;', '\tstruct desc_struct old_desc, new_desc;', '\tconst struct x86_emulate_ops *ops = ctxt->ops;', '', '\t/* Assignment of RIP may only fail in 64-bit mode */', '\tif (ctxt->mode == X86EMUL_MODE_PROT64)', '\t\tops->get_segment(ctxt, &old_sel, &old_desc, NULL,', '\t\t\t\t VCPU_SREG_CS);', '\tif (rc != X86EMUL_CONTINUE) {', '\t\tWARN_ON(ctxt->mode != X86EMUL_MODE_PROT64);', '\t\t/* assigning eip failed; restore the old cs */', '\t\tops->set_segment(ctxt, old_sel, &old_desc, 0, VCPU_SREG_CS);', '\t\treturn rc;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned short sel;', '\tstruct desc_struct new_desc;', '\t/* Error handling is not implemented. */', '\tif (rc != X86EMUL_CONTINUE)', '\t\treturn X86EMUL_UNHANDLEABLE;', '']}
description: arch/x86/kvm/emulate.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.12 does not properly initialize Code Segment (CS) in certain error cases, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from kernel stack memory via a crafted application.

code_evidence: The old CS selector/descriptor is saved only when ctxt->mode == X86EMUL_MODE_PROT64, so old_sel and old_desc remain uninitialized in other modes.
If assign_eip_far fails, the handler warns and calls ops->set_segment(ctxt, old_sel, &old_desc, 0, VCPU_SREG_CS), loading the uninitialized stack values into the guest's CS.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's error path feeds uninitialized stack data into guest CS state, enabling a local guest to read host kernel stack memory, matching CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor. The uninitialized read is the cause; the confidentiality leak is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error-recovery path restores CS from old_sel/old_desc, which are only populated in 64-bit mode. Trigger: a guest jump-far where assign_eip_far returns a non-continue status outside long mode. Consequence: uninitialized host kernel stack contents are copied into guest-visible segment state, exposing sensitive kernel stack memory.

commit_msg:
EAP-pwd: fix side-channel leak where 1 in 2018 handshakes fail

Previously the Hunting and Pecking algorithm of EAP-pwd aborted when
more than 10 iterations are needed. Every iteration has a 50% chance
of finding the password element. This means one in every 2048 handshakes
will fail, in which case an error frame is sent to the client. This
event leaks information that can be abused in an offline password
brute-force attack. More precisely, the adversary learns that all 10
iterations failed for the given random EAP-pwd token. Using the same
techniques as in the Dragonblood attack, this can be used to brute-force
the password.

This patch fixes the above issue by executing enough iterations such that
the password element is always found eventually.

Note that timing and cache leaks remain a risk against the current
implementation of EAP-pwd.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (ctr > 10) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (ctr > 100) {']}
description: In FreeRADIUS 3.0 through 3.0.19, on average 1 in every 2048 EAP-pwd handshakes fails because the password element cannot be found within 10 iterations of the hunting and pecking loop. This leaks information that an attacker can use to recover the password of any user. This information leakage is similar to the "Dragonblood" attack and CVE-2019-9494.

code_evidence: ctr starts at 0 and the loop aborts via goto fail when ctr > 10, so at most 11 iterations are attempted before returning ret = -1.

Each iteration derives x_candidate from HMAC/HKDF of token, peer/server IDs, password and ctr; the point is accepted only if it is on the curve and not at infinity, otherwise continue re-enters the loop.
On abort, ret is set to -1 and cleanup/return occurs, producing a distinguishable failure response compared with the break path at line 112.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-203 fits because the function's behavior differs based on internal search outcome: exhaustion yields a failure return while success yields a point, creating an observable discrepancy. This is not merely a timing leak; the differing error result is the discrepancy, matching the target weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop's iteration cap (10) makes the password-element search probabilistically terminate early; when all attempts fail, the function returns an error rather than a point. The trigger is a token for which no candidate passes the on-curve/cofactor checks within the cap. The observable consequence is a distinct failure response leaking that the iteration budget was exhausted, which an attacker can exploit in offline password brute-forcing.

commit_msg: Add an HTTP/2 related rate limiting
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (cstate.get_received_settings_frame_count() > Http2::max_settings_frames_per_minute) {'], 'added_lines': ['  if (cstate.configured_max_settings_frames_per_minute != 0 &&', '      cstate.get_received_settings_frame_count() > cstate.configured_max_settings_frames_per_minute) {']}
description: The HTTP/2 protocol allows a denial of service (server resource consumption) because request cancellation can reset many streams quickly, as exploited in the wild in August through October 2023.

code_evidence: Each received SETTINGS frame increments a per-connection counter at line 12, then line 13 compares that counter against a fixed global limit Http2::max_settings_frames_per_minute and returns ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM when exceeded. The comparison has no guard for a disabled/zero configured limit, so the throttle is driven by a constant rather than the connection's configured_max_settings_frames_per_minute; the commit adds exactly that guard and uses the per-connection configured value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the throttling point for a limited resource (SETTINGS-frame processing) but does not honor the configured limit, matching CWE-400's lack of throttling for allocated resources. It is not a memory-safety bug; the defect is an uncontrolled-consumption/rate-limit configuration flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the rate check at line 13 uses a fixed global threshold instead of the connection's configured limit, so the only bound on SETTINGS-frame processing is a constant that may be zero/disabled or not aligned with the operator's configured resource budget. Trigger: a peer sends many SETTINGS frames (Rapid Reset-style stream churn). Supported consequence: unbounded per-connection SETTINGS processing and ACK transmission, consuming server CPU/memory until the fixed threshold is hit or the resource is exhausted.

Consequence: the comparison result is corrupted, so max_dur may be updated to a wrong (smaller/larger) fraction, altering the computed movie duration at lines 204-210 rather than a direct memory-safety impact.

description: An issue was discovered in ImageMagick 7.0.7. A memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadPCDImage in coders/pcd.c, which allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Three buffers chroma1, chroma2 and luma are allocated with AcquireQuantumMemory. If any allocation returns NULL, the combined NULL-check at lines 111-112 jumps directly to ThrowReaderException, which unwinds without relinquishing the buffers that did succeed. The pre-patch code had the same leak; the diff shows the fix adding RelinquishMagickMemory calls before throwing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because resources (heap buffers) are not released after their effective lifetime ends on the error path. This is a missing-release weakness, not a buffer overflow or use-after-free, since no freed memory is later dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation-failure branch throws before releasing the already-allocated chroma1/chroma2/luma buffers. Trigger: a crafted PCD file (or memory pressure) makes one of the AcquireQuantumMemory calls fail while the others succeed. Consequence: the successfully allocated buffers are leaked, enabling resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg:
FileURLToFilePath:  Don't unescape '/' and '\\'.

GURL leaves these escaped, and unescaping them in paths changes the
meaning of the path.

Added two values to the UnescapeRule enumeration:
PATH_SEPARATORS and URL_SPECIAL_CHARS_EXCEPT_PATH_SEPARATORS.

In followup CLs, I intend to replace all uses of URL_SPECIAL_CHARS,
in favor of one or both the two new values, and eventually remove
the value, as it's easily to use in an unsafe manner.

BUG=586657

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1704163003

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#377013}

            // Allow any of the prohibited but non-control characters when

-           (first_byte > ' ' && (rules & UnescapeRule::URL_SPECIAL_CHARS)) ||

description: Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.102 on Android mishandles / (slash) and \ (backslash) characters, which allows attackers to conduct directory traversal attacks via a file: URL, related to net/base/escape.cc and net/base/filename_util.cc.

code_evidence: The unescape decision gates whether a percent-encoded byte is decoded and pushed into the result. Line 37 allows decoding of any byte greater than space when URL_SPECIAL_CHARS is set, with no exclusion of '/' or '\'. Decoded bytes at line 42 then flow into the returned string, which callers convert to file paths.

Supported consequence: a path intended to stay under a restricted directory can resolve outside it, enabling directory traversal.

commit_msg:
sctp: avoid BUG_ON on sctp_wait_for_sndbuf

Alexander Popov reported that an application may trigger a BUG_ON in
sctp_wait_for_sndbuf if the socket tx buffer is full, a thread is
waiting on it to queue more data and meanwhile another thread peels off
the association being used by the first thread.

This patch replaces the BUG_ON call with a proper error handling. It
will return -EPIPE to the original sendmsg call, similarly to what would
have been done if the association wasn't found in the first place.

Acked-by: Alexander Popov <alex.popov@linux.com>
Signed-off-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tBUG_ON(sk != asoc->base.sk);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (sk != asoc->base.sk)', '\t\t\tgoto do_error;']}
description: Race condition in the sctp_wait_for_sndbuf function in net/sctp/socket.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.11 allows local users to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and panic) via a multithreaded application that peels off an association in a certain buffer-full state.

code_evidence: The loop releases the socket lock at line 23, sleeps in schedule_timeout at line 24, and then asserts with BUG_ON(sk != asoc->base.sk) at line 25 before reacquiring the lock at line 26. During the unlocked sleep window, another thread can peel off the association, changing asoc->base.sk, so the assertion fails.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unlocked sleep window permits concurrent modification of shared state (asoc->base.sk), violating exclusivity/atomicity; the resulting assertion failure is a race-condition DoS, matching CWE-362. It is a race rather than a simple missing check because the failure depends on interleaving with the concurrent peel-off.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the association's socket pointer is assumed immutable across the release_sock/schedule_timeout/lock_sock window, but the lock is dropped, allowing a concurrent association peel-off to modify it. Trigger: a sender blocked on a full tx buffer while another thread peels off the association. Consequence: the BUG_ON fires, panicking the kernel (DoS).

commit_msg:
libvncserver: scale: cast to 64 bit before shifting

Since pixel_value is 64 bit the data type of the shift operand should
be 64 bit too to prevent integer overflows.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                 pixel_value += (srcptr2[z] << (8 * z));'], 'added_lines': ['                 pixel_value += ((unsigned long)srcptr2[z] << (8 * z));']}
description: An issue was discovered in LibVNCServer before 0.9.13. libvncserver/scale.c has a pixel_value integer overflow.

code_evidence: pixel_value is declared unsigned long (line 37) and reset to 0 (line 51). In the default branch, srcptr2[z] is an unsigned char promoted to int; shifting it left by 8*z (line 58) occurs in int arithmetic. For z=3, a byte >= 0x80 shifted by 24 exceeds INT_MAX and triggers signed integer overflow before the value is added to the wider pixel_value accumulator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The shift computation overflows the int representation, matching CWE-190's integer overflow/wraparound. It is not just a truncating conversion; the unsafe operation is the signed shift that the patch widens to unsigned long.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shift operand srcptr2[z] is promoted to signed int, so 8*z up to 24 can overflow the int representation. Trigger: bytesPerPixel outside {1,2,4} combined with a high-order source byte. Consequence: the shifted value wraps or is UB, corrupting the assembled pixel and downstream scaled output.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/566
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  histogram_image->blob=(BlobInfo *) DetachBlob(histogram_image->blob);', '  histogram_image->blob=CloneBlobInfo(image->blob);', '  image->blob=(BlobInfo *) DetachBlob(image->blob);', '  image->blob=CloneBlobInfo(histogram_image->blob);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: When ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 processes a crafted file in convert, it can lead to a Memory Leak in the WriteHISTOGRAMImage() function in coders/histogram.c.

code_evidence: The function replaces histogram_image->blob and image->blob with cloned BlobInfo objects via DetachBlob and CloneBlobInfo, then calls WriteImage and later destroys histogram_image. The detached original blob references are overwritten without being released, and the cloned blob assigned to image->blob is never freed after its effective lifetime ends.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the code fails to release allocated BlobInfo resources after their effective lifetime, leaking memory. This is a missing-release resource lifetime issue, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the overwritten pointers are simply abandoned.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: DetachBlob returns the existing blob which is then overwritten by CloneBlobInfo, losing the pointer to the original allocation; the replacement blob on image->blob is likewise not released. Trigger: any successful WriteHISTOGRAMImage call, especially repeated processing of crafted files, leaks blob resources. Supported consequence: memory consumption leading to denial of service.

commit_msg:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tFILE *file;', '\tfile = fopen (stats_file, "w");', '\tlist l = vrrp_data->vrrp;', '\telement e;', '\tvrrp_t *vrrp;', '\tfor (e = LIST_HEAD(l); e; ELEMENT_NEXT(e)) {', '\t\tvrrp = ELEMENT_DATA(e);', '\t\tfprintf(file, "  Released master: %d\\n",', '\t\t\tvrrp->stats->release_master);'], 'added_lines': ['\tFILE *file = fopen_safe(stats_file, "w");', '\telement e;', '\tvrrp_t *vrrp;', '\tLIST_FOREACH(vrrp_data->vrrp, vrrp, e) {', '\t\tfprintf(file, "  Released master: %d\\n", vrrp->stats->release_master);']}
description: keepalived 2.0.8 didn't check for pathnames with symlinks when writing data to a temporary file upon a call to PrintData or PrintStats. This allowed local users to overwrite arbitrary files if fs.protected_symlinks is set to 0, as demonstrated by a symlink from /tmp/keepalived.data or /tmp/keepalived.stats to /etc/passwd.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function opens stats_file for writing and writes VRRP statistics; the symlink-following issue is a file-overwrite/arbitrary-write concern (CWE-59/CWE-73 family), not an exposure of sensitive information as required by CWE-200, which the definition itself flags as a commonly misused impact label.

commit_msg:
Always check the number of coefficients

When building the library with NDEBUG, asserts are eliminated
so it's better to always check that the number of coefficients
is inside the array range.

This fixes the 00191-audiofile-indexoob issue in #41
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (numCoefficients < 7 || numCoefficients > 255)', '\t\t\t{', '\t\t\t\t_af_error(AF_BAD_HEADER,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t"Bad number of coefficients");', '\t\t\t\treturn AF_FAIL;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: WAVE.cpp in Audio File Library (aka audiofile) 0.3.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via vectors related to a large number of coefficients.

code_evidence: numCoefficients is read from file input at line 90 and only constrained by an assert at line 91; the value is then stored in m_msadpcmNumCoefficients (line 92) and used as the loop bound writing into m_msadpcmCoefficients at lines 93-97 without any runtime range check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a file-supplied quantity before using it to bound an array write, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing runtime check, not the assert itself, is the validation gap; the resulting index out-of-bounds is the consequence rather than the root weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled numCoefficients from the WAVE ADPC header is trusted after an assert that is compiled out under NDEBUG. Trigger: a crafted file with numCoefficients outside [7,255] passes the assert-free build. Supported consequence: the loop at lines 93-97 writes past the fixed-size m_msadpcmCoefficients array, causing an out-of-bounds write/crash (DoS).

commit_msg: fixed #1734
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (esd) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (esd && esd->decoderConfig) {']}
description: The HintFile function in GPAC 1.0.1 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted file in the MP4Box command.

code_evidence: gf_isom_get_esd may return a non-NULL esd whose decoderConfig is NULL; the guard at line 85 only checks esd, so line 86 dereferences esd->decoderConfig->streamType without validating decoderConfig.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic CWE-476 NULL pointer dereference: a pointer expected valid (decoderConfig) is used without a NULL check, leading to a crash. It is not a buffer or type-confusion issue; the missing constraint is the NULL guard on the nested pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NULL check covers esd but not its nested decoderConfig member. A crafted MP4 file yields an ESD lacking decoderConfig, so dereferencing esd->decoderConfig->streamType crashes MP4Box, causing denial of service.

Return error when there are more mmco params than allocated size

Bug: 25818142

Change-Id: I5c1b23985eeca5192b42703c627ca3d060e4e13d

description: The H.264 decoder in libstagefright in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 mishandles Memory Management Control Operation (MMCO) data, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 25818142.

code_evidence: j is initialized to 0 at line 34 and incremented at line 88 inside the while loop at line 42. Before the fix, each iteration at line 44 indexes ps_dpb_cmds->as_mmc_params[j] and writes u4_mmco at line 45, with no bound check against the array size. The loop terminates only when u4_mmco equals END_OF_MMCO, so a crafted bitstream with many MMCO commands drives j beyond the as_mmc_params array capacity, and line 90 stores the oversized count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked increment of j causes writes through ps_mmc_params at line 45 to fall outside as_mmc_params, which is an out-of-bounds write on a memory buffer, matching CWE-119. The root cause is the missing length constraint before indexing, not a separate type-confusion or integer-overflow issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled MMCO count from the bitstream is used as an array index without validating j against MAX_REF_BUFS. Trigger: a crafted H.264 media file with more MMCO commands than as_mmc_params can hold. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes to memory adjacent to the dpb_commands structure, leading to memory corruption and potential code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13040/MPTCP: Clean up printing DSS suboption.

Do the length checking inline; that means we print stuff up to the point
at which we run out of option data.

First check to make sure we have at least 4 bytes of option, so we have
flags to check.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kim Gwan Yeong.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!(opt_len == 12 && flags & TH_SYN) &&'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!(opt_len == 12 && (flags & TH_SYN)) &&']}
description: The MPTCP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-mptcp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: Length gate: accepts opt only when opt_len is 12 (SYN) or 20 (SYN|ACK), otherwise returns 0; this is the bound that must precede any access.
After the gate, mpc->sub_ver is read and printed without re-verifying opt_len against the struct size; the option is cast from raw packet bytes at line 5.
When opt_len==20, EXTRACT_64BITS reads sender_key and receiver_key via mpc fields, consuming bytes whose availability depends solely on the earlier length check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading data past the end of the intended option buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) because only reads occur, and not CWE-190 since the defect is a missing bound check on access, not arithmetic overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts opt_len to bound accesses to the mp_capable structure but reads fields (sub_ver, sender_key, receiver_key) through a raw cast without confirming the buffer actually provides the bytes implied by that length. Trigger: a crafted MPTCP option where opt_len passes the 12/20 gate but the captured option data is shorter, so the 64-bit key extraction at line 15/17 reads beyond the option buffer. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of packet memory (disclosed by the reporter as buffer over-read), potentially leaking adjacent bytes or crashing.

commit_msg:
Limit max username/password size in SSecurityPlain.

Setting the limit to 1024 which should be still more than enough.

Unlimited ulen and plen can cause various security problems:
  * Overflow in `is->checkNoWait(ulen + plen)` causing it to contine when there is not enough data and then wait forever.
  * Overflow in `new char[plen + 1]` that would allocate zero sized array which succeeds but returns pointer that should not be written into.
  * Allocation failure in `new char[plen + 1]` from trying to allocate too much and crashing the whole server.

All those issues can be triggered by a client before authentication.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (ulen > MaxSaneUsernameLength)', '      throw AuthFailureException("Too long username");', '', '    if (plen > MaxSanePasswordLength)', '      throw AuthFailureException("Too long password");', '']}
description: In TigerVNC 1.7.1 (SSecurityPlain.cxx SSecurityPlain::processMsg), unauthenticated users can crash the server by sending long usernames.

code_evidence: ulen and plen are read directly from the client-controlled input stream as 32-bit values with no range or sanity check before use.
ulen + plen is used to size a checkNoWait call; an overflowing sum can pass the check even though insufficient data is buffered, leading to a blocking wait.
plen + 1 and ulen + 1 size new[] allocations; an overflowing or oversized value can yield a zero-length allocation or an allocation failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts client-supplied length metadata and fails to validate that it has the required bounded properties before processing, which is exactly improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing constraint on ulen/plen is the cause; the resulting hangs and crashes are consequences.

evidence_lines.code:
ulen = is->readU32();
plen = is->readU32();

if (!is->checkNoWait(ulen + plen))
return false;

pw = new char[plen + 1];
uname = new char[ulen + 1];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length fields ulen and plen are consumed from an unauthenticated client and used in arithmetic and allocation without upper-bound validation. A client can send very large lengths, triggering integer overflow in ulen + plen (checkNoWait passes incorrectly, then readBytes blocks) or in plen + 1 (zero-size allocation written past), or causing allocation failure that crashes the server.

commit_msg: fixed #2327
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgf_list_insert(ptr->local_access_entries, ae, i);', '\t\t\tgf_list_insert(ptr->global_access_entries, ae, i);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgf_list_add(ptr->local_access_entries, ae);', '\t\t\tgf_list_add(ptr->global_access_entries, ae);']}
description: GPAC version 2.1-DEV-rev505-gb9577e6ad-master was discovered to contain a memory leak via the afrt_box_read function at box_code_adobe.c.

code_evidence: For each local entry, gf_malloc allocates a GF_AfraEntry (line 15) and it is inserted into ptr->local_access_entries with gf_list_insert at index i (line 17).
Similarly, for each global entry, gf_malloc allocates a GF_GlobalAfraEntry (line 32) and it is inserted via gf_list_insert at index i (line 34).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function allocates memory that becomes untracked when gf_list_insert does not store it, so it is never released. This is a missing release of memory after effective lifetime, not a use-after-free or buffer overflow, since the defect is the lost pointer to live allocated memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop calls gf_malloc for each entry and then inserts the pointer with gf_list_insert at a fixed index. When the index is already occupied or out of range, the new allocation may not be retained in the list, so the pointer to the freshly allocated entry is lost and never freed, leaking memory. The trigger is a malformed afra box with a crafted entry_count/global_entry_count causing list insertion at invalid positions; the supported consequence is memory exhaustion (DoS) over repeated parsing.

commit_msg:
core: set again TLS verification functions after GnuTLS options are changed (closes #1763)

When changing the options weechat.network.gnutls_ca_system or
weechat.network.gnutls_ca_user, the GnuTLS credentials are freed then allocated
again, but the verification function used to check the certificate on
connection is not set again.

As a consequence, any TLS connection is made without checking the certificate.

This regression was introduced in version 3.2, when the options were changed to
automatically load system certificates without having to give the path, and to
let user give an extra custom path with certificates.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        gnutls_certificate_allocate_credentials (&gnutls_xcred);', '#if LIBGNUTLS_VERSION_NUMBER >= 0x02090a /* 2.9.10 */', '        gnutls_certificate_set_verify_function (gnutls_xcred,', '                                                &hook_connect_gnutls_verify_certificates);', '#endif /* LIBGNUTLS_VERSION_NUMBER >= 0x02090a */', '#if LIBGNUTLS_VERSION_NUMBER >= 0x020b00 /* 2.11.0 */', '        gnutls_certificate_set_retrieve_function (gnutls_xcred,', '                                                  &hook_connect_gnutls_set_certificates);', '#else', '        gnutls_certificate_client_set_retrieve_function (gnutls_xcred,', '                                                         &hook_connect_gnutls_set_certificates);', '#endif /* LIBGNUTLS_VERSION_NUMBER >= 0x020b00 */'], 'added_lines': ['        network_allocate_credentials ();']}
description: WeeChat (aka Wee Enhanced Environment for Chat) 3.2 to 3.4 before 3.4.1 does not properly verify the TLS certificate of the server, after certain GnuTLS options are changed, which allows man-in-the-middle attackers to spoof a TLS chat server via an arbitrary certificate. NOTE: this only affects situations where weechat.network.gnutls_ca_system or weechat.network.gnutls_ca_user is changed without a WeeChat restart.

code_evidence: After allocating the GnuTLS credentials into gnutls_xcred, the code loads CA files and then registers the certificate verification callback via gnutls_certificate_set_verify_function.
It also registers the client certificate retrieve callback (version-gated gnutls_certificate_set_retrieve_function or gnutls_certificate_client_set_retrieve_function).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the site where certificate validation is wired to the GnuTLS credentials; failing to preserve that binding leaves certificates unvalidated, which is exactly CWE-295. This is missing validation, not merely a trust-store path issue (CWE-296/297).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The credentials object is allocated and configured here; the verification callback is what enforces certificate checking on each connection. If credentials are later reallocated (e.g. after gnutls_ca_system/user options change) without re-registering this verify function, the connection proceeds with no certificate validation, allowing an attacker to present an arbitrary certificate and spoof the TLS server.

description: A type confusion vulnerability in the merge_param() function of php_http_params.c in PHP's pecl-http extension 3.1.0beta2 (PHP 7) and earlier as well as 2.6.0beta2 (PHP 5) and earlier allows attackers to crash PHP and possibly execute arbitrary code via crafted HTTP requests.

code_evidence: At line 40 ptr is checked as IS_ARRAY and line 41 rebinds ptr to the "value" entry, so ptr may no longer be an array. The while loop at 45-46 iterates over zdata_ptr, and line 48 only confirms test_ptr is an array before assuming ptr is still an array.
Lines 50 and 58 dereference Z_ARRVAL_PP(ptr) without re-checking ptr's type; the fix adds Z_TYPE_PP(ptr) == IS_ARRAY to the line 48 guard.
The else branch at 72-74 handles ptr not being an array by destroying and re-initializing it, showing the code expects a non-array ptr while the array branch assumes an array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code accesses a zval using array macros without verifying its type, i.e. it handles a value as a different type than it is. This is incorrect type conversion/interpretation, matching CWE-704, rather than a memory-safety CWE that only describes the downstream effect.

evidence_lines.code:
if (Z_TYPE_PP(ptr) == IS_ARRAY
&&SUCCESS == zend_hash_find(Z_ARRVAL_PP(ptr), "value", sizeof("value"), (void *) &ptr)
&&SUCCESS == zend_hash_get_current_data(Z_ARRVAL_PP(zdata_ptr), (void *) &zdata_ptr)
while (Z_TYPE_PP(zdata_ptr) == IS_ARRAY
&&SUCCESS == zend_hash_get_current_data(Z_ARRVAL_PP(zdata_ptr), (void *) &test_ptr)
if (Z_TYPE_PP(test_ptr) == IS_ARRAY) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop treats ptr as an array after it was rebound to an arbitrary value from the hash. Trigger: crafted HTTP params where the "value" entry is a non-array but zdata contains nested arrays. Consequence: Z_ARRVAL_PP on a non-array zval causes type confusion, crashing PHP or potentially enabling code execution.

commit_msg:
When a client has a USB device attached over IP, the vhci_hcd driver is
locally leaking a socket pointer address via the

/sys/devices/platform/vhci_hcd/status file (world-readable) and in debug
output when "usbip --debug port" is run.

Fix it to not leak. The socket pointer address is not used at the moment
and it was made visible as a convenient way to find IP address from socket
pointer address by looking up /proc/net/{tcp,tcp6}.

As this opens a security hole, the fix replaces socket pointer address with
sockfd.

Reported-by: Secunia Research <vuln@secunia.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <shuahkh@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t*out += sprintf(*out, "%16p %s",', '\t\t\t\t      vdev->ud.tcp_socket,'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t*out += sprintf(*out, "%u %s",', '\t\t\t\t      vdev->ud.sockfd,']}
description: The vhci_hcd driver in the Linux Kernel before version 4.14.8 and 4.4.114 allows allows local attackers to disclose kernel memory addresses. Successful exploitation requires that a USB device is attached over IP.

code_evidence: When the vdev is in VDEV_ST_USED, line 12 formats vdev->ud.tcp_socket with %16p into the caller-provided *out buffer; line 13 supplies the raw socket pointer and line 14 appends the device name. This status text is written to the world-readable vhci_hcd status file.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly inserts sensitive internal state (a socket pointer address) into an accessible status resource, matching CWE-200's exposure of sensitive information to unauthorized actors. The weakness is the deliberate emission of the pointer, not a downstream confidentiality impact from another flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the status formatter writes a kernel pointer (vdev->ud.tcp_socket) into an output buffer that is exposed through a world-readable sysfs file. Trigger: a USB device is attached over IP so the vdev status is VDEV_ST_USED; any local reader of the status file then receives the pointer. Consequence: disclosure of a kernel/socket address, aiding address-dependent attacks; the pointer is not needed for the file's purpose.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int new_mark_index = mark_index + (mark->end - mark->beg - 1);'], 'added_lines': ['    int new_mark_index = mark_index + (mark->end - mark->beg - n);']}
description: md4c before 0.2.5 has a heap-based buffer overflow because md_split_simple_pairing_mark mishandles splits.

code_evidence: Line 5 computes new_mark_index as mark_index + (mark->end - mark->beg - 1), independent of the split size n, then line 6 forms a pointer into ctx->marks at that index without any bounds check against the marks array capacity.
Line 9 memcpy's a full MD_MARK into dummy, and lines 10-11 mutate mark->end and dummy->beg, writing through the unchecked pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes a full MD_MARK structure through a pointer whose index is not validated against the marks array bounds, which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is the write-side consequence of the incorrect index arithmetic, not merely an integer or bounds-calculation defect.

evidence_lines.code:
mark->end -= n;
dummy->beg = mark->end;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The dummy mark index is derived from a constant offset of -1 instead of the actual split distance n, so when the mark is split and later split again, the computed index can exceed the allocated marks array. The unchecked pointer at line 6 and the memcpy at line 9 then write past the end of the heap buffer, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: fixed #1568
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttmp_strsize =(u32)ptr->size-8;'], 'added_lines': ['\ttmp_strsize =(u32)ptr->size;']}
description: An issue was discovered in gpac before 1.0.1. The abst_box_read function in box_code_adobe.c has a heap-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: Line 18 guards only ptr->size<8, then line 19 computes tmp_strsize=(u32)ptr->size-8, so the buffer allocated at line 20 is 8 bytes smaller than ptr->size. The copy loop (lines 23-30) is bounded by tmp_strsize, not by the allocation, and ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE only decrements ptr->size by 1 per iteration; once tmp_strsize iterations exceed the allocation, tmp_str[i] at line 25 writes/reads past the malloc'd buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads/writes tmp_str beyond its malloc'd extent because the loop bound is derived from an unchecked box size rather than the allocation size, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not merely an integer overflow: the size arithmetic directly yields an under-sized buffer relative to the loop's read range.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size (ptr->size-8) is decoupled from the loop bound, which uses the same decremented counter but the loop can continue reading bytes while the buffer was sized for fewer bytes than ptr->size. Trigger: a crafted abst box whose declared size exceeds the actual remaining data, making the size-driven loop read gf_bs_read_u8 past the allocated tmp_str. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read (and write into tmp_str) leading to crash or memory disclosure.

Trigger: a long input line (or multibyte UTF-8 sequences) causes j to reach or exceed sizeof(szLineConv); the writes at lines 48 and 51 then write past the array, corrupting stack memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!test_bit(KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, &key->flags)) {', '\t\tkey->reject_error = -error;', '\t\tsmp_wmb();', '\t\tset_bit(KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE, &key->flags);', '\t\tset_bit(KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, &key->flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (key->state == KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED) {', '\t\tmark_key_instantiated(key, -error);']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.13.10 does not correctly synchronize the actions of updating versus finding a key in the "negative" state to avoid a race condition, which allows local users to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.

code_evidence: Under key_construction_mutex, the function tests KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, then writes reject_error and sets NEGATIVE and INSTANTIATED bits with only smp_wmb() ordering. The state is spread across separate flags and a unioned error field, so a concurrent reader without the semaphore can observe a rejected state and then read a payload that is no longer the error code.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 is discouraged here: the flaw is a synchronization/race defect (state and error updated non-atomically), not missing validation of attacker-supplied input. The function does not validate an input field; it mishandles concurrent state, so the target CWE is not directly supported.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: instantiation state and rejection error are stored in separate, non-atomic locations, so readers can interleave between the state check and the error/payload read. Trigger: a local user races key rejection/instantiation against key lookup. Consequence: observing an inconsistent key state yields a wrong payload value, causing denial of service or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
crypto: ccm - move cbcmac input off the stack

Commit f15f05b0a5de ("crypto: ccm - switch to separate cbcmac driver")
refactored the CCM driver to allow separate implementations of the
underlying MAC to be provided by a platform. However, in doing so, it
moved some data from the linear region to the stack, which violates the
SG constraints when the stack is virtually mapped.

So move idata/odata back to the request ctx struct, of which we can
reasonably expect that it has been allocated using kmalloc() et al.

Reported-by: Johannes Berg <johannes@sipsolutions.net>
Fixes: f15f05b0a5de ("crypto: ccm - switch to separate cbcmac driver")
Signed-off-by: Ard Biesheuvel <ard.biesheuvel@linaro.org>
Tested-by: Johannes Berg <johannes@sipsolutions.net>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tu8 odata[16];', '\tu8 idata[16];'], 'added_lines': ['\tu8 *odata = pctx->odata;', '\tu8 *idata = pctx->idata;']}
description: crypto/ccm.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x and 4.10.x through 4.10.12 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

code_evidence: odata and idata are fixed 16-byte stack arrays passed into sg_set_buf, so their addresses enter a scatterlist consumed by the MAC driver.
format_input writes the 16-byte control block into odata, and format_adata writes assoclen-derived data into idata before sg_set_buf(&sg[1], idata, ilen).
memset(idata, 0, ilen) and sg_set_buf(&sg[0], idata, ilen) reuse the stack buffer as padding.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function hands stack buffers to scatterlist/DMA operations whose contiguity assumptions they may not satisfy, producing out-of-bounds memory access on the mapped stack region, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer operation. The root cause is the stack placement, not a length miscalculation.

evidence_lines.code:
u8 odata[16];
u8 idata[16];

sg_set_buf(&sg[0], odata, 16);
sg_set_buf(&sg[1], idata, ilen);

memset(idata, 0, ilen);
sg_set_buf(&sg[0], idata, ilen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: stack-allocated buffers are used as DMA scatterlist sources. With CONFIG_VMAP_STACK, a stack buffer can span more than one virtual page, violating scatterlist/DMA assumptions; the driver then operates on memory outside the intended contiguous buffer, causing crash or memory corruption. Trigger: any CCM auth request processed on a virtually mapped stack.

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: correct SH_LINEAR mapping detection in sh_guess_wrmap()

The fix for XSA-243 / CVE-2017-15592 (c/s bf2b4eadcf379) introduced a change
in behaviour for sh_guest_wrmap(), where it had to cope with no shadow linear
mapping being present.

As the name suggests, guest_vtable is a mapping of the guests pagetable, not
Xen's pagetable, meaning that it isn't the pagetable we need to check for the
shadow linear slot in.

The practical upshot is that a shadow HVM vcpu which switches into 4-level
paging mode, with an L4 pagetable that contains a mapping which aliases Xen's
SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START will fool the safety check for whether a SHADOW_LINEAR
mapping is present.  As the check passes (when it should have failed), Xen
subsequently falls over the missing mapping with a pagefault such as:

    (XEN) Pagetable walk from ffff8140a0503880:
    (XEN)  L4[0x102] = 000000046c218063 ffffffffffffffff
    (XEN)  L3[0x102] = 000000046c218063 ffffffffffffffff
    (XEN)  L2[0x102] = 000000046c218063 ffffffffffffffff
    (XEN)  L1[0x103] = 0000000000000000 ffffffffffffffff

This is part of XSA-243.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* Is a shadow linear map is installed in the first place? */', '    sl4p  = v->arch.paging.shadow.guest_vtable;', '    sl4p += shadow_l4_table_offset(SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START);', '    if ( !(shadow_l4e_get_flags(*sl4p) & _PAGE_PRESENT) )', '        return 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    /*', '     * Non-external guests (i.e. PV) have a SHADOW_LINEAR mapping from the', '     * moment their shadows are created.  External guests (i.e. HVM) may not,', '     * but always have a regular linear mapping, which we can use to observe', '     * whether a SHADOW_LINEAR mapping is present.', '     */', '    if ( paging_mode_external(d) )', '    {', '        sl4p =  __linear_l4_table + l4_linear_offset(SH_LINEAR_PT_VIRT_START);', '        if ( !(shadow_l4e_get_flags(*sl4p) & _PAGE_PRESENT) )', '            return 0;', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 HVM guest OS users to cause a denial of service (hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges because self-linear shadow mappings are mishandled for translated guests.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's flaw is a wrong pagetable used for a shadow-linear-mapping presence check, leading to a hypervisor page fault; this is a missing/incorrect validation issue, not exposure of a resource to the wrong control sphere as required by CWE-668.

description: In LibRaw, there is an out-of-bounds read vulnerability within the "LibRaw::parseSonySRF()" function (libraw\src\metadata\sony.cpp) when processing srf files.

code_evidence: entries is read via sget2(cbuf_SR2) before any length check against SR2SubIFDLength; the only guard is entries > 1000.
case 0x7300 reads four 16-bit values at cbuf_SR2 + tag_dataoffset + tag_dataunitlen*c with no bounds check on tag_dataoffset or tag_dataunitlen.
case 0x74a0 passes cbuf_SR2 + tag_dataoffset to sgetreal without verifying tag_dataoffset + 4 <= SR2SubIFDLength.
case 0x7800 indexes cbuf_SR2 + tag_dataoffset + tag_dataunitlen*(i*3+c) up to index 8 without bounds validation.
case 0x787f reads three values at tag_dataoffset + tag_dataunitlen*c without checking the buffer extent.
WB case 0x7480 reads three values at tag_dataoffset + tag_dataunitlen*c with no check.
WB case 0x7480 else-branch reads three values at tag_dataoffset + tag_dataunitlen*c with no check.
case 0x7302 reads four values at tag_dataoffset + tag_dataunitlen*c without verifying the offset/length against the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences pointers derived from file metadata without an upper-bound check, so it reads beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. The weakness is a read overrun rather than an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), since sget2/sgetreal only consume data.

ilm.MaxAp4MaxFocal = sgetreal(tag_type, cbuf_SR2 + tag_dataoffset);
