commit_msg: opj_j2k_write_sot(): fix potential write heap buffer overflow (#991)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (! opj_j2k_write_sot(p_j2k, p_data, &l_current_nb_bytes_written, p_stream,'], 'added_lines': ['    if (! opj_j2k_write_sot(p_j2k, p_data, p_total_data_size,', '                            &l_current_nb_bytes_written, p_stream,']}
description: A size-validation issue was discovered in opj_j2k_write_sot in lib/openjp2/j2k.c in OpenJPEG 2.2.0. The vulnerability causes an out-of-bounds write, which may lead to remote denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow affecting opj_write_bytes_LE in lib/openjp2/cio.c) or possibly remote code execution. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-14152.

code_evidence: opj_j2k_write_sot is invoked without passing p_total_data_size, so the SOT writer has no knowledge of the remaining buffer capacity before writing the 12-byte SOT marker segment.

After the SOT write, p_data is advanced by l_current_nb_bytes_written and p_total_data_size is reduced; subsequent writers (e.g., POC at [45]) receive this reduced size, but the SOT call itself was unchecked against capacity.
opj_j2k_write_sod is passed p_total_data_size, showing the size-aware pattern that the SOT call lacks; an undersized p_data buffer causes SOD/SOT writes to overrun.
opj_write_bytes(l_begin_data + 6, l_nb_bytes_written, 4) writes the accumulated tile-part length into the buffer without validating that the buffer was large enough.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing size argument allows writes past the end of the intended output buffer. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) since the affected writes modify memory beyond the allocated region.

evidence_lines.code:
p_data += l_current_nb_bytes_written;
p_total_data_size -= l_current_nb_bytes_written;

opj_write_bytes(l_begin_data + 6, l_nb_bytes_written,
4);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SOT segment writer is called without the total data size, so it cannot bound-check its writes against the destination buffer. Trigger: an encoder path where the allocated tile-part buffer is smaller than the SOT/SOD output. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds write in opj_write_bytes_LE, leading to memory corruption, DoS, or possible code execution.

Use the proper dest_size in various g_strlcpy calls.

Lines 30-34 copy name into member_object->member_name using long_number < 256 ? long_number : 256 as the destination size, not the actual buffer size of member_name.
Lines 35-38 perform the same copy into mutable_mapping->member_name with the same attacker-influenced size expression.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: g_strlcpy with an incorrect size bound writes past the end of member_name/mutable_mapping->member_name heap buffers, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. The root cause is the missing sizeof-based constraint on the destination size, not merely an integer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
long_number = tvb_get_guint32(tvb, offset_tmp, encoding);
name = tvb_get_string_enc(wmem_packet_scope(), tvb, offset_tmp+4, long_number, ENC_ASCII);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The destination size passed to g_strlcpy is derived from the packet's long_number field rather than sizeof the destination buffer. When long_number is smaller than the destination buffer but larger than the actual allocated member_name size, g_strlcpy writes up to long_number bytes into member_name, overflowing the heap allocation. The attacker controls the RTPS packet length, triggering a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg: fixed #2173
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (nalu_size<2) return GF_NON_COMPLIANT_BITSTREAM;']}
description: gp_rtp_builder_do_hevc in ietf/rtp_pck_mpeg4.c in GPAC 2.0.0 has a heap-based buffer over-read, as demonstrated by MP4Box.

code_evidence: With use_AP and an empty packet, lines 31-32 read nalu[0] and nalu[1] without checking that nalu_size is at least 2.
In the fragmentation branch, line 74 computes bytesLeft = nalu_size - 2 and line 75 sets offset = 2, assuming a NAL header of two bytes exists; lines 84-87 then read nalu[0] and nalu[1] again.
A nalu_size of 0 or 1 makes these accesses read past the end of the nalu buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads beyond the intended nalu buffer via unchecked indexing; the missing length constraint is the cause, and the out-of-bounds read is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
builder->hevc_payload_hdr[0] = nalu[0];
builder->hevc_payload_hdr[1] = (RTP_VVC_AGG_NAL << 3) | (nalu[1] & 0x7);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences nalu[0] and nalu[1] (and derives bytesLeft/offset from nalu_size-2) without enforcing nalu_size >= 2. Trigger: a caller supplies a NAL unit shorter than the 2-byte header. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read, potentially crashing or exposing adjacent memory.

Prevent negative array index for selectnumber and textareanumber

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/12 [CVE-2016-9424]
Origin: https://anonscm.debian.org/cgit/collab-maint/w3m.git/commit/?id=a25fd09f74fb83499396935a96d63bb7cb8e2c58

description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-31. w3m doesn't properly validate the value of tag attribute, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap buffer overflow crash) and possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: HTML_TEXTAREA_INT: parsedtag_get_value writes into n_textarea from ATTR_TEXTAREANUMBER; the guard only checks n_textarea < max_textarea, so a negative value passes and textarea_str[n_textarea] is written out of bounds.
HTML_SELECT_INT: same pattern for n_select from ATTR_SELECTNUMBER; n_select < max_select permits negatives and select_option[n_select] is indexed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lower-bound check leads to an out-of-bounds array access, directly matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer. The negative-index root cause is the cause; the resulting heap overflow is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The tag attribute value is parsed into a signed index and only upper-bounded. A crafted HTML tag supplying a negative number passes the check, causing an out-of-bounds write to textarea_str[] or select_option[]; the heap buffer overflow can crash or corrupt memory.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 0 + 1, depth, error, 7, 16);', '        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 1 - 1, depth, error, 3, 16);', '        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 1 + 0, depth, error, 5, 16);', '        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 1 + 1, depth, error, 1, 16);'], 'added_lines': ['        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 0 + 1, depth, error, 7, 16, width * height);', '        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 1 - 1, depth, error, 3, 16, width * height);', '        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 1 + 0, depth, error, 5, 16, width * height);', '        error_diffuse(data, pos + width * 1 + 1, depth, error, 1, 16, width * height);']}
description: libsixel before 1.10 is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow in libsixel/src/quant.c:867.

code_evidence: pos is computed as y*width+x, then four error_diffuse calls write at pos+1, pos+width-1, pos+width, and pos+width+1. The guard only checks x<width-1 && y<height-1, so the diagonal/right and bottom writes are bounded only when the neighbor indices stay inside the allocated data buffer; the old calls passed no buffer-size limit, so error_diffuse could write past the end of data when pos+width+1 reaches width*height.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds width*height as an explicit size argument to each error_diffuse call, indicating the writes at pos+width+1 and related offsets could exceed the allocated buffer. That is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), not merely an off-by-one read or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the diffusion helper is invoked with computed neighbor offsets but without the total buffer size, and the boundary condition does not itself clamp those offsets to width*height. Trigger: processing a pixel near the right or bottom edge where the computed neighbor index equals or exceeds width*height. Consequence: error_diffuse writes past the end of the data buffer, corrupting memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
[sipmsgops] fix codec_delete_XX() parsing (2)

Issue discovered during OpenSIPS Security Audit 2021,
	by Alfred Farrugia & Sandro Gauci (Enable Security)

https://github.com/OpenSIPS/opensips/security/advisories/GHSA-67w7-g4j8-3wcx
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tend++;'], 'added_lines': ["\tif ( *end == '\\n')", '\t\tend++;']}
description:
OpenSIPS is a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) server implementation. Prior to versions 3.1.7 and 3.2.4, OpenSIPS crashes when a malformed SDP body is received and is processed by the `delete_sdp_line` function in the sipmsgops module. This issue can be reproduced by calling the function with an SDP body that does not terminate by a line feed (i.e. `\n`).

The vulnerability was found while performing black-box fuzzing against an OpenSIPS server running a configuration that made use of the functions `codec_delete_except_re` and `codec_delete_re`. The same issue was also discovered while performing coverage guided fuzzing on the function `codec_delete_except_re`. The crash happens because the function `delete_sdp_line` expects that an SDP line is terminated by a line feed (`\n`).

By abusing this vulnerability, an attacker is able to crash the server. It affects configurations containing functions that rely on the affected code, such as the function `codec_delete_except_re`. Due to the sanity check that is performed in the `del_lump` function, exploitation of this issue will generate an `abort` in the lumps processing function, resulting in a Denial of Service. This issue is patched in versions 3.1.7 and 3.2.4.

code_evidence: The forward scan stops at '\n' or at stream->body.s+stream->body.len, but line 13 unconditionally increments end past the buffer end when no terminating line feed exists, so end can point one byte beyond the SDP body.
Line 14 passes end - start as the lump length to del_lump without checking that the scanned line was actually '\n'-terminated, so an unterminated body yields a length that extends past valid data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate that the input line has the required terminating property before deriving the length passed to del_lump, matching CWE-20's missing input-property validation with availability impact. This is a validation gap, not a transform/encoding issue.

evidence_lines.code: if( del_lump(msg, start - msg->buf, end - start,0) == NULL )

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes every SDP line ends with '\n' and advances end unconditionally after the bounded scan. Trigger: a malformed SDP body whose last line lacks a trailing line feed. The derived lump length then exceeds the body, and del_lump's sanity check aborts, crashing the server (DoS).

commit_msg:
MSG_CTRUNC indicates that we have received fewer fds that we should
have done because the buffer was too small, but we were treating it
as though it indicated that we received *no* fds. If we received any,
we still have to make sure we close them, otherwise they will be leaked.

On the system bus, if an attacker can induce us to leak fds in this
way, that's a local denial of service via resource exhaustion.

Reported-by: Kevin Backhouse, GitHub Security Lab
Fixes: dbus#294
Fixes: CVE-2020-12049
Fixes: GHSL-2020-057
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      if (m.msg_flags & MSG_CTRUNC)', '        {', '          /* Hmm, apparently the control data was truncated. The bad', '             thing is that we might have completely lost a couple of fds', "             without chance to recover them. Hence let's treat this as a", '             serious error. */', '', '          errno = ENOSPC;', '          _dbus_string_set_length (buffer, start);', '          return -1;', '        }', ''], 'added_lines': ['      if (m.msg_flags & MSG_CTRUNC)', '        {', '          unsigned int i;', '', '          /* Hmm, apparently the control data was truncated. The bad', '             thing is that we might have completely lost a couple of fds', "             without chance to recover them. Hence let's treat this as a", '             serious error. */', '', '          /* We still need to close whatever fds we *did* receive,', "           * otherwise they'll never get closed. (CVE-2020-12049) */", '          for (i = 0; i < *n_fds; i++)', '            close (fds[i]);', '', '          *n_fds = 0;', '          errno = ENOSPC;', '          _dbus_string_set_length (buffer, start);', '          return -1;', '        }', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in dbus >= 1.3.0 before 1.12.18. The DBusServer in libdbus, as used in dbus-daemon, leaks file descriptors when a message exceeds the per-message file descriptor limit. A local attacker with access to the D-Bus system bus or another system service's private AF_UNIX socket could use this to make the system service reach its file descriptor limit, denying service to subsequent D-Bus clients.

code_evidence: On MSG_CTRUNC the code immediately sets errno, truncates the buffer and returns -1 without inspecting or closing any SCM_RIGHTS file descriptors that recvmsg already installed into the control buffer.

The SCM_RIGHTS parsing loop (and the memcpy into fds) that would have identified received fds runs only after the MSG_CTRUNC branch, so on truncation the descriptors in m.msg_control are never copied out or closed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failing to release an allocated resource on all paths. Here file descriptors already received are not closed on the truncation return path, matching improper resource release leading to resource-consumption DoS rather than a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the MSG_CTRUNC early-return path abandons the control message before the SCM_RIGHTS descriptors it contains are extracted or closed. Trigger: a local peer sends a message whose ancillary fd data is truncated (e.g. exceeds the per-message fd limit), causing recvmsg to set MSG_CTRUNC. Consequence: the received descriptors remain open in the service, leaking them until the fd limit is exhausted and further D-Bus clients are denied service.

commit_msg:
USB HID: Fix a memory leak.

Replace mismatched g_strdup() + g_free()s with
wmem_strdup_printf(wmem_packet_scope(), ...). Fixes #17124.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    g_free(str);', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: Memory leak in USB HID dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 to 3.4.2 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: Line 6 declares str as NULL; in the USAGE branch with bSize 1 or 2, line 17 assigns str = get_usage_page_item_string(...), an allocated string used only for formatting at lines 18-19.

The function then advances offset (line 63) and, in the before version, frees str at line 64 before returning; the patch removes this unconditional free, so the allocated string's ownership passes to wmem_packet_scope() allocation rather than being leaked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 matches because allocated memory is not released after its effective lifetime, causing resource consumption/DoS. This is a memory-management lifetime issue, not a buffer over-read or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pre-patch code mixed g_strdup()-style allocation with g_free() and, per the commit, mismatched the allocation/free pairing. Trigger: parsing a crafted USB HID report-local Usage item with bSize 1 or 2 repeatedly allocates str. Consequence: unreleased memory accumulates per packet, enabling memory-exhaustion denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix #73832 - leave the table in a safe state if the size is too big.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tht->nTableSize = zend_hash_check_size(nSize);'], 'added_lines': ['\tht->nTableSize = zend_hash_check_size(nSize);']}
description: Zend/zend_hash.c in PHP before 7.0.15 and 7.1.x before 7.1.1 mishandles certain cases that require large array allocations, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (integer overflow, uninitialized memory access, and use of arbitrary destructor function pointers) via crafted serialized data.

code_evidence: ht->nTableSize is computed from the caller-supplied nSize via zend_hash_check_size(nSize) and stored directly into the table size field.
The size-derived value is assigned while the table is being initialized; the destructor pDestructor is installed on the same table, so a corrupted size can later affect bucket access and destruction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow in the size computation that determines allocation size, matching CWE-190's core pattern of a calculation producing a wrapped value used as an allocation/index bound. The uninitialized-memory and destructor-pointer consequences are downstream effects of that overflow, not a separate weakness class.

evidence_lines.code: ht->pDestructor = pDestructor;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nSize is a uint32_t passed to zend_hash_check_size, and the resulting table size is trusted as the basis for allocation and bucket indexing. When crafted serialized data drives a very large nSize, the size computation can overflow/wrap, yielding a too-small or inconsistent table size. Subsequent bucket writes then access memory outside the allocation, corrupting destructor function pointers and enabling arbitrary code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
Fix yet another buffer overflow in the braille table parser

Reported by Henri Salo

Fixes #593
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar pattern[MAXSTRING];'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar pattern[MAXSTRING + 1];']}
description: Liblouis 3.5.0 has a stack-based Buffer Overflow in the function compileHyphenation in compileTranslationTable.c.

code_evidence: The local stack buffer `pattern[MAXSTRING]` is declared with exactly MAXSTRING bytes, leaving no room beyond the valid indices.
In the loop over `hyph.chars`, each non-digit character increments `j` and writes `pattern[++j] = '0'` at the new index; `j` grows with the token length without any bound check against MAXSTRING.
After the loop, `pattern[j + 1] = 0` writes a terminator one byte past the last pattern slot, and `word.chars[j] = 0` similarly depends on the unchecked length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes one byte beyond the end of the stack buffer `pattern` due to a missing length constraint, which is precisely an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The off-by-one buffer sizing is the enabling cause, but the observed unsafe operation is the write past the intended buffer, matching the target CWE rather than a mere array-size defect.

evidence_lines.code: char pattern[MAXSTRING];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pattern array is sized MAXSTRING but the parser indexes it with an unbounded counter derived from attacker-controlled token length, then writes a NUL at j+1. Trigger: a hyphenation table line whose parsed characters push j to MAXSTRING-1 or beyond. Consequence: a stack-based out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent locals such as the following state variables and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
We currently split the close into two, in case we have a ->flush op
that we can't safely handle from non-blocking context. This requires
us to flag the op as uncancelable if we do need to punt it async, and
that means special handling for just this op type.

Use __close_fd_get_file() and grab the files lock so we can get the file
and check if we need to go async in one atomic operation. That gets rid
of the need for splitting this into two steps, and hence the need for
IO_WQ_WORK_NO_CANCEL.

Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* might be already done during nonblock submission */', '\tif (!close->put_file) {', '\t\tret = close_fd_get_file(close->fd, &close->put_file);', '\t\tif (ret < 0)', '\t\t\treturn (ret == -ENOENT) ? -EBADF : ret;', '\tif (close->put_file->f_op->flush && force_nonblock) {', '\t\t/* not safe to cancel at this point */', '\t\treq->work.flags |= IO_WQ_WORK_NO_CANCEL;', '\t\t/* was never set, but play safe */', '\t\treq->flags &= ~REQ_F_NOWAIT;', "\t\t/* avoid grabbing files - we don't need the files */", '\t\treq->flags |= REQ_F_NO_FILE_TABLE;', '\tret = filp_close(close->put_file, req->work.identity->files);', '\tfput(close->put_file);', '\tclose->put_file = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct files_struct *files = current->files;', '\tstruct fdtable *fdt;', '\tstruct file *file;', '\tfile = NULL;', '\tret = -EBADF;', '\tspin_lock(&files->file_lock);', '\tfdt = files_fdtable(files);', '\tif (close->fd >= fdt->max_fds) {', '\t\tspin_unlock(&files->file_lock);', '\t\tgoto err;', '\t}', '\tfile = fdt->fd[close->fd];', '\tif (!file) {', '\t\tspin_unlock(&files->file_lock);', '\t\tgoto err;', '\t}', '', '\tif (file->f_op == &io_uring_fops) {', '\t\tspin_unlock(&files->file_lock);', '\t\tfile = NULL;', '\t\tgoto err;', '\tif (file->f_op->flush && force_nonblock) {', '\t\tspin_unlock(&files->file_lock);', '\tret = __close_fd_get_file(close->fd, &file);', '\tspin_unlock(&files->file_lock);', '\tif (ret < 0) {', '\t\tif (ret == -ENOENT)', '\t\t\tret = -EBADF;', '\t\tgoto err;', '\t}', '', '\tret = filp_close(file, current->files);', 'err:', '\tif (file)', '\t\tfput(file);']}
description: A time-of-check to time-of-use issue exists in io_uring subsystem's IORING_OP_CLOSE operation in the Linux kernel's versions 5.6 - 5.11 (inclusive), which allows a local user to elevate their privileges to root. Introduced in b5dba59e0cf7e2cc4d3b3b1ac5fe81ddf21959eb, patched in 9eac1904d3364254d622bf2c771c4f85cd435fc2, backported to stable in 788d0824269bef539fe31a785b1517882eafed93.

code_evidence: close_fd_get_file() resolves close->fd to a struct file and stores it in close->put_file; the fd-to-file lookup is performed here, separately from later use.
Later, close->put_file->f_op->flush is dereferenced and filp_close(close->put_file, ...) is called, using the file obtained at the earlier check without re-resolving the fd under the files lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits because the resource (the fd's file) is checked/resolved and then used after a window in which its state can change, and the code lacks an atomic hold across check and use. This is the fd-to-file TOCTOU pattern, not a simple missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fd is resolved to a file object in one step (check), then the stored close->put_file is inspected for ->flush and passed to filp_close in a later step (use). Because the fd table is not held across both operations, a concurrent close/dup of the same fd can replace the file between resolution and use, so the file closed or inspected may not correspond to the fd the caller intended. Consequence: closing an unintended file, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. commit_msg:
usb: check RNDIS buffer offsets & length

When processing remote NDIS control message packets,
the USB Net device emulator uses a fixed length(4096) data buffer.
The incoming informationBufferOffset & Length combination could
overflow and cross that range. Check control message buffer
offsets and length to avoid it.

Reported-by: Qinghao Tang <luodalongde@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Message-id: 1455648821-17340-3-git-send-email-ppandit@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (bufoffs + buflen > length)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (buflen > length || bufoffs >= length || bufoffs + buflen > length) {', '    }']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the USB Net device emulator (hw/usb/dev-network.c) in QEMU before 2.5.1 allow local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (QEMU process crash) or obtain sensitive host memory information via a remote NDIS control message packet that is mishandled in the (1) rndis_query_response, (2) rndis_set_response, or (3) usb_net_handle_dataout function.

code_evidence: bufoffs is derived from the untrusted InformationBufferOffset plus 8, and buflen from the untrusted InformationBufferLength; both are attacker-controlled 32-bit fields. The only guard is the single expression 'bufoffs + buflen > length', which itself can wrap: a large bufoffs plus buflen overflowing uint32_t yields a small sum that passes the check. The check also fails to reject bufoffs >= length or buflen > length independently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The guard relies on integer addition whose overflow defeats the intended range validation, matching CWE-189 numeric errors (integer overflow). Contrast with a pure out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the defect is the overflowing calculation, not merely the indexing.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an unchecked arithmetic addition on two guest-controlled offsets used as a bounds check. When the sum wraps, the check passes and the out-of-range bufoffs/buflen are forwarded to ndis_query and later used, enabling out-of-bounds host memory access (info leak) or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix ASN1_INTEGER handling.

Only treat an ASN1_ANY type as an integer if it has the V_ASN1_INTEGER
tag: V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER is an internal only value which is never used
for on the wire encoding.

Thanks to David Benjamin <davidben@google.com> for reporting this bug.

This was found using libFuzzer.

RT#4364 (part)CVE-2016-2108.

Reviewed-by: Emilia Käsper <emilia@openssl.org>

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -16,9 +16,7 @@
         result = 0;             /* They do not have content. */
         break;
     case V_ASN1_INTEGER:
-    case V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER:
     case V_ASN1_ENUMERATED:
-    case V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED:
     case V_ASN1_BIT_STRING:
     case V_ASN1_OCTET_STRING:
     case V_ASN1_SEQUENCE:

description: The ASN.1 implementation in OpenSSL before 1.0.1o and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2c allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (buffer underflow and memory corruption) via an ANY field in crafted serialized data, aka the "negative zero" issue.

code_evidence: The switch treats V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER (line 17) and V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED (line 19) as ordinary string/integer types, though these are internal-only values never valid on the wire.
Both cases fall through to the default branch (lines 37-41), which casts the union's value.ptr to ASN1_STRING and calls ASN1_STRING_cmp on it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-119 covers operations reading/writing outside an intended buffer boundary. Here the erroneous acceptance of internal negative tags causes ASN1_STRING_cmp to process memory outside the buffer's intended bounds, matching the buffer underflow described. It is not merely a type-confusion or logic bug because the supported consequence is out-of-bounds memory access.

case V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER:
case V_ASN1_ENUMERATED:
case V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED:

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Because V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER is accepted as a valid ASN1 type, a crafted ANY field can carry this internal tag; the value is then interpreted through ASN1_STRING_cmp, whose length/data handling for the negative-zero encoding leads to a buffer underflow and memory corruption (CVE-2016-2108). commit_msg:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>

The existing implementation assumed DNS resolv callback will be
called just once, but that's not always the case (apparently,
for multi-homes hosts or something). So, apply array bounds
checking (and do pointer arithmetic only after it, as the C
standard otherwise warns of "undefined behavior"). In such a case,
the port number wasn't set in each entry too, so rework how it's
done.

The issues discovered while resolving archive.ubuntu.com.

code_evidence: ai_state.idx starts at 0 and ai_arr holds only two entries linked in advance; no bound tracking is initialized here.

commit_msg:
sg: Fix double-free when drives detach during SG_IO

In sg_common_write(), we free the block request and return -ENODEV if
the device is detached in the middle of the SG_IO ioctl().

Unfortunately, sg_finish_rem_req() also tries to free srp->rq, so we
end up freeing rq->cmd in the already free rq object, and then free
the object itself out from under the current user.

This ends up corrupting random memory via the list_head on the rq
object. The most common crash trace I saw is this:

  ------------[ cut here ]------------
  kernel BUG at block/blk-core.c:1420!
  Call Trace:
  [<ffffffff81281eab>] blk_put_request+0x5b/0x80
  [<ffffffffa0069e5b>] sg_finish_rem_req+0x6b/0x120 [sg]
  [<ffffffffa006bcb9>] sg_common_write.isra.14+0x459/0x5a0 [sg]
  [<ffffffff8125b328>] ? selinux_file_alloc_security+0x48/0x70
  [<ffffffffa006bf95>] sg_new_write.isra.17+0x195/0x2d0 [sg]
  [<ffffffffa006cef4>] sg_ioctl+0x644/0xdb0 [sg]
  [<ffffffff81170f80>] do_vfs_ioctl+0x90/0x520
  [<ffffffff81258967>] ? file_has_perm+0x97/0xb0
  [<ffffffff811714a1>] SyS_ioctl+0x91/0xb0
  [<ffffffff81602afb>] tracesys+0xdd/0xe2
    RIP [<ffffffff81281e04>] __blk_put_request+0x154/0x1a0

The solution is straightforward: just set srp->rq to NULL in the
failure branch so that sg_finish_rem_req() doesn't attempt to re-free
it.

Additionally, since sg_rq_end_io() will never be called on the object
when this happens, we need to free memory backing ->cmd if it isn't
embedded in the object itself.

KASAN was extremely helpful in finding the root cause of this bug.

Signed-off-by: Calvin Owens <calvinowens@fb.com>
Acked-by: Douglas Gilbert <dgilbert@interlog.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (srp->bio)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (srp->bio) {', '\t\t\tif (srp->rq->cmd != srp->rq->__cmd)', '\t\t\t\tkfree(srp->rq->cmd);', '', '\t\t\tsrp->rq = NULL;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: Double free vulnerability in the sg_common_write function in drivers/scsi/sg.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (memory corruption and system crash) by detaching a device during an SG_IO ioctl call.

code_evidence: On the detaching path, sg_start_req has already allocated srp->rq. When atomic_read(&sdp->detaching) is true and srp->bio is set, blk_end_request_all(srp->rq, -EIO) releases the request, but srp->rq is left pointing at the freed object. sg_finish_rem_req(srp) then operates on that same srp->rq again, re-freeing the request (and rq->cmd) and touching its list_head.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the same request object twice on one path (blk_end_request_all then sg_finish_rem_req), which is exactly CWE-415 Double Free. This is distinct from a use-after-free, since the second sg_finish_rem_req call itself performs the re-free rather than merely reading freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure branch frees the block request via blk_end_request_all without clearing srp->rq, so the subsequent sg_finish_rem_req(srp) releases the same object a second time. Trigger: a local user detaches the device during an SG_IO ioctl after sg_start_req allocated the request and bio. Supported consequence: memory corruption/double free of the request and its cmd buffer, leading to crash or potential privilege escalation.

description: ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 has a large loop vulnerability in the ReadPWPImage function in coders\pwp.c.

code_evidence: filesize is derived from attacker-controlled header bytes (magick[0..2]) at line 77, yielding a value up to 65535*255+256*255+255. The loop at line 78 iterates filesize times, reading a byte and writing it to the temp file each iteration, without any bound tied to actual remaining blob data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-834: the loop's iteration count is not sufficiently limited relative to actual data, allowing attacker-influenced excessive iteration and resource consumption. It is not merely an unchecked read; the weakness is the unbounded iteration derived from attacker-controlled size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The loop count is computed from untrusted header bytes rather than the real available input size, so a crafted file can declare a large filesize. The loop then performs up to ~16.7M read/write iterations, consuming CPU and I/O; once the blob is exhausted ReadBlobByte returns EOF repeatedly and fputc keeps writing, so iteration continues unbounded by input length.

commit_msg:
Prevent division by 0 in common shape functions.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 387712197
Change-Id: Id25c7460e35b68aeeeac23b9a88e455b443ee149
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (ndims == 0)', '      return errors::InvalidArgument(', '          "Number of dims in shape tensor must not be 0");']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions most implementations of convolution operators in TensorFlow are affected by a division by 0 vulnerability where an attacker can trigger a denial of service via a crash. The shape inference [implementation](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/core/framework/common_shape_fns.cc#L577) is missing several validations before doing divisions and modulo operations. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 8a793b5d7f59e37ac7f3cd0954a750a2fe76bad4. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: ndims is derived from shape_vec.size() and used as the divisor in the modulo expression (axes_vec(i) + ndims) % ndims inside the loop; no guard ensures ndims is nonzero before this division.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs a modulo/division by a value (ndims) that can be zero, matching CWE-369's divide-by-zero with an availability impact. The missing validation before the operation, rather than a general bounds issue, is the specific weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shape tensor's element count ndims can be 0, yet it is used as the divisor for the modulo operation on each axis value. Trigger: a caller supplies an empty shape tensor together with a non-empty axes tensor, so the loop executes and evaluates % 0. Consequence: integer division/modulo by zero crashes the process, giving a denial of service.

commit_msg: ffdmx: fix loop index mismatch on side data parsing (fixes #2664)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tffdmx_parse_side_data(&stream->side_data[i], pid);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tffdmx_parse_side_data(&stream->side_data[j], pid);']}
description: GPAC 2.3-DEV-rev605-gfc9e29089-master contains a heap-buffer-overflow in ffdmx_parse_side_data /afltest/gpac/src/filters/ff_dmx.c:202:14 in gpac/MP4Box.

code_evidence: The side-data loop iterates j from 0 to stream->nb_side_data-1, but the indexed element passed to ffdmx_parse_side_data is stream->side_data[i], where i is the outer stream index. The loop counter j is never used for indexing, so when i differs from the valid side-data range the pointer targets the wrong or out-of-bounds element.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the mismatched index lets the side-data parser read/write beyond the side_data buffer, an out-of-bounds write. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the reported consequence is a heap-buffer-overflow write reached through the wrongly indexed structure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: index mismatch between the loop bound (nb_side_data via j) and the element selected (side_data[i]). Trigger: a stream whose index i is >= nb_side_data while nb_side_data > 0, causing ffdmx_parse_side_data to read and process a side-data structure outside the array. Consequence: the parser operates on out-of-bounds memory, matching the reported heap-buffer-overflow write in ffdmx_parse_side_data.

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS replay protection

The DTLS implementation provides some protection against replay attacks
in accordance with RFC6347 section 4.1.2.6.

A sliding "window" of valid record sequence numbers is maintained with
the "right" hand edge of the window set to the highest sequence number we
have received so far. Records that arrive that are off the "left" hand
edge of the window are rejected. Records within the window are checked
against a list of records received so far. If we already received it then
we also reject the new record.

If we have not already received the record, or the sequence number is off
the right hand edge of the window then we verify the MAC of the record.
If MAC verification fails then we discard the record. Otherwise we mark
the record as received. If the sequence number was off the right hand edge
of the window, then we slide the window along so that the right hand edge
is in line with the newly received sequence number.

Records may arrive for future epochs, i.e. a record from after a CCS being
sent, can arrive before the CCS does if the packets get re-ordered. As we
have not yet received the CCS we are not yet in a position to decrypt or
validate the MAC of those records. OpenSSL places those records on an
unprocessed records queue. It additionally updates the window immediately,
even though we have not yet verified the MAC. This will only occur if
currently in a handshake/renegotiation.

This could be exploited by an attacker by sending a record for the next
epoch (which does not have to decrypt or have a valid MAC), with a very
large sequence number. This means the right hand edge of the window is
moved very far to the right, and all subsequent legitimate packets are
dropped causing a denial of service.

A similar effect can be achieved during the initial handshake. In this
case there is no MAC key negotiated yet. Therefore an attacker can send a
message for the current epoch with a very large sequence number. The code
will process the record as normal. If the hanshake message sequence number
(as opposed to the record sequence number that we have been talking about
so far) is in the future then the injected message is bufferred to be
handled later, but the window is still updated. Therefore all subsequent
legitimate handshake records are dropped. This aspect is not considered a
security issue because there are many ways for an attacker to disrupt the
initial handshake and prevent it from completing successfully (e.g.
injection of a handshake message will cause the Finished MAC to fail and
the handshake to be aborted). This issue comes about as a result of trying
to do replay protection, but having no integrity mechanism in place yet.
Does it even make sense to have replay protection in epoch 0? That
issue isn't addressed here though.

This addressed an OCAP Audit issue.

CVE-2016-2181

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (dtls1_process_buffered_records(s) < 0)', '            /* Mark receipt of record. */', '            dtls1_record_bitmap_update(s, bitmap);', '    if (!dtls1_process_record(s)) {', '    dtls1_record_bitmap_update(s, bitmap); /* Mark receipt of record. */'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!dtls1_process_buffered_records(s))', '        /*', '         * TODO: Does it make sense to have replay protection in epoch 0 where', '         * we have no integrity negotiated yet?', '         */', '    if (!dtls1_process_record(s, bitmap)) {']}
description: The Anti-Replay feature in the DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 mishandles early use of a new epoch number in conjunction with a large sequence number, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (false-positive packet drops) via spoofed DTLS records, related to rec_layer_d1.c and ssl3_record.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's numeric handling (epoch/sequence parsing and bitmap window checks) is not shown to involve improper calculation or conversion; the patch concerns replay-window update timing and MAC verification ordering, not a numeric error, so CWE-189 is not directly supported.

commit_msg:
Fix DSA, preserve BN_FLG_CONSTTIME

Operations in the DSA signing algorithm should run in constant time in
order to avoid side channel attacks. A flaw in the OpenSSL DSA
implementation means that a non-constant time codepath is followed for
certain operations. This has been demonstrated through a cache-timing
attack to be sufficient for an attacker to recover the private DSA key.

CVE-2016-2178

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((dsa->flags & DSA_FLAG_NO_EXP_CONSTTIME) == 0) {', '        BN_set_flags(k, BN_FLG_CONSTTIME);', '    }', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '    if ((dsa->flags & DSA_FLAG_NO_EXP_CONSTTIME) == 0) {', '        BN_set_flags(K, BN_FLG_CONSTTIME);', '    }', '']}
description: The dsa_sign_setup function in crypto/dsa/dsa_ossl.c in OpenSSL through 1.0.2h does not properly ensure the use of constant-time operations, which makes it easier for local users to discover a DSA private key via a timing side-channel attack.

code_evidence: BN_FLG_CONSTTIME is set on k, but the value actually used for the exponentiation is K, which is set to kq in the non-NO_EXP_CONSTTIME branch; kq is a separately allocated BIGNUM that never receives the flag.

The conditional builds K = kq (k + q, possibly +q again) only when constant-time mode is requested, so the flag is applied to the wrong object and the exponent used by DSA_BN_MOD_EXP lacks constant-time protection.
DSA_BN_MOD_EXP performs modular exponentiation with K; without BN_FLG_CONSTTIME on K, the exponentiation follows a data-dependent path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's behavior (timing of the exponentiation) depends on secret data and is observable to an attacker, matching CWE-203's observable discrepancy; the missing constant-time constraint is the cause, timing leakage the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
DSA_BN_MOD_EXP(goto err, dsa, r, dsa->g, K, dsa->p, ctx,
dsa->method_mont_p);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: BN_set_flags is applied to k while the exponent passed to the modular exponentiation is K (kq). Trigger: a DSA signing setup with DSA_FLAG_NO_EXP_CONSTTIME clear. Consequence: the exponentiation runs in variable time, leaking timing information correlated with the private key-derived exponent.

commit_msg: Resolve #767
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (state_.size() < sizeof(details::x86_thread_state_t)) {', '          return entry;', '        }', '        if (state_.size() < sizeof(details::x86_thread_state64_t)) {', '          return entry;', '        }', '        if (state_.size() < sizeof(details::arm_thread_state_t)) {', '          return entry;', '        }', '        if (state_.size() < sizeof(details::arm_thread_state64_t)) {', '          return entry;', '        }']}
description: LIEF commit 365a16a was discovered to contain a heap-buffer overflow via the function print_binary at /c/macho_reader.c.

code_evidence: Each architecture case reinterprets state_.data() as a fixed-size thread-state struct and reads the instruction pointer field (eip, rip, r15, pc) without checking that state_ has at least sizeof(that struct) bytes. The cast and field access dereference beyond the allocation when state_ is shorter than the struct.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked out-of-bounds memory access on a heap buffer whose size is not validated against the struct being accessed. This matches the out-of-bounds memory-access family; the patch adds size guards, confirming the missing constraint is the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing length validation before a type-punned access to state_. Trigger: a Mach-O thread command whose state_ buffer is smaller than the expected thread-state struct. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read past the heap buffer, which the fix addresses by returning early when state_.size() is too small.

commit_msg:
polkit: when authorizing via PK let's re-resolve callback/userdata instead of caching it

Previously, when doing an async PK query we'd store the original
callback/userdata pair and call it again after the PK request is
complete. This is problematic, since PK queries might be slow and in the
meantime the userdata might be released and re-acquired. Let's avoid
this by always traversing through the message handlers so that we always
re-resolve the callback and userdata pair and thus can be sure it's
up-to-date and properly valid.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['        sd_event_source_disable_unref(q->defer_event_source);']}
description: A heap use-after-free vulnerability was found in systemd before version v245-rc1, where asynchronous Polkit queries are performed while handling dbus messages. A local unprivileged attacker can abuse this flaw to crash systemd services or potentially execute code and elevate their privileges, by sending specially crafted dbus messages.

code_evidence: async_polkit_query_free releases q->slot, q->request, q->reply, q->action, and q->details, then frees the q struct itself at line 11. The patch adds sd_event_source_disable_unref(q->defer_event_source) before free(q), showing the struct holds an event source reference that was previously left dangling/unreleased. The function performs teardown of an async Polkit query object whose lifetime spans slow asynchronous PK requests.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The free of q while its defer_event_source remains live is a use-after-free: memory belonging to a freed allocation is later referenced. This is CWE-416 rather than a simple memory leak, since the resource can be used after release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the async query's deferred event source was not detached/unreferenced when the AsyncPolkitQuery was freed, and the stored callback/userdata pair outlived the freed query. Trigger: a slow Polkit query completes or the query is freed while the event source still references the query data. Consequence: the event source or callback dereferences freed memory, causing crash or potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fixed heap-buffer-overflow while importing module.

This closes #187 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    text->length = nxt_length(NJS_MODULE_START);', '', '    if (S_ISREG(sb.st_mode) && sb.st_size) {', '        text->length += sb.st_size;', '    text->length += nxt_length(NJS_MODULE_END);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!S_ISREG(sb.st_mode)) {', '        goto fail;', '    text->length = nxt_length(NJS_MODULE_START) + sb.st_size', '                   + nxt_length(NJS_MODULE_END);']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerabilty found in Nginx NJS v.0feca92 allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the njs_module_read in the njs_module.c file.

code_evidence: text->length is computed from NJS_MODULE_START, sb.st_size only when S_ISREG(sb.st_mode) && sb.st_size is true, plus NJS_MODULE_END; for a non-regular file sb.st_size is not added to the allocation size.
The allocation uses text->length, but read() is given sb.st_size as its count and memcpy then writes NJS_MODULE_END at p+n regardless of whether n fits within the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the code copies data (read into the buffer, then memcpy of NJS_MODULE_END) without ensuring the copy size stays below the allocated output buffer size; the size mismatch between text->length and sb.st_size is the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size omits sb.st_size for non-regular files (the S_ISREG/sb.st_size guard), while read() still requests sb.st_size bytes and the trailing NJS_MODULE_END is copied after them. Trigger: opening a module path that is not a regular file but reports a nonzero size. Consequence: the read and final memcpy write past the heap allocation, producing a heap buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
telnet: check sscanf() for correct number of matches

CVE-2021-22898

Bug: https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2021-22898.html
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['          if(sscanf(v->data, "%127[^,],%127s", varname, varval)) {'], 'added_lines': ['          if(sscanf(v->data, "%127[^,],%127s", varname, varval) == 2) {']}
description: curl 7.7 through 7.76.1 suffers from an information disclosure when the `-t` command line option, known as `CURLOPT_TELNETOPTIONS` in libcurl, is used to send variable=content pairs to TELNET servers. Due to a flaw in the option parser for sending NEW_ENV variables, libcurl could be made to pass on uninitialized data from a stack based buffer to the server, resulting in potentially revealing sensitive internal information to the server using a clear-text network protocol.

code_evidence: varname and varval are stack buffers initialized to empty strings at lines 8-9, but the sscanf at line 46 uses '%127[^,],%127s' and the code only checks the truthiness of sscanf's return value. If the input has a comma but no second field, sscanf returns 1, the branch is taken, and varval is still empty; more importantly the match count is not constrained to 2, so a partial parse proceeds to msnprintf (lines 47-49) building NEW_ENV data from varname/varval for transmission at line 57.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to ensure the critical varval buffer is populated before use, matching CWE-909 Missing Initialization of Resource; the information disclosure is the consequence of using an uninitialized resource. CWE-457 (use of uninitialized variable) is a related child, but the target class-level weakness fits the missing-init root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser accepts a partial sscanf result (any nonzero count) instead of requiring both fields, so it can construct and send a NEW_ENV variable/value pair from buffers that were not fully populated by the parse. Trigger: a telnet option variable whose data lacks the expected comma-separated second field. Supported consequence: uninitialized/partial stack-buffer content is sent in cleartext to the TELNET server, disclosing internal data.

commit_msg:
PR25842, Null pointer dereference in nm-new

	PR 25842
	* elf.c (_bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string): Don't segfault on
	NULL nodename.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  version_string = ((base_p || strcmp (symbol->name, nodename))', '\t\t\t    ? nodename : "");'], 'added_lines': ['\t  version_string = "";', '\t  if (base_p', '\t      || nodename == NULL', '\t      || symbol->name == NULL', '\t      || strcmp (symbol->name, nodename) != 0)', '\t    version_string = nodename;']}
description: A Null Pointer Dereference vulnerability exists in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.35, in _bfd_elf_get_symbol_version_string, as demonstrated in nm-new, that can cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 23 loads vd_nodename from the version definition table without verifying it is non-NULL. Line 24 then passes nodename as the second argument to strcmp, which dereferences it; line 25 returns nodename as the version string, propagating the NULL upward.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer it assumes valid (nodename) in strcmp, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read, since the pointer itself is NULL rather than pointing outside a valid object.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vd_nodename can be NULL for a crafted or malformed ELF version definition, and the code passes it directly to strcmp without a NULL check. Trigger: a symbol whose vernum is nonzero and <= cverdefs, with base_p false, reaches line 24. Consequence: strcmp dereferences the NULL nodename, crashing nm-new (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [' int contentlen = 0;', '\t\tcontentlen = atoi(sb);', '\t\t\t\tprintstr(&pp, "<form method=\\"POST\\" action=\\"/U\\"><textarea cols=\\"80\\" rows=\\"30\\" name=\\"conffile\\">");', '\t\t\tint l=0;', '\t\t\tif(!writable || fseek(writable, 0, 0)){', "\t\t\twhile((i = sockgetlinebuf(param, CLIENT, (unsigned char *)buf, LINESIZE - 1, '+', conf.timeouts[STRING_S])) > 0){", '\t\t\t\tbuf[i] = 0;', '\t\t\t\t\tif(strncasecmp(buf, "conffile=", 9)) error = 1;', '\t\t\t\tif(l >= contentlen) break;'], 'added_lines': [' unsigned contentlen = 0;', '\t\tsscanf(sb, "%u", &contentlen);', '\t\tif(contentlen > LINESIZE*1024) contentlen = 0;', '\t\t\t\tprintstr(&pp, "<form method=\\"POST\\" action=\\"/U\\" enctype=\\"application/x-www-form-urlencoded\\"><textarea cols=\\"80\\" rows=\\"30\\" name=\\"conffile\\">");', '\t\t\tunsigned l=0;', '\t\t\tif(!writable || !contentlen || fseek(writable, 0, 0)){', "\t\t\twhile(l < contentlen && (i = sockgetlinebuf(param, CLIENT, (unsigned char *)buf, (contentlen - l) > LINESIZE - 1?LINESIZE - 1:contentlen - l, '+', conf.timeouts[STRING_S])) > 0){", '\t\t\t\t\tif(i<9 || strncasecmp(buf, "conffile=", 9)) error = 1;', '\t\t\t\t\tbuf[i] = 0;']}
description: webadmin.c in 3proxy before 0.8.13 has an out-of-bounds write in the admin interface.

code_evidence: contentlen is declared as a signed int and filled directly from the attacker-controlled Content-Length header via atoi(sb), so it can be negative or arbitrarily large with no upper bound.

In case 'U', the read loop uses contentlen to size the sockgetlinebuf request and then computes i = contentlen - l; if contentlen is negative or smaller than the actual line, this arithmetic yields a negative or oversized value used as an index.
buf[i] = 0 is executed before any check that i is within the LINESIZE buffer, and the loop only exits when l >= contentlen, so a crafted Content-Length drives an out-of-bounds write to buf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a write through buf[i] = 0 where i derives from unvalidated attacker input, directly matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. A related weakness such as integer overflow (CWE-190) may underlie the bad index, but the supported consequence here is the out-of-bounds write itself.

evidence_lines.code: int contentlen = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Content-Length value is trusted as an unvalidated signed integer and used to compute the index i into the fixed LINESIZE buffer. Trigger: an HTTP POST to the admin interface with a negative or excessive Content-Length reaches case 'U'. Consequence: buf[i] writes outside the heap buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': []}
description: NetScaler file parser crash in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.5 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.13 allows denial of service via crafted capture file

code_evidence: A 65536-byte temporary buffer is allocated, and when EOF is reached with a partial page read, memset zero-fills nstrace_buf from bytes_read up to NSPR_PAGESIZE_TRACE; this fill is not bounded by the allocated buffer length.

The loop indexes nstrace_buf[nstrace_buf_offset] and casts &nstrace_buf[nstrace_buf_offset] to nspr_hd_v20_t*; nstrace_ensure_buflen checks space but the offset derives from file-controlled record sizes.
nstrace_buf_offset is advanced by nspr_getv20recordsize(hdp) before dereferencing an nspr_abstime_v20_t at the new offset, so a large record size can move the pointer beyond the page.
The default branch also advances the offset by the attacker-controlled record size before the next loop iteration reads through hdp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memory writes (memset zero-fill and structure access) at offsets not proven to lie within the allocated buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. A pure out-of-bounds read would be CWE-125, but the memset past bytes_read and the cast-based writes make the write variant appropriate.

evidence_lines.code:
nstrace_buf_offset += nspr_getv20recordsize(hdp);
ns_setabstime(nstrace, pletoh32(&((nspr_abstime_v20_t *) &nstrace_buf[nstrace_buf_offset])->abs_Time), pletoh16(&((nspr_abstime_v20_t *) &nstrace_buf[nstrace_buf_offset])->abs_RelTime));
nstrace_buf_offset += nspr_getv20recordsize(hdp);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Record sizes and page offsets come from the crafted capture. The parser advances nstrace_buf_offset by nspr_getv20recordsize(hdp) and then reads/writes structures at the new offset, and the EOF memset writes up to NSPR_PAGESIZE_TRACE regardless of the actual allocation. This yields out-of-bounds memory access, crashing Wireshark (DoS) and potentially corrupting memory.

description: id3/ID3.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, 6.x before 2016-10-01, and 7.0 before 2016-10-01 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (device hang or reboot) via a crafted file, aka internal bug 30744884.

code_evidence: For encoding 0x02, len is computed as n/2 from the attacker-controlled frame size, then used to size a heap allocation and as the loop bound copying from framedata without checking len > 0.

For encoding 0x01, len is likewise derived from n/2; the code allocates len elements and iterates over framedata before validating the endianness marker, and later decrements len after framedata++ without confirming len > 0.
For the eightBit path, frame8 is allocated with len bytes and filled from framedata with no lower-bound check on len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-controlled frame data and length metadata but fails to validate the derived string length before using it for allocation and copying, which is the core of CWE-20. The weakness is improper validation of a derived quantity (length), not a transformation/filtering issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The frame length metadata from the ID3 tag is converted to a string length (n/2) without validating that it is positive or consistent. A crafted file can yield len <= 0, so the allocation is zero/negative-sized and the copy loops or subsequent marker handling operate with invalid lengths, leading to memory corruption or a hang/reboot (DoS) in mediaserver.

commit_msg:
Consult the 'unconditional IO exiting' and 'use IO bitmaps' VM-execution
controls when checking instruction interception. If the 'use IO bitmaps'
VM-execution control is 1, check the instruction access against the IO
bitmaps to determine if the instruction causes a VM-exit.

Signed-off-by: Oliver Upton <oupton@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>

description: A flaw was discovered in the way that the KVM hypervisor handled instruction emulation for an L2 guest when nested virtualisation is enabled. Under some circumstances, an L2 guest may trick the L0 guest into accessing sensitive L1 resources that should be inaccessible to the L2 guest.

code_evidence: vmx_check_intercept only special-cases x86_intercept_rdtscp; all other intercepts, including in/ins/out/outs, fall through to X86EMUL_UNHANDLEABLE without consulting the unconditional-IO-exiting or IO-bitmap VM-execution controls. The function never calls vmx_check_intercept_io, so the nested VMCS12 IO configuration is ignored.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing IO-control check lets an L2 guest reach sensitive L1 resource state, an exposure of information/state to an unauthorized actor, matching CWE-200's confidentiality scope. The underlying error is a missing authorization check on nested IO interception rather than a generic memory-safety bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: instruction interception for IO instructions is not validated against the L1 VMCS12 IO controls. Trigger: an L2 guest executes an IN/OUT/INS/OUTS instruction that is not intercepted under the nested configuration. Consequence: the L0 hypervisor emulates it against L1 host resources, letting L2 access L1 IO state that should be inaccessible.

description: url.cpp in libproxy through 0.4.15 is prone to a buffer overflow when PAC is enabled, as demonstrated by a large PAC file that is delivered without a Content-length header.

code_evidence: The function allocates a fixed PAC_MAX_SIZE heap buffer and zeroes it, establishing the destination capacity for received PAC data.

When no Content-Length is present (content_length == 0), the recv call always uses PAC_HTTP_BLOCK_SIZE and writes at buffer + recvd, with no check that recvd + PAC_HTTP_BLOCK_SIZE stays within PAC_MAX_SIZE.
recvd is incremented by the number of bytes received without any bound, so repeated reads from a large PAC response advance the write offset past the allocated buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer copy/read into a fixed-size output buffer without verifying the input size fits, matching CWE-120. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the recv writes attacker-controlled bytes past the allocated destination.

evidence_lines.code: recvd += r;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the receive loop writes at an offset (recvd) into a fixed PAC_MAX_SIZE buffer and only stops when recv returns <= 0 or a declared content_length is reached; with no Content-length header, content_length stays 0 and the loop never checks accumulated size against the allocation. Trigger: a proxy returns a PAC body larger than PAC_MAX_SIZE without Content-length. Consequence: heap out-of-bounds writes, memory corruption and possible code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20570)

description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing

commit_msg:
The bg_flags field in the block group descripts is only valid if the
uninit_bg or metadata_csum feature is enabled.  We were not
consistently looking at this field; fix this.

Also block group #0 must never have uninitialized allocation bitmaps,
or need to be zeroed, since that's where the root inode, and other
special inodes are set up.  Check for these conditions and mark the
file system as corrupted if they are detected.

This addresses CVE-2018-10876.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199403

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function reads an inode bitmap and validates the bg_flags/block-group-0 condition; it contains no free or reuse of freed memory, so it does not support CWE-416.

description: An issue was discovered in GNU libcdio before 2.0.0. There is a double free in get_cdtext_generic() in lib/driver/_cdio_generic.c.

code_evidence: On the error path where len <= 0 or cdtext_data_init fails, the code calls cdtext_destroy(p_env->cdtext) at line 16 and then free(p_env->cdtext) at line 17 on the same pointer; cdtext_destroy itself releases the structure, so the subsequent free is a second deallocation of already-freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 precisely describes calling free() twice on the same address, which is exactly what lines 16-17 do via the destroy-then-free sequence on p_env->cdtext.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch performs both cdtext_destroy() and free() on the same p_env->cdtext allocation. Trigger: a CD-TEXT block whose computed length is non-positive or whose cdtext_data_init fails. Consequence: the heap chunk is freed twice, enabling heap corruption and potentially arbitrary code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
Actually fail when error occurs in parseFormat

When there's an unsupported number of bits per sample or an invalid
number of samples per block, don't only print an error message using
the error handler, but actually stop parsing the file.

This fixes #35 (also reported at
https://bugzilla.opensuse.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1026983 and
https://blogs.gentoo.org/ago/2017/02/20/audiofile-heap-based-buffer-overflow-in-imadecodeblockwave-ima-cpp/
)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\treturn AF_FAIL;', '\t\t\t\treturn AF_FAIL;']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the decodeBlockWAVE function in IMA.cpp in Audio File Library (aka audiofile) 0.3.6, 0.3.5, 0.3.4, 0.3.3, 0.3.2, 0.3.1, 0.3.0 and 0.2.7 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: When bitsPerSample != 4, the code calls _af_error but does not return, so parsing continues with an invalid IMA configuration.

The bytesPerBlock value is derived from the attacker-controlled samplesPerBlock and channelCount; if the block is inconsistent with blockAlign or samplesPerBlock % 8 != 1, the error is logged but execution falls through.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing return statements let invalid metadata propagate into decompression, producing out-of-bounds memory access in the decode buffer, which fits CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write within a memory buffer. The underlying cause is insufficient validation rather than the memory operation itself, but the supported consequence is buffer-boundary violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: invalid IMA ADPCM parameters (non-4-bit samples or malformed samplesPerBlock) are only reported and not rejected, so the track is configured with inconsistent framesPerPacket/bytesPerPacket values. Trigger: a crafted WAVE_FORMAT_DVI_ADPCM header. Consequence: the later IMA decode path can compute block offsets/lengths from these inconsistent parameters and read or write outside the allocated buffer, causing a heap-based buffer overflow and crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['size_t dsi_writeinit(DSI *dsi, void *buf, const size_t buflen _U_)', '        memmove(buf, dsi->start, bytes);'], 'added_lines': ['size_t dsi_writeinit(DSI *dsi, void *buf, const size_t buflen)', '        memmove(buf, dsi->start, MIN(buflen, bytes));']}
description: This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Netatalk. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. The specific flaw exists within the dsi_writeinit function. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length heap-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of root. Was ZDI-CAN-17646.

code_evidence: Line 4 derives dsi->datasize from the attacker-controlled network header fields dsi_len and dsi_doff. Line 6 computes bytes as the MIN of buffered data and that datasize, without consulting the destination capacity buflen (marked _U_, unused). Line 7 then memmove's bytes into buf, so an attacker-controlled length can exceed the heap allocation of buf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The destination buffer is heap-allocated and its length is unchecked before memmove, matching CWE-122 heap-based buffer overflow. The fix confirms this by clamping the copy to MIN(buflen, bytes); a stack-based variant (CWE-121) would require a stack destination, which is not shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length is bounded only by network-derived DSI header values, never by the destination buffer size. Trigger: a remote DSI write request whose datasize exceeds the heap buffer passed as buf. Consequence: heap memory past buf is overwritten, enabling code execution or crash as described for CVE-2022-43634.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.4. fs/ksmbd/smb2pdu.c in ksmbd does not properly check the UserName value because it does not consider the address of security buffer, leading to an out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: secbuf_len is the security buffer length from the request and is only checked against sizeof(struct authenticate_message); no relation to authblob's actual buffer is enforced here.

name_off and name_len are attacker-controlled offsets/lengths read from authblob->UserName, and the bound check uses auth_msg_len (SecurityBufferOffset + secbuf_len) rather than secbuf_len, so it can permit a UserName range beyond the security buffer.
smb_strndup_from_utf16 reads name_len bytes starting at authblob + name_off, with no guarantee that name_off + name_len stays within the security buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits reading past the end of the security buffer during UTF-16 string duplication, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). This is not CWE-787 because no out-of-bounds write occurs.

evidence_lines.code:
name = smb_strndup_from_utf16((const char *)authblob + name_off,
name_len,
true,
conn->local_nls);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bounds check compares name_off + name_len against auth_msg_len instead of the security buffer length secbuf_len, so an attacker-supplied UserName offset/length can exceed the actual buffer. Trigger: a crafted session setup request. Consequence: out-of-bounds read in smb_strndup_from_utf16, leaking or crashing.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.5 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.13, the NBAP dissector could crash with a large loop that ends with a heap-based buffer overflow. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-nbap.c by prohibiting the self-linking of DCH-IDs.

code_evidence: The while loop follows next_dch links with no limit on iterations or on num_dch_in_flow; each iteration increments num_dch_in_flow and writes dchs_in_flow_list[num_dch_in_flow], so a self-referential or cyclic next_dch chain keeps the loop running and grows the index past the fixed list size, overflowing the buffer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop termination depends solely on next_dch becoming 0, and the DCH-ID linkage can point back to itself, so the attacker-controlled chain never terminates. commit_msg:
In r592_probe, dev->detect_timer was bound with r592_detect_timer.
In r592_irq function, the timer function will be invoked by mod_timer.

If we remove the module which will call hantro_release to make cleanup,
there may be a unfinished work. The possible sequence is as follows,
which will cause a typical UAF bug.

Fix it by canceling the work before cleanup in r592_remove.

CPU0                  CPU1

                    |r592_detect_timer
r592_remove         |
  memstick_free_host|
  put_device;       |
  kfree(host);      |
                    |
                    | queue_work
                    |   &host->media_checker //use

Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230307164338.1246287-1-zyytlz.wz@163.com
Signed-off-by: Ulf Hansson <ulf.hansson@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['\tdel_timer_sync(&dev->detect_timer);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in r592_remove in drivers/memstick/host/r592.c in media access in the Linux Kernel. This flaw allows a local attacker to crash the system at device disconnect, possibly leading to a kernel information leak.

code_evidence: Line 5 stops only the io_thread; the detect_timer armed via mod_timer is never cancelled here.
Lines 15-19 tear down the IRQ, unmap MMIO, release regions and disable the device, then free the host with memstick_free_host.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the host while an outstanding timer/work path may still access it, which is exactly CWE-416. This is a lifetime/synchronization flaw, not merely a leak or double free.

evidence_lines.code:
kthread_stop(dev->io_thread);
r592_enable_device(dev, false);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: r592_detect_timer can still fire after r592_remove begins: the timer callback queues work referencing the host. Because the teardown path frees the host without synchronizing with that timer, the callback can run after memstick_free_host, producing a use-after-free of freed host memory.

commit_msg:
Split the xt_compat_match/xt_compat_target into smaller type-safe functions
performing just one operation. Handle all alignment and size-related
conversions centrally in these function instead of requiring each module to
implement a full-blown conversion function. Replace ->compat callback by
->compat_from_user and ->compat_to_user callbacks, responsible for
converting just a single private structure.

Signed-off-by: Patrick McHardy <kaber@trash.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (m->u.kernel.match->compat)', '\t\tm->u.kernel.match->compat(m, NULL, size, COMPAT_CALC_SIZE);', '\telse', '\t\txt_compat_match(m, NULL, size, COMPAT_CALC_SIZE);'], 'added_lines': ['\t*size += xt_compat_match_offset(m->u.kernel.match);']}
description: A heap out-of-bounds write affecting Linux since v2.6.19-rc1 was discovered in net/netfilter/x_tables.c. This allows an attacker to gain privileges or cause a DoS (via heap memory corruption) through user name space

code_evidence: compat_calc_match receives a match m and a size pointer and dispatches to m->u.kernel.match->compat or xt_compat_match with COMPAT_CALC_SIZE to accumulate size; no bounds or overflow check is performed on the computed *size before it is used by callers to size compat copies.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the defect is an unchecked size computation feeding a write past the end of a heap buffer. It is distinct from a pure integer overflow (CWE-190) since the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds write itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size accumulated for a compat match is computed without validating that it stays within the caller's allocated compat buffer. Trigger: a user-namespace attacker supplies a match whose compat offset makes the computed size exceed the destination buffer. Consequence: callers using this size perform a heap out-of-bounds write, enabling memory corruption, privilege escalation or DoS.
