commit_msg:
Release "3.0.6": Fix crashes in Array for "integer overflow #10"

FossilOrigin-Name: 50642d64b8f0a4e62df68e59fcb2ef0923c3dbec8fc8a15d38b1ddbe655c38d6
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    n = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, obj);'], 'added_lines': ['    n = jsi_SizeOfArray(interp, obj);']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjSetLength in jsish before 3.0.6, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: n is the array length from Jsi_ObjGetLength; if a start argument is supplied, istart is cast from the double nstart to int and only checked against n and zero.
If an end argument is supplied, iend is cast from nend to int and clamped to n at the upper bound, but a large positive nend can wrap during the (int) cast before the iend>=n check.
nsiz = iend-istart+1 is computed as int and only checked for <=0; the loop then indexes obj->arr[i] up to iend.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an integer overflow/wraparound in the int size calculation and casts, matching CWE-190; the out-of-bounds access is the consequence. A pure bounds-check weakness (CWE-125) would not require the arithmetic wrap, and the commit's switch to jsi_SizeOfArray addresses the length/size handling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The (int) casts of attacker-controlled start/end doubles and the int subtraction iend-istart+1 can overflow or wrap, producing an unexpectedly small or negative nsiz that passes or bypasses the <=0 guard while iend remains large. The loop then accesses obj->arr[i] beyond the allocated array, causing memory corruption or crash rather than a benign length check.

commit_msg:
unix: correctly track in-flight fds in sending process user_struct

The commit referenced in the Fixes tag incorrectly accounted the number
of in-flight fds over a unix domain socket to the original opener
of the file-descriptor. This allows another process to arbitrary
deplete the original file-openers resource limit for the maximum of
open files. Instead the sending processes and its struct cred should
be credited.

To do so, we add a reference counted struct user_struct pointer to the
scm_fp_list and use it to account for the number of inflight unix fds.

Fixes: 712f4aad406bb1 ("unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets")
Reported-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tnew_fpl->user = get_uid(fpl->user);']}
description: The Linux kernel before 4.5 allows local users to bypass file-descriptor limits and cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging incorrect tracking of descriptor ownership and sending each descriptor over a UNIX socket before closing it. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2013-4312.

code_evidence: scm_fp_dup copies the scm_fp_list with kmemdup up to offsetof(fp[count]) and, for each copied fd, calls get_file to take an extra file reference; it sets new_fpl->max = new_fpl->count but does not carry over or reference the owning user_struct. The duplicate therefore holds file references without the associated per-user accounting that the original fpl carried.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; here the missing user_struct reference in the duplicated list causes incorrect resource accounting and depletion. This is a resource-management flaw rather than a memory-safety bug, matching the improper tracking of in-flight fds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the duplicated scm_fp_list loses the user_struct ownership reference, so in-flight fds are not charged to the sender's open-file limit. Trigger: a process repeatedly duplicates/sends descriptors over a UNIX socket before closing them; the duplicated lists keep file references without accounting to the correct user. Supported consequence: the per-user file-descriptor/resource limit is bypassed, allowing resource exhaustion and denial of service.

commit_msg: Add negative check in `mrb_str_resize`; fix #4062
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (len < 0) {', '    mrb_raisef(mrb, E_ARGUMENT_ERROR, "negative (or overflowed) string size");', '  }']}
description: The CHECK macro in mrbgems/mruby-sprintf/src/sprintf.c in mruby 1.4.1 contains a signed integer overflow, possibly leading to out-of-bounds memory access because the mrb_str_resize function in string.c does not check for a negative length.

code_evidence: mrb_str_resize accepts mrb_int len without validating its sign; the length is used at line 10 to resize capacity and at line 12 to set the string length, and line 13 writes a NUL terminator at RSTR_PTR(s)[len].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs size arithmetic on len (capacity comparison at line 9 and resize at line 10) without guarding against a negative or overflowed value, which is exactly the integer-overflow/wraparound condition described by CWE-190. The subsequent out-of-bounds write is the downstream consequence, not a separate weakness label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A negative or overflowed len reaches resize_capa and RSTR_SET_LEN unchecked, so the computed capacity/length is treated as valid. The write RSTR_PTR(s)[len]='\0' then indexes memory using that corrupted length, giving out-of-bounds memory access; the root cause is the missing sign/overflow check on len, and the consequence is memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
avformat/asfdec: Fix DoS in asf_build_simple_index()

Fixes: Missing EOF check in loop
No testcase

Found-by: Xiaohei and Wangchu from Alibaba Security Team
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            if (avio_feof(s->pb)) {', '                ret = AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '                goto end;', '            }', '']}
description: In libavformat/asfdec_f.c in FFmpeg 3.3.3, a DoS in asf_build_simple_index() due to lack of an EOF (End of File) check might cause huge CPU consumption. When a crafted ASF file, which claims a large "ict" field in the header but does not contain sufficient backing data, is provided, the for loop would consume huge CPU and memory resources, since there is no EOF check inside the loop.

code_evidence: Line 30 reads the attacker-controlled ict count from the file; line 33 loops i from 0 to ict without any bound or EOF check, and each iteration reads pktnum/pktct (lines 34-35) and adds an index entry. When the file ends early, the loop still runs ict times.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked loop bound lets attacker input control how much CPU/memory work is performed, matching CWE-400 uncontrolled resource consumption. It is not CWE-125/787 because no out-of-bounds buffer access is shown; the defect is unbounded iteration.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the for loop is driven solely by the untrusted ict field with no EOF/error check inside the body. A crafted ASF header claiming a large ict but lacking backing data causes repeated reads and index-entry additions, consuming CPU and memory for the claimed iteration count.

commit_msg:
Fixed bug #73342

Directly listen on socket, instead of duping it to STDIN and
listening on that.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tfpm_globals.listening_socket = dup(wp->listening_socket);']}
description: An issue was discovered in PHP 7.3.x before 7.3.0alpha3, 7.2.x before 7.2.8, and before 7.1.20. The php-fpm master process restarts a child process in an endless loop when using program execution functions (e.g., passthru, exec, shell_exec, or system) with a non-blocking STDIN stream, causing this master process to consume 100% of the CPU, and consume disk space with a large volume of error logs, as demonstrated by an attack by a customer of a shared-hosting facility.

code_evidence: fpm_child_init sets fpm_globals.max_requests and then duplicates the pool's listening socket into fpm_globals.listening_socket without any check on dup() returning -1.

The initialization chain (stdio, log, status, unix, signals, env, php) runs immediately after; on any failure the child logs and calls exit(FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE), terminating without closing the duplicated descriptor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is uncontrolled resource consumption: descriptors and CPU/log volume are not bounded or released, matching CWE-400's availability-impact scope. It is not a single leaked handle but a repeated, unthrottled allocation/restart cycle exhausting limited resources.

evidence_lines.code: fpm_globals.max_requests = wp->config->pm_max_requests;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the duplicated listening socket is a per-child resource acquired before a fallible initialization sequence, and the failure path exits without releasing it. Trigger: repeated child initialization failures (as with the non-blocking STDIN program-execution bug) cause the master to respawn children endlessly; each child leaks its dup'ed descriptor and the master spins, consuming CPU and disk via error logs.

description: The get_client_master_key function in s2_srvr.c in the SSLv2 implementation in OpenSSL before 0.9.8zf, 1.0.0 before 1.0.0r, 1.0.1 before 1.0.1m, and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2a accepts a nonzero CLIENT-MASTER-KEY CLEAR-KEY-LENGTH value for an arbitrary cipher, which allows man-in-the-middle attackers to determine the MASTER-KEY value and decrypt TLS ciphertext data by leveraging a Bleichenbacher RSA padding oracle, a related issue to CVE-2016-0800.

code_evidence: The RSA private decryption of the client master key is performed at lines 101-105, producing the premaster secret directly into the record buffer p.

Lines 106-116 handle a bad decrypt: the error condition (i < 0 or wrong length) is checked with a normal branch, the error queue is cleared, and random bytes replace the decrypted key. The branch taken and the resulting protocol behavior differ based on whether RSA padding/decryption failed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function leaks sensitive cryptographic state (the premaster/master secret) to an unauthorized network actor through an observable padding oracle, which is a confidentiality exposure of protected key material. CWE-200 fits as the exposure of sensitive information; the underlying padding-oracle side channel is the mechanism enabling that disclosure.

evidence_lines.code:
i = ssl_rsa_private_decrypt(s->cert, s->s2->tmp.enc,
&(p[s->s2->tmp.clear]),
&(p[s->s2->tmp.clear]),
(s->s2->ssl2_rollback) ? RSA_SSLV23_PADDING :
RSA_PKCS1_PADDING);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decryption failure is handled with a data-dependent branch and observable protocol responses rather than uniform processing. Trigger: a man-in-the-middle submits crafted CLIENT-MASTER-KEY messages with varying RSA padding. The differing behavior acts as a Bleichenbacher padding oracle, allowing recovery of the MASTER-KEY and decryption of TLS ciphertext.

commit_msg:
openjpeg: Prevent overflows when using opj_aligned_malloc()

BUG=628304
R=thestig@chromium.org, ochang@chromium.org

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2218783002
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / (OPJ_UINT32)sizeof(OPJ_INT32) < datasize) {', '\t\t\t\treturn OPJ_FALSE;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\tif (((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / (OPJ_UINT32)sizeof(opj_flag_t) < flagssize) {', '\t\t\treturn OPJ_FALSE;', '\t\t}']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in OpenJPEG, as used in PDFium in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JPEG 2000 data that is mishandled during opj_aligned_malloc calls in dwt.c and t1.c.

code_evidence: At [10,11] the buffer is freed and reallocated with size datasize * sizeof(OPJ_INT32), where datasize is OPJ_UINT32 and the multiplication is performed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic before being passed to opj_aligned_malloc.
At [22,23] the same pattern occurs for flagssize * sizeof(opj_flag_t), with flagssize derived from w and h without any pre-multiplication bound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs size calculations for memory allocation that can overflow/wrap in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, matching CWE-190. The missing pre-multiplication bound check is the integer-overflow cause; the downstream heap overflow is the consequence, not a separate label.

evidence_lines.code:
opj_aligned_free(t1->data);
t1->data = (OPJ_INT32*) opj_aligned_malloc(datasize * sizeof(OPJ_INT32));

opj_aligned_free(t1->flags);
t1->flags = (opj_flag_t*) opj_aligned_malloc(flagssize * sizeof(opj_flag_t));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation-size products datasize * sizeof(OPJ_INT32) and flagssize * sizeof(opj_flag_t) are computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic and can wrap to a small value when datasize or flagssize is large. Trigger: crafted JPEG 2000 dimensions propagated into w/h yield large datasize/flagssize. The wrapped small allocation is then used by later memset/processing, causing a heap-based buffer overflow (DoS or possible code execution).

commit_msg:
pipe: Fix missing lock in pipe_resize_ring()

pipe_resize_ring() needs to take the pipe->rd_wait.lock spinlock to
prevent post_one_notification() from trying to insert into the ring
whilst the ring is being replaced.

The occupancy check must be done after the lock is taken, and the lock
must be taken after the new ring is allocated.

The bug can lead to an oops looking something like:

 BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in post_one_notification.isra.0+0x62e/0x840
 Read of size 4 at addr ffff88801cc72a70 by task poc/27196
 ...
 Call Trace:
  post_one_notification.isra.0+0x62e/0x840
  __post_watch_notification+0x3b7/0x650
  key_create_or_update+0xb8b/0xd20
  __do_sys_add_key+0x175/0x340
  __x64_sys_add_key+0xbe/0x140
  do_syscall_64+0x5c/0xc0
  entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x44/0xae

Reported by Selim Enes Karaduman @Enesdex working with Trend Micro Zero
Day Initiative.

Fixes: c73be61cede5 ("pipe: Add general notification queue support")

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/*', '\t * We can shrink the pipe, if arg is greater than the ring occupancy.', "\t * Since we don't expect a lot of shrink+grow operations, just free and", '\t * allocate again like we would do for growing.  If the pipe currently', '\t * contains more buffers than arg, then return busy.', '\t */', '\tmask = pipe->ring_size - 1;', '\thead = pipe->head;', '\ttail = pipe->tail;', '\tn = pipe_occupancy(pipe->head, pipe->tail);', '\tif (nr_slots < n)', '\t\treturn -EBUSY;', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '\tspin_lock_irq(&pipe->rd_wait.lock);', '\tmask = pipe->ring_size - 1;', '\thead = pipe->head;', '\ttail = pipe->tail;', '', '\tn = pipe_occupancy(head, tail);', '\tif (nr_slots < n) {', '\t\tspin_unlock_irq(&pipe->rd_wait.lock);', '\t\tkfree(bufs);', '\t\treturn -EBUSY;', '\t}', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&pipe->rd_wait.lock);', '']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's watch queue due to a missing lock in pipe_resize_ring(). The specific flaw exists within the handling of pipe buffers. The issue results from the lack of proper locking when performing operations on an object. This flaw allows a local user to crash the system or escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: The occupancy snapshot (mask, head, tail, n) and the nr_slots < n check are read without any lock, then kcalloc is performed before any synchronization; another context can change pipe->head/tail between the check and the copy.

The copy loop reads pipe->bufs and pipe->ring_size and computes h/t from the stale head/tail snapshot, so a concurrent producer inserting into the ring can make the source indices inconsistent with the data actually copied.

The function then frees pipe->bufs and installs bufs, rewrites ring_size, tail and head, and unlocks/wakes writers, all without holding pipe->rd_wait.lock, so an interfering insertion can target a buffer being replaced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a read-check-modify-swap sequence on shared pipe state (head, tail, bufs, ring_size) with no exclusive lock, allowing an interfering concurrent code sequence to modify the resource in the timing window. This is improper synchronization on a shared resource, matching CWE-362 rather than a pure memory-safety defect, since the missing lock is the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pipe_resize_ring() snapshots and validates ring state and swaps pipe->bufs without taking pipe->rd_wait.lock, so a concurrent post_one_notification() can insert into the ring during replacement. Trigger: a resize racing with a watch-queue notification. The supported consequence is use-after-free/oops from accessing the freed old ring, and possible privilege escalation per the report.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

description: The shared memory manager (associated with pre-authentication compression) in sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4 does not ensure that a bounds check is enforced by all compilers, which might allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging access to a sandboxed privilege-separation process, related to the m_zback and m_zlib data structures.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only selects SSH compression algorithm proposal strings; it contains no memory buffer read/write or bounds operation, so it does not directly support CWE-119.

commit_msg:
x86: don't store possibly stale TLB flush time stamp

While the timing window is extremely narrow, it is theoretically
possible for an update to the TLB flush clock and a subsequent flush
IPI to happen between the read and write parts of the update of the
per-page stamp. Exclude this possibility by disabling interrupts
across the update, preventing the IPI to be serviced in the middle.

This is XSA-241.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            pg[i].tlbflush_timestamp = tlbflush_current_time();'], 'added_lines': ['            page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(&pg[i]);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to execute arbitrary code on the host OS because of a race condition that can cause a stale TLB entry.

code_evidence: For each page being freed, need_tlbflush is set when an owner exists (line 19), and the timestamp is then written directly from tlbflush_current_time() (line 21). This read-then-write update of the per-page timestamp is not protected against a concurrent TLB-flush IPI that could be serviced between the read and the write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code contains a concurrent sequence requiring exclusive access to the per-page flush timestamp, but the read/write update is not atomic with respect to an interfering flush IPI, which is CWE-362. The later fix replaces the direct assignment with page_set_tlbflush_timestamp(), which disables interrupts across the update, confirming the race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-page tlbflush_timestamp update is performed non-atomically while interrupts remain enabled, so a flush IPI can observe/modify state between reading the clock and storing the stamp. Trigger: a concurrent TLB flush IPI during free_heap_pages' timestamp update. Supported consequence: a stale TLB entry can persist, leaving the race window described in XSA-241.

commit_msg:
gnttab: Avoid potential double-put of maptrack entry

Each grant mapping for a particular domain is tracked by an in-Xen
"maptrack" entry.  This entry is is referenced by a "handle", which is
given to the guest when it calls gnttab_map_grant_ref().

There are two types of mapping a particular handle can refer to:
GNTMAP_host_map and GNTMAP_device_map.  A given
gnttab_unmap_grant_ref() call can remove either only one or both of
these entries.  When a particular handle has no entries left, it must
be freed.

gnttab_unmap_grant_ref() loops through its grant unmap request list
twice.  It first removes entries from any host pagetables and (if
appropraite) iommus; then it does a single domain TLB flush; then it
does the clean-up, including telling the granter that entries are no
longer being used (if appropriate).

At the moment, it's during the first pass that the maptrack flags are
cleared, but the second pass that the maptrack entry is freed.

Unfortunately this allows the following race, which results in a
double-free:

 A: (pass 1) clear host_map
 B: (pass 1) clear device_map
 A: (pass 2) See that maptrack entry has no mappings, free it
 B: (pass 2) See that maptrack entry has no mappings, free it #

Unfortunately, unlike the active entry pinning update, we can't simply
move the maptrack flag changes to the second half, because the
maptrack flags are used to determine if iommu entries need to be
added: a domain's iommu must never have fewer permissions than the
maptrack flags indicate, or a subsequent map_grant_ref() might fail to
add the necessary iommu entries.

Instead, free the maptrack entry in the first pass if there are no
further mappings.

This is part of XSA-218.

Reported-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

While the checks", '     * below (with the active entry lock held) will reject any such racing', "     * requests, we still need to make sure we don't attempt to acquire an", '     * invalid lock.', '     */', '    smp_rmb();', '    if ( unlikely(op->ref >= nr_grant_entries(rgt)) )', '        goto unlock_out;', '    act = active_entry_acquire(rgt, op->ref);', '', '    /*', '     * Note that we (ab)use the active entry lock here to protect against', "     * multiple unmaps of the same mapping here. We don't want to hold lgt's", "     * lock, and we only hold rgt's lock for reading (but the latter wouldn't", '     * be the right one anyway). Hence the easiest is to rely on a lock we', '     * hold anyway; see docs/misc/grant-tables.txt\'s "Locking" section.', '     */', '', '    op->flags = read_atomic(&map->flags);', '    smp_rmb();', '    if ( unlikely(!op->flags) || unlikely(map->domid != dom) ||', '         unlikely(map->ref != op->ref) )', '    {', '        gdprintk(XENLOG_WARNING, "Unstable handle %#x\\n", op->handle);', '        rc = GNTST_bad_handle;', '        goto act_release_out;', '    }', '        map->flags &= ~GNTMAP_device_map;', '        map->flags &= ~GNTMAP_host_map;', '    }', '', '    if ( !(map->flags & (GNTMAP_device_map|GNTMAP_host_map)) )', '    {', '        map->flags = 0;', '        put_handle = true;', ' unlock_out:', '', '    if ( put_handle )', '        put_maptrack_handle(lgt, op->handle);']}
description: The grant-table feature in Xen through 4.8.x provides false mapping information in certain cases of concurrent unmap calls, which allows backend attackers to obtain sensitive information or gain privileges, aka XSA-218 bug 1.

code_evidence: Flags are read into op->flags and validated, but the maptrack entry is only referenced through op->map; the active entry is acquired from op->map->ref without re-validation after locking.
The device_map and host_map bits are cleared on op->map->flags in the first pass, but there is no check that the entry still has mappings before clearing, and no maptrack entry release occurs here.
The cleanup path only releases the active entry and rgt lock; it performs no put_maptrack_handle, so freeing of the maptrack entry is deferred elsewhere.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described race lets the same maptrack entry be freed twice, matching CWE-415 (calling free twice on the same address). The function lacks the guard that would make the free conditional and atomic with flag clearing, so the target CWE is directly supported.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the maptrack flags are cleared during the first pass while the maptrack entry is freed later in a second pass, and the active-entry lock does not serialize the two unmaps of the same handle. Trigger: two concurrent gnttab_unmap_grant_ref calls on the same handle each clear one of host_map/device_map; both later observe no remaining mappings and each frees the same maptrack entry, causing a double-free.

coherent_set_tracking.coherent_set_registry_map uses a struct as a key,
but the hash and comparison routines treat keys as a sequence of bytes.
Make sure every key byte is initialized. Fixes #16994.

description: A vulnerability was found in ImageMagick. This security flaw ouccers as an undefined behaviors of casting double to size_t in svg, mvg and other coders (recurring bugs of CVE-2022-32546).

code_evidence: Line 52 computes width by casting the double expression 0.5*draw_info->pointsize*strlen(caption)+0.5 to size_t; pointsize and caption length are attacker-influenced inputs.
Lines 155-157 compute width and height from font metrics and stroke/interline spacing, then cast the double result to size_t for later bounds comparisons.
Lines 188-190 repeat the same double-to-size_t cast of width and height inside the binary-search loop.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe double-to-size_t conversion can yield an integer value outside the intended range, matching CWE-190's integer wraparound/incorrect-representation weakness where a computed size no longer reflects the original value. It is not a plain memory-safety bug; the root cause is the unchecked numeric conversion feeding size/resource logic.

evidence_lines.code: width=(size_t) floor(0.5*draw_info->pointsize*strlen(caption)+0.5);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function computes dimensions as double values that depend on user-controlled caption length and pointsize, then casts them directly to size_t. A large or non-representable double value produces an undefined/incorrect conversion result, so the derived width/height can wrap to a small or unexpected integer. The trigger is a crafted caption or pointsize; the supported consequence is corrupted sizing logic used for resource checks and image extent decisions.

commit_msg:
Issue 761:  Heap overflow reading corrupted 7Zip files

The sample file that demonstrated this had multiple 'EmptyStream'
attributes.  The first one ended up being used to calculate
certain statistics, then was overwritten by the second which
was incompatible with those statistics.

The fix here is to reject any header with multiple EmptyStream
attributes.  While here, also reject headers with multiple
EmptyFile, AntiFile, Name, or Attributes markers.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (h->emptyStreamBools != NULL)', '\t\t\t\treturn (-1);', '\t\t\tif (h->emptyFileBools != NULL)', '\t\t\t\treturn (-1);', '\t\t\tif (h->antiBools != NULL)', '\t\t\t\treturn (-1);', '\t\t\tif (zip->entry_names != NULL)', '\t\t\t\treturn (-1);', '\t\t\tif (h->attrBools != NULL)', '\t\t\t\treturn (-1);']}
description: The read_Header function in archive_read_support_format_7zip.c in libarchive 3.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via multiple EmptyStream attributes in a header in a 7zip archive.

code_evidence: The kEmptyStream case allocates h->emptyStreamBools and computes empty_streams from it without checking whether a prior EmptyStream attribute already populated the buffer; a second EmptyStream marker overwrites the pointer and recomputes empty_streams.

In the post-loop file walk, h->emptyFileBools[eindex] is indexed by eindex, which increments only for entries lacking a stream; eindex is bounded by empty_streams derived from the overwritten emptyStreamBools, not by the size of the emptyFileBools array allocated from an earlier empty_streams value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The observed defect is a read past the end of the emptyFileBools buffer during entry processing, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. The consequence is a read (and DoS), not a write, so CWE-787 does not fit. The duplicate-marker acceptance is the enabling condition, but the directly supported weakness is the out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header parser accepts duplicate EmptyStream/EmptyFile/Anti/Name/Attributes markers, so statistics (empty_streams) and buffers (emptyFileBools, antiBools) can be derived from different, incompatible header instances. Trigger: a crafted 7zip header with multiple EmptyStream attributes causes eindex to exceed the emptyFileBools allocation, and the loop reads h->emptyFileBools[eindex] out of bounds, leading to a crash/DoS (out-of-bounds read).

commit_msg:
Issue #656:  Fix CVE-2016-1541, VU#862384

When reading OS X metadata entries in Zip archives that were stored
without compression, libarchive would use the uncompressed entry size
to allocate a buffer but would use the compressed entry size to limit
the amount of data copied into that buffer.  Since the compressed
and uncompressed sizes are provided by data in the archive itself,
an attacker could manipulate these values to write data beyond
the end of the allocated buffer.

This fix provides three new checks to guard against such
manipulation and to make libarchive generally more robust when
handling this type of entry:
 1. If an OS X metadata entry is stored without compression,
    abort the entire archive if the compressed and uncompressed
    data sizes do not match.
 2. When sanity-checking the size of an OS X metadata entry,
    abort this entry if either the compressed or uncompressed
    size is larger than 4MB.
 3. When copying data into the allocated buffer, check the copy
    size against both the compressed entry size and uncompressed
    entry size.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (rsrc->uncompressed_size != rsrc->compressed_size) {', '\t\t\tarchive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '\t\t\t    "Malformed OS X metadata entry: inconsistent size");', '\t\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_FATAL);', '\t\t}', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_WARN);', '\t}', '\tif (rsrc->compressed_size > (4 * 1024 * 1024)) {', '\t\tarchive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '\t\t    "Mac metadata is too large: %jd > 4M bytes",', '\t\t    (intmax_t)rsrc->compressed_size);', '\t\t\tif ((size_t)bytes_avail > metadata_bytes)', '\t\t\t\tbytes_avail = metadata_bytes;']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the zip_read_mac_metadata function in archive_read_support_format_zip.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via crafted entry-size values in a ZIP archive.

code_evidence: The buffer is sized from rsrc->uncompressed_size, which is checked only against 4MB; the compressed size is not validated against it before allocation.

remaining_bytes is derived from rsrc->compressed_size while metadata_bytes tracks uncompressed_size; bytes_avail is clamped only to remaining_bytes, so memcpy can copy up to the compressed size into a buffer sized by the uncompressed size.
The final copy uses uncompressed_size - metadata_bytes, reflecting the unvalidated size relationship.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-supplied size metadata and fails to validate the required consistency/size property before using it to bound a copy, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The downstream memcpy overflow is the consequence; the missing size check is the validated weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
archive_entry_copy_mac_metadata(entry, metadata,
(size_t)rsrc->uncompressed_size - metadata_bytes);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code trusts attacker-controlled ZIP metadata sizes without validating consistency between compressed and uncompressed sizes. Trigger: a stored (uncompressed) OS X metadata entry whose compressed_size exceeds uncompressed_size. Consequence: memcpy writes past the malloc'd heap buffer, yielding heap overflow and potential code execution.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["      if (line[strlen (line) - 1] == '\\n')", "\tline[strlen (line) - 1] = '\\0';"], 'added_lines': ['      if (strlen (line) > 0)', "\tif (line[strlen (line) - 1] == '\\n')", "\t  line[strlen (line) - 1] = '\\0';"]}
description: idn in libidn before 1.33 might allow remote attackers to obtain sensitive memory information by reading a zero byte as input, which triggers an out-of-bounds read, a different vulnerability than CVE-2015-8948.

code_evidence: getline() at line 57 can return a zero-length line (e.g., a lone NUL byte read from input). When it succeeds, execution reaches line 63, which computes strlen(line) - 1 without first checking that the string is non-empty. For an empty line, strlen==0, so index -1 (size_t underflow) is used to read line[-1] at line 63 and possibly write line[-1] at line 64.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unchecked strlen(line)-1 index reads memory before the start of the allocated line buffer. This is a read past the intended buffer boundary, not merely an integer issue; the underflowed index is the mechanism, and the out-of-bounds access is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the newline-stripping code indexes line[strlen(line)-1] unconditionally, so a zero-length input makes the index underflow and reads one byte before the buffer. Trigger: input that getline returns as an empty string, such as a zero byte. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read (and an out-of-bounds write if that byte equals '\n'), leaking adjacent memory or corrupting it.

commit_msg:
mm: avoid setting up anonymous pages into file mapping

Reading page fault handler code I've noticed that under right
circumstances kernel would map anonymous pages into file mappings: if
the VMA doesn't have vm_ops->fault() and the VMA wasn't fully populated
on ->mmap(), kernel would handle page fault to not populated pte with
do_anonymous_page().

Let's change page fault handler to use do_anonymous_page() only on
anonymous VMA (->vm_ops == NULL) and make sure that the VMA is not
shared.

For file mappings without vm_ops->fault() or shred VMA without vm_ops,
page fault on pte_none() entry would lead to SIGBUS.

Signed-off-by: Kirill A. Shutemov <kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* File mapping without ->vm_ops ? */', '\tif (vma->vm_flags & VM_SHARED)', '\t\treturn VM_FAULT_SIGBUS;']}
description: mm/memory.c in the Linux kernel before 4.1.4 mishandles anonymous pages, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (page tainting) via a crafted application that triggers writing to page zero.

code_evidence: do_anonymous_page() is reached from the page-fault path for a pte_none entry and immediately installs an anonymous/zero page without first checking that the faulting VMA is actually an anonymous, non-shared mapping. Line 12 uses the zero page when not a write fault, and lines 15-18 map it via setpte, so a file mapping lacking vm_ops->fault() (or a shared VMA without vm_ops) gets an anonymous page inserted into a file-backed address space instead of being rejected.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a required property of its input (the VMA must be anonymous and non-shared) before processing, exactly the missing-constraint pattern of CWE-20. The added VM_SHARED guard confirms the missing validation; this is improper validation of input metadata, not a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function never validates the VMA type/shareability before treating the fault as anonymous. Trigger: a crafted application faults on an unpopulated pte of a file mapping without vm_ops->fault() or a shared VMA without vm_ops. Consequence: an anonymous/zero page is mapped into the file mapping, allowing page tainting and privilege escalation or denial of service.

commit_msg:
rfc7468: don't use for (;;) for tvb_find_line_end() loops.

If you're past the end of the tvbuff, tvb_find_line_end() will, when
reassembly is not being done, return a zero-length line without
advancing next_offset, so, unless you check for being past the end of
the tvbuff, you'll loop forever.

Fixes #17801.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for (;;) {', '    for (;;) {', '    for (;;) {'], 'added_lines': ['    while (tvb_offset_exists(tvb, offset)) {', '    while (tvb_offset_exists(tvb, offset)) {', '    while (tvb_offset_exists(tvb, offset)) {']}
description: Crash in the RFC 7468 dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 and 3.4.0 to 3.4.10 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: Each loop is entered unconditionally with for (;;) and only breaks when a boundary/blank-line check matches; the sole exit inside the body is when tvb_find_line_end returns -1.

When offset is past the end of the tvbuff (no reassembly), tvb_find_line_end returns a zero-length line and does not advance next_offset, so line_is_blank/line_is_eb tests never match and the loop repeats with the same offset.
The post-encapsulation loop additionally reallocs databuf and decodes base64 each iteration, so a past-end offset causes unbounded CPU/memory growth rather than termination.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: An iteration whose exit condition cannot be reached at past-end offsets is exactly CWE-835. The missing tvb_offset_exists guard is the unreachable-exit condition; this is not merely an off-by-one read (CWE-125) because the observable defect is non-termination.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loops lack a check that offset is within the tvbuff, relying only on tvb_find_line_end returning -1. Trigger: a crafted/injected packet whose line scanning reaches past the buffer end without a matching pre/post-encapsulation boundary. Consequence: the same offset is re-processed indefinitely, causing CPU (and, in the base64 loop, memory) exhaustion and denial of service.

commit_msg:
[DevTools] Copy objects from debugger context to inspected context properly.

BUG=637594

commit_msg:
Change devm_k*alloc to k*alloc to manually allocate memory

The manual allocation and freeing of memory is necessary because when
the USB radio is disconnected, the memory associated with devm_k*alloc
is freed. Meaning if we still have unresolved references to the radio
device, then we get use-after-free errors.

This patch fixes this by manually allocating memory, and freeing it in
the v4l2.release callback that gets called when the last radio device
exits.

Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+a4387f5b6b799f6becbf@syzkaller.appspotmail.com

Signed-off-by: Luke Nowakowski-Krijger <lnowakow@eng.ucsd.edu>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
[hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl: cleaned up two small checkpatch.pl warnings]
[hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl: prefix subject with driver name]
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+samsung@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tradio = devm_kzalloc(&intf->dev, sizeof(struct raremono_device), GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (radio)', '\t\tradio->buffer = devm_kmalloc(&intf->dev, BUFFER_LENGTH, GFP_KERNEL);', '', '\tif (!radio || !radio->buffer)', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\t\treturn retval;'], 'added_lines': ['\tradio = kzalloc(sizeof(*radio), GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (!radio)', '\tradio->buffer = kmalloc(BUFFER_LENGTH, GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (!radio->buffer) {', '\t\tkfree(radio);', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t}', '\t\tretval = -ENODEV;', '\t\tgoto free_mem;', '\t\tgoto free_mem;', '\tradio->v4l2_dev.release = raremono_device_release;', '', 'free_mem:', '\tkfree(radio->buffer);', '\tkfree(radio);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.6. There is a use-after-free caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/media/v4l2-core/v4l2-dev.c driver because drivers/media/radio/radio-raremono.c does not properly allocate memory.

code_evidence: Lines 6-10 allocate radio and radio->buffer with devm_kzalloc/devm_kmalloc, so both are owned by the interface device and freed automatically on disconnect.
Lines 20-23 return -ENODEV on a non-matching device without releasing the devm allocations.
Lines 27-30 return the v4l2_device_register error directly, again leaving the devm-managed objects to be freed on disconnect.

Lines 41-52 store radio in interface data and driver data, then register the video device; on failure the code only unregisters v4l2_dev and returns, leaving the device's references to radio while disconnect frees it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function leaves pointers to devm-allocated radio/buffer reachable after the device release frees that memory. The patch confirms this by switching to kzalloc/kmalloc with explicit kfree in a release callback, eliminating the dangling references.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: memory backing the radio device is devres-managed, so it is freed when the USB interface is disconnected, yet references (usb_set_intfdata, video_set_drvdata, registered v4l2/video structures) can outlive that free. Trigger: a malicious USB device that disconnects while unresolved references remain. Consequence: use-after-free with potential read/write of freed memory or crash.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that

commit_msg: Fixed bug #69090 (check cached files permissions)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifndef ZEND_WIN32', '\thash_value ^= ZCG(root_hash);', '#endif']}
description: An issue was discovered in PHP 5.x and 7.x, when the configuration uses apache2handler/mod_php or php-fpm with OpCache enabled. With 5.x after 5.6.28 or 7.x after 7.0.13, the issue is resolved in a non-default configuration with the opcache.validate_permission=1 setting. The vulnerability details are as follows. In PHP SAPIs where PHP interpreters share a common parent process, Zend OpCache creates a shared memory object owned by the common parent during initialization. Child PHP processes inherit the SHM descriptor, using it to cache and retrieve compiled script bytecode ("opcode" in PHP jargon). Cache keys vary depending on configuration, but filename is a central key component, and compiled opcode can generally be run if a script's filename is known or can be guessed. Many common shared-hosting configurations change EUID in child processes to enforce privilege separation among hosted users (for example using mod_ruid2 for the Apache HTTP Server, or php-fpm user settings). In these scenarios, the default Zend OpCache behavior defeats script file permissions by sharing a single SHM cache among all child PHP processes. PHP scripts often contain sensitive information: Think of CMS configurations where reading or running another user's script usually means gaining privileges to the CMS database.

code_evidence: The lookup key is reduced to a hash via zend_inline_hash_func and then modulo accel_hash->max_num_entries to select a bucket; no per-user or per-process identity, such as ZCG(root_hash), is mixed into the key.
Matching entries are accepted solely on hash_value, key_length and memcmp of key; on match the cached data is returned directly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's lookup does not incorporate the identity that distinguishes privileged users, so cached bytecode crosses permission boundaries; this is a permissions/access-control management weakness matching CWE-264, not merely a hash collision issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cache key and lookup ignore the calling process's privilege/root identity, so a shared SHM cache is searched with only filename-derived hashes. Trigger: a child process with a reduced EUID looks up a script whose filename is known or guessable. Supported consequence: it can retrieve another user's cached opcode, defeating script file permissions.

description: abrt-dbus in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) allows local users to delete or change the ownership of arbitrary files via the problem directory argument to the (1) ChownProblemDir, (2) DeleteElement, or (3) DeleteProblem method.

code_evidence: The function's only guard on the caller-supplied dirname is dir_is_in_dump_location, which merely checks the path prefix; it does not confirm the path is a direct sub-directory or a regular directory before the value is used downstream.

The privileged branch validates the dump directory with lstat, S_ISDIR, ownership and group checks, but this validation is applied only when g_settings_privatereports is true; the alternate else branch (line 36) delegates to dump_dir_accessible_by_uid without this stat-based validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing/incorrect validation of a caller-supplied path before it is processed, which is the core of CWE-20. It is not a canonicalization or encoding issue; the defect is that required properties (direct sub-directory, ownership) are not enforced on all paths.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dirname argument is trusted after a weak prefix check, and the stat-based ownership/type validation is conditional on g_settings_privatereports. Trigger: a caller supplies a path that passes the prefix check but is not a valid dump directory, when privatereports is disabled. Consequence: the path flows into dd_opendir, spawn_event_handler_child and delete_dump_dir without adequate validation, enabling access to unintended paths.

description: The ConnectionBase::preparseNewBytes function in resip/stack/ConnectionBase.cxx in reSIProcate through 1.10.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow) or possibly execute arbitrary code when TLS communication is enabled.

code_evidence: In the PartialBody state, mBufferPos is advanced by the attacker-influenced bytesRead, but the message is completed only when mBufferPos == contentLength; body data beyond contentLength in the same read is not accounted for and the buffer is handed off without any overhang handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a missing size constraint on the amount copied into the message body buffer: contentLength is trusted while the actual received data can be larger, and the copy/handoff at lines 282-283 proceeds without checking for overhang, matching CWE-120's unchecked input-size copy. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the excess data is written into the message buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a SIP body spans multiple reads and the final read contains more bytes than needed to reach contentLength, mBufferPos exceeds contentLength; the equality check at line 280 fails, so the overhang is never split off and the extra data is mishandled on the next processing pass, corrupting buffer state. This is the crash/overflow trigger described in the commit message.

commit_msg:
Fix a use-after-free in RegExp.prototype.compile

Fixes #4056.

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Dániel Bátyai daniel.batyai@h-lab.eu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* ecma_op_create_regexp_from_bytecode will never throw an error while re-initalizing the regexp object, so we', '     * can deref the old bytecode without leaving a dangling pointer. */', '    return ecma_op_create_regexp_from_bytecode (this_obj_p, bc_p);', '  ecma_value_t ret_value = ecma_op_create_regexp_from_pattern (this_obj_p, pattern_arg, flags_arg);'], 'added_lines': ['  ecma_value_t ret_value;', '    ret_value = ecma_op_create_regexp_from_bytecode (this_obj_p, bc_p);', '', '    return ret_value;', '  ret_value = ecma_op_create_regexp_from_pattern (this_obj_p, pattern_arg, flags_arg);']}
description: An issue was discovered in JerryScript 2.4.0. There is a heap-use-after-free in ecma_bytecode_ref in ecma-helpers.c file.

code_evidence: old_bc_p is loaded from re_obj_p->u.class_prop.u.value before the reinitialization. In the pattern-is-regexp branch, ecma_ref_object(this_obj_p) is called, then ecma_bytecode_deref frees old_bc_p, and only afterward ecma_op_create_regexp_from_bytecode(this_obj_p, bc_p) is invoked. If that call reads or reinitializes state holding the just-freed bytecode, it dereferences freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees old_bc_p via ecma_bytecode_deref and subsequently invokes a call that can still reference the freed bytecode through this_obj_p. This is a direct use-after-free, not merely a double free or null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the old compiled bytecode is dereferenced (freed) before ecma_op_create_regexp_from_bytecode completes reinitializing the regexp object, despite the removed comment assuming the call cannot throw or leave a dangling pointer. Trigger: calling RegExp.prototype.compile with a RegExp pattern. Consequence: heap use-after-free, potentially read/modify of freed memory, crash, or worse.

commit_msg:
In dm1105_probe, it called dm1105_ir_init and bound
&dm1105->ir.work with dm1105_emit_key.
When it handles IRQ request with dm1105_irq,
it may call schedule_work to start the work.

When we call dm1105_remove to remove the driver, there
may be a sequence as follows:

Fix it by finishing the work before cleanup in dm1105_remove

CPU0                  CPU1

                    |dm1105_emit_key
dm1105_remove      |
  dm1105_ir_exit       |
    rc_unregister_device |
    rc_free_device  |
    rc_dev_release  |
    kfree(dev);     |
                    |
                    | rc_keydown
                    |   //use

Fixes: 34d2f9bf189c ("V4L/DVB: dm1105: use dm1105_dev & dev instead of dm1105dvb")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcancel_work_sync(&dev->ir.work);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.2. A use-after-free was found in dm1105_remove in drivers/media/pci/dm1105/dm1105.c.

code_evidence: dm1105_remove frees the device with kfree(dev) at line 25 after calling dm1105_ir_exit at line 7, but the IR work item bound to dm1105_emit_key is never canceled or synchronized. The work may be scheduled by dm1105_irq and run concurrently during teardown, accessing dev after it is freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function tears down shared state concurrently with an asynchronously scheduled work item without exclusivity, a race between remove and the IR work path. This fits CWE-362; the use-after-free is the consequence of the unsynchronized concurrent access, not a separate labeling target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: teardown does not synchronize with the pending IR work before releasing resources and freeing dev. Trigger: an IRQ schedules the work while dm1105_remove runs; the work executes after rc_unregister_device/kfree releases the device. Consequence: use-after-free of dev in the work callback, causing instability or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix empty inputs for Upper/LowerBound.

For upper/lower-bound searches via `tf.searchsorted`, if the sorted input is empty,
the previous code resulted in a `nullptr` dereference.  For emtpy inputs, any
sorted search should return a value of 0, meaning that a value would be inserted
into the first slot of the array.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 460971165
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    // For empty inputs, all values will be placed at the zeroth position.', '    if (sorted_inputs.size() == 0) {', '      functor::SetZeroFunctor<Device, OutType> set_zero;', '      set_zero(ctx->eigen_device<Device>(), output);', '      return;', '    }', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. If `LowerBound` or `UpperBound` is given an empty`sorted_inputs` input, it results in a `nullptr` dereference, leading to a segfault that can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit bce3717eaef4f769019fd18e990464ca4a2efeea. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: sorted_inputs and values are flattened views of the input tensors; when sorted_inputs_t is empty, the flat view holds no elements. The call to LowerBoundFunctor::Compute is made unconditionally with sorted_inputs_t.dim_size(0) and dim_size(1) as sizes, so the functor receives a zero-length input.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing empty-input guard lets the functor dereference a null data pointer, matching CWE-476's null dereference with availability impact. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the failure is dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no guard for an empty sorted_inputs tensor before invoking the lower-bound functor, which assumes at least one element is present and dereferences the underlying data pointer. Trigger: a caller supplies a sorted_inputs tensor with zero elements. Consequence: a NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (segfault), i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* check directory for duplicate names.  Need to sort directory first */', '\tsort_directory(dir);', '\tif(check_directory(dir) == FALSE) {', '\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: directory has duplicate names\\n");', '\t\tgoto corrupted;', '\t}']}
description: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

code_evidence: The function reads directory entries and builds a linked list of dir_ent nodes, storing each entry's name via strdup(dire->name) at line 82 along with its type, start_block and offset. It validates individual names with check_name (line 72) but never checks whether two entries share the same name within the directory before returning the list.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-59: file access (writing the later duplicate entry) is performed by name without preventing that name from resolving through a symlink to an unintended resource. The missing duplicate-name constraint is what enables the link to be followed; the fix adds sort_directory and check_directory to close this gap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: squashfs_opendir builds a directory listing without rejecting duplicate filenames, so a crafted filesystem can hold a symlink entry and a same-named regular file entry. The caller processes the symlink first, creating a link pointing outside the destination, then writes through the identical name, following the link. Consequence: files are written outside the destination directory.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>

Message-id: 20170213135235.12274-8-pbonzini@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    nbd_coroutine_end(client, &request);'], 'added_lines': ['    nbd_coroutine_end(bs, &request);']}
description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

code_evidence: When the BDRV_REQ_FUA flag is set, the function asserts that the negotiated server flags include NBD_FLAG_SEND_FUA before setting the FUA request flag.
A second assert enforces bytes <= NBD_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE on the caller-supplied request length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 applies because the function contains reachable assert() statements whose failure exits the application when input/state violates the assumed invariant. This is a reachable-assertion availability weakness, distinct from a memory-safety bug that the assertion might otherwise guard against.

evidence_lines.code: assert(bytes <= NBD_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function assumes the client session's negotiated flags and the request size satisfy its internal invariants. If a peer or caller drives a write with BDRV_REQ_FUA while NBD_FLAG_SEND_FUA was not negotiated, or with a length exceeding NBD_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE, the assert aborts the process. The reachable abort terminates the qemu-nbd server, causing denial of service rather than a controlled error return.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13690/IKEv2: Fix some bounds checks.

Use a pointer of the correct type in ND_TCHECK(), or use ND_TCHECK2()
and provide the correct length.

While we're at it, remove the blank line between some checks and the
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY()s they protect.

Also, note the places where we print the entire payload.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* Print the entire payload in hex */']}
description: The IKEv2 parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: ND_TCHECK(*ext) validates only sizeof(struct isakmp_gen) bytes for the base header, then UNALIGNED_MEMCPY copies sizeof(e) from ext, which is the same header size, so e.len is attacker-controlled from the wire.
The length check only tests 4 < ntohs(e.len); rawprint then reads ntohs(e.len) - 4 bytes starting at ext + 1 without verifying that many bytes remain in the captured buffer.
The return advances by ntohs(e.len) without confirming the payload length fits in the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads beyond the intended buffer because it trusts an unvalidated length field, which is exactly CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not an out-of-bounds write, since no data is written past the buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
ND_TCHECK(*ext);
UNALIGNED_MEMCPY(&e, ext, sizeof(e));
return (const u_char *)ext + ntohs(e.len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header length field e.len is trusted as a payload size without a bounds check against the actual captured data. Trigger: a crafted IKEv1 VID payload declaring a length larger than the available bytes. Consequence: rawprint and the pointer arithmetic read past the end of the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds over-read (crash/DoS and potential memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
Release "3.0.6": Fix crashes in Array for "integer overflow #10"

FossilOrigin-Name: 50642d64b8f0a4e62df68e59fcb2ef0923c3dbec8fc8a15d38b1ddbe655c38d6
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    n = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, obj);', '        Jsi_ObjSetLength(interp, obj, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    n = jsi_SizeOfArray(interp, obj);', '        Jsi_ObjSetLength(interp, obj, curlen=0);']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjSetLength in jsish before 3.0.6, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 13 obtains the array length n and copies it to curlen without bounding it; the patch replaces Jsi_ObjGetLength with jsi_SizeOfArray, indicating the raw length could be negative/oversized.
Lines 32-36 compute rhowmany = n-istart and then overwrite it from the caller-supplied howmany, clamping only to n-istart; a negative or huge nstart/nhow feeds directly into loop bounds.

Lines 60-65 compute curlen -= j and newlen = curlen + argc - ... then call Jsi_ObjArraySizer(interp, obj, newlen+3); newlen+3 is an int arithmetic result used as an allocation/size argument with no overflow check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is integer arithmetic on lengths that can wrap before use as an allocation size, exactly CWE-190; the wrapped value then drives array sizing and indexing. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the unsafe operation is the unchecked signed addition feeding the sizer.

evidence_lines.code:
n = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, obj);
curlen = n;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: array length and splice counts (curlen, argc, ilen) are combined in signed int arithmetic (newlen = curlen + argc - ...) and passed as newlen+3 to Jsi_ObjArraySizer without overflow validation. Trigger: a large array length or splice count causes the sum to wrap negative. Consequence: undersized allocation followed by indexed writes at lines 68-69/79, yielding memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: Prevent buffer overflow in BMP coder (bug report from pwchen of tencent).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    bmp_info.image_size=(unsigned int) (bytes_per_line*image->rows);'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((image->columns != (signed int) image->columns) ||', '        (image->rows != (signed int) image->rows))', '      ThrowWriterException(ImageError,"WidthOrHeightExceedsLimit");', '    bmp_info.image_size=(unsigned long) (bytes_per_line*image->rows);']}
description: Integer overflow in the BMP coder in ImageMagick before 7.0.2-10 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via crafted height and width values, which triggers an out-of-bounds write.

code_evidence: Line 117 computes bytes_per_line as 4*((image->columns*bmp_info.bits_per_pixel+31)/32) using size_t arithmetic; with attacker-controlled large columns this multiplication can wrap.
Line 150 casts the product bytes_per_line*image->rows to unsigned int for bmp_info.image_size, truncating the size, and line 151 adds that truncated value to file_size.
Lines 171-176 allocate and zero only bmp_info.image_size bytes, while later pixel loops (e.g., lines 278-285, 303-312) write bytes_per_line per row for image->rows rows, exceeding the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an integer overflow/wraparound in a size calculation whose result is assumed to remain valid; the truncated size is then used for allocation and copying, matching CWE-190. The out-of-bounds write is the consequence, not the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: bytes_per_line=4*((image->columns*bmp_info.bits_per_pixel+31)/32);

bmp_info.image_size=(unsigned int) (bytes_per_line*image->rows);
bmp_info.file_size+=bmp_info.image_size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked arithmetic on attacker-supplied width/height: bytes_per_line*image->rows is computed in size_t then truncated to unsigned int at line 150, producing a small image_size. The buffer is allocated and zeroed using this truncated size (lines 171-176), but the per-row writing loops use the true bytes_per_line and image->rows, so writes run past the allocation, causing an out-of-bounds write and crash/corruption.

commit_msg:
net/vmxnet3: Refine l2 header validation

Validation of l2 header length assumed minimal packet size as
eth_header + 2 * vlan_header regardless of the actual protocol.

This caused crash for valid non-IP packets shorter than 22 bytes, as
'tx_pkt->packet_type' hasn't been assigned for such packets, and
'vmxnet3_on_tx_done_update_stats()' expects it to be properly set.

Refine header length validation in 'vmxnet_tx_pkt_parse_headers'.
Check its return value during packet processing flow.

As a side effect, in case IPv4 and IPv6 header validation failure,
corrupt packets will be dropped.

Signed-off-by: Dana Rubin <dana.rubin@ravellosystems.com>
Signed-off-by: Shmulik Ladkani <shmulik.ladkani@ravellosystems.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (bytes_read < ETH_MAX_L2_HDR_LEN) {', '    } else {', '        l2_hdr->iov_len = eth_get_l2_hdr_length(l2_hdr->iov_base);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (bytes_read < sizeof(struct eth_header)) {', '    }', '', '    l2_hdr->iov_len = sizeof(struct eth_header);', '    switch (be16_to_cpu(PKT_GET_ETH_HDR(l2_hdr->iov_base)->h_proto)) {', '    case ETH_P_VLAN:', '        l2_hdr->iov_len += sizeof(struct vlan_header);', '        break;', '    case ETH_P_DVLAN:', '        l2_hdr->iov_len += 2 * sizeof(struct vlan_header);', '        break;', '    }', '', '    if (bytes_read < l2_hdr->iov_len) {', '        l2_hdr->iov_len = 0;', '        return false;']}
description: QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) built with a VMWARE VMXNET3 paravirtual NIC emulator support is vulnerable to crash issue. It occurs when a guest sends a Layer-2 packet smaller than 22 bytes. A privileged (CAP_SYS_RAWIO) guest user could use this flaw to crash the QEMU process instance resulting in DoS.

code_evidence: The function reads up to ETH_MAX_L2_HDR_LEN bytes from the guest-supplied packet into l2_hdr->iov_base and rejects the packet only when bytes_read < ETH_MAX_L2_HDR_LEN. Otherwise it derives l2_hdr->iov_len from eth_get_l2_hdr_length() on the raw buffer, without checking that the guest-provided L2 length is consistent with the actual bytes read or with the protocol implied by the header.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is improper validation of guest-supplied packet input: the code does not verify that the header length is consistent with the actual data and protocol before processing. This is an input-validation weakness (CWE-20), not a mere bounds error, because the missing constraint on derived metadata enables the crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the L2 header length is computed from packet contents and assumed valid once a fixed 22-byte read succeeds, so short non-IP packets pass validation with an unset/inconsistent packet type. Trigger: a privileged guest sends a Layer-2 packet smaller than 22 bytes. Consequence: downstream code such as vmxnet3_on_tx_done_update_stats() dereferences the unassigned tx_pkt->packet_type, crashing the QEMU process (DoS).

commit_msg:
io_uring/fdinfo: lock SQ thread while retrieving thread cpu/pid

We could race with SQ thread exit, and if we do, we'll hit a NULL pointer
dereference when the thread is cleared. Grab the SQPOLL data lock before
attempting to get the task cpu and pid for fdinfo, this ensures we have a
stable view of it.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=218032
Reviewed-by: Gabriel Krisman Bertazi <krisman@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct io_sq_data *sq = NULL;', '\t\tsq = ctx->sq_data;', '\t\tif (!sq->thread)', '\t\t\tsq = NULL;', '\tseq_printf(m, "SqThread:\\t%d\\n", sq ? task_pid_nr(sq->thread) : -1);', '\tseq_printf(m, "SqThreadCpu:\\t%d\\n", sq ? task_cpu(sq->thread) : -1);'], 'added_lines': ['\tint sq_pid = -1, sq_cpu = -1;', '\t\tstruct io_sq_data *sq = ctx->sq_data;', '', '\t\tif (mutex_trylock(&sq->lock)) {', '\t\t\tif (sq->thread) {', '\t\t\t\tsq_pid = task_pid_nr(sq->thread);', '\t\t\t\tsq_cpu = task_cpu(sq->thread);', '\t\t\t}', '\t\t\tmutex_unlock(&sq->lock);', '\t\t}', '\tseq_printf(m, "SqThread:\\t%d\\n", sq_pid);', '\tseq_printf(m, "SqThreadCpu:\\t%d\\n", sq_cpu);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.5.9. During a race with SQ thread exit, an io_uring/fdinfo.c io_uring_show_fdinfo NULL pointer dereference can occur.

code_evidence: After mutex_trylock(&ctx->uring_lock), the SQPOLL branch reads ctx->sq_data into sq and checks sq->thread without holding sq->lock. The check at line 76 and the later dereferences task_pid_nr(sq->thread)/task_cpu(sq->thread) at lines 79-80 are not atomic with SQ thread exit, so sq->thread can be cleared between the check and use, yielding a NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences a pointer (sq->thread) that can become NULL due to the race, matching CWE-476. It is not merely an unchecked return; the check exists but is racy, so the NULL dereference is the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a missing synchronization on sq->lock around reading and using sq->thread, allowing a race with SQ thread exit. Trigger: fdinfo read concurrent with SQPOLL thread teardown; the thread pointer is cleared after the NULL check, and task_pid_nr/task_cpu dereference NULL, causing a kernel crash (DoS).

eap, line_to_free) == FAIL)

commit_msg:
drm/amd/display: prevent memory leak

In dcn*_create_resource_pool the allocated memory should be released if
construct pool fails.

Reviewed-by: Harry Wentland <harry.wentland@amd.com>
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alex Deucher <alexander.deucher@amd.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tkfree(pool);']}
description: Memory leaks in *create_resource_pool() functions under drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc in the Linux kernel through 5.3.11 allow attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption). This affects the dce120_create_resource_pool() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce120/dce120_resource.c, the dce110_create_resource_pool() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce110/dce110_resource.c, the dce100_create_resource_pool() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce100/dce100_resource.c, the dcn10_create_resource_pool() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dcn10/dcn10_resource.c, and the dce112_create_resource_pool() function in drivers/gpu/drm/amd/display/dc/dce112/dce112_resource.c, aka CID-104c307147ad.

code_evidence: Line 5-6 allocates 'pool' with kzalloc and stores the only reference. If construct() fails at line 9, the function takes the line 11-12 path and returns NULL without freeing 'pool', so the allocated memory becomes unreachable and leaks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory is allocated and remains unreleased after its effective lifetime on the error path. This is a missing release in this function, not a use-after-free or double-free.

Trigger: construct(num_virtual_links, dc, pool) returns nonzero, which is the error condition. Consequence: the resource pool allocation is lost on each failed call, causing repeated leaks and memory exhaustion (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix an integer overflow in opj_tcd_get_decoded_tile_size().

Based on suggested patch by reporter.
BUG=629919

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2182683002
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (*p_data_size == (OPJ_UINT32)-1) {', '                return OPJ_FALSE;', '        }', '']}
description: Integer overflow in the opj_tcd_get_decoded_tile_size function in tcd.c in OpenJPEG, as used in PDFium in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JPEG 2000 data.

code_evidence: Line 184 assigns the result of opj_tcd_get_decoded_tile_size() into *p_data_size without checking whether the computation overflowed; the commit adds a sentinel check for (OPJ_UINT32)-1 immediately after this call, confirming the returned size can wrap. Line 185 then reads tile geometry fields from the same tile structure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer wraparound in a size calculation that is assumed to remain valid; the caller uses the wrapped value as a data size, matching CWE-190. It is distinct from a mere missing bounds check because the arithmetic itself overflows, and the added sentinel check directly guards that overflow outcome.

*p_tile_x0 = p_j2k->m_tcd->tcd_image->tiles->x0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoded tile size computed from attacker-controlled JPEG 2000 tile dimensions/components can wrap in 32-bit arithmetic, yielding a very small or sentinel value. Trigger: crafted codestream producing large tile dimensions. Consequence: the undersized size is later used for buffer sizing, leading to heap-based buffer overflow / DoS. The fix rejects the (OPJ_UINT32)-1 sentinel before returning success.

commit_msg:
run: Only compare the lowest 32 ioctl arg bits for TIOCSTI

Closes #2782.

Closes: #2783
Approved by: alexlarsson
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    {SCMP_SYS (ioctl), &SCMP_A1 (SCMP_CMP_EQ, (int) TIOCSTI)},'], 'added_lines': ['    {SCMP_SYS (ioctl), &SCMP_A1 (SCMP_CMP_MASKED_EQ, 0xFFFFFFFFu, (int) TIOCSTI)},']}
description: Flatpak before 1.0.8, 1.1.x and 1.2.x before 1.2.4, and 1.3.x before 1.3.1 allows a sandbox bypass. Flatpak versions since 0.8.1 address CVE-2017-5226 by using a seccomp filter to prevent sandboxed apps from using the TIOCSTI ioctl, which could otherwise be used to inject commands into the controlling terminal so that they would be executed outside the sandbox after the sandboxed app exits. This fix was incomplete: on 64-bit platforms, the seccomp filter could be bypassed by an ioctl request number that has TIOCSTI in its 32 least significant bits and an arbitrary nonzero value in its 32 most significant bits, which the Linux kernel would treat as equivalent to TIOCSTI.

code_evidence: Line 33 defines the seccomp blacklist rule for ioctl using SCMP_A1(SCMP_CMP_EQ, (int) TIOCSTI), an exact 64-bit equality comparison on argument 1.
Lines 107-108 install this arg-filtered rule via seccomp_rule_add, so only an ioctl request equal to TIOCSTI is blocked; a request differing in high bits is not matched.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The filter fails to validate all relevant bits of the ioctl request input, accepting a nonconforming value as safe; this is improper input validation (CWE-20). The consequence is a security-control bypass, distinct from the later command injection itself.

evidence_lines.code: {SCMP_SYS (ioctl), &SCMP_A1 (SCMP_CMP_EQ, (int) TIOCSTI)},

if (syscall_blacklist[i].arg)
r = seccomp_rule_add (seccomp, SCMP_ACT_ERRNO (EPERM), scall, 1, *syscall_blacklist[i].arg);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an exact-equality comparison of the ioctl request against TIOCSTI, which fails to account for the kernel treating request numbers with the same low 32 bits as equivalent. A sandboxed process can issue such a crafted request to bypass the filter and inject terminal input, escaping the sandbox.
