commit_msg:
The syzbot fuzzer found a bug in the p54 USB wireless driver.  The
issue involves a race between disconnect and the firmware-loader
callback routine, and it has several aspects.

One big problem is that when the firmware can't be loaded, the
callback routine tries to unbind the driver from the USB _device_ (by
calling device_release_driver) instead of from the USB _interface_ to
which it is actually bound (by calling usb_driver_release_interface).

The race involves access to the private data structure.  The driver's
disconnect handler waits for a completion that is signalled by the
firmware-loader callback routine.  As soon as the completion is
signalled, you have to assume that the private data structure may have
been deallocated by the disconnect handler -- even if the firmware was
loaded without errors.  However, the callback routine does access the
private data several times after that point.

Another problem is that, in order to ensure that the USB device
structure hasn't been freed when the callback routine runs, the driver
takes a reference to it.  This isn't good enough any more, because now
that the callback routine calls usb_driver_release_interface, it has
to ensure that the interface structure hasn't been freed.

Finally, the driver takes an unnecessary reference to the USB device
structure in the probe function and drops the reference in the
disconnect handler.  This extra reference doesn't accomplish anything,
because the USB core already guarantees that a device structure won't
be deallocated while a driver is still bound to any of its interfaces.

To fix these problems, this patch makes the following changes:

	Call usb_driver_release_interface() rather than
	device_release_driver().

	Don't signal the completion until after the important
	information has been copied out of the private data structure,
	and don't refer to the private data at all thereafter.

	Lock udev (the interface's parent) before unbinding the driver
	instead of locking udev->parent.

	During the firmware loading process, take a reference to the
	USB interface instead of the USB device.

	Don't take an unnecessary reference to the device during probe
	(and then don't drop it during disconnect).

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+200d4bb11b23d929335f@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Acked-by: Christian Lamparter <chunkeey@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tusb_get_dev(udev);', '\tif (err) {', '\t\tusb_put_dev(udev);', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (err)']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.1. There is a use-after-free caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/net/wireless/intersil/p54/p54usb.c driver.

code_evidence: The probe stores the interface and device pointers in the private structure (priv->udev, priv->intf) and takes an extra usb_get_dev(udev) reference at line 22.
After p54u_load_firmware returns, the error path calls usb_put_dev(udev) and p54_free_common(dev), dropping the device reference and freeing the private data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function establishes the shared private-data/device-pointer state and reference lifetime that the disconnect/firmware-callback race later misuses, matching CWE-416 use-after-free rather than a simple double-free or NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The probe takes a reference to the USB device but not to the interface, and the firmware-loading callback can race with disconnect; disconnect waits on a completion and may free the private structure while the callback still dereferences priv->udev and priv->intf. The stale references then access freed memory.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Rewrite guest %cr4 handling from scratch

The PV cr4 logic is almost impossible to follow, and leaks bits into guest
context which definitely shouldn't be visible (in particular, VMXE).

The biggest problem however, and source of the complexity, is that it derives
new real and guest cr4 values from the current value in hardware - this is
context dependent and an inappropriate source of information.

Rewrite the cr4 logic to be invariant of the current value in hardware.

First of all, modify write_ptbase() to always use mmu_cr4_features for IDLE
and HVM contexts.  mmu_cr4_features *is* the correct value to use, and makes
the ASSERT() obviously redundant.

For PV guests, curr->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] remains the guests view of cr4, but
all logic gets reworked in terms of this and mmu_cr4_features only.

Two masks are introduced; bits which the guest has control over, and bits
which are forwarded from Xen's settings.  One guest-visible change here is
that Xen's VMXE setting is no longer visible at all.

pv_make_cr4() follows fairly closely from pv_guest_cr4_to_real_cr4(), but
deliberately starts with mmu_cr4_features, and only alters the minimal subset
of bits.

The boot-time {compat_,}pv_cr4_mask variables are removed, as they are a
remnant of the pre-CPUID policy days.  pv_fixup_guest_cr4() gains a related
derivation from the policy.

Another guest visible change here is that a 32bit PV guest can now flip
FSGSBASE in its view of CR4.  While the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE instructions are
unusable outside of a 64bit code segment, the ability to modify FSGSBASE
matches real hardware behaviour, and avoids the need for any 32bit/64bit
differences in the logic.

Overall, this patch shouldn't have a practical change in guest behaviour.
VMXE will disappear from view, and an inquisitive 32bit kernel can now see
FSGSBASE changing, but this new logic is otherwise bug-compatible with before.

This is part of XSA-293.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        curr->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] = pv_guest_cr4_fixup(curr, val);', '        write_cr4(pv_guest_cr4_to_real_cr4(curr));'], 'added_lines': ['        curr->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4] = pv_fixup_guest_cr4(curr, val);', '        write_cr4(pv_make_cr4(curr));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: Case 4 handles a guest write to CR4: the guest-supplied val is passed to pv_guest_cr4_fixup() and stored in curr->arch.pv.ctrlreg[4], then the resulting real CR4 is written via write_cr4(pv_guest_cr4_to_real_cr4(curr)). The guest controls val, and the fixup/derivation is the only constraint applied before the value becomes the guest's view of CR4 and is loaded into hardware.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts guest-controlled CR4 input and relies on fixup/derivation rather than validating that the resulting bit set is safe, which is the improper-validation-of-input pattern described by CWE-20; the weakness is the missing/incorrect constraint on the guest-supplied value, not a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guest's CR4 value is derived from a context-dependent source and the fixup/forwarding logic does not correctly constrain which bits the guest may set, so guest-controlled CR4 bits leak into the real/hardware value. Trigger: a PV guest issuing a CR4 write with crafted bits. Supported consequence: guest can manipulate virtualised %cr4 incompatibly with the guest kernel, giving DoS or privilege escalation.

Added a bunch of `assert(b)`'s to address CVE-2018-17073
See https://github.com/wernsey/bitmap/issues/1

description: wernsey/bitmap before 2018-08-18 allows a NULL pointer dereference via a 4-bit image.

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The security vulnerability results in FractionalMax(AVG)Pool with illegal pooling_ratio. Attackers using Tensorflow can exploit the vulnerability. They can access heap memory which is not in the control of user, leading to a crash or remote code execution. commit_msg:
The function l2cap_get_conf_opt will return L2CAP_CONF_OPT_SIZE + opt->len
as length value. The opt->len however is in control over the remote user
and can be used by an attacker to gain access beyond the bounds of the
actual packet.

To prevent any potential leak of heap memory, it is enough to check that
the resulting len calculation after calling l2cap_get_conf_opt is not
below zero. A well formed packet will always return >= 0 here and will
end with the length value being zero after the last option has been
parsed. In case of malformed packets messing with the opt->len field the
length value will become negative. If that is the case, then just abort
and ignore the option.

In case an attacker uses a too short opt->len value, then garbage will
be parsed, but that is protected by the unknown option handling and also
the option parameter size checks.

Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hedberg <johan.hedberg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (len < 0)', '\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: A heap address information leak while using L2CAP_GET_CONF_OPT was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.1-rc1.

code_evidence: The loop condition checks len >= L2CAP_CONF_OPT_SIZE, then subtracts the return value of l2cap_get_conf_opt, which is L2CAP_CONF_OPT_SIZE + opt->len with opt->len controlled by the remote packet; without the added len < 0 check, a large opt->len makes len negative while the loop still proceeds into the switch.

For L2CAP_CONF_RFC, if olen equals sizeof(rfc), memcpy copies olen bytes from val into the local rfc struct; val points into the received buffer, so an oversized olen can copy beyond the buffer's actual bounds.
For L2CAP_CONF_EWS, txwin_ext is set from val when olen == 2, reading a value derived from the same attacker-controlled buffer region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the intended received buffer (memcpy from val and val-derived txwin_ext) because the length accounting permits negative len. This is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); it is not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: l2cap_get_conf_opt returns a length computed from the attacker-controlled opt->len, so the running len can go negative; the loop then continues parsing subsequent options and memcpy/val reads occur at offsets beyond the actual received packet buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read that leaks heap memory.

commit_msg:
USB: core: harden cdc_parse_cdc_header

Andrey Konovalov reported a possible out-of-bounds problem for the
cdc_parse_cdc_header function.  He writes:
	It looks like cdc_parse_cdc_header() doesn't validate buflen
	before accessing buffer[1], buffer[2] and so on. The only check
	present is while (buflen > 0).

So fix this issue up by properly validating the buffer length matches
what the descriptor says it is.

Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t}', '\t\tif ((buflen < elength) || (elength < 3)) {', '\t\t\tdev_err(&intf->dev, "invalid descriptor buffer length\\n");', '\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: The cdc_parse_cdc_header function in drivers/usb/core/message.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device.

code_evidence: The loop condition only checks buflen > 0, then reads buffer[1] and buffer[2] without verifying that two or three bytes remain in the buffer.
After processing, buflen is decremented by elength and buffer is advanced by elength, so a descriptor length larger than the remaining buflen can drive subsequent iterations past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory locations outside the supplied buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write, but it still falls within the buffer-boundary class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts the descriptor length byte (buffer[0]) and accesses buffer[1]/buffer[2] with only a buflen > 0 guard. A crafted USB descriptor with a short or oversized length causes out-of-bounds reads at the initial accesses and after advancing buffer, leading to a kernel crash or undefined read impact.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The API of `tf.raw_ops.SparseCross` allows combinations which would result in a `CHECK`-failure and denial of service. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/3d782b7d47b1bf2ed32bd4a246d6d6cadc4c903d/tensorflow/core/kernels/sparse_cross_op.cc#L114-L116) is tricked to consider a tensor of type `tstring` which in fact contains integral elements. Fixing the type confusion by preventing mixing `DT_STRING` and `DT_INT64` types solves this issue. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

The shapes loop reads shapes_list_in[i].vec<int64>() at line 46 without verifying that the shape tensor's dtype is DT_INT64, so a tstring-backed tensor is interpreted as int64.
The dense loop checks only that each dense tensor is a matrix; it does not verify dtype against the expected string internal type.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: ValidateInput trusts caller-supplied tensors' declared shapes but not their actual element types. A tstring tensor containing integral elements passes validation and later is accessed via vec<int64>(), so the buffer is reinterpreted with an incompatible type; the mismatch triggers a CHECK failure and denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                    /* Check, if fragment is still small enough to fit datagram size.', '                     * `offset` is 0, as this is the first fragment so it does not have to be added', '                     * here. */', '                    if (frag_size > entry.super->datagram_size) {', '                        DEBUG_PUTS(', '                           "6lo rfrag: fragment too big for resulting datagram, "', '                           "discarding datagram\\n"', '                        );', '                        gnrc_pktbuf_release(entry.rbuf->pkt);', '                        gnrc_pktbuf_release(pkt);', '                        gnrc_sixlowpan_frag_rb_remove(entry.rbuf);', '                        return RBUF_ADD_ERROR;', '                    }']}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. In version 2023.01 and prior, an attacker can send a crafted frame to the device resulting in an out of bounds write in the packet buffer. The overflow can be used to corrupt other packets and the allocator metadata. Corrupting a pointer will easily lead to denial of service. While carefully manipulating the allocator metadata gives an attacker the possibility to write data to arbitrary locations and thus execute arbitrary code. This issue is fixed in pull request 19680. As a workaround, disable support for fragmented IP datagrams.

code_evidence: For SFR first fragments (offset 0), line 152 decrements entry.super->datagram_size without verifying that the first fragment's frag_size still fits the reduced datagram size.

Line 158 resizes the reassembly buffer based on the (now smaller) datagram_size, then line 164 memcpy's frag_size bytes at offset into entry.rbuf->pkt->data, so frag_size can exceed the buffer capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a memcpy whose length (frag_size) can exceed the destination buffer size derived from datagram_size, writing past the end of the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), distinct from a mere integer underflow since the write itself crosses the buffer boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SFR branch shrinks datagram_size by one but never checks frag_size against it, so the reassembly buffer is sized too small. Trigger: an attacker sends a crafted first 6LoWPAN SFR fragment whose payload exceeds the decremented datagram size. Consequence: the memcpy at line 164 writes past the allocated packet buffer, corrupting adjacent packets or allocator metadata, enabling DoS and potentially arbitrary code execution.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. A `GraphDef` from a TensorFlow `SavedModel` can be maliciously altered to cause a TensorFlow process to crash due to encountering a `StatusOr` value that is an error and forcibly extracting the value from it. We have patched the issue in multiple GitHub commits and these will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0 and TensorFlow 2.7.1, as both are affected.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-754 fits because the function fails to check an unusual/exceptional error condition (a failed StatusOr) before proceeding, and the unchecked condition causes a crash. This is a missing check, not merely incorrect error propagation; the fix adds the explicit !ctor_type.ok() guard.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return status of full_type::SpecializeType is not checked before ValueOrDie() is called. Trigger: a maliciously altered GraphDef node whose attributes cause type specialization to fail, producing an error StatusOr. commit_msg:
net: mcf: limit buffer descriptor count

ColdFire Fast Ethernet Controller uses buffer descriptors to manage
data flow to/fro receive & transmit queues. While transmitting
packets, it could continue to read buffer descriptors if a buffer
descriptor has length of zero and has crafted values in bd.flags.
Set upper limit to number of buffer descriptors.

Reported-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Reviewed-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jason Wang <jasowang@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int len;', '    while (1) {'], 'added_lines': ['    int len, descnt = 0;', '    while (descnt++ < FEC_MAX_DESC) {']}
description: The mcf_fec_do_tx function in hw/net/mcf_fec.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) does not properly limit the buffer descriptor count when transmitting packets, which allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and QEMU process crash) via vectors involving a buffer descriptor with a length of 0 and crafted values in bd.flags.

code_evidence: The transmit loop is entered with an unconditional `while (1)`, so loop termination depends entirely on the in-loop break condition.
The only exit is the `break` when `(bd.flags & FEC_BD_R) == 0`; a descriptor that keeps FEC_BD_R set never triggers it.

`len = bd.length` is not checked for zero, and the `frame_size + len > FEC_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` clamp only bounds oversized lengths, so a zero-length descriptor passes through without advancing frame_size.
Descriptor advancement is driven by `bd.flags`: when FEC_BD_W is clear, `addr += 8`; the guest-crafted flags can keep the loop re-reading descriptors indefinitely.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the iteration's exit condition is not reachable for crafted descriptor flags, producing an unbounded loop. This is a loop-termination defect, not merely an out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code: while (1) {

if ((bd.flags & FEC_BD_R) == 0) {
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop lacks any bound on descriptor iterations and relies solely on guest-controlled bd.flags to terminate. A zero-length descriptor with crafted flags keeps the FEC_BD_R bit set, so the loop never reaches its break and repeatedly reads descriptors, causing an infinite loop and QEMU process hang/crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
jbd2: fix use-after-free of transaction_t race

jbd2_journal_wait_updates() is called with j_state_lock held. But if
there is a commit in progress, then this transaction might get committed
and freed via jbd2_journal_commit_transaction() ->
jbd2_journal_free_transaction(), when we release j_state_lock.
So check for journal->j_running_transaction everytime we release and
acquire j_state_lock to avoid use-after-free issue.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/948c2fed518ae739db6a8f7f83f1d58b504f87d0.1644497105.git.ritesh.list@gmail.com
Fixes: 4f98186848707f53 ("jbd2: refactor wait logic for transaction updates into a common function")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+afa2ca5171d93e44b348@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Signed-off-by: Ritesh Harjani <riteshh@linux.ibm.com>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttransaction_t *commit_transaction = journal->j_running_transaction;', '\tif (!commit_transaction)', '\t\treturn;', '\tspin_lock(&commit_transaction->t_handle_lock);', '\twhile (atomic_read(&commit_transaction->t_updates)) {', '\t\tDEFINE_WAIT(wait);', '\t\t\t\t\tTASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE);', '\t\tif (atomic_read(&commit_transaction->t_updates)) {', '\t\t\tspin_unlock(&commit_transaction->t_handle_lock);', '\t\t\twrite_unlock(&journal->j_state_lock);', '\t\t\tschedule();', '\t\t\twrite_lock(&journal->j_state_lock);', '\t\t\tspin_lock(&commit_transaction->t_handle_lock);', '\tspin_unlock(&commit_transaction->t_handle_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tDEFINE_WAIT(wait);', '\twhile (1) {', '\t\t/*', '\t\t * Note that the running transaction can get freed under us if', '\t\t * this transaction is getting committed in', '\t\t * jbd2_journal_commit_transaction() ->', '\t\t * jbd2_journal_free_transaction(). This can only happen when we', '\t\t * release j_state_lock -> schedule() -> acquire j_state_lock.', '\t\t * Hence we should everytime retrieve new j_running_transaction', '\t\t * value (after j_state_lock release acquire cycle), else it may', '\t\t * lead to use-after-free of old freed transaction.', '\t\t */', '\t\ttransaction_t *transaction = journal->j_running_transaction;', '\t\tif (!transaction)', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tspin_lock(&transaction->t_handle_lock);', '\t\t\t\tTASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE);', '\t\tif (!atomic_read(&transaction->t_updates)) {', '\t\t\tspin_unlock(&transaction->t_handle_lock);', '\t\t\tfinish_wait(&journal->j_wait_updates, &wait);', '\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\tspin_unlock(&transaction->t_handle_lock);', '\t\twrite_unlock(&journal->j_state_lock);', '\t\tschedule();', '\t\twrite_lock(&journal->j_state_lock);']}
description: jbd2_journal_wait_updates in fs/jbd2/transaction.c in the Linux kernel before 5.17.1 has a use-after-free caused by a transaction_t race condition.

code_evidence: Line 3 caches the running transaction pointer once before the wait loop.
Lines 13-16 release j_state_lock, call schedule(), then reacquire the lock and re-lock commit_transaction->t_handle_lock; the cached commit_transaction is never re-read.
Lines 7 and 11 test t_updates on the cached pointer; after the lock is dropped another thread can commit and free that transaction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function relies on j_state_lock for exclusive access to journal->j_running_transaction, but the drop-and-reacquire window lets an interfering commit sequence free and replace it, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization over a shared resource. The use-after-free is the consequence of this race, not a separate weakness.

evidence_lines.code: transaction_t *commit_transaction = journal->j_running_transaction;

while (atomic_read(&commit_transaction->t_updates)) {
if (atomic_read(&commit_transaction->t_updates)) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the transaction pointer is read once and reused across a j_state_lock release/reacquire cycle, violating exclusivity over the shared transaction. Trigger: while the caller sleeps in schedule(), a concurrent commit path frees the running transaction. Reacquiring the lock and dereferencing the stale pointer yields a use-after-free, supporting a crash/instability consequence.

commit_msg:
x86/traps: Use an Interrupt Stack Table for #DB

PV guests can use architectural corner cases to cause #DB to be raised after
transitioning into supervisor mode.

Use an interrupt stack table for #DB to prevent the exception being taken with
a guest controlled stack pointer.

This is part of XSA-260 / CVE-2018-8897

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    set_ist(&idt[TRAP_debug],         IST_NONE);']}
description: A statement in the System Programming Guide of the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual (SDM) was mishandled in the development of some or all operating-system kernels, resulting in unexpected behavior for #DB exceptions that are deferred by MOV SS or POP SS, as demonstrated by (for example) privilege escalation in Windows, macOS, some Xen configurations, or FreeBSD, or a Linux kernel crash. The MOV to SS and POP SS instructions inhibit interrupts (including NMIs), data breakpoints, and single step trap exceptions until the instruction boundary following the next instruction (SDM Vol. 3A; section 6.8.3). (The inhibited data breakpoints are those on memory accessed by the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction itself.) Note that debug exceptions are not inhibited by the interrupt enable (EFLAGS.IF) system flag (SDM Vol. 3A; section 2.3). If the instruction following the MOV to SS or POP to SS instruction is an instruction like SYSCALL, SYSENTER, INT 3, etc. that transfers control to the operating system at CPL < 3, the debug exception is delivered after the transfer to CPL < 3 is complete. OS kernels may not expect this order of events and may therefore experience unexpected behavior when it occurs.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only clears IST assignments in IDT entries; it contains no concurrent code sequence, shared resource, or synchronization window, so it does not demonstrate a race condition (CWE-362).

commit_msg:
floppy: fix out-of-bounds read in copy_buffer

This fixes a global out-of-bounds read access in the copy_buffer
function of the floppy driver.

The FDDEFPRM ioctl allows one to set the geometry of a disk.  The sect
and head fields (unsigned int) of the floppy_drive structure are used to
compute the max_sector (int) in the make_raw_rw_request function.  It is
possible to overflow the max_sector.  Next, max_sector is passed to the
copy_buffer function and used in one of the memcpy calls.

An unprivileged user could trigger the bug if the device is accessible,
but requires a floppy disk to be inserted.

The patch adds the check for the .sect * .head multiplication for not
overflowing in the set_geometry function.

The bug was found by syzkaller.

Signed-off-by: Denis Efremov <efremov@ispras.ru>
Tested-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -4,8 +4,10 @@
 	int cnt;
 
 	/* sanity checking for parameters. */
-	if (g->sect <= 0 ||
-	    g->head <= 0 ||
+	if ((int)g->sect <= 0 ||
+	    (int)g->head <= 0 ||
+	    /* check for overflow in max_sector */
+	    (int)(g->sect * g->head) <= 0 ||
 	    /* check for zero in F_SECT_PER_TRACK */
 	    (unsigned char)((g->sect << 2) >> FD_SIZECODE(g)) == 0 ||
 	    g->track <= 0 || g->track > UDP->tracks >> STRETCH(g) ||
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (g->sect <= 0 ||', '\t    g->head <= 0 ||'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((int)g->sect <= 0 ||', '\t    (int)g->head <= 0 ||', '\t    /* check for overflow in max_sector */', '\t    (int)(g->sect * g->head) <= 0 ||']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.2.3, set_geometry in drivers/block/floppy.c does not validate the sect and head fields, as demonstrated by an integer overflow and out-of-bounds read. It can be triggered by an unprivileged local user when a floppy disk has been inserted. NOTE: QEMU creates the floppy device by default.

code_evidence: The sanity check only rejects non-positive sect and head individually; it never bounds their product, so a large sect and head can each pass while their multiplication overflows.

user_params[drive] = *g stores the unvalidated geometry, and SUPBOUND(buffer_max, user_params[drive].sect) derives buffer sizing from it, so the overflowing product later feeds max_sector used by copy_buffer's memcpy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is an unchecked integer multiplication whose wrapped result is used as a size/offset, matching CWE-190. The out-of-bounds read is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
if (g->sect <= 0 ||
g->head <= 0 ||

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: set_geometry accepts attacker-controlled sect and head without constraining their product. When make_raw_rw_request multiplies them, the int max_sector overflows to a small or negative value, and copy_buffer uses it in a memcpy, producing an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    appendToHeader(entry->value(), value);'], 'added_lines': ['    const uint64_t added_size = appendToHeader(entry->value(), value);', '    addSize(added_size);']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

code_evidence: Line 2 looks up an existing inline entry by key; when found (line 3), line 4 appends the new value to the existing entry and returns immediately.
When no entry exists, lines 7-11 copy the key and value into new HeaderString objects and insert them, growing the map by one entry per call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function's design lets an attacker drive unbounded growth of a limited resource (header storage and CPU) without throttling or aggregate size enforcement. The consequence is resource-consumption DoS, matching CWE-400's availability scope; the fix adds cached byte-size accounting rather than correcting a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Each addCopy call either appends to an existing header value or inserts a new entry without tracking the map's aggregate byte size. A remote peer can send many small, distinct headers that each stay under the per-request limit; the map grows unbounded and repeated size verification requires iterating all entries, yielding O(n^2) CPU consumption and denial of service. The root cause is missing internal accounting of accumulated header bytes, not the individual copies.

commit_msg:
vfs: make AIO use the proper rw_verify_area() area helpers

We had for some reason overlooked the AIO interface, and it didn't use
the proper rw_verify_area() helper function that checks (for example)
mandatory locking on the file, and that the size of the access doesn't
cause us to overflow the provided offset limits etc.

Instead, AIO did just the security_file_permission() thing (that
rw_verify_area() also does) directly.

This fixes it to do all the proper helper functions, which not only
means that now mandatory file locking works with AIO too, we can
actually remove lines of code.

Reported-by: Manish Honap <manish_honap_vit@yahoo.co.in>

commit_msg:
ext4: fix use-after-free in ext4_xattr_set_entry

Hulk Robot reported a issue:
==================================================================
BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in ext4_xattr_set_entry+0x18ab/0x3500
Write of size 4105 at addr ffff8881675ef5f4 by task syz-executor.0/7092

CPU: 1 PID: 7092 Comm: syz-executor.0 Not tainted 4.19.90-dirty #17
Call Trace:
[...]
 memcpy+0x34/0x50 mm/kasan/kasan.c:303
 ext4_xattr_set_entry+0x18ab/0x3500 fs/ext4/xattr.c:1747
 ext4_xattr_ibody_inline_set+0x86/0x2a0 fs/ext4/xattr.c:2205
 ext4_xattr_set_handle+0x940/0x1300 fs/ext4/xattr.c:2386
 ext4_xattr_set+0x1da/0x300 fs/ext4/xattr.c:2498
 __vfs_setxattr+0x112/0x170 fs/xattr.c:149
 __vfs_setxattr_noperm+0x11b/0x2a0 fs/xattr.c:180
 __vfs_setxattr_locked+0x17b/0x250 fs/xattr.c:238
 vfs_setxattr+0xed/0x270 fs/xattr.c:255
 setxattr+0x235/0x330 fs/xattr.c:520
 path_setxattr+0x176/0x190 fs/xattr.c:539
 __do_sys_lsetxattr fs/xattr.c:561 [inline]
 __se_sys_lsetxattr fs/xattr.c:557 [inline]
 __x64_sys_lsetxattr+0xc2/0x160 fs/xattr.c:557
 do_syscall_64+0xdf/0x530 arch/x86/entry/common.c:298
 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x44/0xa9
RIP: 0033:0x459fe9
RSP: 002b:00007fa5e54b4c08 EFLAGS: 00000246 ORIG_RAX: 00000000000000bd
RAX: ffffffffffffffda RBX: 000000000051bf60 RCX: 0000000000459fe9
RDX: 00000000200003c0 RSI: 0000000020000180 RDI: 0000000020000140
RBP: 000000000051bf60 R08: 0000000000000001 R09: 0000000000000000
R10: 0000000000001009 R11: 0000000000000246 R12: 0000000000000000
R13: 00007ffc73c93fc0 R14: 000000000051bf60 R15: 00007fa5e54b4d80
[...]
==================================================================

Above issue may happen as follows:
-------------------------------------
ext4_xattr_set
  ext4_xattr_set_handle
    ext4_xattr_ibody_find
      >> s->end < s->base
      >> no EXT4_STATE_XATTR
      >> xattr_check_inode is not executed
    ext4_xattr_ibody_set
      ext4_xattr_set_entry
       >> size_t min_offs = s->end - s->base
       >> UAF in memcpy

we can easily reproduce this problem with the following commands:
    mkfs.ext4 -F /dev/sda
    mount -o debug_want_extra_isize=128 /dev/sda /mnt
    touch /mnt/file
    setfattr -n user.cat -v `seq -s z 4096|tr -d '[:digit:]'` /mnt/file

In ext4_xattr_ibody_find, we have the following assignment logic:
  header = IHDR(inode, raw_inode)
         = raw_inode + EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE + i_extra_isize
  is->s.base = IFIRST(header)
             = header + sizeof(struct ext4_xattr_ibody_header)
  is->s.end = raw_inode + s_inode_size

In ext4_xattr_set_entry
  min_offs = s->end - s->base
           = s_inode_size - EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE - i_extra_isize -
	     sizeof(struct ext4_xattr_ibody_header)
  last = s->first
  free = min_offs - ((void *)last - s->base) - sizeof(__u32)
       = s_inode_size - EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE - i_extra_isize -
         sizeof(struct ext4_xattr_ibody_header) - sizeof(__u32)

In the calculation formula, all values except s_inode_size and
i_extra_size are fixed values. When i_extra_size is the maximum value
s_inode_size - EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE, min_offs is -4 and free is -8.
The value overflows. As a result, the preceding issue is triggered when
memcpy is executed.

Therefore, when finding xattr or setting xattr, check whether
there is space for storing xattr in the inode to resolve this issue.

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Reported-by: Hulk Robot <hulkci@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Baokun Li <libaokun1@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Ritesh Harjani (IBM) <ritesh.list@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220616021358.2504451-3-libaokun1@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (EXT4_I(inode)->i_extra_isize == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!EXT4_INODE_HAS_XATTR_SPACE(inode))', '']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerability was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem in the way it handled the extra inode size for extended attributes. This flaw could allow a privileged local user to cause a system crash or other undefined behaviors.

code_evidence: The only guard before the set operation is a check that i_extra_isize is zero; any nonzero extra inode size, including the maximum value, passes.
ext4_xattr_set_entry is then called unconditionally with the search state s derived from the inode, and its error return is the only gate before header and s->first are dereferenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The reported consequence is use-after-free (write to freed slab memory) reached through the unchecked inode geometry; CWE-416 captures reuse of freed memory. The root defect is a missing space/geometry check rather than a plain integer overflow alone, so the UAF label fits the demonstrated memory-reuse consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
if (EXT4_I(inode)->i_extra_isize == 0)
return -ENOSPC;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When i_extra_isize is maximal (s_inode_size - EXT4_GOOD_OLD_INODE_SIZE), the ibody search range yields a negative min_offs/free; the insufficient guard admits this state, and ext4_xattr_set_entry performs an out-of-bounds write via memcpy, corrupting/reusing freed slab memory. Trigger is a crafted setxattr on an inode with oversized extra_isize.

description: Heap-based buffer overflow in sqbaselib.cpp in SQUIRREL 3.2 due to lack of a certain sq_reservestack call.

Trigger: calling a thread with enough arguments to exceed the thread stack's free space causes Push/sq_move to write past the allocated buffer. commit_msg: Fix #9913 - oobread in anal.dalvik
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (len > 2) {', '\t\tif (len > 2) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (len > 3) {', '\t\tif (len > 5) {']}
description: In radare2 2.5.0, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in the dalvik_op function (libr/anal/p/anal_dalvik.c). Remote attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted DEX file. Note that this issue is different from CVE-2018-8809, which was patched earlier.

code_evidence: Case 0x29 (goto/16) guards only with len > 2 but then reads data[2] and data[3], requiring at least 4 bytes; with len==3 data[3] is read past the supplied buffer.
Case 0x2a (goto/32) guards only with len > 2 but then reads data[2] through data[5], requiring at least 6 bytes; with len in 3..5 data[3..5] are read out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code reads data beyond the bounds of the intended buffer because the guard does not cover all accessed indices, which is exactly CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not a write or an integer overflow; the defect is an insufficient length constraint on read indices.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length check is smaller than the number of operand bytes actually consumed by the jump decoding. Trigger: a crafted DEX instruction stream where the goto/16 or goto/32 opcode is followed by fewer operand bytes than the read requires (len==3 for 0x29, len 3–5 for 0x2a). Consequence: reads past the end of the heap buffer, potentially crashing (DoS) or disclosing adjacent memory.

description: The dnxhd_decode_header function in libavcodec/dnxhddec.c in FFmpeg 3.0 through 3.3.2 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted DNxHD file.

code_evidence: mb_height is taken directly from the attacker-controlled header byte buf[0x16d] (line 95).

The loop at line 118 iterates i < ctx->mb_height and reads AV_RB32(buf + 0x170 + (i << 2)) from the input buffer, so an oversized mb_height drives reads past the supplied buffer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the HR2 branch computes data_offset from the untrusted mb_height without enforcing the mb_height limit that the non-HR2 branch applies. Trigger: a crafted DNxHD file with an HR2 header and large buf[0x16d] value. Consequence: the scan-index loop reads beyond the input buffer (out-of-bounds read), causing DoS or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
Prevent null pointer dereference in `mutable_graph_view`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409684472
Change-Id: I577eb9d9ac470fcec0501423171e739a4ec0cb5c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (input_node == nullptr) {', '      return false;', '    }']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. Under certain scenarios, Grappler component of TensorFlow can trigger a null pointer dereference. There are 2 places where this can occur, for the same malicious alteration of a `SavedModel` file (fixing the first one would trigger the same dereference in the second place). First, during constant folding, the `GraphDef` might not have the required nodes for the binary operation. If a node is missing, the correposning `mul_*child` would be null, and the dereference in the subsequent line would be incorrect. We have a similar issue during `IsIdentityConsumingSwitch`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 9 obtains a NodeDef* from graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node()), where tensor_id is derived from the attacker-controlled SavedModel node input. Line 10 immediately dereferences input_node via IsSwitch(*input_node) without any null check, so a missing node yields a null pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 directly matches: a pointer expected to be valid is dereferenced while null, and the fix adds an explicit nullptr check before use. This is a null-dereference issue, not an out-of-bounds or type-confusion weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
NodeDef* input_node = graph.GetNode(tensor_id.node());
return IsSwitch(*input_node);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of GetNode is assumed non-null and dereferenced unconditionally. Trigger: a malformed GraphDef/SavedModel where the referenced input node does not exist, causing GetNode to return nullptr. Supported consequence: null pointer dereference, leading to a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix an integer overflow in opj_tcd_get_decoded_tile_size().

Based on suggested patch by reporter.
BUG=629919

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2182683002
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                l_data_size += l_size_comp * (OPJ_UINT32)((l_res->x1 - l_res->x0) * (l_res->y1 - l_res->y0));'], 'added_lines': ['        OPJ_UINT32 l_temp;', "                l_temp = (OPJ_UINT32)((l_res->x1 - l_res->x0) * (l_res->y1 - l_res->y0)); /* x1*y1 can't overflow */", '', '                if (l_size_comp && ((OPJ_UINT32)-1) / l_size_comp < l_temp) {', '                        return (OPJ_UINT32)-1;', '                }', '                l_temp *= l_size_comp;', '', '                if (l_temp > ((OPJ_UINT32)-1) - l_data_size) {', '                        return (OPJ_UINT32)-1;', '                }', '                l_data_size += l_temp;', '']}
description: Integer overflow in the opj_tcd_get_decoded_tile_size function in tcd.c in OpenJPEG, as used in PDFium in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JPEG 2000 data.

code_evidence: l_size_comp is derived from the component precision via shifts and rounding (lines 12-19), yielding a small per-sample byte count used as a multiplier.

Line 21 computes l_data_size += l_size_comp * (OPJ_UINT32)((l_res->x1 - l_res->x0) * (l_res->y1 - l_res->y0)) with no overflow check on either the per-resolution product or the running accumulation, so attacker-influenced image dimensions and precision can wrap the OPJ_UINT32 result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs size arithmetic intended to produce a larger value but can wrap to a small number, exactly the CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound pattern. The consequence is a miscalculated size used for memory operations, matching the weakness's security-critical size-determination scope; this is distinct from a simple out-of-bounds read because the arithmetic itself is the defect.

evidence_lines.code:
l_res = l_tile_comp->resolutions + l_tile_comp->minimum_num_resolutions - 1;
l_data_size += l_size_comp * (OPJ_UINT32)((l_res->x1 - l_res->x0) * (l_res->y1 - l_res->y0));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoded tile size is accumulated in a 32-bit unsigned integer without validating that the resolution-area times component-size product, nor the running sum, stays within OPJ_UINT32. Crafted JPEG 2000 data with large resolution extents or component precision triggers wraparound, producing an undersized l_data_size that later drives heap allocation/copy, causing heap-based buffer overflow or DoS.

commit_msg:
Unsquashfs: fix write outside destination directory exploit

An issue on Github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
shows how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and ..) can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by checking all names for
validity.

In doing so I have also added checks for '.' and for names that
are shorter than they should be (names in the file system should
not have '\0' terminators).

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\t/* check name for invalid characters (i.e /, ., ..) */', '\t\t\tif(check_name(dire->name, dire->size + 1) == FALSE) {', '\t\t\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: invalid characters in name\\n");', '\t\t\t\tgoto corrupted;', '\t\t\t}', '']}
description: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-1.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 stores the filename in the directory entry; this is then used by unsquashfs to create the new file during the unsquash. The filename is not validated for traversal outside of the destination directory, and thus allows writing to locations outside of the destination.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts external input (on-disk names) and builds a name intended for use under the destination directory without neutralizing '..' or '/' elements, directly matching CWE-22 path traversal. The missing check_name validation is the specific constraint whose absence permits escaping the restricted directory.

evidence_lines.code:
strcpy(dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].name, dire->name);
dir->dirs[dir->dir_count].start_block =

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: filenames from a crafted squashfs image are trusted and copied without rejecting path separators or '..' components. Trigger: a malicious filesystem contains a directory entry whose name includes '/' or '..'. Consequence: the stored name is later used to create files, resolving outside the destination directory and allowing writes to arbitrary locations.

commit_msg:
malloc() adds some overhead to the requested size, which may result in
an integer overflow and subsequent buffer overflow if it is close to
SIZE_MAX.  It should fail if size is large enough for this to happen.

Further, it's not legal for a C object to be larger than
PTRDIFF_MAX (half of SIZE_MAX) as pointer arithmetic within it could
overflow.  So return failure immediately if size is greater than that.

CVE-2021-31873

Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Various additions below will overflow if size is close to', "\t   SIZE_MAX.  Further, it's not legal for a C object to be", '\t   larger than PTRDIFF_MAX (half of SIZE_MAX) as pointer', '\t   arithmetic within it could overflow. */', '\tif (size > PTRDIFF_MAX) {', '\t\terrno = ENOMEM;', '\t\treturn NULL;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in klibc before 2.0.9. Additions in the malloc() function may result in an integer overflow and a subsequent heap buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Only a zero-size check; no upper-bound validation before size arithmetic.
size is rounded up via (size + 2*sizeof(arena_header) - 1) & ARENA_SIZE_MASK; if size is near SIZE_MAX this addition wraps to a small value.
The wrapped size is then used for block search and fsize = (size + MALLOC_CHUNK_MASK) & ~MALLOC_CHUNK_MASK, driving allocation size and subsequent __malloc_from_block(fp, size).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the size calculation wraps before being used as an allocation size, and the wrapped value is trusted as the buffer size. This is integer overflow leading to undersized allocation rather than merely a missing bounds check.

evidence_lines.code: fsize = (size + MALLOC_CHUNK_MASK) & ~MALLOC_CHUNK_MASK;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: malloc() performs additive rounding on an attacker-controlled size_t without rejecting values close to SIZE_MAX. Trigger: a large size argument makes the additions wrap to a small value. Supported consequence: the allocator returns a block smaller than requested, so callers writing the requested length overflow the heap buffer.

commit_msg:
gnttab: split maptrack lock to make it fulfill its purpose again

The way the lock is currently being used in get_maptrack_handle(), it
protects only the maptrack limit: The function acts on current's list
only, so races on list accesses are impossible even without the lock.

Otoh list access races are possible between __get_maptrack_handle() and
put_maptrack_handle(), due to the invocation of the former for other
than current from steal_maptrack_handle(). Introduce a per-vCPU lock
for list accesses to become race free again. This lock will be
uncontended except when it becomes necessary to take the steal path,
i.e. in the common case there should be no meaningful performance
impact.

When in get_maptrack_handle adds a stolen entry to a fresh, empty,
freelist, we think that there is probably no concurrency.  However,
this is not a fast path and adding the locking there makes the code
clearly correct.

Also, while we are here: the stolen maptrack_entry's tail pointer was
not properly set.  Set it.

This is CVE-2017-12136 / XSA-228.

Reported-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    spin_lock(&v->maptrack_freelist_lock);', '', '        {', '            spin_unlock(&v->maptrack_freelist_lock);', '        }', '        {', '            spin_unlock(&v->maptrack_freelist_lock);', '        }', '    spin_unlock(&v->maptrack_freelist_lock);', '']}
description: Race condition in the grant table code in Xen 4.6.x through 4.9.x allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (free list corruption and host crash) or gain privileges on the host via vectors involving maptrack free list handling.

code_evidence: The function reads v->maptrack_head and maptrack_entry(t, head).ref, then conditionally updates the head via cmpxchg in a loop, with early returns at lines 10 and 13. No lock is held around these accesses in the shown function, so the shared per-vCPU maptrack free-list head and entry links can be concurrently modified by put_maptrack_handle() or by steal_maptrack_handle() invoking this function on another vCPU. The early return paths also leave the sequence without any exclusive access guarantee.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function performs a concurrent read-modify-write on a shared resource without proper synchronization, allowing an interfering code sequence to violate atomicity. This is not merely a missing check; it is a timing-window race on shared state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the maptrack free-list head and entry links are read and updated without holding a per-vCPU lock, so another concurrent free-list operation can interleave between the read of head/next and the cmpxchg. Trigger: concurrent get/put (or steal) operations on the same maptrack free list. Supported consequence: free-list corruption leading to host crash or privilege escalation.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of division in TFLite is [vulnerable to a division by 0 error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/div.cc). commit_msg:
Fix handling of parameter-entity references

There were two bugs where parameter-entity references could lead to an
unexpected change of the input buffer in xmlParseNameComplex and
xmlDictLookup being called with an invalid pointer.

Percent sign in DTD Names
=========================

The NEXTL macro used to call xmlParserHandlePEReference. When parsing
"complex" names inside the DTD, this could result in entity expansion
which created a new input buffer. The fix is to simply remove the call
to xmlParserHandlePEReference from the NEXTL macro. This is safe because
no users of the macro require expansion of parameter entities.

- xmlParseNameComplex
- xmlParseNCNameComplex
- xmlParseNmtoken

The percent sign is not allowed in names, which are grammatical tokens.

- xmlParseEntityValue

Parameter-entity references in entity values are expanded but this
happens in a separate step in this function.

- xmlParseSystemLiteral

Parameter-entity references are ignored in the system literal.

- xmlParseAttValueComplex
- xmlParseCharDataComplex
- xmlParseCommentComplex
- xmlParsePI
- xmlParseCDSect

Parameter-entity references are ignored outside the DTD.

- xmlLoadEntityContent

This function is only called from xmlStringLenDecodeEntities and
entities are replaced in a separate step immediately after the function
call.

This bug could also be triggered with an internal subset and double
entity expansion.

This fixes bug 766956 initially reported by Wei Lei and independently by
Chromium's ClusterFuzz, Hanno Böck, and Marco Grassi. Thanks to everyone
involved.

xmlParseNameComplex with XML_PARSE_OLD10
========================================

When parsing Names inside an expanded parameter entity with the
XML_PARSE_OLD10 option, xmlParseNameComplex would call xmlGROW via the
GROW macro if the input buffer was exhausted. At the end of the
parameter entity's replacement text, this function would then call
xmlPopInput which invalidated the input buffer.

There should be no need to invoke GROW in this situation because the
buffer is grown periodically every XML_PARSER_CHUNK_SIZE characters and,
at least for UTF-8, in xmlCurrentChar. This also matches the code path
executed when XML_PARSE_OLD10 is not set.

This fixes bugs 781205 (CVE-2017-9049) and 781361 (CVE-2017-9050).
Thanks to Marcel Böhme and Thuan Pham for the report.

Additional hardening
====================

A separate check was added in xmlParseNameComplex to validate the
buffer size.

Check the buffer size to avoid passing an invalid', '         * pointer to xmlDictLookup.', '         */', '        xmlFatalErr(ctxt, XML_ERR_INTERNAL_ERROR,', '                    "unexpected change of input buffer");', '        return (NULL);', '    }']}
description: parser.c in libxml2 before 2.9.5 mishandles parameter-entity references because the NEXTL macro calls the xmlParserHandlePEReference function in the case of a '%' character in a DTD name.

code_evidence: In the XML_PARSE_OLD10 branch, when CUR_CHAR returns 0 the loop calls GROW and re-reads CUR_CHAR without re-validating that the input buffer still holds len characters; GROW/xmlPopInput at the end of a parameter entity's replacement text can replace the buffer.

After the loop, len accumulated from the old buffer is used to compute ctxt->input->cur - len (or -(len+1)) and pass it to xmlDictLookup, so a shrunk/changed buffer yields a pointer before the buffer base.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect allows a read operation outside the intended input-buffer boundary via a stale length/pointer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory access. It is not merely a logic error: the dangling pointer is dereferenced, so the buffer-bounds class fits the supported consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser tracks name length across a buffer-changing GROW triggered by a '%' parameter-entity reference at end of an expanded entity. Trigger: a DTD name inside an expanded parameter entity under XML_PARSE_OLD10. Consequence: xmlDictLookup reads from a pointer outside the current input buffer, causing out-of-bounds read and possible crash.

array.c: fix `mrb_ary_shift_m` initialization bug.

The `ARY_PTR` and `ARY_LEN` may be modified in `mrb_get_args`.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  struct RArray *a = mrb_ary_ptr(self);', '  mrb_int len = ARY_LEN(a);', '  mrb_value val;', '  };'], 'added_lines': ['  }', '', '  struct RArray *a = mrb_ary_ptr(self);', '  mrb_int len = ARY_LEN(a);', '  mrb_value val;', '']}
description: mruby is vulnerable to NULL Pointer Dereference

code_evidence: Array pointer `a` and cached length `len` are captured at lines 4-5 before `mrb_get_args` runs at line 8; when no argument is given the function returns via `mrb_ary_shift` at line 9, but on the argument path it continues with the stale `a` and `len` and calls `ary_modify_check(mrb, a)` at line 11.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale `a` may no longer point to a valid array structure, and subsequent ARY_PTR/ARY_LEN accesses dereference that invalid pointer, matching CWE-476. This is a use-after-invalidation of a pointer rather than an out-of-bounds index issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `mrb_get_args` can invoke Ruby code that mutates the receiver array, invalidating the previously cached `ARY_PTR`/`ARY_LEN` in `a`. Trigger: calling shift with an integer argument whose conversion executes user code. The stale pointer is then dereferenced downstream (e.g. `ARY_PTR(a)` at line 15), giving a NULL or freed pointer dereference and a crash.

allocate a temporary structure that will be dropped once packet dissection is

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (!rlcinf) {', '            rlcinf = wmem_new0(wmem_packet_scope(), rlc_info);', '        }', '        if (!macinf) {', '            macinf = wmem_new0(wmem_packet_scope(), umts_mac_info);', '        }']}
description: epan/dissectors/packet-umts_fp.c in the UMTS FP dissector in Wireshark 2.x before 2.0.6 does not ensure that memory is allocated for certain data structures, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (invalid write access and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: Lines 36-37 fetch rlc_info and umts_mac_info from packet proto-data; before the patch these pointers could be NULL when no RLC/MAC dissector had stored them.
Lines 34-35 declare macinf/rlcinf as raw pointers with no allocation or NULL check at this site.
The inner loop over no_of_pdus[n] (lines 126-127) writes macinf->content[j], macinf->lchid[j], rlcinf->li_size[j] and rlcinf->rbid[j] using attacker-controlled j and n from the PDU block header.
The per-PDU dissectors at lines 144-145 are invoked with the same pinfo, so the write targets are the structures later consumed by those sub-dissectors.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the observed unsafe operation is a write through macinf/rlcinf array members at attacker-influenced indices into memory not guaranteed to be allocated or large enough for those indices, i.e., writing outside the intended buffer. A NULL-pointer dereference alone would be CWE-476, but the code indexes the structures and the commit fixes allocation, so the out-of-bounds write characterization is the supported weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
rlcinf = (rlc_info *)p_get_proto_data(wmem_file_scope(), pinfo, proto_rlc, 0);
macinf = (umts_mac_info *)p_get_proto_data(wmem_file_scope(), pinfo, proto_umts_mac, 0);

umts_mac_info *macinf;
rlc_info *rlcinf;

next_tvb = tvb_new_subset_length(tvb, offset, (gint)pdu_length[n]);
call_dissector_with_data(mac_fdd_hsdsch_handle, next_tvb, pinfo, top_level_tree, data);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function dereferences rlc_info/umts_mac_info pointers obtained from p_get_proto_data without ensuring they were allocated or that j stays within the fixed array bounds. Trigger: a crafted HS-DSCH data frame whose PDU block header yields large no_of_pdus values causes writes through macinf/rlcinf into memory that was never allocated or is sized for fewer entries. Consequence: invalid write access and application crash (DoS), matching the described invalid write access.

description: xorg-x11-server before 1.19.5 had wrong extra length check in ProcXIChangeHierarchy function allowing malicious X client to cause X server to crash or possibly execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 12 derives the remaining buffer length as the request's length field (in 4-byte units) minus sizeof(xXIAnyHierarchyChangeInfo), while the actual payload begins at &stuff[1] after the xXIChangeHierarchyReq header (line 13). Subtracting the wrong structure size makes len larger than the real payload, so the bounds checks at lines 15 and 21 against attacker-controlled any->length and the per-iteration decrement at line 76 no longer reflect the true remaining buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function receives a length field from the client and fails to correctly validate/derive it before using it to bound parsing, matching CWE-20's improper validation of input metadata (specified length). The wrong sizeof produces an incorrect derived quantity, so the subsequent checks do not constrain the input to the actual buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length of the client-supplied request body is computed by subtracting the wrong header size, so the derived remaining-length value is not validated against the actual data available. Trigger: a malicious X client sends an XIChangeHierarchy request with crafted num_changes/length values. Consequence: the loop reads or advances past the real buffer, causing an out-of-bounds access that can crash the X server or potentially allow code execution.

commit_msg:
USB HID: Fix a memory leak.

Replace mismatched g_strdup() + g_free()s with
wmem_strdup_printf(wmem_packet_scope(), ...). Fixes #17124.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return g_strdup_printf(str, id);'], 'added_lines': ['    return wmem_strdup_printf(wmem_packet_scope(), str, id);']}
description: Memory leak in USB HID dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 to 3.4.2 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: Line 120 returns a heap allocation from g_strdup_printf(str, id); the caller receives ownership of this g_malloc-backed buffer, and nothing in this function frees it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the root cause is an unreleased heap allocation whose lifetime is not managed after use, with the supported consequence being memory-consumption/availability impact. A use-after-free or double-free would require a release or reuse of the buffer, which is not present here.

evidence_lines.code: return g_strdup_printf(str, id);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function allocates a formatted string with g_strdup_printf and returns it to the caller without any release path. When the dissector is invoked repeatedly on crafted or injected USB HID packets, each call leaves an allocation that is not tracked for later g_free, so memory accumulates over the capture-processing lifetime and can exhaust resources or destabilize the process.

commit_msg:
Fix #196 and #199: Out of bound reads security issues

Check args before calling memmove() and memset() in remap_struct()
function to avoid out of bound reads which would possibly lead to
unknown code execution and/or sadf command crash.

Signed-off-by: Sebastien GODARD <sysstat@users.noreply.github.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t    arch_64, endian_mismatch, oneof)) != 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t    arch_64, endian_mismatch, oneof, sizeof(rec_hdr_tmp))) != 0)']}
description: An issue was discovered in sysstat 12.1.1. The remap_struct function in sa_common.c has an out-of-bounds read during a memmove call, as demonstrated by sadf.

code_evidence: rec_hdr_tmp is a fixed-size local buffer of MAX_RECORD_HEADER_SIZE. read_record_hdr is called with rec_hdr_tmp and a record header pointer but no length for the temporary buffer, so the callee cannot bound how many bytes it writes into rec_hdr_tmp before the subsequent memmove/memset. The patch adds sizeof(rec_hdr_tmp) to the call, confirming the missing size argument was the defect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing length argument lets the header read exceed the intended rec_hdr_tmp buffer, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read past the intended buffer. It is not merely an integer issue: the defect is the unbounded access to the fixed-size buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read_record_hdr is invoked without the size of the caller's stack buffer rec_hdr_tmp, so it may copy more header bytes than the buffer holds. Trigger: reading a crafted sa file whose record header length exceeds MAX_RECORD_HEADER_SIZE. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write of stack memory, potentially crashing sadf or enabling code execution.

description: The (1) t1_parse_font_matrix function in type1/t1load.c, (2) cid_parse_font_matrix function in cid/cidload.c, (3) t42_parse_font_matrix function in type42/t42parse.c, and (4) ps_parser_load_field function in psaux/psobjs.c in FreeType before 2.5.4 do not check return values, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (uninitialized memory access and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted font.

code_evidence: `count` is declared `FT_UInt` and set from `T1_ToInt( parser )` on attacker-controlled font bytes without checking for negative or unreasonable values; a negative value is cast to a huge unsigned count.

In immediates-only mode `charcode` is set to `n`, and the `/`-name branch uses `charcode` as an index into `char_table` without validating it against the table size; `T1_Skip_PS_Token` can also advance the cursor to the limit.
The final `else` branch on an unrecognized encoding token sets `Invalid_File_Format` rather than validating or rejecting the input cleanly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes untrusted font input and fails to validate derived quantities (count, charcode) before using them for allocation and indexing, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). The missing sign/bounds checks are the cause; the crash is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
FT_UInt      count, n;
count = (FT_UInt)T1_ToInt( parser );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts numeric fields (`count`, `charcode`) and token structure from a crafted Type1/CID font without bounds or sign validation. Trigger: a font supplying a negative count or an out-of-range immediate charcode. Consequence: huge allocations or out-of-bounds table indexing, leading to uninitialized memory access and crash (DoS).

commit_msg: disable Unix-domain socket forwarding when privsep is disabled
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    !no_port_forwarding_flag && !options.disable_forwarding) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t    !no_port_forwarding_flag && !options.disable_forwarding &&', '\t    use_privsep) {']}
description: sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4, when privilege separation is not used, creates forwarded Unix-domain sockets as root, which might allow local users to gain privileges via unspecified vectors, related to serverloop.c.

code_evidence: The forwarding gate checks only allow_streamlocal_forwarding, no_port_forwarding_flag and options.disable_forwarding; it does not consider whether privilege separation is enabled.
When the gate passes, channel_connect_to_path(target, ...) is invoked to create the forwarded Unix-domain socket, with target taken from the client-supplied packet string (line 7).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an access-control decision over a privileged operation (creating a socket as root) using an incomplete permission condition, matching CWE-264's scope of permissions/privileges management. The missing constraint, not the socket operation itself, is the weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((options.allow_streamlocal_forwarding & FORWARD_LOCAL) != 0 &&
!no_port_forwarding_flag && !options.disable_forwarding) {

c = channel_connect_to_path(target,
"direct-streamlocal@openssh.com", "direct-streamlocal");

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the authorization condition for local streamlocal forwarding lacks a privilege-separation check, so the privileged sshd process handles the request. Trigger: a local user requests direct-streamlocal forwarding while privsep is disabled, passing the allow/disable checks. Consequence: the forwarded Unix-domain socket is created with root privileges, enabling privilege gain.

commit_msg:
Jann Horn reported that SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS implementations
are racy, as af_unix can concurrently change sk_peer_pid and sk_peer_cred.

In order to fix this issue, this patch adds a new spinlock that needs
to be used whenever these fields are read or written.

Jann also pointed out that l2cap_sock_get_peer_pid_cb() is currently
reading sk->sk_peer_pid which makes no sense, as this field
is only possibly set by AF_UNIX sockets.
We will have to clean this in a separate patch.
This could be done by reverting b48596d1dc25 "Bluetooth: L2CAP: Add get_peer_pid callback"
or implementing what was truly expected.

Fixes: 109f6e39fa07 ("af_unix: Allow SO_PEERCRED to work across namespaces.")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Cc: Eric W. Biederman <ebiederm@xmission.com>
Cc: Luiz Augusto von Dentz <luiz.von.dentz@intel.com>
Cc: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_lock_init(&sk->sk_peer_lock);', '']}
description: A use-after-free read flaw was found in sock_getsockopt() in net/core/sock.c due to SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS race with listen() (and connect()) in the Linux kernel. In this flaw, an attacker with a user privileges may crash the system or leak internal kernel information.

code_evidence: Initializes sk_peer_pid and sk_peer_cred to NULL and then proceeds to initialize other fields, but the patch shows the needed spin_lock_init(&sk->sk_peer_lock) is added between lines 41 and 42; the shown function body lacks any lock protecting these peer credential fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the weakness is improper synchronization over shared sk_peer_pid/sk_peer_cred state allowing an interfering code sequence to modify the resource during a read. The missing spinlock init and absence of locking in this initialization path directly supports the race-condition classification rather than a generic memory-safety label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sk_peer_pid and sk_peer_cred are shared socket fields written during initialization and concurrently read/modified by SO_PEERCRED/SO_PEERGROUPS paths without exclusive locking. Trigger: a concurrent listener/connect path changes these fields while sock_getsockopt reads them, producing a race. Supported consequence: use-after-free read leading to crash or kernel memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
mnt: Add a per mount namespace limit on the number of mounts

CAI Qian <caiqian@redhat.com> pointed out that the semantics
of shared subtrees make it possible to create an exponentially
increasing number of mounts in a mount namespace.

    mkdir /tmp/1 /tmp/2
    mount --make-rshared /
    for i in $(seq 1 20) ; do mount --bind /tmp/1 /tmp/2 ; done

Will create create 2^20 or 1048576 mounts, which is a practical problem
as some people have managed to hit this by accident.

As such CVE-2016-6213 was assigned.

Ian Kent <raven@themaw.net> described the situation for autofs users
as follows:

> The number of mounts for direct mount maps is usually not very large because of
> the way they are implemented, large direct mount maps can have performance
> problems. There can be anywhere from a few (likely case a few hundred) to less
> than 10000, plus mounts that have been triggered and not yet expired.
>
> Indirect mounts have one autofs mount at the root plus the number of mounts that
> have been triggered and not yet expired.
>
> The number of autofs indirect map entries can range from a few to the common
> case of several thousand and in rare cases up to between 30000 and 50000. I've
> not heard of people with maps larger than 50000 entries.
>
> The larger the number of map entries the greater the possibility for a large
> number of active mounts so it's not hard to expect cases of a 1000 or somewhat
> more active mounts.

So I am setting the default number of mounts allowed per mount
namespace at 100,000.  This is more than enough for any use case I
know of, but small enough to quickly stop an exponential increase
in mounts.  Which should be perfect to catch misconfigurations and
malfunctioning programs.

For anyone who needs a higher limit this can be changed by writing
to the new /proc/sys/fs/mount-max sysctl.

Tested-by: CAI Qian <caiqian@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: "Eric W. Biederman" <ebiederm@xmission.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct mnt_namespace *ns = dest_mnt->mnt_ns;', '', '\t/* Is there space to add these mounts to the mount namespace? */', '\tif (!parent_path) {', '\t\terr = count_mounts(ns, source_mnt);', '\t\tif (err)', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t}', '\t\tchild->mnt_parent->mnt_ns->pending_mounts = 0;', '\tns->pending_mounts = 0;']}
description: fs/namespace.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9 does not restrict how many mounts may exist in a mount namespace, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption and deadlock) via MS_BIND mount system calls, as demonstrated by a loop that triggers exponential growth in the number of mounts.

code_evidence: attach_recursive_mnt performs the mount attachment: when parent_path is NULL it calls mnt_set_mountpoint/commit_tree to add source_mnt into dest_mnt's namespace, and when parent_path is non-NULL it detaches and attaches the mount to the new parent.
No check constrains how many mounts may exist in the destination mount namespace before these attach operations run.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly performs an allocation/maintenance operation (adding mounts) on a limited system resource—the mount namespace—without throttling the number of allocated resources, matching CWE-400's lack of control over resource consumption. The patch adds count_mounts to enforce exactly this limit, confirming the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the attach path accepts and commits a new mount (and, via propagate_mnt, its propagated subtree) into the mount namespace without any per-namespace mount-count limit. Trigger: a local user repeatedly issues MS_BIND mount syscalls, and shared-subtree propagation makes each bind multiply the number of mounts. Consequence: unbounded memory consumption in the mount namespace, leading to denial of service (memory exhaustion and potential deadlock).

commit_msg:
Avoid uninitialized memory

As reported by https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=16856
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    } else {', "        matvar->name[tmp - 1] = '\\0';"]}
description: Mat_VarReadNextInfo4 in mat4.c in MATIO 1.5.17 omits a certain '\0' character, leading to a heap-based buffer over-read in strdup_vprintf when uninitialized memory is accessed.

code_evidence: The name buffer is allocated with malloc(tmp) and filled by fread(matvar->name,1,tmp,...) with exactly tmp bytes. If the read succeeds, the function proceeds to line 140 without ever writing a '\0' terminator into the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function hands out a buffer whose string terminator was never initialized, so later string operations access uninitialized resource content; this matches CWE-908 (Use of Uninitialized Resource). It is not merely a missing-bound check (CWE-125) because the defect is the absent initialization of the terminator, not an unchecked length.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: matvar->name is treated as a C string but no terminator is stored after the file-supplied name bytes. Trigger: a MAT-file whose name field length tmp is read fully, so the buffer holds tmp non-NUL bytes; subsequent string consumers read past the allocated region into uninitialized/heap memory. Consequence: heap-based over-read of uninitialized data, potentially exposing memory contents or crashing.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Allow g_variant_byteswap() to operate on tree-form variants

This avoids needing to always serialise a variant before byteswapping it.
With variants in non-normal forms, serialisation can result in a large
increase in size of the variant, and a lot of allocations for leaf
`GVariant`s. This can lead to a denial of service attack.

Avoid that by changing byteswapping so that it happens on the tree form
of the variant if the input is in non-normal form. If the input is in
normal form (either serialised or in tree form), continue using the
existing code as byteswapping an already-serialised normal variant is
about 3× faster than byteswapping on the equivalent tree form.

The existing unit tests cover byteswapping well, but need some
adaptation so that they operate on tree form variants too.

I considered dropping the serialised byteswapping code and doing all
byteswapping on tree-form variants, as that would make maintenance
simpler (avoiding having two parallel implementations of byteswapping).
However, most inputs to `g_variant_byteswap()` are likely to be
serialised variants (coming from a byte array of input from some foreign
source) and most of them are going to be in normal form (as corruption
and malicious action are rare). So getting rid of the serialised
byteswapping code would impose quite a performance penalty on the common
case.

Signed-off-by: Philip Withnall <pwithnall@endlessos.org>

Fixes: #2797

commit_msg:
Do stricter error checking when parsing path nodes

The SVG spec mandates that path parsing should terminate on the first
error encountered, and an error be reported. To improve the handling
of corrupt files, implement such error handling, and also limit the
number of QPainterPath elements to a reasonable range.

Fixes: QTBUG-96044
