commit_msg: fixed mqtt variable length header issue
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  size_t new_pos = ofs;', '  uint32_t bytes_consumed;', '      prop->iv = decode_variable_length((char *) i, &bytes_consumed);', '      new_pos += bytes_consumed;'], 'added_lines': ['  uint8_t *end = (uint8_t *) msg->dgram.ptr + msg->dgram.len;', '  size_t new_pos = ofs, len;', '      len = decode_varint(i, (size_t) (end - i), (size_t *) &prop->iv);', '      new_pos = (!len) ? 0 : new_pos + len;']}
description: Due to a failure in validating the length of a provided MQTT_CMD_PUBLISH parsed message with a variable length header, Cesanta Mongoose, an embeddable web server, version 7.10 is susceptible to a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the default configuration. Version 7.9 and prior does not appear to be vulnerable. This issue is resolved in version 7.11.

code_evidence: The pointer i is derived from msg->dgram.ptr + msg->props_start + ofs, but the bounds check at line 7 occurs only after prop->id = i[0] at line 6 dereferences i, so the first read can be out of bounds.
For STRING_PAIR, key and value lengths are read from i[0..3] and i is advanced by 2 + key.len with no check against the datagram end, so subsequent reads/writes can exceed the buffer.
For VARIABLE_INT, decode_variable_length is called without passing the remaining buffer length, so the decoder has no bound to stop at.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length/offset arithmetic lets property parsing write and read past the end of the heap dgram buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) rather than a mere out-of-bounds read, since the parser advances and processes data beyond the allocated region.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is missing upper-bound validation: offsets and decoded lengths are trusted after only a lower-bound check, and the variable-length decoder receives no remaining-length argument. A crafted MQTT PUBLISH property block makes i or new_pos advance beyond dgram.len, causing out-of-bounds reads/writes on the heap and potential memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
LBMPDM: fix heap-buffer-overflow (write) in dissect_segment_ofstable

id_list and ofs_list contain offsets read directly from the packet.
While the field type is FT_UINT32, it is somehow interpreted as signed
number. This means that ofs_table->offset_list[id_list[idx]]=... could
in fact result in an arbitrary write before "ofs_table->offset_list" due
to id_list[idx] being negative.

Another way for id_list[idx] to remain negative (-1) is for the loop to
terminate before all "field_count" elements are set. Thus, remove the
"datalen_remaining >= L_LBMPDM_OFFSET_ENTRY_T" check, if the offset is
invalid the proto_tree_add_item accessors will throw an exception.

Fixes the crash in the linked bug. Regression tested against the 8
capture files from bug 9718, its dissection results are still the same.

Bug: 15132
Change-Id: If5d2f11ee47578acb80bc43ba7ed16adb27e0c02
Fixes: v1.11.3-rc1-2270-g2f4ca9c8d9 ("Initial checkin of LBM aka 29West dissectors. See Bug 9718.")
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/30300
Petri-Dish: Peter Wu <peter@lekensteyn.nl>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 5797f602741a7505c18c2e0c505e963ca3349153)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/30347
Reviewed-by: Peter Wu <peter@lekensteyn.nl>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int datalen_remaining = 0;', '    datalen_remaining = datalen;', '    for (idx = 0; (idx < field_count) && (datalen_remaining >= L_LBMPDM_OFFSET_ENTRY_T); idx++, ofs += L_LBMPDM_OFFSET_ENTRY_T)'], 'added_lines': ['    for (idx = 0; idx < field_count; idx++, ofs += L_LBMPDM_OFFSET_ENTRY_T)', '        if (id_list[idx] < 0 || ofs_list[idx] < 0) {', '            THROW(ReportedBoundsError);', '        }']}
description: In Wireshark 2.6.0 to 2.6.4 and 2.4.0 to 2.4.10, the LBMPDM dissector could crash. In addition, a remote attacker could write arbitrary data to any memory locations before the packet-scoped memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-lbmpdm.c by disallowing certain negative values.

code_evidence: field_count derives from packet datalen, and the id_list and ofs_list arrays are sized to field_count entries.
id_list[idx] and ofs_list[idx] are cast to gint32 from packet-fetched uint32 values, so a crafted value can become a negative index.
Only a greater-than check updates max_index; negative ids are not excluded, so max_index and the allocation size in line 55 can be inconsistent with later indexing.
offset_list is allocated with ofs_table->num_flds = max_index + 1 entries.
The final loop indexes offset_list by the unvalidated id_list[idx], which can be negative.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because line 62 performs a write to ofs_table->offset_list[id_list[idx]] where the signed index can be negative, placing the write before the allocated buffer. This is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read or NULL dereference.

evidence_lines.code:
id_list[idx] = (gint32)lbmpdm_fetch_uint32_encoded(tvb, ofs + O_LBMPDM_OFFSET_ENTRY_T_ID, encoding);
ofs_list[idx] = (gint32)lbmpdm_fetch_uint32_encoded(tvb, ofs + O_LBMPDM_OFFSET_ENTRY_T_OFFSET, encoding);

ofs_table->num_flds = max_index + 1;
ofs_table->offset_list = wmem_alloc_array(wmem_packet_scope(), gint32, ofs_table->num_flds);

for (idx = 0; idx < field_count; ++idx)
ofs_table->offset_list[id_list[idx]] = ofs_list[idx];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Packet-controlled offset-table entries are cast to signed 32-bit integers without a lower-bound check. A negative id_list[idx] is used to index ofs_table->offset_list, writing ofs_list[idx] before the allocated buffer (and min_set_offset may take that address). The trigger is a crafted LBMPDM offset table; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write before packet-scoped memory, causing a crash and potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Issue #846: Handle the case where a client tries to send too-large commands
in an effort to DoS the server.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['         * them another chance?'], 'added_lines': ['  unsigned int too_large_count = 0;', '         * them a few more chances, with minor delays?', '        too_large_count++;', '        pr_timer_usleep(250 * 1000);', '', '        if (too_large_count > 3) {', '          return -1;', '        }', '']}
description: ProFTPD before 1.3.6b and 1.3.7rc before 1.3.7rc2 allows remote unauthenticated denial-of-service due to incorrect handling of overly long commands because main.c in a child process enters an infinite loop.

code_evidence: The while(TRUE) loop at line 16 repeatedly calls pr_netio_telnet_gets2; on E2BIG (line 22) it takes continue at line 23, returning to the top without any counter, delay, or cap, so an oversized command is retried indefinitely.
After the loop, lines 33-38 truncate/terminate only when cmd_buflen > cmd_bufsz, which never triggers for the E2BIG path since that branch already continued.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the iteration at line 16 has no reachable exit when errno==E2BIG: the continue at line 23 guarantees re-entry with the same condition and no state change, and the truncation guard at lines 33-38 is bypassed. This is an infinite loop, not merely a buffer-size issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the E2BIG handler unconditionally continues the unbounded while(TRUE) loop. Trigger: a remote unauthenticated client sends an overly long command so pr_netio_telnet_gets2 returns E2BIG. Consequence: the child process spins forever, consuming CPU and denying service; the loop's exit condition (break at line 31) is never reached on this path.

commit_msg:
Remove an abort in the bfd library and add a check for an integer overflow when mapping sections to segments.

	PR 23932
	* elf.c (IS_CONTAINED_BY_LMA): Add a check for a negative section
	size.
	(rewrite_elf_program_header): If no sections are mapped into a
	segment return an error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  BFD_ASSERT (map->count > 0);'], 'added_lines': ['   && (section->lma + SECTION_SIZE (section, segment) >= section->lma)\t\\', '\t  /* PR 23932.  A corrupt input file may contain sections that cannot', '\t     be assigned to any segment - because for example they have a', '\t     negative size - or segments that do not contain any sections.  */', '\t  if (map->count == 0)', '\t    {', '\t      bfd_set_error (bfd_error_bad_value);', '\t      free (sections);', '\t      return FALSE;', '\t    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils through 2.31. There is an integer overflow and infinite loop caused by the IS_CONTAINED_BY_LMA macro in elf.c.

code_evidence: IS_CONTAINED_BY_LMA computes section->lma + SECTION_SIZE(section, segment) and compares it to SEGMENT_END, with no overflow guard; a corrupt section size can wrap the sum below the segment end.
The do-loop uses IS_CONTAINED_BY_LMA to accept a section, then hits abort() when the alignment check at line 318 fails (map->count==0), aborting the process.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an unchecked addition of two bfd_vma values whose result is assumed to remain above section->lma; wraparound of that sum is exactly CWE-190. The patch adds a (sum >= section->lma) check, confirming the intended integer-overflow guard rather than a separate bounds or logic weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
#define IS_CONTAINED_BY_LMA(section, segment, base)\
(section->lma >= base\
&& (section->lma + SECTION_SIZE (section, segment)\
<= SEGMENT_END (segment, base)))

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the containment macro adds an attacker-controlled section size to section->lma without checking for wraparound, so the sum can wrap to a small value and falsely satisfy the containment test. Trigger: a malformed input ELF with an oversized section size. Consequence: the wrapped comparison misclassifies the section, leading to the abort() path at line 326 (DoS).

commit_msg: Fixes #704
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '  obj1 = fileSpec.dictLookup("Desc");', '  if (obj1.isString())', '    desc = obj1.getString()->copy();'], 'added_lines': ['', '    obj1 = fileSpec.dictLookup("Desc");', '    if (obj1.isString()) {', '      desc = obj1.getString()->copy();', '    }']}

commit_msg:
drivers: hamradio: 6pack: fix UAF bug caused by mod_timer()

When a 6pack device is detaching, the sixpack_close() will act to cleanup
necessary resources. Although del_timer_sync() in sixpack_close()
won't return if there is an active timer, one could use mod_timer() in
sp_xmit_on_air() to wake up timer again by calling userspace syscall such
as ax25_sendmsg(), ax25_connect() and ax25_ioctl().

This unexpected waked handler, sp_xmit_on_air(), realizes nothing about
the undergoing cleanup and may still call pty_write() to use driver layer
resources that have already been released.

One of the possible race conditions is shown below:

      (USE)                      |      (FREE)
ax25_sendmsg()                   |
 ax25_queue_xmit()               |
  ...                            |
  sp_xmit()                      |
   sp_encaps()                   | sixpack_close()
    sp_xmit_on_air()             |  del_timer_sync(&sp->tx_t)
     mod_timer(&sp->tx_t,...)    |  ...
                                 |  unregister_netdev()
                                 |  ...
     (wait a while)              | tty_release()
                                 |  tty_release_struct()
                                 |   release_tty()
    sp_xmit_on_air()             |    tty_kref_put(tty_struct) //FREE
     pty_write(tty_struct) //USE |    ...

The corresponding fail log is shown below:
===============================================================
BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in __run_timers.part.0+0x170/0x470
Write of size 8 at addr ffff88800a652ab8 by task swapper/2/0
...
Call Trace:
  ...
  queue_work_on+0x3f/0x50
  pty_write+0xcd/0xe0pty_write+0xcd/0xe0
  sp_xmit_on_air+0xb2/0x1f0
  call_timer_fn+0x28/0x150
  __run_timers.part.0+0x3c2/0x470
  run_timer_softirq+0x3b/0x80
  __do_softirq+0xf1/0x380
  ...

This patch reorders the del_timer_sync() after the unregister_netdev()
to avoid UAF bugs. Because the unregister_netdev() is well synchronized,
it flushs out any pending queues, waits the refcount of net_device
decreases to zero and removes net_device from kernel. There is not any
running routines after executing unregister_netdev(). Therefore, we could
not arouse timer from userspace again.

Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Reviewed-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\tunregister_netdev(sp->dev);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunregister_netdev(sp->dev);', '']}
description: A use-after-free vulnerabilitity was discovered in drivers/net/hamradio/6pack.c of linux that allows an attacker to crash linux kernel by simulating ax25 device using 6pack driver from user space.

code_evidence: sixpack_close stops the queue, then deletes tx_t/resync_t timers before unregister_netdev, so the timer teardown ordering is the changed cleanup path.
After unregister_netdev, buffers and the net_device are freed, while the timer callbacks (sp_xmit_on_air) can still re-arm tx_t via mod_timer from user-triggered AX.25 paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's ordering permits a timer callback to operate on resources freed during close, matching CWE-416 use-after-free. The weakness is not merely a double-free; the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory by sp_xmit_on_air after teardown.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: del_timer_sync for tx_t runs before unregister_netdev, so a concurrent sp_xmit_on_air can re-arm the timer after deletion but while cleanup proceeds. Trigger: user-space AX.25 send/connect/ioctl reaches sp_xmit while sixpack_close unregisters and releases the tty/net_device. The re-armed timer later fires and dereferences freed resources, causing a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
This reverts commit 84ecc2f6eb1cb12e6d44818f94fa49b50f06e6ac.

con_insert_unipair() is working with a sparse 3-dimensional array:

- p->uni_pgdir[] is the top layer
- p1 points to a middle layer
- p2 points to a bottom layer

If it needs to allocate a new middle layer, and then fails to allocate
a new bottom layer, it would previously free only p2, and now it frees
both p1 and p2.  But since the new middle layer was already registered
in the top layer, it was not leaked.

However, if it looks up an *existing* middle layer and then fails to
allocate a bottom layer, it now frees both p1 and p2 but does *not*
free any other bottom layers under p1.  So it *introduces* a memory
leak.

The error path also cleared the wrong index in p->uni_pgdir[],
introducing a use-after-free.

Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
Fixes: 84ecc2f6eb1c ("consolemap: Fix a memory leaking bug in drivers/tty/vt/consolemap.c")
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (!p2) {', '\t\t\tkfree(p1);', '\t\t\tp->uni_pgdir[n] = NULL;', '\t\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!p2) return -ENOMEM;']}
description: An issue was discovered in con_insert_unipair in drivers/tty/vt/consolemap.c in the Linux kernel through 5.1.5. There is a memory leak in a certain case of an ENOMEM outcome of kmalloc. NOTE: This id is disputed as not being an issue

code_evidence: p1 is fetched from p->uni_pgdir at line 14; if an existing middle layer exists, p2 is looked up next. When the kmalloc_array for p2 fails at line 16, the error path at 17-21 frees p1 and clears p->uni_pgdir[n], but n at line 19 is the bottom-layer index (unicode>>6)&0x1f, not the top-layer index unicode>>11, so the wrong slot is cleared and the freed p1 pointer may remain referenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the error path abandons allocated bottom-layer entries without releasing them, leaving memory unavailable for reuse. The wrong-index clear is a related dangling-pointer concern, but the leak of p1's children is the supported missing-release weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ENOMEM path frees the middle layer p1 without freeing its existing bottom-layer children and clears the wrong p->uni_pgdir index; trigger is a failed bottom-layer allocation when p1 already existed. Supported consequence: the child p2 allocations under p1 become unreachable, a memory leak, and the mismatched index can leave a dangling p1 reference.

commit_msg:
babeld: fix #10502 #10503 by repairing the checks on length

This patch repairs the checking conditions on length in four functions:
babel_packet_examin, parse_hello_subtlv, parse_ihu_subtlv, and parse_update_subtlv

Signed-off-by: qingkaishi <qingkaishi@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        type = a[0];', '        if(i + 1 > alen) {', '        if(i + len > alen) {'], 'added_lines': ['        type = a[i];', '        if(i + 1 >= alen) {', '        if(i + len + 2 > alen) {']}
description: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in FRRouting through 8.1.0 due to a wrong check on the input packet length in the babel_packet_examin function in babeld/message.c.

code_evidence: Line 6 loops while i < alen, but line 7 reads type from a[0] instead of a[i], so the loop never advances past the first byte's type. Line 12 checks i + 1 > alen, allowing i + 1 == alen to pass; line 17 then reads a[i + 1] at index alen, one past the buffer. Line 18 checks i + len > alen, ignoring the two-byte header, so a len reaching the end still passes and line 26 reads a + i + 2 through DO_NTOHL beyond alen.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory outside the intended packet buffer because the bounds checks do not account for header bytes and the loop index. That is an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer's bounds, matching CWE-119; the specific manifestation is an out-of-bounds read rather than a write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The length guards use off-by-one/off-by-two comparisons (i + 1 > alen, i + len > alen) and the type read ignores i. A truncated Hello sub-TLV with i + 1 == alen or len extending to the buffer end passes validation, and the subsequent a[i + 1] or DO_NTOHL read at a + i + 2 crosses the intended buffer boundary, causing an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
virt: vbox: Only copy_from_user the request-header once

In vbg_misc_device_ioctl(), the header of the ioctl argument is copied from
the userspace pointer 'arg' and saved to the kernel object 'hdr'. Then the
'version', 'size_in', and 'size_out' fields of 'hdr' are verified.

Before this commit, after the checks a buffer for the entire request would
be allocated and then all data including the verified header would be
copied from the userspace 'arg' pointer again.

Given that the 'arg' pointer resides in userspace, a malicious userspace
process can race to change the data pointed to by 'arg' between the two
copies. By doing so, the user can bypass the verifications on the ioctl
argument.

This commit fixes this by using the already checked copy of the header
to fill the header part of the allocated buffer and only copying the
remainder of the data from userspace.

Signed-off-by: Wenwen Wang <wang6495@umn.edu>
Reviewed-by: Hans de Goede <hdegoede@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (copy_from_user(buf, (void *)arg, hdr.size_in)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t*((struct vbg_ioctl_hdr *)buf) = hdr;', '\tif (copy_from_user(buf + sizeof(hdr), (void *)arg + sizeof(hdr),', '\t\t\t   hdr.size_in - sizeof(hdr))) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.2. vbg_misc_device_ioctl() in drivers/virt/vboxguest/vboxguest_linux.c reads the same user data twice with copy_from_user. The header part of the user data is double-fetched, and a malicious user thread can tamper with the critical variables (hdr.size_in and hdr.size_out) in the header between the two fetches because of a race condition, leading to severe kernel errors, such as buffer over-accesses. This bug can cause a local denial of service and information leakage.

code_evidence: Line 10 copies the ioctl header from userspace pointer arg into kernel hdr, and lines 14-15 validate hdr.size_in and hdr.size_out against sizeof(hdr). Line 17 derives size from those validated fields, and line 30 re-reads from the same userspace arg using hdr.size_in. The userspace memory behind arg is not locked between the first copy and the second, so the values used at line 30 can differ from the checked ones.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is a time-of-check/time-of-use race: an untrusted concurrent writer modifies shared userspace data between the validation and the second copy, violating atomicity of the check-then-use sequence. This directly matches CWE-362's concurrent access to a shared resource without proper synchronization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the same userspace buffer is fetched twice, with validation applied only to the first fetch. A malicious thread racing on arg can change size_in after the check but before line 30, causing a copy length inconsistent with the validated size and the allocated buffer, leading to over-access or mismatched data. Consequence: kernel memory corruption/DoS and possible information leakage.

commit_msg:
qcow2: Fix NULL dereference in qcow2_open() error path (CVE-2014-0146)

The qcow2 code assumes that s->snapshots is non-NULL if s->nb_snapshots
!= 0. By having the initialisation of both fields separated in
qcow2_open(), any error occuring in between would cause the error path
to dereference NULL in qcow2_free_snapshots() if the image had any
snapshots.

Signed-off-by: Kevin Wolf <kwolf@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Max Reitz <mreitz@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    s->snapshots_offset = header.snapshots_offset;', '    s->nb_snapshots = header.nb_snapshots;', ''], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Internal snapshots */', '    s->snapshots_offset = header.snapshots_offset;', '    s->nb_snapshots = header.nb_snapshots;']}
description: The qcow2_open function in the (block/qcow2.c) in QEMU before 1.7.2 and 2.x before 2.0.0 allows local users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted image which causes an error, related to the initialization of the snapshot_offset and nb_snapshots fields.

code_evidence: Lines 167-168 initialize s->snapshots_offset and s->nb_snapshots from the header before any validation of the L1 table, refcount handling, extensions, or backing file.
Lines 242-245 call qcow2_read_snapshots(bs) and jump to the fail label on error; qcow2_read_snapshots only allocates s->snapshots when s->nb_snapshots != 0.

The fail block at lines 320-323 unconditionally calls qcow2_free_snapshots(bs), which iterates/frees s->snapshots even though a prior error between 168 and 242 left it NULL while nb_snapshots is nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences s->snapshots while it is NULL because nb_snapshots is nonzero but allocation was skipped; this is exactly CWE-476. It is not a mere uninitialized read, since the pointer is NULL and the failure is an availability-impacting crash.

evidence_lines.code:
s->snapshots_offset = header.snapshots_offset;
s->nb_snapshots = header.nb_snapshots;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the snapshot count and offset fields are committed to the state before the snapshot array is allocated, so the shared error path frees snapshots that were never allocated. Trigger: a crafted qcow2 image with nb_snapshots != 0 that causes an error (e.g., invalid L1/refcount table or backing file) before qcow2_read_snapshots is reached. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference in qcow2_free_snapshots, crashing QEMU (DoS).

description: The d_walk function in fs/dcache.c in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 does not properly maintain the semantics of rename_lock, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock and system hang) via a crafted application.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is a debugging dump routine that only walks subdirectories and logs dentry data; it contains no resource allocation, throttling, or rename_lock handling, and the diff merely renames the list_entry member, so it does not support CWE-400.

commit_msg:
Fix handling of symbolic link ACLs

On Linux ACLs on symbolic links are not supported.
We must avoid calling acl_set_file() on symbolic links as their
targets are modified instead.

While here, do not try to set default ACLs on non-directories.

Fixes #1565
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    struct archive_acl *abstract_acl,'], 'added_lines': ['    struct archive_acl *abstract_acl, __LA_MODE_T mode,', '\t}', '', '\tif (S_ISLNK(mode)) {', '\t\t/* Linux does not support ACLs on symbolic links */', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_OK);', '\t}', '', '\tif (acl_type == ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT && !S_ISDIR(mode)) {', '\t\terrno = EINVAL;', '\t\tarchive_set_error(a, errno,', '\t\t    "Cannot set default ACL on non-directory");', '\t\treturn (ARCHIVE_WARN);']}
description: An improper link resolution flaw while extracting an archive can lead to changing the access control list (ACL) of the target of the link. An attacker may provide a malicious archive to a victim user, who would trigger this flaw when trying to extract the archive. A local attacker may use this flaw to change the ACL of a file on the system and gain more privileges.

code_evidence: set_acl's signature lacks any mode/type parameter; it receives a path name and an fd but no information about whether name refers to a symbolic link or the link's target.

The else branch calls acl_set_file(name, acl_type, acl) directly on the caller-supplied path with no lstat check, so when name is a symlink the ACL is applied to the resolved target rather than the link itself.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the function accesses a file by name and fails to prevent that name from being a link resolving to an unintended resource, exactly the improper link-resolution-before-access pattern. The flaw is link following, not merely wrong ACL type handling.

evidence_lines.code:
static int
set_acl(struct archive *a, int fd, const char *name,
struct archive_acl *abstract_acl,
int ae_requested_type, const char *tname)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: set_acl resolves the archive-controlled path via acl_set_file without verifying that the path is not a symbolic link, so the operation follows the link. Trigger: a malicious archive containing a symlink entry with an ACL causes extraction to modify the ACL of the link's target. Supported consequence: the target file's permissions/ACL are changed, potentially bypassing access controls and enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
v2: FontNames.c  return a NULL list whenever a single
length field from the server is incohent.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (rep.length < (INT_MAX >> 2)) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (rep.length < (INT_MAX >> 2) &&', '\t(rep.length >> 1) == rep.numKeyPerModifier) {']}
description: The XListFonts function in X.org libX11 before 1.6.4 might allow remote X servers to gain privileges via vectors involving length fields, which trigger out-of-bounds write operations.

code_evidence: The reply length field rep.length from the server is only checked against INT_MAX>>2; allocation size nbytes = rep.length<<2 and the read length passed to _XReadPad are both derived from it without validating consistency with rep.numKeyPerModifier.
res->max_keypermod is set from rep.numKeyPerModifier while the buffer is sized solely by rep.length, so consumers expecting (numKeyPerModifier * 8) bytes may index beyond the allocated map.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked length relationship lets a remote server induce an out-of-bounds write on a heap buffer, matching CWE-787. This is not merely an integer overflow (CWE-190) since the guard exists but fails to validate the length/keypermodifier consistency.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the server-controlled rep.length is trusted to size the modifier map buffer without cross-checking the declared numKeyPerModifier. A malicious X server sends an inconsistent reply, so the allocated buffer is smaller than the logical map implied by max_keypermod, and subsequent accesses write/read out of bounds.

description: decoder/impeg2d_dec_hdr.c in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file that triggers a certain negative value, aka internal bug 26070014.

code_evidence: u2_index is taken directly from ps_dec->u2_motion_type and used to index ps_func_bi_direct[u2_index] with no bounds check against the array size.
The selected function pointer pf_func_mb_params is then invoked, so an out-of-range index yields a pointer read outside the array.
The forward/back path repeats the same pattern: u2_index = ps_dec->u2_motion_type indexes ps_func_forw_or_back[u2_index] unchecked.
That unchecked pointer is likewise dereferenced and called via pf_func_mb_params(ps_dec).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads a function-pointer table at an attacker-controlled index outside the intended buffer boundary, which is exactly an out-of-bounds memory operation within CWE-119's scope. The missing upper-bound constraint on u2_index before indexing the arrays is the memory-safety defect; this is not merely a null-pointer issue, since the index itself is unvalidated.

evidence_lines.code:
UWORD16 u2_index       = (ps_dec->u2_motion_type);
ps_dec_mb_params = &ps_dec->ps_func_bi_direct[u2_index];
ps_dec_mb_params->pf_func_mb_params(ps_dec);
ps_dec_mb_params->pf_func_mb_params(ps_dec);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-influenced u2_motion_type (derived from stream bits, lines 45/79/89) is used as an array subscript without validating it against the ps_func_bi_direct/ps_func_forw_or_back table bounds. Trigger: a crafted media file supplies a motion type value outside the valid range. The out-of-bounds pointer read can yield an invalid function pointer whose call causes memory corruption, matching the described DoS/arbitrary code execution consequence.

The verifier considers this program as safe by mistakenly pruning unsafe
code paths. In the above func#0, code lines 0-10 are of interest. In line
0-3 registers r6 to r9 are initialized with known scalar values. In line 4
the register r6 is reset to an unknown scalar given the verifier does not
track modulo operations. Due to this, the verifier can also not determine
precisely which branches in line 6 and 9 are taken, therefore it needs to
explore them both.

As can be seen, the verifier starts with exploring the false/fall-through
paths first. The 'from 19 to 21' path has both r6=0 and r9=0 and the pointer
arithmetic on r0 += r6 is therefore considered safe. Given the arithmetic,
r6 is correctly marked for precision tracking where backtracking kicks in
where it walks back the current path all the way where r6 was set to 0 in
the fall-through branch.

Next, the pruning logics pops the path 'from 9 to 11' from the stack. Also
here, the state of the registers is the same, that is, r6=0 and r9=0, so
that at line 19 the path can be pruned as it is considered safe. It is
interesting to note that the conditional in line 9 turned r6 into a more
precise state, that is, in the fall-through path at the beginning of line
10, it is R6=scalar(umin=1), and in the branch-taken path (which is analyzed
here) at the beginning of line 11, r6 turned into a known const r6=0 as
r9=0 prior to that and therefore (unsigned) r6 <= 0 concludes that r6 must
be 0 (**):

  [...]                                 ; R6_w=scalar()
  9: (bd) if r6 <= r9 goto pc+1         ; R6=scalar(umin=1) R9=0
  [...]

  from 9 to 11: R1=ctx(off=0,imm=0) R6=0 R7=0 R8=0 R9=0 R10=fp0
  [...]

The next path is 'from 6 to 9'. The verifier considers the old and current
state equivalent, and therefore prunes the search incorrectly. Looking into
the two states which are being compared by the pruning logic at line 9, the
old state consists of R6_rwD=Pscalar() R9_rwD=0 R10=fp0 and the new state
consists of R1=ctx(off=0,imm=0) R6_w=scalar(umax=18446744071562067968)
R7_w=0 R8_w=0 R9_w=-2147483648 R10=fp0. While r6 had the reg->precise flag
correctly set in the old state, r9 did not. Both r6'es are considered as
equivalent given the old one is a superset of the current, more precise one,
however, r9's actual values (0 vs 0x80000000) mismatch. Given the old r9
did not have reg->precise flag set, the verifier does not consider the
register as contributing to the precision state of r6, and therefore it
considered both r9 states as equivalent. However, for this specific pruned
path (which is also the actual path taken at runtime), register r6 will be
0x400 and r9 0x80000000 when reaching line 21, thus oob-accessing the map.

The purpose of precision tracking is to initially mark registers (including
spilled ones) as imprecise to help verifier's pruning logic finding equivalent
states it can then prune if they don't contribute to the program's safety
aspects. For example, if registers are used for pointer arithmetic or to pass
constant length to a helper, then the verifier sets reg->precise flag and
backtracks the BPF program instruction sequence and chain of verifier states
to ensure that the given register or stack slot including their dependencies
are marked as precisely tracked scalar. This also includes any other registers
and slots that contribute to a tracked state of given registers/stack slot.
This backtracking relies on recorded jmp_history and is able to traverse
entire chain of parent states. This process ends only when all the necessary
registers/slots and their transitive dependencies are marked as precise.

The backtrack_insn() is called from the current instruction up to the first
instruction, and its purpose is to compute a bitmask of registers and stack
slots that need precision tracking in the parent's verifier state. For example,
if a current instruction is r6 = r7, then r6 needs precision after this
instruction and r7 needs precision before this instruction, that is, in the
parent state. Hence for the latter r7 is marked and r6 unmarked.

For the class of jmp/jmp32 instructions, backtrack_insn() today only looks
at call and exit instructions and for all other conditionals the masks
remain as-is. However, in the given situation register r6 has a dependency
on r9 (as described above in **), so also that one needs to be marked for
precision tracking. In other words, if an imprecise register influences a
precise one, then the imprecise register should also be marked precise.
Meaning, in the parent state both dest and src register need to be tracked
for precision and therefore the marking must be more conservative by setting
reg->precise flag for both. The precision propagation needs to cover both
for the conditional: if the src reg was marked but not the dst reg and vice
versa.

description:
Incorrect verifier pruning in BPF in Linux Kernel >=5.4 leads to unsafe
code paths being incorrectly marked as safe, resulting in arbitrary read/write in
kernel memory, lateral privilege escalation, and container escape.

code_evidence: For BPF_JMP/BPF_JMP32 instructions, the function only handles BPF_CALL and BPF_EXIT; all other conditional opcodes fall through with *reg_mask left unchanged. In particular, for a register-to-register conditional (dreg <cond> sreg), nothing marks the source register as precise when the destination is tracked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The verifier performs an incorrect calculation of the precision bitmask (failing to include sreg for dreg<cond>sreg), and that flawed result drives a security-critical pruning decision, matching CWE-682's incorrect calculation used in a protection mechanism.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: backtrack_insn omits precision propagation for register-based conditional jumps, so an imprecise source register that influences a precise destination is never marked precise. Trigger: a conditional comparing a tracked scalar against another register whose value differs between states. Consequence: the verifier's pruning logic treats non-equivalent states as equivalent, incorrectly marking an unsafe path safe and permitting out-of-bounds map access.

commit_msg:
Btrfs: fix truncation of compressed and inlined extents

When truncating a file to a smaller size which consists of an inline
extent that is compressed, we did not discard (or made unusable) the
data between the new file size and the old file size, wasting metadata
space and allowing for the truncated data to be leaked and the data
corruption/loss mentioned below.
We were also not correctly decrementing the number of bytes used by the
inode, we were setting it to zero, giving a wrong report for callers of
the stat(2) syscall. The fsck tool also reported an error about a mismatch
between the nbytes of the file versus the real space used by the file.

Now because we weren't discarding the truncated region of the file, it
was possible for a caller of the clone ioctl to actually read the data
that was truncated, allowing for a security breach without requiring root
access to the system, using only standard filesystem operations. The
scenario is the following:

   1) User A creates a file which consists of an inline and compressed
      extent with a size of 2000 bytes - the file is not accessible to
      any other users (no read, write or execution permission for anyone
      else);

   2) The user truncates the file to a size of 1000 bytes;

   3) User A makes the file world readable;

   4) User B creates a file consisting of an inline extent of 2000 bytes;

   5) User B issues a clone operation from user A's file into its own
      file (using a length argument of 0, clone the whole range);

   6) User B now gets to see the 1000 bytes that user A truncated from
      its file before it made its file world readbale. User B also lost
      the bytes in the range [1000, 2000[ bytes from its own file, but
      that might be ok if his/her intention was reading stale data from
      user A that was never supposed to be public.

Note that this contrasts with the case where we truncate a file from 2000
bytes to 1000 bytes and then truncate it back from 1000 to 2000 bytes. In
this case reading any byte from the range [1000, 2000[ will return a value
of 0x00, instead of the original data.

This problem exists since the clone ioctl was added and happens both with
and without my recent data loss and file corruption fixes for the clone
ioctl (patch "Btrfs: fix file corruption and data loss after cloning
inline extents").

So fix this by truncating the compressed inline extents as we do for the
non-compressed case, which involves decompressing, if the data isn't already
in the page cache, compressing the truncated version of the extent, writing
the compressed content into the inline extent and then truncate it.

The following test case for fstests reproduces the problem. In order for
the test to pass both this fix and my previous fix for the clone ioctl
that forbids cloning a smaller inline extent into a larger one,
which is titled "Btrfs: fix file corruption and data loss after cloning
inline extents", are needed. Without that other fix the test fails in a
different way that does not leak the truncated data, instead part of
destination file gets replaced with zeroes (because the destination file
has a larger inline extent than the source).

  seq=`basename $0`
  seqres=$RESULT_DIR/$seq
  echo "QA output created by $seq"
  tmp=/tmp/$$
  status=1	# failure is the default!
  trap "_cleanup; exit \$status" 0 1 2 3 15

  _cleanup()
  {
      rm -f $tmp.*
  }

  # get standard environment, filters and checks
  . ./common/rc
  . ./common/filter

  # real QA test starts here
  _need_to_be_root
  _supported_fs btrfs
  _supported_os Linux
  _require_scratch
  _require_cloner

  rm -f $seqres.full

  _scratch_mkfs >>$seqres.full 2>&1
  _scratch_mount "-o compress"

  # Create our test files. File foo is going to be the source of a clone operation
  # and consists of a single inline extent with an uncompressed size of 512 bytes,
  # while file bar consists of a single inline extent with an uncompressed size of
  # 256 bytes. For our test's purpose, it's important that file bar has an inline
  # extent with a size smaller than foo's inline extent.
  $XFS_IO_PROG -f -c "pwrite -S 0xa1 0 128"   \
          -c "pwrite -S 0x2a 128 384" \
          $SCRATCH_MNT/foo | _filter_xfs_io
  $XFS_IO_PROG -f -c "pwrite -S 0xbb 0 256" $SCRATCH_MNT/bar | _filter_xfs_io

  # Now durably persist all metadata and data. We do this to make sure that we get
  # on disk an inline extent with a size of 512 bytes for file foo.
  sync

  # Now truncate our file foo to a smaller size. Because it consists of a
  # compressed and inline extent, btrfs did not shrink the inline extent to the
  # new size (if the extent was not compressed, btrfs would shrink it to 128
  # bytes), it only updates the inode's i_size to 128 bytes.
  $XFS_IO_PROG -c "truncate 128" $SCRATCH_MNT/foo

  # Now clone foo's inline extent into bar.
  # This clone operation should fail with errno EOPNOTSUPP because the source
  # file consists only of an inline extent and the file's size is smaller than
  # the inline extent of the destination (128 bytes < 256 bytes). However the
  # clone ioctl was not prepared to deal with a file that has a size smaller
  # than the size of its inline extent (something that happens only for compressed
  # inline extents), resulting in copying the full inline extent from the source
  # file into the destination file.
  #
  # Note that btrfs' clone operation for inline extents consists of removing the
  # inline extent from the destination inode and copy the inline extent from the
  # source inode into the destination inode, meaning that if the destination
  # inode's inline extent is larger (N bytes) than the source inode's inline
  # extent (M bytes), some bytes (N - M bytes) will be lost from the destination
  # file. Btrfs could copy the source inline extent's data into the destination's
  # inline extent so that we would not lose any data, but that's currently not
  # done due to the complexity that would be needed to deal with such cases
  # (specially when one or both extents are compressed), returning EOPNOTSUPP, as
  # it's normally not a very common case to clone very small files (only case
  # where we get inline extents) and copying inline extents does not save any
  # space (unlike for normal, non-inlined extents).
  $CLONER_PROG -s 0 -d 0 -l 0 $SCRATCH_MNT/foo $SCRATCH_MNT/bar

  # Now because the above clone operation used to succeed, and due to foo's inline
  # extent not being shinked by the truncate operation, our file bar got the whole
  # inline extent copied from foo, making us lose the last 128 bytes from bar
  # which got replaced by the bytes in range [128, 256[ from foo before foo was
  # truncated - in other words, data loss from bar and being able to read old and
  # stale data from foo that should not be possible to read anymore through normal
  # filesystem operations. Contrast with the case where we truncate a file from a
  # size N to a smaller size M, truncate it back to size N and then read the range
  # [M, N[, we should always get the value 0x00 for all the bytes in that range.

  # We expected the clone operation to fail with errno EOPNOTSUPP and therefore
  # not modify our file's bar data/metadata. So its content should be 256 bytes
  # long with all bytes having the value 0xbb.
  #
  # Without the btrfs bug fix, the clone operation succeeded and resulted in
  # leaking truncated data from foo, the bytes that belonged to its range
  # [128, 256[, and losing data from bar in that same range. So reading the
  # file gave us the following content:
  #
  # 0000000 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1 a1
  # *
  # 0000200 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a 2a
  # *
  # 0000400
  echo "File bar's content after the clone operation:"
  od -t x1 $SCRATCH_MNT/bar

  # Also because the foo's inline extent was not shrunk by the truncate
  # operation, btrfs' fsck, which is run by the fstests framework everytime a
  # test completes, failed reporting the following error:
  #
  #  root 5 inode 257 errors 400, nbytes wrong

  status=0
  exit

description: fs/btrfs/inode.c in the Linux kernel before 4.3.3 mishandles compressed inline extents, which allows local users to obtain sensitive pre-truncation information from a file via a clone action.

code_evidence: The inline-extent branch only truncates the extent item when compression, encryption and other_encoding are all zero; a compressed inline extent (compression != 0) fails this guard and falls to the else-if.
For the uncompressed case the code computes size = new_size - found_key.offset and shrinks the item via btrfs_truncate_item, discarding the truncated region.

In the compressed/other-encoded case the function only adjusts inode accounting (inode_sub_bytes) and never shrinks or rewrites the inline extent, so the bytes between new_size and item_end remain stored and readable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly enables disclosure of data the owner truncated and expected to be gone; the leftover bytes are exposed to unauthorized actors. This is an information exposure caused by improper truncation, matching CWE-200 rather than a simple memory-safety defect.

Trigger: a user truncates a file with a compressed inline extent to a smaller size. Consequence: stale data past the new size persists and can be read by others (e.g., via clone), leaking sensitive pre-truncation content.

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

commit_msg:
Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

Signed-off-by: Graham Chapman <graham_chapman@ca.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tAssert_VM_true(J9_ARE_NO_BITS_SET(resolveFlags, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CP_UPDATE));']}
description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: Computes ramCPEntry, invokeCacheIndex and the ramClass->invokeCache slot, then reads result = *invokeCache before any resolution or initialization occurs.
The resolution path (resolveClassRef and sendResolveOpenJDKInvokeHandle) runs only when result is NULL and canRunJavaCode is true, so entries are resolved lazily, not eagerly initialized.
On success the result is published via staticCompareAndSwapObject; if the CAS loses, result is re-read from invokeCache.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because a critical resource (the invoke-cache entry and the class initialization it depends on) is used without being initialized, and the function returns an uninitialized or unresolved value. This is missing initialization of a resource rather than a memory-safety flaw; the added assertion only guards a flag, not the initialization itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The invoke-cache slot is treated as a lazily populated resource and is read before it is initialized. If the slot is NULL and Java code cannot run (canRunJavaCode false), or if resolution fails, the uninitialized slot value (NULL or a stale entry) is returned to the caller. The caller can then invoke the handle without the class having been initialized, exposing uninitialized static values or causing a null dereference.

commit_msg: ok_jpg: Fix invalid DHT (#11)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ok_jpg_generate_huffman_table(table, buffer);', '        if (table->count > 0) {', '            if (table->count > 256 || table->count > length) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!ok_jpg_generate_huffman_table(table, buffer)) {', '            ok_jpg_error(jpg, OK_JPG_ERROR_INVALID, "Invalid DHT");', '            return false;', '        } else if (table->count > 0) {', '            if (table->count > length) {']}
description: David Brackeen ok-file-formats dev version is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow. When the function of the ok-file-formats project is used, a heap-buffer-overflow occurred in function ok_jpg_generate_huffman_table() in "/ok_jpg.c:403".

code_evidence: ok_jpg_generate_huffman_table() populates table->count from the DHT code-length bytes; its return value is ignored. The only guard is table->count > 256 || table->count > length, so a table with count > 256 but <= length still passes and ok_read writes table->count bytes into table->val.
length is decremented by 17 and then by table->count; a crafted DHT can make count exceed the real remaining segment, so the fixed-size table->val is filled beyond its bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced count bytes into a fixed-size heap table without a capacity constraint, which is an out-of-bounds write. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the write itself is the supported consequence.

length -= 17;
length -= table->count;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the count produced by huffman-table generation is not validated against the table->val capacity before ok_read writes count bytes. Trigger: a DHT segment whose code counts yield a count over 256 while length is large enough to pass the length check. Consequence: heap-buffer-overflow write past table->val (CWE-787).

commit_msg:
Fix UAF in ~CallbackEnv

com_android_bluetooth_btservice_AdapterService does not null its local
JNI environment variable after detaching the thread (which frees the
environment context), allowing UAF under certain conditions.

Null the variable in this case.

Testing here was done through a custom unit test; see patchsets 4-6 for
contents.  However, unit testing of the JNI layer is problematic in
production, so that part of the patch is omitted for final merge.

Bug: 291500341
Test: atest bluetooth_test_gd_unit, atest net_test_stack_btm
Tag: #security
Ignore-AOSP-First: Security
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:7a5c71c32d382c0e14083f0d093ae4f5420968ff)
Merged-In: I3e5e3c51412640aa19f0981caaa809313d6ad030
Change-Id: I3e5e3c51412640aa19f0981caaa809313d6ad030
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    callbackEnv = NULL;']}
description: In callback_thread_event of com_android_bluetooth_btservice_AdapterService.cpp, there is a possible memory corruption due to a use after free. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: On ASSOCIATE_JVM, AttachCurrentThread stores the JNI environment in the global callbackEnv and marks the thread as attached.

On DISASSOCIATE_JVM, DetachCurrentThread is called and sHaveCallbackThread is cleared, but the function shown does not reset callbackEnv; the diff adds callbackEnv = NULL after detach. After detach frees the environment context, callbackEnv still points to freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function keeps a pointer to memory freed by detach and allows subsequent references; the missing null assignment is exactly the stale-pointer condition. This is not just a leak because the pointer remains usable and can be dereferenced after free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the global callbackEnv retains a pointer to the JNI environment after DetachCurrentThread releases it, and the function does not clear it. A later use of callbackEnv, such as another callback path or re-association, dereferences freed memory, causing memory corruption or code execution.

commit_msg: saslserv/main: free sasl_sourceinfo_t after use
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tobject_unref(req.si);']}
description: Memory leak in the login_user function in saslserv/main.c in saslserv/main.so in Atheme 7.2.7 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to consume memory and cause a denial of service. This is fixed in 7.2.8.

code_evidence: login_user allocates a sasl_sourceinfo_t via sasl_sourceinfo_create(p) into req.si at line 8 and passes it to hook_call_user_can_login at line 11. When the hook denies login, the branch at lines 12-15 logs the failure and returns NULL without releasing req.si; the early-return paths later in the function likewise never unref it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because a created resource outlives its effective lifetime and is never released on an early-return path. This is a missing-release/lifetime defect, not a use-after-free (CWE-416) or double-free: the object is simply leaked, matching the availability impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The resource acquired at line 8 is only meant to live through the login check, but the denial path (lines 12-15) returns before any release, so each failed LOGIN from a remote unauthenticated client leaks one sasl_sourceinfo_t. commit_msg:
Security: update Lua struct package for security.

During an auditing Apple found that the "struct" Lua package
we ship with Redis (http://www.inf.puc-rio.br/~roberto/struct/) contains
a security problem. A bound-checking statement fails because of integer
overflow. The bug exists since we initially integrated this package with
Lua, when scripting was introduced, so every version of Redis with
EVAL/EVALSHA capabilities exposed is affected.

Instead of just fixing the bug, the library was updated to the latest
version shipped by the author.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["    case 'c': return getnum(L, fmt, 1);", '      int sz = getnum(L, fmt, sizeof(int));'], 'added_lines': ["    case 'c': return getnum(fmt, 1);", '      int sz = getnum(fmt, sizeof(int));']}
description: An Integer Overflow issue was discovered in the struct library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2, leading to a failure of bounds checking.

code_evidence: optsize returns a size derived from getnum(L, fmt, 1) for option 'c', using the parsed numeric value as the element size without any upper bound.
For 'i'/'I', getnum(L, fmt, sizeof(int)) computes sz, which is then only compared against MAXINTSIZE (sz > MAXINTSIZE) before being returned as the size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow that defeats a bounds check: the code assumes the computed size is valid and only compares it to a limit, matching CWE-190 (overflow/wraparound leading to failed bounds checking). It is not a plain missing length check but a faulty numeric computation whose overflow invalidates the guard.

evidence_lines.code: case 'c': return getnum(L, fmt, 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size returned by getnum is used as an element width, and the only guard is a comparison sz > MAXINTSIZE rather than a check on the arithmetic that produces the size. If getnum's internal computation wraps or overflows, the resulting sz can be small or negative, so the bounds check passes and a wrong (undersized) size is returned. That size then drives later packing/unpacking bounds logic, allowing out-of-bounds access.

commit_msg:
x86/hvm: Disallow the creation of HVM domains without Local APIC emulation

There are multiple problems, not necesserily limited to:

 * Guests which configure event channels via hvmop_set_evtchn_upcall_vector(),
   or which hit %cr8 emulation will cause Xen to fall over a NULL vlapic->regs
   pointer.

 * On Intel hardware, disabling the TPR_SHADOW execution control without
   reenabling CR8_{LOAD,STORE} interception means that the guests %cr8
   accesses interact with the real TPR.  Amongst other things, setting the
   real TPR to 0xf blocks even IPIs from interrupting this CPU.

 * On hardware which sets up the use of Interrupt Posting, including
   IOMMU-Posting, guests run without the appropriate non-root configuration,
   which at a minimum will result in dropped interrupts.

Whether no-LAPIC mode is of any use at all remains to be seen.

This is XSA-256.

Reported-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -6,7 +6,7 @@
         if ( is_hardware_domain(d) &&
              emflags != (XEN_X86_EMU_LAPIC|XEN_X86_EMU_IOAPIC) )
             return false;
-        if ( !is_hardware_domain(d) && emflags &&
+        if ( !is_hardware_domain(d) &&
              emflags != XEN_X86_EMU_ALL && emflags != XEN_X86_EMU_LAPIC )
             return false;
     }
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ( !is_hardware_domain(d) && emflags &&'], 'added_lines': ['        if ( !is_hardware_domain(d) &&']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.8.x through 4.10.x allowing x86 PVH guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and hypervisor crash) by leveraging the mishandling of configurations that lack a Local APIC.

code_evidence: For non-hardware HVM domains, the guard only rejects emflags when they are nonzero and not XEN_X86_EMU_ALL or XEN_X86_EMU_LAPIC. The original condition also required emflags to be nonzero (`emflags &&`), so a call with emflags == 0 (no Local APIC emulation) passes this check and the function returns true, permitting an HVM domain to be created without Local APIC emulation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference of vlapic->regs when Local APIC emulation is absent, matching CWE-476. The function's missing constraint on emflags permits the unsafe configuration; it is not a separate weakness such as improper input validation alone, since the concrete impact is the NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation accepts emflags == 0 for non-hardware HVM domains, allowing domains that lack Local APIC emulation. Trigger: a guest configures event channels via hvmop_set_evtchn_upcall_vector() or accesses %cr8, reaching code that dereferences vlapic->regs. Because no vlapic exists, that pointer is NULL, causing a NULL pointer dereference and hypervisor crash (DoS).

We need to put an upper bound on "user_len" so the memcpy() doesn't
overflow.

Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>

commit_msg:
v2: Protect against integer overflow (Alan Coopersmith)

Reviewed-by: Alan Coopersmith <alan.coopersmith@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Jeremy Huddleston Sequoia <jeremyhu@apple.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Cristau <jcristau@debian.org>
Signed-off-by: Nathan Kidd <nkidd@opentext.com>
Signed-off-by: Julien Cristau <jcristau@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return BadAlloc;'], 'added_lines': ['        return BadLength;']}
description: xorg-x11-server before 1.19.5 was vulnerable to integer overflow in ProcDbeGetVisualInfo function allowing malicious X client to cause X server to crash or possibly execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 10 validates stuff->n against UINT32_MAX / sizeof(DbeSwapInfoRec) before line 12 computes stuff->n * sizeof(xDbeSwapInfo) for REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE. The guard prevents the multiplication from wrapping, so the function itself already performs the overflow check rather than the vulnerable unchecked computation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code guards a multiplication used for size validation, and the check at line 10 directly addresses integer wraparound in the size computation. The function demonstrates the overflow-prevention pattern rather than an exploitable overflow, but the relevant arithmetic and constraint are present.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an integer multiplication (stuff->n * sizeof(xDbeSwapInfo)) that could wrap if the client-supplied count is large. The trigger is a malicious X client sending a large n; the guard at line 10 constrains n so the product cannot exceed UINT32_MAX, and the return value only affects the error code (BadAlloc vs BadLength). The guard's presence means this function does not itself exhibit the overflow; the supported consequence of a missing guard would be incorrect size validation and potential out-of-bounds handling, but here it is blocked.

commit_msg:
On a I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA read request, if data->block[0] is
greater than I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX + 1, the underlying I2C driver writes
data out of the msgbuf1 array boundary.

It is possible from a user application to run into that issue by
calling the I2C_SMBUS ioctl with data.block[0] greater than
I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX + 1.

This patch makes the code compliant with
Documentation/i2c/dev-interface by raising an error when the requested
size is larger than 32 bytes.

Call Trace:
 [<ffffffff8139f695>] dump_stack+0x67/0x92
 [<ffffffff811802a4>] panic+0xc5/0x1eb
 [<ffffffff810ecb5f>] ? vprintk_default+0x1f/0x30
 [<ffffffff817456d3>] ? i2cdev_ioctl_smbus+0x303/0x320
 [<ffffffff8109a68b>] __stack_chk_fail+0x1b/0x20
 [<ffffffff817456d3>] i2cdev_ioctl_smbus+0x303/0x320
 [<ffffffff81745aed>] i2cdev_ioctl+0x4d/0x1e0
 [<ffffffff811f761a>] do_vfs_ioctl+0x2ba/0x490
 [<ffffffff81336e43>] ? security_file_ioctl+0x43/0x60
 [<ffffffff811f7869>] SyS_ioctl+0x79/0x90
 [<ffffffff81a22e97>] entry_SYSCALL_64_fastpath+0x12/0x6a

Signed-off-by: Jeremy Compostella <jeremy.compostella@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Wolfram Sang <wsa@the-dreams.de>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (msg[0].len > I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX + 1) {', '\t\t\t\tdev_err(&adapter->dev,', '\t\t\t\t\t"Invalid block write size %d\\n",', '\t\t\t\t\tdata->block[0]);', '\t\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (data->block[0] > I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX) {', '\t\t\tdev_err(&adapter->dev, "Invalid block %s size %d\\n",', '\t\t\t\tread_write == I2C_SMBUS_READ ? "read" : "write",', '\t\t\t\tdata->block[0]);', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '\t\t}', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in drivers/i2c/i2c-core-smbus.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.15. There is an out of bounds write in the function i2c_smbus_xfer_emulated.

code_evidence: msgbuf1 is declared with I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX+2 bytes (line 7). In the I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA read path, msg[1].len is set directly from the user-controlled data->block[0] with no upper-bound check (lines 96-97). i2c_transfer then fills msgbuf1 according to that length, and the copy-back loop at lines 147-148 iterates to data->block[0].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic out-of-bounds write: an unchecked length controls how many bytes are written into a fixed-size stack buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read because the driver writes received data past msgbuf1's end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The read branch of I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA assigns msg[1].len = data->block[0] without validating it against I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX, while the write branch has such a check. A user passing data.block[0] larger than the buffer via the I2C_SMBUS ioctl causes the underlying driver to write past msgbuf1 (and the copy-back to overrun data->block), corrupting memory/stack.

commit_msg:
ati: use vga_read_byte in ati_cursor_define

This makes sure reads are confined to vga video memory.

v3: use uint32_t, fix cut+paste bug.
v2: fix ati_cursor_draw_line too.

Reported-by: xu hang <flier_m@outlook.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: BALATON Zoltan <balaton@eik.bme.hu>
Reviewed-by: Philippe Mathieu-Daudé <philmd@redhat.com>
Message-id: 20190917111441.27405-3-kraxel@redhat.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint8_t *src;', '    src = s->vga.vram_ptr + s->cursor_offset + (scr_y - vga->hw_cursor_y) * 16;', '        uint8_t abits = src[i];', '        uint8_t xbits = src[i + 8];'], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t srcoff;', '    srcoff = s->cursor_offset + (scr_y - vga->hw_cursor_y) * 16;', '        uint8_t abits = vga_read_byte(vga, srcoff + i);', '        uint8_t xbits = vga_read_byte(vga, srcoff + i + 8);']}
description: In QEMU 4.1.0, an out-of-bounds read flaw was found in the ATI VGA implementation. It occurs in the ati_cursor_define() routine while handling MMIO write operations through the ati_mm_write() callback. A malicious guest could abuse this flaw to crash the QEMU process, resulting in a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 12 computes src as vram_ptr + cursor_offset + (scr_y - hw_cursor_y) * 16, using guest-controlled cursor_offset and hw_cursor_y without validating that the cursor region lies within vram_size.

The loop at line 15 reads src[i] and src[i+8] (lines 17-18) directly from that pointer; the earlier guard only checks scr_y bounds and CRTC enable, not the cursor offset range, so reads can extend past the allocated VRAM buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads bytes past the end of the intended VRAM buffer via an unchecked computed pointer. It is not a write overflow (CWE-787) since the dereference is a read used to compute pixel colors.

evidence_lines.code: src = s->vga.vram_ptr + s->cursor_offset + (scr_y - vga->hw_cursor_y) * 16;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cursor_offset and hw_cursor_y derive from guest MMIO registers and are added to vram_ptr with no bounds check against vram_size. Trigger: a malicious guest programs an out-of-range cursor offset, so ati_cursor_draw_line dereferences memory beyond the VRAM allocation. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read that can crash the QEMU process (DoS) and expose adjacent host memory.

description: codecs/on2/dec/SoftVPX.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-05-01 does not validate VPX output buffer sizes, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, as demonstrated by obtaining Signature or SignatureOrSystem access, aka internal bug 27597103.

code_evidence: Line 40 sets outHeader->nFilledLen from outputBufferWidth()*outputBufferHeight()*3/2 without comparing it to outHeader->nAllocLen. Lines 42 and 49 then use outHeader->pBuffer as dst and copy a full YV12 frame into it via copyYV12FrameToOutputBuffer, so the copy size is derived from dimensions rather than the allocated buffer capacity.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function omits the buffer-size check that would constrain writes, matching the target category's access/privilege-management concern as demonstrated by obtaining Signature-level access. The direct memory flaw is an out-of-bounds write; CWE-264 captures the resulting privilege escalation described for this bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder output buffer capacity (nAllocLen) is never validated against the frame size written (nFilledLen) before the YV12 copy. Trigger: a crafted stream producing frame dimensions larger than the supplied output buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write past pBuffer, corrupting adjacent memory and enabling privilege escalation in mediaserver.

commit_msg:
Proper global init/deinit of GnuTLS

These are reference counted so it is important to retain symmetry
between the calls. Failure to do so will result in bad memory access
and crashes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    initGlobal();', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: The Xvnc server in TigerVNC allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (invalid memory access and crash) by terminating a TLS handshake early.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no buffer allocation, indexing, or length arithmetic; the only memory-related defect is reference-count asymmetry in initGlobal/deinit causing invalid access, which is a lifecycle/initialization flaw rather than an out-of-bounds buffer operation.

commit_msg:
Track byteSize of HeaderMap internally.

Introduces a cached byte size updated internally in HeaderMap. The value
is stored as an optional, and is cleared whenever a non-const pointer or
reference to a HeaderEntry is accessed. The cached value can be set with
refreshByteSize() which performs an iteration over the HeaderMap to sum
the size of each key and value in the HeaderMap.

Signed-off-by: Asra Ali <asraa@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      cached_byte_size_.reset();']}
description: Upon receiving each incoming request header data, Envoy will iterate over existing request headers to verify that the total size of the headers stays below a maximum limit. The implementation in versions 1.10.0 through 1.11.1 for HTTP/1.x traffic and all versions of Envoy for HTTP/2 traffic had O(n^2) performance characteristics. A remote attacker may craft a request that stays below the maximum request header size but consists of many thousands of small headers to consume CPU and result in a denial-of-service attack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown get() function only performs a linear lookup and resets a cached byte size; it contains no header-size accounting or iteration logic that could exhibit the O(n^2) resource-consumption flaw described, so the target CWE-400 is not directly supported by this function.

commit_msg:
Fixed OOB read in update_read_cache_bitmap_v3_order

CVE-2020-11096 thanks @antonio-morales for finding this.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbitsPerPixelId = BPP_CBR2[cache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp];'], 'added_lines': ['\tBOOL rc;', '\tbitsPerPixelId = get_bpp_bmf(cache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp, &rc);', '\tif (!rc)', '\t\treturn FALSE;']}
description: In FreeRDP before version 2.1.2, there is a global OOB read in update_read_cache_bitmap_v3_order. As a workaround, one can disable bitmap cache with -bitmap-cache (default). This is fixed in version 2.1.2.

code_evidence: Line 8 indexes BPP_CBR2 directly with cache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp without any bounds check.

The resulting bitsPerPixelId is shifted left by 3 and ORed into *flags, so an attacker-controlled out-of-range bitmapBpp value drives an out-of-bounds table read whose result is propagated into output flags.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads past the end of the BPP_CBR2 buffer due to a missing index validation, matching CWE-125. Unlike CWE-787, the defect is an out-of-bounds read, not a write.

evidence_lines.code: bitsPerPixelId = BPP_CBR2[cache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the unchecked indexing of the fixed BPP_CBR2 lookup table by cache_bitmap_v2->bitmapBpp. When bitmapBpp exceeds the table bounds, the read accesses memory past the array, producing a global out-of-bounds read whose value flows into the flags field.

commit_msg:
Use new libostree APIs to reject world-writable/suid content

This uses the new libostree APIs that landed recently to ensure
that we reject any files with mode outside of `0775` for system
helper pulls, and we also mask directory modes during checkout.

However, this does *not* fix up any already downloaded content.
For that, one could uninstall/reinstall; or a future patch could
do a one-time fixup pass.

Note that I am not aware of a way for flatpak applications to escalate their
privileges directly with this flaw; the bubblewrap `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` turns
of setuid. However, in combination with code execution on the host via another
mechanism (e.g. unsandboxed app), a setuid app injected could be used to gain
full host privileges.

At this time we're not aware of any flatpak content exploiting this issue.

Closes: https://github.com/flatpak/flatpak/issues/845
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  OstreeRepoPullFlags flags = OSTREE_REPO_PULL_FLAGS_UNTRUSTED;'], 'added_lines': ['  /* The latter flag was introduced in https://github.com/ostreedev/ostree/pull/926 */', '  const OstreeRepoPullFlags flags = OSTREE_REPO_PULL_FLAGS_UNTRUSTED |OSTREE_REPO_PULL_FLAGS_BAREUSERONLY_FILES;']}
description: In Flatpak before 0.8.7, a third-party app repository could include malicious apps that contain files with inappropriate permissions, for example setuid or world-writable. The files are deployed with those permissions, which would let a local attacker run the setuid executable or write to the world-writable location. In the case of the "system helper" component, files deployed as part of the app are owned by root, so in the worst case they could be setuid root.

code_evidence: Line 12 builds the pull flags as only OSTREE_REPO_PULL_FLAGS_UNTRUSTED, with no flag restricting file modes.
Lines 31-32 serialize these flags into the pull options variant sent to libostree.
Lines 54-55 pass that options variant to ostree_repo_pull_with_options, so the resulting checkout inherits whatever modes the untrusted repository supplies.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 fits because the pull path effectively accepts permission settings for security-critical deployed resources that grant more access than intended. This is an incorrect permission assignment during deployment, not a missing authorization check on an operation.

evidence_lines.code: OstreeRepoPullFlags flags = OSTREE_REPO_PULL_FLAGS_UNTRUSTED;

g_variant_builder_add (&builder, "{s@v}", "flags",
g_variant_new_variant (g_variant_new_int32 (flags)));

res = ostree_repo_pull_with_options (self, url, g_variant_builder_end (&builder),
progress, cancellable, error);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the untrusted pull is performed without constraining the modes of checked-out files, so a malicious third-party repository can ship setuid or world-writable files that are deployed as-is. Trigger: a user pulls from such a repository. Consequence: locally deployed files carry unsafe permissions, and in the system-helper case they are root-owned, enabling privilege escalation or modification by unintended actors.

commit_msg:
Fix various overflows in util/ (CVE-2017-11704)

* Add a check in decompileIF to avoid overflows.

    Avoid processing block when sact->numActions is 0, as
    sact->numActions - 1 may be used as index when accessing
    sact->Actions array.

* Fix overflow in readUInt32.

    o Fix declaration of readUInt32 and readSInt32 in util/read.h:
      return types should be unsigned long and long.
    o readUInt32: Avoid calling all readUInt8(f) in one line, order of
      evaluation is not guaranteed in the C standard.
    o readUInt32: Cast result of readUInt8(f) before << 24 to avoid
      overflow.

* Fix overflow in readMovie.

    length has int type but according to the specification it should be able
    to store unsigned 32bit numbers. Instead of changing the type of
    length, which would be a major refactoring, we verify that the value
    returned by readUInt32 is smaller than INT_MAX and update length if
    it's the case. Otherwise we print a warning and ignore the block.

This commit fixes CVE-2017-11704.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tlength = readUInt32 (f);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tunsigned long real_length = readUInt32 (f);', '', '                        if (real_length > INT_MAX) {', '\t\t            SWF_warn(" Could not process long block with length %lu:"', '                                     " blocks with length > %d not supported on this system\\n",', '                                     real_length, INT_MAX);', '                            continue;', '                        } else {', '                            length = (int) real_length;', '                        }']}
description: A heap-based buffer over-read was found in the function decompileIF in util/decompile.c in Ming 0.4.8, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: When the short length field is 63, the function reads a 32-bit block length into the signed int variable length via readUInt32; no bound is enforced before use.
That length is used to compute nextFrame = fileOffset+length and is passed to filelen_check_fails(length) and blockParse(f, length, type).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked oversized length causes the parser to read past the intended block/buffer boundaries, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). This is distinct from an out-of-bounds write because the observed consequence is reading memory beyond the buffer, though the root cause is an integer overflow in length handling.

evidence_lines.code:
length = readUInt32 (f);
}

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an attacker-controlled 32-bit SWF block length is stored in a signed int without validating it against INT_MAX, so values above INT_MAX become negative and the fileOffset+length computation can wrap. Trigger: a crafted SWF with a length-63 block whose extended length exceeds INT_MAX. Consequence: the length checks and blockParse operate on an incorrect/negative length, leading to out-of-bounds reads (and possible crash/DoS).
