commit_msg:
sys/base64: Use void pointer for buffers in API

This is a non-breaking change, as `unsigned char *` can implicitly be converted
to `void *`.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static char getsymbol(unsigned char code, bool urlsafe)'], 'added_lines': ['static char getsymbol(uint8_t code, bool urlsafe)']}
description: RIOT 2020.04 has a buffer overflow in the base64 decoder. The decoding function base64_decode() uses an output buffer estimation function to compute the required buffer capacity and validate against the provided buffer size. The base64_estimate_decode_size() function calculates the expected decoded size with an arithmetic round-off error and does not take into account possible padding bytes. Due to this underestimation, it may be possible to craft base64 input that causes a buffer overflow.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown getsymbol function only maps a single byte to a character and performs no buffer indexing; the described overflow arises from base64_estimate_decode_size/base64_decode, not this function.

commit_msg:
Invalid generator were not removed from list

fluid_list_remove() should receive the beginning of a list, so it can adjust the predecessor of the element to be removed. Otherwise the element would remain in the list, which in this case led to a use-after-free afterwards.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    fluid_list_t *p, *p2, *p3, *dup, **hz = NULL;', '        p2 = ((SFInst *)(p->data))->zone;', '                    *hz = fluid_list_remove(*hz, p2->data);', '                    delete_zone((SFZone *)fluid_list_get(p2));'], 'added_lines': ['    fluid_list_t *p, *p2, *p3, *dup, **hz = NULL, *start_of_zone_list;', '        start_of_zone_list = p2 = ((SFInst *)(p->data))->zone;', '                    SFZone * izone = fluid_list_get(p2);', '                    *hz = fluid_list_remove(start_of_zone_list, izone);', '                    delete_zone(izone);']}
description: fluidsynth is a software synthesizer based on the SoundFont 2 specifications. A use after free violation was discovered in fluidsynth, that can be triggered when loading an invalid SoundFont file.

code_evidence: hz points to the zone-list head (or &p2) and is used as the list base for removal; line 138 calls fluid_list_remove(*hz, p2->data) and line 139 then delete_zone(fluid_list_get(p2)) frees the zone. Because *hz may not be the actual list head, fluid_list_remove can fail to unlink p2, so the freed zone node remains in the list and is revisited by p2 = fluid_list_next(p2) at line 153.

The relocation branch removes p2 via SLADVREM(*hz, p2), prepends the saved data and continues, showing the list base is manipulated through hz; this confirms the removal helper must receive the true list head to correctly adjust links.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code frees a zone object and later dereferences/advances the stale list node, which is exactly reuse of freed memory (CWE-416). It is not merely a memory leak or double free; the freed object remains reachable and is used afterward.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the invalid-global-zone path frees the zone with delete_zone while removing it using *hz, which may not be the list head, so the node can stay linked. Trigger: a crafted SoundFont with an invalid global zone. Consequence: the loop advances onto the freed zone (use-after-free), enabling memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix divide-by-zero vulnerability in scroll_cursor_bot.
Fix #12528
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    int width2 = width1 + curwin_col_off2();', '\t    // similar formula is used in curs_columns()', '\t    if (curwin->w_skipcol > width1)', '\t\tskip_lines += (curwin->w_skipcol - width1) / width2 + 1;', '\t    else if (curwin->w_skipcol > 0)', '\t\tskip_lines = 1;', '', '\t    top_plines -= skip_lines;', '\t    if (top_plines > curwin->w_height)', '\t    {', '\t\tscrolled += (top_plines - curwin->w_height);'], 'added_lines': ['\t    if (width1 > 0) {', '\t\tint width2 = width1 + curwin_col_off2();', '\t\t// similar formula is used in curs_columns()', '\t\tif (curwin->w_skipcol > width1)', '\t\t    skip_lines += (curwin->w_skipcol - width1) / width2 + 1;', '\t\telse if (curwin->w_skipcol > 0)', '\t\t    skip_lines = 1;', '', '\t\ttop_plines -= skip_lines;', '\t\tif (top_plines > curwin->w_height)', '\t\t{', '\t\t    scrolled += (top_plines - curwin->w_height);', '\t\t}']}
description: Divide By Zero in vim/vim from 9.0.1367-1 to 9.0.1367-3

code_evidence: Line 103 computes width1 = curwin->w_width - curwin_col_off(); line 104 computes width2 = width1 + curwin_col_off2(). When width1 is zero or negative, width2 can be zero, and line 106 divides (curwin->w_skipcol - width1) by width2 with no guard on width2.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 fits because the function performs a division whose divisor (width2) can be zero due to an unvalidated window-width calculation. This is a direct divide-by-zero, not merely an out-of-bounds or overflow issue.

commit_msg:
USB: uas: fix bug in handling of alternate settings

The uas driver has a subtle bug in the way it handles alternate
settings.  The uas_find_uas_alt_setting() routine returns an
altsetting value (the bAlternateSetting number in the descriptor), but
uas_use_uas_driver() then treats that value as an index to the
intf->altsetting array, which it isn't.

Normally this doesn't cause any problems because the various
alternate settings have bAlternateSetting values 0, 1, 2, ..., so the
value is equal to the index in the array.  But this is not guaranteed,
and Andrey Konovalov used the syzkaller fuzzer with KASAN to get a
slab-out-of-bounds error by violating this assumption.

This patch fixes the bug by making uas_find_uas_alt_setting() return a
pointer to the altsetting entry rather than either the value or the
index.  Pointers are less subject to misinterpretation.

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
CC: Oliver Neukum <oneukum@suse.com>
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint r, alt;', '', '\tif (alt < 0)', '\tr = uas_find_endpoints(&intf->altsetting[alt], eps);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct usb_host_interface *alt;', '\tint r;', '\tif (!alt)', '\tr = uas_find_endpoints(alt, eps);']}
description: The uas driver in the Linux kernel before 4.13.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted USB device, related to drivers/usb/storage/uas-detect.h and drivers/usb/storage/uas.c.

code_evidence: alt is declared as int and receives the return of uas_find_uas_alt_setting(), which is a bAlternateSetting descriptor value, not an array index. Line 13 then uses that value to index intf->altsetting[alt] before passing the element to uas_find_endpoints(). A crafted USB device can supply a bAlternateSetting value that exceeds the number of alternate settings, so the index is not bounded by the array size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Using an unvalidated descriptor value as an array index and reading intf->altsetting[alt] past the intended buffer is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The defect is not merely an incorrect value check; the unchecked index causes memory to be read beyond the array.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the driver conflates a descriptor bAlternateSetting number with an array index and dereferences intf->altsetting[alt] without validating alt against intf->num_altsetting. Trigger: a malicious USB device reports an alternate setting number larger than the array bounds. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the altsetting array, leading to a KASAN slab-out-of-bounds and possible crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
display-store: Pass the display object rather than the id in the removed signal

By the time GdmDisplayStore emits the "display-removed" signal, the display
is no longer in the store and gdm_display_store_lookup will not work in
signal handlers.

Change the "display-removed" parameter from the display id to the GdmDisplay
object, so that signal handers can perform any cleanup they need to do

CVE-2018-14424

Closes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gdm/issues/401
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        char *id;', '', '        gdm_display_get_id (stored_display->display, &id, NULL);', '', '                       id);', '        g_free (id);'], 'added_lines': ['                       stored_display->display);']}
description: The daemon in GDM through 3.29.1 does not properly unexport display objects from its D-Bus interface when they are destroyed, which allows a local attacker to trigger a use-after-free via a specially crafted sequence of D-Bus method calls, resulting in a denial of service or potential code execution.

code_evidence: stored_display_free emits the DISPLAY_REMOVED signal, passing the display id obtained earlier from the display object; the object itself is not passed to handlers.
Immediately after emitting the signal, the function unrefs stored_display->display, potentially destroying it, and then frees the StoredDisplay.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The core issue is that a display object is freed while still reachable through its D-Bus interface, and subsequent operations reference that freed memory, which is CWE-416. This is not merely a missing cleanup or resource leak; the freed object remains accessible to external callers.

evidence_lines.code:
g_signal_emit (G_OBJECT (stored_display->store),
signals[DISPLAY_REMOVED],
0,
id);
g_object_unref (stored_display->display);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Because the signal only carries the id, signal handlers cannot reliably retrieve the display from the store (it is already removed) and thus do not unexport it from D-Bus before its final unref. The display's D-Bus object outlives the freed GObject, and later D-Bus method calls reach freed memory, causing a use-after-free and possible DoS or code execution.

code_evidence: The only guard on ref_function_name_length before the copy loop is the signed cast check `(int) ref_function_name_length < 0`; since the length is a ut32 read from the file, values above INT_MAX or any large positive value pass this check.

code_evidence: The function accepts only a byte pointer fin and an offset pointer; it derives bloc from *offset and then walks the Huffman tree, calling get_bit(fin) on each iteration without any parameter or check bounding how many bits may be read.

Specify type for matching Subject Alternative Name. (#18628)


Signed-off-by: Pradeep Rao <pcrao@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  // Only match against URI SAN since SPIFFE specification does not restrict values in other SAN', '  // types. See the discussion: https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/issues/15392', '    if (general_name->type == GEN_URI) {', '      const std::string san = Utility::generalNameAsString(general_name);', '      for (const auto& config_san_matcher : subject_alt_name_matchers_) {', '        if (config_san_matcher.match(san)) {', '          return true;', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['    for (const auto& config_san_matcher : subject_alt_name_matchers_) {', '      if (config_san_matcher->match(general_name)) {', '        return true;']}
description: Envoy is an open source edge and service proxy, designed for cloud-native applications. The default_validator.cc implementation used to implement the default certificate validation routines has a "type confusion" bug when processing subjectAltNames. This processing allows, for example, an rfc822Name or uniformResourceIndicator to be authenticated as a domain name. This confusion allows for the bypassing of nameConstraints, as processed by the underlying OpenSSL/BoringSSL implementation, exposing the possibility of impersonation of arbitrary servers. As a result Envoy will trust upstream certificates that should not be trusted.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over every GENERAL_NAME in the certificate's subjectAltName extension, but the only type check is general_name->type == GEN_URI at line 7. Only GEN_URI entries are converted with Utility::generalNameAsString at line 8 and passed to config_san_matcher.match(san) at line 10. Other SAN types, such as GEN_DNS, GEN_EMAIL (rfc822Name) or GEN_URI mismatches, are silently skipped because they are treated as if they were the string form expected by the matcher.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-843 fits because the GENERAL_NAME resource is interpreted using an incompatible type: non-URI SAN values are handled through the same string-matching path intended for URI names, and the type field is not used to constrain the comparison. This is a logical type confusion leading to an incorrect trust decision, not a mere parsing error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the matcher consumes a SAN string without verifying that the GENERAL_NAME type matches the matcher's expected type, so a value of one SAN type (e.g. URI or rfc822Name) can be compared as if it were a DNS name. Trigger: a certificate carrying a SAN of an unexpected type whose value matches a configured name. Consequence: the name constraint check is bypassed and a certificate for an unintended identity is accepted, enabling impersonation of arbitrary servers.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix race among timer ioctls

ALSA timer ioctls have an open race and this may lead to a
use-after-free of timer instance object.  A simplistic fix is to make
each ioctl exclusive.  We have already tread_sem for controlling the
tread, and extend this as a global mutex to be applied to each ioctl.

The downside is, of course, the worse concurrency.  But these ioctls
aren't to be parallel accessible, in anyway, so it should be fine to
serialize there.

description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 uses an incorrect type of mutex, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition, use-after-free, and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: The ioctl dispatch reads user-controlled cmd and immediately performs put_user without any locking protecting tu or its timer state.
Multiple ioctl cases such as GINFO, SELECT and PARAMS call helper functions that mutate or tear down the shared timer instance with no exclusive access held across the dispatch.
Only the TREAD case takes tu->tread_sem, and it releases it before returning; all other command paths run unprotected, so concurrent ioctls on the same file can interleave.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a shared resource (tu and its timer) to concurrent ioctl sequences without a common exclusive lock, exactly the improper synchronization described by CWE-362. The use-after-free is a consequence of that missing exclusivity, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ioctl handler serializes only the TREAD subcommand and leaves the shared snd_timer_user/timer instance unprotected for all other commands. Trigger: two threads issue ioctls (e.g. SELECT/PARAMS versus a teardown path) on the same timer file concurrently, so one frees or reinitializes the timer while another still uses it, yielding a use-after-free and crash.

commit_msg:
io_uring: check that we have a file table when allocating update slots

If IORING_FILE_INDEX_ALLOC is set asking for an allocated slot, the
helper doesn't check if we actually have a file table or not. The non
alloc path does do that correctly, and returns -ENXIO if we haven't set
one up.

Do the same for the allocated path, avoiding a NULL pointer dereference
when trying to find a free bit.

Fixes: a7c41b4687f5 ("io_uring: let IORING_OP_FILES_UPDATE support choosing fixed file slots")
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>

description: A NULL pointer dereference issue was discovered in the Linux kernel in io_files_update_with_index_alloc. A local user could use this flaw to potentially crash the system causing a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop calls io_fixed_fd_install with IORING_FILE_INDEX_ALLOC, which allocates a fixed-file slot by searching the file table's bitmap; no check confirms req->ctx->file_data (the file table) exists before this call, so the allocation path can dereference a NULL table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a missing constraint on a pointer (req->ctx->file_data) that is later dereferenced, exactly matching CWE-476. It is not a generic input-validation issue: the direct consequence is a NULL dereference during slot allocation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocated-slot path lacks the file_data existence check that the non-alloc path performs. Trigger: a user submits IORING_OP_FILES_UPDATE with IORING_FILE_INDEX_ALLOC before any registered file table is set up, so io_fixed_fd_install's free-bit search dereferences a NULL file table. Consequence: kernel NULL pointer dereference, crashing the system (DoS).

commit_msg:
x86/mm/32: Enable full randomization on i386 and X86_32

Currently on i386 and on X86_64 when emulating X86_32 in legacy mode, only
the stack and the executable are randomized but not other mmapped files
(libraries, vDSO, etc.). This patch enables randomization for the
libraries, vDSO and mmap requests on i386 and in X86_32 in legacy mode.

By default on i386 there are 8 bits for the randomization of the libraries,
vDSO and mmaps which only uses 1MB of VA.

This patch preserves the original randomness, using 1MB of VA out of 3GB or
4GB. We think that 1MB out of 3GB is not a big cost for having the ASLR.

The first obvious security benefit is that all objects are randomized (not
only the stack and the executable) in legacy mode which highly increases
the ASLR effectiveness, otherwise the attackers may use these
non-randomized areas. But also sensitive setuid/setgid applications are
more secure because currently, attackers can disable the randomization of
these applications by setting the ulimit stack to "unlimited". This is a
very old and widely known trick to disable the ASLR in i386 which has been
allowed for too long.

Another trick used to disable the ASLR was to set the ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE
personality flag, but fortunately this doesn't work on setuid/setgid
applications because there is security checks which clear Security-relevant
flags.

This patch always randomizes the mmap_legacy_base address, removing the
possibility to disable the ASLR by setting the stack to "unlimited".

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int nvmx_handle_vmwrite(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)'], 'added_lines': ['static int nvmx_handle_vmwrite(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

code_evidence: decode_vmx_inst is checked and returns X86EMUL_EXCEPTION on failure, so decode/operand are only used after a successful decode.
The only guard before using VMX state is checking nv_vvmcxaddr against INVALID_PADDR; there is no check that nested virt was enabled or that the nvmx structure was initialised.

set_vvmcs_safe(v, vmcs_encoding, operand) is called with the vcpu and decoded operand, and its result is only used to trigger vmfail; the call itself is not gated by any privilege or nested-virt-enabled check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described failure is a host-side NULL pointer dereference caused by operating on an uninitialized nvmx structure, matching CWE-476. The missing nested-virt privilege check is the trigger, but the supported consequence is the NULL dereference rather than a generic access-control flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The handler performs VMX operations without first verifying that nested virtualization is enabled or that the nvmx structure has been initialized. When a guest executes VMWRITE while nested virt is off, the zeroed vcpu state makes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() appear true, so set_vvmcs_safe proceeds into uninitialized nvmx data, leading to a host NULL-pointer dereference and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Patch series "Fix several device private page reference counting issues",
v2

This series aims to fix a number of page reference counting issues in
drivers dealing with device private ZONE_DEVICE pages.  These result in
use-after-free type bugs, either from accessing a struct page which no
longer exists because it has been removed or accessing fields within the
struct page which are no longer valid because the page has been freed.

During normal usage it is unlikely these will cause any problems.  However
without these fixes it is possible to crash the kernel from userspace. 
These crashes can be triggered either by unloading the kernel module or
unbinding the device from the driver prior to a userspace task exiting. 
In modules such as Nouveau it is also possible to trigger some of these
issues by explicitly closing the device file-descriptor prior to the task
exiting and then accessing device private memory.

This involves some minor changes to both PowerPC and AMD GPU code. 
Unfortunately I lack hardware to test either of those so any help there
would be appreciated.  The changes mimic what is done in for both Nouveau
and hmm-tests though so I doubt they will cause problems.


This patch (of 8):

When the CPU tries to access a device private page the migrate_to_ram()
callback associated with the pgmap for the page is called.  However no
reference is taken on the faulting page.  Therefore a concurrent migration
of the device private page can free the page and possibly the underlying
pgmap.  This results in a race which can crash the kernel due to the
migrate_to_ram() function pointer becoming invalid.  It also means drivers
can't reliably read the zone_device_data field because the page may have
been freed with memunmap_pages().

Close the race by getting a reference on the page while holding the ptl to
ensure it has not been freed.  Unfortunately the elevated reference count
will cause the migration required to handle the fault to fail.  To avoid
this failure pass the faulting page into the migrate_vma functions so that
if an elevated reference count is found it can be checked to see if it's
expected or not.

description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel. It has been classified as problematic. Affected is an unknown function of the file mm/memory.c of the component Driver Handler. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211020.

code_evidence: svm_bo is obtained from the work item via container_of and then conditionally referenced with svm_bo_ref_unless_zero, returning early if the refcount is already zero.

The eviction_fence's mm is fetched and pinned with mmget_not_zero; if that fails, svm_bo is unreferenced and the worker returns, showing the object lifetime is reference-counted and can be torn down concurrently.

After the migration loop, the worker signals eviction_fence->base and then calls svm_range_bo_unref(svm_bo); the WARN_ONCE on the kref read indicates the code depends on svm_bo being the last reference at that point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses memory (svm_bo and its fields) whose lifetime is managed by reference counting, and the patch context shows the missing reference on the faulting page allowed the object to be freed before use. This is a use-after-free (CWE-416), not merely a race, because the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the worker dereferences svm_bo (and its eviction_fence/mm fields) after only a conditional reference, while concurrent eviction/unbinding can drop the last reference and free the object. Trigger: a racing teardown frees svm_bo between the ref_unless_zero check and later uses such as line 44. Consequence: use-after-free reads/writes of the freed svm_bo, potentially crashing the kernel.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!data || payload_len <= 0 || payload_len > 65535) {', '        tcpedit_setwarn(tcpedit, "%s", "Unable to checksum packets with no L3+ data");'], 'added_lines': ['    if (!data || payload_len < (int)sizeof(*ipv4) || payload_len > 0xffff) {', '        tcpedit_setwarn(tcpedit, "%s", "Unable to checksum packet with no L3+ data");', '        if (payload_len < sizeof(*ipv6)) {', '            tcpedit_setwarn(tcpedit, "%s", "Unable to checksum IPv6 packet with insufficient data");', '            return TCPEDIT_WARN;', '        }', '']}
description: Buffer Overflow in Tcpreplay v4.3.2 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service via the 'do_checksum' function in 'checksum.c'. It can be triggered by sending a crafted pcap file to the 'tcpreplay-edit' binary. This issue is different than CVE-2019-8381.

code_evidence: The entry guard only rejects payload_len <= 0; a small positive length (e.g., 1..3) passes, then ipv4 = (ipv4_hdr_t *)data and ipv4->ip_v is read from a buffer shorter than the header.

In the IPv6 branch, get_ipv6_l4proto and get_layer4_v6 are called with payload_len + sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t) while payload_len already describes the L3+ buffer, and ip_hl is derived from the resulting layer pointer.

For TCP, tcp = data + ip_hl is dereferenced (tcp->th_sum = 0) and do_checksum_math((uint16_t *)tcp, payload_len) reads payload_len bytes, where ip_hl can exceed the actual buffer and payload_len is adjusted without revalidating against the remaining buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs reads and writes through header pointers derived from insufficiently validated lengths, so operations fall outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. It is not merely a length-value error; the concrete impact is out-of-bounds memory access.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!data || payload_len <= 0 || payload_len > 65535) {
}

tcp = (tcp_hdr_t *)(data + ip_hl);
sum += do_checksum_math((uint16_t *)tcp, payload_len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length checks do not ensure the buffer holds a full IPv4/IPv6 header before casting and dereferencing, and the IPv6 path computes ip_hl/payload_len from a possibly inconsistent length. Trigger: a crafted pcap yielding a short or malformed L3/L4 length. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads (and writes such as tcp->th_sum) past the packet buffer, causing a crash/DoS and possible memory disclosure.

commit_msg:
We're holding the request reference, but we need to go one higher
to ensure that the ctx remains valid after the request has finished.
If the ring is closed with pending task_work inflight, and the
given io_kiocb finishes sync during issue, then we need a reference
to the ring itself around the task_work execution cycle.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v5.7+
Reported-by: syzbot+9b260fc33297966f5a8e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tpercpu_ref_get(&req->ctx->refs);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8.2. fs/io_uring.c has a use-after-free related to io_async_task_func and ctx reference holding, aka CID-6d816e088c35.

code_evidence: Line 4 initializes req->task_work to run io_req_task_submit, and line 5 queues it via io_req_task_work_add without first taking a reference on req->ctx->refs. The queued task_work can execute asynchronously after the current issue path returns and the request/ring context may be released, so the deferred callback dereferences a freed ctx.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the deferred task_work accesses req->ctx after its lifetime ended; the missing percpu_ref_get is the missing lifetime constraint. This is a lifetime/use-after-free flaw, not a simple null-pointer or logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
init_task_work(&req->task_work, io_req_task_submit);
ret = io_req_task_work_add(req, &req->task_work);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function schedules asynchronous task_work referencing req->ctx but does not hold a ctx reference across that deferred execution. Trigger: the ring is closed with the task_work still pending, or the request completes synchronously during issue. Consequence: io_req_task_submit uses the freed io_ring_ctx, yielding a use-after-free (crash, memory corruption).

commit_msg:
Check bounds for reads and writes in scatter_nd

PiperOrigin-RevId: 463365479
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  reference_ops::ScatterNd(', '  return kTfLiteOk;'], 'added_lines': ['  return reference_ops::ScatterNd(']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The `ScatterNd` function takes an input argument that determines the indices of of the output tensor. An input index greater than the output tensor or less than zero will either write content at the wrong index or trigger a crash. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit b4d4b4cb019bd7240a52daa4ba61e3cc814f0384. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: ScatterNd forwards the indices tensor shape/data, updates tensor shape/data, and output tensor shape/data directly to reference_ops::ScatterNd without any bounds validation on index values. The wrapper performs no check that each index lies within the output tensor's dimensions before passing control to the reference implementation, which writes updates into the output buffer at positions derived from indices.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function enables an index-driven write into the output tensor without validating index bounds, directly matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) because the affected operation stores updates at the computed index.

evidence_lines.code:
reference_ops::ScatterNd(
GetTensorShape(indices), GetTensorData<IndicesT>(indices),
GetTensorShape(updates), GetTensorData<UpdatesT>(updates),
GetTensorShape(output), GetTensorData<UpdatesT>(output));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: caller-supplied indices are used to compute write offsets into the output buffer without verifying 0 <= index < output dimension. Trigger: an index greater than the output tensor size or negative. Consequence: writes land before/after the intended output buffer, corrupting memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
Commit 086d49058cd8 ("ipv6: annotate some data-races around sk->sk_prot")
fixed some data-races around sk->sk_prot but it was not enough.

Some functions in inet6_(stream|dgram)_ops still access sk->sk_prot
without lock_sock() or rtnl_lock(), so they need READ_ONCE() to avoid
load tearing.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Signed-off-by: Kuniyuki Iwashima <kuniyu@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (sk->sk_prot->sendpage)', '\t\treturn sk->sk_prot->sendpage(sk, page, offset, size, flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct proto *prot;', '\t/* IPV6_ADDRFORM can change sk->sk_prot under us. */', '\tprot = READ_ONCE(sk->sk_prot);', '\tif (prot->sendpage)', '\t\treturn prot->sendpage(sk, page, offset, size, flags);']}
description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function inet6_stream_ops/inet6_dgram_ops of the component IPv6 Handler. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211090 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 7 dereferences sk->sk_prot to test the sendpage callback, and line 8 dereferences sk->sk_prot again to invoke it, with no lock_sock() or rtnl_lock() and no READ_ONCE() to stabilize the pointer between the two accesses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits: the function performs a concurrent check-then-use sequence on the shared sk->sk_prot resource without exclusive access or atomicity. This is a synchronization race, not a simple null-pointer dereference, because the defect is the unsynchronized re-read of a concurrently mutable pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
if (sk->sk_prot->sendpage)
return sk->sk_prot->sendpage(sk, page, offset, size, flags);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: sk->sk_prot is a shared pointer that IPV6_ADDRFORM can change concurrently. Because the check and the call each reload sk->sk_prot without synchronization, the pointer can be replaced between them, so the callback tested is not necessarily the one invoked, or a torn load can produce an invalid pointer. The supported consequence is a race-induced crash or instability in the IPv6 sendpage path.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

    (thread 1)          |        (thread 2)
                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

Although rose_destroy_socket() calls rose_stop_heartbeat(),
it could not stop the timer that is running.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdel_timer(&sk->sk_timer);', '\tadd_timer(&sk->sk_timer);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsk_stop_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer);', '\tsk_reset_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer, sk->sk_timer.expires);']}
description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: rose_start_heartbeat() arms sk->sk_timer with del_timer()/add_timer() but never takes a reference on the owning sock. del_timer() only removes a pending timer; it cannot stop a handler already executing, so the timer callback rose_heartbeat_expiry can run while the sock is being torn down and freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unmanaged timer lifetime permits the sock to be freed while its timer handler still references it, which is exactly CWE-416. This is distinct from a simple race or double-free; the supported consequence is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the timer is armed without holding a sock reference, and del_timer() cannot synchronize with an in-flight handler. Trigger: a timer expiry racing socket release/teardown, which frees sk via sock_put(). Consequence: rose_heartbeat_expiry then dereferences freed sk (e.g., locking the socket), yielding a use-after-free that can crash the kernel.

commit_msg:
pinctrl: amd: Use devm_pinctrl_register() for pinctrl registration

Use devm_pinctrl_register() for pin control registration and clean
error path.

Signed-off-by: Laxman Dewangan <ldewangan@nvidia.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Walleij <linus.walleij@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpinctrl_unregister(gpio_dev->pctrl);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: In the Linux kernel before 4.7, the amd_gpio_remove function in drivers/pinctrl/pinctrl-amd.c calls the pinctrl_unregister function, leading to a double free.

code_evidence: amd_gpio_remove retrieves gpio_dev from platform drvdata, removes the gpiochip with gpiochip_remove, then unconditionally calls pinctrl_unregister(gpio_dev->pctrl). No check guards whether the pinctrl object was already released or is managed elsewhere, so the same pctrl pointer is passed to the unregister path again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the function issues a second pinctrl_unregister/free on the same pctrl pointer during teardown. This is a double-free of a resource, not merely a missing null check or an unrelated cleanup ordering issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: teardown calls pinctrl_unregister on gpio_dev->pctrl without verifying ownership or prior release. Trigger: a remove path where that pinctrl was already unregistered (e.g., devm-managed cleanup) causes the same pointer to be freed/unregistered twice. Consequence: double free of the pinctrl memory, potentially leading to memory corruption or use-after-free behavior.

commit_msg:
admin: Add query_info_on_read/write functionality

Admin backend doesn't implement query_info_on_read/write which might
potentially lead to some race conditions which aren't really wanted
especially in case of admin backend. For example, in file_copy_fallback(),
g_file_query_info() is used if g_file_input_stream_query_info() is not
supported, which in theory means that the info might be obtained from
the different file then it is opened. Let's add this missing
functionality to prevent this possibility.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  backend_class->query_info_on_read = do_query_info_on_read;', '  backend_class->query_info_on_write = do_query_info_on_write;']}
description: An issue was discovered in GNOME gvfs 1.29.4 through 1.41.2. daemon/gvfsbackendadmin.c has race conditions because the admin backend doesn't implement query_info_on_read/write.

code_evidence: The class init registers open_for_read, query_info, and read handlers on the admin backend but omits query_info_on_read; the patch adds those missing vtable entries, indicating the backend previously had no atomic query-on-open-stream capability.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing vtable handlers force a non-atomic open-then-query sequence over a shared filesystem resource that another process can modify concurrently, matching CWE-362's improper synchronization window. This is a TOCTOU-style race rather than a simple null dereference or permission check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the admin backend lacked query_info_on_read/on_write, so callers like file_copy_fallback fall back to a separate g_file_query_info() on the path after opening the stream. Between open and query the file can be replaced, causing the info to describe a different file than the opened stream; the consequence is a time-of-check/time-of-use race affecting file metadata/identity.

commit_msg:
Fixed a 1-byte buffer overrun in the BMP decoder

Fixes issue #35
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tiw_byte buf[255];'], 'added_lines': ['\tiw_byte buf[256];', '\t\t\t\tif(n_bytes>sizeof(buf)) goto done;']}
description: libimageworsener.a in ImageWorsener 1.3.2 has a buffer overflow in the bmpr_read_rle_internal function in imagew-bmp.c.

code_evidence: Line 5 declares a fixed 255-byte stack buffer buf; n_bytes is computed from the attacker-controlled RLE run length n_pix (line 31). For RLE8, n_bytes = ((n_pix+1)/2)*2 (line 35), which can reach 256 when n_pix is 255, and this value is passed to iwbmp_read(rctx,buf,n_bytes) at line 37, overflowing the 255-byte buffer by one byte.
For RLE4, line 32 computes n_bytes = ((n_pix+3)/4)*2, which for n_pix up to 255 yields at most 128, so that path stays within bounds; the overrun is specific to the RLE8 calculation at line 35.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the intended boundary of a fixed-size memory buffer, which is exactly the out-of-bounds write described by CWE-119; the missing size constraint on n_bytes relative to sizeof(buf) is the direct cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a stack buffer sized 255 bytes receives n_bytes bytes where the RLE8 formula rounds n_pix=255 up to 256, without any bounds check before the read. Trigger: a crafted BMP with an RLE8 encoded run whose length byte is 255. Consequence: iwbmp_read writes one byte past buf, corrupting adjacent stack memory and potentially enabling memory modification or a crash.

commit_msg: gnrc_sixlowpan_iphc: fix buffer overflow in gnrc_sixlowpan_iphc_recv()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        /* for a fragmented datagram we know the overall length already */', '    if ((rbuf == NULL) &&', '        (gnrc_pktbuf_realloc_data(ipv6, uncomp_hdr_len + payload_len) != 0)) {', '        DEBUG("6lo iphc: no space left to copy payload\\n");', '        _recv_error_release(sixlo, ipv6, rbuf);', '        return;', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['        if ((ipv6->size < sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t)) &&', '            (gnrc_pktbuf_realloc_data(ipv6, sizeof(ipv6_hdr_t)) != 0)) {', '            DEBUG("6lo iphc: no space to decompress IPHC\\n");', '            _recv_error_release(sixlo, ipv6, rbuf);', '            return;', '        }', '            /* for a fragmented datagram we know the overall length already */', '    if (rbuf == NULL) {', '        if (gnrc_pktbuf_realloc_data(ipv6, uncomp_hdr_len + payload_len) != 0) {', '            DEBUG("6lo iphc: no space left to copy payload\\n");', '            _recv_error_release(sixlo, ipv6, rbuf);', '            return;', '        }', '    }', '    else {', '        if (ipv6->size < (uncomp_hdr_len + (sixlo->size - payload_offset))) {', '            DEBUG("6lo iphc: not enough space to copy payload.\\n");', '            DEBUG("6lo iphc: potentially malicious datagram size received.\\n");', '            _recv_error_release(sixlo, ipv6, rbuf);', '            return;', '        }', '    }', '']}
description: RIOT-OS, an operating system that supports Internet of Things devices, contains a network stack with the ability to process 6LoWPAN frames. Prior to version 2022.10, an attacker can send a crafted frame to the device resulting in an out of bounds write in the packet buffer. The overflow can be used to corrupt other packets and the allocator metadata. Corrupting a pointer will easily lead to denial of service. While carefully manipulating the allocator metadata gives an attacker the possibility to write data to arbitrary locations and thus execute arbitrary code. Version 2022.10 fixes this issue. As a workaround, disable support for fragmented IP datagrams or apply the patches manually.

code_evidence: After the realloc branch, the destination buffer is ipv6->data with ipv6->size bytes and the copy length is sixlo->size - payload_offset. In the fragmented rbuf != NULL path there is no realloc and no size check before this memcpy, so the copy length is not bounded by ipv6->size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked memcpy length relative to the destination allocation is a classic out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The fix adds an explicit ipv6->size bound check in the rbuf path, confirming the missing length constraint rather than an integer overflow or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When rbuf is non-NULL (fragmented datagram reassembly), the code neither reallocs ipv6 nor validates that ipv6->size can hold uncomp_hdr_len + (sixlo->size - payload_offset). A crafted 6LoWPAN frame with an inconsistent datagram/fragment size makes the memcpy at line 135 write past the end of the packet buffer, corrupting adjacent packets and allocator metadata; this can cause DoS or, with allocator manipulation, arbitrary write.

commit_msg:
The requirement is that events have type in range
EXTENSION_EVENT_BASE..lastEvent, but it was tested
only for first event of all.

Signed-off-by: Michal Srb <msrb@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
Signed-off-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int ret;', '    if (!((EXTENSION_EVENT_BASE <= first->u.u.type) &&', '          (first->u.u.type < lastEvent))) {', '        client->errorValue = first->u.u.type;', '        return BadValue;'], 'added_lines': ['    int ret, i;', '    for (i = 0; i < stuff->num_events; i++) {', '        if (!((EXTENSION_EVENT_BASE <= first[i].u.u.type) &&', '            (first[i].u.u.type < lastEvent))) {', '            client->errorValue = first[i].u.u.type;', '            return BadValue;', '        }']}
description: In the X.Org X server before 2017-06-19, a user authenticated to an X Session could crash or execute code in the context of the X Server by exploiting a stack overflow in the endianness conversion of X Events.

code_evidence: Length check derives expected size from client-controlled stuff->count and stuff->num_events, so it bounds the request only against itself, not the actual number of events present.
Zero-event case returns early, but any positive num_events proceeds.
Only first->u.u.type (index 0) is range-checked; the remaining num_events-1 events are never validated.
list is computed as first + stuff->num_events and events are passed to SendEvent with stuff->num_events, so unvalidated event types flow into endianness conversion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked event types drive buffer operations beyond the intended validated region, reading/writing outside the buffer bounds, matching CWE-119. The missing per-event bound check is the root cause; crash or code execution in the server is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
if (stuff->num_events == 0)
return ret;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that the event-type range check validates only the first event while the subsequent events are used based on the client-supplied num_events. A client can supply extra events whose types are outside EXTENSION_EVENT_BASE..lastEvent; these reach SendEvent and the endianness conversion, causing out-of-bounds access in the X server.

commit_msg:
Make extensions use a correct same-origin check.

GURL::GetOrigin does not do the right thing for all types of URLs.

BUG=573317

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1658913002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#373381}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  bool url_not_allowed = (url != GURL(url::kAboutBlankURL)) &&', '      (url.GetOrigin() != extension_url_.GetOrigin());'], 'added_lines': ['  bool url_not_allowed = url != GURL(url::kAboutBlankURL) &&', '                         !url::IsSameOriginWith(url, extension_url_);']}
description: The Extensions subsystem in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.75 incorrectly relies on GetOrigin method calls for origin comparisons, which allows remote attackers to bypass the Same Origin Policy and obtain sensitive information via a crafted extension.

code_evidence: Line 3 resolves attacker-influenced src against extension_url_, producing url. Lines 4-5 compute url_not_allowed by comparing url.GetOrigin() with extension_url_.GetOrigin(); this origin check is the only access constraint before navigation. Line 6 then decides whether to redirect to about:blank, and line 7 performs the redirect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the function fails to correctly enforce the access restriction that only same-origin content may be loaded. The flaw is a faulty enforcement mechanism in the origin check, not merely a generic input-validation issue; a precise same-origin comparison is the missing control.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the access decision relies on GetOrigin, which does not yield a correct same-origin comparison for all URL types. Trigger: a crafted URL whose GetOrigin value appears equal to the extension origin passes the check at lines 4-5. Consequence: the guest navigates to a URL that is not actually same-origin with the extension, bypassing the intended origin restriction and exposing extension-context data.

description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: rose_stop_idletimer() calls del_timer() directly on the socket's idletimer. del_timer() only removes a pending timer; it does not synchronize with a handler that is already executing on another CPU. joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the timer callback accesses the sock after it has been deallocated. This is distinct from a mere race condition: the defect is reuse of freed memory, and the patch replaces del_timer() with sk_stop_timer() to manage the sock reference.

evidence_lines.code: del_timer(&rose_sk(sk)->idletimer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stop path uses del_timer(), which cannot wait for a concurrently running timer callback, and no reference is held on the sock. Trigger: the idletimer fires while rose_release/rose_destroy_socket frees the sock via sock_put(). Consequence: the timer handler dereferences freed memory (bh_lock_sock), yielding a use-after-free crash and potential memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix DTLS buffered message DoS attack

DTLS can handle out of order record delivery. Additionally since
handshake messages can be bigger than will fit into a single packet, the
messages can be fragmented across multiple records (as with normal TLS).
That means that the messages can arrive mixed up, and we have to
reassemble them. We keep a queue of buffered messages that are "from the
future", i.e. messages we're not ready to deal with yet but have arrived
early. The messages held there may not be full yet - they could be one
or more fragments that are still in the process of being reassembled.

The code assumes that we will eventually complete the reassembly and
when that occurs the complete message is removed from the queue at the
point that we need to use it.

However, DTLS is also tolerant of packet loss. To get around that DTLS
messages can be retransmitted. If we receive a full (non-fragmented)
message from the peer after previously having received a fragment of
that message, then we ignore the message in the queue and just use the
non-fragmented version. At that point the queued message will never get
removed.

Additionally the peer could send "future" messages that we never get to
in order to complete the handshake. Each message has a sequence number
(starting from 0). We will accept a message fragment for the current
message sequence number, or for any sequence up to 10 into the future.
However if the Finished message has a sequence number of 2, anything
greater than that in the queue is just left there.

So, in those two ways we can end up with "orphaned" data in the queue
that will never get removed - except when the connection is closed. At
that point all the queues are flushed.

An attacker could seek to exploit this by filling up the queues with
lots of large messages that are never going to be used in order to
attempt a DoS by memory exhaustion.

I will assume that we are only concerned with servers here. It does not
seem reasonable to be concerned about a memory exhaustion attack on a
client. They are unlikely to process enough connections for this to be
an issue.

A "long" handshake with many messages might be 5 messages long (in the
incoming direction), e.g. ClientHello, Certificate, ClientKeyExchange,
CertificateVerify, Finished. So this would be message sequence numbers 0
to 4. Additionally we can buffer up to 10 messages in the future.
Therefore the maximum number of messages that an attacker could send
that could get orphaned would typically be 15.

The maximum size that a DTLS message is allowed to be is defined by
max_cert_list, which by default is 100k. Therefore the maximum amount of
"orphaned" memory per connection is 1500k.

Message sequence numbers get reset after the Finished message, so
renegotiation will not extend the maximum number of messages that can be
orphaned per connection.

As noted above, the queues do get cleared when the connection is closed.
Therefore in order to mount an effective attack, an attacker would have
to open many simultaneous connections.

Issue reported by Quan Luo.

CVE-2016-2179

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    dtls1_clear_record_buffer(s);'], 'added_lines': ['    dtls1_clear_sent_buffer(s);']}
description: The DTLS implementation in OpenSSL before 1.1.0 does not properly restrict the lifetime of queue entries associated with unused out-of-order messages, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by maintaining many crafted DTLS sessions simultaneously, related to d1_lib.c, statem_dtls.c, statem_lib.c, and statem_srvr.c.

code_evidence: dtls1_stop_timer resets timers and then calls dtls1_clear_record_buffer(s), a buffer-clearing routine reached on every timer stop. The function itself contains no length, count, or lifetime check on the buffered DTLS message queue; it only clears the record buffer, leaving queue entries in place.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources such as memory. The function's buffer-clearing call does not bound or release retained DTLS queue memory, matching this resource-management category rather than a parsing or authentication weakness.

evidence_lines.code: dtls1_clear_record_buffer(s);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that the timer-stop path clears only the record buffer, not the orphaned buffered-message queue entries, so queued future or fragmented messages can persist for the connection lifetime. A peer that keeps many DTLS sessions open with crafted messages accumulates memory; the supported consequence is resource exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg:
Commit 086d49058cd8 ("ipv6: annotate some data-races around sk->sk_prot")
fixed some data-races around sk->sk_prot but it was not enough.

Some functions in inet6_(stream|dgram)_ops still access sk->sk_prot
without lock_sock() or rtnl_lock(), so they need READ_ONCE() to avoid
load tearing.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Signed-off-by: Kuniyuki Iwashima <kuniyu@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn sk->sk_prot->setsockopt(sk, level, optname, optval, optlen);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* IPV6_ADDRFORM can change sk->sk_prot under us. */', '\treturn READ_ONCE(sk->sk_prot)->setsockopt(sk, level, optname, optval, optlen);']}
description: A vulnerability has been found in Linux Kernel and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects the function inet6_stream_ops/inet6_dgram_ops of the component IPv6 Handler. The manipulation leads to race condition. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211090 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: Line 4 loads sk->sk_prot and line 5 immediately dereferences it to call setsockopt. The function takes no lock (no lock_sock/rtnl_lock) and performs no READ_ONCE, so the pointer is read once and used without synchronization while another sequence can change it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the code sequence requires exclusive access to the shared sk->sk_prot resource yet permits an interfering concurrent modification, violating atomicity/exclusivity. The missing READ_ONCE is the concrete unsynchronized access, not a separate weakness class.

evidence_lines.code:
struct sock *sk = sock->sk;
return sk->sk_prot->setsockopt(sk, level, optname, optval, optlen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sk->sk_prot is a shared field that IPV6_ADDRFORM can rewrite concurrently, but this setsockopt path reads and dereferences it without exclusive access or an atomic load. Trigger: a concurrent ADDRFORM transition between the load and the call. Consequence: the call may dispatch through a stale or torn protocol pointer, causing inconsistent behavior or a crash.

drivers/gpu/drm/radeon/radeon_atombios.c: range check issues

This change makes the array larger, "MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING_V1_2" is 3
and the original size "MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING" is 2.

Also there were checks that were off by one.

Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <error27@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alex Deucher <alexdeucher@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Dave Airlie <airlied@redhat.com>

description: In the Linux kernel before 2.6.34, a range check issue in drivers/gpu/drm/radeon/atombios.c could cause an off by one (buffer overflow) problem. NOTE: At least one Linux maintainer believes that this CVE is incorrectly assigned and should be rejected because the value is hard coded and are not user-controllable where it is used

code_evidence: Case 1 rejects only when index > MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING, then indexes tv_info->aModeTimings[index]; an index exactly equal to the maximum passes the check and addresses one element past the array.

Case 2 similarly rejects only index > MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING_V1_2, then computes dtd_timings = &tv_info_v1_2->aModeTimings[index], so index equal to the maximum yields an out-of-bounds pointer used for subsequent reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-193 fits because the maximum valid index is computed/used incorrectly: the check is off by one, allowing one more element than the array holds. This is an index-limit error, not merely a generic buffer overflow; the overflow stems from the incorrect boundary value.

evidence_lines.code:
if (index > MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING)
return false;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The bounds checks use a strict greater-than comparison against the array maximum instead of rejecting index equal to it. When the caller supplies index equal to MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING (case 1) or MAX_SUPPORTED_TV_TIMING_V1_2 (case 2), the function proceeds to read the one-past-end element, causing an out-of-bounds read of the BIOS data and possibly corrupted mode values.

commit_msg:
tiocspgrp() takes two tty_struct pointers: One to the tty that userspace
passed to ioctl() (`tty`) and one to the TTY being changed (`real_tty`).
These pointers are different when ioctl() is called with a master fd.

To properly lock real_tty->pgrp, we must take real_tty->ctrl_lock.

This bug makes it possible for racing ioctl(TIOCSPGRP, ...) calls on
both sides of a PTY pair to corrupt the refcount of `struct pid`,
leading to use-after-free errors.

Fixes: 47f86834bbd4 ("redo locking of tty->pgrp")
CC: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jiri Slaby <jirislaby@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tspin_lock_irq(&tty->ctrl_lock);', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&tty->ctrl_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tspin_lock_irq(&real_tty->ctrl_lock);', '\tspin_unlock_irq(&real_tty->ctrl_lock);']}
description: A locking issue was discovered in the tty subsystem of the Linux kernel through 5.9.13. drivers/tty/tty_jobctrl.c allows a use-after-free attack against TIOCSPGRP, aka CID-54ffccbf053b.

code_evidence: The critical section mutates real_tty->pgrp (put_pid/get_pid) but acquires spin_lock_irq(&tty->ctrl_lock), locking a different tty_struct than the one modified; when tty and real_tty differ (master fd), the update to real_tty->pgrp is not serialized by real_tty->ctrl_lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the function does not properly acquire the lock guarding the resource it updates: the mutex/spinlock protecting real_tty->pgrp is not held during its modification, violating the intended locking discipline. This is a locking-consistency flaw, not merely a missing check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lock is taken on tty while the shared state real_tty->pgrp is modified, so the wrong lock protects the resource. Trigger: racing ioctl(TIOCSPGRP) on both sides of a PTY pair, where tty != real_tty. Consequence: concurrent get_pid/put_pid on the same struct pid corrupt its refcount, allowing a use-after-free.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-17 Q16, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in coders/sixel.c in the ReadSIXELImage function, related to the sixel_decode function.

code_evidence: The buffer is allocated with size `length` (MagickPathExtent) but ReadBlobString writes up to MagickPathExtent bytes at p; the loop reads *p and *(p+1) at lines 45 and 47 without ensuring a NUL terminator or spare byte exists, and calls strlen(p) at line 49 on data that may not be terminated within the allocation.
The resulting buffer is passed to sixel_decode at line 61, which parses it as a string; without the fix a missing NUL terminator allows reads past the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory beyond the allocated sixel_buffer while parsing attacker-controlled input, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. It is not an out-of-bounds write, since the defect concerns reading past the buffer's end rather than writing beyond it.

evidence_lines.code: if (sixel_decode((unsigned char *) sixel_buffer,&sixel_pixels,&image->columns,&image->rows,&sixel_palette,&image->colors) == MagickFalse)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sixel_buffer is allocated without extra room for a terminator and is never explicitly NUL-terminated, yet ReadBlobString/strlen and the later sixel_decode treat it as a C string. A crafted SIXEL file that fills the buffer without a terminating byte triggers out-of-bounds reads in the loop and in sixel_decode, causing a heap over-read (crash/information disclosure).

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/873
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return(DestroyImageList(image));'], 'added_lines': ['        {', '          xpm_colors=DestroySplayTree(xpm_colors);', '          xpm_buffer=DestroyString(xpm_buffer);', '          return(DestroyImageList(image));', '        }']}
description: In ImageMagick 7.0.7-12 Q16, a memory leak vulnerability was found in the function ReadXPMImage in coders/xpm.c, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted xpm image file.

code_evidence: At line 162 the code calls SetImageExtent; if it fails (line 163), line 164 returns DestroyImageList(image) immediately.
The splay tree xpm_colors is allocated at lines 105-106 and xpm_buffer is allocated earlier at line 49; both remain owned by this function at the failure point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-772: heap resources (splay tree and buffer) are not released after their effective lifetime ends on an early-return error path. It is a missing-release leak, not a use-after-free or out-of-bounds access, so CWE-772 fits directly.

A crafted XPM file that triggers extent allocation failure thus leaks these resources, and repeated processing accumulates memory, supporting a denial of service.

commit_msg: Fixed check for the number of pixels that will be allocated.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((number_pixels*number_planes) != (size_t) (number_pixels*number_planes))', '    pixel_info_length=image->columns*image->rows*MagickMax(number_planes,4);'], 'added_lines': ['    number_planes_filled,', '    number_planes_filled=(number_planes % 2 == 0) ? number_planes :', '      number_planes+1;', '    if ((number_pixels*number_planes_filled) != (size_t) (number_pixels*', '         number_planes_filled))', '    pixel_info_length=image->columns*image->rows*number_planes_filled;']}
description: The ReadRLEImage function in coders/rle.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via vectors related to the number of pixels.

code_evidence: number_pixels is columns*rows and number_planes is incremented when alpha is present; the pre-patch check only tests number_pixels*number_planes and allocates pixel_info_length=columns*rows*MagickMax(number_planes,4).
ByteDataOp computes offset from rows, columns, number_planes and plane, then validates offset+(operand*number_planes) against pixel_info_length before writing through p=pixels+offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading data past the end of pixel_info because the allocation-size and offset-stride calculations were inconsistent. This is CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read), not merely an integer overflow, since the check can be bypassed and the subsequent access reads past the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocated pixel_info_length did not consistently match the per-pixel stride number_planes used in offset arithmetic. When the plane count and allocation size diverged, the bounds check at the ByteDataOp/RunDataOp handlers could pass while p=pixels+offset and the p+=number_planes loop indexed beyond the allocated buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read.

commit_msg:
Reported as

  https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=738

* src/sfnt/sfobjs.c (sfnt_init_face): While setting number of
instances to zero for `CFF' fonts table, ensure that there is no `glyf'
present also (which gets priority).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["      /* we don't support Multiple Master CFFs yet */", '      if ( !face->goto_table( face, TTAG_CFF, stream, 0 ) )', '        num_instances = 0;', ''], 'added_lines': ["      /* we don't support Multiple Master CFFs yet */", '      if ( face->goto_table( face, TTAG_glyf, stream, 0 ) &&', '           !face->goto_table( face, TTAG_CFF, stream, 0 ) )', '        num_instances = 0;', '']}
description: FreeType 2 before 2017-03-07 has an out-of-bounds write related to the TT_Get_MM_Var function in truetype/ttgxvar.c and the sfnt_init_face function in sfnt/sfobjs.c.

code_evidence: CFF presence forces num_instances to zero without checking whether a glyf table exists; glyf takes priority, so a font with both tables keeps its fvar instance count.
The default-value loop reads num_axes entries into default_values, which was allocated as num_axes*2 bytes, so its bound is consistent with the allocation.
The instance loop iterates i < num_instances and reads num_axes*2 bytes into instance_values, also allocated as num_axes*2, so each individual read matches the buffer size.
When no default instance matches, num_instances is incremented after the loop, so the count can exceed the number of instances actually present in the fvar table.

instance_index is compared against the possibly inflated num_instances; a negative face_instance_index with an out-of-range instance_index sets num_instances to 0 rather than rejecting, and style_flags is derived from this count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function supplies the miscounted num_instances that later drives buffer sizing/allocation in variation handling, enabling writes past the end of an intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is not merely a logic error, since the miscount is the precondition for the out-of-bounds write.

evidence_lines.code:
if ( !face->goto_table( face, TTAG_CFF, stream, 0 ) )
num_instances = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is an incorrect instance-count guard: the CFF check ignores glyf priority and the post-loop increment can raise num_instances beyond the real fvar instance count. Downstream consumers trusting this count (e.g., TT_Get_MM_Var building variation arrays) can write past allocated buffers. The trigger is a crafted font with both glyf and CFF tables and inconsistent fvar instance data; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
Kernel: User pointer validation should reject kernel-only addresses

We were happily allowing syscalls with pointers into kernel-only
regions (virtual address >= 0xc0000000).

This patch fixes that by only considering user regions in the current
process, and also double-checking the Region::is_user_accessible() flag
before approving an access.

Thanks to Fire30 for finding the bug! :^)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    auto* region = region_from_vaddr(process, vaddr);', '    return region && region->is_readable();'], 'added_lines': ['    auto* region = user_region_from_vaddr(const_cast<Process&>(process), vaddr);', '    return region && region->is_user_accessible() && region->is_readable();']}
description: Kernel/VM/MemoryManager.cpp in SerenityOS before 2019-12-30 does not reject syscalls with pointers into the kernel-only virtual address space, which allows local users to gain privileges by overwriting a return address that was found on the kernel stack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only validates a user pointer against region metadata; it performs no memory-buffer access or bounds computation, so the out-of-bounds buffer operation required by CWE-119 is not shown in this function.

The missing allocation bitmap check is the specific constraint whose absence permits these out-of-bounds accesses; the heap overflow is the resultant impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the teardown loops trust the driver-supplied actualcount as the bound for indexing m_out_mem_ptr and m_inp_mem_ptr and free every entry unconditionally. If the client negotiates a larger buffer count than was allocated (or frees on a partially allocated port), the loop indexes past the allocated arrays, producing out-of-bounds reads/frees on heap memory. Consequence: heap corruption potentially leading to privilege escalation, as described in the advisory.

commit_msg:
patch 8.2.4245: ":retab 0" may cause illegal memory access

Problem:    ":retab 0" may cause illegal memory access.
Solution:   Limit the value of 'tabstop' to 10000.

description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.

code_evidence: The tabstop value comes from getdigits(&ptr) on the user argument and is rejected only when new_ts < 0 or new_ts > 9999; a value of 0 is then replaced by curbuf->b_p_ts.
In the non-VARTABS path, new_ts drives arithmetic: temp = new_ts - (start_vcol % new_ts), num_tabs += num_spaces / new_ts, and the remainder computation.
new_line is heap-allocated with alloc(old_len - col + start_col + len + 1); len is derived from num_spaces and num_tabs, then tab/space bytes are written for col < len.

commit_msg:
netlink: limit recursion depth in policy validation

Now that we have nested policies, we can theoretically
recurse forever parsing attributes if a (sub-)policy
refers back to a higher level one. This is a situation
that has happened in nl80211, and we've avoided it there
by not linking it.

Add some code to netlink parsing to limit recursion depth.

Signed-off-by: Johannes Berg <johannes.berg@intel.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t    extack, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t    extack, NULL, 0);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8. lib/nlattr.c allows attackers to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion) via a nested Netlink policy with a back reference.

code_evidence: The function forwards directly to __nla_validate_parse, passing extack and NULL as the final arguments. In the patched version the call adds a depth argument (0), but the function body shown here contains no bound, counter, or check of its own; the recursion control is delegated entirely to the callee.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the weakness is an unbounded recursive parse path triggered by attacker-supplied nested policy back references. The function supports it only as the entry point that invokes the parser without depth state; the actual limiting logic lives in __nla_validate_parse, so the evidence is indirect.

evidence_lines.code:
return __nla_validate_parse(head, len, maxtype, policy, validate,
extack, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The wrapper performs no recursion-depth accounting before entering the parser; with a self-referential nested Netlink policy, the parse path can re-enter validation indefinitely, exhausting the stack and causing denial of service. The added constant 0 is the initial depth supplied to the callee, not a limit enforced here.

commit_msg:
KVM: x86: Forbid VMM to set SYNIC/STIMER MSRs when SynIC wasn't activated

Setting non-zero values to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs activates certain features,
this should not happen when KVM_CAP_HYPERV_SYNIC{,2} was not activated.

Note, it would've been better to forbid writing anything to SYNIC/STIMER
MSRs, including zeroes, however, at least QEMU tries clearing
HV_X64_MSR_STIMER0_CONFIG without SynIC. HV_X64_MSR_EOM MSR is somewhat
'special' as writing zero there triggers an action, this also should not
happen when SynIC wasn't activated.

Signed-off-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20220325132140.25650-4-vkuznets@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>

description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s KVM when attempting to set a SynIC IRQ. This issue makes it possible for a misbehaving VMM to write to SYNIC/STIMER MSRs, causing a NULL pointer dereference. This flaw allows an unprivileged local attacker on the host to issue specific ioctl calls, causing a kernel oops condition that results in a denial of service.

code_evidence: The guard at lines 6-7 returns early only when SynIC is inactive and the write is not from the host, so a host-originated MSR write with non-zero data proceeds even if SynIC was never activated.
The HV_X64_MSR_EOM case at lines 47-52 unconditionally iterates over synic->sint and calls kvm_hv_notify_acked_sint for each entry without checking synic->active.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences pointers (via kvm_hv_notify_acked_sint) that are only valid when SynIC is active, without enforcing that precondition, matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). This is distinct from merely writing MSR values; the supported consequence is the NULL dereference caused by the missing activation check.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!synic->active && !host)
return 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When SynIC is not activated, a VMM-issued write to HV_X64_MSR_EOM passes the insufficient guard and reaches the EOM loop. The loop invokes kvm_hv_notify_acked_sint on SINT entries whose underlying state was never initialized because SynIC was inactive, leading to a NULL pointer dereference and kernel oops (DoS). The root cause is the missing synic->active check on the EOM path; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory accesses while loading .a2m files

Missing checks and wrong calculations in src/a2m.cpp cause
multiple heap-based buffer overflows and out-of-bounds reads
in heap, stack, and static data.

Bugs addressed in this commit:
* Check the number of patterns. Too big values can cause reads
  past the end of the len array.
* Reading a not packed data block with odd length will allocate
  a buffer which is one byte too small and write past the end
  of it (issue #88). Change the allocation/deallocation code
  to fix that in both places.
* Check that data blocks (afer unpacking if applicable) are big
  enough for the expected data before accessing the memory.
* Ensure that the length byte for author, song name, and instrument
  names doesn't exceed the maximum size available.
* Also change the accessor functions for these strings to call
  the proper std::string constructors for char arrays.
* Avoid reads past the end of convfx/newconvfx arrays while
  converting track data.

This commit fixes CVE-2019-14732.
