commit_msg:
evdns: name_parse(): fix remote stack overread

@asn-the-goblin-slayer:
  "the name_parse() function in libevent's DNS code is vulnerable to a buffer overread.

   971         if (cp != name_out) {
   972             if (cp + 1 >= end) return -1;
   973             *cp++ = '.';
   974         }
   975         if (cp + label_len >= end) return -1;
   976         memcpy(cp, packet + j, label_len);
   977         cp += label_len;
   978         j += label_len;
   No check is made against length before the memcpy occurs.

   This was found through the Tor bug bounty program and the discovery should be credited to 'Guido Vranken'."

Reproducer for gdb (https://gist.github.com/azat/e4fcf540e9b89ab86d02):
  set $PROT_NONE=0x0
  set $PROT_READ=0x1
  set $PROT_WRITE=0x2
  set $MAP_ANONYMOUS=0x20
  set $MAP_SHARED=0x01
  set $MAP_FIXED=0x10
  set $MAP_32BIT=0x40

  start

  set $length=202
  # overread
  set $length=2
  # allocate with mmap to have a seg fault on page boundary
  set $l=(1<<20)*2
  p mmap(0, $l, $PROT_READ|$PROT_WRITE, $MAP_ANONYMOUS|$MAP_SHARED|$MAP_32BIT, -1, 0)
  set $packet=(char *)$1+$l-$length
  # hack the packet
  set $packet[0]=63
  set $packet[1]='/'

  p malloc(sizeof(int))
  set $idx=(int *)$2
  set $idx[0]=0
  set $name_out_len=202

  p malloc($name_out_len)
  set $name_out=$3

  # have WRITE only mapping to fail on read
  set $end=$1+$l
  p (void *)mmap($end, 1<<12, $PROT_NONE, $MAP_ANONYMOUS|$MAP_SHARED|$MAP_FIXED|$MAP_32BIT, -1, 0)
  set $m=$4

  p name_parse($packet, $length, $idx, $name_out, $name_out_len)
  x/2s (char *)$name_out

Before this patch:
$ gdb -ex 'source gdb' dns-example
$1 = 1073741824
$2 = (void *) 0x633010
$3 = (void *) 0x633030
$4 = (void *) 0x40200000

Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
__memcpy_sse2_unaligned () at memcpy-sse2-unaligned.S:33

After this patch:
$ gdb -ex 'source gdb' dns-example
$1 = 1073741824
$2 = (void *) 0x633010
$3 = (void *) 0x633030
$4 = (void *) 0x40200000
$5 = -1
0x633030:       "/"
0x633032:       ""
(gdb) p $m
$6 = (void *) 0x40200000
(gdb) p $1
$7 = 1073741824
(gdb) p/x $1
$8 = 0x40000000
(gdb) quit

P.S. plus drop one condition duplicate.

Fixes: #317
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (j >= length) return -1;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (j + label_len > length) return -1;']}
description: The name_parse function in evdns.c in libevent before 2.1.6-beta allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via vectors involving the label_len variable, which triggers an out-of-bounds stack read.

code_evidence: At line 30, the only bound check before the copy is against the output buffer end (cp + label_len >= end). Line 31 then calls memcpy(cp, packet + j, label_len) reading label_len bytes from the input packet at offset j, but nothing verifies that j + label_len stays within the input buffer length (line 33 advances j by label_len).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the unsafe memcpy reads data beyond the intended input buffer boundary; the missing j + label_len > length check is precisely an out-of-bounds read, not a write (the destination is checked).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the source-side bounds check is missing; the function validates the destination buffer (end) but not the input packet extent before memcpy. Trigger: a crafted DNS label with a large label_len (up to 63) near the end of the packet makes packet + j + label_len exceed length. Consequence: memcpy reads past the input buffer, causing an out-of-bounds stack read (crash/DoS and possible memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
x86: avoid leaking PKRU and BND* between vCPU-s

PKRU is explicitly "XSAVE-managed but not XSAVE-enabled", so guests
might access the register (via {RD,WR}PKRU) without setting XCR0.PKRU.
Force context switching as well as migrating the register as soon as
CR4.PKE is being set the first time.

For MPX (BND<n>, BNDCFGU, and BNDSTATUS) the situation is less clear,
and the SDM has not entirely consistent information for that case.
While experimentally the instructions don't change register state as
long as the two XCR0 bits aren't both 1, be on the safe side and enable
both if BNDCFGS.EN is being set the first time.

This is XSA-220.

Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>

netfilter: ebtables: CONFIG_COMPAT: don't trust userland offsets

We need to make sure the offsets are not out of range of the
total size.
Also check that they are in ascending order.

The WARN_ON triggered by syzkaller (it sets panic_on_warn) is
changed to also bail out, no point in continuing parsing.

Briefly tested with simple ruleset of
-A INPUT --limit 1/s' --log
plus jump to custom chains using 32bit ebtables binary.

Reported-by: <syzbot+845a53d13171abf8bf29@syzkaller.appspotmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>

description: A flaw was found in the Linux 4.x kernel's implementation of 32-bit syscall interface for bridging. This allowed a privileged user to arbitrarily write to a limited range of kernel memory.

code_evidence: offsets[0] is fixed to sizeof(struct ebt_entry), but offsets[1..3] are copied directly from the user-supplied entry->watchers_offset, targets_offset and entries_offset fields without any range or ordering check.
The loop computes buf = buf_start + offsets[i] and size = offsets[j] - offsets[i]; offsets[i] can exceed offsets[j], so size underflows and match32 points beyond the entry buffer.
offsets_update[i] = offsets[j] + new_offset writes a user-derived offset into kernel buffer memory at buf_start, allowing out-of-range values to be written.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked offsets drive a write past the intended buffer via offsets_update into kernel memory and out-of-bounds parsing. The missing ascending/range constraint is the enabling defect; a pure read-overrun (CWE-125) would not capture the write to offsets_update.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: userland offsets in the compat ebtables entry are trusted without validating they are within *total or ascending. Trigger: a crafted 32-bit ebtables rule with offsets[j] < offsets[i] or offsets beyond the entry makes size underflow and match32 point out of bounds. Consequence: ebt_size_mwt parses from an out-of-bounds pointer and offsets_update writes attacker-influenced offsets into kernel memory, enabling limited out-of-bounds writes.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code assigns and then checks realloc's return, but the unsafe direct assignment to the tracked pointer means the failure path leaks memory rather than cleanly handling the error; the missing constraint is preserving the original pointer until success. CWE-252 fits the unchecked failure handling that produces the unexpected state.

Trigger: allocation failure when finalNbRects < nbRects. Consequence: memory leak, and the function returns FALSE with region->data pointing at empty_region.

commit_msg:

The module is typically executed as root and would sometimes
open files or follow symlinks that could be controlled from the
outside.

Drop privileges to the target user before opening any files.

Fixes CVE-2019-12209.

Thanks to Matthias Gerstner of the SUSE Security Team for reporting
the issue.

If the debug option is enabled in the PAM configuration, part of the file contents of a symlink target will be logged, possibly revealing sensitive information.

When openasuser is false, line 119 calls get_devices_from_authfile on cfg->auth_file (built from pw->pw_dir) while still at euid 0, so the file in the user's $HOME is opened as root. Lines 111-112/122-123 show the seteuid switch is skipped entirely in that path.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the authfile path under the user-controlled home directory is opened with root privileges unless openasuser is explicitly configured. Trigger: an attacker places a symlink at $HOME/.config/Yubico/u2f_keys pointing to a root-owned file; the root process follows it. Consequence: disclosure of sensitive file contents (logged when debug is enabled) and access to unintended resources.

commit_msg:
internal redirect: fix a lifetime bug (#785)

Signed-off-by: Alyssa Wilk <alyssar@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Matt Klein <mklein@lyft.com>
Signed-off-by: Pradeep Rao <pcrao@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  active_request_->response_encoder_.runResetCallbacks(reason);', '  connection_.dispatcher().deferredDelete(std::move(active_request_));'], 'added_lines': ['  if (active_request_) {', '    active_request_->response_encoder_.runResetCallbacks(reason);', '    connection_.dispatcher().deferredDelete(std::move(active_request_));', '  }']}
description: Envoy is a cloud-native high-performance edge/middle/service proxy. In versions prior to 1.22.1 if Envoy attempts to send an internal redirect of an HTTP request consisting of more than HTTP headers, there’s a lifetime bug which can be triggered. If while replaying the request Envoy sends a local reply when the redirect headers are processed, the downstream state indicates that the downstream stream is not complete. On sending the local reply, Envoy will attempt to reset the upstream stream, but as it is actually complete, and deleted, this result in a use-after-free. Users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade are advised to disable internal redirects if crashes are observed.

code_evidence: onResetStream unconditionally dereferences active_request_ (line 2) and then moves it into deferredDelete (line 3). There is no null check or ownership/lifetime guard before these operations, so the handler assumes active_request_ still refers to a live request object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the handler references and passes ownership of a request object after its lifetime has ended; the missing validity check permits use of freed memory. This is distinct from a plain null-pointer dereference, since the issue is stale object lifetime rather than an absent pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
active_request_->response_encoder_.runResetCallbacks(reason);
connection_.dispatcher().deferredDelete(std::move(active_request_));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reset callback path does not verify that active_request_ is still valid. Trigger: an internal redirect replay causes a local reply, resetting an upstream stream that is already complete and deleted, so active_request_ is stale when onResetStream runs. The dereference on line 2 and the move on line 3 then operate on freed memory, supporting a use-after-free crash or memory corruption.

description: loadImage() in tools/tiffcrop.c in LibTIFF through 4.5.0 has a heap-based use after free via a crafted TIFF image.

At line 318 read_buff = *read_ptr reuses a prior buffer; when non-NULL, the else branch reallocates only if prev_readsize < buffsize, otherwise it skips reallocation and proceeds with the stale buffer.
After the realloc-or-keep path, line 351 checks only !read_buff; there is no check that the buffer is actually at least buffsize bytes when prev_readsize >= buffsize.
Lines 356-358 unconditionally write three guard bytes at read_buff[buffsize], [buffsize+1], [buffsize+2] on whatever buffer was retained.
Line 359 then records prev_readsize = buffsize, cementing the incorrect size assumption for later calls.

This is distinct from a pure use-after-free: the write target is a live but undersized buffer, and the consequence is heap corruption rather than dereferencing freed memory.

evidence_lines.code:
prev_readsize = buffsize;
*read_ptr = read_buff;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stale static prev_readsize is trusted as the current allocation size, so a reused read_buff can be smaller than buffsize while the code skips reallocation. Trigger: a caller (e.g., rotateImage) reallocates the buffer to a different size without updating prev_readsize, then loadImage is invoked with a larger buffsize; the guard-byte writes at [buffsize..buffsize+2] and subsequent read functions write past the actual allocation, corrupting heap memory.

commit_msg:
Make sure binding security checks don't pass if the frame is remote.

Blink assumes that remote frames will always fail the security origin
check. Unfortunately, reality is not that simple. There are several
instances where this assumption fails to hold. For example:

  1. Navigate to a.com.
  2. a.com opens a new window.
  3. Navigate the new window to b.com via the omnibox.
  4. Click a link to c.com in both windows.

Because browser-initiated navigations go cross-process but
renderer-initiated navigations do not [1], the two c.com windows will
end up in different renderer processes.

Both windows have the same origin but see each other as RemoteFrames.
This means that SecurityOrigin's canAccess check will pass… but this
ends up violating many assumptions in Blink that passing the security
check implies a local frame.

[1] https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/process-models#Caveats

BUG=601629
CQ_INCLUDE_TRYBOTS=tryserver.chromium.linux:linux_site_isolation

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1887553002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#387087}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow(targetFrameOrigin, accessingWindow))'], 'added_lines': ["    // It's important to check that targetWindow is a LocalDOMWindow: it's", '    // possible for a remote frame and local frame to have the same security', '    // origin, depending on the model being used to allocate Frames between', '    // processes. See https://crbug.com/601629.', '    if (targetWindow && targetWindow->isLocalDOMWindow() && isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow(targetFrameOrigin, accessingWindow))']}
description: Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.94, does not ensure that frames satisfy a check for the same renderer process in addition to a Same Origin Policy check, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted web site, related to BindingSecurity.cpp and DOMWindow.cpp.

code_evidence: The guard at line 3 only asserts that a targetWindow with a frame equals that frame's domWindow; it does not establish that the window is local. Line 4 then calls isOriginAccessibleFromDOMWindow for any targetWindow and returns true on a same-origin match, without checking targetWindow->isLocalDOMWindow(). A remote frame sharing the origin therefore passes the access check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a required property of its input (targetWindow must be a local DOMWindow) before processing it under the security check, which matches CWE-20's invalid validation of required input properties. This is a missing validation constraint, not a mere filtering or encoding issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the access decision relies solely on the Same Origin Policy check and treats a same-origin result as sufficient, omitting validation that the target is a local DOMWindow. Trigger: a remote frame with the same security origin as the accessing window. Consequence: binding security checks incorrectly pass, violating Blink's assumption that a successful check implies a local frame, leading to memory corruption/DoS as described.

commit_msg:
Fix auth digest refcount integer overflow (#585)

This fixes a possible overflow of the nonce reference counter in the
digest authentication scheme, found by security researchers
@synacktiv.

It changes `references` to be an 64 bits unsigned integer. This makes
overflowing the counter impossible in practice.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    assert(nonce->references != 0); // no overflows']}
description: An issue was discovered in Squid before 5.0.2. A remote attacker can replay a sniffed Digest Authentication nonce to gain access to resources that are otherwise forbidden. This occurs because the attacker can overflow the nonce reference counter (a short integer). Remote code execution may occur if the pooled token credentials are freed (instead of replayed as valid credentials).

code_evidence: Line 4 only asserts the nonce pointer is non-NULL; line 5 unconditionally increments nonce->references with no bound check, so the counter wraps when it reaches its maximum value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because line 5 performs an increment whose result can exceed the counter's representable range and wrap, exactly the integer overflow/wraparound pattern. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the missing constraint is on the arithmetic value itself.

evidence_lines.code:
assert(nonce != NULL);
++nonce->references;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reference counter is a narrow integer and authDigestNonceLink increments it without checking for saturation. Trigger: an attacker replays a sniffed nonce enough times to drive references past its maximum, wrapping it to zero. Consequence: the wrapped count misrepresents the number of live references, enabling premature release of pooled credentials and potential use-after-free or unauthorized access.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The implementation of `OpLevelCostEstimator::CalculateOutputSize` is vulnerable to an integer overflow if an attacker can create an operation which would involve tensors with large enough number of elements. We can have a large enough number of dimensions in `output_shape.dim()` or just a small number of dimensions being large enough to cause an overflow in the multiplication. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over output_shape.dim() and multiplies the running output_size by each dim.size() with no overflow check or bound on dimension count/magnitude.
The product is accumulated into total_output_size and returned; a wrapped negative or small value propagates to callers as a size estimate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs multiplication of integer dimension values assuming the result stays representable, exactly the CWE-190 pattern of wraparound from unchecked arithmetic. It is not merely a signedness or truncation issue; the missing overflow constraint on the multiply is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unchecked int64_t multiplication over attacker-influenced tensor dimensions. Trigger: an operation whose output shape has many dimensions or large dim sizes, so output_size *= dim.size() exceeds INT64_MAX and wraps. Consequence: a corrupted (negative/small) size estimate is returned and accumulated, yielding incorrect cost/execution logic; the commit notes the API returns a negative value on overflow.

When the key is small relative to the digest (1024-bit key, 64-byte
hash, 61-byte salt length), the internal message to hash is larger than

In the non-LONG_SALT branch, m and s are set directly to pkcsBlock (line 87), then RSA_PSS_PAD_SZ zero bytes and inputLen input bytes are written via XMEMSET/XMEMCPY without any bound check against pkcsBlockLen.

description: In Wireshark through 2.0.13 and 2.2.x through 2.2.7, the openSAFETY dissector could crash or exhaust system memory. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-opensafety.c by adding length validation. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-9350.

code_evidence: payloadSize is read from attacker-controlled packet bytes via tvb_get_letohl, and calcDataLength is derived from the frame's dataLength byte minus header offsets; dataLength is a guint8 read at line 25, so calcDataLength can be negative.
The fragmented branch at line 155 calls fragment_add_seq_check with calcDataLength as the length argument before any check that calcDataLength is non-negative.
The only guard, calcDataLength >= 0 at line 169, is applied to proto_tree_add_item but placed after the reassembly call, so it does not constrain the length passed to fragment_add_seq_check.

payloadSize = tvb_get_letohl(message_tvb, payloadOffset - 4);
calcDataLength = dataLength - (payloadOffset - db0Offset);

if ( fragmentId != 0 && packet->payload.ssdo->sacmd.segmented )
fragmentId, NULL, 0, calcDataLength, TRUE );

proto_tree_add_item(ssdo_tree, hf_oss_ssdo_payload, message_tvb, payloadOffset, calcDataLength, ENC_NA );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the derived length calcDataLength is passed to the reassembly routine without first verifying it is non-negative. commit_msg: fix #55 : check too big code point value for single byte value in next_state_val()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (*vs > 0xff)', '          return ONIGERR_INVALID_CODE_POINT_VALUE;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in Oniguruma 6.2.0, as used in Oniguruma-mod in Ruby through 2.4.1 and mbstring in PHP through 7.1.5. A heap out-of-bounds write or read occurs in next_state_val() during regular expression compilation. Octal numbers larger than 0xff are not handled correctly in fetch_token() and fetch_token_in_cc(). A malformed regular expression containing an octal number in the form of '\700' would produce an invalid code point value larger than 0xff in next_state_val(), resulting in an out-of-bounds write memory corruption.

code_evidence: In the CCS_VALUE/CCV_SB branch, *vs is used directly as a bit index for BITSET_SET_BIT(cc->bs, (int)(*vs)) with no upper-bound check on *vs.

By contrast, the CCS_RANGE/CCV_SB branch validates *vs and v against 0xff and returns ONIGERR_INVALID_CODE_POINT_VALUE before calling bitset_set_range, showing the missing constraint in the single-value path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked oversized index is written past the end of the class bitset buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The read/range counterpart is a related consequence, but the direct unsafe operation here is a write beyond the buffer bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
if (*type == CCV_SB) {
BITSET_SET_BIT(cc->bs, (int )(*vs));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a single-byte class value (CCV_SB) whose code point exceeds 0xff is not rejected before being cast to int and used as a bitset index. A malformed regex such as an octal escape '\700' produces such a value, so BITSET_SET_BIT writes outside the intended bitset buffer, causing out-of-bounds memory corruption.

commit_msg: Prevent buffer overflow in SIXEL, PDB, MAP, and CALS coders (bug report from Donghai Zhu)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  sixel_pixels =(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(image->columns * image->rows,1);'], 'added_lines': ['  sixel_pixels =(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(image->columns , image->rows);']}
description: Buffer overflow in the WriteMAPImage function in coders/map.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.5-8 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or have other unspecified impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 89 allocates sixel_pixels as image->columns * image->rows bytes (multiplication before the size argument), while the write loop at lines 94-95 indexes sixel_pixels[y * image->columns + x] over rows and columns, so the allocation size and index range depend on the same product and overflow of that product can under-allocate the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The write loop stores into sixel_pixels at indices derived from image dimensions that can exceed the allocation, an out-of-bounds buffer write, matching CWE-119. A size-calculation integer overflow is the underlying cause, but the observable weakness is improper restriction of buffer-bound operations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size expression image->columns * image->rows is evaluated in a width that can overflow, so AcquireQuantumMemory may allocate fewer bytes than the index y*image->columns+x requires. Trigger: a crafted image with large dimensions makes the product wrap. Consequence: the loop writes pixel indices beyond the allocated buffer, causing heap corruption and crash.

commit_msg:
Add a container structure struct bpf_sanitize_info which holds
the current aux info, and update call-sites to sanitize_ptr_alu()
to pass it in. This is needed for passing in additional state
later on.

Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct bpf_insn_aux_data tmp_aux = {};', '\t\t\t\t       &tmp_aux, false);', '\t\t\t\t       &tmp_aux, true);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct bpf_sanitize_info info = {};', '\t\t\t\t       &info, false);', '\t\t\t\t       &info, true);']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.7 enforces incorrect limits for pointer arithmetic operations, aka CID-bb01a1bba579. This can be abused to perform out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory, leading to local privilege escalation to root. In particular, there is a corner case where the off reg causes a masking direction change, which then results in an incorrect final aux->alu_limit.

code_evidence: The function allocates a fresh per-call 'struct bpf_insn_aux_data tmp_aux = {};' to hold alu_limit state produced by sanitize_ptr_alu().

In the pre-adjustment sanitization path, sanitize_ptr_alu() is invoked with &tmp_aux and false; the resulting alu_limit in tmp_aux is discarded after the call, so it never constrains subsequent pointer arithmetic.
After bounds deduction, a second sanitize_ptr_alu() call with &tmp_aux and true again writes into this local temporary rather than persistent verifier aux state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing persistent limit means a pointer value can be used to write past the intended buffer, which is the out-of-bounds write described by CWE-787. The root cause is the discarded sanitization state, not merely incorrect arithmetic, so CWE-787 fits as the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code: struct bpf_insn_aux_data tmp_aux = {};

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: sanitize_ptr_alu() computes the masking limit for pointer arithmetic but stores it in a stack-local tmp_aux that is reset per invocation and never persisted into env->insn_aux_data. The verifier therefore cannot enforce the computed alu_limit when the pointer is later dereferenced, allowing the masked offset to exceed the intended bounds and enabling out-of-bounds memory access.

commit_msg: Zero pixel buffer
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  (void) ResetMagickMemory(jpeg_pixels,0,image->columns*', '    jpeg_info.output_components*sizeof(*jpeg_pixels));']}
description: The ReadJPEGImage function in coders/jpeg.c in ImageMagick before 7.0.6-1 allows remote attackers to obtain sensitive information from uninitialized memory locations via a crafted file.

code_evidence: jpeg_pixels is obtained from a virtual-memory blob sized for image->columns*output_components bytes per scanline, then used as scanline[0].
On a short/failed jpeg_read_scanlines the loop continues without filling jpeg_pixels; subsequent code reads *p from that buffer and writes it into image pixels.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function converts uninitialized buffer contents into output pixels that an attacker can retrieve, directly exposing sensitive in-process memory to an unauthorized actor, which matches CWE-200. The underlying uninitialized-read could also be described as CWE-457, but here the observable defect is the resulting information exposure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the scanline buffer is not initialized before use. Trigger: a crafted JPEG whose decompression yields fewer than one scanline (jpeg_read_scanlines != 1), so the continue path skips refilling jpeg_pixels; the pixel-conversion loops then read stale/uninitialized JSAMPLE values and store them into the output image. Supported consequence: uninitialized heap memory is exposed to the caller as image pixel data.

commit_msg:
cirrus: handle negative pitch in cirrus_invalidate_region()

cirrus_invalidate_region() calls memory_region_set_dirty()
on a per-line basis, always ranging from off_begin to
off_begin+bytesperline. With a negative pitch off_begin
marks the top most used address and thus we need to do an
initial shift backwards by a line for negative pitches of
backward blits, otherwise the first iteration covers the
line going from the start offset forwards instead of
backwards.
Additionally since the start address is inclusive, if we
shift by a full `bytesperline` we move to the first address
*not* included in the blit, so we only shift by one less
than bytesperline.

Signed-off-by: Wolfgang Bumiller <w.bumiller@proxmox.com>
Message-id: 1485352137-29367-1-git-send-email-w.bumiller@proxmox.com

[ kraxel: codestyle fixes ]

Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (off_pitch < 0) {', '        off_begin -= bytesperline - 1;', '    }', '', '        assert(off_cur_end >= off_cur);']}
description: The cirrus_invalidate_region function in hw/display/cirrus_vga.c in Qemu allows local OS guest privileged users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access and QEMU process crash) via vectors related to negative pitch.

code_evidence: The loop derives off_cur_end from off_cur + bytesperline masked by cirrus_addr_mask, then passes the range [off_cur, off_cur_end) to memory_region_set_dirty. With a negative off_pitch, off_begin initially marks the topmost address of the backward blit, so the first iteration computes a range that extends forward past the intended lines rather than backward, reading/marking an out-of-bounds region of vram.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect causes the computed range to extend past the intended buffer region when pitch is negative, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read past the intended buffer. It is not merely an arithmetic wrap; the missing negative-pitch adjustment is what places the range outside the blit's intended lines.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop does not adjust off_begin for negative pitch before computing the first range, so off_cur and off_cur_end do not describe the intended backward line. Trigger: a guest-supplied negative pitch reaches this function. Consequence: memory_region_set_dirty is invoked over an out-of-bounds range, leading to an out-of-bounds access and QEMU process crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_bad_inode(inode))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fuse_is_bad(inode))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

commit_msg:
use signed 64 bit instead for dataWindow calculation

Signed-off-by: Peter Hillman <peterh@wetafx.co.nz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    Int64 tileMaxX = Int64(tileMin[0]) + tileDesc.xSize - 1;', '    Int64 tileMaxY = Int64(tileMin[1]) + tileDesc.ySize - 1;', '    V2i tileMax = V2i (std::min (tileMaxX, Int64(levelMax[0])),', '\t\t   std::min (tileMaxY, Int64(levelMax[1])));'], 'added_lines': ['    int64_t tileMaxX = int64_t(tileMin[0]) + tileDesc.xSize - 1;', '    int64_t tileMaxY = int64_t(tileMin[1]) + tileDesc.ySize - 1;', '    V2i tileMax = V2i (std::min (tileMaxX, int64_t(levelMax[0])),', '\t\t   std::min (tileMaxY, int64_t(levelMax[1])));']}
description: A flaw found in function dataWindowForTile() of IlmImf/ImfTiledMisc.cpp. An attacker who is able to submit a crafted file to be processed by OpenEXR could trigger an integer overflow, leading to an out-of-bounds write on the heap. The greatest impact of this flaw is to application availability, with some potential impact to data integrity as well.

code_evidence: tileMin is computed in 32-bit int arithmetic from minX + dx * tileDesc.xSize and minY + dy * tileDesc.ySize; the multiplication and addition can wrap before any widening.
tileMaxX/tileMaxY widen tileMin[0]/tileMin[1] to Int64 only after tileMin has already been computed, so the widening cannot recover a value corrupted by 32-bit overflow.
tileMax is clamped against levelMax and returned as Box2i(tileMin, tileMax); the potentially wrapped tileMin/tileMax feed the returned tile data window.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs arithmetic that can exceed the int range and assumes results remain valid, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound; the wrap yields a small or negative tile origin that later corrupts memory. The diff's widening of tileMax does not address the earlier 32-bit tileMin computation.

evidence_lines.code:
V2i tileMin = V2i (minX + dx * tileDesc.xSize,
minY + dy * tileDesc.ySize);

Int64 tileMaxX = Int64(tileMin[0]) + tileDesc.xSize - 1;
Int64 tileMaxY = Int64(tileMin[1]) + tileDesc.ySize - 1;

V2i tileMax = V2i (std::min (tileMaxX, Int64(levelMax[0])),
std::min (tileMaxY, Int64(levelMax[1])));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tile-origin calculation at lines 8-9 uses 32-bit int multiplication/addition, so large dx/dy or xSize/ySize values wrap. Trigger: a crafted file supplying tile coordinates or tile dimensions that overflow int. Consequence: tileMin (and the derived tileMax) become incorrect, and the returned Box2i drives downstream heap out-of-bounds writes.

commit_msg:
Prevent array index out of bounds for symbol

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/38
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    Strcat_charp(tmp, symbol[(int)c]);'], 'added_lines': ['\t    Strcat_charp(tmp, symbol[(unsigned char)c % N_SYMBOL]);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-33. w3m allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap buffer overflow and crash) via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: Line 16/19 computes c as a signed char offset from SYMBOL_BASE, which can be negative or exceed the symbol table range. Line 29 indexes symbol[(int)c] without any bounds check, reading an out-of-bounds pointer from the symbol array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads symbol[(int)c] outside the intended bounds of the symbol array, an out-of-bounds memory access matching CWE-119. The fix's modulo N_SYMBOL and unsigned cast confirm the missing bound restriction; this is the direct buffer-boundary weakness rather than a mere NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the index c derived from attacker-controlled HTML character data is used directly to index the symbol pointer array with no range validation. Trigger: a crafted page produces a PC_SYMBOL character whose computed c falls outside [0, N_SYMBOL). Consequence: out-of-bounds read of a char* from the symbol array, likely dereferenced by Strcat_charp, causing heap buffer overflow and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
bits: stabilize bit_utf8_to_TU for invalid strings

Fixes both fuzzer bugs GH #681 poc0.bit_utf8_to_TU and poc1.bit_wcs2nlen
hexhive: nice fuzzer!
description: LibreDWG v0.12.5 was discovered to contain a heap buffer overflow via the function bit_wcs2nlen at bits.c.

code_evidence: wstr is allocated with calloc(2, len+1) using the initial strlen-derived len, but the loop later mutates len and indexes wstr via i without rechecking capacity.
For a 2-byte sequence the guard is only len>=1, yet the code reads str[1] and writes wstr[i++] while decrementing len and advancing str; a truncated sequence can still consume a write slot.

For a 3-byte sequence the guard is len>=2, but the code reads str[1] and str[2] and writes an element while decrementing len twice and advancing str twice, so continuation-byte handling can desynchronize len from the remaining input.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through wstr[i++] without validating i against the calloc'd element count, and the patch wraps the multibyte writes in braces so len/str updates occur only when the write happens. That is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), not merely an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: wstr = (BITCODE_TU)calloc (2, len + 1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination buffer is sized from the original string length, while the decode loop decrements len and increments i based on byte consumption that does not strictly match output writes for invalid/truncated UTF-8. Trigger: malformed multibyte input where continuation handling consumes bytes without a corresponding bounded write. Supported consequence: wstr[i++] can advance past the allocated buffer, producing a heap out-of-bounds write.

commit_msg:
mctp: defer the kfree of object mdev->addrs

when a netcard detaches. However, a running routine may be unaware of
this and cause the use-after-free of the mdev->addrs object.

 cleanup thread               another thread

unregister_netdev()       |  mctp_sendmsg()

Acked-by: Jeremy Kerr <jk@codeconstruct.com.au>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tkfree(mdev->addrs);']}
description: A flaw was found in the MCTP protocol in the Linux kernel. The function mctp_unregister() reclaims the device's relevant resource when a netcard detaches. However, a running routine may be unaware of this and cause the use-after-free of the mdev->addrs object, potentially leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: mctp_dev_put() decrements mdev->refs and, when it reaches zero, releases mdev->dev and schedules mdev itself via kfree_rcu; the commit adds kfree(mdev->addrs) at this point so the addrs array is reclaimed only when the last reference is dropped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a use-after-free (CWE-416): the addrs object is freed while a live reference path still dereferences it. Deferring the kfree to the refcount-zero path in mctp_dev_put() ensures the object outlives all holders, confirming the target CWE.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mdev->addrs was previously freed during mctp_unregister() while other threads could still hold a reference to mdev (e.g., via a route object) and dereference rt->dev->addrs[0]. Trigger: a concurrent detach/unregister races with mctp_sendmsg, freeing addrs while a sender reads it. Supported consequence: use-after-free read of freed memory, causing crash/DoS and potentially memory corruption.

commit_msg: fix for zz_rootsize #41
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (zz_entries < 0 || zz_rootseek < 0 || zz_rootseek < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (zz_entries < 0 || zz_rootseek < 0 || zz_rootsize < 0)']}
description: An issue was discovered in ZZIPlib 0.13.68. There is a bus error caused by the __zzip_parse_root_directory function of zip.c. Attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted zip file.

code_evidence: zz_rootsize is read from the disk trailer, and the guard checks zz_rootseek twice instead of validating zz_rootsize, so a negative rootsize passes the corruption check.
malloc(zz_rootsize) is called with the unvalidated signed value; a negative size converts to a huge size_t allocation, and the subsequent directory parsing proceeds on that assumption.
zz_rootsize + zz_fd_gap is used as the mmap length, again derived from the unvalidated value.
The loop bounds compare zz_offset against zz_rootsize; with a negative rootsize these bounds checks are ineffective, so parsing can run past the intended directory buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing negative-size constraint lets directory parsing operate outside the allocated buffer's intended bounds, matching CWE-119. The specific root cause is an incorrect/incomplete validation check rather than an unconditional integer overflow, but the supported consequence is out-of-bounds memory access.

evidence_lines.code:
_zzip_mmap(io->fd.sys, fd, zz_rootseek - zz_fd_gap,
zz_rootsize + zz_fd_gap);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the validation at line 19 repeats zz_rootseek and never rejects a negative zz_rootsize. A crafted zip trailer supplying a negative directory size bypasses the corruption guard, causing malloc and mmap to receive a huge converted size and the loop bound checks to be meaningless, leading to out-of-bounds buffer operations and a crash (bus error/DoS).

commit_msg:
Don't allow setting hostname if not unsharing UTS namespace

This is normally verified on argument validation, but it may happen
if someone managed to send custom priv-sep operations via e.g. ptrace.

See https://github.com/projectatomic/bubblewrap/issues/107

Closes: #108
Approved by: alexlarsson

description: Bubblewrap before 0.1.3 sets the PR_SET_DUMPABLE flag, which might allow local users to gain privileges by attaching to the process, as demonstrated by sending commands to a PrivSep socket.

code_evidence: The PRIV_SEP_OP_SET_HOSTNAME branch calls sethostname(arg1, strlen(arg1)) directly, with no check that opt_unshare_uts authorizes hostname changes in the current namespace. In the pre-patch function, any privileged_op invocation reaching this case performs the operation unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission and privilege management. Here a privileged operation is performed without verifying the caller is authorized (UTS namespace unshared), so the target category fits; this is an access-control gap, not a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the privileged operation dispatch lacks a permission/namespace check before sethostname. Trigger: a crafted priv-sep operation (e.g., via ptrace) sends PRIV_SEP_OP_SET_HOSTNAME with a chosen arg1. Consequence: the hostname of the original namespace is modified, an unauthorized privileged action; the commit's fix adds the opt_unshare_uts guard.

commit_msg:
sctp: validate chunk len before actually using it

Andrey Konovalov reported that KASAN detected that SCTP was using a slab
beyond the boundaries. It was caused because when handling out of the
blue packets in function sctp_sf_ootb() it was checking the chunk len
only after already processing the first chunk, validating only for the
2nd and subsequent ones.

The fix is to just move the check upwards so it's also validated for the
1st chunk.

Reported-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Tested-by: Andrey Konovalov <andreyknvl@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Neil Horman <nhorman@tuxdriver.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t/* Report violation if chunk len overflows */', '\t\tch_end = ((__u8 *)ch) + SCTP_PAD4(ntohs(ch->length));', '\t\tif (ch_end > skb_tail_pointer(skb))', '\t\t\treturn sctp_sf_violation_chunklen(net, ep, asoc, type, arg,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t  commands);', ''], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\treturn sctp_sf_violation_chunklen(net, ep, asoc, type, arg,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t  commands);', '', '\t\t/* Report violation if chunk len overflows */', '\t\tch_end = ((__u8 *)ch) + SCTP_PAD4(ntohs(ch->length));', '\t\tif (ch_end > skb_tail_pointer(skb))']}
description: The sctp_sf_ootb function in net/sctp/sm_statefuns.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.8 lacks chunk-length checking for the first chunk, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds slab access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted SCTP data.

code_evidence: The first chunk is only checked for a minimum header length (ntohs(ch->length) < sizeof(sctp_chunkhdr_t)); no upper bound relative to the skb is enforced before the loop body uses the chunk.
ch_end is computed as ((__u8 *)ch) + SCTP_PAD4(ntohs(ch->length)) and compared to skb_tail_pointer(skb); this overflow check occurs only after the chunk's type and error fields have been read.
ch is advanced to ch_end and the loop continues while ch_end < skb_tail_pointer(skb), so a first chunk whose declared length exceeds the buffer is dereferenced before validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads chunk type and error fields from a chunk whose declared length may exceed the received buffer, i.e., reads past the end of the intended buffer. This directly matches CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read), distinct from a write-based weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
ch = (sctp_chunkhdr_t *) ch_end;
} while (ch_end < skb_tail_pointer(skb));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the out-of-bounds chunk-length check is placed after the first chunk's header/error fields are read, so the initial chunk is trusted. Trigger: a crafted SCTP packet whose first chunk declares a length extending past skb_tail_pointer. Consequence: out-of-bounds slab read, causing KASAN-detected access and possible denial of service.

commit_msg:
button->xkb_acts is supposed to be an array sufficiently large for all
our buttons, not just a single XkbActions struct. Allocating
insufficient memory here means when we memcpy() later in
XkbSetDeviceInfo we write into memory that wasn't ours to begin with,
leading to the usual security ooopsiedaisies.

CVE-2023-6377, ZDI-CAN-22412, ZDI-CAN-22413

This vulnerability was discovered by:
Jan-Niklas Sohn working with Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        int last_num_buttons = master->button->numButtons;', '', '        if (last_num_buttons < maxbuttons) {', '            master->button->xkb_acts = xnfreallocarray(master->button->xkb_acts,', '                                                       maxbuttons,', '                                                       sizeof(XkbAction));', '            memset(&master->button->xkb_acts[last_num_buttons],', '                   0,', '                   (maxbuttons - last_num_buttons) * sizeof(XkbAction));', '        }']}
description: A flaw was found in xorg-server. Querying or changing XKB button actions such as moving from a touchpad to a mouse can result in out-of-bounds memory reads and writes. This may allow local privilege escalation or possible remote code execution in cases where X11 forwarding is involved.

code_evidence: The guard only checks that master->button->numButtons differs from the newly computed maxbuttons. Line 27 then overwrites numButtons with maxbuttons without resizing master->button->xkb_acts, and line 28 copies maxbuttons Atom entries from master->button->labels into the event.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from buffers (labels/xkb_acts) whose allocated size is smaller than the count used, which is a classic out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not merely an integer issue; the direct consequence is reading beyond the intended buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-button xkb_acts/labels storage is sized for the old button count but numButtons is updated to the larger maxbuttons derived from attached slave devices. Trigger: attaching a device with more buttons causes the mismatch. The subsequent memcpy and later XkbSetDeviceInfo operations read past the end of the undersized allocation, giving out-of-bounds reads (and writes), potentially leaking memory or causing crashes.

commit_msg: libvncserver: add missing NULL pointer checks
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  newspan->_next = before;', '  newspan->_prev = before->_prev;', '  before->_prev->_next = newspan;', '  before->_prev = newspan;'], 'added_lines': ['  if(newspan && before) {', '    newspan->_next = before;', '    newspan->_prev = before->_prev;', '    before->_prev->_next = newspan;', '    before->_prev = newspan;', '  }']}
description: An issue was discovered in LibVNCServer before 0.9.13. libvncserver/rfbregion.c has a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: sraSpanInsertBefore unconditionally dereferences newspan (lines 3-4) and before (lines 4-5) without validating either argument. Line 5 further dereferences before->_prev, so a NULL before or a before whose _prev is NULL crashes. The patch adds an if(newspan && before) guard, confirming these pointers could be NULL at call sites.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts caller-supplied span pointers and dereferences them (including the chained before->_prev) without a NULL check. Trigger: a call passing NULL newspan or before, or a before with NULL _prev. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
avformat/mxfdec: Fix DoS issues in mxf_read_index_entry_array()

Fixes: 20170829A.mxf

Co-Author: 张洪亮(望初)" <wangchu.zhl@alibaba-inc.com>
Found-by: Xiaohei and Wangchu from Alibaba Security Team
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if(segment->nb_index_entries && length < 11)', '        return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '        if(avio_feof(pb))', '            return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;']}
description: In libavformat/mxfdec.c in FFmpeg 3.3.3 -> 2.4, a DoS in mxf_read_index_entry_array() due to lack of an EOF (End of File) check might cause huge CPU consumption. When a crafted MXF file, which claims a large "nb_index_entries" field in the header but does not contain sufficient backing data, is provided, the loop would consume huge CPU resources, since there is no EOF check inside the loop. Moreover, this big loop can be invoked multiple times if there is more than one applicable data segment in the crafted MXF file.

code_evidence: Line 4 reads the attacker-controlled nb_index_entries count from the file header and line 5 reads length, with no validation bounding the count against remaining input size.

The loop at lines 13-19 iterates i from 0 to nb_index_entries, calling avio_r8/avio_rb64 each pass. If the file lacks backing data, these reads hit EOF but the loop keeps iterating, so the declared count fully controls the iteration count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 covers loops whose iteration count is insufficiently limited and attacker-influenced, leading to resource exhaustion. Here the file-declared count drives the loop with no EOF guard, matching excessive iteration rather than a fixed-size buffer issue.

evidence_lines.code:
segment->nb_index_entries = avio_rb32(pb);
length = avio_rb32(pb);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound nb_index_entries is taken directly from the file without an EOF or size check inside the loop. Trigger: a crafted MXF claiming a huge entry count with insufficient backing data. Consequence: excessive CPU consumption (DoS), amplified when multiple segments trigger the loop.

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>

'P' : '-',", "                       evtchn_port_is_masked(d, info->evtchn) ? 'M' : '-',", "                       info->masked ? 'M' : '-',"], 'added_lines': ['                struct evtchn *evtchn;', '                unsigned int pending = 2, masked = 2;', '', '                evtchn = evtchn_from_port(d, info->evtchn);', '                local_irq_disable();', '                if ( spin_trylock(&evtchn->lock) )', '                {', '                    pending = evtchn_is_pending(d, evtchn);', '                    masked = evtchn_is_masked(d, evtchn);', '                    spin_unlock(&evtchn->lock);', '                }', '                local_irq_enable();', '                       d->domain_id, pirq, "-P?"[pending],', '                       "-M?"[masked], info->masked ? \'M\' : \'-\',']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: After resolving info, the loop reads info->evtchn and calls evtchn_port_is_pending()/evtchn_port_is_masked() with no event or per-channel lock held, while only desc->lock is held. These helpers dereference the evtchn obtained from a potentially changing port mapping, so a concurrent evtchn_reset() can free or reallocate that channel between lookup and use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a concurrent read of a shared event-channel structure without the exclusive access required to keep it stable against evtchn_reset(), which is the shared-resource race described by CWE-362. The missing synchronization is the cause; the memory-safety impact is a consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the guest event-channel state is read locklessly from dump_irqs(), which does not synchronize with evtchn_reset() that may change d->evtchn_port_ops and max_evtchns(d). Trigger: a racing reset while the dump iterates guest channels. Consequence: stale/out-of-range evtchn pointer use leading to out-of-bounds access or bug checks (DoS, possibly privilege escalation for PV guests).

commit_msg:
nfc: st21nfca: Fix potential buffer overflows in EVT_TRANSACTION

It appears that there are some buffer overflows in EVT_TRANSACTION.
This happens because the length parameters that are passed to memcpy
come directly from skb->data and are not guarded in any way.

Signed-off-by: Jordy Zomer <jordy@pwning.systems>
Reviewed-by: Krzysztof Kozlowski <krzysztof.kozlowski@canonical.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t/* Checking if the length of the AID is valid */', '\t\tif (transaction->aid_len > sizeof(transaction->aid))', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '', '', '\t\t/* Total size is allocated (skb->len - 2) minus fixed array members */', '\t\tif (transaction->params_len > ((skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction)))', '\t\t\treturn -EINVAL;', '']}
description: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received in drivers/nfc/st21nfca/se.c in the Linux kernel through 5.16.12 has EVT_TRANSACTION buffer overflows because of untrusted length parameters.

code_evidence: Line 19 reads transaction->aid_len directly from skb->data[1] without any bound check, and lines 20-21 use it as the memcpy length into the fixed-size transaction->aid array.
Line 25 reads transaction->params_len directly from skb->data[transaction->aid_len + 3] without validation, and lines 26-27 use it as the memcpy length into the fixed-size transaction->params array.

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tjs_Ast *a;', '\tINCREC();', '\ta = assignment(J, notin);', "\twhile (jsP_accept(J, ','))", '\tDECREC();'], 'added_lines': ['\tjs_Ast *a = assignment(J, notin);', '\tSAVEREC();', "\twhile (jsP_accept(J, ',')) {", '\t\tINCREC();', '\t}', '\tPOPREC();']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: The function increments the recursion counter once (line 4) before parsing an assignment, then loops over comma operators (lines 6-7), repeatedly calling assignment() without incrementing the counter per iteration. The single DECREC() at line 8 only releases the initial increment, so the loop's nested parse depth is never accounted for.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to properly track and bound recursion depth for binary comma expressions, directly matching CWE-674's uncontrolled recursion consuming stack resources. The missing per-iteration depth accounting is the root cause; the resulting stack exhaustion is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The recursion-depth counter is incremented only once around the whole comma-expression loop rather than per parsed operand, so each comma-separated assignment is parsed at the same recorded depth. A crafted file with many comma operands drives unbounded nested parsing/recursion, exhausting the stack and causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Checks against the IO bitmap are useful for both instruction emulation
and VM-exit reflection. Refactor the IO bitmap checks into a helper
function.

Signed-off-by: Oliver Upton <oupton@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Vitaly Kuznetsov <vkuznets@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tgpa_t bitmap, last_bitmap;', '\tu8 b;', '\tlast_bitmap = (gpa_t)-1;', '\tb = -1;', '', '\twhile (size > 0) {', '\t\tif (port < 0x8000)', '\t\t\tbitmap = vmcs12->io_bitmap_a;', '\t\telse if (port < 0x10000)', '\t\t\tbitmap = vmcs12->io_bitmap_b;', '\t\telse', '\t\t\treturn true;', '\t\tbitmap += (port & 0x7fff) / 8;', '', '\t\tif (last_bitmap != bitmap)', '\t\t\tif (kvm_vcpu_read_guest(vcpu, bitmap, &b, 1))', '\t\t\t\treturn true;', '\t\tif (b & (1 << (port & 7)))', '\t\t\treturn true;', '', '\t\tport++;', '\t\tsize--;', '\t\tlast_bitmap = bitmap;', '\t}', '', '\treturn false;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn nested_vmx_check_io_bitmaps(vcpu, port, size);']}
description: A flaw was discovered in the way that the KVM hypervisor handled instruction emulation for an L2 guest when nested virtualisation is enabled. Under some circumstances, an L2 guest may trick the L0 guest into accessing sensitive L1 resources that should be inaccessible to the L2 guest.

code_evidence: The loop reads the L1-defined IO bitmap bytes (io_bitmap_a/io_bitmap_b) via kvm_vcpu_read_guest and, for each port in the emulated range, returns false when the bit is clear so the IO instruction is executed on behalf of the L2 guest. Ports >= 0x10000 return true, but the bitmap address is taken directly from vmcs12 without validating it lies outside L1-sensitive memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is unauthorized exposure of L1 information to the L2 guest through unvalidated bitmap handling, matching CWE-200's confidentiality impact. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the flaw is the missing authorization constraint on the referenced L1 resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the IO bitmap GPA from the L2-controlled vmcs12 is used directly for guest reads and to decide whether to emulate an IO access, with no check that the bitmap address is a legitimate L1 resource. Trigger: an L2 guest sets an IO bitmap pointing at sensitive L1 memory and issues a port IO; the unchecked read/decision lets L2 influence access to L1 resources. Consequence: L1-confidential data may be exposed to L2.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (quantum_info != (QuantumInfo *) NULL)', '      quantum_info=DestroyQuantumInfo(quantum_info);', '    if (clone_info)', '      clone_info=DestroyImageInfo(clone_info);']}
description: The ReadMATImage function in coders/mat.c in ImageMagick through 6.9.9-3 and 7.x through 7.0.6-3 has memory leaks involving the quantum_info and clone_info data structures.

code_evidence: quantum_info and clone_info are declared as heap-allocated resource handles.
clone_info is assigned via CloneImageInfo inside the per-frame loop.
quantum_info is assigned via AcquireQuantumInfo.
After the loop, only BImgBuff is released; the added checks destroy quantum_info and clone_info, but the pre-patch function lacked these releases, leaving both resources allocated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the function fails to release allocated resources (quantum_info, clone_info) after use, matching the patch that adds DestroyQuantumInfo/DestroyImageInfo calls. This is a missing-release weakness, not a use-after-free or double-free, since no stale access occurs.

evidence_lines.code:
QuantumInfo *quantum_info;
ImageInfo *clone_info;
clone_info=CloneImageInfo(image_info);
quantum_info=AcquireQuantumInfo(clone_info,image);

RelinquishMagickMemory(BImgBuff);
clone_info=DestroyImageInfo(clone_info);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function allocates QuantumInfo (AcquireQuantumInfo) and ImageInfo (CloneImageInfo) but the original loop exit path only frees BImgBuff, so these handles are not released after their effective lifetime. Trigger: reading a MAT file that reaches the normal end-of-reading path. Consequence: memory leaks that accumulate across reads, enabling resource-consumption denial of service.

strips + tiles is not allowed in TIFF
DNG uses a separate codepath

Regression since da5b3d002862d1e105002a6dc1567e6551860896.

Fixes: NULL pointer dereference
Fixes: poc1

AV_LOG_WARNING : AV_LOG_ERROR, "Tiled TIFF is not allowed to strip\\n");', '        if (!tiled_dng)', '            return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '    if (!s->is_tiled || has_strip_bits) {']}
description: An issue was discovered in decode_frame in libavcodec/tiff.c in FFmpeg version 4.3, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: When both tile and strip tags are present, the code only logs a warning and continues instead of rejecting the inconsistent TIFF.
init_image() is then called to allocate and set up the frame buffers for the image.

The subsequent strip-handling block runs for non-tiled images, initializing stripsizes/stripdata only when stripoffsets exist and then requiring s->rps > 0; for a tiled image incorrectly carrying strip bits, these per-strip fields may be unset and the strip unpack path can proceed with NULL/uninitialized strip data.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((ret = init_image(s, &frame)) < 0)
return ret;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts a TIFF that declares both tiled and stripped layout, so the strip path can execute with strip metadata (strip offsets/sizes, rps) that were never validly initialized. Trigger: a crafted TIFF with both tile and strip tags; the missing early return lets decoding reach strip unpacking, dereferencing an invalid/NULL pointer. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = t->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tconst struct xt_table_info *private = xt_table_get_private_protected(t);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: get_info() acquires the ARP table pointer t via xt_request_find_table_lock() and then reads t->private directly into the local private pointer.
That raw private pointer is subsequently dereferenced for hook_entry, underflow, number and size copies, so the reads depend entirely on the table info still being valid at this point.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences table info that the concurrent replacement path can free, matching reuse of memory after it has been freed. The fix replaces the raw read with xt_table_get_private_protected(), confirming the missing lifetime guard rather than a mere NULL check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the table's private info is read without the protected accessor, so it is not synchronized against the concurrent replacement path that frees the old table info. Trigger: a concurrent iptables rules replacement racing with get_info() on another CPU; the replacement may free the private info while this thread still dereferences it. Supported consequence: use-after-free read of freed table data, leading to crash or disclosure.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels

Bug 689699: Avoid buffer overrun.

When cleaning a pdf file, various lists (of pdf_xref_len length) are
defined early on.

If we trigger a repair during the clean, this can cause pdf_xref_len
to increase causing an overrun.

Fix this by watching for changes in the length, and checking accesses
to the list for validity.

This also appears to fix bugs 698700-698703.

description: pdf/pdf-write.c in Artifex MuPDF before 1.12.0 mishandles certain length changes when a repair operation occurs during a clean operation, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted PDF document.

commit_msg:
It is possible to trigger heap overflows due to an integer overflow
while parsing images and a signedness issue while parsing comments.

The integer overflow occurs because the chosen limit 0x10000 for
dimensions is too large for 32 bit systems, because each pixel takes
4 bytes. Properly chosen values allow an overflow which in turn will
lead to less allocated memory than needed for subsequent reads.

The signedness bug is triggered by reading the length of a comment
as unsigned int, but casting it to int when calling the function
XcursorCommentCreate. Turning length into a negative value allows the
check against XCURSOR_COMMENT_MAX_LEN to pass, and the following
addition of sizeof (XcursorComment) + 1 makes it possible to allocate
less memory than needed for subsequent reads.

Signed-off-by: Tobias Stoeckmann <tobias@stoeckmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (width < 0 || height < 0)', '       return NULL;', '    if (width > XCURSOR_IMAGE_MAX_SIZE || height > XCURSOR_IMAGE_MAX_SIZE)', '       return NULL;']}
description: libXcursor before 1.1.15 has various integer overflows that could lead to heap buffer overflows when processing malicious cursors, e.g., with programs like GIMP. It is also possible that an attack vector exists against the related code in cursor/xcursor.c in Wayland through 1.14.0.

code_evidence: The allocation size is computed as sizeof(XcursorImage) + width * height * sizeof(XcursorPixel) without validating width or height. The multiplication width * height can wrap for large dimensions, and the addition can wrap as well, so malloc receives a small size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operation is an integer calculation whose wrapped result is used as an allocation size; the missing dimension constraint is the direct cause. The heap overflow is the downstream consequence, not the primary weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
image = malloc (sizeof (XcursorImage) +
width * height * sizeof (XcursorPixel));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size expression width * height * sizeof(XcursorPixel) is evaluated in int arithmetic with unchecked, attacker-influenced dimensions, allowing wraparound before conversion to size_t. Trigger: cursor image dimensions large enough that the product or sum overflows. Consequence: a smaller buffer than the width/height imply is allocated, and subsequent pixel reads/writes exceed it, causing a heap buffer overflow.

security fixes

https://hhvm.com/blog/2021/02/25/security-update.html
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['inline void StringData::setSize(int len) {'], 'added_lines': ['inline void StringData::setSize(int64_t len) {']}
description: xbuf_format_converter, used as part of exif_read_data, was appending a terminating null character to the generated string, but was not using its standard append char function. As a result, if the buffer was full, it would result in an out-of-bounds write. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.56.3, all versions between 4.57.0 and 4.80.1, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.93.1, and versions 4.94.0, 4.95.0, 4.96.0, 4.97.0, 4.98.0.

code_evidence: setSize writes a terminating null at mutableData()[len] after only asserting len <= capacity(). The assert is compiled out in release builds, so a len equal to capacity() indexes exactly one past the last valid byte, and len > capacity() writes further out of bounds. The earlier callers in xbuf_format_converter pass a value derived from the buffer state, so this bound is reachable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing mutableData()[len] = 0 when len == capacity() places data one byte past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. The missing constraint is a strict len < capacity() check; the assert does not enforce it in release builds.

evidence_lines.code:
assertx(len >= 0 && len <= capacity());
mutableData()[len] = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the null terminator is written at index len without a runtime check that len < capacity(), relying solely on an assert. Trigger: a caller supplies len equal to (or greater than) the buffer capacity. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past the allocated string buffer, corrupting adjacent memory.

description: A null pointer dereference vulnerability in compose_group_nonknockout_nonblend_isolated_allmask_common() in base/gxblend.c of Artifex Software GhostScript v9.50 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via a crafted PDF file. This is fixed in v9.51.

commit_msg:
crypto: pcrypt - fix freeing pcrypt instances

pcrypt is using the old way of freeing instances, where the ->free()
method specified in the 'struct crypto_template' is passed a pointer to
the 'struct crypto_instance'.  But the crypto_instance is being
kfree()'d directly, which is incorrect because the memory was actually
allocated as an aead_instance, which contains the crypto_instance at a
nonzero offset.  Thus, the wrong pointer was being kfree()'d.

Fix it by switching to the new way to free aead_instance's where the
->free() method is specified in the aead_instance itself.

Reported-by: syzbot <syzkaller@googlegroups.com>
Fixes: 0496f56065e0 ("crypto: pcrypt - Add support for new AEAD interface")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.2+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tinst->free = pcrypt_free;', '']}
description: crypto/pcrypt.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.13 mishandles freeing instances, allowing a local user able to access the AF_ALG-based AEAD interface (CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_AEAD) and pcrypt (CONFIG_CRYPTO_PCRYPT) to cause a denial of service (kfree of an incorrect pointer) or possibly have unspecified other impact by executing a crafted sequence of system calls.

code_evidence: The instance is allocated with kzalloc(sizeof(*inst) + sizeof(*ctx)) as an aead_instance, so inst points to the aead_instance base, not the embedded crypto_instance.
On registration failure the code jumps to out_drop_aead and then out_free_inst, where kfree(inst) releases the aead_instance allocation.
The error path frees inst directly rather than through the instance release callback; the commit adds inst->free = pcrypt_free so the aead_instance's own free method performs the correct release.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-763 covers returning a memory resource with the wrong release function or incorrect release. Here kfree(inst) on an aead_instance that requires its own free method is exactly a wrong/invalid release, matching the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path releases the aead_instance using kfree on the wrong pointer/lifetime mechanism instead of the instance's designated free callback. Trigger: aead_register_instance or an earlier setup step fails after allocation, reaching out_free_inst. Consequence: incorrect release of the instance memory, enabling memory corruption/DoS as a local AF_ALG user.

Fix another buffer overflow in table parsing reported by Henri Salo

Fixes #575 and CVE-2018-11440
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tif (out >= MAXSTRING) {', '\t\t\t\tresult->length = lastOutSize;', '\t\t\t\treturn 1;', '\t\t\t}']}
