commit_msg:
Patch series "Fix several device private page reference counting issues",
v2

This series aims to fix a number of page reference counting issues in
drivers dealing with device private ZONE_DEVICE pages.  These result in
use-after-free type bugs, either from accessing a struct page which no
longer exists because it has been removed or accessing fields within the
struct page which are no longer valid because the page has been freed.

During normal usage it is unlikely these will cause any problems.  However
without these fixes it is possible to crash the kernel from userspace. 
These crashes can be triggered either by unloading the kernel module or
unbinding the device from the driver prior to a userspace task exiting. 
In modules such as Nouveau it is also possible to trigger some of these
issues by explicitly closing the device file-descriptor prior to the task
exiting and then accessing device private memory.

This involves some minor changes to both PowerPC and AMD GPU code. 
Unfortunately I lack hardware to test either of those so any help there
would be appreciated.  The changes mimic what is done in for both Nouveau
and hmm-tests though so I doubt they will cause problems.


This patch (of 8):

When the CPU tries to access a device private page the migrate_to_ram()
callback associated with the pgmap for the page is called.  However no
reference is taken on the faulting page.  Therefore a concurrent migration
of the device private page can free the page and possibly the underlying
pgmap.  This results in a race which can crash the kernel due to the
migrate_to_ram() function pointer becoming invalid.  It also means drivers
can't reliably read the zone_device_data field because the page may have
been freed with memunmap_pages().

Close the race by getting a reference on the page while holding the ptl to
ensure it has not been freed.  Unfortunately the elevated reference count
will cause the migration required to handle the fault to fail.  To avoid
this failure pass the faulting page into the migrate_vma functions so that
if an elevated reference count is found it can be checked to see if it's
expected or not.

description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel. It has been classified as problematic. Affected is an unknown function of the file mm/memory.c of the component Driver Handler. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211020.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fault handler reads zone_device_data and uses the derived pvt values without taking a page reference, so a racing migration can free the device private page and underlying pgmap. The stale struct page and pvt fields are then used, yielding use-after-free and potential kernel crash.

commit_msg:
Reimplement httpd's support for byte ranges.

The previous implementation loaded all the output into a single output
buffer and used its size to determine the Content-Length of the body.

The new implementation calculates the body length first and writes the
individual ranges in an async way using the bufferevent mechanism.

This prevents httpd from using too much memory and applies the
watermark and throttling mechanisms to range requests.

Problem reported by Pierre Kim (pierre.kim.sec at gmail.com)

description: httpd in OpenBSD allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a series of requests for a large file using an HTTP Range header.

code_evidence: The request allocates a fresh evbuffer via evbuffer_new() for each partial request; no cap on its size is imposed here.
For multipart ranges (nranges > 1), the loop iterates once per requested range, appending headers and file data into the same evbuffer and accumulating content_length.
Each iteration calls evbuffer_add_printf and buffer_add_range, growing the buffer by the range's data length; the number of ranges and their sizes come from the client's Range header.
The entire accumulated evbuffer is then written at once via server_bufferevent_write_buffer, so memory usage is proportional to the full response body.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates memory (evbuffer growth) on behalf of the requester without limiting the number or total size of ranges, so resource consumption is unbounded and client-controlled.

evidence_lines.code:
if (server_bufferevent_write_buffer(clt, evb) == -1)
goto fail;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the client-controlled Range header determines both the number of ranges and their total data, and the code buffers the whole multipart body in one evbuffer before writing. Trigger: a request for a large file with many/large byte ranges. Consequence: server memory consumption proportional to the requested body, causing denial of service.

0002 | XStoreName (

0006 | {

description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: XStoreName passes the caller-supplied name and its strlen(name) length into XChangeProperty, which encodes the length as a CARD16 protocol field; the length is not capped at USHRT_MAX, so an oversized name produces a length that overflows the 16-bit field.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits the missing size check on input copied into a fixed-size protocol field, where the unchecked length allows data to exceed the destination length and overflow it.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the string length is truncated when encoded as a 16-bit protocol length because no upper bound is checked before the property request is built. Trigger: a caller supplies a name longer than USHRT_MAX. Consequence: the server misinterprets trailing bytes as additional X requests, enabling arbitrary request execution.

commit_msg:
warc: consume data once read

The warc decoder only used read ahead, it wouldn't actually consume
data that had previously been printed. This means that if you specify
an invalid content length, it will just reprint the same data over
and over and over again until it hits the desired length.

This means that a WARC resource with e.g.
Content-Length: 666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666666665
but only a few hundred bytes of data, causes a quasi-infinite loop.

Consume data in subsequent calls to _warc_read.

Found with an AFL + afl-rb + qsym setup.

commit_msg:
As part of CVE-2013-4288, the D-Bus clients were allowed (and
encouraged) to submit the UID of the subject of authorization checks
to avoid races against UID changes (notably using executables
set-UID to root).

However, that also allowed any client to submit an arbitrary UID, and
that could be used to bypass "can only ask about / affect the same UID"
checks in CheckAuthorization / RegisterAuthenticationAgent /
UnregisterAuthenticationAgent.  This allowed an attacker:

- With CheckAuthorization, to cause the registered authentication
  agent in victim's session to pop up a dialog, or to determine whether
  the victim currently has a temporary authorization to perform an
  operation.

  (In principle, the attacker can also determine whether JavaScript
  rules allow the victim process to perform an operation; however,
  usually rules base their decisions on information determined from
  the supplied UID, so the attacker usually won't learn anything new.)

- With RegisterAuthenticationAgent, to prevent the victim's
  authentication agent to work (for a specific victim process),
  or to learn about which operations requiring authorization
  the victim is attempting.

To fix this, expose internal _polkit_unix_process_get_owner() /
obsolete polkit_unix_process_get_owner() as a private
polkit_unix_process_get_racy_uid__() (being more explicit about the
dangers on relying on it), and use it in
polkit_backend_session_monitor_get_user_for_subject() to return
a boolean indicating whether the subject UID may be caller-chosen.

Then, in the permission checks that require the subject to be
equal to the caller, fail on caller-chosen UIDs (and continue
through the pre-existing code paths which allow root, or root-designated
server processes, to ask about arbitrary subjects.)

Signed-off-by: Miloslav Trmač <mitr@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                                                        caller,'], 'added_lines': ['                                                                        caller, NULL,']}
description: A flaw was found in polkit before version 0.116. The implementation of the polkit_backend_interactive_authority_check_authorization function in polkitd allows to test for authentication and trigger authentication of unrelated processes owned by other users. This may result in a local DoS and information disclosure.

code_evidence: The caller's user is resolved via polkit_backend_session_monitor_get_user_for_subject, which in the pre-patch state allowed a client-supplied UID to be used, so user_of_caller could reflect an arbitrary UID rather than the actual caller.

The only gate is identity_is_root_user(user_of_caller); once a spoofed root UID passes, the function continues to get_authentication_session_for_uid_and_cookie using the caller-supplied uid and cookie.
No check ties the session owner or the requested uid to the real caller, so a non-root caller can obtain and complete an authentication session for another user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function fails to enforce that the caller is authorized to act on the supplied session/uid; the root check is the only authorization gate and it is bypassable due to the unverified caller-derived UID. This is missing authorization rather than mere authentication: the authenticated identity is accepted without confirming the caller's right to the target session.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller identity is derived from an attacker-influenced UID without verifying it belongs to the actual caller, and the function only rejects non-root after that weak derivation. Trigger: a local client supplies a cookie/uid for a victim's session while the resolved user is made to appear root (or the racy UID path is relied upon). Consequence: the session is marked authenticated and authenticated_identity set, enabling authorization bypass and disclosure about the victim's pending operations.

commit_msg:
unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets

It is possible for a process to allocate and accumulate far more FDs than
the process' limit by sending them over a unix socket then closing them
to keep the process' fd count low.

This change addresses this problem by keeping track of the number of FDs
in flight per user and preventing non-privileged processes from having
more FDs in flight than their configured FD limit.

Mitigates: CVE-2013-4312 (Linux 2.0+)

Signed-off-by: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

commit_msg:
Open bind mount sources from the host userns

The source of the bind mount might not be accessible in a different user
namespace because a component of the source path might not be traversed
under the users and groups mapped inside the user namespace. This caused
errors such as the following:

  # time="2020-06-22T13:48:26Z" level=error msg="container_linux.go:367:
  starting container process caused: process_linux.go:459:
  container init caused: rootfs_linux.go:58:
  mounting \"/tmp/busyboxtest/source-inaccessible/dir\"
  to rootfs at \"/tmp/inaccessible\" caused:
  stat /tmp/busyboxtest/source-inaccessible/dir: permission denied"

To solve this problem, this patch performs the following:

1. in nsexec.c, it opens the source path in the host userns (so we have
   the right permissions to open it) but in the container mntns (so the
   kernel cross mntns mount check let us mount it later:
   https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v5.8/fs/namespace.c#L2312).

2. in nsexec.c, it passes the file descriptors of the source to the
   child process with SCM_RIGHTS.

3. In runc-init in Golang, it finishes the mounts while inside the
   userns even without access to the some components of the source
   paths.

Passing the fds with SCM_RIGHTS is necessary because once the child
process is in the container mntns, it is already in the container userns
so it cannot temporarily join the host mntns.

This patch uses the existing mechanism with _LIBCONTAINER_* environment
variables to pass the file descriptors from runc to runc init.

This patch uses the existing mechanism with the Netlink-style bootstrap
to pass information about the list of source mounts to nsexec.c.

Rootless containers don't use this bind mount sources fdpassing
mechanism because we can't setns() to the target mntns in a rootless
container (we don't have the privileges when we are in the host userns).

This patch takes care of using O_CLOEXEC on mount fds, and close them
early.

Fixes: #2484.

Signed-off-by: Alban Crequy <alban@kinvolk.io>
Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Campos <rodrigo@kinvolk.io>
Co-authored-by: Rodrigo Campos <rodrigo@kinvolk.io>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tcase MOUNT_SOURCES_ATTR:', '\t\t\tconfig->mountsources = current;', '\t\t\tconfig->mountsources_len = payload_len;', '\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: runc is a CLI tool for spawning and running containers on Linux according to the OCI specification. In runc, netlink is used internally as a serialization system for specifying the relevant container configuration to the `C` portion of the code (responsible for the based namespace setup of containers). In all versions of runc prior to 1.0.3, the encoder did not handle the possibility of an integer overflow in the 16-bit length field for the byte array attribute type, meaning that a large enough malicious byte array attribute could result in the length overflowing and the attribute contents being parsed as netlink messages for container configuration. This vulnerability requires the attacker to have some control over the configuration of the container and would allow the attacker to bypass the namespace restrictions of the container by simply adding their own netlink payload which disables all namespaces. The main users impacted are those who allow untrusted images with untrusted configurations to run on their machines (such as with shared cloud infrastructure). runc version 1.0.3 contains a fix for this bug. As a workaround, one may try disallowing untrusted namespace paths from your container. It should be noted that untrusted namespace paths would allow the attacker to disable namespace protections entirely even in the absence of this bug.

code_evidence: Line 21 bounds the parsing loop by current < data + size, but line 23 computes payload_len as nlattr->nla_len - NLA_HDRLEN from an attacker-influenced 16-bit nla_len without first verifying nla_len >= NLA_HDRLEN or that the attribute fits within the remaining buffer. Line 24 then advances current by NLA_HDRLEN and line 62 advances by NLA_ALIGN(payload_len), so a too-small nla_len underflows payload_len and a large aligned value can move current past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The subtraction nlattr->nla_len - NLA_HDRLEN on an unsigned length wraps when nla_len is smaller than the header, producing a very large size_t; this is integer underflow/wraparound (CWE-190) that corrupts the parser's size and offset arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nla_len is used in subtraction and alignment without validating header length or remaining payload. Trigger: a crafted netlink attribute with a short or oversized length. Consequence: payload_len underflows to a huge size_t, corrupting loop bounds and allowing out-of-bounds reads/parsing of attribute data as configuration.

commit_msg: Lock down search_path in SPI calls
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Lock down search_path */', '\tres = SPI_exec("SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);', '\tif (res < 0)', '\t\tereport(ERROR, (errcode(ERRCODE_INTERNAL_ERROR), (errmsg("could not set search_path"))));']}
description:
TimescaleDB, an open-source time-series SQL database, has a privilege escalation vulnerability in versions 2.8.0 through 2.9.2. During installation, TimescaleDB creates a telemetry job that is runs as the installation user. The queries run as part of the telemetry data collection were not run with a locked down `search_path`, allowing malicious users to create functions that would be executed by the telemetry job, leading to privilege escalation. In order to be able to take advantage of this vulnerability, a user would need to be able to create objects in a database and then get a superuser to install TimescaleDB into their database. When TimescaleDB is installed as trusted extension, non-superusers can install the extension without help from a superuser.

Version 2.9.3 fixes this issue. As a mitigation, the `search_path` of the user running the telemetry job can be locked down to not include schemas writable by other users. The vulnerability is not exploitable on instances in Timescale Cloud and Managed Service for TimescaleDB due to additional security provisions in place on those platforms.

code_evidence: After SPI_connect, the function executes a query without first restricting search_path; only the function names are schema-qualified, while the earlier code path runs as the telemetry job's privileged user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is failure to constrain the privileged execution context (search_path) for the telemetry job, an improper privilege-management weakness enabling a lower-privileged actor to gain the telemetry user's privileges; the patch adds SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp to close it.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function runs SPI queries as the installation/telemetry user without locking search_path, so unqualified name resolution can be hijacked by objects in attacker-writable schemas. A malicious user creates a function/operator that the privileged telemetry query resolves and executes, yielding privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
avcodec/aacdec: Fix pulse position checks in decode_pulses()

Fixes out of array read
Fixes: asan_static-oob_1efed25_1887_cov_2013541199_HeyYa_RA10_AAC_192K_30s.rm
Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michaelni@gmx.at>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (pulse->pos[0] > 1023)', '        if (pulse->pos[i] > 1023)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (pulse->pos[0] >= swb_offset[num_swb])', '        if (pulse->pos[i] >= swb_offset[num_swb])']}
description: A vulnerability classified as problematic has been found in FFmpeg 2.0. This affects the function decode_pulses. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: pulse->pos[0] is derived from swb_offset[pulse_swb] plus a 5-bit value and only checked against the fixed constant 1023, not the actual swb_offset[num_swb] bound.
Each subsequent pulse->pos[i] accumulates get_bits(gb,5) onto the prior position and is likewise only compared to 1023, allowing positions beyond the valid swb_offset range.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked positions lead to writes past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The missing constraint is a boundary check against swb_offset[num_swb], not merely a mismatched numeric limit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The pulse positions are validated against a hard-coded 1023 instead of the real spectral-band boundary swb_offset[num_swb]. A crafted AAC stream can produce pulse positions that pass this check but exceed the allocated coefficient array, so later use of these positions indexes out of bounds and corrupts memory.

description: A stack overflow vulnerability exists in gpac 1.1.0 via the gf_bifs_dec_proto_list function, which causes a segmentation fault and application crash.

The buffer is later consumed by `strlen(name)` and `gf_node_set_id`, so a name longer than 999 bytes plus terminator overflows the stack buffer before this use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing beyond the 1000-byte `name` array is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an out-of-bounds read; the decoded name data is written past the buffer end, matching the target weakness.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

Reviewed-by: Simon Horman <simon.horman@corigine.com>

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) at line 27 returns a local pointer without taking a reference; the NULL check at 28-31 only guards the failure path.

The pointer is stored into llcp_sock->local at line 33 via nfc_llcp_local_get(local), and line 35 dereferences local->raw_sockets; the reference is acquired after the lookup rather than atomically with it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a struct nfc_llcp_local pointer that can be freed by a concurrent unregister before the reference is taken, matching CWE-416. This is distinct from a plain NULL-dereference because the object was valid at lookup and is freed afterward.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lookup and reference acquisition are not atomic, so a concurrent nfc_llcp_unregister_device can drop the last reference and free the local object between line 27 and line 33. Trigger: a bind racing with device unregistration. Consequence: line 35 dereferences freed memory, yielding a use-after-free read/write on the local structure.

commit_msg: fixed #1970
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (codec->UseName) gf_bifs_dec_name(bs, name);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (codec->UseName) gf_bifs_dec_name(bs, name, 1000);']}
description: A stack overflow vulnerability exists in gpac 1.1.0 via the gf_bifs_dec_proto_list function, which causes a segmentation fault and application crash.

code_evidence: Line 8 declares a fixed 1000-byte stack buffer 'name'. Line 13 calls gf_bifs_dec_name(bs, name) with no length argument, so the callee has no knowledge of the buffer's size and can write decoded name bytes past its end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes attacker-influenced decoded name data into a fixed-size stack buffer without a length constraint, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is a buffer overflow caused by missing bounds, distinct from mere out-of-bounds read, since the callee writes into 'name'.

evidence_lines.code:
char name[1000];
if (codec->UseName) gf_bifs_dec_name(bs, name);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination buffer 'name' is fixed at 1000 bytes but is passed to gf_bifs_dec_name without a capacity bound, so attacker-controlled name data from the bitstream can overflow the stack buffer. Trigger: parsing a route with codec->UseName set and an overlong encoded name. Consequence: stack memory corruption leading to segmentation fault/crash and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
http: make length/offset-related variables unsigned.

Fixes #5992, reported and found by Paul Cher <paulcher@icloud.com>.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int remaining = s->icy_metaint - s->icy_data_read;', '    if (remaining < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    uint64_t remaining;', '    if (s->icy_metaint < s->icy_data_read)', '    remaining = s->icy_metaint - s->icy_data_read;']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in libavformat/http.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.10, 3.0.x before 3.0.5, 3.1.x before 3.1.6, and 3.2.x before 3.2.2 allows remote web servers to execute arbitrary code via a negative chunk size in an HTTP response.

code_evidence: Line 4 computes `remaining` as a signed int from `s->icy_metaint - s->icy_data_read`; if icy_data_read exceeds icy_metaint the subtraction overflows to a negative value, caught only by the line 5 check.

When remaining is zero, line 15 derives `len = ch * 16` from the attacker-controlled metadata length byte, and line 16 reads `len` bytes into the fixed 4081-byte stack array `data` declared at line 13; line 19 then writes `data[len + 1] = 0`, one past the bytes read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to a fixed-size buffer using a length not bounded to the buffer's capacity, which is an operation outside the intended memory boundary as described by CWE-119. The signed-overflow handling in the patch is related but the direct memory-safety issue is the unbounded length/offset into `data`.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signed subtraction in line 4 and the unchecked multiplication/offset in lines 15 and 19 allow a length derived from the remote metadata byte to exceed the fixed buffer size of `data`. Trigger: an HTTP response with a crafted ICY metadata byte (and icy_metaint/icy_data_read relationship) causes http_read_stream_all to write beyond `data` and line 19 to terminate past the buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write on the stack, potentially memory corruption.

commit_msg:
unix: correctly track in-flight fds in sending process user_struct

The commit referenced in the Fixes tag incorrectly accounted the number
of in-flight fds over a unix domain socket to the original opener
of the file-descriptor. This allows another process to arbitrary
deplete the original file-openers resource limit for the maximum of
open files. Instead the sending processes and its struct cred should
be credited.

To do so, we add a reference counted struct user_struct pointer to the
scm_fp_list and use it to account for the number of inflight unix fds.

Fixes: 712f4aad406bb1 ("unix: properly account for FDs passed over unix sockets")
Reported-by: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: David Herrmann <dh.herrmann@gmail.com>
Cc: Willy Tarreau <w@1wt.eu>
Cc: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Frederic Sowa <hannes@stressinduktion.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void unix_notinflight(struct file *fp)', '\tfp->f_cred->user->unix_inflight--;'], 'added_lines': ['void unix_notinflight(struct user_struct *user, struct file *fp)', '\tuser->unix_inflight--;']}
description: The Linux kernel before 4.5 allows local users to bypass file-descriptor limits and cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by leveraging incorrect tracking of descriptor ownership and sending each descriptor over a UNIX socket before closing it. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2013-4312.

code_evidence: The decrement of the in-flight fd counter is charged to fp->f_cred->user, i.e., the credentials of the process that originally opened the file, not the process that sent the descriptor over the socket.
The decrement occurs under unix_gc_lock but is keyed to a user_struct derived from the file's opener, so the counter credited during send and the counter debited here belong to different processes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) covers improper management of system resources; misattributing the in-flight fd counter to the wrong user_struct mismanages the per-user fd resource limit, matching the target category. It is not a memory-safety flaw; the issue is accounting of a finite resource quota.

evidence_lines.code:
void unix_notinflight(struct file *fp)
fp->f_cred->user->unix_inflight--;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: in-flight fd accounting is attributed to the file opener's user_struct rather than the sending process's credentials. Trigger: a local user repeatedly sends descriptors over a UNIX socket and closes them; the debit lands on the victim opener's user->unix_inflight while the sender's own limit is never reduced. Consequence: the original opener's RLIMIT_NOFILE-derived in-flight budget is arbitrarily depleted, enabling denial of service through resource exhaustion; it is a cause, not itself the memory consumption.

commit_msg:
Fix wild free.

`huffdata` is initially allocated using `aligned_dealloc` but can be
replaced with `data2` which is allocated using `custom_calloc`.
This can cause a wild free when `aligned_dealloc(huffdata)` is called.
Fix by replacing allocation sites with aligned_alloc.

Noticed and fixed a similar problem with `hdrdata`.

description: Dropbox Lepton v1.2.1-185-g2a08b77 was discovered to contain a heap-buffer-overflow in the function aligned_dealloc():src/lepton/bitops.cc:108.

code_evidence: The function subtracts the byte value stored immediately before `data` (`data[-1]`) from the pointer, then passes the result to `custom_free`. It performs no validation that `data` came from the matching aligned allocator or that `data[-1]` is a bounded, trustworthy offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked subtraction `data -= data[-1]` can move the pointer before the start of the intended buffer, and the following `custom_free` accesses/writes memory outside that buffer. The missing constraint on the offset byte and allocator provenance is the cause; the out-of-bounds pointer operation is the supported consequence.

data -= data[-1];
custom_free(data);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: `aligned_dealloc` blindly trusts the prefix byte `data[-1]` and rewinds the pointer by that amount without bounds or provenance checks. Trigger: a pointer allocated by a different allocator (e.g., `custom_calloc`) or with a corrupted/oversized prefix byte is passed in. Consequence: the rewound pointer can lie outside the intended allocation, so the subsequent free operates on an out-of-bounds/wild address, corrupting heap metadata or crashing.

commit_msg:
RTPS: Check for signed overflow

The offset is a signed integer, and we use negative offsets
to mean "offset counting from the end of the tvb." That means
that we can still have an excessive loop without unsigned overflow
or running off the end of the tvb, if the result of adding a large
unsigned integer to the offset results in a small negative number.

Just check if the result of the addition makes the offset move
backwards.

Fix #19322
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static guint32 check_offset_addition(guint32 offset, guint32 value, proto_tree *tree, packet_info *pinfo, tvbuff_t *tvb)', '    if (offset > G_MAXUINT32 - value) {', '    return offset + value;'], 'added_lines': ['static gint check_offset_addition(gint offset, guint32 value, proto_tree *tree, packet_info *pinfo, tvbuff_t *tvb)', '    gint new_offset = offset + (gint)value;', '    if (new_offset < offset) {', '    return new_offset;']}
description: RTPS dissector memory leak in Wireshark 4.0.0 to 4.0.8 and 3.6.0 to 3.6.16 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: check_offset_addition takes a guint32 offset and guint32 value, rejects only when offset > G_MAXUINT32 - value (unsigned overflow guard), then returns offset + value. A large value added to a negative-to-be offset is not prevented from wrapping into a small/negative result.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked offset arithmetic allows an unbounded loop driven by attacker-controlled packet data, exhausting resources without a limit — matching CWE-770 (allocation of resources without limits/throttling). It is not merely an integer-overflow correctness bug; the supported consequence is resource-consumption DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function validates only unsigned 32-bit overflow while the offset is later treated as signed (negative means 'from end of tvb'). Adding a large unsigned value can wrap into a small negative result that passes the check, so the caller's loop condition remains true and repeats unboundedly, consuming CPU/memory (DoS). Root cause: missing signed-overflow/backwards-movement constraint; trigger: crafted packet with large offset value.

description: Contiki-NG is an open-source, cross-platform operating system for Next-Generation IoT devices. An out-of-bounds read can be triggered by 6LoWPAN packets sent to devices running Contiki-NG 4.6 and prior. The IPv6 header decompression function (uncompress_hdr_iphc) does not perform proper boundary checks when reading from the packet buffer. Hence, it is possible to construct a compressed 6LoWPAN packet that will read more bytes than what is available from the packet buffer. As of time of publication, there is not a release with a patch available. Users can apply the patch for this vulnerability out-of-band as a workaround.

The size arguments passed are buffer_size (UIP_BUFSIZE or SICSLOWPAN_FIRST_FRAGMENT_SIZE), not the actual received packet length, so the decompressor has no real bound on how far it may read from the packet buffer.

Trigger: a crafted compressed 6LoWPAN packet with truncated/malformed header fields. Consequence: reads past the packet buffer (out-of-bounds read), leaking memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
Unsquashfs: additional write outside destination directory exploit fix

An issue on github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
showed how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and '..') can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

Since then it has been shown that specially crafted Squashfs filesystems
that contain a symbolic link pointing outside of the destination directory,
coupled with an identically named file within the same directory, can
cause Unsquashfs to write files outside of the destination directory.

Specifically the symbolic link produces a pathname pointing outside
of the destination directory, which is then followed when writing the
duplicate identically named file within the directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by explictly checking for duplicate
filenames within a directory.  As directories in v2.1, v3.x, and v4.0
filesystems are sorted, this is achieved by checking for consecutively
identical filenames.  Additionally directories are checked to
ensure they are sorted, to avoid attempts to evade the duplicate
check.

Version 1.x and 2.0 filesystems (where the directories were unsorted)
are sorted and then the above duplicate filename check is applied.

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif(needs_sorting)', '\t\tsort_directory(dir);', '', '\t/* check directory for duplicate names and sorting */', '\tif(check_directory(dir) == FALSE) {', '\t\tif(needs_sorting)', '\t\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: directory has duplicate names\\n");', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: directory has duplicate names or is unsorted\\n");', '\t\tgoto corrupted;', '\t}']}
description: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-2.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 allows Directory Traversal, a different vulnerability than CVE-2021-40153. A squashfs filesystem that has been crafted to include a symbolic link and then contents under the same filename in a filesystem can cause unsquashfs to first create the symbolic link pointing outside the expected directory, and then the subsequent write operation will cause the unsquashfs process to write through the symbolic link elsewhere in the filesystem.

code_evidence: Lines 72-75 validate only characters in each name via check_name, rejecting invalid characters but not detecting a duplicate name that matches an earlier symlink entry.

Lines 79-92 build the directory entry list, appending each entry (name, start_block, offset, type) without comparing against existing entries for identical names; no duplicate-name or ordering check is performed before returning.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-59 fits because the missing constraint lets a filename resolve to a symlink created earlier, so a subsequent file access follows the link to an unintended resource. This is link following rather than mere path traversal (CWE-22), since the attack relies on a symlink entry resolving the duplicate name outside the destination.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function builds a directory listing from attacker-controlled Squashfs metadata and never verifies that entries are sorted or unique. A crafted filesystem can contain a symlink entry pointing outside the destination plus an identically named regular file entry; the symlink is created first, then the duplicate write follows the link. Root cause is missing duplicate-name/sorting validation; consequence is writes through the symlink outside the destination directory.

commit_msg:
netfilter: x_tables: fix unconditional helper

Ben Hawkes says:

 In the mark_source_chains function (net/ipv4/netfilter/ip_tables.c) it
 is possible for a user-supplied ipt_entry structure to have a large
 next_offset field. This field is not bounds checked prior to writing a
 counter value at the supplied offset.

Problem is that mark_source_chains should not have been called --
the rule doesn't have a next entry, so its supposed to return
an absolute verdict of either ACCEPT or DROP.

However, the function conditional() doesn't work as the name implies.
It only checks that the rule is using wildcard address matching.

However, an unconditional rule must also not be using any matches
(no -m args).

The underflow validator only checked the addresses, therefore
passing the 'unconditional absolute verdict' test, while
mark_source_chains also tested for presence of matches, and thus
proceeeded to the next (not-existent) rule.

Unify this so that all the callers have same idea of 'unconditional rule'.

Reported-by: Ben Hawkes <hawkes@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tpr_err("Underflows must be unconditional and "', '\t\t\t\t       "use the STANDARD target with "', '\t\t\t\t       "ACCEPT/DROP\\n");'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tpr_debug("Underflows must be unconditional and "', '\t\t\t\t\t "use the STANDARD target with "', '\t\t\t\t\t "ACCEPT/DROP\\n");']}
description: The netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel through 4.5.2 does not validate certain offset fields, which allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (heap memory corruption) via an IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt call.

code_evidence: Lines 12-14 bound e->next_offset against limit, but this check alone does not ensure the underflow entry is a genuine unconditional absolute-verdict rule.

Lines 32-39 accept any entry whose offset equals underflows[h] when check_underflow(e) passes, then store it as the underflow target without verifying that matches are absent; the commit notes check_underflow only validated addresses, so a rule with matches passes while mark_source_chains later follows next_offset into non-existent memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The consequence is a write to a memory location outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds operation. The root cause is the inconsistent unconditional-rule check, but the supported weakness is the resulting out-of-bounds write rather than a pure input-validation flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the underflow validator and mark_source_chains disagree on what 'unconditional' means, so a user-supplied ipt_entry with matches and a large next_offset passes validation. mark_source_chains then walks past the rule's intended end and writes a counter value at the supplied offset, causing heap memory corruption (privilege escalation or DoS).

It is a missing-release lifetime bug, not merely a memory leak, because the ctx is subsequently dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The task_work callback holds a reference to the io_ring_ctx but never releases it on either exit path. When the ring is closed with this task_work still inflight, the missing percpu_ref_put leaves the reference unbalanced, so the ctx can be torn down while the callback still accesses ctx (e.g., completion_lock, refs), yielding a use-after-free.

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/43
Origin: https://anonscm.debian.org/cgit/collab-maint/w3m.git/commit/?id=716bc126638393c733399d11d3228edb82877faa
Origin: https://anonscm.debian.org/cgit/collab-maint/w3m.git/commit/?id=88110c2658ad9badd292430c75ebb0444c3312eb
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmap_size = pcs_ucs_map_size[f - WC_F_PCS_BASE];']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-33. w3m allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (global buffer overflow and crash) via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: The case WC_CCS_A_PCS branch validates only the encoding index f against WC_F_PCS_BASE/WC_F_PCS_END before selecting map = pcs_ucs_map[f - WC_F_PCS_BASE]. Unlike the CS94W, CS96W and PCSW branches (lines 36, 49, 80), it never sets map_size from a corresponding size table, so map_size retains the default 0x80. The guard at line 172 then uses this incorrect bound before the read map[cc.code] at line 174. cc.code is masked to 7 bits at line 74, so the read can exceed the actual pcs_ucs_map entry when that entry is shorter than 128 elements.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function indexes a memory buffer using an incorrect size bound, producing an out-of-bounds read of a global array, which is an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer (CWE-119). The missing size assignment is the defect; CWE-125 would be the more specific read-flavored child, but the target is the parent class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PCS branch omits loading the per-entry map size, leaving the default 0x80 bound. Trigger: a crafted HTML page yields a PCS character set whose map entry is smaller than 0x80 and a cc.code value within 0x7f. Consequence: map[cc.code] reads past the global map array (global buffer overflow), causing a crash/DoS as described.

commit_msg:
Fixes #86

FossilOrigin-Name: 9c3099ff5a311d4fa71612ceba3b14030aacf7581b102c2705e0a13b04e35fab
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['    if (obj->modifying)', '      return Jsi_LogError("already modifying");', '    obj->modifying = 1;', '    obj->modifying = 0;']}
description: Jsish v3.5.0 was discovered to contain a heap-use-after-free via SortSubCmd in src/jsiArray.c. This vulnerability can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS).

code_evidence: The function sorts obj->arr via qsort/qsort_r using SortSubCmd; the user-supplied comparator (si.compare) is invoked during sorting and can re-enter array mutation while the original sort loop still holds obj->arr and curlen.

The unique-dedup loop later walks obj->arr[i] and calls Jsi_DecrRefCount on duplicates, then writes obj->arr[n] = obj->arr[i]; if the array was resized/freed by a reentrant comparator, these accesses reference stale storage.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported weakness is reuse of freed heap memory: obj->arr elements are read and decremented after reentrant mutation may have freed them. This is CWE-416 rather than a mere out-of-bounds read because the stale pointer is used after the backing allocation is released.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sort/dedup operates on obj->arr without guarding against reentrant modification; the comparator supplied via args can execute script that changes the array. Trigger: a comparator that mutates/frees the array during qsort or during the dedup SortSubCmd calls. Consequence: stale obj->arr/obj->arr[i] pointers are dereferenced and refcounted, giving heap use-after-free and potential DoS.

commit_msg: Add missing authorization checking in Helper::flushPageCache()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!isCallerAuthorized()) {', '        return {};', '    }', '']}
description: KDiskMark before 3.1.0 lacks authorization checking for D-Bus methods such as Helper::flushPageCache.

code_evidence: The function checks isCallerAuthorized() and returns an error reply before any privileged action, so this branch enforces authorization for the caller.
Only after the authorization gate does the function open /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches for writing and write "1", performing the privileged cache-flush action.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-862 fits because the function previously performed a privileged action (writing to drop_caches) without verifying the caller's authorization; the guard now prevents unauthorized actors from invoking it.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause addressed is the absence of an authorization gate before the privileged cache-flush operation; the added isCallerAuthorized() check with an early error return ensures unprivileged callers cannot reach the write to /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches. Without it, any D-Bus caller could trigger the flush.

commit_msg:
CVE-2023-0494, ZDI-CAN-19596

This vulnerability was discovered by:
Jan-Niklas Sohn working with Trend Micro Zero Day Initiative

Signed-off-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        else'], 'added_lines': ['        else {', '            to->button->xkb_acts = NULL;', '        }']}
description: A vulnerability was found in X.Org. This issue occurs due to a dangling pointer in DeepCopyPointerClasses that can be exploited by ProcXkbSetDeviceInfo() and ProcXkbGetDeviceInfo() to read and write into freed memory. This can lead to local privilege elevation on systems where the X server runs privileged and remote code execution for ssh X forwarding sessions.

code_evidence: When from->button->xkb_acts is NULL, the else branch frees to->button->xkb_acts at line 73 but does not clear the pointer; the pre-patch code left to->button->xkb_acts dangling. On a later DeepCopyPointerClasses call with a non-NULL from->button->xkb_acts, line 64's `!to->button->xkb_acts` check sees the stale non-NULL pointer, skips allocation, and line 69 memcpy writes sizeof(XkbAction) into freed memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code frees memory and retains a pointer to it, then dereferences that pointer for memcpy and later reads, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. The fix adds `to->button->xkb_acts = NULL` to prevent the stale reference. This is not a double free or plain memory leak, since the freed pointer is reused rather than re-freed or merely orphaned.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: freeing to->button->xkb_acts without nulling it leaves a dangling pointer in the ButtonClassRec. Trigger: a subsequent copy where the source supplies xkb_acts causes the stale pointer to be treated as valid, so memcpy writes into freed memory and later reads via ProcXkbGetDeviceInfo return freed data. Supported consequence: use-after-free read/write, enabling privilege escalation or RCE in privileged X servers.

description: In radare2 prior to 3.1.1, the parseOperand function inside libr/asm/p/asm_x86_nz.c may allow attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash via a stack-based buffer overflow) by crafting an input file, a related issue to CVE-2018-20456.

code_evidence: When a register token is followed by '+', '-', or ']', the code writes op->regs[reg_index] and op->scale[reg_index] using reg_index without any bound check, then increments reg_index.

In the else branch the same unchecked reg_index indexes op->regs for X86R_UNDEFINED; reg_index is only incremented in the first branch, but repeated register/offset tokens in one memory operand can still grow it.

description: The ZipCommon::isValidPath() function in Zip/src/ZipCommon.cpp in POCO C++ Libraries before 1.8 does not properly restrict the filename value in the ZIP header, which allows attackers to conduct absolute path traversal attacks during the ZIP decompression, and possibly create or overwrite arbitrary files, via a crafted ZIP file, related to a "file path injection vulnerability".

code_evidence: Entry filename from the ZIP header is taken as dirName and only checked by ZipCommon::isValidPath before being combined with _outDir and used to create directories.
For file entries, fileName is checked by isValidPath, then combined with _outDir into dest and opened for writing via FileOutputStream and populated by StreamCopier.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits: external ZIP header input is used to build a pathname intended to stay under _outDir, but special path elements are not neutralized, so the resolved path can leave the restricted directory. The consequence is file write outside the intended extraction root, not merely an error message issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The attacker-controlled ZIP header filename flows into path construction (_outDir, dirName/fileName) and subsequent directory creation and file writes. The only guard is isValidPath; the commit description states this check does not properly restrict the filename, allowing crafted entries (e.g. absolute or parent-directory paths) to escape the extraction directory, causing arbitrary file creation/overwrite outside _outDir.

asn1: don't increment a buffer beyond its end.

Change-Id: I04cbb822f0e77c8e0ac8513e3a5c13116920ca6e

(cherry picked from commit 45a3d0787f3c9f6f5fb5b53a8c29771b3f28e406)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/33736
Petri-Dish: Dario Lombardo <lomato@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    /* Ensure the buffer len and its content are coherent */', '    DISSECTOR_ASSERT(lenE < len - 1);', '']}
description: In Wireshark 3.0.0 to 3.0.2, 2.6.0 to 2.6.9, and 2.4.0 to 2.4.15, the ASN.1 BER dissector and related dissectors could crash. This was addressed in epan/asn1.c by properly restricting buffer increments.

code_evidence: lenE is derived from the exponent-length bits of octet and is at most 3, but nothing verifies that the remaining buffer (len after line 9) actually holds lenE exponent octets. The loop at 35-42 dereferences *p lenE times and advances p, so a short buffer causes an out-of-bounds read.
After the exponent loop, lenN = len - lenE can underflow when lenE exceeds the remaining len; the loop at 51-54 then dereferences *p lenN times, reading beyond the buffer end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loops perform memory reads beyond the intended buffer boundary due to missing length validation, which is an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer (CWE-119). The added DISSECTOR_ASSERT(lenE < len - 1) confirms the missing bound check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the ASN.1 header's encoded exponent length without checking it against the actual buffer length. Trigger: a crafted BER REAL where the exponent-length field exceeds the remaining bytes. The exponent and mantissa loops then read past the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bluetooth: sco: Fix lock_sock() blockage by memcpy_from_msg()

The sco_send_frame() also takes lock_sock() during memcpy_from_msg()
call that may be endlessly blocked by a task with userfaultd
technique, and this will result in a hung task watchdog trigger.

Just like the similar fix for hci_sock_sendmsg() in commit
92c685dc5de0 ("Bluetooth: reorganize functions..."), this patch moves
the  memcpy_from_msg() out of lock_sock() for addressing the hang.

This should be the last piece for fixing CVE-2021-3640 after a few
already queued fixes.

Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\terr = sco_send_frame(sk, msg, len);'], 'added_lines': ['\tvoid *buf;', '\tbuf = kmalloc(len, GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (!buf)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '', '\tif (memcpy_from_msg(buf, msg, len)) {', '\t\tkfree(buf);', '\t\treturn -EFAULT;', '\t}', '', '\t\terr = sco_send_frame(sk, buf, len, msg->msg_flags);', '\tkfree(buf);']}
description: A flaw use-after-free in function sco_sock_sendmsg() of the Linux kernel HCI subsystem was found in the way user calls ioct UFFDIO_REGISTER or other way triggers race condition of the call sco_conn_del() together with the call sco_sock_sendmsg() with the expected controllable faulting memory page. A privileged local user could use this flaw to crash the system or escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: lock_sock(sk) is taken, then sk->sk_state is checked against BT_CONNECTED and sco_send_frame(sk, msg, len) is called while the lock is held; release_sock(sk) follows. The send path reads from the user msg buffer inside the locked region, so a faulting user page can stall the operation while holding the socket lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function takes exclusive access to the shared socket via lock_sock() but keeps it across a blocking user-memory operation, allowing a concurrent code sequence (connection deletion) to be blocked and thereby violating the intended progress/atomicity of the locked sequence. This is a synchronization/race-liveness flaw rather than a use-after-free in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The socket lock is held across the entire send, including the user-buffer access performed by sco_send_frame. If that access blocks on a userfaultfd-controlled page, the lock stays held; a concurrent sco_conn_del()/close path needing the same lock waits, producing a hung task/lockup. The root cause is holding exclusive socket state across a potentially blocking user copy; the supported consequence is denial of service via lockup, not memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Issue 717:  Fix integer overflow when computing location of volume descriptor

The multiplication here defaulted to 'int' but calculations
of file positions should always use int64_t.  A simple cast
suffices to fix this since the base location is always 32 bits
for ISO, so multiplying by the sector size will never overflow
a 64-bit integer.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tskipsize = LOGICAL_BLOCK_SIZE * vd->location;', '\t\tskipsize = LOGICAL_BLOCK_SIZE * vd->location;'], 'added_lines': ['\tskipsize = LOGICAL_BLOCK_SIZE * (int64_t)vd->location;', '\t\tskipsize = LOGICAL_BLOCK_SIZE * (int64_t)vd->location;']}
description: Integer overflow in the ISO parser in libarchive before 3.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted ISO file.

code_evidence: vd->location is read from the ISO volume descriptor into a 32-bit field, but the product LOGICAL_BLOCK_SIZE * vd->location is evaluated in int arithmetic before assignment to the int64_t skipsize; a crafted large location can wrap the 32-bit product.
The same int multiplication at line 39 is then reduced by current_position and passed to __archive_read_consume, so the wrapped/negative value drives the subsequent seek and parsing position.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a direct integer overflow/wraparound in an offset calculation whose result is assumed to grow, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a signedness issue, since the arithmetic itself wraps before the value is used as a file position.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sector-size times descriptor-location multiplication is performed in 32-bit int and only then widened to int64_t, so a crafted ISO location overflows and yields a small or negative skipsize. The trigger is an attacker-supplied ISO volume descriptor; the resulting bad offset is passed to __archive_read_consume, causing the parser to read from an incorrect position and crash (DoS).

description: An issue was discovered in Erlang/OTP 18.x. Erlang's generation of compiled regular expressions is vulnerable to a heap overflow. description: The consume_init_expr function in wasm.c in radare2 1.3.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted Web Assembly file.

code_evidence: The loop advances i while buf + i < max and buf[i] != eoc, so it stops when buf + i reaches max without dereferencing past max.
After the loop, buf[i] is read unconditionally; if the loop terminated because buf + i == max (no eoc found), this dereference reads one byte at max, i.e., past the intended buffer end.
The return value i + 1 and offset increment i + 1 also exceed the consumed bytes when eoc was never found, but the primary unsafe read is at line 6.

return 0;

*offset += i + 1;
return i + 1;

USB: core: Fix free-while-in-use bug in the USB S-Glibrary

FuzzUSB (a variant of syzkaller) found a free-while-still-in-use bug
in the USB scatter-gather library:

BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in atomic_read
include/asm-generic/atomic-instrumented.h:26 [inline]
BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in usb_hcd_unlink_urb+0x5f/0x170
drivers/usb/core/hcd.c:1607
Read of size 4 at addr ffff888065379610 by task kworker/u4:1/27

CPU: 1 PID: 27 Comm: kworker/u4:1 Not tainted 5.5.11 #2
Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS
1.10.2-1ubuntu1 04/01/2014
Workqueue: scsi_tmf_2 scmd_eh_abort_handler
Call Trace:
 __dump_stack lib/dump_stack.c:77 [inline]
 dump_stack+0xce/0x128 lib/dump_stack.c:118
 print_address_description.constprop.4+0x21/0x3c0 mm/kasan/report.c:374
 __kasan_report+0x153/0x1cb mm/kasan/report.c:506
 kasan_report+0x12/0x20 mm/kasan/common.c:639
 check_memory_region_inline mm/kasan/generic.c:185 [inline]
 check_memory_region+0x152/0x1b0 mm/kasan/generic.c:192
 __kasan_check_read+0x11/0x20 mm/kasan/common.c:95
 atomic_read include/asm-generic/atomic-instrumented.h:26 [inline]
 usb_hcd_unlink_urb+0x5f/0x170 drivers/usb/core/hcd.c:1607
 usb_unlink_urb+0x72/0xb0 drivers/usb/core/urb.c:657
 usb_sg_cancel+0x14e/0x290 drivers/usb/core/message.c:602
 usb_stor_stop_transport+0x5e/0xa0 drivers/usb/storage/transport.c:937

This bug occurs when cancellation of the S-G transfer races with
transfer completion.  When that happens, usb_sg_cancel() may continue
to access the transfer's URBs after usb_sg_wait() has freed them.

The bug is caused by the fact that usb_sg_cancel() does not take any
sort of reference to the transfer, and so there is nothing to prevent
the URBs from being deallocated while the routine is trying to use
them.  The fix is to take such a reference by incrementing the
transfer's io->count field while the cancellation is in progres and
decrementing it afterward.  The transfer's URBs are not deallocated
until io->complete is triggered, which happens when io->count reaches
zero.

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: Kyungtae Kim <kt0755@gmail.com>
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/Pine.LNX.4.44L0.2003281615140.14837-100000@netrider.rowland.org
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: usb_sg_cancel in drivers/usb/core/message.c in the Linux kernel before 5.6.8 has a use-after-free because a transfer occurs without a reference, aka CID-056ad39ee925.

code_evidence: The early-out only checks io->status; it does not check io->count, so cancellation can proceed even when the transfer has no outstanding reference and usb_sg_wait() may already free the URBs.
After setting io->status, the function drops io->lock and iterates over io->urbs[i], calling usb_block_urb() and usb_unlink_urb() on each URB without holding any reference to keep them alive.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function dereferences URB objects after their lifetime has ended due to the missing reference; the fix adds io->count reference handling to prevent the free-while-in-use race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: usb_sg_cancel() accesses the transfer's URBs without taking a reference on the transfer. Trigger: concurrent transfer completion, where usb_sg_wait() frees the URBs while cancellation is still iterating. Supported consequence: use-after-free reads/writes on freed URB memory, as seen in the reported KASAN trace during usb_unlink_urb().

commit_msg:
ptrace: Fix ->ptracer_cred handling for PTRACE_TRACEME

Fix two issues:

When called for PTRACE_TRACEME, ptrace_link() would obtain an RCU
reference to the parent's objective credentials, then give that pointer
to get_cred().  However, the object lifetime rules for things like
struct cred do not permit unconditionally turning an RCU reference into
a stable reference.

PTRACE_TRACEME records the parent's credentials as if the parent was
acting as the subject, but that's not the case.  If a malicious
unprivileged child uses PTRACE_TRACEME and the parent is privileged, and
at a later point, the parent process becomes attacker-controlled
(because it drops privileges and calls execve()), the attacker ends up
with control over two processes with a privileged ptrace relationship,
which can be abused to ptrace a suid binary and obtain root privileges.

Fix both of these by always recording the credentials of the process
that is requesting the creation of the ptrace relationship:
current_cred() can't change under us, and current is the proper subject
for access control.

This change is theoretically userspace-visible, but I am not aware of
any code that it will actually break.

Fixes: 64b875f7ac8a ("ptrace: Capture the ptracer's creds not PT_PTRACE_CAP")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\trcu_read_lock();', '\t__ptrace_link(child, new_parent, __task_cred(new_parent));', '\trcu_read_unlock();'], 'added_lines': ['\t__ptrace_link(child, new_parent, current_cred());']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.1.17, ptrace_link in kernel/ptrace.c mishandles the recording of the credentials of a process that wants to create a ptrace relationship, which allows local users to obtain root access by leveraging certain scenarios with a parent-child process relationship, where a parent drops privileges and calls execve (potentially allowing control by an attacker). One contributing factor is an object lifetime issue (which can also cause a panic). Another contributing factor is incorrect marking of a ptrace relationship as privileged, which is exploitable through (for example) Polkit's pkexec helper with PTRACE_TRACEME. NOTE: SELinux deny_ptrace might be a usable workaround in some environments.

code_evidence: ptrace_link() takes an RCU read lock and passes __task_cred(new_parent), an RCU-protected pointer to the parent's credentials, into __ptrace_link(), which records those credentials as the basis of the ptrace relationship. The subject whose privileges are captured is the parent, not the process requesting the relationship, and the RCU reference is converted into a stable credential reference without the proper lifetime rule.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function improperly assigns privilege for the ptrace actor by recording the parent's credentials instead of the requester's, creating an unintended privileged sphere of control exploitable for escalation. This is an access-control/privilege-assignment mistake, matching CWE-269 rather than merely describing the escalation impact.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ptrace relationship's privilege is derived from the parent's (new_parent) credentials rather than the requesting task's current credentials. Trigger: an unprivileged child calls PTRACE_TRACEME against a privileged parent that later drops privileges and execs attacker-controlled code. Consequence: the attacker obtains a ptrace relationship marked privileged, enabling tracing of a suid binary to gain root; the RCU-to-stable conversion also risks a lifetime/panic issue.

commit_msg:
If the target ring is configured with IOPOLL, then we always need to hold
the target ring uring_lock before posting CQEs. We could just grab it
unconditionally, but since we don't expect many target rings to be of this
type, make grabbing the uring_lock conditional on the ring type.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/io-uring/Y8krlYa52%2F0YGqkg@ip-172-31-85-199.ec2.internal/
Reported-by: Xingyuan Mo <hdthky0@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tret = io_msg_ring_data(req);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tret = io_msg_ring_data(req, issue_flags);']}
description: A vulnerability was found due to missing lock for IOPOLL flaw in io_cqring_event_overflow() in io_uring.c in Linux Kernel. This flaw allows a local attacker with user privilege to trigger a Denial of Service threat.

code_evidence: In the IORING_MSG_DATA case, the function calls io_msg_ring_data(req) without forwarding issue_flags. The sibling IORING_MSG_SEND_FD case at line 13 passes issue_flags to io_msg_send_fd, showing the flag is available but dropped for the data path. This dispatch is the call site that determines whether the target ring's uring_lock is acquired before posting CQEs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing lock acquisition for IOPOLL target rings is a failure to properly acquire a lock on a shared resource before posting CQEs, matching CWE-667 (Improper Locking). This is not a generic race on data but specifically an omitted locking step in the message-ring data path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: io_msg_ring_data is invoked without the issue_flags needed to conditionally acquire the target ring's uring_lock for IOPOLL rings. Trigger: a local user posts an IORING_MSG_DATA message to an IOPOLL-configured target ring. Consequence: CQEs are posted without the required lock, causing an unsynchronized state that can lead to a denial of service.

commit_msg:
The SendEvent request holds xEvent which is exactly 32 bytes long, no more,
no less. Both ProcSendEvent and SProcSendEvent verify that the received data
exactly match the request size. However nothing stops the client from passing
in event with xEvent::type = GenericEvent and any value of
xGenericEvent::length.

In the case of ProcSendEvent, the event will be eventually passed to
WriteEventsToClient which will see that it is Generic event and copy the
arbitrary length from the receive buffer (and possibly past it) and send it to
the other client. This allows clients to copy unitialized heap memory out of X
server or to crash it.

In case of SProcSendEvent, it will attempt to swap the incoming event by
calling a swapping function from the EventSwapVector array. The swapped event
is written to target buffer, which in this case is local xEvent variable. The
xEvent variable is 32 bytes long, but the swapping functions for GenericEvents
expect that the target buffer has size matching the size of the source
GenericEvent. This allows clients to cause stack buffer overflows.

Signed-off-by: Michal Srb <msrb@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
Signed-off-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        client->errorValue = stuff->event.u.u.type;', '        return BadValue;', '    }', '    /* Generic events can have variable size, but SendEvent request holds', '       exactly 32B of event data. */', '    if (stuff->event.u.u.type == GenericEvent) {']}
description: In the X.Org X server before 2017-06-19, a user authenticated to an X Session could crash or execute code in the context of the X Server by exploiting a stack overflow in the endianness conversion of X Events.

code_evidence: ProcSendEvent only checks the 32-byte request size and validates the event type range, but never rejects GenericEvent before the event is forwarded to DeliverEventsToWindow. The type is masked and range-checked, yet GenericEvent passes these checks and its attacker-controlled xGenericEvent::length is not constrained.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked GenericEvent length causes a read that exceeds the intended bounds of the fixed 32-byte event buffer, matching CWE-119. This is specifically an out-of-bounds read rather than a stack overwrite, which would fit the related SProcSendEvent path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the request is validated only by REQUEST_SIZE_MATCH and a type-range test, so a GenericEvent with an arbitrary xGenericEvent::length is accepted. When the event is delivered, code treats it as a variable-length GenericEvent and copies the declared length from the 32-byte buffer, reading past the buffer boundary. Supported consequence: disclosure of uninitialized or out-of-bounds heap memory, or a server crash.

commit_msg:
The return value of devm_kzalloc() needs to be checked.
To avoid use of null pointer in case of thefailure of alloc.

Fixes: 46233e91fa24 ("media: mtk-vcodec: move firmware implementations into their own files")
Signed-off-by: Jiasheng Jiang <jiasheng@iscas.ac.cn>
Reviewed-by: Tzung-Bi Shih <tzungbi@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!fw)', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.16-rc6. mtk_vcodec_fw_vpu_init in drivers/media/platform/mtk-vcodec/mtk_vcodec_fw_vpu.c lacks check of the return value of devm_kzalloc() and will cause the null pointer dereference.

code_evidence: Line 22 assigns the result of devm_kzalloc() to fw without checking it, and lines 23-25 immediately dereference fw via fw->type, fw->ops and fw->pdev. If allocation fails, fw is NULL and these writes target address zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL after failed allocation, matching CWE-476. The missing NULL check on the allocation result is the direct cause, not a separate resource-leak issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the devm_kzalloc() return value is used unconditionally. Trigger: memory allocation failure returns NULL. Consequence: the subsequent member writes dereference a NULL pointer, causing a kernel crash (DoS) and potentially memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix a seg-fault in the ELF note parser when a note with an excessively large alignment is encountered.

	PR 22788
	* elf.c (elf_parse_notes): Reject notes with excessuively large
	alignments.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (align != 4 && align != 8)', '    return FALSE;']}
description: The elf_parse_notes function in elf.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.30, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and segmentation violation) via a note with a large alignment.

code_evidence: The parameter align is only bounded below (align < 4 becomes 4); there is no upper constraint on align before it is used.

in.descdata is computed as p + ELF_NOTE_DESC_OFFSET(in.namesz, align), so an excessively large align drives descdata far past the buffer; the subsequent bounds check compares in.descdata against buf + size but the offset computation itself can place it beyond the object, and descpos is derived from that pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked alignment causes reads relative to a pointer computed beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). It is not merely an integer overflow; the defect is the missing alignment constraint that lets descdata escape the buffer before it is dereferenced.

evidence_lines.code:
if (align < 4)
align = 4;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the alignment value from the note is not validated against a sane maximum, so ELF_NOTE_DESC_OFFSET can produce a pointer outside the note buffer. Trigger: a crafted ELF note with a very large alignment. Consequence: out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic/read leading to a segmentation violation (denial of service).

commit_msg:
[builtins] Fix Array.prototype.concat bug

Array.prototype.concat did not work correct with complex elements on the
receiver or the prototype chain.

BUG=chromium:594574
LOG=y

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1804963002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#34798}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  ElementsKind origin_kind = array->map()->elements_kind();'], 'added_lines': ['  ElementsKind origin_kind = array->GetElementsKind();']}
description: The Array.prototype.concat implementation in builtins.cc in Google V8, as used in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.108, does not properly consider element data types, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JavaScript code.

code_evidence: Line 11 reads origin_kind from array->map()->elements_kind() rather than the array's actual elements kind, so a receiver whose prototype chain or complex elements differ can report a stale kind.
Lines 19-20 and 29-31 derive target_kind (FAST_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS/FAST_ELEMENTS) from that origin_kind, and line 37 compares it to the same possibly-wrong origin_kind before transitioning at line 39.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale kind causes fast-path element access to operate beyond the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119 out-of-bounds read. It is not merely a logic bug: the supported consequence is memory read outside bounds.

evidence_lines.code:
ElementsKind origin_kind = array->map()->elements_kind();
if (IsDictionaryElementsKind(origin_kind)) return false;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The origin_kind is taken from the map instead of GetElementsKind, so a mismatched kind is used as the baseline for the transition decision. When crafted elements make target_kind equal the stale origin_kind, the transition is skipped, leaving array storage with a kind inconsistent with its contents; subsequent fast-element access in concat then indexes outside intended bounds, causing an out-of-bounds read (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix error overflow bug
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  // GPR_ASSERT((*err)->ints[which] == UINT8_MAX); // TODO, enforce this'], 'added_lines': ['    if (slot == UINT8_MAX) {', '      gpr_log(GPR_ERROR, "Error %p is full, dropping int {\\"%s\\":%" PRIiPTR "}", *err,', '              error_int_name(which), value);', '      return;', '    }']}
description: Google gRPC before 2017-04-05 has an out-of-bounds write caused by a heap-based buffer overflow related to core/lib/iomgr/error.c.

code_evidence: Line 3 reads a slot index from (*err)->ints[which]; when it equals UINT8_MAX, line 5 calls get_placement to obtain a new slot. The returned slot is written unconditionally into (*err)->ints[which] on line 7 and used to index (*err)->arena on line 8, with no check that get_placement succeeded (i.e., did not return UINT8_MAX or an out-of-range slot).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked slot value indexes and writes into the fixed arena buffer, producing a write past the end of the intended buffer, which matches CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write). A related CWE-125 read is not applicable because the unsafe operation is a write on line 8.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the slot returned by get_placement is trusted without validating it against the arena capacity or the UINT8_MAX sentinel. Trigger: an error object whose arena is exhausted causes get_placement to return UINT8_MAX (or an invalid index). Consequence: line 8 writes (*err)->arena[slot] out of bounds, corrupting heap memory (the described heap-based buffer overflow / out-of-bounds write).

commit_msg:
SampleTable.cpp: Fixed a regression caused by a fix for bug
28076789.

Detail: Before the original fix
(Id207f369ab7b27787d83f5d8fc48dc53ed9fcdc9) for 28076789, the
code allowed a time-to-sample table size to be 0. The change
made in that fix disallowed such situation, which in fact should
be allowed. This current patch allows it again while maintaining
the security of the previous fix.

Bug: 28288202
Bug: 28076789
Change-Id: I1c9a60c7f0cfcbd3d908f24998dde15d5136a295
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!mTimeToSample.empty() || data_size < 8) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (mHasTimeToSample || data_size < 8) {', '', '    mHasTimeToSample = true;']}
description: SampleTable.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-06-01 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (device hang or reboot) via a crafted file, aka internal bug 28076789.

code_evidence: The guard rejects only a non-empty table or data_size < 8; it does not reject a zero count in the header, so a zero-entry table is accepted.
mTimeToSampleCount is read from attacker-controlled header bytes and only an upper bound is checked; a count of 0 passes the bound and is used as the vector size.
getVector is called with mTimeToSampleCount * 2, which is 0 when the count is zero, so no table data is read and processing continues.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The declared count is input metadata that is not validated for the required nonzero property before use, matching CWE-20. This is improper validation of an input-derived quantity rather than a memory-safety defect; the missing lower-bound check is the validation failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function validates the declared table count only against an upper bound and never enforces a minimum, so a crafted file with a zero time-to-sample count is accepted. Trigger: a malicious file whose header declares count 0. Consequence: an empty table flows onward into downstream sample-table consumers, supporting the reported device hang/reboot denial of service.
