description: A stack-based buffer over-read exists in setbit() at iptree.h of TCPFLOW 1.5.0, due to received incorrect values causing incorrect computation, leading to denial of service during an address_histogram call or a get_histogram call.

code_evidence: The loop bound is addrlen*8/2, so index i ranges up to addrlen*4-1. Line 3 calls setbit(addr1,i) and line 4 calls setbit(addr2,i) with that index, but the buffers' sizes are given by addr12len, which is never consulted. If addr12len is smaller than addrlen*4, setbit reads/writes past the end of addr1/addr2. The patch adds sizeof(addr1)/sizeof(addr2) arguments, showing the missing size constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the index computed from addrlen indexes beyond the intended addr1/addr2 buffers during a read-modify access in setbit, matching out-of-bounds read. A write-based CWE would also apply, but the reported over-read in setbit is directly supported by the unchecked index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bit index derived from addrlen is used to address addr1/addr2 without validating it against addr12len. Trigger: caller supplies addrlen whose derived index exceeds the destination buffer size. Consequence: setbit reads/writes memory beyond the buffer, causing out-of-bounds access and possible crash/DoS during histogram calls.

commit_msg:
avcodec/jpeg2000dwt: Check ndeclevels before calling dwt_decode*()

Fixes out of array access
Fixes: 01859c9a9ac6cd60a008274123275574/asan_heap-oob_1dff571_8250_50d3d1611e294c3519fd1fa82198b69b.avi

Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (s->ndeclevels == 0)', '        return 0;', '']}
description: The ff_dwt_decode function in libavcodec/jpeg2000dwt.c in FFmpeg before 2.8.4 does not validate the number of decomposition levels before proceeding with Discrete Wavelet Transform decoding, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JPEG 2000 data.

code_evidence: ff_dwt_decode dispatches directly to dwt_decode97_float, dwt_decode97_int, or dwt_decode53 based solely on s->type, with no check on s->ndeclevels before calling these decoders. The decoders use the number of decomposition levels to size/iterate buffers, so a crafted JPEG 2000 stream yielding ndeclevels==0 reaches them unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked decomposition-level count causes the DWT routines to read/write memory outside intended buffer bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds buffer operation. CWE-119 covers the resultant OOB access; the missing ndeclevels check is the root cause enabling it.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation of s->ndeclevels before invoking the DWT decode routines. Trigger: crafted JPEG 2000 data sets ndeclevels to an invalid value (e.g., 0); the switch then calls a decoder that computes buffer offsets from that level count. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds array access, leading to crash/DoS or memory corruption.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C. In versions of PJSIP prior to 2.13 the PJSIP parser, PJMEDIA RTP decoder, and PJMEDIA SDP parser are affeced by a buffer overflow vulnerability. Users connecting to untrusted clients are at risk. This issue has been patched and is available as commit c4d3498 in the master branch and will be included in releases 2.13 and later. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: Line 5 dereferences *(scanner->curptr+1) and compares it to '=' without first confirming that curptr+1 is within the scanner buffer (curptr < end).

Line 9 likewise dereferences *(scanner->curptr+2) and compares it to '0' without verifying that curptr+2 is within the buffer, so either dereference can read past the end when the scanner is near or at the end of its input.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds curptr+N >= end guards, showing the missing size/length check was the defect. However, the unsafe operations are out-of-bounds reads, not a buffer copy, so CWE-120 (buffer copy without input-size checking) does not accurately describe this function; CWE-125 would better fit the read overrun.

evidence_lines.code: if (*(scanner->curptr+1) != '=') {
if (*(scanner->curptr+2) != '0') {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parse_version reads fixed offsets curptr+1 and curptr+2 from the scanner cursor before any bounds check against scanner->end. Trigger: a truncated SDP version line (e.g. ending at or shortly after 'v') makes these offsets point past the allocated buffer. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read that can crash the parser or leak adjacent memory; it is not a copy into a destination buffer.

commit_msg:
passthrough: quarantine PCI devices

When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for
that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The
IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that
the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However,
when the guest domain is torn down the device is assigned back to dom0,
thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data.

This patch introduces a 'quarantine' for PCI devices using dom_io. When
the toolstack makes a device assignable (by binding it to pciback), it
will now also assign it to DOMID_IO and the device will only be assigned
back to dom0 when the device is made unassignable again. Whilst device is
assignable it will only ever transfer between dom_io and guest domains.
dom_io is actually only used as a sentinel domain for quarantining purposes;
it is not configured with any IOMMU mappings. Assignment to dom_io simply
means that the device's initiator (requestor) identifier is not present in
the IOMMU's device table and thus any DMA transactions issued will be
terminated with a fault condition.

In addition, a fix to assignment handling is made for VT-d.  Failure
during the assignment step should not lead to a device still being
associated with its prior owner. Hand the device to DomIO temporarily,
until the assignment step has completed successfully.  Remove the PI
hooks from the source domain then earlier as well.

Failure of the recovery reassign_device_ownership() may not go silent:
There e.g. may still be left over RMRR mappings in the domain assignment
to which has failed, and hence we can't allow that domain to continue
executing.

NOTE: This patch also includes one printk() cleanup; the
      "XEN_DOMCTL_assign_device: " tag is dropped in iommu_do_pci_domctl(),
      since similar printk()-s elsewhere also don't log such a tag.

This is XSA-302.

Signed-off-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <ian.jackson@eu.citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device. This occurs because passed through PCI devices may corrupt host memory after deassignment. When a PCI device is assigned to an untrusted domain, it is possible for that domain to program the device to DMA to an arbitrary address. The IOMMU is used to protect the host from malicious DMA by making sure that the device addresses can only target memory assigned to the guest. However, when the guest domain is torn down, or the device is deassigned, the device is assigned back to dom0, thus allowing any in-flight DMA to potentially target critical host data. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function handles PCI device assignment and IOMMU/DMA ownership; it contains no OS command construction or execution, so it does not support CWE-78.

to reduce the coverage of struct_mutex, with a view to removing the last

Fixed bug #73342

Directly listen on socket, instead of duping it to STDIN and

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (wp->listening_socket != STDIN_FILENO) {', '\t\tif (0 > dup2(wp->listening_socket, STDIN_FILENO)) {', '\t\t\tzlog(ZLOG_SYSERROR, "failed to init child stdio: dup2()");', '\t\t\treturn -1;', '\t\t}', '\t}'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in PHP 7.3.x before 7.3.0alpha3, 7.2.x before 7.2.8, and before 7.1.20. The php-fpm master process restarts a child process in an endless loop when using program execution functions (e.g., passthru, exec, shell_exec, or system) with a non-blocking STDIN stream, causing this master process to consume 100% of the CPU, and consume disk space with a large volume of error logs, as demonstrated by an attack by a customer of a shared-hosting facility.

code_evidence: The function dups the worker's listening socket onto STDIN_FILENO via dup2, replacing the child's inherited stdin. This makes the listening socket the child's standard input, so program-execution functions reading stdin operate on the listening socket.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code enables an endless child-restart loop that exhausts CPU and disk/log resources, matching uncontrolled resource consumption. The dup2 onto STDIN is the concrete unsafe operation; removing it (as the patch does) avoids the loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that the child's STDIN is bound to the listening socket, so spawned processes reading non-blocking stdin repeatedly error or fail; the FPM master then restarts the child in a loop. Trigger is any program execution with a non-blocking STDIN stream, causing unbounded CPU and log/disk consumption (CWE-400).

commit_msg:
gmarkup: Fix crash in error handling path for closing elements

If something which looks like a closing tag is left unfinished, but
isn’t paired to an opening tag in the document, the error handling code
would do a null pointer dereference. Avoid that, at the cost of
introducing a new translatable error message.

Includes a test case, courtesy of pdknsk.

Signed-off-by: Philip Withnall <withnall@endlessm.com>

description: In GNOME GLib 2.56.1, g_markup_parse_context_end_parse() in gmarkup.c has a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: In the close-tag error states, the code calls current_element(context) as a printf-style argument to set_error without first verifying that context->tag_stack is non-NULL. current_element() derives the element name from the tag stack, so when the document ends inside a close tag for an element that was never opened, the stack is empty and this dereference path yields a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the function dereferences an expected-valid pointer (the tag stack via current_element) without a NULL check, leading to a crash. This is not a generic parse error; the defect is the missing validity constraint on the pointer before use.

case STATE_INSIDE_CLOSE_TAG_NAME:
case STATE_AFTER_CLOSE_TAG_NAME:

_("Document ended unexpectedly inside the close tag for "
"element “%s”"), current_element (context));
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the STATE_AFTER_CLOSE_TAG_SLASH/INSIDE_CLOSE_TAG_NAME/AFTER_CLOSE_TAG_NAME branch unconditionally reads the current element from context->tag_stack. Trigger: an input that ends while inside a close tag with no matching opening element, leaving tag_stack NULL. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a crash (DoS) in g_markup_parse_context_end_parse().

commit_msg:
brcmfmac: fix possible buffer overflow in brcmf_cfg80211_mgmt_tx()

The lower level nl80211 code in cfg80211 ensures that "len" is between
25 and NL80211_ATTR_FRAME (2304).  We subtract DOT11_MGMT_HDR_LEN (24) from
"len" so thats's max of 2280.  However, the action_frame->data[] buffer is
only BRCMF_FIL_ACTION_FRAME_SIZE (1800) bytes long so this memcpy() can
overflow.

	memcpy(action_frame->data, &buf[DOT11_MGMT_HDR_LEN],
	       le16_to_cpu(action_frame->len));

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 3.9.x
Fixes: 18e2f61db3b70 ("brcmfmac: P2P action frame tx.")
Reported-by: "freenerguo(郭大兴)" <freenerguo@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Arend van Spriel <arend.vanspriel@broadcom.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

code_evidence: Line 50 stores len - DOT11_MGMT_HDR_LEN into the 16-bit action_frame->len without validating len against the destination capacity.
Lines 58-59 copy that many bytes from buf[DOT11_MGMT_HDR_LEN] into action_frame->data, the fixed-size BRCMF_FIL_ACTION_FRAME_SIZE buffer, with no upper-bound check.

commit_msg:
Fix packet length handling.

Treat the packet length as unsigned - it shouldn't be negative in the
file.  If it is, that'll probably cause the sscanf to fail, so we'll
report the file as bad.

Check it against WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE to make sure we don't try to
allocate a huge amount of memory, just as we do in other file readers.

Use the now-validated packet size as the length in
ws_buffer_assure_space(), so we are certain to have enough space, and
don't allocate too much space.

Merge the header and packet data parsing routines while we're at it.

Bug: 12396
Change-Id: I7f981f9cdcbea7ecdeb88bfff2f12d875de2244f
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/15176
Reviewed-by: Guy Harris <guy@alum.mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint\t\tpkt_len;', '\tchar\t\tcap_int[NETSCREEN_MAX_INT_NAME_LENGTH];', '\tgboolean\tcap_dir;', '\tchar\t\tcap_dst[13];', '\tpkt_len = parse_netscreen_rec_hdr(phdr, line, cap_int, &cap_dir,', '\t    cap_dst, err, err_info);', '\tif (pkt_len == -1)', '\t\treturn FALSE;', '', '\tif (!parse_netscreen_hex_dump(wth->random_fh, pkt_len, cap_int,', '\t    cap_dst, phdr, buf, err, err_info))', '\t\treturn FALSE;', '\treturn TRUE;'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn parse_netscreen_packet(wth->random_fh, phdr, buf, line,', '\t    err, err_info);']}
description: wiretap/netscreen.c in the NetScreen file parser in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 and 2.x before 2.0.4 mishandles sscanf unsigned-integer processing, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: parse_netscreen_rec_hdr returns a length into signed int pkt_len, derived from the file header via sscanf; no upper bound or unsigned validation is applied.
The only check is pkt_len == -1, so any other value (e.g. negative values other than -1, or very large lengths) passes through.
That unvalidated length is passed directly as the length argument to parse_netscreen_hex_dump, which uses it to size/consume buffer space.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts file-derived metadata (packet length) without validating that it is non-negative and within WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE before using it, which is improper input validation of a specified quantity. The signed/unsigned mishandling and missing size constraint are the validation failures; CWE-20 captures this root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
pkt_len = parse_netscreen_rec_hdr(phdr, line, cap_int, &cap_dir,
cap_dst, err, err_info);

if (pkt_len == -1)
return FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the packet length read from the attacker-controlled file is stored in a signed int and only compared to -1, so negative or oversized values are not rejected. Trigger: a crafted NetScreen capture file whose header length is negative or exceeds WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE. Consequence: the unchecked length drives buffer sizing/parsing, leading to allocation of a huge amount of memory or a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
ovl: fix permission checking for setattr

[Al Viro] The bug is in being too enthusiastic about optimizing ->setattr()
away - instead of "copy verbatim with metadata" + "chmod/chown/utimes"
(with the former being always safe and the latter failing in case of
insufficient permissions) it tries to combine these two.  Note that copyup
itself will have to do ->setattr() anyway; _that_ is where the elevated
capabilities are right.  Having these two ->setattr() (one to set verbatim
copy of metadata, another to do what overlayfs ->setattr() had been asked
to do in the first place) combined is where it breaks.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <miklos@szeredi.hu>

description: The ovl_setattr function in fs/overlayfs/inode.c in the Linux kernel through 4.3.3 attempts to merge distinct setattr operations, which allows local users to bypass intended access restrictions and modify the attributes of arbitrary overlay files via a crafted application.

code_evidence: The function branches on whether an upper dentry already exists. When one exists, it directly calls notify_change on the upper inode with the caller-supplied attr (lines 9-12). Only when no upper dentry exists does it route through ovl_copy_up_last(dentry, attr, false) (line 14). Thus the metadata-verbatim copyup and the requested setattr are merged in this single path rather than being performed as separate operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a permission/access-control failure: the function bypasses intended access restrictions when modifying file attributes. This matches CWE-264 (Permissions, Privileges, and Access Controls), which covers improper management of permissions and privileges during access-controlled operations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ovl_setattr applies the requested attribute change directly to the upper inode without first performing a permission-checked copyup. Trigger: a local user invokes setattr on an overlay file that has an upper dentry, supplying a crafted iattr. The combined operation lets the attribute modification proceed without the access restriction that the separated copyup/setattr sequence would enforce, so arbitrary overlay file attributes can be changed.

commit_msg:
[tflite] Ensure `MatchingDim` does not allow buffer overflow.

We check in `MatchingDim` that both arguments have the same dimensionality, however that is a `DCHECK` only enabled if building in debug mode. Hence, it could be possible to cause buffer overflows by passing in a tensor with larger dimensions as the second argument. To fix, we now make `MatchingDim` return the minimum of the two sizes.

A much better fix would be to return a status object but that requires refactoring a large part of the codebase for minor benefits.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 332526127
Change-Id: If627d0d2c80a685217b6e0d1e64b0872dbf1c5e4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return shape1.Dims(index1);'], 'added_lines': ['  return std::min(shape1.Dims(index1), shape2.Dims(index2));']}
description: In tensorflow-lite before versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1 and 2.3.1, when determining the common dimension size of two tensors, TFLite uses a `DCHECK` which is no-op outside of debug compilation modes. Since the function always returns the dimension of the first tensor, malicious attackers can craft cases where this is larger than that of the second tensor. In turn, this would result in reads/writes outside of bounds since the interpreter will wrongly assume that there is enough data in both tensors. The issue is patched in commit 8ee24e7949a203d234489f9da2c5bf45a7d5157d, and is released in TensorFlow versions 1.15.4, 2.0.3, 2.1.2, 2.2.1, or 2.3.1.

code_evidence: Line 3 relies on TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ to require that shape1.Dims(index1) and shape2.Dims(index2) are equal, but this check compiles to a no-op in non-debug builds. Line 4 then unconditionally returns shape1.Dims(index1), so the returned dimension is not constrained by shape2's actual size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked, mismatched dimension propagates into buffer accesses that write beyond the intended allocation. The missing release-mode constraint on the returned size is the direct cause; the memory corruption is the consequence, distinguishing it from a pure out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code:
TFLITE_DCHECK_EQ(shape1.Dims(index1), shape2.Dims(index2));
return shape1.Dims(index1);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the only equality constraint between the two tensor dimensions is a debug-only DCHECK, and the function returns the first shape's dimension regardless. Trigger: a caller supplies a second tensor whose dimension at index2 is smaller than shape1's. The interpreter, trusting the returned value, assumes both tensors hold enough elements and performs reads/writes past the smaller tensor's bounds, yielding an out-of-bounds write (and read).

avformat/rtmppkt: Convert ff_amf_get_field_value() to bytestream2

Fixes: out of array accesses

Found-by: JunDong Xie of Ant-financial Light-Year Security Lab
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int namelen = strlen(name);', '    int len;', '    while (*data != AMF_DATA_TYPE_OBJECT && data < data_end) {', '        len = ff_amf_tag_size(data, data_end);', '        if (len < 0)', '            len = data_end - data;', '        data += len;', '    }', '    if (data_end - data < 3)', '    data++;', '    for (;;) {', '        int size = bytestream_get_be16(&data);', '        if (!size)', '            break;', '        if (size < 0 || size >= data_end - data)', '            return -1;', '        data += size;', '        if (size == namelen && !memcmp(data-size, name, namelen)) {', '            switch (*data++) {', '            case AMF_DATA_TYPE_NUMBER:', '                snprintf(dst, dst_size, "%g", av_int2double(AV_RB64(data)));', '                break;', '            case AMF_DATA_TYPE_BOOL:', '                snprintf(dst, dst_size, "%s", *data ? "true" : "false");', '                break;', '            case AMF_DATA_TYPE_STRING:', '                len = bytestream_get_be16(&data);', '                av_strlcpy(dst, data, FFMIN(len+1, dst_size));', '                break;', '            default:', '                return -1;', '            }', '            return 0;', '        }', '        len = ff_amf_tag_size(data, data_end);', '        if (len < 0 || len >= data_end - data)', '            return -1;', '        data += len;', '    }', '    return -1;'], 'added_lines': ['    GetByteContext gb;', '    if (data >= data_end)', '', '    bytestream2_init(&gb, data, data_end - data);', '', '    return amf_get_field_value2(&gb, name, dst, dst_size);']}
description: The ff_amf_get_field_value function in libavformat/rtmppkt.c in FFmpeg 3.3.2 allows remote RTMP servers to cause a denial of service (Segmentation Violation and application crash) via a crafted stream.

code_evidence: The initial scan advances data by ff_amf_tag_size() but when len<0 it sets len=data_end-data, so data can land exactly on data_end; the loop condition dereferences *data before checking data<data_end, allowing a read past the buffer.

The for(;;) loop reads a 16-bit size via bytestream_get_be16(&data) with no check that two bytes remain, and the size check `size >= data_end - data` is off-by-one relative to the following data += size.
After matching a field name, the switch reads the type byte via *data++ and for NUMBER calls AV_RB64(data), reading 8 bytes without verifying data_end - data >= 8.
For STRING, len is read via bytestream_get_be16 and av_strlcpy(dst, data, FFMIN(len+1, dst_size)) copies from data without confirming that len bytes remain before data_end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate derived length/offset properties of untrusted input before using them, matching CWE-20's improper validation of size and position metadata. The consequence is out-of-bounds access; CWE-20 fits as the missing-validation root cause, whereas the memory read itself would be a lower-level consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser consumes attacker-controlled AMF tag sizes and length prefixes from a remote RTMP stream without validating that the remaining buffer is large enough before dereferencing or reading. Trigger: a crafted stream with truncated tags, mismatched size fields, or a NUMBER/STRING field near data_end. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads causing segmentation fault and application crash (DoS), as fixed by converting to bounded bytestream2 accessors.

commit_msg: http2.c: fix incorrect trailer buffer size
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* 3 is for ":" and "\\r\\n". */', '    uint32_t n = (uint32_t)(namelen + valuelen + 3);'], 'added_lines': ['    /* 4 is for ": " and "\\r\\n". */', '    uint32_t n = (uint32_t)(namelen + valuelen + 4);']}
description: libcurl 7.49.0 to and including 7.57.0 contains an out bounds read in code handling HTTP/2 trailers. It was reported (https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/2231) that reading an HTTP/2 trailer could mess up future trailers since the stored size was one byte less than required. The problem is that the code that creates HTTP/1-like headers from the HTTP/2 trailer data once appended a string like `:` to the target buffer, while this was recently changed to `: ` (a space was added after the colon) but the following math wasn't updated correspondingly. When accessed, the data is read out of bounds and causes either a crash or that the (too large) data gets passed to client write. This could lead to a denial-of-service situation or an information disclosure if someone has a service that echoes back or uses the trailers for something.

code_evidence: Line 47 computes the stored trailer record size as namelen + valuelen + 3, but the actual serialized record written at lines 51-54 includes name, a two-byte ": " separator, value, and a three-byte "\r\n\0" terminator, totaling namelen + valuelen + 5. The size prefix written at line 50 is therefore two bytes short of the bytes actually appended, and the ": " literal at line 52 is the two-byte separator the math fails to account for.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the defect is an incorrect size that causes data to be read beyond the intended trailer buffer. It is not a write overflow (CWE-787): the append operations themselves fit their buffers; the error is in the length metadata used on later reads.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stored length prefix underestimates the serialized trailer record because the separator/terminator accounting was not updated to match the ": " plus "\r\n\0" writes. Trigger: receiving an HTTP/2 trailer after bodystarted. Consequence: consumers trusting the stored size can read past the trailer buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read, crash/DoS, or disclosure of adjacent memory passed to the client write.

commit_msg:
Add missing validations in dillation ops.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 372037158
Change-Id: I4ee304c84a02550c030288a6534000b934fc1599
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!context->status().ok()) return;']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. An attacker can write outside the bounds of heap allocated arrays by passing invalid arguments to `tf.raw_ops.Dilation2DBackpropInput`. This is because the implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/afd954e65f15aea4d438d0a219136fc4a63a573d/tensorflow/core/kernels/dilation_ops.cc#L321-L322) does not validate before writing to the output array. The values for `h_out` and `w_out` are guaranteed to be in range for `out_backprop` (as they are loop indices bounded by the size of the array). However, there are no similar guarantees relating `h_in_max`/`w_in_max` and `in_backprop`. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: ParseSizes populates out_rows/out_cols and other size variables, and the function proceeds immediately to use them without first checking context->status(); the patch adds that status check right after this call.
The OP_REQUIRES validates only the out_backprop dimensions against batch/out_rows/out_cols/depth; it does not constrain the input dimensions used to derive the write region.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a write past the end of an allocated output buffer (filter_backprop), which matches CWE-787. The missing status/bounds validation is the enabling cause, not a separate weakness; the supported consequence is the out-of-bounds heap write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ParseSizes can fail or produce sizes that are not validated before being used, and no check ensures the derived input-side bounds fit the allocated filter_backprop buffer. Trigger: invalid arguments to the op make h_in_max/w_in_max fall outside filter_backprop. Consequence: the functor writes past the heap buffer, corrupting memory or crashing.

netfilter: x_tables: make sure e->next_offset covers remaining blob size

Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>

description: The IPT_SO_SET_REPLACE setsockopt implementation in the netfilter subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly obtain sensitive information from kernel heap memory by leveraging in-container root access to provide a crafted offset value that leads to crossing a ruleset blob boundary.

Consequence: the match/target iteration reads beyond the blob, causing out-of-bounds kernel heap read (DoS or info leak).

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

description: The IP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-ip.c:ip_printts().

code_evidence: Line 30 checks only option_len bytes at cp before dispatch, but the IPOPT_TS branch calls ip_printts at line 35 and discards its return value, so any out-of-bounds read detected inside ip_printts is not propagated to the trunc label.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits: the function permits reading memory beyond the intended option buffer when parsing a crafted timestamp option. The missing propagation of the failure return is the enabling condition; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read, not a write or injection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The caller bounds-checks the option block with ND_TCHECK2 but does not verify that timestamp-option parsing stays within that block; ip_printts may read past the option data. Because its -1 return is ignored, the over-read proceeds rather than jumping to trunc, enabling a buffer over-read on malformed IP timestamp options.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.8. There is a NULL pointer dereference caused by a malicious USB device in the sound/usb/helper.c (motu_microbookii) driver.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes usb_pipe_endpoint always returns a valid endpoint and dereferences it unconditionally. Trigger: a malicious USB device supplies a pipe whose endpoint lookup fails, making ep NULL; the dereference then faults, causing a kernel crash/DoS. The consequence is a NULL pointer dereference, not a type confusion.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (len_nm + len_cl >= USHRT_MAX)', '            return 1;']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Lines 10-11 compute attacker-influenced name/class lengths with safestrlen and line 12 allocates len_nm+len_cl+2 bytes without any upper bound; the pre-patch code lacks the length check. Lines 14 and 20 strcpy the res_name/res_class strings into that buffer, then lines 23-25 send len_nm+len_cl+2 as the property length via XChangeProperty.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies attacker-controlled strings into a buffer sized from unchecked lengths, matching CWE-120's unchecked buffer copy; the consequence here is protocol length truncation and request injection. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, and the missing upper-bound check distinguishes it from a size-calculation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sum of the two string lengths is passed to Xmalloc and later to XChangeProperty without ensuring it fits the protocol's CARD16 length field. Trigger: a client supplies color/class-hint strings whose combined length exceeds USHRT_MAX. The oversized length is truncated when encoded in the X protocol, so data beyond the declared size is interpreted by the server as additional requests, enabling unauthorized commands rather than a direct heap overflow.

commit_msg:
[NBAP] Prevent crash.

If no previous conversation exists, a memcpy will try to copy from NULL destination.

Bug: 11835
Change-Id: I445480bb425834c5a918f1ffa148cb83d6c9750c
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/12326
Reviewed-by: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Petri-Dish: Michael Mann <mmann78@netscape.net>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot <buildbot-no-reply@wireshark.org>
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#line 1845 "../../asn1/nbap/nbap.cnf"'], 'added_lines': ['#line 1846 "../../asn1/nbap/nbap.cnf"']}
description: epan/dissectors/packet-nbap.c in the NBAP dissector in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.9 and 2.0.x before 2.0.1 does not validate conversation data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: Lines 10-13 return early when the packet was already visited or when transportLayerAddress_ipv4 or BindingID_port is zero, so a conversation entry is only created after both dissected fields are non-zero.

Lines 14-15 nonetheless derive a destination address from transportLayerAddress_ipv4 and copy it into nbap_hsdsch_channel_info[hsdsch_macdflow_id].crnc_address without validating hsdsch_macdflow_id or confirming the conversation slot was previously initialized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The dissector accepts packet-derived identifiers and address data and proceeds to use them without validating the required conversation state, which matches CWE-20's improper input validation leading to a crash. This is not merely a null check on a parsed field; the missing constraint is on the conversation/index data used for the copy.

evidence_lines.code:
set_address(&dst_addr, AT_IPv4, 4, &transportLayerAddress_ipv4);
copy_address(&(nbap_hsdsch_channel_info[hsdsch_macdflow_id].crnc_address),&dst_addr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function creates and copies conversation data using the dissector-provided hsdsch_macdflow_id and address fields, but does not validate that the indexed conversation entry exists or was initialized. When a crafted packet causes the copy path to run with an uninitialized/NULL destination, the memcpy in copy_address dereferences invalid memory, crashing the application. The root cause is missing validation of conversation/index state; the consequence is a NULL-pointer dereference DoS.

commit_msg: issue #30 issue #31 issue #32: no multiple format chunks in WAV or W64
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    int format_chunk = 0;', '', '            if (format_chunk++) {', '                error_line ("%s is not a valid .W64 file!", infilename);', '                return WAVPACK_SOFT_ERROR;', '            }']}
description: An issue was discovered in WavPack 5.1.0 and earlier. The WAV parser component contains a vulnerability that allows writing to memory because ParseRiffHeaderConfig in riff.c does not reject multiple format chunks.

code_evidence: The fmt chunk handler at [41-46] reads a chunk whose size is only checked to be between 16 and sizeof(WaveHeader), so a second fmt chunk overwrites the same WaveHeader and config state established by the first.

The data chunk handler at [124-152] computes total_samples and config->bytes_per_sample from WaveHeader.BlockAlign/NumChannels; these values derive from whichever fmt chunk was processed last, while earlier state may already have been committed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing rejection of multiple format chunks permits inconsistent parsed metadata that leads to writing past the intended buffer during later processing. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely an input-validation or parsing-state issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Without a single-format-chunk constraint, a crafted W64 file can supply multiple fmt chunks. Later parsing uses WaveHeader-derived values (BlockAlign, NumChannels, bytes_per_sample) that may be inconsistent with previously stored configuration, allowing subsequent sample handling to write beyond the intended buffer. The added format_chunk counter rejects the second fmt chunk, confirming the missing constraint is the root cause.

commit_msg:
Regardless of whether the flex_bg feature is set, we should always
check to make sure the bits we are setting in the block bitmap are
within the block group bounds.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=199865

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint flex_bg = 0;', '\tif (ext4_has_feature_flex_bg(sb))', '\t\tflex_bg = 1;', '', '\tif (!flex_bg || ext4_block_in_group(sb, tmp, block_group))', '\tif (!flex_bg || ext4_block_in_group(sb, tmp, block_group))', '\t\tif (!flex_bg || ext4_block_in_group(sb, tmp, block_group))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ext4_block_in_group(sb, tmp, block_group))', '\tif (ext4_block_in_group(sb, tmp, block_group))', '\t\tif (ext4_block_in_group(sb, tmp, block_group))']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bounds write and a denial of service or unspecified other impact is possible by mounting and operating a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: flex_bg is set solely from the on-disk feature flag via ext4_has_feature_flex_bg(sb), so a crafted image can make flex_bg=1 regardless of actual layout.
For the block bitmap, when flex_bg is set the ext4_block_in_group() bounds check is skipped (short-circuit !flex_bg), so ext4_set_bit(EXT4_B2C(sbi, tmp - start)) runs unconditionally.
Same pattern for the inode bitmap: the in-group check is bypassed and the computed bit index is written into bh->b_data.
The inode table loop likewise skips ext4_block_in_group() when flex_bg is set, writing EXT4_B2C(sbi, tmp - start) for each table block without confirming it lies within this block group.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function computes a bit offset from attacker-influenced on-disk block numbers and writes it into a fixed-size bitmap buffer without a group-bounds check, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The missing constraint is the in-group validation, not a mere integer overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
if (ext4_has_feature_flex_bg(sb))
flex_bg = 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the !flex_bg short-circuit makes ext4_block_in_group() the only bounds check, and it is skipped whenever the flex_bg feature bit is set. A crafted ext4 image sets flex_bg and supplies out-of-group bitmap/inode-table block numbers, so tmp - start yields an index beyond the group's bitmap buffer. ext4_set_bit writes past bh->b_data, corrupting memory and enabling DoS or other impact.

commit_msg:
Security: more cmsgpack fixes by @soloestoy.

@soloestoy sent me this additional fixes, after searching for similar
problems to the one reported in mp_pack(). I'm committing the changes
because it was not possible during to make a public PR to protect Redis
users and give Redis providers some time to patch their systems.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    luaL_checkstack(L, 1, "in function mp_encode_lua_table_as_array");']}
description: Memory Corruption was discovered in the cmsgpack library in the Lua subsystem in Redis before 3.2.12, 4.x before 4.0.10, and 5.x before 5.0 RC2 because of stack-based buffer overflows.

code_evidence: mp_encode_lua_table_as_array encodes each array element by pushing index j and calling lua_gettable, then recurses via mp_encode_lua_type for every element. The loop at lines 8-11 performs repeated Lua stack pushes without any luaL_checkstack guard before the loop; the patch adds that guard at line 7.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing stack-capacity check lets stack pushes and recursive encoding write past the end of the Lua stack buffer, corrupting memory. This is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely an unchecked return value; the missing luaL_checkstack allows the write to occur.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive encoding loop pushes Lua stack values (index and fetched element) on each iteration without verifying remaining stack capacity. Trigger: a deeply nested or large Lua table causes recursion and repeated pushes to exhaust the Lua stack, writing beyond the allocated stack buffer. Supported consequence: stack-based buffer overflow leading to memory corruption, as described in the cmsgpack advisory.

commit_msg:
Remove `CHECK`-fails from `IsSimplifiableReshape`

PiperOrigin-RevId: 409164987
Change-Id: I58c7dd459ff348c3dbae95e00c4c5e63b30a4e65
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  CHECK_LE(2, node.input_size());', '  CHECK_EQ(1, outputs.size());'], 'added_lines': ['  if (2 > node.input_size()) {', '    return errors::Internal("Node ", node.name(),', '                            " must have at most 2 inputs but has ",', '                            node.input_size());', '  }', '  if (outputs.size() != 1) {', '    return errors::Internal("Node ", node.name(),', '                            " must have exactly 1 output but has ",', '                            outputs.size());', '  }']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The Grappler optimizer in TensorFlow can be used to cause a denial of service by altering a `SavedModel` such that `IsSimplifiableReshape` would trigger `CHECK` failures. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: IsSimplifiableReshape receives an attacker-controlled NodeDef from a SavedModel graph. After confirming the node is a Reshape, line 460 uses CHECK_LE(2, node.input_size()) to enforce the input count, and line 461 unconditionally reads node.input(1). A crafted Reshape node with fewer than two inputs reaches the CHECK and aborts the process.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because the reachable CHECK_LE terminates the application on attacker-influenced input instead of returning an errors::Internal status like the surrounding checks. This is not a mere input-validation gap; the specific consequence is an assertion-triggered abort.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a hard CHECK assertion guards a shape assumption about untrusted graph input rather than returning an error status. Trigger: a malformed Reshape node with fewer than two inputs supplied via a SavedModel during Grappler optimization. Consequence: the CHECK fails and terminates the process, a denial of service.

commit_msg:
[lite] Check for overflow when creating required bytes.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 417629001
Change-Id: Ia7feb3ea8e988f4fd4b3c98c1a1fed4557d99fd7
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int embedding_size = 1;', '  int lookup_size = 1;', '    const int dim = dense_shape->data.i32[i];', '    lookup_size *= dim;', '    const int dim = SizeOfDimension(value, i);', '    embedding_size *= dim;', '  const int output_size = lookup_size * embedding_size;'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t embedding_size = 1;', '  size_t lookup_size = 1;', '    const size_t dim = dense_shape->data.i32[i];', '    TF_LITE_ENSURE_MSG(', '        context,', '        MultiplyAndCheckOverflow(lookup_size, dim, &lookup_size) == kTfLiteOk,', '        "Lookup size overflowed.");', '    const size_t dim = SizeOfDimension(value, i);', '    TF_LITE_ENSURE_MSG(context,', '                       MultiplyAndCheckOverflow(embedding_size, dim,', '                                                &embedding_size) == kTfLiteOk,', '                       "Embedding size overflowed.");', '  const size_t output_size = lookup_size * embedding_size;', '  // Makes sure reallocation was successful.', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, output_ptr != nullptr);']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. An attacker can craft a TFLite model that would cause an integer overflow in embedding lookup operations. Both `embedding_size` and `lookup_size` are products of values provided by the user. Hence, a malicious user could trigger overflows in the multiplication. In certain scenarios, this can then result in heap OOB read/write. Users are advised to upgrade to a patched version.

code_evidence: lookup_size is a 32-bit int multiplied by dim, which comes from dense_shape->data.i32[i], so multiple user-controlled dimensions can wrap lookup_size to a small or negative value.
embedding_size is likewise an int multiplied by each value dimension via SizeOfDimension(value, i), allowing wraparound when the product exceeds INT_MAX.
output_size is computed as lookup_size * embedding_size and passed as output_size * sizeof(float) to TfLiteTensorRealloc, so a wrapped small/negative size under-allocates the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs size calculations (multiplications) on user-controlled dimensions that can wrap, exactly the integer overflow/wraparound of CWE-190; the overflowed size then feeds a memory allocation, making it security critical. This is a size-computation overflow rather than a mere out-of-bounds index check.

evidence_lines.code:
const int output_size = lookup_size * embedding_size;
TfLiteTensorRealloc(output_size * sizeof(float), output);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size products lookup_size and embedding_size use signed 32-bit int without overflow checks, and output_size is their unchecked product. Trigger: a crafted TFLite model supplies dense_shape and value dimensions whose products exceed INT_MAX. Consequence: the wrapped output_size leads to an undersized allocation, after which the later fill and offset writes exceed the buffer, causing heap OOB write.

commit_msg:
The functions that were used in the emulation of fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt and
sidt were originally meant for task switching, and as such they did not
check privilege levels.  This is very bad when the same functions are used
in the emulation of unprivileged instructions.  This is CVE-2018-10853.

The obvious fix is to add a new argument to ops->read_std and ops->write_std,
which decides whether the access is a "system" access or should use the
processor's CPL.

Fixes: 129a72a0d3c8 ("KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std", 2017-01-12)
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t      unsigned int bytes, struct x86_exception *exception)', '\t\t\t\t\t   PFERR_WRITE_MASK, exception);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t      unsigned int bytes, struct x86_exception *exception,', '\t\t\t      bool system)', '\tu32 access = PFERR_WRITE_MASK;', '', '\tif (!system && kvm_x86_ops->get_cpl(vcpu) == 3)', '\t\taccess |= PFERR_USER_MASK;', '\t\t\t\t\t   access, exception);']}
description: A flaw was found in the way Linux kernel KVM hypervisor before 4.18 emulated instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor. It did not check current privilege(CPL) level while emulating unprivileged instructions. An unprivileged guest user/process could use this flaw to potentially escalate privileges inside guest.

code_evidence: emulator_write_std derives the vcpu but forwards a fixed PFERR_WRITE_MASK to kvm_write_guest_virt_helper without consulting the current privilege level (CPL); no system/CPL argument or check exists before the virtual write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to check or encode the actor's privilege level when performing the emulated write, so privilege assignment is not enforced for an unprivileged actor. That is improper privilege management (CWE-269); the resulting guest privilege escalation is the impact, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the emulated standard write always uses the same access flags and never distinguishes a system access from a user-mode (CPL 3) access. Trigger: an unprivileged guest in ring 3 executes an instruction whose emulation reaches this write path. Consequence: the write is performed with system-level semantics, bypassing privilege checks and allowing an unprivileged guest user to act outside its intended sphere of control.

commit_msg:
Add bounds checks in btif_avrcp_audio_track.cc

Fuzz testing reveals that the transcodeQ*ToFloat family of functions are
not bounds checked, causing a potential OOB write.

Check these functions against bounds of the destination array.

Bug: 275895309
Test: atest bluetooth_test_gd_unit, net_test_stack_btm
Tag: #security
Ignore-AOSP-First: Security
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:46803ae95d63ee133eae83d885e7c051964dc8ed)
Merged-In: I7a13261429797769cf5b913912a30e249668ac93
Change-Id: I7a13261429797769cf5b913912a30e249668ac93
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  for (; i <= length / sampleSize; i++) {'], 'added_lines': ['  for (; i < std::min(trackHolder->bufferLength, length / sampleSize); i++) {']}
description: In transcodeQ*ToFloat of btif_avrcp_audio_track.cc, there is a possible out of bounds write due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to paired device escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: Line 5 loops while i <= length / sampleSize, and line 6 writes trackHolder->buffer[i] without comparing i against trackHolder->bufferLength. The buffer length is never consulted, so the destination array bounds are not enforced before the indexed store.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code writes through an index into a fixed destination array without a bounds check, directly matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). The missing constraint on the destination capacity, not merely an off-by-one read, is the cause of the memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound derives only from the input length/sample size and omits the destination buffer capacity, allowing i to reach and exceed bufferLength. Trigger: a length large enough that length/sampleSize is at or beyond the buffer size. Consequence: an out-of-bounds write past trackHolder->buffer, corrupting adjacent memory.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix integer overflows

There were various issues related to the limited size of integers used in
the verifier:
 - `off + size` overflow in __check_map_access()
 - `off + reg->off` overflow in check_mem_access()
 - `off + reg->var_off.value` overflow or 32-bit truncation of
   `reg->var_off.value` in check_mem_access()
 - 32-bit truncation in check_stack_boundary()

Make sure that any integer math cannot overflow by not allowing
pointer math with large values.

Also reduce the scope of "scalar op scalar" tracking.

Fixes: f1174f77b50c ("bpf/verifier: rework value tracking")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (!src_known &&', '\t    opcode != BPF_ADD && opcode != BPF_SUB && opcode != BPF_AND) {', '\t\t__mark_reg_unknown(dst_reg);', '\t\treturn 0;', '\t}']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (integer overflow and memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging unrestricted integer values for pointer arithmetic.

code_evidence: src_known/dst_known are derived from tnum_is_const, and the switch dispatches into per-opcode arithmetic without a guard that rejects unknown-source operands for non-ADD/SUB/AND opcodes; the patch inserts that guard before the switch.

In BPF_MUL, when both operands are <= U32_MAX the code computes umin_value *= umin_val and umax_value *= umax_val in u64 with no overflow check, then compares the product to S64_MAX; a product wrapping in u64 yields a small umax_value and bogus bounds.

In BPF_LSH, umax_val is checked against insn_bitness, but the shift amounts umin_val/umax_val are then applied to umin_value/umax_value with only a umax_value > 1ULL << (63 - umax_val) guard; the shift can overflow/wrap the u64 bounds, and the tnum is set from tnum_unknown when src is not const.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operations are integer multiplications and shifts whose results can exceed the u64 representation and wrap, producing values smaller than the operands; the code assumes the product/shift is larger and derives bounds from it. The consequence is unsound pointer-arithmetic bounds feeding memory checks, not merely a logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier's scalar min/max tracking performs u64 multiplications and shifts on attacker-influenced register bounds without fully preventing wraparound, and permits unknown-source operands in operations where bounds then become unsound. Trigger: a BPF program whose scalar registers carry large or non-constant values reaching BPF_MUL or BPF_LSH. Consequence: wrapped/incorrect bounds propagate into later memory-access checks, enabling out-of-bounds access (memory corruption) or verifier misbehavior.

commit_msg:
Fix memory leak in xmlParseBalancedChunkMemoryRecover

When doc is NULL, namespace created in xmlTreeEnsureXMLDecl
is bind to newDoc->oldNs, in this case, set newDoc->oldNs to
NULL and free newDoc will cause a memory leak.

Found with libFuzzer.

Closes #82.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    newDoc->oldNs = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['    if(doc != NULL)', '\tnewDoc->oldNs = NULL;']}
description: xmlParseBalancedChunkMemoryRecover in parser.c in libxml2 before 2.9.10 has a memory leak related to newDoc->oldNs.

code_evidence: When doc == NULL, the else branch at line 61 sets ctxt->myDoc = newDoc but never assigns newDoc->oldNs; namespace created later in xmlTreeEnsureXMLDecl gets bound to newDoc->oldNs.
At cleanup, line 116 unconditionally clears newDoc->oldNs before xmlFreeDoc(newDoc) at line 117, detaching the namespace list so xmlFreeDoc cannot free it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because a pointer to allocated namespace structures is discarded without being freed, leaving memory allocated after its effective lifetime. This is not a use-after-free: no later dereference occurs; the defect is the missing release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: newDoc->oldNs is populated during parsing when doc is NULL, but the cleanup path unconditionally nulls the pointer before xmlFreeDoc. Trigger: calling xmlParseBalancedChunkMemoryRecover with doc == NULL on input that creates a namespace declaration. Supported consequence: the namespace list becomes unreachable and is never released, leaking memory.

commit_msg: check divide by zero, fixing #86

description: The allocate_channel_framebuffer function in uncompressed_components.hh in Dropbox Lepton 1.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and application crash) via a malformed JPEG image.

code_evidence: total_req_blocks is initialized to 0 and only incremented in the loop over components bounded by header_.size() and cmpc_ [4,5,6,7]. The second loop then computes max_cmp_bc /= total_req_blocks [13] without any check that total_req_blocks is nonzero. If header_ is empty or cmpc_ is 0, the loop body never executes, total_req_blocks stays 0, and the division at line 13 divides by zero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-369 directly matches: a value is divided by a variable that can be zero because the missing nonzero check on total_req_blocks is not enforced before the division. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds or null-pointer issue; the crash stems specifically from the zero divisor.

Trigger: a malformed JPEG where cmpc_ is 0 or no components satisfy the loop bound, making the divisor zero. Consequence: an integer divide-by-zero raises a hardware exception and crashes the process, giving denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fixes CVE-2023-3138: X servers could return values from XQueryExtension
that would cause Xlib to write entries out-of-bounds of the arrays to
store them, though this would only overwrite other parts of the Display
struct, not outside the bounds allocated for that structure.

Reported-by: Gregory James DUCK <gjduck@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Alan Coopersmith <alan.coopersmith@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (event_number < 0 ||', '\t    event_number > LastExtensionEvent) {', '\t    fprintf(stderr, "Xlib: ignoring invalid extension event %d\\n",', '\t\t    event_number);', '\t    return (EventToWireType)_XUnknownNativeEvent;', '\t}']}
description: A vulnerability was found in libX11. The security flaw occurs because the functions in src/InitExt.c in libX11 do not check that the values provided for the Request, Event, or Error IDs are within the bounds of the arrays that those functions write to, using those IDs as array indexes. They trust that they were called with values provided by an Xserver adhering to the bounds specified in the X11 protocol, as all X servers provided by X.Org do. As the protocol only specifies a single byte for these values, an out-of-bounds value provided by a malicious server (or a malicious proxy-in-the-middle) can only overwrite other portions of the Display structure and not write outside the bounds of the Display structure itself, possibly causing the client to crash with this memory corruption.

code_evidence: event_number is used directly as an index into dpy->wire_vec for both reading (line 9) and writing (line 10) without any bounds check against the array size; the caller-supplied value is trusted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked array index produces a write past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787. It is an out-of-bounds write rather than an out-of-bounds read because line 10 stores proc into the array; the missing range check is the direct cause.

evidence_lines.code:
oldproc = dpy->wire_vec[event_number];
dpy->wire_vec[event_number] = proc;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no validation that event_number lies within wire_vec bounds before indexing. Trigger: a malicious X server or proxy supplies an out-of-range extension event number. Consequence: the write at line 10 lands outside wire_vec, corrupting adjacent Display struct memory and potentially crashing the client.

commit_msg:
There's a goto missing in nvmet_setup_auth(), causing a kernel oops
when nvme_auth_extract_key() fails.

Reported-by: Tal Lossos <tallossos@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Hannes Reinecke <hare@suse.de>
Reviewed-by: Sagi Grimberg <sagi@grimberg.me>

Signed-off-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>

description: A NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in the Linux kernel NVMe functionality, in nvmet_setup_auth(), allows an attacker to perform a Pre-Auth Denial of Service (DoS) attack on a remote machine. Affected versions v6.0-rc1 to v6.0-rc3, fixed in v6.0-rc4.

code_evidence: nvme_auth_extract_key() may return an ERR_PTR; on failure ctrl->ctrl_key is reset to NULL at line 64.
Execution then falls through to the pr_debug at lines 66-69, which unconditionally dereferences ctrl->ctrl_key (->hash, ->len, ->key) even though it is NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences ctrl->ctrl_key after explicitly setting it to NULL on the error path, matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). This is not an uninitialized-pointer issue; the pointer is knowingly NULL and used without a validity check.

ctrl->ctrl_key->hash > 0 ?
nvme_auth_hmac_name(ctrl->ctrl_key->hash) : "none",
(int)ctrl->ctrl_key->len, ctrl->ctrl_key->key);

Trigger: a host with a dhchap_ctrl_secret whose key extraction fails. Consequence: NULL dereference of ctrl->ctrl_key, causing a kernel oops/DoS.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization is vulnerable to an exponential blowup issue where a crafted GVariant can cause excessive processing, leading to denial of service.

code_evidence: gvs_variable_sized_array_get_child derives child bounds from framing offsets via gvs_offsets_get_offset_n for index_-1 and index_ without verifying the offsets are ordered or non-overlapping (lines 15,21). The only guard start < end && end <= value.size && end <= offsets.data_size (line 22) accepts an end offset smaller than start, producing an empty child, and does not detect overlapping elements when offsets are out of order. Untrusted serialized data therefore controls start/end and the resulting child size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reconstructs elements from attacker-supplied serialized bytes and the missing ordering constraint means invalid deserialized data is accepted, matching CWE-502's untrusted-data deserialization without validation. A plain bounds/out-of-bounds CWE does not fit because the flaw is absent structural validation of deserialized offsets, not a direct memory access error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: deserialization of untrusted GVariant framing offsets without enforcing monotonic, non-overlapping boundaries, so child elements can overlap. Trigger: a crafted serialized variable-sized array whose offsets are out of order. Supported consequence: inconsistent/overlapping child views that let a GVariant normalize to a much larger type, enabling resource-consumption denial of service.

commit_msg: Fix improper cast that could cause an overflow as demonstrated in #347.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            length=(MagickSizeType) ReadBlobByte(image);'], 'added_lines': ['            length=(MagickSizeType) (unsigned char) ReadBlobByte(image);']}
description: coders/psd.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact by leveraging an improper cast, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: ReadBlobByte returns a signed int; assigning it to the unsigned MagickSizeType length sign-extends negative byte values (0xFF becomes a huge value). The check 'length > 0' then passes and ReadBlob writes length bytes into the fixed layer_info[i].name buffer, and name[length] is written past its bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to layer_info[i].name and its index using an attacker-influenced length without bounding it to the buffer size, so operations occur outside the intended memory buffer, directly matching CWE-119. The improper cast is the mechanism producing the out-of-bounds length, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing unsigned-char cast on the byte read into length, so a crafted PSD layer-name length byte of 0xFF produces a large length. Triggering that byte causes ReadBlob to copy far more than the name buffer holds and the trailing name[length]='\0' write to fall outside the buffer, yielding a heap-based buffer overflow.

Fixed CVE-2018-8789

Thanks to Eyal Itkin from Check Point Software Technologies.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int ntlm_read_message_fields_buffer(wStream* s, NTLM_MESSAGE_FIELDS* fields)', '\t\tif ((fields->BufferOffset + fields->Len) > Stream_Length(s))'], 'added_lines': ['static int ntlm_read_message_fields_buffer(wStream* s, NTLM_MESSAGE_FIELDS* fields)', '\t\tconst UINT64 offset = (UINT64)fields->BufferOffset + (UINT64)fields->Len;', '', '\t\tif (offset > Stream_Length(s))']}
description: FreeRDP prior to version 2.0.0-rc4 contains several Out-Of-Bounds Reads in the NTLM Authentication module that results in a Denial of Service (segfault).

code_evidence: The bounds check computes fields->BufferOffset + fields->Len in the width of the operand types; if both are 32-bit, the sum can wrap and pass the comparison against Stream_Length(s).
After the check, Stream_SetPosition uses fields->BufferOffset and Stream_Read reads fields->Len bytes into the allocated buffer, so a wrapped offset is trusted for the read.

Stream_Read(s, fields->Buffer, fields->Len);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the offset/length sum can integer-overflow before being compared to the stream length, so an attacker-controlled NTLM message field with a large BufferOffset can bypass the bounds check. Trigger: a crafted message where BufferOffset + Len wraps below Stream_Length(s). The subsequent Stream_Read then reads outside the stream buffer, giving an out-of-bounds read that can crash (DoS).
