commit_msg:
Avoid crash on crash report when a bad function pointer was called (#11298)

If Redis crashes due to calling an invalid function pointer,
the `backtrace` function will try to dereference this invalid pointer
which will cause a crash inside the crash report and will kill
the processes without having all the crash report information.

Example:

```
=== REDIS BUG REPORT START: Cut & paste starting from here ===
198672:M 19 Sep 2022 18:06:12.936 # Redis 255.255.255 crashed by signal: 11, si_code: 1
198672:M 19 Sep 2022 18:06:12.936 # Accessing address: 0x1
198672:M 19 Sep 2022 18:06:12.936 # Crashed running the instruction at: 0x1
// here the processes is crashing
```

This PR tries to fix this crash be:
1. Identify the issue when it happened.
2. Replace the invalid pointer with a pointer to some dummy function
   so that `backtrace` will not crash.

I identification is done by comparing `eip` to `info->si_addr`, if they
are the same we know that the crash happened on the same address it tries to
accesses and we can conclude that it tries to call and invalid function pointer.

To replace the invalid pointer we introduce a new function, `setMcontextEip`,
which is very similar to `getMcontextEip` and it knows to set the Eip for the
different supported OS's. After printing the trace we retrieve the old `Eip` value.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    void *eip = getMcontextEip(uc);', '    logStackTrace(getMcontextEip(uc), 1);'], 'added_lines': ['    void *eip = getAndSetMcontextEip(uc, NULL);', '    if (eip == info->si_addr) {', "        /* When eip matches the bad address, it's an indication that we crashed when calling a non-mapped", '         * function pointer. In that case the call to backtrace will crash trying to access that address and we', "         * won't get a crash report logged. Set it to a valid point to avoid that crash. */", '', '        /* This trick allow to avoid compiler warning */', '        void *ptr;', '        invalidFunctionWasCalledType *ptr_ptr = (invalidFunctionWasCalledType*)&ptr;', '        *ptr_ptr = invalidFunctionWasCalled;', '        getAndSetMcontextEip(uc, ptr);', '    }', '', '    logStackTrace(eip, 1);', '', '    if (eip == info->si_addr) {', '        /* Restore old eip */', '        getAndSetMcontextEip(uc, eip);', '    }']}
description: ** DISPUTED ** A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in Redis up to 6.2.7/7.0.5. Affected is the function sigsegvHandler of the file debug.c of the component Crash Report. The manipulation leads to denial of service. The complexity of an attack is rather high. The exploitability is told to be difficult. The real existence of this vulnerability is still doubted at the moment. Upgrading to version 6.2.8 and 7.0.6 is able to address this issue. The patch is identified as 0bf90d944313919eb8e63d3588bf63a367f020a3. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211962 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability. NOTE: The vendor claims that this is not a DoS because it applies to the crash logging mechanism which is triggered after a crash has occurred.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function does not manage or release a resource; the crash-report recursion stems from dereferencing an invalid function pointer, not from improper resource shutdown or release, so it does not support CWE-404.

commit_msg:
Currently, locking of ->session is very inconsistent; most places
protect it using the legacy tty mutex, but disassociate_ctty(),
__do_SAK(), tiocspgrp() and tiocgsid() don't.
Two of the writers hold the ctrl_lock (because they already need it for
->pgrp), but __proc_set_tty() doesn't do that yet.

On a PREEMPT=y system, an unprivileged user can theoretically abuse
this broken locking to read 4 bytes of freed memory via TIOCGSID if
tiocgsid() is preempted long enough at the right point. (Other things
might also go wrong, especially if root-only ioctls are involved; I'm
not sure about that.)

Change the locking on ->session such that:

 - tty_lock() is held by all writers: By making disassociate_ctty()
   hold it. This should be fine because the same lock can already be
   taken through the call to tty_vhangup_session().
   The tricky part is that we need to shorten the area covered by
   siglock to be able to take tty_lock() without ugly retry logic; as
   far as I can tell, this should be fine, since nothing in the
   signal_struct is touched in the `if (tty)` branch.
 - ctrl_lock is held by all writers: By changing __proc_set_tty() to
   hold the lock a little longer.
 - All readers that aren't holding tty_lock() hold ctrl_lock: By
   adding locking to tiocgsid() and __do_SAK(), and expanding the area
   covered by ctrl_lock in tiocspgrp().

Cc: stable@kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Jiri Slaby <jirislaby@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsession = tty->session;'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long flags;', '', '\tspin_lock_irqsave(&tty->ctrl_lock, flags);', '\tsession = get_pid(tty->session);', '\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&tty->ctrl_lock, flags);', '\tput_pid(session);']}
description: A locking inconsistency issue was discovered in the tty subsystem of the Linux kernel through 5.9.13. drivers/tty/tty_io.c and drivers/tty/tty_jobctrl.c may allow a read-after-free attack against TIOCGSID, aka CID-c8bcd9c5be24.

code_evidence: session = tty->session reads the shared tty->session pointer without holding tty->ctrl_lock (the lock that the commit establishes for all writers/readers of ->session); the diff shows this line being replaced by a locked get_pid()/unlock sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-667 fits because the function accesses a shared resource (tty->session) without properly acquiring the lock that other writers hold, violating the required locking discipline. The consequence (stale/freed pid traversal) is the downstream effect, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code: session = tty->session;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: __do_SAK() dereferences tty->session without synchronization while disassociate_ctty()/__proc_set_tty() can concurrently clear or replace it. Trigger: SAK processing racing a session change. Consequence: session may be stale/freed, so do_each_pid_task walks a stale pid, enabling use-after-free or corrupted task iteration (supporting the described read-after-free).

commit_msg:
Fix potential abort in btu_av_act.cc

Partner analysis shows that bta_av_rc_msg does not respect handling
established for a null browse packet, instead dispatching the null
pointer to bta_av_rc_free_browse_msg.  Strictly speaking this does
not cause a UAF, as osi_free_and_reset will find the null and abort,
but it will lead to improper program termination.

Handle the case instead.

Bug: 269253349
Test: atest bluetooth_test_gd_unit
Tag: #security
Ignore-AOSP-First: Security
(cherry picked from https://googleplex-android-review.googlesource.com/q/commit:d3ee136851de30261e56c62fbb488541dc564b94)
Merged-In: I14dc4910476c733b246bcf7ff292afe9b7c0cc3d
Change-Id: I14dc4910476c733b246bcf7ff292afe9b7c0cc3d
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    bta_av_rc_free_browse_msg(p_cb, p_data);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (p_data->rc_msg.opcode == AVRC_OP_BROWSE &&', '        p_data->rc_msg.msg.browse.p_browse_pkt != NULL) {', '      bta_av_rc_free_browse_msg(p_cb, p_data);', '    }']}
description: In bta_av_rc_msg of bta_av_act.cc, there is a possible use after free due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: For AVRC_OP_BROWSE, the browse packet pointer p_data->rc_msg.msg.browse.p_browse_pkt and its data are propagated into av.meta_msg, and evt is set to BTA_AV_META_MSG_EVT.

After dispatching evt through the callback, bta_av_rc_free_browse_msg is called unconditionally whenever evt != 0, with no check that the opcode is browse or that the browse packet pointer is non-null.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the browse packet memory is released while a reference to it may still be used by the dispatched callback. This is not merely a null dereference; the root cause is freeing memory without confirming the message type and pointer ownership.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The browse message buffer is freed after being handed to the callback, but the free path is taken for any nonzero event, including non-browse messages whose browse pointer is null or stale. The missing opcode/pointer guard means an unrelated message can trigger a free of the browse packet, and the callback may retain a reference to the freed buffer, enabling use-after-free or improper termination.

commit_msg:
gsocketclient: Fix criticals

This ensures the parent GTask is kept alive as long as an enumeration
is running and trying to connect.

Closes #1646
Closes #1649
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      enumerator_next_async (data);'], 'added_lines': ['      enumerator_next_async (data, FALSE);']}
description: gio/gsocketclient.c in GNOME GLib 2.59.2 does not ensure that a parent GTask remains alive during the execution of a connection-attempting enumeration, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (g_socket_client_connected_callback mishandling and application crash) via a crafted web site, as demonstrated by GNOME Web (aka Epiphany).

code_evidence: The callback calls g_tls_connection_handshake_finish and branches on its success; the failure path at lines 16-19 unrefs object and retries via enumerator_next_async(data) without any guard against the parent task being gone.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code fails to check the exceptional condition that the parent GTask is no longer alive before continuing the enumeration, matching CWE-754's improper check for unusual conditions; this is a missing lifetime guard rather than a memory-safety flaw itself, though the crash is the consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: On TLS handshake failure, the else branch unconditionally invokes enumerator_next_async while the parent GTask may already have been finalized; the missing lifetime/state check lets the retry operate on freed data, causing g_socket_client_connected_callback mishandling and an application crash.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12993/Juniper: Add more bounds checks.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Add tests using the capture files supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        ND_TCHECK2(p[0], 3);', '', 'trunc:', '\tND_PRINT((ndo, "[|juniper_atm2]"));', '\treturn l2info.header_len;']}
description: The Juniper protocols parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-juniper.c, several functions.

code_evidence: After advancing p by l2info.header_len, the code reads l2info.cookie[7] and then calls EXTRACT_24BITS(p), which reads three bytes at p without first verifying that the remaining captured data holds at least three bytes.

llc_print is called with l2info.length/caplen, and p[0] plus isoclns_print(p+1, l2info.length-1) are used; the length values may exceed the bytes actually present at p, so these reads can run past the captured buffer.

Consequence: EXTRACT_24BITS and related accesses read past the buffer end (the commit adds ND_TCHECK2(p[0],3) to guard this).

commit_msg:
Fix illegal memory access triggered when parsing a PE binary with a corrupt data dictionary.

	PR 22373
	* peicode.h (pe_bfd_read_buildid): Check for invalid size and data
	offset values.

commit_msg: Fix heap buffer overflow in de_dotdot
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t(void) memmove( cp, cp + 2, strlen( file ) - 1 );'], 'added_lines': ['\t(void) memmove( cp, cp + 2, strlen( cp ) - 1 );']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in the de_dotdot function in libhttpd.c in sthttpd before 2.27.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (daemon crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted filename.

code_evidence: Line 14 locates the substring "/./" within file and stores its position in cp. Line 15 then calls memmove(cp, cp + 2, strlen(file) - 1), using the length of the whole remaining file buffer as the copy size instead of the length of the tail starting at cp. Because cp is an interior pointer, strlen(file) - 1 exceeds the bytes available from cp + 2 through the end of the string, so memmove reads and writes past the intended buffer boundary.

It is a length-calculation error rather than an off-by-one index or NULL dereference, so CWE-119 fits the supplied target.

while ( ( cp = strstr( file, "/./") ) != (char*) 0 )
(void) memmove( cp, cp + 2, strlen( file ) - 1 );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length is computed from the full file string rather than from the substring at cp, so the memmove span extends beyond the buffer when "/./" appears before the end of file. Trigger: a crafted filename containing an interior "/./" pattern. Consequence: out-of-bounds read/write of heap memory, causing a daemon crash or other memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Fix invalid memory write on lua stack overflow {CVE-2021-32626}

When LUA call our C code, by default, the LUA stack has room for 20
elements. In most cases, this is more than enough but sometimes it's not
and the caller must verify the LUA stack size before he pushes elements.

On 3 places in the code, there was no verification of the LUA stack size.
On specific inputs this missing verification could have lead to invalid
memory write:
1. On 'luaReplyToRedisReply', one might return a nested reply that will
   explode the LUA stack.
2. On 'redisProtocolToLuaType', the Redis reply might be deep enough
   to explode the LUA stack (notice that currently there is no such
   command in Redis that returns such a nested reply, but modules might
   do it)
3. On 'ldbRedis', one might give a command with enough arguments to
   explode the LUA stack (all the arguments will be pushed to the LUA
   stack)

This commit is solving all those 3 issues by calling 'lua_checkstack' and
verify that there is enough room in the LUA stack to push elements. In
case 'lua_checkstack' returns an error (there is not enough room in the
LUA stack and it's not possible to increase the stack), we will do the
following:
1. On 'luaReplyToRedisReply', we will return an error to the user.
2. On 'redisProtocolToLuaType' we will exit with panic (we assume this
   scenario is rare because it can only happen with a module).
3. On 'ldbRedis', we return an error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    if (!lua_checkstack(lua, 5)) {', '        /*', '         * Increase the Lua stack if needed, to make sure there is enough room', '         * to push 5 elements to the stack. On failure, exit with panic.', '\xa0 \xa0 \xa0 \xa0 \xa0* Notice that we need, in the worst case, 5 elements because redisProtocolToLuaType_Aggregate', '\xa0 \xa0 \xa0 \xa0 \xa0* might push 5 elements to the Lua stack.*/', '        serverPanic("lua stack limit reach when parsing redis.call reply");', '    }', '']}
description: Redis is an open source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions specially crafted Lua scripts executing in Redis can cause the heap-based Lua stack to be overflowed, due to incomplete checks for this condition. This can result with heap corruption and potentially remote code execution. This problem exists in all versions of Redis with Lua scripting support, starting from 2.6. The problem is fixed in versions 6.2.6, 6.0.16 and 5.0.14. For users unable to update an additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent users from executing Lua scripts. This can be done using ACL to restrict EVAL and EVALSHA commands.

code_evidence: redisProtocolToLuaType dispatches on the reply type byte and delegates to helpers such as redisProtocolToLuaType_Aggregate for '*', '%' and '~', and to Int/Bulk/Status/Error/Null/Bool/Double for the other cases. Each helper pushes values onto the Lua stack, but the function performs no lua_checkstack call before dispatch, so the caller-provided lua_State may have insufficient free slots when a deeply nested or large reply is parsed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The absence of a capacity check before stack pushes allows data to be written beyond the Lua stack buffer, directly matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an integer or input-validation issue; the supported harm is memory written past the intended buffer boundary.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function parses an untrusted Redis reply and forwards it to helpers that push onto the Lua stack without first verifying available stack capacity. Trigger: a sufficiently deep/nested reply (e.g. from a module) drives the aggregate helper to push more elements than the default stack permits. Supported consequence: writes past the Lua stack buffer, causing heap corruption and potential code execution or crash.

description: Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in WebKit/Source/platform/v8_inspector/V8Debugger.cpp in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML into the Developer Tools (aka DevTools) subsystem via a crafted web site, aka "Universal XSS (UXSS)."

Lines 6-12 install privileged callback functions (bind, getInternalProperties, objectHasOwnProperty, etc.) as own properties on that host object, exposing them to script that can reach the inherited prototype chain.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the injected-script host object is created with the default prototype, so page/context script can tamper with or traverse the prototype chain and reach the privileged inspector callbacks. Trigger: a crafted page manipulates Object.prototype or the host's prototype, letting attacker script invoke the injected host functions in the inspected context. diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstride = (fz_colorspace_n(ctx, colorspace) + s + alpha) * w;'], 'added_lines': ['\tint n;', '\tn = fz_colorspace_n(ctx, colorspace) + s + alpha;', '\tif (w > INT_MAX / n)', '\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_GENERIC, "Overly wide image");', '\tstride = n * w;']}

code_evidence: The stride is computed as (fz_colorspace_n(ctx, colorspace) + s + alpha) * w in a signed int without any overflow check. The resulting stride is passed directly to fz_new_pixmap_with_data, which allocates the backing buffer using this size. If the multiplication overflows, the allocated buffer is smaller than the actual row size expected by consumers.

The integer overflow is the root cause; the write past the buffer is the supported consequence, distinguishing it from a pure integer-overflow label.

Trigger: a crafted image with a very large width causes the product to wrap to a small or negative value. Consequence: the pixmap buffer is under-allocated, so subsequent row/stride-based writes run past the buffer end, corrupting heap memory (out-of-bounds write).

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: get_busid_priv() returns the shared busid_priv entry; its status fields are read here, but the early return at line 14 exits without releasing any busid entry lock, leaving the entry unprotected after inspection.
The busid_priv fields shutdown_busid, sdev, udev and status are written directly with no lock held, and the success return at line 49 likewise does not release the busid entry lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a check-then-act sequence on a shared resource lacking synchronization, matching CWE-362's concurrent access to a shared resource with improper synchronization. The fix routes all exits through put_busid_priv() to release the lock, confirming the missing exclusivity; the NULL deref/UAF are consequences, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: stub_probe() reads and mutates the shared busid_priv entry without holding the finer-grained busid lock across the check-then-update sequence. Concurrent probe/disconnect/rebind paths can interleave between the status check and the writes, so the entry can be freed or reset concurrently, yielding a NULL-pointer dereference or use-after-free.

A local attacker could exploit this when a net namespace with a netnsid is assigned to cause a kernel panic and a denial of service.

description: FreeType 2 before 2017-03-08 has an out-of-bounds write caused by a heap-based buffer overflow related to the TT_Get_MM_Var function in truetype/ttgxvar.c and the sfnt_init_face function in sfnt/sfobjs.c.

code_evidence: When glyf is absent but CFF present, num_instances is forced to 0, discarding the fvar-derived instance count. The guard omits the CFF2 tag, so a CFF2 font with an fvar table retains a nonzero num_instances.
The loop reads instances and increments num_instances when no default match is found, then later code (TT_Get_MM_Var) uses this count to size buffers.
The increment at line 136 can leave num_instances inconsistent with the actual CFF2 table, feeding an inflated count downstream.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a heap buffer overflow writing past an allocation sized from the mismatched num_instances, matching CWE-787 (write past end of intended buffer). It is not merely an incorrect count; the count drives an out-of-bounds write.

Trigger: a crafted CFF2 font with an fvar table. Downstream TT_Get_MM_Var allocates based on this count and writes instance data, producing a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

description: Out-of-bounds read in `r_bin_ne_get_relocs` function in GitHub repository radareorg/radare2 prior to 5.6.8. This vulnerability may allow attackers to read sensitive information or cause a crash.

code_evidence: The bounds check only rejects rel.index greater than ModRefs; when rel.index equals ModRefs or is zero, the else branch executes offset = modref[rel.index - 1] + ... .
modref is allocated with ModRefs ut16 entries; indexing modref[rel.index - 1] with rel.index == 0 reads modref[-1], before the allocated buffer.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an off-by-one/zero boundary error. The guard uses rel.index > ModRefs instead of a strict > 0 && < ModRefs check, so rel.index == 0 (and == ModRefs) passes into the array access, and rel.index - 1 underflows to -1, reading before modref. description: In Wireshark 3.2.0 to 3.2.1, 3.0.0 to 3.0.8, and 2.6.0 to 2.6.14, the EAP dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-eap.c by using more careful sscanf parsing.

code_evidence: identity is split on '@.' and token count checked to be 6; tokens[2] and tokens[3] are used assuming they contain 'mnc'/'mcc' prefixes of at least 3 chars.
sscanf(tokens[2] + 3, ...) and sscanf(tokens[3] + 3, ...) advance the pointer by 3 bytes without verifying the token length, so a short token makes the pointer skip past the NUL terminator.
tokens[0] is compared against tokens[2] + 3 and then strlen(tokens[2])/strlen(tokens[3]) are used for tree offsets.
Later tree additions compute offsets and lengths from strlen(tokens[2]) and strlen(tokens[3]) minus 'mnc'/'mcc' length, which can underflow for short tokens.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads beyond the intended token buffer due to missing length validation before pointer arithmetic, which directly matches CWE-125 out-of-bounds read. The fix replaces the pointer offset with a bounded sscanf format that skips exactly 3 characters without reading past the buffer.

evidence_lines.code:
proto_tree_add_uint(eap_identity_tree, hf_eap_identity_wlan_mcc_mnc,
tvb, offset + (guint)strlen(tokens[0]) + (guint)strlen("@wlan.") +
(guint)strlen("mnc"), (guint)strlen(tokens[2]) - (guint)strlen("mnc"),
mcc_mnc);
proto_tree_add_uint(eap_identity_tree, hf_eap_identity_wlan_mcc,
tvb, offset + (guint)(strlen(tokens[0]) + strlen("@wlan.") +
strlen(tokens[2]) + 1 + strlen("mcc")),
(guint)(strlen(tokens[3]) - strlen("mcc")), mcc);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser assumes the MNC and MCC tokens are longer than 3 bytes and unconditionally adds 3 to their pointers before sscanf and string comparison. A crafted EAP identity with a short token (e.g., 'mnc' with no digits) causes reads past the end of the token buffer, leading to a crash/DoS in the dissector.

description: The ReadHDRImage function in coders/hdr.c in ImageMagick 6.x and 7.x allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via a crafted HDR file.

code_evidence: The value-collection loop at line 117 reads bytes into value and advances c via ReadBlobByte at line 121, but its only exit conditions are c=='\n' or c=='\0'. ReadBlobByte returns EOF on end of input, which is neither '\n' nor '\0', so at end-of-file the loop condition stays true and c is repeatedly set to EOF without ever reaching an exit condition.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is precisely an iteration whose exit condition cannot be reached for the EOF input, matching CWE-835's definition of an infinite loop with availability impact. The sscanf return-value checks in the same patch are unrelated robustness fixes and do not support this label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop termination test omits EOF, while ReadBlobByte signals end of file with EOF. Trigger: a crafted HDR file whose header ends (or whose value line ends) without a trailing newline or NUL causes c to become EOF inside the loop. Consequence: the loop never exits, consuming CPU indefinitely and denying service.

commit_msg:
The Layer 2 Update frame is used to update bridges when a station roams
to another AP even if that STA does not transmit any frames after the
reassociation. This behavior was described in IEEE Std 802.11F-2003 as
something that would happen based on MLME-ASSOCIATE.indication, i.e.,
before completing 4-way handshake. However, this IEEE trial-use
recommended practice document was published before RSN (IEEE Std
802.11i-2004) and as such, did not consider RSN use cases. Furthermore,
IEEE Std 802.11F-2003 was withdrawn in 2006 and as such, has not been
maintained amd should not be used anymore.

Sending out the Layer 2 Update frame immediately after association is
fine for open networks (and also when using SAE, FT protocol, or FILS
authentication when the station is actually authenticated by the time
association completes). However, it is not appropriate for cases where
RSN is used with PSK or EAP authentication since the station is actually
fully authenticated only once the 4-way handshake completes after
authentication and attackers might be able to use the unauthenticated
triggering of Layer 2 Update frame transmission to disrupt bridge
behavior.

Fix this by postponing transmission of the Layer 2 Update frame from
station entry addition to the point when the station entry is marked
authorized. Similarly, send out the VLAN binding update only if the STA
entry has already been authorized.

Signed-off-by: Jouni Malinen <jouni@codeaurora.org>
Reviewed-by: Johannes Berg <johannes@sipsolutions.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tint layer2_update;', '\tlayer2_update = sdata->vif.type == NL80211_IFTYPE_AP_VLAN ||', '\t\tsdata->vif.type == NL80211_IFTYPE_AP;', '', '\tif (layer2_update)', '\t\tcfg80211_send_layer2_update(sta->sdata->dev, sta->sta.addr);', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: An exploitable denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel prior to mainline 5.3. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by triggering AP to send IAPP location updates for stations before the required authentication process has completed. This could lead to different denial-of-service scenarios, either by causing CAM table attacks, or by leading to traffic flapping if faking already existing clients in other nearby APs of the same wireless infrastructure. An attacker can forge Authentication and Association Request packets to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: The function initializes rate control when WLAN_STA_ASSOC is set, but this does not require WLAN_STA_AUTHORIZED; the station can still be mid-4-way-handshake.
layer2_update is set purely from the interface type (AP_VLAN or AP), with no check of the station's authorization state.
After sta_info_insert_rcu succeeds, cfg80211_send_layer2_update is called unconditionally for AP/AP_VLAN, broadcasting the Layer 2 Update frame for a station that may not yet be authenticated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function acts on a station identity claim (association) without enforcing that authentication/authorization has completed before triggering network-visible state changes; this is improper authentication of the claimed identity. It is not merely a missing authorization check, since the core flaw is treating an unauthenticated association as sufficient.

evidence_lines.code:
layer2_update = sdata->vif.type == NL80211_IFTYPE_AP_VLAN ||
sdata->vif.type == NL80211_IFTYPE_AP;

if (layer2_update)
cfg80211_send_layer2_update(sta->sdata->dev, sta->sta.addr);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Layer 2 update is sent based only on association/interface type rather than on completed authentication (authorized flag). Trigger: an attacker forges Authentication/Association frames so a station entry is added before the 4-way handshake completes, causing the AP to emit IAPP Layer 2 updates. Consequence: bridge/forwarding-table disruption (traffic flapping or CAM-table attacks) leading to denial of service.

description: Moonlight-common-c contains the core GameStream client code shared between Moonlight clients. Moonlight-common-c is vulnerable to buffer overflow starting in commit f57bd745b4cbed577ea654fad4701bea4d38b44c. A malicious game streaming server could exploit a buffer overflow vulnerability to crash a moonlight client. Achieving RCE is possible but unlikely, due to stack canaries in use by modern compiler toolchains. The published binaries for official clients Qt, Android, iOS/tvOS, and Embedded are built with stack canaries, but some unofficial clients may not use stack canaries. This vulnerability takes place after the pairing process, so it requires the client to be tricked into pairing to a malicious host. It is not possible to perform using a man-in-the-middle due to public key pinning that takes place during the pairing process. The bug was addressed in commit b2497a3918a6d79808d9fd0c04734786e70d5954.

code_evidence: sendMessageTcp allocates sizeof(*packet)+paylen bytes, stores the caller-supplied paylen into packet->payloadLength, then memcpy copies paylen bytes from payload into &packet[1]. No check constrains paylen against the actual size of the payload buffer or any maximum, so the size written is taken directly from the argument.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a buffer copy via memcpy using an unvalidated input length, matching CWE-120's 'buffer copy without checking size of input'. The unchecked length drives both the allocation and the copy, so the write can exceed the destination buffer; this is a classic overflow rather than an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy length paylen is attacker-influenced and never validated against the source buffer's real size or an upper bound. Trigger: a malicious server causes a caller to pass a payload whose length field exceeds the actual data. Consequence: memcpy reads past the source buffer and writes past the allocated packet region, corrupting heap memory and potentially crashing the client or enabling code execution.

commit_msg:
If a pattern contains '?' character, any character in the string is skipped,
even if it is '\0'. The rest of the matching then reads invalid memory.

Reviewed-by: Peter Hutterer <peter.hutterer@who-t.net>
Signed-off-by: Julien Cristau <jcristau@debian.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    if (*string++ == XK_minus)'], 'added_lines': ['\t    if ((t = *string++) == XK_minus)', '\t    if (!t)', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: In the PatternMatch function in fontfile/fontdir.c in libXfont through 1.5.2 and 2.x before 2.0.2, an attacker with access to an X connection can cause a buffer over-read during pattern matching of fonts, leading to information disclosure or a crash (denial of service). This occurs because '\0' characters are incorrectly skipped in situations involving ? characters.

code_evidence: In the '?' case, the code unconditionally advances the string pointer with *string++ and only checks whether the skipped character equals XK_minus; it never verifies that the skipped character is non-NUL. When the current string position holds '\0', the pointer is advanced past the terminator, so the loop continues matching against memory beyond the intended string buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory beyond the bounds of the intended string buffer because the '?' branch skips the '\0' terminator and continues matching. This is a read past the end of a buffer, matching CWE-125 rather than an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the '?' wildcard consumes a character without checking for the NUL terminator, unlike the '*' case which tests !t after reading. Trigger: a pattern containing '?' matched against a string that ends (or has a NUL) at that position. Consequence: subsequent iterations read past the end of the string buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read that may disclose memory or crash.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20568)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                              tree);'], 'added_lines': ['                                              tree, 1);']}
description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: The function iterates over caller-supplied policy_oids and, when no matching node exists in auth_nodes but an anyPolicy node is present, creates a new policy-data node via ossl_policy_data_new and attaches it with ossl_policy_level_add_node(NULL, extra, anyPolicy->parent, tree, 1). The final argument 1 is the fix's added flag controlling node duplication/counting; before the patch this call passed no such argument, allowing repeated policy-OID entries to create excessive policy nodes during chain verification.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness lies in the X.509 certificate-chain policy-constraint verification path, directly supporting CWE-295's improper certificate validation scope. It is a resource-exhaustion consequence within certificate validation, distinct from signature or identity-check failures.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the policy-constraint processing path adds nodes without bounding the work done per user-supplied policy OID, so a malicious certificate chain with many policy OIDs and an anyPolicy node triggers exponential resource consumption during X.509 verification. Consequence is denial of service, not a validation bypass.

commit_msg:
The current code performs the cancel of a delayed work at the late
stage of disconnection procedure, which may lead to the access to the
already cleared state.

This patch assures to call cancel_delayed_work_sync() at the beginning
of the disconnection procedure for avoiding that race.  The delayed

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Don't have %cr4.fsgsbase active behind a guest kernels back

Currently, a 64bit PV guest can appear to set and clear FSGSBASE in %cr4, but
the bit remains set in hardware.  Therefore, the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE are usable
even when the guest kernel believes that they are disabled.

The FSGSBASE feature isn't currently supported in Linux, and its context
switch path has some optimisations which rely on userspace being unable to use
the WR{FS,GS}BASE instructions.  Xen's current behaviour undermines this
expectation.

In 64bit PV guest context, always load the guest kernels setting of FSGSBASE
into %cr4.  This requires adjusting how Xen uses the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE
instructions.

 * Delete the cpu_has_fsgsbase helper.  It is no longer safe, as users need to
   check %cr4 directly.
 * The raw __rd{fs,gs}base() helpers are only safe to use when %cr4.fsgsbase
   is set.  Comment this property.
 * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}{base,shadow}() and read_msr() helpers are updated to use
   the current %cr4 value to determine which mechanism to use.
 * toggle_guest_mode() and save_segments() are update to avoid reading
   fs/gsbase if the values in hardware cannot be stale WRT struct vcpu.  A
   consequence of this is that the write_cr() path needs to cache the current
   bases, as subsequent context switches will skip saving the values.
 * write_cr4() is updated to ensure that the shadow %cr4.fsgsbase value is
   observed in a safe way WRT the hardware setting, if an interrupt happens to
   hit in the middle.
 * load_segments() is updated to use the VMLOAD optimisation if FSGSBASE is
   unavailable, even if only gs_shadow needs updating.  As a minor perf
   improvement, check cpu_has_svm first to short circuit a context-dependent
   conditional on Intel hardware.
 * pv_make_cr4() is updated for 64bit PV guests to use the guest kernels
   choice of FSGSBASE.

This is part of XSA-293.

Reported-by: Andy Lutomirski <luto@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    get_cpu_info()->cr4 = val;', '    asm volatile ( "mov %0,%%cr4" : : "r" (val) );'], 'added_lines': ['    struct cpu_info *info = get_cpu_info();', '', '    /*', "     * On hardware supporting FSGSBASE, the value in %cr4 is the kernel's", '     * choice for 64bit PV guests, which impacts whether Xen can use the', '     * instructions.', '     *', '     * The {rd,wr}{fs,gs}base() helpers use info->cr4 to work out whether it', '     * is safe to execute the {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE instruction, falling back to', '     * the MSR path if not.  Some users require interrupt safety.', '     *', '     * If FSGSBASE is currently or about to become clear, reflect this in', '     * info->cr4 before updating %cr4, so an interrupt which hits in the', "     * middle won't observe FSGSBASE set in info->cr4 but clear in %cr4.", '     */', '    info->cr4 = val & (info->cr4 | ~X86_CR4_FSGSBASE);', '', '    asm volatile ( "mov %[val], %%cr4"', '                   : "+m" (info->cr4) /* Force ordering without a barrier. */', '                   : [val] "r" (val) );', '', '    info->cr4 = val;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges because a guest can manipulate its virtualised %cr4 in a way that is incompatible with Linux (and possibly other guest kernels).

code_evidence: write_cr4 accepts caller-supplied cr4 value val and stores it directly into get_cpu_info()->cr4 before executing mov %0,%%cr4. The only check is an ASSERT that PGE and PCIDE are not both set; this is a debug assertion, not a runtime validation of FSGSBASE or other guest-controlled cr4 bits, and it does not constrain the value written to hardware.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the cr4 value is external input that is accepted and applied without adequate validation of its FSGSBASE property, allowing an inconsistent state. The weakness is missing validation of an input's required properties, not merely a logic ordering bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function blindly records and loads the requested cr4 value without validating that FSGSBASE is consistent with the guest kernel's expectation. Trigger: a 64-bit PV guest manipulates its virtualized cr4 so the FSGSBASE bit differs from the hardware state, leaving {RD,WR}{FS,GS}BASE usable while the guest believes they are disabled. Consequence: the guest can subvert Linux context-switch assumptions, supporting privilege escalation or denial of service.

description: A use-after-free vulnerability was found in systemd. commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&lchn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&lchn->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long  flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&lchn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&lchn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: evtchn_send acquires the per-channel lock with plain spin_lock() and releases it with plain spin_unlock() at the out label, without disabling interrupts.
The lock protects lchn state and the interdomain/IPI notification paths (lines 18-36), which can be reached from interrupt context via send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the critical section lacks IRQ-safe synchronization, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence (the interrupt handler) to access the shared evtchn resource. The fix to spin_lock_irqsave/irqrestore confirms the missing interrupt-exclusion constraint; this is a race-condition/synchronization flaw, not merely a memory-safety defect.

evidence_lines.code: spin_lock(&lchn->lock);
spin_unlock(&lchn->lock);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-channel lock is taken without masking interrupts, so an interrupt handler on the same CPU can attempt to acquire the same lock while evtchn_send holds it, violating exclusivity/atomicity. Trigger: a local interrupt that invokes the virq-sending path during the critical section. Supported consequence: lock recursion/deadlock, corrupt channel state, or bug checks leading to DoS.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the backward scan lacks a target == output guard, so the loop condition permits target to reach output and then the body dereferences it after further decrements. Trigger: a crafted path such as "x/../y" processed after target has advanced without an intervening slash. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds access before the output buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
lib: limit size of vty buffer to 4096 bytes

This removes the automatic resizing of the vty input buffer and places a
hard size cap of 4096 bytes. It also fixes a potentially unsafe strcpy.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Young <qlyoung@cumulusnetworks.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int len = strlen (str);', '  vty_write (vty, str, len);', '  strcpy (&vty->buf[vty->cp], str);', '  vty->cp += len;'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t nwrite = MIN ((int) strlen (str), VTY_BUFSIZ - vty->cp);', '  vty_write (vty, str, nwrite);', '  strncpy (&vty->buf[vty->cp], str, nwrite);', '  vty->cp += nwrite;']}
description: All versions of Quagga, 0.93 through 1.1.0, are vulnerable to an unbounded memory allocation in the telnet 'vty' CLI, leading to a Denial-of-Service of Quagga daemons, or even the entire host. When Quagga daemons are configured with their telnet CLI enabled, anyone who can connect to the TCP ports can trigger this vulnerability, prior to authentication. Most distributions restrict the Quagga telnet interface to local access only by default. The Quagga telnet interface 'vty' input buffer grows automatically, without bound, so long as a newline is not entered. This allows an attacker to cause the Quagga daemon to allocate unbounded memory by sending very long strings without a newline. Eventually the daemon is terminated by the system, or the system itself runs out of memory. This is fixed in Quagga 1.1.1 and Free Range Routing (FRR) Protocol Suite 2017-01-10.

code_evidence: Line 4 computes len as the full strlen of the attacker-influenced str without comparing it to the remaining space in vty->buf. Line 6 then calls strcpy(&vty->buf[vty->cp], str), copying len+1 bytes (including the NUL) at offset cp with no bound, so the destination write can extend past the end of vty->buf when cp+len exceeds the buffer size. Lines 5 and 7 propagate the same unchecked len to vty_write and vty->cp.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the code performs a write operation outside the intended bounds of vty->buf. The unchecked strcpy is the concrete out-of-bounds write; the broader unbounded-allocation DoS is a related consequence rather than the direct memory-safety defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function copies str into vty->buf using strcpy with a length derived only from the input, ignoring the destination capacity and current offset cp. Trigger: a long input string (e.g., vty input without a newline) reaches this function, making cp+len+1 exceed the buffer. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds write in vty->buf, corrupting adjacent memory and enabling crash or memory corruption; the unbounded growth also supports memory exhaustion/DoS.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12902/Zephyr: Fix bounds checking.

Use ND_TTEST() rather than comparing against ndo->ndo_snapend ourselves;
it's easy to get the tests wrong.

Check for running out of packet data before checking for running out of
captured data, and distinguish between running out of packet data (which
might just mean "no more strings") and running out of captured data
(which means "truncated").

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

description: The Zephyr parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-zephyr.c, several functions.

code_evidence: The scan loop dereferences **pptr at line 10 and increments *pptr at line 11 while only comparing *pptr to ndo_snapend; the comparison does not account for the size of the dereferenced byte and the post-loop dereference/increment at lines 14-15 occurs after the loop exits, without re-validating that the current position is still within captured data.
Line 16 checks *len < 0 and *pptr > ndo_snapend only after lines 14-15 already incremented *pptr and *len, so the pointer may have advanced past the captured buffer before the check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads captured packet memory past its intended bounds: the terminator scan and post-loop increment can move *pptr beyond ndo_snapend, and the returned pointer is dereferenced by the caller. This is a read overrun, not a write, so it is out-of-bounds read rather than CWE-787.

evidence_lines.code:
if (*len < 0 || *pptr > (const char *) ndo->ndo_snapend)
return NULL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop bound is checked with a pointer comparison against ndo_snapend rather than ND_TTEST, and the NUL terminator (or end of packet) is never guaranteed before the post-loop increment. Trigger: a Zephyr packet whose string field reaches the end of captured data without a NUL terminator. Consequence: lines 14-15 advance *pptr past ndo_snapend, and the returned string is then read by callers, producing an out-of-bounds read (buffer over-read).

commit_msg: mRLE: decoding bounds
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void mrled(u8 * RESTRICT in, u8 * RESTRICT out, s32 outlen) {', '    while (op < outlen) {', '            for (run = 0; (pc = in[ip++]) == 255; run += 255)'], 'added_lines': ['static int mrled(u8 * RESTRICT in, u8 * RESTRICT out, s32 outlen, s32 maxin) {', '    if(maxin < 32)', '        return 1;', '', '    while (op < outlen && ip < maxin) {', '            for (run = 0; (pc = in[ip++]) == 255 && ip < maxin; run += 255)', '', '    return op != outlen;']}
description: An issue was discovered in libbzip3.a in bzip3 before 1.2.3. There is a bz3_decode_block out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: The header loop reads 32 bytes via in[ip++] without any check that the input buffer actually contains 32 bytes, so a short input causes reads past the end of in.

The main decode loop runs while op < outlen and reads in[ip++] with no bound on ip relative to the input length; the run-length loop at line 13 also dereferences in[ip++] repeatedly on 0xFF bytes, advancing ip without any input-length limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function dereferences in[ip++] past the end of the supplied input buffer; the weakness is a read beyond the buffer boundary, not a write, so it is an out-of-bounds read rather than an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mrled receives only the output length outlen and never an input length, so neither the 32-byte header read nor the per-symbol and run-byte reads are bounded by the size of in. Trigger: a truncated or malformed compressed block whose data ends before outlen output bytes are produced. Consequence: in[ip++] reads beyond the input buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (crash or disclosure).

description: NULL Pointer Dereference in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3.0-DEV.

code_evidence: The WAVE fmt chunk parses ctx->ch (channel count) and ctx->sr (sample rate) directly from untrusted packet bytes via gf_bs_read_u16_le/gf_bs_read_u32_le; no check rejects zero values.
ctx->ch drives layout selection, but when it is 0 none of the branches set a valid layout (else ctx->layout = 0).

After header probe, wav_ok is not set false for zero ch/sr, so control proceeds to ctx->probe_wave = 2 and pcmreframe_configure_pid, where zero channel count/sample rate propagate into downstream frame-size and division computations.

This matches CWE-476, where a pointer expected valid is NULL; it is not merely an integer overflow because the added checks target zero values before use.

Trigger: a crafted WAVE header with ch=0 or sr=0 reaches pcmreframe_configure_pid, which relies on these values for frame sizing/division. Supported consequence: a crash (DoS) from a NULL or invalid dereference/division path, consistent with the reported NULL pointer dereference.

commit_msg:
saslserv/main: Track EID we're pending login to

The existing model does not remember that we've sent a SVSLOGIN for a
given SASL session, and simply assumes that if a client is introduced
with a SASL session open, that session must have succeeded. The security
of this approach requires ircd to implicitly abort SASL sessions on
client registration.

This also means that if a client successfully authenticates and then
does something else its pending login is forgotten about, even though a
SVSLOGIN has been sent for it, and the ircd is going to think it's
logged in.

This change removes the dependency on ircd's state machine by keeping
explicit track of the pending login, i.e. the one we've most recently
sent a SVSLOGIN for. The next commit will ensure that a client abort
(even an implicit one) doesn't blow that information away.

description: Atheme IRC Services before 7.2.12, when used in conjunction with InspIRCd, allows authentication bypass by ending an IRC handshake at a certain point during a challenge-response login sequence.

code_evidence: When mu is NULL, the function trusts p->authzeid as the identity to log in; the only guard is a non-empty check, so a session whose SASL exchange was aborted but whose authzeid remains populated proceeds to myuser_find_uid and login.

If u->myuser already differs from mu, the function performs a logout, but when ircd_on_logout fails (was_killed false) it falls through and calls myuser_login for the new mu, completing an authentication/login transition without re-verifying that the SASL session actually succeeded.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the product accepts an identity claim (authzeid) without sufficiently proving that the SASL challenge-response actually completed successfully, allowing an actor to assume another user's identity. This is a missing-verification flaw in the authentication decision, not merely a session-management or logging issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code derives the authenticated identity from the session's authzeid field and assumes any introduced session with a SASL session open has succeeded, instead of tracking an explicit pending/successful login state. Trigger: a client ends the IRC handshake at a chosen point during the challenge-response sequence, leaving authzeid set while SASL has not succeeded. Consequence: myuser_login binds the client to the account, granting an authenticated identity (authentication bypass).

commit_msg:
Don't change the state of the ETM flags until CCS processing

Changing the ciphersuite during a renegotiation can result in a crash
leading to a DoS attack. ETM has not been implemented in 1.1.0 for DTLS
so this is TLS only.

The problem is caused by changing the flag indicating whether to use ETM
or not immediately on negotiation of ETM, rather than at CCS. Therefore,
during a renegotiation, if the ETM state is changing (usually due to a
change of ciphersuite), then an error/crash will occur.

Due to the fact that there are separate CCS messages for read and write
we actually now need two flags to determine whether to use ETM or not.

CVE-2017-3733

Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    s->s3->flags &= ~TLS1_FLAGS_ENCRYPT_THEN_MAC;', '                s->s3->flags |= TLS1_FLAGS_ENCRYPT_THEN_MAC;'], 'added_lines': ['    s->tlsext_use_etm = 0;', '                s->tlsext_use_etm = 1;']}
description: During a renegotiation handshake if the Encrypt-Then-Mac extension is negotiated where it was not in the original handshake (or vice-versa) then this can cause OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0e to crash (dependent on ciphersuite). Both clients and servers are affected.

code_evidence: At function entry line 16 the server-hello extension scanner clears TLS1_FLAGS_ENCRYPT_THEN_MAC, and at lines 196-199, upon parsing a TLSEXT_TYPE_encrypt_then_mac extension, it sets that same flag immediately when the negotiated cipher is neither AEAD nor RC4. The flag is set at extension-parse time, before the CCS phase where the new cipher state actually takes effect.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts the peer-supplied encrypt_then_mac extension and applies it without validating that the change is consistent with the current record-layer state and handshake phase, i.e., it fails to enforce the required state constraint on the input. This matches CWE-20's improper validation of input properties; it is not a memory-safety bug in itself, the crash follows from the unvalidated state transition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ETM state is committed during ServerHello extension parsing rather than deferred until CCS, so during renegotiation the flag can change while the existing record layer still uses the previous ETM state. Trigger: a peer negotiates a ciphersuite change that flips ETM on or off in a renegotiation handshake. Consequence: the record layer and the negotiated state disagree, causing a crash and a denial of service.

commit_msg:
Protect against size_t overflows in pb_dec_bytes/pb_dec_string.

Possible consequences of bug:
1) Denial of service by causing a crash
   Possible when all of the following apply:
      - Untrusted data is passed to pb_decode()
      - The top-level message contains a static string field as the first field.
   Causes a single write of '0' byte to 1 byte before the message struct.

2) Remote code execution
   Possible when all of the following apply:
      - 64-bit platform
      - The message or a submessage contains a static/pointer string field.
      - Decoding directly from a custom pb_istream_t
      - bytes_left on the stream is set to larger than 4 GB
   Causes a write of up to 4 GB of data past the string field.

3) Possible heap corruption or remote code execution
   Possible when all of the following apply:
      - less than 64-bit platform
      - The message or a submessage contains a pointer-type bytes field.
   Causes a write of sizeof(pb_size_t) bytes of data past a 0-byte long
   malloc()ed buffer. On many malloc() implementations, this causes at
   most a crash. However, remote code execution through a controlled jump
   cannot be ruled out.

--

Detailed analysis follows

In the following consideration, I define "platform bitness" as equal to
number of bits in size_t datatype. Therefore most 8-bit platforms are
regarded as 16-bit for the purposes of this discussion.

1. The overflow in pb_dec_string

The overflow happens in this computation:

uint32_t size;
size_t alloc_size;
alloc_size = size + 1;

There are two ways in which the overflow can occur: In the uint32_t
addition, or in the cast to size_t. This depends on the platform
bitness.

On 32- and 64-bit platforms, the size has to be UINT32_MAX for the
overflow to occur. In that case alloc_size will be 0.

On 16-bit platforms, overflow will happen whenever size is more than
UINT16_MAX, and resulting alloc_size is attacker controlled.

For static fields, the alloc_size value is just checked against the
field data size. For pointer fields, the alloc_size value is passed to
malloc(). End result in both cases is the same, the storage is 0 or
just a few bytes in length.

On 16-bit platforms, another overflow occurs in the call to pb_read(),
when passing the original size. An attacker will want the passed value
to be larger than the alloc_size, therefore the only reasonable choice
is to have size = UINT16_MAX and alloc_size = 0. Any larger multiple
will truncate to the same values.

At this point we have read atleast the tag and the string length of the
message, i.e. atleast 3 bytes. The maximum initial value for stream
bytes_left is SIZE_MAX, thus at this point at most SIZE_MAX-3 bytes are
remaining.

On 32-bit and 16-bit platforms this means that the size passed to
pb_read() is always larger than the number of remaining bytes. This
causes pb_read() to fail immediately, before reading any bytes.

On 64-bit platforms, it is possible for the bytes_left value to be set
to a value larger than UINT32_MAX, which is the wraparound point in
size calculation. In this case pb_read() will succeed and write up to 4
GB of attacker controlled data over the RAM that comes after the string
field.

On all platforms, there is an unconditional write of a terminating null
byte. Because the size of size_t typically reflects the size of the
processor address space, a write at UINT16_MAX or UINT32_MAX bytes
after the string field actually wraps back to before the string field.
Consequently, on 32-bit and 16-bit platforms, the bug causes a single
write of '0' byte at one byte before the string field.

If the string field is in the middle of a message, this will just
corrupt other data in the message struct. Because the message contents
is attacker controlled anyway, this is a non-issue. However, if the
string field is the first field in the top-level message, it can
corrupt other data on the stack/heap before it. Typically a single '0'
write at a location not controlled by attacker is enough only for a
denial-of-service attack.

When using pointer fields and malloc(), the attacker controlled
alloc_size will cause a 0-size allocation to happen. By the same logic
as before, on 32-bit and 16-bit platforms this causes a '0' byte write
only. On 64-bit platforms, however, it will again allow up to 4 GB of
malicious data to be written over memory, if the stream length allows
the read.

2. The overflow in pb_dec_bytes

This overflow happens in the PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE macro:

The computation is done in size_t data type this time. This means that
an overflow is possible only when n is larger than SIZE_MAX -
offsetof(..). The offsetof value in this case is equal to
sizeof(pb_size_t) bytes.

Because the incoming size value is limited to 32 bits, no overflow can
happen here on 64-bit platforms.

The size will be passed to pb_read(). Like before, on 32-bit and 16-bit
platforms the read will always fail before writing anything.

This leaves only the write of bdest->size as exploitable. On statically
allocated fields, the size field will always be allocated, regardless
of alloc_size. In this case, no buffer overflow is possible here, but
user code could possibly use the attacker controlled size value and
read past a buffer.

If the field is allocated through malloc(), this will allow a write of
sizeof(pb_size_t) attacker controlled bytes to past a 0-byte long
buffer. In typical malloc implementations, this will either fit in
unused alignment padding area, or cause a heap corruption and a crash.
Under very exceptional situation it could allow attacker to influence
the behaviour of malloc(), possibly jumping into an attacker-controlled
location and thus leading to remote code execution.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!allocate_field(stream, dest, PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size), 1))', '        if (PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size) > field->data_size)', '    }', '    ', '    if (size > PB_SIZE_MAX)', '    {', '        PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "bytes overflow");'], 'added_lines': ['    size_t alloc_size;', '    ', '    if (size > PB_SIZE_MAX)', '        PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "bytes overflow");', '    ', '    alloc_size = PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size);', '    if (size > alloc_size)', '        PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "size too large");', '        if (!allocate_field(stream, dest, alloc_size, 1))', '        if (alloc_size > field->data_size)']}
description: Nanopb before 0.3.1 allows size_t overflows in pb_dec_bytes and pb_dec_string.

code_evidence: Untrusted length is decoded into a 32-bit size from the stream; no bound is enforced on it before it drives allocation and buffer sizing.
For pointer fields, PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size) is passed to allocate_field without validating that the computed allocation covers size bytes.
For static fields, the same macro result is compared to field->data_size, again relying on a possibly wrapped size computation.
The PB_SIZE_MAX check occurs only after allocation/validation, too late to prevent a wrapped allocation size.
bdest->size is set from size and pb_read copies size bytes into bdest->bytes, which may exceed the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes attacker-controlled data beyond the allocated destination buffer due to an unchecked size computation. It is an out-of-bounds write rather than merely an integer overflow: the overflow is the cause, the past-end write in pb_read is the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code: if (!allocate_field(stream, dest, PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size), 1))

if (PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size) > field->data_size)
PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "bytes overflow");

bdest->size = (pb_size_t)size;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size_t allocation size computed by PB_BYTES_ARRAY_T_ALLOCSIZE(size) can wrap for large attacker-controlled size, and the size>PB_SIZE_MAX guard runs after allocation. Consequence: allocate_field/malloc returns an undersized buffer, then pb_read writes size bytes past it, causing out-of-bounds write, heap corruption, crash or possible code execution.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.5-5, the ReadPCDImage function in pcd.c allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory leak) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 50 allocates header via AcquireQuantumMemory; line 52's ThrowReaderException on allocation failure is a macro that returns without freeing header (though header is NULL there).

Lines 55-57: when the header count/magic validation fails, ThrowReaderException is invoked while header still holds the 0x800*3 allocation; the macro long-jumps/returns, so header is never relinquished.
Lines 60-62: the number_images>65535 check throws before the RelinquishMagickMemory(header) at line 62, leaking the header buffer on that error path.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header buffer allocated at line 50 is freed only at line 62, after two error-return branches (lines 55-57 and 60-61) that exit via ThrowReaderException without releasing it. A crafted PCD file with a bad magic/header size or number_images>65535 triggers the early return, leaking the 0x800*3 buffer per read; repeated processing of such files consumes memory (DoS). The consequence is memory exhaustion, not corruption or disclosure.

commit_msg:
Fix a padding oracle in PKCS7_dataDecode and CMS_decrypt_set1_pkey

An attack is simple, if the first CMS_recipientInfo is valid but the
second CMS_recipientInfo is chosen ciphertext. If the second
recipientInfo decodes to PKCS #1 v1.5 form plaintext, the correct
encryption key will be replaced by garbage, and the message cannot be
decoded, but if the RSA decryption fails, the correct encryption key is
used and the recipient will not notice the attack.

As a work around for this potential attack the length of the decrypted
key must be equal to the cipher default key length, in case the
certifiate is not given and all recipientInfo are tried out.

The old behaviour can be re-enabled in the CMS code by setting the
CMS_DEBUG_DECRYPT flag.

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/9777)

(cherry picked from commit 5840ed0cd1e6487d247efbc1a04136a41d7b3a37)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                               PKCS7_RECIP_INFO *ri, EVP_PKEY *pkey)', '                         ri->enc_key->data, ri->enc_key->length) <= 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['                               PKCS7_RECIP_INFO *ri, EVP_PKEY *pkey,', '                               size_t fixlen)', '                         ri->enc_key->data, ri->enc_key->length) <= 0', '            || eklen == 0', '            || (fixlen != 0 && eklen != fixlen)) {']}
description: In situations where an attacker receives automated notification of the success or failure of a decryption attempt an attacker, after sending a very large number of messages to be decrypted, can recover a CMS/PKCS7 transported encryption key or decrypt any RSA encrypted message that was encrypted with the public RSA key, using a Bleichenbacher padding oracle attack. Applications are not affected if they use a certificate together with the private RSA key to the CMS_decrypt or PKCS7_decrypt functions to select the correct recipient info to decrypt. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1d (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1c). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.0l (Affected 1.1.0-1.1.0k). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2t (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2s).

code_evidence: The second EVP_PKEY_decrypt call is the only failure check on the RSA/PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption result. The function returns 0 only when the call itself fails; it does not verify that the recovered plaintext has the expected key length, so any successfully decrypted block is accepted and returned via *pek/*peklen.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is in the use of RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption without countermeasures against a known Bleichenbacher oracle, making the cryptographic protocol risky to use. This fits CWE-327; it is a protocol-level cryptographic weakness rather than a generic improper input check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The recipient-info decryption path accepts any RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption that returns non-error, without binding the result length to the expected content-encryption key length. An attacker supplying a crafted recipientInfo can distinguish a valid PKCS#1 v1.5 padding from a failure based on whether the correct key is later used, exposing a padding oracle that leaks the transport key.

commit_msg:
xen/events: avoid removing an event channel while handling it

Today it can happen that an event channel is being removed from the
system while the event handling loop is active. This can lead to a
race resulting in crashes or WARN() splats when trying to access the
irq_info structure related to the event channel.

Fix this problem by using a rwlock taken as reader in the event
handling loop and as writer when deallocating the irq_info structure.

As the observed problem was a NULL dereference in evtchn_from_irq()
make this function more robust against races by testing the irq_info
pointer to be not NULL before dereferencing it.

And finally make all accesses to evtchn_to_irq[row][col] atomic ones
in order to avoid seeing partial updates of an array element in irq
handling. Note that irq handling can be entered only for event channels
which have been valid before, so any not populated row isn't a problem
in this regard, as rows are only ever added and never removed.

This is XSA-331.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Reported-by: Jinoh Kang <luke1337@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tread_lock(&evtchn_rwlock);', '', '\tread_unlock(&evtchn_rwlock);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.9.1, as used with Xen through 4.14.x. drivers/xen/events/events_base.c allows event-channel removal during the event-handling loop (a race condition). This can cause a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by a dom0 crash via events for an in-reconfiguration paravirtualized device, aka CID-073d0552ead5.

code_evidence: The do-while loop clears vcpu_info->evtchn_upcall_pending, calls xen_evtchn_handle_events(cpu) to process pending event channels, and re-reads the pending flag to decide whether to iterate again. In the before state this loop runs without any lock protecting the event-channel/irq_info structures that xen_evtchn_handle_events traverses, so concurrent removal of an event channel can free irq_info while the handler dereferences it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is a concurrent code sequence lacking exclusive access to shared event-channel state; an interfering deallocation path can modify that resource mid-loop, violating exclusivity/atomicity, which matches CWE-362. The NULL dereference is a downstream symptom rather than the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the event-handling loop accesses event-channel state without synchronization, while another path can remove/deallocate an event channel concurrently. Trigger: a pending upcall processed in this loop races with event-channel deallocation. Supported consequence: use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference in the handler, leading to crash/instability.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix race between read and ioctl

The read from ALSA timer device, the function snd_timer_user_tread(),
may access to an uninitialized struct snd_timer_user fields when the
read is concurrently performed while the ioctl like
snd_timer_user_tselect() is invoked.  We have already fixed the races
among ioctls via a mutex, but we seem to have forgotten the race
between read vs ioctl.

This patch simply applies (more exactly extends the already applied
range of) tu->ioctl_lock in snd_timer_user_tread() for closing the
race window.

Reported-by: Alexander Potapenko <glider@google.com>
Tested-by: Alexander Potapenko <glider@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tmutex_lock(&tu->ioctl_lock);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&tu->ioctl_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&tu->ioctl_lock);', '\t\t\tmutex_unlock(&tu->ioctl_lock);', '\t\t\tmutex_lock(&tu->ioctl_lock);', '\tmutex_unlock(&tu->ioctl_lock);']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.11.5 is vulnerable to a data race in the ALSA /dev/snd/timer driver resulting in local users being able to read information belonging to other users, i.e., uninitialized memory contents may be disclosed when a read and an ioctl happen at the same time.

code_evidence: Line 9 reads tu->tread to pick a unit size, then line 10 takes only qlock; the queue index and count are updated at lines 34-37 under qlock, but the unlock at line 37 drops that protection before the copy at lines 40-46, which only holds ioctl_lock. The tqueue/queue contents and tread flag can thus change between the qused check and the copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies kernel queue memory to a user buffer without holding the lock that guards concurrent reconfiguration, so another user's or uninitialized contents can be exposed. This is an unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data, matching CWE-200; the race is the enabling mechanism, not a separate target label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: read and ioctl paths do not share a consistent lock, so a concurrent tselect ioctl can reallocate or reinitialize the queue and tread after qhead/qused are captured. Trigger: one thread calls read while another performs the ioctl. Consequence: copy_to_user at lines 40-46 sends stale or uninitialized queue memory to the user, disclosing kernel data to a local reader.
