description: Oniguruma before 6.9.3 allows Stack Exhaustion in regcomp.c because of recursion in regparse.c.

code_evidence: parse_char_class increments env->parse_depth at entry and only rejects when it exceeds ParseDepthLimit, returning ONIGERR_PARSE_DEPTH_LIMIT_OVER.
The TK_CC_CC_OPEN case recursively calls parse_char_class(&anode, tok, &p, end, env) for a nested '[' within a character class, so each nested class open adds a stack frame.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly recurses on attacker-controlled nested class syntax with only a depth counter as a constraint, matching CWE-674's uncontrolled recursion consuming program stack. This is recursion depth control, not merely an input-size or allocation limit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nested character-class openings trigger self-recursion in parse_char_class, and the only guard is the depth counter check at entry. Trigger: a pattern with deeply nested '[' class-open tokens. Consequence: unbounded stack growth leading to stack exhaustion before the limit is reached or when the limit is too permissive, causing a crash/DoS during compilation.

commit_msg:
"nt_len - CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE" is passed directly from
ksmbd_decode_ntlmssp_auth_blob to ksmbd_auth_ntlmv2. Malicious requests
can set nt_len to less than CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE, which results in a negative
number (or large unsigned value) used for a subsequent memcpy in
ksmbd_auth_ntlvm2 and can cause a panic.

Fixes: e2f34481b24d ("cifsd: add server-side procedures for SMB3")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: William Liu <will@willsroot.io>
Signed-off-by: Hrvoje Mišetić <misetichrvoje@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Namjae Jeon <linkinjeon@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (blob_len < (u64)dn_off + dn_len || blob_len < (u64)nt_off + nt_len)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (blob_len < (u64)dn_off + dn_len || blob_len < (u64)nt_off + nt_len ||', '\t    nt_len < CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE)']}
description: A bug affects the Linux kernel’s ksmbd NTLMv2 authentication and is known to crash the OS immediately in Linux-based systems.

code_evidence: nt_off and nt_len are read from the attacker-controlled NtChallengeResponse fields; the bounds check only verifies blob_len against nt_off + nt_len, not that nt_len is at least CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE.
nt_len - CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE is computed with unsigned short arithmetic and passed as the length to ksmbd_auth_ntlmv2, which uses it for a memcpy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The underflowed length drives a memcpy that writes beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds Write). The arithmetic underflow is the cause; the out-of-bounds write and crash are the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
ret = ksmbd_auth_ntlmv2(conn, sess,
(struct ntlmv2_resp *)((char *)authblob + nt_off),
nt_len - CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE,
domain_name, conn->ntlmssp.cryptkey);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is a missing lower-bound check on nt_len before subtracting CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE. A malicious request can set nt_len below CIFS_ENCPWD_SIZE, so the subtraction underflows to a large unsigned value that is used as a memcpy length in ksmbd_auth_ntlmv2, writing past the destination buffer and crashing the kernel.

commit_msg:
x86/shadow: fix refcount overflow check

Commit c385d27079 ("x86 shadow: for multi-page shadows, explicitly track
the first page") reduced the refcount width to 25, without adjusting the
overflow check. Eliminate the disconnect by using a manifest constant.

Interestingly, up to commit 047782fa01 ("Out-of-sync L1 shadows: OOS
snapshot") the refcount was 27 bits wide, yet the check was already
using 26.

This is XSA-249.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ( unlikely(nx >= 1U<<26) )'], 'added_lines': ['    if ( unlikely(nx >= (1U << PAGE_SH_REFCOUNT_WIDTH)) )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing guest OS users to cause a denial of service (host OS crash) or gain host OS privileges by leveraging an incorrect mask for reference-count overflow checking in shadow mode.

code_evidence: Lines 7-8 read the 25-bit shadow refcount into x and compute nx = x + 1. Line 9 checks overflow against a hard-coded 1U<<26 threshold instead of the actual PAGE_SH_REFCOUNT_WIDTH of 25. When the check passes, line 15 writes nx back into the fixed-width sp->u.sh.count bitfield.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The mismatched mask lets the increment write past the intended range of the fixed-width bitfield buffer, so the operation falls outside the field's bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root cause is the incorrect bound constant, not merely an integer wrap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The overflow guard uses a mask wider than the refcount field, so a count reaching the 25-bit limit is not rejected and nx wraps or truncates when stored into sp->u.sh.count. Trigger: repeated reference acquisition on a shadow page. Consequence: corrupted reference count, permitting premature free/reuse of shadow memory and host crash or privilege escalation.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/271
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (map_length >= 64)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (map_length >= 32)']}
description: The ReadPCXImage function in coders/pcx.c in ImageMagick 7.0.4.9 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (attempted large memory allocation and application crash) via a crafted file. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2016-8862 and CVE-2016-8866.

code_evidence: Line 76 reads attacker-controlled map_length as an unsigned char; line 77 only rejects values >= 64, permitting up to 63.
Line 80 computes map_length = 1 << map_length, so a value of 63 yields an enormous shift result used as a size/count.
Lines 108-109 allocate number_colormaps * 3 * map_length bytes using that shifted value.
Lines 113-115 iterate x < map_length and write *p++ into the colormap buffer, so the loop bound derives from the same oversized value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the loop at lines 113-115 operates on a buffer whose length is derived from an insufficiently bounded value, permitting writes outside the intended buffer boundary. The primary observable effect reported is large allocation leading to crash, but the underlying buffer-bound weakness is CWE-119.

evidence_lines.code:
one=1;
map_length=one << map_length;

colormap=(unsigned char *) AcquireQuantumMemory(number_colormaps,
3*map_length*sizeof(*colormap));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the header field map_length is validated against 64 rather than a bound consistent with the buffer sizing arithmetic, and it is then left-shifted to form the colormap length. A crafted file with a large map_length produces an attempted huge allocation (line 108) and, if allocation succeeds or is partially handled, the line 114 loop writes past the intended colormap extent. Trigger is a crafted RLE file; supported consequence is resource exhaustion/DoS and potential out-of-bounds write.

description: The gf_hinter_track_new function in GPAC 1.0.1 allows attackers to read memory via a crafted file in the MP4Box command.

commit_msg:
chanserv/flags: make Anope FLAGS compatibility an option

Previously, ChanServ FLAGS behavior could be modified by registering or
dropping the keyword nicks "LIST", "CLEAR", and "MODIFY".
Now, a configuration option is available that when turned on (default),
disables registration of these keyword nicks and enables this
compatibility feature. When turned off, registration of these keyword
nicks is possible, and compatibility to Anope's FLAGS command is
disabled.

Fixes atheme/atheme#397
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\telse if (!strcasecmp(target, "LIST") && myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL)', '\telse if (!strcasecmp(target, "CLEAR") && myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL)', '\telse if (!strcasecmp(target, "MODIFY") && myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL)'], 'added_lines': ['\telse if (anope_flags_compat && !strcasecmp(target, "LIST") && myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL)', '\telse if (anope_flags_compat && !strcasecmp(target, "CLEAR") && myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL)', '\telse if (anope_flags_compat && !strcasecmp(target, "MODIFY") && myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL)']}
description: modules/chanserv/flags.c in Atheme before 7.2.7 allows remote attackers to modify the Anope FLAGS behavior by registering and dropping the (1) LIST, (2) CLEAR, or (3) MODIFY keyword nicks.

code_evidence: The special target keywords LIST, CLEAR, and MODIFY are matched only by strcasecmp and myentity_find_ext(target) == NULL, with no check of the anope_flags_compat configuration flag, so any user can trigger these compatibility branches by supplying the reserved keyword as target.

The CLEAR branch deletes every non-founder access entry via object_unref while iterating mc->chanacs; the only gate is chanacs_source_has_flag(mc, si, CA_FOUNDER) checked after target is freed, so the branch is reachable by keyword rather than by an entity lookup.

The MODIFY branch rewrites target from parv[2] and proceeds into the general flag-modification path; because it is keyed on the literal keyword, the reserved name collides with normal access-list processing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the function fails to enforce the intended access-control policy: the compatibility behavior is a restricted mode that should be disabled by configuration, yet the branches run regardless, letting keyword nicks drive privilege-affecting access-list operations. This is an enforcement failure of an access restriction rather than a memory-safety issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: reserved compatibility keywords are recognized unconditionally instead of being gated by anope_flags_compat, so the keyword nicks LIST/CLEAR/MODIFY are treated as command modifiers. Trigger: a user registers or drops these keyword nicks and issues FLAGS with the keyword as target. Consequence: the Anope FLAGS compatibility behavior (including the CLEAR path that mass-removes access entries) is activated outside the intended configuration, altering channel access control.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: make the internal memory data base the default

Having a file backed data base has the only advantage of being capable
to dump the contents of it while Xenstore is running, and potentially
using less swap space in case the data base can't be kept in memory.

It has the major disadvantage of a huge performance overhead: switching
to keep the data base in memory only speeds up live update of xenstored
with 120000 nodes from 20 minutes to 11 seconds. A complete tree walk
of this configuration will be reduced from 7 seconds to 280 msecs
(measured by "xenstore-control check").

So make the internal memory data base the default and enhance the
"--internal-db" command line parameter to take an optional parameter
allowing to switch the internal data base back to the file based one.

This is part of XSA-419.

Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        snprintf(cmdline, 512, "--event %d --internal-db %s", rv, param);', '        snprintf(cmdline, 512, "--event %d --internal-db", rv);'], 'added_lines': ['        snprintf(cmdline, 512, "--event %d %s", rv, param);', '        snprintf(cmdline, 512, "--event %d", rv);']}
description: Xenstore: Cooperating guests can create arbitrary numbers of nodes T[his CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] Since the fix of XSA-322 any Xenstore node owned by a removed domain will be modified to be owned by Dom0. This will allow two malicious guests working together to create an arbitrary number of Xenstore nodes. This is possible by domain A letting domain B write into domain A's local Xenstore tree. Domain B can then create many nodes and reboot. The nodes created by domain B will now be owned by Dom0. By repeating this process over and over again an arbitrary number of nodes can be created, as Dom0's number of nodes isn't limited by Xenstore quota.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only formats a xenstore command line and manages domain setup; it contains no evidence of an unreleased allocation, and the patch merely removes the --internal-db flag, so CWE-401 is not supported.

commit_msg:
Fix security vulnerability with AvgPoolGrad

PiperOrigin-RevId: 461724457
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      output_shape.AddDim(shape_vec(i));'], 'added_lines': ['      OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, output_shape.AddDimWithStatus(shape_vec(i)));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The `AvgPoolOp` function takes an argument `ksize` that must be positive but is not checked. A negative `ksize` can trigger a `CHECK` failure and crash the program. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 3a6ac52664c6c095aa2b114e742b0aa17fdce78f. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds to this issue.

code_evidence: The loop reads each element of the user-supplied `tensor_in_shape` (input 0) and passes it to `output_shape.AddDim(shape_vec(i))`. The value is an int32 taken directly from the input tensor with no positivity or bound check before being used as a dimension.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because the unchecked input leads to a reachable assertion/CHECK failure that terminates the program. This is distinct from a mere input-validation gap (CWE-20): the demonstrated impact is process abort from an assertion, matching the Reachable Assertion description.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shape vector from `tensor_in_shape` is trusted and fed into `AddDim` without validating that each dimension is non-negative. A crafted input tensor with a negative value reaches `AddDim`, whose internal `CHECK`/assert fails, aborting the process. The trigger is attacker-controlled input shape data; the supported consequence is a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg: Prevent memory use after free
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  (void) CloseBlob(pwp_image);', '  pwp_image=DestroyImage(pwp_image);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the ReadPWPImage function in coders/pwp.c in ImageMagick 6.9.5-5 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or have other unspecified impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: Line 110 closes the blob of pwp_image and line 111 destroys pwp_image, freeing the image object that was initially assigned to image at line 35.

After freeing pwp_image, line 112 calls EOFBlob(image) and lines 117-118 use image->filename; since image still aliases the destroyed pwp_image when no next_image was linked, these are uses of freed memory. Line 121 then calls CloseBlob(image) on the same stale pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly destroys pwp_image and then dereferences image, which aliases that freed object, matching CWE-416 use after free. This is not a double free; the defect is post-free access through the stale image pointer.

evidence_lines.code:
(void) CloseBlob(pwp_image);
pwp_image=DestroyImage(pwp_image);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pwp_image is destroyed while image may still reference the same object (image=pwp_image at line 35). Trigger: a crafted PWP file that reaches the cleanup path without replacing image via next_image. Consequence: EOFBlob and image->filename access freed memory, causing a crash (DoS) or other undefined behavior.

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20570)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (!tree_link_nodes(curr, cache))'], 'added_lines': ['        if (!tree_link_nodes(curr, cache, tree))']}
description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over every policy level from index 1, fetching each level's policy cache and linking nodes via tree_link_nodes(curr, cache) without passing the policy tree, so node linking cannot enforce tree-wide constraints.
The conditional linking of any-policy nodes via tree_link_any(curr, cache, tree) is also performed per level without bounding work, and tree_prune is invoked on each level.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements X.509 certificate-chain policy validation; its unbounded per-level linking causes verification of attacker-supplied certificates to consume excessive resources. This is a validation-handling flaw in the certificate verification path, fitting CWE-295, though the impact is DoS rather than direct acceptance of a bad certificate.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: policy-tree node linking is done per level without a tree-wide bound, so a malicious certificate chain with policy constraints drives repeated (exponential) traversal during verification. Trigger: enabling policy processing and supplying a crafted chain. Consequence: excessive CPU consumption, a denial of service during certificate validation.

description: The exif_process_IFD_TAG function in ext/exif/exif.c in PHP before 5.5.35, 5.6.x before 5.6.21, and 7.x before 7.0.6 does not properly construct spprintf arguments, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted header data.

code_evidence: NumDirEntries is read from dir_start (line 10) before any check that two bytes are available at dir_start; the bound check on line 11 uses the just-read value and computes dir_start+2+NumDirEntries*12, so a short buffer is read out of bounds at line 10.

The for loop iterates de up to NumDirEntries and calls exif_process_IFD_TAG with dir_start+2+12*de (line 16); the loop bound depends on the untrusted entry count validated only by the overflow-prone expression on line 11.

After the loop, php_ifd_get32u reads four bytes at dir_start+2+12*de (line 24); the check on line 26 tests the resulting NextDirOffset against offset_base+IFDlength, not the read address, so the 4-byte read can exceed the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs memory reads outside the intended IFD buffer boundary due to missing length constraints, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read within a memory buffer; the added upstream checks confirm the missing bound validation as the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function reads IFD header fields (entry count and next-IFD offset) from crafted JPEG data without first ensuring the corresponding bytes lie within the IFD buffer, and the size check on line 11 does not guard the initial 2-byte read. Trigger: a crafted Exif header with a truncated or oversized IFD. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap reads, leading to denial of service or possible information disclosure.

commit_msg:
The X protocol uses CARD16 values to represent the length so
this would overflow.

CVE-2021-31535

Signed-off-by: Matthieu Herrb <matthieu@herrb.eu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (n >= USHRT_MAX)', '            return(0);']}
description: LookupCol.c in X.Org X through X11R7.7 and libX11 before 1.7.1 might allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. The libX11 XLookupColor request (intended for server-side color lookup) contains a flaw allowing a client to send color-name requests with a name longer than the maximum size allowed by the protocol (and also longer than the maximum packet size for normal-sized packets). The user-controlled data exceeding the maximum size is then interpreted by the server as additional X protocol requests and executed, e.g., to disable X server authorization completely. For example, if the victim encounters malicious terminal control sequences for color codes, then the attacker may be able to take full control of the running graphical session.

code_evidence: Line 14 computes n = strlen(spec) with no upper bound. For non-'#' names, line 15's branch is skipped, so no length validation occurs before the XLookupColor request. Line 68 truncates n into a CARD16 nbytes, line 69 computes req->length from the full n, and line 70 copies all n bytes via Data, so a name longer than USHRT_MAX desynchronizes the protocol length and overruns the fixed request packet.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer copy (Data at line 70) of input whose size is not checked against the destination request size, matching CWE-120's unchecked-size copy. It is not merely an integer truncation issue: the unchecked copy of oversized input is the direct cause of the overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unbounded user-controlled color name is copied into a fixed-size X protocol request without checking that its length fits the CARD16 length field. Trigger: a client passes a spec longer than USHRT_MAX (e.g., via terminal color control sequences). Consequence: excess bytes are interpreted as additional X requests, enabling injected commands such as disabling server authorization.

The fixed version adds a check that encJoinAcceptSize does not exceed LORAMAC_JOIN_ACCEPT_FRAME_MAX_SIZE before this copy.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no validation that the attacker-influenced encJoinAcceptSize fits the destination decJoinAccept before the memcpy1. Trigger: a received JoinAccept frame with an oversized size value. Consequence: a write past the end of decJoinAccept, corrupting adjacent memory (integrity/availability), with potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Fixes #264.

The JP2 decoder was allowing the decoding of a code stream to be
attempted when the stream has inconsistent values for the number of
components and/or the component types.  For such invalid streams,
only a warning would be issued and decoding would proceed.  This is
dangerous, however, as it can lead to many unexpected paths through
the code, which in some cases have been demonstrated to result in
security vulnerabilities.  This code change makes decoding of these
types invalid code streams a hard error.

commit_msg:
evtchn: evtchn_reset() shouldn't succeed with still-open ports

While the function closes all ports, it does so without holding any
lock, and hence racing requests may be issued causing new ports to get
opened. This would have been problematic in particular if such a newly
opened port had a port number above the new implementation limit (i.e.
when switching from FIFO to 2-level) after the reset, as prior to
"evtchn: relax port_is_valid()" this could have led to e.g.
evtchn_close()'s "BUG_ON(!port_is_valid(d2, port2))" to trigger.

Introduce a counter of active ports and check that it's (still) no
larger then the number of Xen internally used ones after obtaining the
necessary lock in evtchn_reset().

As to the access model of the new {active,xen}_evtchns fields - while
all writes get done using write_atomic(), reads ought to use
read_atomic() only when outside of a suitably locked region.

Note that as of now evtchn_bind_virq() and evtchn_bind_ipi() don't have
a need to call check_free_port().

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    rc = get_free_port(ld);', '    port = rc;'], 'added_lines': ['    port = rc = get_free_port(ld);', '    write_atomic(&ld->xen_evtchns, ld->xen_evtchns + 1);', '', '    check_free_port(ld, port);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: get_free_port(ld) selects a free port under ld->event_lock, and evtchn_from_port maps it into chn for subsequent setup.

The out label releases ld->event_lock and returns rc<0 ? rc : port; the newly allocated port is only marked active after the lock is dropped, leaving a window where the port state and internal bookkeeping are not yet consistent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the allocation and the port-accounting update are not performed as one exclusive atomic sequence on the shared event-channel resource; an interfering reset can interleave. This is a synchronization/timing flaw, not merely a bounds error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function reserves a free port and returns it while the port's active-accounting update is not performed atomically with the allocation. A concurrent evtchn_reset() can observe the port as not yet active, close/reset channels, and then the racing allocation completes, leaving an open port inconsistent with reset state. This violates the exclusivity/atomicity of the shared event-channel state and can lead to invalid port assumptions, bug checks, out-of-bounds access, or privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
xen/events: avoid removing an event channel while handling it

Today it can happen that an event channel is being removed from the
system while the event handling loop is active. This can lead to a
race resulting in crashes or WARN() splats when trying to access the
irq_info structure related to the event channel.

Fix this problem by using a rwlock taken as reader in the event
handling loop and as writer when deallocating the irq_info structure.

As the observed problem was a NULL dereference in evtchn_from_irq()
make this function more robust against races by testing the irq_info
pointer to be not NULL before dereferencing it.

And finally make all accesses to evtchn_to_irq[row][col] atomic ones
in order to avoid seeing partial updates of an array element in irq
handling. Note that irq handling can be entered only for event channels
which have been valid before, so any not populated row isn't a problem
in this regard, as rows are only ever added and never removed.

This is XSA-331.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Reported-by: Jinoh Kang <luke1337@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.9.1, as used with Xen through 4.14.x. drivers/xen/events/events_base.c allows event-channel removal during the event-handling loop (a race condition). This can cause a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by a dom0 crash via events for an in-reconfiguration paravirtualized device, aka CID-073d0552ead5.

code_evidence: xen_free_irq reads the shared irq_info via info_for_irq(irq), then removes it from the list, clears the global mapping with set_info_for_irq(irq, NULL), and frees it with kfree(info). In the shown function these operations are unsynchronized, so a concurrent event-handling loop dereferencing the same irq_info can observe a freed or NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's teardown of a shared structure races with a concurrent reader lacking mutual exclusion, matching CWE-362's non-atomic/exclusivity violation. A related UAF is only the downstream consequence; the weakness is the unsynchronized concurrent access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared irq_info is torn down (list_del, set_info_for_irq NULL, kfree) without exclusive synchronization against the event-handling loop that reads it. Trigger: an event channel is removed while the handler is concurrently dereferencing its irq_info. Consequence: NULL dereference or use-after-free, yielding crashes/WARN splats (DoS).

commit_msg:
Prevent KDC unset status assertion failures

Assign status values if S4U2Self padata fails to decode, if an
S4U2Proxy request uses invalid KDC options, or if an S4U2Proxy request
uses an evidence ticket which does not match the canonicalized request
server principal name.  Reported by Samuel Cabrero.

If a status value is not assigned during KDC processing, default to
"UNKNOWN_REASON" rather than failing an assertion.  This change will
prevent future denial of service bugs due to similar mistakes, and
will allow us to omit assigning status values for unlikely errors such
as small memory allocation failures.

CVE-2017-11368:

In MIT krb5 1.7 and later, an authenticated attacker can cause an
assertion failure in krb5kdc by sending an invalid S4U2Self or
S4U2Proxy request.

  CVSSv3 Vector: AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H/E:H/RL:O/RC:C

ticket: 8599 (new)
target_version: 1.15-next
target_version: 1.14-next
tags: pullup
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (errcode != 0)', '        assert (state->status != 0);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (errcode != 0 && state->status == NULL)', '        state->status = "UNKNOWN_REASON";']}
description: In MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) 1.7 and later, an authenticated attacker can cause a KDC assertion failure by sending invalid S4U2Self or S4U2Proxy requests.

code_evidence: At the egress label, when errcode is nonzero the code asserts state->status != 0, requiring an error-status string to have been assigned; otherwise the assertion aborts the KDC.

Early error paths such as the initial 'if (errcode) goto egress;' jump to egress without assigning state->status, so a request that fails before any status assignment reaches the assertion with status still NULL.
A later block only sets state->status from emsg after the assertion point, so it cannot prevent the abort for those paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains an assert() reachable via attacker-controlled request processing, and firing it terminates the server process. This matches CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion), whose impact is DoS via crash/exit; the weakness is the reachable assertion itself, not a memory-safety flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
if (errcode)
goto egress;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the egress error path unconditionally asserts that state->status was set for any nonzero errcode, but several failure paths (e.g. the initial errcode check) reach egress without assigning it. An authenticated attacker sending a request that triggers such an early failure causes the assertion to fire, aborting the krb5kdc process and denying service to other clients.

commit_msg:
tcp: fix SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS for normal skbs

__sock_recv_timestamp can be called for both normal skbs (for
receive timestamps) and for skbs on the error queue (for transmit
timestamps).

Commit 1c885808e456
(tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING)
assumes any skb passed to __sock_recv_timestamp are from
the error queue, containing OPT_STATS in the content of the skb.
This results in accessing invalid memory or generating junk
data.

To fix this, set skb->pkt_type to PACKET_OUTGOING for packets
on the error queue. This is safe because on the receive path
on local sockets skb->pkt_type is never set to PACKET_OUTGOING.
With that, copy OPT_STATS from a packet, only if its pkt_type
is PACKET_OUTGOING.

Fixes: 1c885808e456 ("tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING")
Reported-by: JongHwan Kim <zzoru007@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Soheil Hassas Yeganeh <soheil@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Willem de Bruijn <willemb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tskb_set_err_queue(skb);']}
description: The TCP stack in the Linux kernel through 4.10.6 mishandles the SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS feature, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from the kernel's internal socket data structures or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via crafted system calls, related to net/core/skbuff.c and net/socket.c.

code_evidence: The function accepts an skb and enqueues it onto sk->sk_error_queue without marking it as an error-queue skb (no pkt_type/tag set here in the before state).

It only manipulates skb ownership, truesize accounting and dst refcount before tail-queuing the skb, so a normal receive-path skb can reach the error queue indistinguishable from a genuine error-queue skb.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The downstream consumer reads a field past the intended skb content because this function fails to establish the distinguishing constraint, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. It is not merely a logic flaw: the misclassification directly causes reading beyond valid buffer content.

evidence_lines.code:
skb_dst_force(skb);
skb_queue_tail(&sk->sk_error_queue, skb);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: enqueued skbs are not tagged as belonging to the error queue, so later __sock_recv_timestamp cannot distinguish normal skbs from error-queue skbs and reads OPT_STATS content that is not present. Trigger: a skb passed here from the normal receive path is later consumed by the timestamping path. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of skb data, leaking kernel memory or causing a crash.

commit_msg:
[gsm] Delay the creation of the GsmXSMPClient until it really exists

We used to create the GsmXSMPClient before the XSMP connection is really
accepted. This can lead to some issues, though. An example is:
https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=598211#c19. Quoting:

 "What is happening is that a new client (probably metacity in your
 case) is opening an ICE connection in the GSM_MANAGER_PHASE_END_SESSION
 phase, which causes a new GsmXSMPClient to be added to the client
 store. The GSM_MANAGER_PHASE_EXIT phase then begins before the client
 has had a chance to establish a xsmp connection, which means that
 client->priv->conn will not be initialized at the point that xsmp_stop
 is called on the new unregistered client."

The fix is to create the GsmXSMPClient object when there's a real XSMP
connection. This implies moving the timeout that makes sure we don't
have an empty client to the XSMP server.

https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=598211

description: Bad reference counting in the context of accept_ice_connection() in gsm-xsmp-server.c in old versions of gnome-session up until version 2.29.92 allows a local attacker to establish ICE connections to gnome-session with invalid authentication data (an invalid magic cookie). Each failed authentication attempt will leak a file descriptor in gnome-session. When the maximum number of file descriptors is exhausted in the gnome-session process, it will enter an infinite loop trying to communicate without success, consuming 100% of the CPU. The graphical session associated with the gnome-session process will stop working correctly, because communication with gnome-session is no longer possible.

commit_msg:
Chain binding only requires the rule addition/insertion command within
the same transaction. Removal of rules from chain bindings within the
same transaction makes no sense, userspace does not utilize this
feature. Replace nft_chain_is_bound() check to nft_chain_binding() in
rule deletion commands. Replace command implies a rule deletion, reject
this command too.

Rule flush command can also safely rely on this nft_chain_binding()
check because unbound chains are not allowed since 62e1e94b246e
("netfilter: nf_tables: reject unbound chain set before commit phase").

Fixes: d0e2c7de92c7 ("netfilter: nf_tables: add NFT_CHAIN_BINDING")
Reported-by: Kevin Rich <kevinrich1337@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (nft_chain_binding(chain)) {', '\t\t\terr = -EOPNOTSUPP;', '\t\t\tgoto err_destroy_flow_rule;', '\t\t}', '']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's netfilter: nf_tables component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

Addition and removal of rules from chain bindings within the same transaction causes leads to use-after-free.

We recommend upgrading past commit f15f29fd4779be8a418b66e9d52979bb6d6c2325.

code_evidence: Line 46-47 rejects chains where nft_chain_is_bound() is true, but this predicate does not cover chains marked as binding chains (NFT_CHAIN_BINDING), so a binding chain can reach the rule-replace path.

At lines 151-160 the NLM_F_REPLACE branch calls nft_delrule(&ctx, old_rule) to schedule deletion of the existing rule and then adds the new rule adjacent to old_rule->list; the added guard in the patch rejects this path via nft_chain_binding(chain), confirming the missing constraint.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the unsafe operation is reuse of a rule object after nft_delrule schedules its destruction within the same transaction; the fix adds a missing binding-chain constraint rather than fixing an unrelated weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (nft_chain_is_bound(chain))
return -EOPNOTSUPP;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pre-patch check only blocks bound chains, not binding chains, allowing a rule replacement inside a binding chain to enqueue a deletion and re-add a rule in the same transaction. Trigger: a netlink NEWRULE request with NLM_F_REPLACE targeting a chain that is a binding. Consequence: the old rule is freed at commit while the transaction still references/reorders it, yielding use-after-free and possible local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Check outbuf length in mutt_to_base64()

The obuf can be overflowed in auth_cram.c, and possibly auth_gss.c.

Thanks to Jeriko One for the bug report.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  len = mutt_b64_decode(obuf, idata->buf + 2);'], 'added_lines': ['  len = mutt_b64_decode(obuf, idata->buf + 2, sizeof(obuf));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Mutt before 1.10.1 and NeoMutt before 2018-07-16. They have a buffer overflow via base64 data.

code_evidence: Line 3 declares obuf as a fixed LONG_STRING stack buffer. Line 23 calls mutt_b64_decode(obuf, idata->buf + 2) without passing the destination size, so the server-controlled base64 data is decoded into obuf with no bound. Line 29 then writes obuf[len] = '\0' at the attacker-influenced length.

Lines 32-33 reuse obuf: snprintf writes the user name plus a space and mutt_md5_toascii writes the HMAC ASCII at obuf + off, both operating on the same buffer whose contents were just filled by the unbounded decode.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a buffer copy operation (mutt_b64_decode writing into obuf) without checking that the input size is less than the output buffer size, matching CWE-120's classic buffer overflow. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); the copy writes past obuf's end.

evidence_lines.code:
int off = snprintf(obuf, sizeof(obuf), "%s ", idata->conn->account.user);
mutt_md5_toascii(hmac_response, obuf + off);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the CRAM-MD5 challenge from the server is base64-decoded into the fixed-size obuf with no destination-length check, so a long challenge overflows the stack buffer during the copy. The trigger is a malicious or oversized server response to AUTHENTICATE CRAM-MD5. The supported consequence is memory corruption of the stack, potentially leading to crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
can: usb_8dev: usb_8dev_start_xmit(): fix double dev_kfree_skb() in error path

There is no need to call dev_kfree_skb() when usb_submit_urb() fails
because can_put_echo_skb() deletes original skb and
can_free_echo_skb() deletes the cloned skb.

Fixes: 0024d8ad1639 ("can: usb_8dev: Add support for USB2CAN interface from 8 devices")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20220311080614.45229-1-hbh25y@gmail.com
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Hangyu Hua <hbh25y@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (unlikely(err))', '\t\tgoto failed;', '\telse if (atomic_read(&priv->active_tx_urbs) >= MAX_TX_URBS)', 'failed:', '\tcan_free_echo_skb(netdev, context->echo_index, NULL);', '', '\tusb_unanchor_urb(urb);', '\tusb_free_coherent(priv->udev, size, buf, urb->transfer_dma);', '', '\tatomic_dec(&priv->active_tx_urbs);', '', '\tif (err == -ENODEV)', '\t\tnetif_device_detach(netdev);', '\telse', '\t\tnetdev_warn(netdev, "failed tx_urb %d\\n", err);', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tif (unlikely(err)) {', '\t\tcan_free_echo_skb(netdev, context->echo_index, NULL);', '', '\t\tusb_unanchor_urb(urb);', '\t\tusb_free_coherent(priv->udev, size, buf, urb->transfer_dma);', '', '\t\tatomic_dec(&priv->active_tx_urbs);', '', '\t\tif (err == -ENODEV)', '\t\t\tnetif_device_detach(netdev);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tnetdev_warn(netdev, "failed tx_urb %d\\n", err);', '\t\tstats->tx_dropped++;', '\t} else if (atomic_read(&priv->active_tx_urbs) >= MAX_TX_URBS)']}
description: usb_8dev_start_xmit in drivers/net/can/usb/usb_8dev.c in the Linux kernel through 5.17.1 has a double free.

code_evidence: Line 51 clones the skb into the echo buffer via can_put_echo_skb(); if usb_submit_urb() at line 53 fails, control jumps to the failed label at line 65.
The failed block (lines 65-73) calls can_free_echo_skb() to release the cloned skb, then falls through to nomembuf/nomem and dev_kfree_skb(skb) at line 77, freeing the original skb as well.
Because the error path does not return after can_free_echo_skb(), both the echo-buffer clone and the original skb are freed on the same failure path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same skb allocation is freed on two paths within one invocation: can_free_echo_skb() releases the clone and dev_kfree_skb() releases the original, a double free. This is not merely a use-after-free; the defect is the duplicate release itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the usb_submit_urb() error path frees the echo skb via can_free_echo_skb() but then falls through to dev_kfree_skb(skb) without returning. Trigger: any usb_submit_urb() failure (e.g., -ENODEV). Consequence: the skb is released twice, corrupting the allocator and potentially enabling memory modification or code execution.

commit_msg:
Issue 719:  Fix for TALOS-CAN-154

A RAR file with an invalid zero dictionary size was not being
rejected, leading to a zero-sized allocation for the dictionary
storage which was then overwritten during the dictionary initialization.

Thanks to the Open Source and Threat Intelligence project at Cisco for
reporting this.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      if (rar->dictionary_size == 0) {', '\t      archive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '                          "Invalid zero dictionary size");', '\t      return (ARCHIVE_FATAL);', '      }', '']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the parse_codes function in archive_read_support_format_rar.c in libarchive before 3.2.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a RAR file with a zero-sized dictionary.

code_evidence: Line 25 derives rar->dictionary_size from attacker-controlled bits; when ppmd_flags has 0x20, the value is (byte+1)<<20, so it is nonzero, but the PPMd path at 37-55 allocates with this size and initializes the context at 67.

Lines 210-227: when dictionary_size is zero or lzss.window is NULL, new_size is computed from unp_size and realloc allocates that buffer, then line 226 memsets rar->dictionary_size bytes. If unp_size is 0, new_size is 0, realloc(ptr,0) may return a minimal/non-NULL block, and memset with size 0 is harmless; the overflow arises when dictionary_size is set to a value larger than the allocated new_size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes beyond the intended buffer boundary (memset of dictionary_size into a smaller allocation), which is an out-of-bounds memory operation, matching CWE-119. It is not merely improper input validation; the memory-buffer violation is the direct supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dictionary_size derived from untrusted RAR data can be zero or inconsistent with the allocated lzss.window size. Trigger: a crafted RAR with a zero/invalid dictionary leads to a zero-sized or undersized allocation, then memset at line 226 writes dictionary_size bytes into that buffer. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write, potentially code execution or crash.

commit_msg: Fix use-after-free in PlayerGeneric destructor
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (mixer)', '\t\tdelete mixer;', '\t\tif (mixer->isActive() && !mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (mixer && mixer->isActive() && !mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player))', '\t', '\tif (mixer)', '\t\tdelete mixer;']}
description: PlayerGeneric.cpp in MilkyTracker through 1.02.00 has a use-after-free in the PlayerGeneric destructor.

code_evidence: Line 4 deletes the mixer object; lines 7-8 then dereference mixer via mixer->isActive() and mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player) without re-checking mixer for null, so the freed pointer is used after delete. The later delete player on line 9 runs in the same block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function explicitly deletes mixer and then reads through the same pointer in mixer->isActive()/isDeviceRemoved. Contrast with CWE-476: the defect is not merely a missing null check but use of memory after it was freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destructor frees mixer before the player cleanup block that dereferences mixer, and the dereference at line 7 lacks a null/liveness guard. Trigger: a PlayerGeneric instance whose mixer is non-null and player is non-null, so destruction enters both branches. Consequence: the freed mixer pointer is dereferenced, enabling memory corruption, crash, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
media: xirlink_cit: add missing descriptor sanity checks

Make sure to check that we have two alternate settings and at least one
endpoint before accessing the second altsetting structure and
dereferencing the endpoint arrays.

This specifically avoids dereferencing NULL-pointers or corrupting
memory when a device does not have the expected descriptors.

Note that the sanity check in cit_get_packet_size() is not redundant as
the driver is mixing looking up altsettings by index and by number,
which may not coincide.

Fixes: 659fefa0eb17 ("V4L/DVB: gspca_xirlink_cit: Add support for camera with a bcd version of 0.01")
Fixes: 59f8b0bf3c12 ("V4L/DVB: gspca_xirlink_cit: support bandwidth changing for devices with 1 alt setting")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>     # 2.6.37
Cc: Hans de Goede <hdegoede@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Hans Verkuil <hverkuil-cisco@xs4all.nl>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab+huawei@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (alt->desc.bNumEndpoints < 1)', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.6.1, drivers/media/usb/gspca/xirlink_cit.c (aka the Xirlink camera USB driver) mishandles invalid descriptors, aka CID-a246b4d54770.

code_evidence: Line 6 retrieves the alternate setting by number; lines 7-10 validate only that the returned altsetting pointer is non-NULL before proceeding.
Line 11 unconditionally dereferences alt->endpoint[0] without checking alt->desc.bNumEndpoints, so a descriptor with zero endpoints leaves the endpoint array empty.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function assumes a valid endpoint exists and dereferences the endpoint array entry without a bounds guard; the descriptor-driven trigger yields an invalid pointer access consistent with CWE-476. It is not a plain missing NULL check on alt, which lines 7-10 already handle.

evidence_lines.code: return le16_to_cpu(alt->endpoint[0].desc.wMaxPacketSize);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is a missing check that the selected altsetting actually contains at least one endpoint before indexing endpoint[0]. A malicious or malformed USB device descriptor advertising zero endpoints triggers an out-of-bounds access on the endpoint array, leading to invalid memory read/corruption or a crash rather than a NULL-pointer check failure.

commit_msg:
gryphon: Create pkt_info if it doesn't exist

Try to retrieve the per packet info data first, and create it if
it doesn't exist, rather than assuming it is there on the second
pass. Prevents segfaults in cases with strange TCP sequence issues
(that still show up as bugs in the TCP dissector.) Fix #17737.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (!pinfo->fd->visited) {', '    else {', '        pkt_info = (gryphon_pkt_info_t*)p_get_proto_data(wmem_file_scope(), pinfo, proto_gryphon, (guint32)tvb_raw_offset(tvb));', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['    pkt_info = (gryphon_pkt_info_t*)p_get_proto_data(wmem_file_scope(), pinfo, proto_gryphon, (guint32)tvb_raw_offset(tvb));', '', '    if (!pkt_info) {']}
description: Crash in the Gryphon dissector in Wireshark 3.4.0 to 3.4.10 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file

code_evidence: On the first pass (!pinfo->fd->visited) a gryphon_pkt_info_t is allocated and stored via p_add_proto_data; on later passes the else branch retrieves it with p_get_proto_data into pkt_info. If lookup fails, pkt_info stays NULL.
pkt_info is then dereferenced unconditionally at pkt_info->ioctl_command, pkt_info->req_frame_num, pkt_info->req_time and pkt_info->ioctl_command passed to cmd_ioctl_resp, without a NULL check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences pkt_info without verifying that the p_get_proto_data lookup succeeded, directly matching CWE-476 (NULL Pointer Dereference). The crash is the consequence of the missing NULL check, not a separate memory-safety defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes per-packet proto data created on the first pass is always retrievable on subsequent passes. Trigger: a packet whose stored data cannot be found (e.g., strange TCP sequence handling causing a second pass without prior creation) leaves pkt_info NULL. Consequence: the dereferences crash the dissector, enabling denial of service via crafted capture or injected packets.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int nvmx_handle_vmclear(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)'], 'added_lines': ['static int nvmx_handle_vmclear(struct cpu_user_regs *regs)']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.9.x through 4.11.x, on Intel x86 platforms, allowing x86 HVM and PVH guests to cause a host OS denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact because nested VT-x is not properly restricted.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only changes linkage to static; it contains no NULL dereference, and the described flaw (missing nested-virt/VMXE privilege check and uninitialized nvmx state in callers) is not visible in this function.

commit_msg:
bpf: Fix leakage under speculation on mispredicted branches

The verifier only enumerates valid control-flow paths and skips paths that
are unreachable in the non-speculative domain. And so it can miss issues
under speculative execution on mispredicted branches.

For example, a type confusion has been demonstrated with the following
crafted program:

  // r0 = pointer to a map array entry
  // r6 = pointer to readable stack slot
  // r9 = scalar controlled by attacker
  1: r0 = *(u64 *)(r0) // cache miss
  2: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 4
  3: r6 = r9
  4: if r0 != 0x1 goto line 6
  5: r9 = *(u8 *)(r6)
  6: // leak r9

Since line 3 runs iff r0 == 0 and line 5 runs iff r0 == 1, the verifier
concludes that the pointer dereference on line 5 is safe. But: if the
attacker trains both the branches to fall-through, such that the following
is speculatively executed ...

  r6 = r9
  r9 = *(u8 *)(r6)
  // leak r9

... then the program will dereference an attacker-controlled value and could
leak its content under speculative execution via side-channel. This requires
to mistrain the branch predictor, which can be rather tricky, because the
branches are mutually exclusive. However such training can be done at
congruent addresses in user space using different branches that are not
mutually exclusive. That is, by training branches in user space ...

  A:  if r0 != 0x0 goto line C
  B:  ...
  C:  if r0 != 0x0 goto line D
  D:  ...

... such that addresses A and C collide to the same CPU branch prediction
entries in the PHT (pattern history table) as those of the BPF program's
lines 2 and 4, respectively. A non-privileged attacker could simply brute
force such collisions in the PHT until observing the attack succeeding.

Alternative methods to mistrain the branch predictor are also possible that
avoid brute forcing the collisions in the PHT. A reliable attack has been
demonstrated, for example, using the following crafted program:

  // r0 = pointer to a [control] map array entry
  // r7 = *(u64 *)(r0 + 0), training/attack phase
  // r8 = *(u64 *)(r0 + 8), oob address
  // [...]
  // r0 = pointer to a [data] map array entry
  1: if r7 == 0x3 goto line 3
  2: r8 = r0
  // crafted sequence of conditional jumps to separate the conditional
  // branch in line 193 from the current execution flow
  3: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 5
  4: if r0 == 0x0 goto exit
  5: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 7
  6: if r0 == 0x0 goto exit
  [...]
  187: if r0 != 0x0 goto line 189
  188: if r0 == 0x0 goto exit
  // load any slowly-loaded value (due to cache miss in phase 3) ...
  189: r3 = *(u64 *)(r0 + 0x1200)
  // ... and turn it into known zero for verifier, while preserving slowly-
  // loaded dependency when executing:
  190: r3 &= 1
  191: r3 &= 2
  // speculatively bypassed phase dependency
  192: r7 += r3
  193: if r7 == 0x3 goto exit
  194: r4 = *(u8 *)(r8 + 0)
  // leak r4

As can be seen, in training phase (phase != 0x3), the condition in line 1
turns into false and therefore r8 with the oob address is overridden with
the valid map value address, which in line 194 we can read out without
issues. However, in attack phase, line 2 is skipped, and due to the cache
miss in line 189 where the map value is (zeroed and later) added to the
phase register, the condition in line 193 takes the fall-through path due
to prior branch predictor training, where under speculation, it'll load the
byte at oob address r8 (unknown scalar type at that point) which could then
be leaked via side-channel.

One way to mitigate these is to 'branch off' an unreachable path, meaning,
the current verification path keeps following the is_branch_taken() path
and we push the other branch to the verification stack. Given this is
unreachable from the non-speculative domain, this branch's vstate is
explicitly marked as speculative. This is needed for two reasons: i) if
this path is solely seen from speculative execution, then we later on still
want the dead code elimination to kick in in order to sanitize these
instructions with jmp-1s, and ii) to ensure that paths walked in the
non-speculative domain are not pruned from earlier walks of paths walked in
the speculative domain. Additionally, for robustness, we mark the registers
which have been part of the conditional as unknown in the speculative path
given there should be no assumptions made on their content.

The fix in here mitigates type confusion attacks described earlier due to
i) all code paths in the BPF program being explored and ii) existing
verifier logic already ensuring that given memory access instruction
references one specific data structure.

An alternative to this fix that has also been looked at in this scope was to
mark aux->alu_state at the jump instruction with a BPF_JMP_TAKEN state as
well as direction encoding (always-goto, always-fallthrough, unknown), such
that mixing of different always-* directions themselves as well as mixing of
always-* with unknown directions would cause a program rejection by the
verifier, e.g. programs with constructs like 'if ([...]) { x = 0; } else
{ x = 1; }' with subsequent 'if (x == 1) { [...] }'. For unprivileged, this
would result in only single direction always-* taken paths, and unknown taken
paths being allowed, such that the former could be patched from a conditional
jump to an unconditional jump (ja). Compared to this approach here, it would
have two downsides: i) valid programs that otherwise are not performing any
pointer arithmetic, etc, would potentially be rejected/broken, and ii) we are
required to turn off path pruning for unprivileged, where both can be avoided
in this work through pushing the invalid branch to the verification stack.

The issue was originally discovered by Adam and Ofek, and later independently
discovered and reported as a result of Benedict and Piotr's research work.

Fixes: b2157399cc98 ("bpf: prevent out-of-bounds speculation")

description: In kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel before 5.12.13, a branch can be mispredicted (e.g., because of type confusion) and consequently an unprivileged BPF program can read arbitrary memory locations via a side-channel attack, aka CID-9183671af6db.

code_evidence: When the verifier proves a conditional branch is statically taken (pred == 1) or not taken (pred == 0), it follows only that single path and returns without pushing the other branch onto the verification stack. The other, non-speculative-dead branch is never simulated, so its register types are never validated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The verifier permits a register to be dereferenced as a pointer on a path where it was assigned a scalar, i.e., the same resource is accessed using an incompatible type, matching CWE-843. The missing speculative-path simulation is the mechanism that allows this type confusion to survive verification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the verifier prunes the statically-dead branch instead of simulating it under speculative execution, so a register that is a scalar on one path and a pointer on the other is never reconciled. Trigger: a crafted BPF program with two mutually exclusive conditions that the attacker mistrains the branch predictor on. Consequence: the speculatively-executed path dereferences an attacker-controlled scalar as a pointer (type confusion), enabling out-of-bounds read and side-channel leakage.

commit_msg:
As reported by Jann, ihold() does not in fact guarantee inode
persistence. And instead of making it so, replace the usage of inode
pointers with a per boot, machine wide, unique inode identifier.

This sequence number is global, but shared (file backed) futexes are
rare enough that this should not become a performance issue.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tatomic64_set(&inode->i_sequence, 0);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel’s futex implementation. This flaw allows a local attacker to corrupt system memory or escalate their privileges when creating a futex on a filesystem that is about to be unmounted. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to confidentiality, integrity, as well as system availability.

code_evidence: inode_init_always initializes a fresh inode but sets no unique identity/sequence value; it only sets i_sb, i_blkbits, i_flags, i_count and the operation pointers. The patch adds atomic64_set(&inode->i_sequence, 0) here, showing this function is the allocation path where a per-inode identifier is established.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the underlying flaw is continued use of an inode reference after the inode can be freed and reallocated. The missing stable inode identifier in inode_init_always is the initialization-side evidence for that lifetime problem, distinct from a simple NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: inode identity is derived from the inode pointer, and ihold() does not guarantee the inode stays allocated. When a file-backed futex relies on that pointer while the filesystem is unmounted and the inode freed, later use of the stale pointer can access reused memory, corrupting memory or enabling privilege escalation. The trigger is creating a futex on a filesystem being unmounted; the consequence is use-after-free of the inode structure.

commit_msg:
Issue 23433 in oss-fuzz: Heap-buffer-overflow in findNextBorderPixel()
* Check pix boundary when looking for the next pixel.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (npx < 0 || npx >= w || npy < 0 || npy >= h)', '            continue;']}
description: Leptonica before 1.80.0 allows a heap-based buffer over-read in findNextBorderPixel in ccbord.c.

code_evidence: Neighbor coordinates npx and npy are computed from px/py plus offset tables without any bounds check, then used directly to index the image: line = data + npy * wpl and GET_DATA_BIT(line, npx).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked npx/npy are used to compute a line pointer and bit offset, producing a read past the intended image buffer, which is exactly CWE-125. It is a read, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the neighbor coordinate calculation lacks a clamp against the image width w and height h, so npx/npy can fall outside [0,w)/[0,h). Trigger: findNextBorderPixel is called on a border pixel near an image edge, producing an out-of-range neighbor. Consequence: data + npy*wpl and GET_DATA_BIT read outside the allocated pixel buffer, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read (the reported heap-buffer-overflow).

description: Integer overflow in the xml_utf8_encode function in ext/xml/xml.c in PHP before 7.0.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via a long argument to the utf8_encode function, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Line 3 stores the caller-supplied length in size_t pos; line 17 computes the allocation size as len * 4 using zend_string_alloc, a multiplication with no overflow check. The loop bounds are driven by the same len (line 19, decremented at line 36), so each input byte can write up to four output bytes into the buffer sized by that unchecked product.

The subsequent out-of-bounds write is the downstream consequence; the missing overflow check on the size computation is the root cause.

Trigger: a very long input to utf8_encode such that len * 4 exceeds SIZE_MAX. Consequence: an undersized heap allocation followed by the encode loop writing beyond it, producing a heap-based buffer overflow (DoS or memory corruption).

description: In LibRaw, there is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability within the "new_node()" function (libraw\src\x3f\x3f_utils_patched.cpp) that can be triggered via a crafted X3F file.

commit_msg:
xen: Make coherent PV IOMMU discipline

In order for a PV domain to set up DMA from a passed-through device to
one of its pages, the page must be mapped in the IOMMU.  On the other
hand, before a PV page may be used as a "special" page type (such as a
pagetable or descriptor table), it _must not_ be writable in the IOMMU
(otherwise a malicious guest could DMA arbitrary page tables into the
memory, bypassing Xen's safety checks); and Xen's current rule is to
have such pages not in the IOMMU at all.

At the moment, in order to accomplish this, the code borrows HVM
domain's "physmap" concept: When a page is assigned to a guest,
guess_physmap_add_entry() is called, which for PV guests, will create
a writable IOMMU mapping; and when a page is removed,
guest_physmap_remove_entry() is called, which will remove the mapping.

Additionally, when a page gains the PGT_writable page type, the page
will be added into the IOMMU; and when the page changes away from a
PGT_writable type, the page will be removed from the IOMMU.

Unfortunately, borrowing the "physmap" concept from HVM domains is
problematic.  HVM domains have a lock on their p2m tables, ensuring
synchronization between modifications to the p2m; and all hypercall
parameters must first be translated through the p2m before being used.

Trying to mix this locked-and-gated approach with PV's lock-free
approach leads to several races and inconsistencies:

* A race between a page being assigned and it being put into the
  physmap; for example:
  - P1: call populate_physmap() { A = allocate_domheap_pages() }
  - P2: Guess page A's mfn, and call decrease_reservation(A).  A is owned by the domain,
        and so Xen will clear the PGC_allocated bit and free the page
  - P1: finishes populate_physmap() { guest_physmap_add_entry() }

  Now the domain has a writable IOMMU mapping to a page it no longer owns.

* Pages start out as type PGT_none, but with a writable IOMMU mapping.
  If a guest uses a page as a page table without ever having created a
  writable mapping, the IOMMU mapping will not be removed; the guest
  will have a writable IOMMU mapping to a page it is currently using
  as a page table.

* A newly-allocated page can be DMA'd into with no special actions on
  the part of the guest; However, if a page is promoted to a
  non-writable type, the page must be mapped with a writable type before
  DMA'ing to it again, or the transaction will fail.

To fix this, do away with the "PV physmap" concept entirely, and
replace it with the following IOMMU discipline for PV guests:
 - (type == PGT_writable) <=> in iommu (even if type_count == 0)
 - Upon a final put_page(), check to see if type is PGT_writable; if so,
   iommu_unmap.

In order to achieve that:

- Remove PV IOMMU related code from guest_physmap_*

- Repurpose cleanup_page_cacheattr() into a general
  cleanup_page_mappings() function, which will both fix up Xen
  mappings for pages with special cache attributes, and also check for
  a PGT_writable type and remove pages if appropriate.

- For compatibility with current guests, grab-and-release a
  PGT_writable_page type for PV guests in guest_physmap_add_entry().
  This will cause most "normal" guest pages to start out life with
  PGT_writable_page type (and thus an IOMMU mapping), but no type
  count (so that they can be used as special cases at will).

Also, note that there is one exception to to the "PGT_writable => in
iommu" rule: xenheap pages shared with guests may be given a
PGT_writable type with one type reference.  This reference prevents
the type from changing, which in turn prevents page from gaining an
IOMMU mapping in get_page_type().  It's not clear whether this was
intentional or not, but it's not something to change in a security
update.

This is XSA-288.

Reported-by: Paul Durrant <paul.durrant@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        return need_iommu_pt_sync(p2m->domain) ?', '            iommu_legacy_unmap(p2m->domain, _dfn(mfn), page_order) : 0;'], 'added_lines': ['    /* IOMMU for PV guests is handled in get_page_type() and put_page(). */', '        return 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.11.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service or gain privileges by leveraging incorrect use of the HVM physmap concept for PV domains.

code_evidence: For non-translated (PV) domains, p2m_remove_page previously called iommu_legacy_unmap guarded only by need_iommu_pt_sync; the surrounding p2m entry updates (lines 15-27) are not performed under the HVM p2m lock that the physmap model relied on.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect stems from mixing a lock-free PV path with a lock-and-gated HVM physmap discipline, leaving IOMMU state changes unsynchronized with page-type changes—an improper-locking/lack of synchronization weakness (CWE-667), distinct from a simple missing bounds check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the PV IOMMU mapping is removed in a separate, unsynchronized path from the page-type transitions that establish it (get_page_type/put_page). Trigger: a PV guest racing page assignment, promotion to PGT_writable, or removal causes the IOMMU mapping and p2m/page type to diverge. Consequence: writable IOMMU mappings to pages now used as page tables or no longer owned, enabling privilege escalation or DoS.

patch 9.0.0483: illegal memory access when replacing in virtualedit mode

Problem:    Illegal memory access when replacing in virtualedit mode.
Solution:   Check for replacing NUL after Tab.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t    PBYTE(curwin->w_cursor, c);', '\t\t}', '\t    }', '\t    else if (virtual_op && curwin->w_cursor.lnum == oap->end.lnum)'], 'added_lines': ['\t    int done = FALSE;', '', '\t\t    done = TRUE;', '\t\t    // with "coladd" set may move to just after a TAB', '\t\t    if (gchar_cursor() != NUL)', '\t\t    {', '\t\t\tPBYTE(curwin->w_cursor, c);', '\t\t\tdone = TRUE;', '\t\t    }', '\t\t}', '\t    }', '\t    if (!done && virtual_op && curwin->w_cursor.lnum == oap->end.lnum)']}
description: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 9.0.0483.

code_evidence: In the non-block replace loop, when the cursor is on a TAB the code calls coladvance_force(getviscol()) to position after the TAB, then unconditionally executes PBYTE(curwin->w_cursor, c) without checking that gchar_cursor() is non-NUL. The fix adds exactly this check before PBYTE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unguarded PBYTE writes past the line buffer's allocated end, matching heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122). It is not merely an off-by-one read; the operation is a write, and the fix inserts a bounds/NUL check, confirming the write was the defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: coladvance_force with 'coladd'/virtualedit can move the cursor to just past a TAB, i.e. beyond the end of the line buffer. The unguarded PBYTE then writes at that out-of-range position. Trigger: replace operation in virtualedit mode over a TAB at the end of the operand. Consequence: illegal/out-of-bounds memory write (heap corruption or crash), as the commit message reports an illegal memory access.

commit_msg:
mptcp: fix subflow traversal at disconnect time

At disconnect time the MPTCP protocol traverse the subflows
list closing each of them. In some circumstances - MPJ subflow,
passive MPTCP socket, the latter operation can remove the
subflow from the list, invalidating the current iterator.

Address the issue using the safe list traversing helper
variant.

Reported-by: van fantasy <g1042620637@gmail.com>
Fixes: b29fcfb54cd7 ("mptcp: full disconnect implementation")
Tested-by: Matthieu Baerts <matthieu.baerts@tessares.net>
Reviewed-by: Mat Martineau <mathew.j.martineau@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Mat Martineau <mathew.j.martineau@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct mptcp_subflow_context *subflow;', '\tmptcp_for_each_subflow(msk, subflow) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct mptcp_subflow_context *subflow, *tmp;', '\tlist_for_each_entry_safe(subflow, tmp, &msk->conn_list, node) {']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference issue was discovered in the Linux kernel in the MPTCP protocol when traversing the subflow list at disconnect time. A local user could use this flaw to potentially crash the system causing a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over msk's subflow list using mptcp_for_each_subflow and, for each entry, calls __mptcp_close_ssk with the subflow. __mptcp_close_ssk can remove the current subflow from the list (MPJ subflow, passive socket), which invalidates the iterator; the next iteration then dereferences a freed/NULL subflow via mptcp_subflow_tcp_sock(subflow).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a dereference of an invalid/NULL subflow pointer during list traversal, matching CWE-476. The traversal flaw is the cause; the NULL dereference is the direct weakness manifesting as a crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unsafe list traversal that does not tolerate removal of the current element during iteration. Trigger: closing an MPJ subflow on a passive MPTCP socket at disconnect time, where __mptcp_close_ssk unlinks the subflow. Consequence: the iterator advances to an invalid entry and dereferences it, causing a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash (DoS).

On a read-component failure the loop merely sets i=ncmpts and result=false (lines 92-96) instead of aborting; the crafted-image dimension/step relationship is what drives the out-of-bounds write in readComponent8u.
