commit_msg: Fix bug #72241: get_icu_value_internal out-of-bounds read
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tfor( i=0 ; i< max_value; i++ ){  ', '\t\t\tsnprintf( cur_key_name , 30, "%s%d", key_name , i);\t'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tfor( i=0 ; i< max_value; i++ ){', '\t\t\tsnprintf( cur_key_name , 30, "%s%d", key_name , i);']}
description: The get_icu_value_internal function in ext/intl/locale/locale_methods.c in PHP before 5.5.36, 5.6.x before 5.6.22, and 7.x before 7.0.7 does not ensure the presence of a '\0' character, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted locale_get_primary_language call.

code_evidence: The loop builds cur_key_name via snprintf(cur_key_name, 30, ...) into a 31-byte stack buffer, then passes strlen(cur_key_name)+1 as the length to zend_hash_find.

snprintf truncates and NUL-terminates, so the lookup key is bounded; the appended value comes from Z_STRVAL_PP(ele_value) with Z_STRLEN_PP(ele_value) via smart_str_appendl, which copies exactly the recorded length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the defect is a read beyond the intended buffer during string copying, not a write overflow (CWE-787) nor a format-string issue. The missing '\0' guarantee means the copy length can exceed valid data, directly producing an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code: smart_str_appendl(loc_name, Z_STRVAL_PP(ele_value) , Z_STRLEN_PP(ele_value));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a string whose stored length may exceed its actual NUL-terminated content: smart_str_appendl at line 55 copies Z_STRLEN_PP(ele_value) bytes from Z_STRVAL_PP(ele_value). If a crafted locale value lacks a '\0' within its declared length, the copy reads past the allocated string buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and potential crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix rare race condition when claiming sessions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif(session->source && session->source->transport) {', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tjanus_mutex_lock(&session->mutex);', '\t\tif(session->source && session->source->transport)', '\t\tjanus_mutex_unlock(&session->mutex);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Janus through 0.9.1. janus.c has multiple concurrent threads that misuse the source property of a session, leading to a race condition when claiming sessions.

code_evidence: In the destroy branch, the code checks session->source and calls its transport's session_over without holding session->mutex, so a concurrent thread can free or replace session->source between the check and the dereference.

The claim branch takes session->mutex while reading, destroying, and reassigning session->source, showing the same shared field is mutated under that lock elsewhere; the destroy path's unlocked access is therefore an unsynchronized concurrent access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a concurrent sequence whose exclusive access to the shared session->source field is not enforced, allowing an interfering thread to modify it mid-sequence; this is exactly a race condition (CWE-362). The consequence use-after-free is downstream of the missing synchronization rather than the labeled weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destroy path accesses session->source without acquiring session->mutex, while the claim path concurrently destroys and reassigns the same pointer under that mutex. Trigger: a 'destroy' request racing with a 'claim' request on the same session. Consequence: the unlocked check-and-dereference can operate on a freed or replaced source, causing a use-after-free or crash (availability impact).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    while((packet = pcap_next(local_handle,&header))) {'], 'added_lines': ['    while((packet = safe_pcap_next(local_handle,&header))) {']}
description: Tcpreplay v4.3.0 beta1 contains a heap-based buffer over-read. The get_next_packet() function in the send_packets.c file uses the memcpy() function unsafely to copy sequences from the source buffer pktdata to the destination (*prev_packet)->pktdata. This will result in a Denial of Service (DoS) and potentially Information Exposure when the application attempts to process a file.

code_evidence: Line 30 obtains packets via pcap_next, which trusts the capture header; the header's caplen (bytes actually read) is not compared with len (claimed packet length). Line 32 copies the whole struct pcap_pkthdr, then line 33 allocates sched[i].pkthdr.len and line 34 memcpy's that many bytes from packet, so a corrupt file whose len exceeds caplen causes memcpy to read beyond the captured buffer.
Line 48 computes size_payload from ip_len without validating it against the actual captured length, and line 69 stores that possibly underflowed/oversized value for later use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy copies header.len bytes from a buffer only guaranteed to hold caplen bytes, i.e. reading past the end of the intended buffer, which is CWE-125. This is an out-of-bounds read rather than an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), since the destination is sized to len but the source is too short.

evidence_lines.code:
size_payload = ntohs(iphdr->ip_len) - (size_ip + (size_tcp));
sched[i].size_payload = size_payload;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop uses pcap_next without validating that header.len (capture length) is within the actual caplen and a sane maximum. Trigger: a corrupt/attacker-supplied PCAP where len is larger than the bytes returned. Consequence: memcpy at line 34 over-reads the heap buffer (and size_payload at line 48 can be inconsistent), leading to DoS and potential information exposure.

commit_msg:
Currently, we have a bug where a simultaneous DROPTAG ioctl and socket
close may race, as we attempt to remove a key from lists twice, and
perform an unref for each removal operation. This may result in a uaf
when we attempt the second unref.

This change fixes the race by making __mctp_key_remove tolerant to being
called on a key that has already been removed from the socket/net lists,
and only performs the unref when we do the actual remove. We also need
to hold the list lock on the ioctl cleanup path.

This fix is based on a bug report and comprehensive analysis from
butt3rflyh4ck <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>, found via syzkaller.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: 63ed1aab3d40 ("mctp: Add SIOCMCTP{ALLOC,DROP}TAG ioctls for tag control")
Reported-by: butt3rflyh4ck <butterflyhuangxx@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Jeremy Kerr <jk@codeconstruct.com.au>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tspin_lock_irqsave(&key->lock, flags);', '\t\t__mctp_key_remove(key, net, flags, MCTP_TRACE_KEY_DROPPED);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tunsigned long fl2;', '\t\t/* Unwind our key allocation: the keys list lock needs to be', '\t\t * taken before the individual key locks, and we need a valid', '\t\t * flags value (fl2) to pass to __mctp_key_remove, hence the', '\t\t * second spin_lock_irqsave() rather than a plain spin_lock().', '\t\t */', '\t\tspin_lock_irqsave(&net->mctp.keys_lock, flags);', '\t\tspin_lock_irqsave(&key->lock, fl2);', '\t\t__mctp_key_remove(key, net, fl2, MCTP_TRACE_KEY_DROPPED);', '\t\tspin_unlock_irqrestore(&net->mctp.keys_lock, flags);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel MCTP (Management Component Transport Protocol) functionality. This issue occurs when a user simultaneously calls DROPTAG ioctl and socket close happens, which could allow a local user to crash the system or potentially escalate their privileges on the system.

code_evidence: On the copy_to_user failure path, the code takes only key->lock, calls __mctp_key_remove(key, net, flags, ...) and then mctp_key_unref(key). It does not take net->mctp.keys_lock, the list lock that serializes removal of the key from the socket/net lists against a concurrent socket close.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The double removal leads to a double unref and then to a second use of freed key memory, which matches CWE-416. The defect is not a simple double free, because the second removal and unref operate on memory that is already freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unwind path removes the key without holding net->mctp.keys_lock, so a simultaneous socket close can also remove the same key from the lists. The key is unref'd twice, and the second unref frees an already-freed key. Trigger: a user causes the copy_to_user failure while another thread closes the socket; the supported consequence is a use-after-free, which can crash the system or potentially enable privilege escalation.

commit_msg: fixed trivial auth detection for pubkeys
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tcli_ses.is_trivial_auth = 0;'], 'added_lines': []}
description: An issue was discovered in Dropbear through 2020.81. Due to a non-RFC-compliant check of the available authentication methods in the client-side SSH code, it is possible for an SSH server to change the login process in its favor. This attack can bypass additional security measures such as FIDO2 tokens or SSH-Askpass. Thus, it allows an attacker to abuse a forwarded agent for logging on to another server unnoticed.

commit_msg:
In kobject_get_path(), if kobj->name is changed between calls
get_kobj_path_length() and fill_kobj_path() and the length becomes
longer, then fill_kobj_path() will have an out-of-bounds bug.

The actual current problem occurs when the ixgbe probe.

In ixgbe_mii_bus_init(), if the length of netdev->dev.kobj.name
length becomes longer, out-of-bounds will occur.

cpu0                                         cpu1
ixgbe_probe
 register_netdev(netdev)
  netdev_register_kobject
   device_add
    kobject_uevent // Sending ADD events
                                             systemd-udevd // rename netdev
                                              dev_change_name
                                               device_rename
                                                kobject_rename
 ixgbe_mii_bus_init                             |
  mdiobus_register                              |
   __mdiobus_register                           |
    device_register                             |
     device_add                                 |
      kobject_uevent                            |
       kobject_get_path                         |
        len = get_kobj_path_length // old name  |
        path = kzalloc(len, gfp_mask);          |
                                                kobj->name = name;
                                                /* name length becomes
                                                 * longer
                                                 */
        fill_kobj_path /* kobj path length is
                        * longer than path,
                        * resulting in out of
                        * bounds when filling path
                        */

This is the kasan report:

==================================================================
BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in fill_kobj_path+0x50/0xc0
Write of size 7 at addr ff1100090573d1fd by task kworker/28:1/673

 Workqueue: events work_for_cpu_fn
 Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 dump_stack_lvl+0x34/0x48
 print_address_description.constprop.0+0x86/0x1e7
 print_report+0x36/0x4f
 kasan_report+0xad/0x130
 kasan_check_range+0x35/0x1c0
 memcpy+0x39/0x60
 fill_kobj_path+0x50/0xc0
 kobject_get_path+0x5a/0xc0
 kobject_uevent_env+0x140/0x460
 device_add+0x5c7/0x910
 __mdiobus_register+0x14e/0x490
 ixgbe_probe.cold+0x441/0x574 [ixgbe]
 local_pci_probe+0x78/0xc0
 work_for_cpu_fn+0x26/0x40
 process_one_work+0x3b6/0x6a0
 worker_thread+0x368/0x520
 kthread+0x165/0x1a0
 ret_from_fork+0x1f/0x30

This reproducer triggers that bug:

while:
do
    rmmod ixgbe
    sleep 0.5
    modprobe ixgbe
    sleep 0.5

When calling fill_kobj_path() to fill path, if the name length of
kobj becomes longer, return failure and retry. This fixes the problem.

Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")
Signed-off-by: Wang Hai <wanghai38@huawei.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221220012143.52141-1-wanghai38@huawei.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfill_kobj_path(kobj, path, len);'], 'added_lines': ['retry:', '\tif (fill_kobj_path(kobj, path, len)) {', '\t\tkfree(path);', '\t\tgoto retry;', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in lib/kobject.c in the Linux kernel before 6.2.3. With root access, an attacker can trigger a race condition that results in a fill_kobj_path out-of-bounds write.

code_evidence: len is computed from get_kobj_path_length(kobj) at line 5 and used to allocate path via kzalloc(len) at line 8; fill_kobj_path(kobj, path, len) at line 11 then copies the kobject name into that buffer without re-checking the current name length, so if kobj->name grows between the length computation and the fill, the write exceeds the allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a buffer sized from a stale length and then writes the path into it, so a longer current name produces a write past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 Out-of-bounds Write. The race is the trigger; the out-of-bounds write is the direct weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size is computed once from the kobject name length and then used to fill the path while the name can be concurrently changed to a longer value. Trigger: a race where another thread renames the kobject after get_kobj_path_length but before fill_kobj_path. Supported consequence: fill_kobj_path writes past the kzalloc'd buffer, causing a slab out-of-bounds write (memory corruption/crash).

commit_msg:
tcp: take care of truncations done by sk_filter()

With syzkaller help, Marco Grassi found a bug in TCP stack,
crashing in tcp_collapse()

Root cause is that sk_filter() can truncate the incoming skb,
but TCP stack was not really expecting this to happen.
It probably was expecting a simple DROP or ACCEPT behavior.

We first need to make sure no part of TCP header could be removed.
Then we need to adjust TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->end_seq

Many thanks to syzkaller team and Marco for giving us a reproducer.

Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Marco Grassi <marco.gra@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Vladis Dronov <vdronov@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (sk_filter(sk, skb))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (tcp_filter(sk, skb))', '\tth = (const struct tcphdr *)skb->data;', '\thdr = ipv6_hdr(skb);']}
description: The TCP stack in the Linux kernel before 4.8.10 mishandles skb truncation, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) via a crafted application that makes sendto system calls, related to net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c and net/ipv6/tcp_ipv6.c.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs packet reception and filtering in the TCP stack; the bug is a skb truncation/sequence-update mishandling causing a crash, not an access-control restriction failure matching CWE-284.

commit_msg:
tracing/syscalls: Ignore numbers outside NR_syscalls' range

ARM has some private syscalls (for example, set_tls(2)) which lie
outside the range of NR_syscalls.  If any of these are called while
syscall tracing is being performed, out-of-bounds array access will
occur in the ftrace and perf sys_{enter,exit} handlers.

 # trace-cmd record -e raw_syscalls:* true && trace-cmd report
 ...
 true-653   [000]   384.675777: sys_enter:            NR 192 (0, 1000, 3, 4000022, ffffffff, 0)
 true-653   [000]   384.675812: sys_exit:             NR 192 = 1995915264
 true-653   [000]   384.675971: sys_enter:            NR 983045 (76f74480, 76f74000, 76f74b28, 76f74480, 76f76f74, 1)
 true-653   [000]   384.675988: sys_exit:             NR 983045 = 0
 ...

 # trace-cmd record -e syscalls:* true
 [   17.289329] Unable to handle kernel paging request at virtual address aaaaaace
 [   17.289590] pgd = 9e71c000
 [   17.289696] [aaaaaace] *pgd=00000000
 [   17.289985] Internal error: Oops: 5 [#1] PREEMPT SMP ARM
 [   17.290169] Modules linked in:
 [   17.290391] CPU: 0 PID: 704 Comm: true Not tainted 3.18.0-rc2+ #21
 [   17.290585] task: 9f4dab00 ti: 9e710000 task.ti: 9e710000
 [   17.290747] PC is at ftrace_syscall_enter+0x48/0x1f8
 [   17.290866] LR is at syscall_trace_enter+0x124/0x184

Fix this by ignoring out-of-NR_syscalls-bounds syscall numbers.

Commit cd0980fc8add "tracing: Check invalid syscall nr while tracing syscalls"
added the check for less than zero, but it should have also checked
for greater than NR_syscalls.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/p/1414620418-29472-1-git-send-email-rabin@rab.in

Fixes: cd0980fc8add "tracing: Check invalid syscall nr while tracing syscalls"
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 2.6.33+
Signed-off-by: Rabin Vincent <rabin@rab.in>
Signed-off-by: Steven Rostedt <rostedt@goodmis.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (syscall_nr < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (syscall_nr < 0 || syscall_nr >= NR_syscalls)']}
description: kernel/trace/trace_syscalls.c in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 does not properly handle private syscall numbers during use of the perf subsystem, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and OOPS) or bypass the ASLR protection mechanism via a crafted application.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function guards against a NULL pointer at lines 16-17 and 21-22; the actual defect is an out-of-bounds array access at line 15 due to a missing upper-bound check on syscall_nr, which supports CWE-125/CWE-129, not CWE-476.

commit_msg:
evtchn: convert per-channel lock to be IRQ-safe

... in order for send_guest_{global,vcpu}_virq() to be able to make use
of it.

This is part of XSA-343.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    spin_lock(&chn->lock);', '    spin_unlock(&chn->lock);'], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long  flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&chn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&chn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The channel lock protecting the shared evtchn structure is taken with plain spin_lock and released with spin_unlock, so the critical section that sets chn->state, chn->u.pirq.irq and links the port is not IRQ-safe; an interrupt handler on the same CPU can re-enter and mutate chn concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function contains a concurrent sequence needing exclusive access to shared chn state, but the non-IRQ-safe lock leaves a window for an interfering interrupt handler to modify it, matching CWE-362. It is not merely a missing lock; the lock exists but is improperly synchronized.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-channel lock is acquired without disabling interrupts. Trigger: an interrupt arriving while this CPU holds chn->lock runs handler code that takes the same lock and modifies chn state. Consequence: the critical section is not exclusive, so chn state transitions can interleave, violating internal assumptions and enabling out-of-bounds accesses or bug checks (host privilege escalation/DoS).

commit_msg:
Commit 326587b84078 ("sched: fix goto retry in pick_next_task_rt()")
removed any path which could make pick_next_rt_entity() return NULL.
However, BUG_ON(!rt_se) in _pick_next_task_rt() (the only caller of
pick_next_rt_entity()) still checks the error condition, which can
never happen, since list_entry() never returns NULL.
Remove the BUG_ON check, and instead emit a warning in the only
possible error condition here: the queue being empty which should
never happen.

Fixes: 326587b84078 ("sched: fix goto retry in pick_next_task_rt()")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Phil Auld <pauld@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Steven Rostedt (Google) <rostedt@goodmis.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230128-list-entry-null-check-sched-v3-1-b1a71bd1ac6b@diag.uniroma1.it
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tBUG_ON(!rt_se);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (unlikely(!rt_se))', '\t\t\treturn NULL;']}
description: In the Linux kernel, pick_next_rt_entity() may return a type confused entry, not detected by the BUG_ON condition, as the confused entry will not be NULL, but list_head.The buggy error condition would lead to a type confused entry with the list head,which would then be used as a type confused sched_rt_entity,causing memory corruption.

code_evidence: pick_next_rt_entity(rt_rq) returns rt_se, and the code only checks BUG_ON(!rt_se); a list_head pointer that is not NULL passes this check.
rt_se is then passed to group_rt_rq(rt_se), which interprets it as a sched_rt_entity, and the loop continues while rt_rq is non-NULL.
Finally rt_task_of(rt_se) is used to derive the task from the same pointer, so the mismatched object propagates to the return value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts a pointer of one type (list_head) and accesses it as an incompatible type (sched_rt_entity) because the BUG_ON(!rt_se) guard misses non-NULL type-confused values. This is exactly access of a resource using an incompatible type, so CWE-843 fits.

evidence_lines.code:
rt_se = pick_next_rt_entity(rt_rq);
BUG_ON(!rt_se);
rt_rq = group_rt_rq(rt_se);
return rt_task_of(rt_se);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error detection only tests for NULL, but the failure mode yields a list_head pointer rather than NULL. Trigger: an empty or inconsistent RT queue causes pick_next_rt_entity() to return a list_head-derived pointer. Consequence: the pointer is dereferenced as a sched_rt_entity by group_rt_rq() and rt_task_of(), leading to memory corruption.

commit_msg:
evtchn: avoid NULL derefs

Commit fbbd5009e6 ("evtchn: refactor low-level event channel port ops")
added a de-reference of the struct evtchn pointer for a port without
first making sure the bucket pointer is non-NULL. This de-reference is
actually entirely unnecessary, as all relevant callers (beyond the
problematic do_poll()) already hold the port number in their hands, and
the actual leaf functions need nothing else.

For FIFO event channels there's a second problem in that the ordering
of reads and updates to ->num_evtchns and ->event_array[] was so far
undefined (the read side isn't always holding the domain's event lock).
Add respective barriers.

This is XSA-221.

Reported-by: Ankur Arora <ankur.a.arora@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                            const struct evtchn *evtchn)', '    return d->evtchn_port_ops->is_pending(d, evtchn);'], 'added_lines': ['                                            evtchn_port_t port)', '    return d->evtchn_port_ops->is_pending(d, port);']}
description: Xen through 4.8.x does not validate the port numbers of polled event channel ports, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and host OS crash) or possibly obtain sensitive information, aka XSA-221.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function is only a thin inline wrapper passing a port to evtchn_port_ops->is_pending; it contains no pointer dereference, NULL check, or port validation, so it does not itself exhibit CWE-476.

commit_msg:
[set] Make all operators null-safe again

Changed my mind.

Also for hb_map_clear().

Part of https://github.com/harfbuzz/harfbuzz/pull/3162
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (unlikely (hb_object_is_immutable (set)))', '    return;', ''], 'added_lines': ['  /* Immutible-safe. */']}
description: HarfBuzz 2.9.0 has an out-of-bounds write in hb_bit_set_invertible_t::set (called from hb_sparseset_t<hb_bit_set_invertible_t>::set and hb_set_copy).

code_evidence: hb_set_clear checks hb_object_is_immutable(set) and returns early, so an immutable set is never cleared; otherwise it calls set->clear() on the caller-supplied pointer without any bounds/null check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the reachable clear() operation can write past the end of the set's internal buffer, and the function provides no constraint preventing that mutation. This is a buffer-write weakness rather than a mere logic error; the immutability guard is a related access-control check, not the out-of-bounds condition itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function forwards the caller-provided set to set->clear() with no validation of the pointer or the set's internal state. If an immutable set is passed, the early return prevents mutation; if a mutable set is passed, clear() mutates its internal buffer. The root cause is the missing guard on the object's mutability/state, not a length check; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds write inside the set's clear path when the internal buffer state is inconsistent.

commit_msg:
In renesas_usb3_probe, role_work is bound with renesas_usb3_role_work.
renesas_usb3_start will be called to start the work.

If we remove the driver which will call usbhs_remove, there may be
an unfinished work. The possible sequence is as follows:

CPU0                  			CPU1

                    			 renesas_usb3_role_work
renesas_usb3_remove
usb_role_switch_unregister
device_unregister
kfree(sw)
//free usb3->role_sw
                    			 usb_role_switch_set_role
                    			 //use usb3->role_sw

The usb3->role_sw could be freed under such circumstance and then
used in usb_role_switch_set_role.

This bug was found by static analysis. And note that removing a
driver is a root-only operation, and should never happen in normal
case. But the root user may directly remove the device which
will also trigger the remove function.

Fix it by canceling the work before cleanup in the renesas_usb3_remove.

Fixes: 39facfa01c9f ("usb: gadget: udc: renesas_usb3: Add register of usb role switch")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Reviewed-by: Yoshihiro Shimoda <yoshihiro.shimoda.uh@renesas.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230320062931.505170-1-zyytlz.wz@163.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcancel_work_sync(&usb3->role_work);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.2. A use-after-free was found in renesas_usb3_remove in drivers/usb/gadget/udc/renesas_usb3.c.

code_evidence: re renesas_usb3_remove unregisters usb3->role_sw and tears down the gadget without first cancelling the pending role_work that was scheduled by renesas_usb3_start. The work handler renesas_usb3_role_work later calls usb_role_switch_set_role(usb3->role_sw), so the remove path can free the switch while the work still uses it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because two concurrent sequences (remove and role_work) access the shared usb3->role_sw without exclusive synchronization, producing a timing window. The consequence is use-after-free, but the underlying weakness is the unsynchronized race, not merely the free itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the remove sequence lacks synchronization with the concurrently scheduled role_work, so unregister/free of usb3->role_sw races with the work handler's access. Trigger: driver removal while role_work is pending or running. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the role switch, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg: Fix #10498 - Fix crash in fuzzed java files (#10511)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (attr->info.code_attr.code == NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!attr->info.code_attr.code) {']}
description: The r_bin_java_annotation_new function in shlr/java/class.c in radare2 2.7.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted .class file because of missing input validation in r_bin_java_line_number_table_attr_new.

code_evidence: Line 18 reads code_length from the untrusted buffer and line 21 allocates that many bytes. Line 29 copies the ut32 code_length into a signed int len, and line 30 memsets the allocation. Line 31 checks offset + len >= sz but line 32 sets len = sz and returns without copying, so the guard is against the buffer size rather than the allocation; when the guard passes, line 35 memcpy reads len bytes from buffer + offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Line 35 reads from buffer beyond its intended bounds because the length used for memcpy is derived from attacker-controlled code_length and is not constrained to the remaining input, which directly matches CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code_length value taken from the class file drives both the heap allocation and the later memcpy length without validating that offset + len stays within the supplied buffer sz. Trigger: a crafted .class file with a large code_length makes line 31 pass and line 35 copy len bytes past the end of buffer. Supported consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Some TCP peers announce a very small MSS option in their SYN and/or
SYN/ACK messages.

This forces the stack to send packets with a very high network/cpu
overhead.

Linux has enforced a minimal value of 48. Since this value includes
the size of TCP options, and that the options can consume up to 40
bytes, this means that each segment can include only 8 bytes of payload.

In some cases, it can be useful to increase the minimal value
to a saner value.

We still let the default to 48 (TCP_MIN_SND_MSS), for compatibility
reasons.

Note that TCP_MAXSEG socket option enforces a minimal value
of (TCP_MIN_MSS). David Miller increased this minimal value
in commit c39508d6f118 ("tcp: Make TCP_MAXSEG minimum more correct.")
from 64 to 88.

We might in the future merge TCP_MIN_SND_MSS and TCP_MIN_MSS.

Acked-by: Neal Cardwell <ncardwell@google.com>

description: Jonathan Looney discovered that the Linux kernel default MSS is hard-coded to 48 bytes. This allows a remote peer to fragment TCP resend queues significantly more than if a larger MSS were enforced. A remote attacker could use this to cause a denial of service. This has been fixed in stable kernel releases 4.4.182, 4.9.182, 4.14.127, 4.19.52, 5.1.11, and is fixed in commits 967c05aee439e6e5d7d805e195b3a20ef5c433d6 and 5f3e2bf008c2221478101ee72f5cb4654b9fc363.

code_evidence: Line 12-13 clamps mss_now to the peer-advertised mss_clamp, so a remote SYN/SYN-ACK with a tiny MSS option drives mss_now down to that attacker-chosen value.
Line 14 subtracts icsk_ext_hdr_len, then line 15-16 floors the result at the hardcoded TCP_MIN_SND_MSS (48), which includes TCP option space, leaving only ~8 bytes of payload per segment.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates per-segment TCP send resources (skb/queue/CPU) governed by an MSS floor that imposes no effective restriction on the number of segments a remote peer can induce. if (mss_now > tp->rx_opt.mss_clamp)
mss_now = tp->rx_opt.mss_clamp;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the MSS floor is a fixed constant that does not account for per-socket resource limits, so a remote peer can force very small segments. Trigger: an attacker advertises a minimal MSS in SYN/SYN-ACK; the clamp at line 12-13 and the constant floor at line 15-16 yield tiny segments, inflating segment count and CPU/queue overhead. Supported consequence is denial of service via excessive resource consumption.

commit_msg:
settings: Add support for defaults to keyfile backend

Stacked databases and locks are dconf features that allow
management software like Fleet Commander to set system-wide
defaults and overrides centrally for applications.

This patch adds minimal support for the same to the keyfile
backend. We look for a keyfile named 'defaults' and a
lock-list named 'locks'.

Suitable files can be produced from a dconf database with
dconf dump and dconf list-locks, respectively.

The default location for these files is /etc/glib-2.0/settings/.
For test purposes, this can be overwritten with the
GSETTINGS_DEFAULTS_DIR environment variable.

Writes always go to the per-user keyfile.

commit_msg:
gnttab: fix pin count / page reference race

Dropping page references before decrementing pin counts is a bad idea
if assumptions are being made that a non-zero pin count implies a valid
page. Fix the order of operations in gnttab_copy_release_buf(), but at
the same time also remove the assertion that was found to trigger:
map_grant_ref() also has the potential of causing a race here, and
changing the order of operations there would likely be quite a bit more
involved.

This is CVE-2017-15597 / XSA-236.

Reported-by: Pawel Wieczorkiewicz <wipawel@amazon.de>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>

description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x. Grant copying code made an implication that any grant pin would be accompanied by a suitable page reference. Other portions of code, however, did not match up with that assumption. When such a grant copy operation is being done on a grant of a dying domain, the assumption turns out wrong. A malicious guest administrator can cause hypervisor memory corruption, most likely resulting in host crash and a Denial of Service. Privilege escalation and information leaks cannot be ruled out.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only reorders cleanup operations (unmapping, page-type drop, page put, grant release); it contains no buffer indexing or memory access that demonstrates an out-of-bounds operation, so the target CWE-119 is not directly supported.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12897/ISO CLNS: Use ND_TTEST() for the bounds checks in isoclns_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Don't pass the remaining caplen - that's too hard to get right, and we

description: The ISO CLNS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isoclns_print().

code_evidence: After the header is parsed, p is advanced by hdrlen and length/caplen are decremented by hdrlen, but caplen is still forwarded to the ISO CLNS parser.
When SSAP/DSAP are LLCSAP_ISONS and control is LLC_UI, isoclns_print(ndo, p, length, caplen) is invoked with the remaining caplen, which the callee used for bounds checks in a way that over-read.

description: radare2 through 3.5.1 mishandles the RParse API, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact, as demonstrated by newstr buffer overflows during replace operations. This affects libr/asm/asm.c and libr/parse/parse.c.

code_evidence: The input `data` determines `len`, and `buf` is allocated with `len+1` and filled by `memcpy`; the tokenization then copies substrings into fixed-size stack buffers.

Each `strncpy(wN, ptr, WSZ - 1)` writes at most WSZ-1 bytes into arrays of size WSZ, but the pointers `ptr`/`optr` reference positions within `buf`, so the copied spans depend on attacker-controlled comma/space delimiters.

The `wa[]` array holds the five token buffers, `nw` counts non-empty tokens, and `replace(nw, wa, str)` is invoked with these stack buffers; the return value is only cast to void, so any overflow inside replace is neither prevented nor reported.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because `replace` writes beyond the intended `w0`-`w4` buffer bounds during replacement; the code only suppresses the return value, not the overflow. This is a write past buffer end, not merely an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function passes attacker-influenced fixed-size stack token buffers to `replace`, whose internal writes are not bounded by the caller. Trigger: crafted input with many/long comma- or space-delimited tokens reaches `replace(nw, wa, str)`. Supported consequence: an out-of-bounds write during replacement can corrupt stack memory and crash or alter state.

commit_msg:
bpf: fix 32-bit ALU op verification

32-bit ALU ops operate on 32-bit values and have 32-bit outputs.
Adjust the verifier accordingly.

Fixes: f1174f77b50c ("bpf/verifier: rework value tracking")
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>

This includes', '\t\t\t * shifts by a negative number.', '\t\tif (umax_val > 63) {', '\t\t\t/* Shifts greater than 63 are undefined.  This includes', '\t\t\t * shifts by a negative number.'], 'added_lines': ['\tu64 insn_bitness = (BPF_CLASS(insn->code) == BPF_ALU64) ? 64 : 32;', '', '\t\tif (umax_val >= insn_bitness) {', '\t\t\t/* Shifts greater than 31 or 63 are undefined.', '\t\t\t * This includes shifts by a negative number.', '\t\tif (umax_val >= insn_bitness) {', '\t\t\t/* Shifts greater than 31 or 63 are undefined.', '\t\t\t * This includes shifts by a negative number.', '\tif (BPF_CLASS(insn->code) != BPF_ALU64) {', '\t\t/* 32-bit ALU ops are (32,32)->32 */', '\t\tcoerce_reg_to_size(dst_reg, 4);', '\t\tcoerce_reg_to_size(&src_reg, 4);', '\t}', '']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging mishandling of 32-bit ALU ops.

code_evidence: 32-bit ALU operands are coerced to 4 bytes at function entry, before the switch, so the register bounds used for the operation are truncated to 32-bit ranges.
The LSH guard rejects only umax_val > 63, allowing shifts of 32-63 even for 32-bit ALU ops whose inputs were coerced to 32-bit values.
The RSH guard likewise uses umax_val > 63 rather than the instruction bitness, permitting oversized shift counts for 32-bit ops.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The incorrect 32-bit ALU verification yields wrong register bounds that the verifier relies on for memory-access safety, allowing operations outside intended buffer boundaries, matching CWE-119.

if (umax_val > 63) {
mark_reg_unknown(env, regs, insn->dst_reg);

if (umax_val > 63) {
mark_reg_unknown(env, regs, insn->dst_reg);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shift-range check uses a fixed 64-bit limit instead of the ALU instruction's 32-bit width, and truncation happens before the operation rather than after. A 32-bit shift with count 32-63 passes verification, producing tracked bounds inconsistent with actual 32-bit semantics; the verifier then permits later memory accesses based on incorrect bounds, leading to out-of-bounds reads/writes.

commit_msg:
Fix ASN1_INTEGER handling.

Only treat an ASN1_ANY type as an integer if it has the V_ASN1_INTEGER
tag: V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER is an internal only value which is never used
for on the wire encoding.

Thanks to David Benjamin <davidben@google.com> for reporting this bug.

This was found using libFuzzer.

RT#4364 (part)CVE-2016-2108.

Reviewed-by: Emilia Käsper <emilia@openssl.org>
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -71,9 +71,7 @@
         break;
 
     case V_ASN1_INTEGER:
-    case V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER:
     case V_ASN1_ENUMERATED:
-    case V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED:
         /*
          * These are all have the same content format as ASN1_INTEGER
          */
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    case V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER:', '    case V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED:'], 'added_lines': []}
description: The ASN.1 implementation in OpenSSL before 1.0.1o and 1.0.2 before 1.0.2c allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (buffer underflow and memory corruption) via an ANY field in crafted serialized data, aka the "negative zero" issue.

code_evidence: For an ANY field, utype is taken from typ->type (the on-wire tag) and pval is redirected to typ->value.asn1_value.
Otherwise utype comes from *putype, so the switch dispatch depends on the decoded type value.
The integer case lumps V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER and V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED with V_ASN1_INTEGER, routing them to i2c_ASN1_INTEGER on the ASN1_STRING value.
The resulting cont/len are copied with memcpy(cout, cont, len), so an inconsistent len yields an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect causes operations (length computation and memcpy) outside the intended buffer boundary of the integer content, matching CWE-119. It is not merely a type-confusion label: the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds memory read during encoding.

evidence_lines.code:
case V_ASN1_INTEGER:
case V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER:
case V_ASN1_ENUMERATED:
case V_ASN1_NEG_ENUMERATED:
return i2c_ASN1_INTEGER((ASN1_INTEGER *)*pval, cout ? &cout : NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: internal negative-tag values (V_ASN1_NEG_INTEGER/ENUMERATED) are accepted as integer content during i2c encoding, so a crafted ANY field whose type is a negative tag is treated as an ASN1_INTEGER. The integer encoder then computes a length inconsistent with the actual buffer, and the final memcpy reads len bytes from cont beyond the intended buffer, corrupting output or reading out of bounds.

description: epan/dissectors/packet-qnet6.c in the QNX6 QNET dissector in Wireshark 2.x before 2.0.6 mishandles MAC address data, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted packet.

code_evidence: After fetching name[i] via tvb_get_string_enc for the address entries, the code checks strlen(p) and reads *(p + 1) without ensuring the buffer is at least 2 bytes; the MAC branch then adds p+2 and later the column code dereferences p+2..p+7.

In the request case, p = name[2] is tested only with strlen(p) and *(p + 1), then the COL_INFO format reads *(p + 2) through *(p + 7) unconditionally, so a short address string causes reads past the allocated string.
The reply case repeats the same pattern: p = name[2], the same insufficient length check, and the format string dereferences p+2..p+7, again reading beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads bytes before the beginning/end of the intended buffer (p+2..p+7) due to missing length validation. This is an out-of-bounds read, not merely an invalid string conversion or display issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dissector treats a variable-length packet-derived address string as a fixed 8-byte MAC layout, validating only strlen(p) and *(p+1). Trigger: a crafted QNET6 LR packet whose address field is shorter than the offsets dereferenced. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads of packet-scope string memory, potentially crashing the dissector (DoS).

description: An issue was discovered in ksmbd in the Linux kernel 5.15 through 5.19 before 5.19.2. fs/ksmbd/smb2misc.c has an out-of-bounds read and OOPS for SMB2_TREE_CONNECT.

code_evidence: Lines 7-9 return early when hdr->Status is nonzero and StructureSize matches an error response, leaving *off and *len at 0 and skipping the command-specific extraction and the bounds checks below.
Lines 15-17 extract attacker-controlled PathOffset and PathLength from a TREE_CONNECT request when the early return is not taken.
Lines 78-85 validate *off and *off+*len against MAX_STREAM_PROT_LEN and return -EINVAL; these checks are bypassed when the early return at line 9 fires.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading data past the end of the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not a write or null dereference: the consequence is an out-of-bounds read leading to crash/DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an error-status request with a matching error StructureSize causes the function to return successfully with zeroed offset/length, so the caller believes the request is valid and processing continues. Trigger: a TREE_CONNECT request carrying nonzero Status and a long PathLength. The missing length validation lets the path be read past the buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and kernel oops.

description: The ZipCommon::isValidPath() function in Zip/src/ZipCommon.cpp in POCO C++ Libraries before 1.8 does not properly restrict the filename value in the ZIP header, which allows attackers to conduct absolute path traversal attacks during the ZIP decompression, and possibly create or overwrite arbitrary files, via a crafted ZIP file, related to a "file path injection vulnerability".

code_evidence: The directory-entry branch takes the untrusted ZIP header filename via hdr.getFileName() (line 7), validates it with ZipCommon::isValidPath(dirName) (line 8), then builds Poco::Path dir(_outDir, dirName) (line 10) and calls aFile.createDirectories() (line 13).

The file-entry branch takes hdr.getFileName() (line 19), validates it at line 26, builds Poco::Path file(fileName) (line 28) and Poco::Path dest(_outDir, file) (line 30), creates parent directories (line 34-35) and opens Poco::FileOutputStream out(dest.toString()) (line 37), writing attacker-influenced paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because the function restricts writes to _outDir but relies on a filename check that fails to neutralize path elements, allowing traversal/absolute paths to escape the restricted directory. This is path traversal rather than, e.g., a mere exception-message issue, since the constructed path directly reaches filesystem creation and write operations.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The ZIP header filename is external input used to construct an output path under _outDir. The only guard is ZipCommon::isValidPath, which before the fix did not properly restrict the filename value; when it fails to reject absolute or parent-directory elements, dest resolves outside _outDir, so directory creation and FileOutputStream can create or overwrite arbitrary files. The cause is insufficient path neutralization; the consequence is out-of-directory file write.

description: Miniaudio 0.10.35 has a Double free vulnerability that could cause a buffer overflow in ma_default_vfs_close__stdio in miniaudio.h.

code_evidence: On failure of ma_decoder_init__internal or ma_decoder__postinit, the error path unconditionally calls ma_vfs_or_default_close(pVFS, pDecoder->backend.vfs.file) without checking whether the file handle was already closed and reset to NULL by an earlier ma_decoder_uninit() during the internal init steps.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the same resource (file handle) is released twice through the unconditional close at line 41 after internal cleanup already closed it. The guard on a NULL check is the missing constraint; a mere leak or use-after-free would not match this double-release pattern.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure handler closes pDecoder->backend.vfs.file without verifying it is non-NULL, even though internal initialization may have already uninitialized the decoder and closed/nullified that handle. Trigger: a decoder backend init failing after it has released the file. Consequence: the same file handle is closed twice (double free), risking memory corruption or a crash.

commit_msg:
xen/events: avoid removing an event channel while handling it

Today it can happen that an event channel is being removed from the
system while the event handling loop is active. This can lead to a
race resulting in crashes or WARN() splats when trying to access the
irq_info structure related to the event channel.

Fix this problem by using a rwlock taken as reader in the event
handling loop and as writer when deallocating the irq_info structure.

As the observed problem was a NULL dereference in evtchn_from_irq()
make this function more robust against races by testing the irq_info
pointer to be not NULL before dereferencing it.

And finally make all accesses to evtchn_to_irq[row][col] atomic ones
in order to avoid seeing partial updates of an array element in irq
handling. Note that irq handling can be entered only for event channels
which have been valid before, so any not populated row isn't a problem
in this regard, as rows are only ever added and never removed.

This is XSA-331.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Reported-by: Jinoh Kang <luke1337@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (WARN(irq >= nr_irqs, "Invalid irq %d!\\n", irq))', '\treturn info_for_irq(irq)->evtchn;'], 'added_lines': ['\tconst struct irq_info *info = NULL;', '', '\tif (likely(irq < nr_irqs))', '\t\tinfo = info_for_irq(irq);', '\tif (!info)', '\treturn info->evtchn;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 5.9.1, as used with Xen through 4.14.x. drivers/xen/events/events_base.c allows event-channel removal during the event-handling loop (a race condition). This can cause a use-after-free or NULL pointer dereference, as demonstrated by a dom0 crash via events for an in-reconfiguration paravirtualized device, aka CID-073d0552ead5.

code_evidence: evtchn_from_irq() validates irq against nr_irqs with WARN, then immediately dereferences the result of info_for_irq(irq) at line 5 without any lock or recheck. The irq_info pointer is shared state that can be removed concurrently by the deallocation path during event handling; the function performs a check-then-use over that shared structure with no synchronization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses shared irq_info state without exclusive synchronization, allowing an interfering code sequence to modify/remove it mid-use — a timing-window race (CWE-362). The NULL dereference is the resulting consequence, not the root weakness; the fix's rwlock and NULL recheck confirm the missing synchronization constraint.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the lookup of irq_info and its dereference are not protected against concurrent removal of the event channel, so the pointer can become NULL or freed between retrieval and access. Trigger: an event channel is deallocated while the event-handling loop calls this function. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference or use-after-free, causing a crash or WARN splat (denial of service).

commit_msg: Fix error overflow bug
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (slot == UINT8_MAX) {', '    gpr_log(GPR_ERROR, "Error %p is full, dropping error %p = %s", *err, new,', '            grpc_error_string(new));', '    GRPC_ERROR_UNREF(new);', '    return;', '  }']}
description: Google gRPC before 2017-04-05 has an out-of-bounds write caused by a heap-based buffer overflow related to core/lib/iomgr/error.c.

code_evidence: Line 3 obtains a placement slot from get_placement for a grpc_linked_error; the returned uint8_t slot is used without validating that it is within the arena bounds.
Line 15 then performs memcpy((*err)->arena + slot, &new_last, sizeof(grpc_linked_error)), writing the structure at the returned offset directly into the arena buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes a grpc_linked_error through memcpy to an arena offset that can exceed the buffer, directly producing an out-of-bounds write. This is a write past the end of the intended buffer, not a read or integer-only defect.

evidence_lines.code: uint8_t slot = get_placement(err, sizeof(grpc_linked_error));
memcpy((*err)->arena + slot, &new_last, sizeof(grpc_linked_error));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the slot returned by get_placement is trusted as a valid arena offset and used as the destination of a memcpy without a bounds check. Trigger: when the arena cannot accommodate another grpc_linked_error, get_placement returns UINT8_MAX (255), which is used as the offset. Consequence: memcpy writes past the end of the heap-based arena buffer, an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt memory or crash.

description: In ImageMagick 7.0.6-8, the load_level function in coders/xcf.c lacks offset validation, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (load_tile memory exhaustion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: ntiles is derived from attacker-controlled width and height read from the file (lines 25-26), and the loop iterates over every tile without any bound on ntiles.
offset2 is read from the blob; when zero it is synthesized as offset + TILE_WIDTH*TILE_WIDTH*4*1.5, and the code seeks to offset without validating offset2 against the blob size.
load_tile/load_tile_rle are invoked with the size (offset2-offset), which can be arbitrarily large, driving per-tile allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates tile resources proportional to attacker-controlled values without limiting their size or count, matching CWE-770's resource allocation without throttling and its availability/memory-consumption impact. This is not CWE-190 integer overflow; the weakness is the absent allocation bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the XCF loader trusts width/height and tile offsets from the file, computing ntiles and a tile byte count with no upper bound or blob-size check. Trigger: a crafted XCF with large dimensions or a large/zero offset2 causes many iterations and oversized load_tile/load_tile_rle allocations, exhausting memory (DoS). The missing offset2 validation added in the patch only partially addresses this.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer read overrun by ensuring that DWARF sections containing strings always end in a NUL byte.

	PR 22047
	* dwarf2.c (read_section): If necessary add a terminating NUL byte
	to dwarf string sections.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '      /* Paranoia - if we are reading in a string section, make sure that it', '\t is NUL terminated.  This is to prevent string functions from running', '\t off the end of the buffer.  Note - knowing the size of the buffer is', '\t not enough as some functions, eg strchr, do not have a range limited', '\t equivalent.', '', '\t FIXME: We ought to use a flag in the dwarf_debug_sections[] table to', '\t determine the nature of a debug section, rather than checking the', '\t section name as we do here.  */', '      if (*section_size > 0', '\t  && (*section_buffer)[*section_size - 1] != 0', '\t  && (strstr (section_name, "_str") || strstr (section_name, "names")))', '\t{', '\t  bfd_byte * new_buffer = malloc (*section_size + 1);', '', '\t  _bfd_error_handler (_("warning: dwarf string section \'%s\' is not NUL terminated"),', '\t\t\t      section_name);', '\t  memcpy (new_buffer, *section_buffer, *section_size);', '\t  new_buffer[*section_size] = 0;', '\t  free (*section_buffer);', '\t  *section_buffer = new_buffer;', '\t}']}
description: The read_section function in dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (parse_comp_unit heap-based buffer over-read and application crash) via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: read_section allocates exactly *section_size bytes from the section's rawsize/size and copies the section contents into that buffer, with no extra byte for a terminator.
The only bounds check rejects an offset >= *section_size; it does not ensure the last byte of a string section is NUL, so downstream string scanning can run past the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading memory beyond the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-787 because the faulty access is a read, not a write; the missing NUL terminator is the precondition enabling the out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: string sections are read into an exactly-sized heap buffer without guaranteeing NUL termination. Trigger: a crafted ELF whose DWARF string/name section lacks a trailing NUL byte. Consequence: string routines (e.g. strchr) read past the buffer end, causing a heap-based out-of-bounds read and crash (DoS).

description: The iseries_check_file_type function in wiretap/iseries.c in the iSeries file parser in Wireshark 2.0.x before 2.0.2 does not consider that a line may lack the "OBJECT PROTOCOL" substring, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: buf is a fixed stack buffer whose contents depend on file_gets; when file_gets fails the function returns FALSE without inspecting buf, but on success buf is passed to ascii_strup_inplace and sscanf.

sscanf uses format "%*[ \n\t]OBJECT PROTOCOL%*[ .:\n\t]%8s" and writes up to 8 chars into protocol[9]; the scan is only meaningful if the line contains the OBJECT PROTOCOL prefix, and the code does not guard against lines lacking it before parsing.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function parses attacker-controlled file lines with sscanf into a fixed-length protocol buffer and only checks the extracted token against ETHERNET. A crafted file can drive reads/parsing beyond the intended line structure, producing an out-of-bounds read and crash (the described DoS). The root cause is missing validation of the line format and buffer-boundary handling; the crash is the consequence.

description: The trad_enc_decrypt_update function in archive_read_support_format_zip.c in libarchive before 3.2.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds heap read and crash) via a crafted zip file, related to reading the password.

code_evidence: ENC_HEADER_SIZE is defined as 12 and the function calls __archive_read_ahead(a, ENC_HEADER_SIZE, NULL) to obtain a pointer to the encryption header without first verifying that the entry actually contains at least 12 bytes.
The returned pointer p is passed to trad_enc_init along with ENC_HEADER_SIZE, so the decryption routine reads 12 header bytes from p.
After consuming the header, entry_bytes_remaining is decremented by ENC_HEADER_SIZE without any prior check that it is >= 12.

The unchecked subtraction of ENC_HEADER_SIZE from entry_bytes_remaining further corrupts the remaining-length accounting.

net/mlx5: prevent memory leak in mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq

In mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq if mlx5_vector2eqn fails the allocated
memory should be released.

Fixes: 537a50574175 ("net/mlx5: FPGA, Add high-speed connection routines")
Signed-off-by: Navid Emamdoost <navid.emamdoost@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Saeed Mahameed <saeedm@mellanox.com>

description: A memory leak in the mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq() function in drivers/net/ethernet/mellanox/mlx5/core/fpga/conn.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.11 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) by triggering mlx5_vector2eqn() failures, aka CID-c8c2a057fdc7.

code_evidence: Line 28 allocates the create_cq_in buffer 'in' with kvzalloc; on allocation failure it jumps to err_cqwq without needing to free.
Line 33 calls mlx5_vector2eqn; if it returns an error, line 34-35 jumps to err_cqwq while 'in' is still allocated and never freed.
The err_cqwq label at lines 63-64 only destroys conn->cq.wq_ctrl and returns err; it does not release 'in', so the buffer allocated at line 28 leaks on this error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because memory allocated at line 28 is not released when the mlx5_vector2eqn error branch is taken, leaving allocated memory unreachable after its effective lifetime. This is a missing-release-on-error-path leak, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path after mlx5_vector2eqn() failure exits via err_cqwq without freeing the kvzalloc'd 'in' buffer. Trigger: mlx5_vector2eqn() returns a nonzero error. Supported consequence: the inlen-sized buffer becomes unreachable, leaking kernel memory and enabling memory-consumption denial of service if the path is repeatedly triggered.

- Don't attempt to use the nonexistant "sddm-check" PAM service

description: An issue was discovered in SDDM through 0.17.0. If configured with ReuseSession=true, the password is not checked for users with an already existing session. Any user with access to the system D-Bus can therefore unlock any graphical session. This is related to daemon/Display.cpp and helper/backend/PamBackend.cpp.

Fix buffer overflows in TGA and troff exports (addresses #53, #54)

Each sprintf call writes its formatted bytes plus a terminating NUL, so the cursor advances by one extra byte per call; the header writes cumulatively exceed the 18 reserved bytes.
caca_render_canvas then writes w*h*4 bytes at the shifted cursor, so the total write extends past the malloc'd region.

cur = data = malloc(*bytes);
caca_render_canvas(cv, f, cur, w, h, 4 * w);

We were making the decision to use box blurs, instead of a true
Gaussian kernel, based on the size of *both* x and y dimensions.  Do
them individually instead.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    gboolean use_box_blur;', '    /* For small radiuses, use a true gaussian kernel; otherwise use three box blurs with', '     * clever offsets.', '     */', '    if (sx < 10.0 && sy < 10.0)', '        use_box_blur = FALSE;', '    else', '        use_box_blur = TRUE;', ''], 'added_lines': ['        gboolean use_box_blur;', '', '        /* For small radiuses, use a true gaussian kernel; otherwise use three box blurs with', '         * clever offsets.', '         */', '        if (sx < 10.0)', '            use_box_blur = FALSE;', '        else', '            use_box_blur = TRUE;', '        gboolean use_box_blur;', '', '        /* For small radiuses, use a true gaussian kernel; otherwise use three box blurs with', '         * clever offsets.', '         */', '        if (sy < 10.0)', '            use_box_blur = FALSE;', '        else', '            use_box_blur = TRUE;']}
description: A SIGFPE is raised in the function box_blur_line of rsvg-filter.c in GNOME librsvg 2.40.17 during an attempted parse of a crafted SVG file, because of incorrect protection against division by zero.

code_evidence: use_box_blur is decided once from the combined condition sx < 10.0 && sy < 10.0, so it is TRUE whenever either axis is large.

In the horizontal pass (sx != 0.0), if use_box_blur is TRUE, compute_box_blur_width(sx) is called even when sx is small; its result box_width is then passed to box_blur_line, which divides by box_width.

In the vertical pass (sy != 0.0), the same combined flag is reused; compute_box_blur_width(sy) is called for small sy, producing a zero box_height that is passed to box_blur_line, where division by zero raises SIGFPE.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes a computed box dimension that can be zero as a divisor into box_blur_line, directly producing division by zero. This matches CWE-369 (Divide By Zero); it is not merely a general integer issue, since the crash stems specifically from a zero divisor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a single combined sx/sy decision controls box-blur selection for both independent passes, so one small axis is misrouted into the box-blur path. Trigger: a crafted SVG blur with one small radius (e.g., sx<10) and one large radius causes compute_box_blur_width to return 0, and box_blur_line divides by that zero width/height, crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
btrfs: fix deadlock with concurrent chunk allocations involving system chunks

When a task attempting to allocate a new chunk verifies that there is not
currently enough free space in the system space_info and there is another
task that allocated a new system chunk but it did not finish yet the
creation of the respective block group, it waits for that other task to
finish creating the block group. This is to avoid exhaustion of the system
chunk array in the superblock, which is limited, when we have a thundering
herd of tasks allocating new chunks. This problem was described and fixed
by commit eafa4fd0ad0607 ("btrfs: fix exhaustion of the system chunk array
due to concurrent allocations").

However there are two very similar scenarios where this can lead to a
deadlock:

1) Task B allocated a new system chunk and task A is waiting on task B
   to finish creation of the respective system block group. However before
   task B ends its transaction handle and finishes the creation of the
   system block group, it attempts to allocate another chunk (like a data
   chunk for an fallocate operation for a very large range). Task B will
   be unable to progress and allocate the new chunk, because task A set
   space_info->chunk_alloc to 1 and therefore it loops at
   btrfs_chunk_alloc() waiting for task A to finish its chunk allocation
   and set space_info->chunk_alloc to 0, but task A is waiting on task B
   to finish creation of the new system block group, therefore resulting
   in a deadlock;

2) Task B allocated a new system chunk and task A is waiting on task B to
   finish creation of the respective system block group. By the time that
   task B enter the final phase of block group allocation, which happens
   at btrfs_create_pending_block_groups(), when it modifies the extent
   tree, the device tree or the chunk tree to insert the items for some
   new block group, it needs to allocate a new chunk, so it ends up at
   btrfs_chunk_alloc() and keeps looping there because task A has set
   space_info->chunk_alloc to 1, but task A is waiting for task B to
   finish creation of the new system block group and release the reserved
   system space, therefore resulting in a deadlock.

In short, the problem is if a task B needs to allocate a new chunk after
it previously allocated a new system chunk and if another task A is
currently waiting for task B to complete the allocation of the new system
chunk.

Unfortunately this deadlock scenario introduced by the previous fix for
the system chunk array exhaustion problem does not have a simple and short
fix, and requires a big change to rework the chunk allocation code so that
chunk btree updates are all made in the first phase of chunk allocation.
And since this deadlock regression is being frequently hit on zoned
filesystems and the system chunk array exhaustion problem is triggered
in more extreme cases (originally observed on PowerPC with a node size
of 64K when running the fallocate tests from stress-ng), revert the
changes from that commit. The next patch in the series, with a subject
of "btrfs: rework chunk allocation to avoid exhaustion of the system
chunk array" does the necessary changes to fix the system chunk array
exhaustion problem.

Reported-by: Naohiro Aota <naohiro.aota@wdc.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-btrfs/20210621015922.ewgbffxuawia7liz@naota-xeon/
Fixes: eafa4fd0ad0607 ("btrfs: fix exhaustion of the system chunk array due to concurrent allocations")
CC: stable@vger.kernel.org # 5.12+
Tested-by: Shin'ichiro Kawasaki <shinichiro.kawasaki@wdc.com>
Tested-by: Naohiro Aota <naohiro.aota@wdc.com>
Signed-off-by: Filipe Manana <fdmanana@suse.com>
Tested-by: David Sterba <dsterba@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: David Sterba <dsterba@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct btrfs_transaction *cur_trans = trans->transaction;', '\tatomic64_sub(trans->chunk_bytes_reserved, &cur_trans->chunk_bytes_reserved);', '\tcond_wake_up(&cur_trans->chunk_reserve_wait);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: btrfs in the Linux kernel before 5.13.4 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) via processes that trigger allocation of new system chunks during times when there is a shortage of free space in the system space_info.

code_evidence: Early return when trans->chunk_bytes_reserved is zero skips all release logic, so any accounting/wakeup tied to a nonzero reservation is bypassed.
The function decrements cur_trans->chunk_bytes_reserved and wakes waiters on cur_trans->chunk_reserve_wait, coordinating other tasks waiting for reserved system chunk space.
The reservation counter is reset to zero only after the release and wakeup, tying the wakeup ordering to the accounting update.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function manages synchronization state (reservation counter plus condition wakeup) for concurrent chunk allocation; the deadlock arises from improper coordination of this lock-like reservation protocol, fitting CWE-667. It is not simply a race on data, but a lock/wait-ordering flaw causing indefinite blocking.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!trans->chunk_bytes_reserved)
return;

atomic64_sub(trans->chunk_bytes_reserved, &cur_trans->chunk_bytes_reserved);
cond_wake_up(&cur_trans->chunk_reserve_wait);
trans->chunk_bytes_reserved = 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: chunk reservation accounting and waiter wakeup are coupled to transaction/chunk allocation ordering, so a task holding a chunk reservation can block on another task that is waiting for the reservation to be released. Trigger: concurrent chunk allocations where one task waits for a system block group completion while the reserving task needs another chunk. Consequence: deadlock and denial of service, as described in the commit message.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Harden slave timer list handling

A slave timer instance might be still accessible in a racy way while
operating the master instance as it lacks of locking.  Since the
master operation is mostly protected with timer->lock, we should cope
with it while changing the slave instance, too.  Also, some linked
lists (active_list and ack_list) of slave instances aren't unlinked
immediately at stopping or closing, and this may lead to unexpected
accesses.

This patch tries to address these issues.  It adds spin lock of
timer->lock (either from master or slave, which is equivalent) in a
few places.  For avoiding a deadlock, we ensure that the global
slave_active_lock is always locked at first before each timer lock.

Also, ack and active_list of slave instances are properly unlinked at
snd_timer_stop() and snd_timer_close().

Last but not least, remove the superfluous call of _snd_timer_stop()
at removing slave links.  This is a noop, and calling it may confuse
readers wrt locking.  Further cleanup will follow in a later patch.

Actually we've got reports of use-after-free by syzkaller fuzzer, and
this hopefully fixes these issues.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tspin_lock_irq(&slave_active_lock);', '\t\t\t_snd_timer_stop(slave, 1, SNDRV_TIMER_EVENT_RESOLUTION);', '\t\t\tspin_unlock_irq(&slave_active_lock);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tspin_lock_irq(&slave_active_lock);', '\t\tspin_lock(&timer->lock);', '\t\t\tlist_del_init(&slave->ack_list);', '\t\t\tlist_del_init(&slave->active_list);', '\t\tspin_unlock(&timer->lock);', '\t\tspin_unlock_irq(&slave_active_lock);']}
description: sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 employs a locking approach that does not consider slave timer instances, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition, use-after-free, and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: The slave iteration walks timeri->slave_list_head and mutates each slave (open_list move, master/timer nulling) while only slave_active_lock is taken per iteration; the master timer->lock is not held, so a concurrent slave operation can access the same instance.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a shared-resource update (slave list/fields) under incomplete synchronization, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to modify the same resource. That is CWE-362; it is not merely a memory-safety bug, since the underlying defect is the missing exclusive access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: slave instances are modified without holding timer->lock, so a concurrent master/slave operation races on slave fields and list membership. Trigger: a crafted ioctl operating on the master while a slave is being closed/stopped. Supported consequence: use-after-free/race leading to crash, matching the reported DoS.

commit_msg:
usb: check RNDIS buffer offsets & length

When processing remote NDIS control message packets,
the USB Net device emulator uses a fixed length(4096) data buffer.
The incoming informationBufferOffset & Length combination could
overflow and cross that range. Check control message buffer
offsets and length to avoid it.

Reported-by: Qinghao Tang <luodalongde@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Message-id: 1455648821-17340-3-git-send-email-ppandit@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (bufoffs + buflen > length)'], 'added_lines': ['    if (buflen > length || bufoffs >= length || bufoffs + buflen > length) {', '    }']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in the USB Net device emulator (hw/usb/dev-network.c) in QEMU before 2.5.1 allow local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (QEMU process crash) or obtain sensitive host memory information via a remote NDIS control message packet that is mishandled in the (1) rndis_query_response, (2) rndis_set_response, or (3) usb_net_handle_dataout function.

code_evidence: InformationBufferOffset is read from the packet and incremented by 8 into bufoffs; InformationBufferLength is read into buflen. The only guard is the single comparison bufoffs + buflen > length, which itself performs an unchecked 32-bit addition of two attacker-controlled values before comparing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The guard relies on an addition whose result can wrap, an improper numeric calculation permitting out-of-bounds access; this matches CWE-189 numeric errors. It differs from a pure bounds-check omission because the missing constraint is the overflow of the computed offset-plus-length sum.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bufoffs + buflen is computed without overflow checking, so a large buflen (or large offset) wraps the sum to a small value that passes the length check. Trigger: a crafted RNDIS set message with overflowing offset/length. Consequence: the check is bypassed, and ndis_set is invoked with bufoffs + (uint8_t *)buf and buflen, reading/writing beyond the 4096-byte buffer, causing host memory disclosure or a QEMU crash.

commit_msg:
netlink: fix possible spoofing from non-root processes

Non-root user-space processes can send Netlink messages to other
processes that are well-known for being subscribed to Netlink
asynchronous notifications. This allows ilegitimate non-root
process to send forged messages to Netlink subscribers.

The userspace process usually verifies the legitimate origin in
two ways:

a) Socket credentials. If UID != 0, then the message comes from
   some ilegitimate process and the message needs to be dropped.

b) Netlink portID. In general, portID == 0 means that the origin
   of the messages comes from the kernel. Thus, discarding any
   message not coming from the kernel.

However, ctnetlink sets the portID in event messages that has
been triggered by some user-space process, eg. conntrack utility.
So other processes subscribed to ctnetlink events, eg. conntrackd,
know that the event was triggered by some user-space action.

Neither of the two ways to discard ilegitimate messages coming
from non-root processes can help for ctnetlink.

This patch adds capability validation in case that dst_pid is set
in netlink_sendmsg(). This approach is aggressive since existing
applications using any Netlink bus to deliver messages between
two user-space processes will break. Note that the exception is
NETLINK_USERSOCK, since it is reserved for netlink-to-netlink
userspace communication.

Still, if anyone wants that his Netlink bus allows netlink-to-netlink
userspace, then they can set NL_NONROOT_SEND. However, by default,
I don't think it makes sense to allow to use NETLINK_ROUTE to
communicate two processes that are sending no matter what information
that is not related to link/neighbouring/routing. They should be using
NETLINK_USERSOCK instead for that.

Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tnl_table[NETLINK_USERSOCK].nl_nonroot = NL_NONROOT_SEND;']}
description: The netlink_sendmsg function in net/netlink/af_netlink.c in the Linux kernel before 3.5.5 does not validate the dst_pid field, which allows local users to have an unspecified impact by spoofing Netlink messages.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only initializes the NETLINK_USERSOCK table entry (groups, listeners, module, registered flag); it contains no dst_pid handling or sender/credential validation, so it does not itself demonstrate the improper access control described.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. An attacker can craft a TFLite model that would allow limited reads and writes outside of arrays in TFLite. This exploits missing validation in the conversion from sparse tensors to dense tensors. The fix is included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range. Users are advised to upgrade as soon as possible.

code_evidence: At line 25 shape_of_level and metadata are read from dim_metadata_ without bounds checks. Line 32's sparse branch indexes array_segments[prev_idx] and array_segments[prev_idx+1] (line 35) without validating prev_idx against the segment size. Line 37 writes indices[level] and line 38 recurses using i as the new prev_idx, so an attacker-controlled sparse model can drive prev_idx past the segment array size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked indexing writes past the end of the indices buffer (and reads past metadata arrays), which is an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read because line 37 stores into indices[level] beyond its intended range.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing validation that prev_idx and i remain within dim_metadata_ segment/indices bounds during sparse-tensor traversal. Trigger: a crafted TFLite sparse model whose segment metadata yields out-of-range prev_idx. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of array_segments/array_indices and out-of-bounds write to indices[level], corrupting memory.
