description: xbuf_format_converter, used as part of exif_read_data, was appending a terminating null character to the generated string, but was not using its standard append char function. As a result, if the buffer was full, it would result in an out-of-bounds write. This issue affects HHVM versions prior to 4.56.3, all versions between 4.57.0 and 4.80.1, all versions between 4.81.0 and 4.93.1, and versions 4.94.0, 4.95.0, 4.96.0, 4.97.0, 4.98.0.

code_evidence: strncpy copies std::min(size, kFileNameMax) bytes from the Attr string into the fixed frame->file_name buffer; if size >= kFileNameMax the copy fills the buffer without a null terminator.
Same pattern for class_name: the copy length is clamped to kClassNameMax, which can fill the whole destination buffer.
Same pattern for function: the copy length is clamped to kFunctionMax, again allowing a full-buffer write with no terminator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The write to a fixed-size destination buffer whose length is not constrained to leave space for the terminator is a classic out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely CWE-125 (read) because the defect is in the write length to frame buffers.

strncpy(frame->function,
val(function_name).pstr->data(),
std::min(val(function_name).pstr->size(),
strobelight::kFunctionMax));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the copy count is not reduced to leave room for the terminating null, so a string whose size reaches the buffer maximum fills the entire destination. The subsequent explicit write of '\0' at index kMax-1 then overwrites the last byte, and the string is not properly terminated at a safe boundary; with attacker-controlled backtrace field lengths this yields an out-of-bounds/incorrect buffer write in the fixed-size frame.

commit_msg:
fixed local DoS when UnregisterHandler was called for a not existing handler

Any user with DBUS access could cause a SEGFAULT in tcmu-runner by
running something like this:

dbus-send --system --print-reply --dest=org.kernel.TCMUService1 /org/kernel/TCMUService1/HandlerManager1 org.kernel.TCMUService1.HandlerManager1.UnregisterHandler string:123

description: The tcmu-runner daemon in tcmu-runner version 1.0.5 to 1.2.0 is vulnerable to a local denial of service attack

code_evidence: Line 7 resolves the caller-supplied subtype string via find_handler_by_subtype; line 8 immediately dereferences the returned handler->opaque before the NULL check at line 9. When the subtype does not match any handler, handler is NULL and line 8 dereferences a null pointer, so the intended unknown-subtype error path at lines 10-13 is never reached.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accepts attacker-controlled input (the subtype) and fails to validate that it maps to an existing handler before processing, i.e., dereferencing the derived handler pointer. This matches CWE-20's improper validation of input properties; the crash is the resulting availability impact, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the externally supplied subtype from a DBus UnregisterHandler call is looked up, but the lookup result is dereferenced before being validated for existence. description: Integer overflow in tools/tiffcp.c in LibTIFF 4.0.7, 3.9.3, 3.9.4, 3.9.5, 3.9.6, 3.9.7, 4.0.0alpha4, 4.0.0alpha5, 4.0.0alpha6, 4.0.0beta7, 4.0.0, 4.0.1, 4.0.2, 4.0.3, 4.0.4, 4.0.4beta, 4.0.5 and 4.0.6 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted image, which triggers a heap-based buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The parameter inskew is declared as int; the patch changes it to int64 to avoid 32-bit wraparound.
After copying each row, the pointer in is advanced by in += inskew; a large or negative skew can wrap the 32-bit int arithmetic before being applied to the pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is integer wraparound in the skew arithmetic used to compute a memory offset; the patch widens inskew to int64 specifically to prevent this overflow. The out-of-bounds read is the consequence of the wrapped offset, not a separate root-cause weakness.

evidence_lines.code: uint32 rows, uint32 cols, int outskew, int inskew)

out += outskew;
in += inskew;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: inskew is a 32-bit int, so the per-row pointer increment in += inskew is computed in 32-bit arithmetic and can overflow/wrap when callers pass large or negative skews. Trigger: a crafted image causes a large strip/tile geometry that yields an out-of-range skew. Consequence: in points outside the intended buffer, so the next row's *out++ = *in++ reads from an invalid location, supporting heap out-of-bounds access/corruption.

commit_msg:
Prevent another div by 0 in optimized pooling implementations TFLite

PiperOrigin-RevId: 370800091
Change-Id: I2119352f57fb5ca4f2051e0e2d749403304a979b
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  // Prevent division by 0 in optimized pooling implementations', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, params->stride_height > 0);', '  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, params->stride_width > 0);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Optimized pooling implementations in TFLite fail to check that the stride arguments are not 0 before calling `ComputePaddingHeightWidth`(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/3f24ccd932546416ec906a02ddd183b48a1d2c83/tensorflow/lite/kernels/pooling.cc#L90). Since users can craft special models which will have `params->stride_{height,width}` be zero, this will result in a division by zero. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function reads attacker-controllable pooling parameters from node->builtin_data (line 2) and passes params->stride_height and params->stride_width directly into ComputePaddingHeightWidth without validating they are nonzero. This call is the operation that divides by the stride values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Passing an unchecked zero stride into a routine that divides by it directly matches CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). It is not merely an unchecked input issue; the specific consequence is division by zero, so the base weakness fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: GenericPrepare performs no zero check on params->stride_height/stride_width before ComputePaddingHeightWidth uses them as divisors. Trigger: a crafted model sets a stride to 0. Consequence: integer division by zero during preparation, causing a crash (DoS).

description: A denial of service vulnerability was found in tildearrow Furnace. It has been classified as problematic. This is due to an incomplete fix of CVE-2022-1211. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely but it requires user interaction. The issue got fixed with the patch 0eb02422d5161767e9983bdaa5c429762d3477ce.

code_evidence: For an effect cell with pat->data[i][index] != -1, the value is passed to sprintf at line 179 and compared against thresholds starting at line 180. The value is only treated as an extended effect (>=0xe0) at line 196/198, where line 199 indexes extFxColors[pat->data[i][index]-0xe0] with no upper bound. pat->data[i][index] is an int from the pattern data; the code never checks it against the size of extFxColors, so a value such as 0x1FF (or any value >0xe0 beyond the array) yields an out-of-bounds index at line 199.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers improper handling of resource release; here the relevant resource is the extFxColors lookup table, and the code fails to bound-check its index before use, allowing an out-of-range access that disrupts availability. The missing upper-bound check on the pattern value, not merely a formatting error, is the defect the fix's '>0xff' guard addresses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extended-effect branch assumes any value >=0xe0 indexes extFxColors within its bounds, but the pattern value is not validated against the array size. Trigger: a pattern cell containing an effect value above the extFxColors range (e.g., 0x1FF) is rendered by patternRow. The unbounded subtraction and index produce an out-of-bounds read; the sprintf at line 179 also writes it without validation. The supported consequence is an out-of-bounds array access that can crash the process (denial of service), consistent with the referenced incomplete-fix crash report.

Release "3.0.6": Fix crashes in Array for "integer overflow #10"

FossilOrigin-Name: 50642d64b8f0a4e62df68e59fcb2ef0923c3dbec8fc8a15d38b1ddbe655c38d6

description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjSetLength in jsish before 3.0.6, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 11 obtains the array length n via Jsi_ObjGetLength (the pre-fix call). Line 15 declares a double nstart; line 20 converts the user-supplied start value to int istart via a cast, and lines 21-26 compare istart to n and adjust negatives without validating that the cast result is representable or that n+istart cannot wrap.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because an integer value derived from a double-to-int conversion and used in index arithmetic can wrap to a small or negative number, and the logic assumes it stays within the array bounds. This is distinct from a bounds-check omission alone: the defect is the unchecked arithmetic conversion enabling the wrapped index.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The user-controlled start value is cast from a double to int (line 20) without a range check; a large magnitude value truncates/wraps to an arbitrary int. The subsequent comparisons against n and the negative adjustment (lines 23-24) then operate on a corrupted index, so the loop at line 33 can compute out-of-bounds offsets into obj->arr, leading to memory corruption or crash. Root cause is the unchecked numeric conversion feeding index arithmetic; trigger is a crafted start argument.

commit_msg:
KEYS: Fix race between updating and finding a negative key

Consolidate KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE and the rejection
error into one field such that:

 (1) The instantiation state can be modified/read atomically.

 (2) The error can be accessed atomically with the state.

 (3) The error isn't stored unioned with the payload pointers.

This deals with the problem that the state is spread over three different
objects (two bits and a separate variable) and reading or updating them
atomically isn't practical, given that not only can uninstantiated keys
change into instantiated or rejected keys, but rejected keys can also turn
into instantiated keys - and someone accessing the key might not be using
any locking.

The main side effect of this problem is that what was held in the payload
may change, depending on the state.  For instance, you might observe the
key to be in the rejected state.  You then read the cached error, but if
the key semaphore wasn't locked, the key might've become instantiated
between the two reads - and you might now have something in hand that isn't
actually an error code.

The state is now KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED, KEY_IS_POSITIVE or a negative error
code if the key is negatively instantiated.  The key_is_instantiated()
function is replaced with key_is_positive() to avoid confusion as negative
keys are also 'instantiated'.

Additionally, barriering is included:

 (1) Order payload-set before state-set during instantiation.

 (2) Order state-read before payload-read when using the key.

Further separate barriering is necessary if RCU is being used to access the
payload content after reading the payload pointers.

Fixes: 146aa8b1453b ("KEYS: Merge the type-specific data with the payload data")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v4.4+
Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (test_bit(KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, &key->flags) &&', '\t\t    !test_bit(KEY_FLAG_NEGATIVE, &key->flags) &&', '\t\t    key->type->destroy)', '\t\tif (test_bit(KEY_FLAG_INSTANTIATED, &key->flags))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tshort state = key->state;', '', '\t\tif (state == KEY_IS_POSITIVE && key->type->destroy)', '\t\tif (state != KEY_IS_UNINSTANTIATED)']}

commit_msg:
Eric Dumazet says:

====================
Juha-Matti Tilli reported that malicious peers could inject tiny
packets in out_of_order_queue, forcing very expensive calls
to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for
every incoming packet.

With tcp_rmem[2] default of 6MB, the ooo queue could
contain ~7000 nodes.

This patch series makes sure we cut cpu cycles enough to
render the attack not critical.

We might in the future go further, like disconnecting
or black-holing proven malicious flows.
====================

Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\ttcp_collapse(sk, NULL, &tp->out_of_order_queue,', '\t\t\t\t     head, skb, start, end);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu32 range_truesize, sum_tiny = 0;', '\trange_truesize = skb->truesize;', '\t\t\t/* Do not attempt collapsing tiny skbs */', '\t\t\tif (range_truesize != head->truesize ||', '\t\t\t    end - start >= SKB_WITH_OVERHEAD(SK_MEM_QUANTUM)) {', '\t\t\t\ttcp_collapse(sk, NULL, &tp->out_of_order_queue,', '\t\t\t\t\t     head, skb, start, end);', '\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\tsum_tiny += range_truesize;', '\t\t\t\tif (sum_tiny > sk->sk_rcvbuf >> 3)', '\t\t\t\t\treturn;', '\t\t\t}', '\t\trange_truesize += skb->truesize;']}
description: Linux kernel versions 4.9+ can be forced to make very expensive calls to tcp_collapse_ofo_queue() and tcp_prune_ofo_queue() for every incoming packet which can lead to a denial of service.

code_evidence: The function walks the out-of-order queue in a loop that repeatedly calls tcp_collapse() whenever a range boundary is reached, then restarts via new_range. Each incoming packet can trigger this O(n) collapse over the full queue, and the loop has no bound on how many ranges it processes per call.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the function fails to throttle the maintenance work triggered by attacker-controlled queue contents, leading to CPU resource exhaustion (DoS).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the out-of-order queue maintenance loop performs tcp_collapse() for each range without limiting work per invocation. A peer injecting many tiny out-of-order packets fills the queue, forcing expensive collapse calls for every packet and exhausting CPU.

description: The swiotlb_print_info function in lib/swiotlb.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.14 allows local users to obtain sensitive address information by reading dmesg data from a "software IO TLB" printk call.

code_evidence: When the allocated order differs from the requested size, the fallback branch logs the allocated size via printk(KERN_WARNING ...) into the kernel ring buffer; this message is readable through dmesg by local users.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code explicitly inserts internal allocation information into a log resource (dmesg) that unauthorized local users can read, matching CWE-200's exposure of sensitive internal state to actors not authorized for it. This is a deliberate logging disclosure, not an indirect consequence of another memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function writes a diagnostic message revealing software IO TLB allocation details into the kernel log, which is accessible to unprivileged local users via dmesg. The trigger is the allocation-order mismatch path at line 26; the supported consequence is disclosure of kernel memory-allocation state to unauthorized actors.

commit_msg:
Fix memory leak parsing group addresses without a display name.

When there was a group address terminator with no previous
addresses (including the group display-name), an address would be
allocated but not attached to the address list.

Change this to only allocate when last exists.

It would be more correct to not allocate at all unless we are inside a
group list, but I will address that in a separate commit to master.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      cur = rfc822_new_address ();', '\tlast->next = cur;', '\tlast = cur;'], 'added_lines': ['\tlast->next = rfc822_new_address ();', '\tlast = last->next;']}
description: rfc822.c in Mutt through 2.0.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (mailbox unavailability) by sending email messages with sequences of semicolon characters in RFC822 address fields (aka terminators of empty groups). A small email message from the attacker can cause large memory consumption, and the victim may then be unable to see email messages from other persons.

code_evidence: In the ';' (group terminator) branch, rfc822_new_address() is called unconditionally at line 119, assigning a fresh ADDRESS to cur. The block only links it into the list (last->next = cur; last = cur) when last is non-NULL; when last is NULL the allocated cur is never attached to top and no pointer to it is retained, so it cannot be freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory and loses the only reference without releasing it, which is exactly missing release of memory after effective lifetime (CWE-401). It is not a use-after-free or double-free, since the block is simply never freed; the unsupported consequence is memory growth from attacker-controlled input.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a heap allocation is performed before checking whether a list anchor exists. Trigger: an RFC822 address field containing a group terminator ';' with no preceding address (last == NULL). The orphaned allocation is unreachable and never released, so repeated terminators in one message accumulate memory, supporting resource-consumption DoS / mailbox unavailability.

  #3 0x44393f in localtime_rz lib/time_rz.c:290
  #4 0x41e4fe in parse_datetime2 lib/parse-datetime.y:1798

A minimized reproducer is the following 120 byte TZ value,
which goes beyond the value of ABBR_SIZE_MIN (119) on x86_64.
Extend the aa...b portion to overwrite more of the heap.

  date -d $(printf 'TZ="aaa%020daaaaaab%089d"')

localtime_rz and mktime_z were affected since commit 4bc76593.
parse_datetime was affected since commit 4e6e16b3f.

* lib/time_rz.c (save_abbr): Rearrange the calculation determining
whether there is enough buffer space available.  The rearrangement
ensures we're only dealing with positive numbers, thus avoiding
the problematic promotion of signed to unsigned causing an invalid
comparison when zone_copy is more than ABBR_SIZE_MIN bytes beyond
the start of the buffer.
* tests/test-parse-datetime.c (main): Add a test case written by
Paul Eggert, which overwrites enough of the heap so that
standard glibc will fail with "free(): invalid pointer"
without the patch applied.
Reported and analyzed at https://bugzilla.redhat.com/1444774
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['              if (zone_size < tz->abbrs + ABBR_SIZE_MIN - zone_copy)'], 'added_lines': ['              size_t zone_used = zone_copy - tz->abbrs;', '              if (SIZE_MAX - zone_used < zone_size)', '                {', '                  errno = ENOMEM;', '                  return false;', '                }', '              if (zone_used + zone_size < ABBR_SIZE_MIN)']}
description: Gnulib before 2017-04-26 has a heap-based buffer overflow with the TZ environment variable. The error is in the save_abbr function in time_rz.c.

code_evidence: Line 29 computes zone_size from the external TZ-derived abbreviation string. Line 30's bounds check compares zone_size against the pointer-arithmetic expression tz->abbrs + ABBR_SIZE_MIN - zone_copy; when zone_copy is more than ABBR_SIZE_MIN bytes past tz->abbrs, the unsigned subtraction wraps, making the comparison pass incorrectly and calling extend_abbrs (line 31) to write past the buffer.
The else branch at 32-39 only allocates a new timezone when the flawed check fails; the wrap makes the safe path unreachable for the overflow case.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe write in extend_abbrs targets a memory location outside the abbrs buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within buffer bounds; the flawed comparison is the cause enabling the out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size check mixes pointer subtraction with unsigned arithmetic, so a large offset makes the computed remaining space wrap to a huge value. Trigger: a TZ abbreviation longer than the remaining abbrs buffer (e.g., >ABBR_SIZE_MIN bytes) reaches save_abbr. Consequence: extend_abbrs writes zone_size bytes beyond tz->abbrs, a heap buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
Prevent leak of SecurityServer and ClientServer.

They are created in SConnection's and CConnection's constructors but never destroyed.

There is no reason for the indirection, so lets make them direct members.

description: In TigerVNC 1.7.1 (CConnection.cxx CConnection::CConnection), an unauthenticated client can cause a small memory leak in the server.

code_evidence: The constructor body allocates a SecurityClient via 'security = new SecurityClient();' and then the constructor ends at line 8 without any corresponding delete or ownership transfer to a member that would be destroyed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 covers failing to release a resource after its effective lifetime. The raw 'new SecurityClient()' with no matching release in the function directly instantiates that missing-release pattern; the leak is a consequence of the unmanaged allocation, not a separate weakness such as improper input validation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor unconditionally allocates a SecurityClient object and no destructor or cleanup path releases it, so the resource outlives its effective lifetime. Trigger: each CConnection construction (e.g., per unauthenticated client connection) performs the allocation. commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> guard(mInternalData->mLock);']}
description: In multiple functions of MetaDataBase.cpp, there is a possible UAF write due to a race condition. This could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

code_evidence: The loop iterates mInternalData->mItems and, on each iteration, calls keyAt(i) and valueAt(i) to read the shared KeyedVector. No lock is held in this version, so a concurrent thread modifying mItems (e.g., insert/remove) can change its size or reallocate its backing store between these accesses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a multi-step read of a shared resource with no exclusive-access guarantee, exactly the timing window in which an interfering sequence can modify the resource; this is CWE-362. The fix adds a mutex lock_guard, confirming the missing synchronization rather than a separate memory-safety root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unsynchronized concurrent access to the shared mItems KeyedVector. Trigger: another thread mutates mItems while toString() reads keyAt(i)/valueAt(i), so the index or element reference becomes stale after a size change or reallocation. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds or use-after-free reads/writes on the vector storage (the commit describes a UAF write and privilege escalation).

description: Race condition in Oracle MySQL before 5.5.52, 5.6.x before 5.6.33, 5.7.x before 5.7.15, and 8.x before 8.0.1; MariaDB before 5.5.52, 10.0.x before 10.0.28, and 10.1.x before 10.1.18; Percona Server before 5.5.51-38.2, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-78-1, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-8; and Percona XtraDB Cluster before 5.5.41-37.0, 5.6.x before 5.6.32-25.17, and 5.7.x before 5.7.14-26.17 allows local users with certain permissions to gain privileges by leveraging use of my_copystat by REPAIR TABLE to repair a MyISAM table.

code_evidence: The patched function init_common_variables sets server_start_time and initializes replication/binlog filters (lines 8-9); the diff adds my_disable_copystat_in_redel = 1 immediately after line 8, a global flag that disables the my_copystat behavior in the server. The function itself contains no synchronization primitive around this global state, so the flag is set during startup without any locking.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the underlying weakness is a timing window in a concurrent file-copy sequence lacking exclusive access to a shared resource; the function's role is to disable the racy helper at startup. It is not CWE-667 (improper locking) generally, since the specific issue is a copy race.

evidence_lines.code:
server_start_time= flush_status_time= my_time(0);
rpl_filter= new Rpl_filter;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the server previously performed REPAIR TABLE via my_copystat, which copies file metadata/attributes non-atomically, allowing a concurrent process to race the copy and alter the file or permissions. The fix disables my_copystat in the server by setting the global flag during initialization. Trigger: a local user with repair privileges issues REPAIR TABLE on a MyISAM table while a concurrent code sequence modifies the underlying file. Supported consequence: privilege escalation or race-induced corruption, as the description states.

commit_msg:
driver core: platform: fix race condition with driver_override

The driver_override implementation is susceptible to race condition when
different threads are reading vs storing a different driver override.
Add locking to avoid race condition.

Fixes: 3d713e0e382e ("driver core: platform: add device binding path 'driver_override'")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Adrian Salido <salidoa@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn sprintf(buf, "%s\\n", pdev->driver_override);'], 'added_lines': ['\tssize_t len;', '\tdevice_lock(dev);', '\tlen = sprintf(buf, "%s\\n", pdev->driver_override);', '\tdevice_unlock(dev);', '\treturn len;']}
description: The driver_override implementation in drivers/base/platform.c in the Linux kernel before 4.12.1 allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging a race condition between a read operation and a store operation that involve different overrides.

code_evidence: driver_override_show reads pdev->driver_override via sprintf without holding device_lock, while the store path can concurrently replace the pointer, so the read of the shared pointer is unsynchronized.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the read sequence lacks exclusive access to a shared resource that another concurrent sequence can modify; the missing lock creates the timing window. This is improper synchronization of a shared resource, not merely a length or format bug.

evidence_lines.code:
struct platform_device *pdev = to_platform_device(dev);
return sprintf(buf, "%s\n", pdev->driver_override);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the show function dereferences the shared driver_override pointer with no lock, so a concurrent store can free/replace the string between read and use. Trigger: one thread reads the attribute while another writes a different override. Supported consequence: a race causing use of a stale/freed pointer, potentially leading to corruption or privilege escalation as described.

commit_msg:
Fixed wrong condition for copying arguments on stack; fix #4926

This bug was introduced in 694089f to address #4832
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        mrb_bool nocopy = altmode || argv_on_stack ? TRUE : FALSE;'], 'added_lines': ['        mrb_bool nocopy = altmode || argv_on_stack ? FALSE : TRUE;']}
description: In mruby 2.1.0, there is a use-after-free in hash_values_at in mrbgems/mruby-hash-ext/src/hash-ext.c.

code_evidence: The '*' branch computes nocopy from altmode/argv_on_stack, then, when argc>i, either aliases the live stack/array argv via *var=argv+i (nocopy path) or copies into a new array via mrb_ary_new_from_values and exposes RARRAY_PTR(args) via *var. The fixed condition flips which branch is taken.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The exposed RARRAY_PTR of a temporary array whose reference was cleared can outlive that allocation, so later access is a use-after-free, matching CWE-416. The bug is the inverted condition controlling whether memory is borrowed or copied, not a bounds issue (CWE-125/787).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the wrong ternary inverted the copy decision, so for stack arguments the function returned a pointer into a freshly allocated, only-implicitly-referenced array (RARRAY(args)->c cleared) instead of a stable stack slice (or vice versa). The returned *var can then be used after the temporary array is collected/freed, yielding a dangling pointer read/write.

commit_msg:
Signed-off-by: Vincent Pelletier <plr.vincent@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Christie <mchristi@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchap_binaryhex_to_asciihex(challenge_asciihex, chap->challenge,'], 'added_lines': ['\tbin2hex(challenge_asciihex, chap->challenge,']}
description: A security flaw was found in the chap_server_compute_md5() function in the ISCSI target code in the Linux kernel in a way an authentication request from an ISCSI initiator is processed. An unauthenticated remote attacker can cause a stack buffer overflow and smash up to 17 bytes of the stack. The attack requires the iSCSI target to be enabled on the victim host. Depending on how the target's code was built (i.e. depending on a compiler, compile flags and hardware architecture) an attack may lead to a system crash and thus to a denial-of-service or possibly to a non-authorized access to data exported by an iSCSI target. Due to the nature of the flaw, privilege escalation cannot be fully ruled out, although we believe it is highly unlikely. Kernel versions 4.18.x, 4.14.x and 3.10.x are believed to be vulnerable.

code_evidence: Line 8 declares a fixed stack buffer challenge_asciihex sized CHAP_CHALLENGE_LENGTH*2+1 and zeroes it at line 10. Line 11 fills chap->challenge with CHAP_CHALLENGE_LENGTH random bytes. Line 14-15 convert that challenge into challenge_asciihex via chap_binaryhex_to_asciihex, then line 16 appends the string to c_str with sprintf, advancing *c_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The overwritten object is a local stack array (challenge_asciihex), and the overflow arises from an unchecked copy into it, matching CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow. It is distinct from heap or global overflow because the affected buffer is allocated on the stack.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the unsafe chap_binaryhex_to_asciihex conversion writing hex output into the fixed stack buffer challenge_asciihex without a bounds check; the trigger is the challenge conversion path exercised during an iSCSI authentication request. The supported consequence is a stack-based overflow that can overwrite adjacent stack memory, enabling crash/DoS and potentially further memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Don't go past the end of a page in a NetScaler file.

Records in a properly formatted NetScaler file shouldn't go past the end
of a page, but nothing guarantees that a NetScaler file will be properly
formatted.

NetScaler 3.x files allow record bodies to go past the end of a page,
but 1.x and 2.x files don't, so treat record headers that go past the
end of a page, and record bodies in 1.x and 2.x files that go past the
end of a page, as errors.

Clean up some stuff while we're at it.

Bug: 13430
Change-Id: I3b1d56086e3bb14b246406f306e3d730df337561
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/20326
Reviewed-by: Guy Harris <guy@alum.mit.edu>
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/20329
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    gint32 nstrace_buf_offset = nstrace->nstrace_buf_offset;', '    gint32 nstrace_buflen = nstrace->nstrace_buflen;', '    }while((nstrace_buflen > 0) && (bytes_read = file_read(nstrace_buf, nstrace_buflen, wth->fh)) && (bytes_read == nstrace_buflen));'], 'added_lines': ['    guint32 nstrace_buf_offset = nstrace->nstrace_buf_offset;', '    guint32 nstrace_buflen = nstrace->nstrace_buflen;', '    }while((nstrace_buflen > 0) && (bytes_read = file_read(nstrace_buf, nstrace_buflen, wth->fh)) > 0 && ((guint32)bytes_read == nstrace_buflen));']}
description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.4 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.10, there is a NetScaler file parser crash, triggered by a malformed capture file. This was addressed in wiretap/netscaler.c by validating the relationship between pages and records.

code_evidence: The loop guard only checks that at least sizeof(ph_RecordType) bytes remain, not that the full record header/body fits within the page buffer.

The record type is read via pletoh16 at nstrace_buf_offset, and each case advances nstrace_buf_offset by the attacker-controlled nsprRecordSize from the record header, without verifying that offset + RecordSize stays within nstrace_buflen.
The do-while condition relies on file_read results; the signed gint32 buffer length/offset types make the bounds comparison fragile, and no check rejects records that run past the page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function processes untrusted file metadata (record sizes/offsets) without validating the required relationship between records and page bounds, which is improper input validation. This directly matches CWE-20; the consequence is an availability impact from unvalidated malformed input.

evidence_lines.code:
while ((nstrace_buf_offset < nstrace_buflen) &&
((nstrace_buflen - nstrace_buf_offset) >= ((gint32)sizeof((( nspr_header_v10_t*)&nstrace_buf[nstrace_buf_offset])->ph_RecordType))))
}while((nstrace_buflen > 0) && (bytes_read = file_read(nstrace_buf, nstrace_buflen, wth->fh)) && (bytes_read == nstrace_buflen));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser trusts the record size field in the NetScaler file and advances nstrace_buf_offset by it without confirming the record lies within the current page. A malformed capture with an oversized or malformed record causes out-of-bounds reads past the page buffer, leading to a parser crash (DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if ((*pkthdr)->len > MAX_PCAP_PACKET_LEN) {', '                    file, funcname, line, (*pkthdr)->len, MAX_PCAP_PACKET_LEN);'], 'added_lines': ['        if ((*pkthdr)->len > MAXPACKET) {', '                    file, funcname, line, (*pkthdr)->len, MAXPACKET);']}
description: Tcpreplay v4.3.0 beta1 contains a heap-based buffer over-read. The get_next_packet() function in the send_packets.c file uses the memcpy() function unsafely to copy sequences from the source buffer pktdata to the destination (*prev_packet)->pktdata. This will result in a Denial of Service (DoS) and potentially Information Exposure when the application attempts to process a file.

code_evidence: Line 5 obtains packet metadata from pcap_next_ex; lines 6-11 only reject a packet whose length exceeds MAX_PCAP_PACKET_LEN, but no check ensures the returned buffer actually contains caplen bytes. The length/caplen relationship is validated later (line 12), yet the buffer returned by libpcap may be shorter than the header claims, so downstream consumers reading caplen bytes can read past the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading beyond the returned packet buffer is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), matching the described unsafe memcpy from pktdata. A write overflow (CWE-787) is not supported because the missing constraint concerns read length, not a write bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the pcap header's caplen and never constrains it against the actual buffer size returned by pcap_next_ex. Trigger: a crafted capture file or truncated packet where caplen exceeds the real data. Consequence: downstream memcpy/reads walk past the buffer end, causing heap over-read, DoS or information exposure.

commit_msg: wqfix issues 1368:exist a issues of freeing uninitialized pointer in src/bin/jp2/opj_decompress.c，that will cause a segfault
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        dirptr = (dircnt_t*)malloc(sizeof(dircnt_t));'], 'added_lines': ['        dirptr = (dircnt_t*)calloc(1, sizeof(dircnt_t));']}
description: A flaw was found in the opj2_decompress program in openjpeg2 2.4.0 in the way it handles an input directory with a large number of files. When it fails to allocate a buffer to store the filenames of the input directory, it calls free() on an uninitialized pointer, leading to a segmentation fault and a denial of service.

code_evidence: dirptr is allocated with malloc, so its fields are uninitialized until the later memset at line 29.

filename_buf is allocated; if this allocation fails, the code sets failed and jumps to fin before memset of the buffer is relevant, but dirptr->filename_buf itself was zeroed by the memset at line 29.
At fin, the cleanup reads dirptr->filename and dirptr->filename_buf and frees them; these reads depend on the struct having been initialized before any goto fin path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-665 fits because the resource (heap struct) is allocated without initialization, so its pointer members hold indeterminate values that are later used in the cleanup path; this is improper initialization rather than a classic use-after-free or double-free, which would require prior valid initialization.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The struct is obtained with malloc and only zero-initialized by a separate memset after the allocation check. If control reaches the fin cleanup before that memset (e.g., an early error path after allocation), the pointer fields are read and freed while uninitialized, producing undefined behavior and a likely crash/DoS.

commit_msg: fixed trivial auth detection for pubkeys
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tcli_ses.is_trivial_auth = 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Dropbear through 2020.81. Due to a non-RFC-compliant check of the available authentication methods in the client-side SSH code, it is possible for an SSH server to change the login process in its favor. This attack can bypass additional security measures such as FIDO2 tokens or SSH-Askpass. Thus, it allows an attacker to abuse a forwarded agent for logging on to another server unnoticed.

code_evidence: The realsign branch builds a signature buffer and calls cli_buf_put_sign, but in the provided function body it never clears cli_ses.is_trivial_auth; the commit adds that reset after signing. The function only distinguishes realsign versus non-realsign via the realsign byte at line 15 and the if(realsign) block.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect concerns client-side authentication state not being proven/updated correctly, allowing a server to influence whether real authentication occurred, which fits CWE-287 (Improper Authentication). It is not merely a protocol-format bug: the missing state reset directly affects authentication trust decisions.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pubkey authentication path leaves the client's trivial-auth state set after a real signature is sent, so the client-side authentication state does not reflect that a genuine pubkey signature occurred. Trigger: an SSH server manipulates the advertised/available auth methods so the client takes this path. Consequence: the server can steer the login process and bypass additional authentication measures or abuse a forwarded agent.

The discovering of sas port is driven by workqueue in libsas. When libsas
is processing port events or phy events in workqueue, new events may rise
up and change the state of some structures such as asd_sas_phy.  This may
cause some problems such as follows:

==>thread 1                       ==>thread 2

                                  ==>phy up
                                  ==>phy_up_v3_hw()
                                    ==>oob_mode = SATA_OOB_MODE;

                                    ==>sas_ha->notify_phy_event()
                                    ==>sas_phy_disconnected()
                                      ==>oob_mode = OOB_NOT_CONNECTED
==>workqueue wakeup
==>sas_form_port()
  ==>sas_discover_domain()
    ==>sas_get_port_device()
      ==>oob_mode is OOB_NOT_CONNECTED and device
         is wrongly taken as expander

This at last lead to the panic when libsas trying to issue a command to
discover the device.

description: In the Linux kernel through 5.4.6, there is a NULL pointer dereference in drivers/scsi/libsas/sas_discover.c because of mishandling of port disconnection during discovery, related to a PHY down race condition, aka CID-f70267f379b5.

code_evidence: In the pre-patch else branch, dev->frame_rcvd is cast to struct sas_identify_frame and dev_type/iproto/tproto are read from it whenever the SATA condition at line 22 fails, without checking port->oob_mode.

If a PHY-down race sets oob_mode to OOB_NOT_CONNECTED, frame_rcvd may not contain a valid identify frame, so id->dev_type yields an unintended value; the switch then falls through to default, rphy stays NULL, and line 65 returns through sas_put_device without dereferencing rphy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit's crash is a NULL pointer dereference during expander discovery (CWE-476), rooted in the missing oob_mode check in this function. It is not a direct NULL dereference within this function; the function supplies the misclassification that leads to the NULL dereference downstream.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code interprets frame_rcvd as an identify frame without verifying that the port's oob_mode still indicates a connected link. Trigger: a PHY-down event during discovery changes oob_mode, causing a wrong dev_type to be derived; the resulting NULL rphy is handled, but the misclassified device later drives discovery of a nonexistent expander, leading to the reported NULL dereference.

commit_msg:
IB/security: Restrict use of the write() interface

The drivers/infiniband stack uses write() as a replacement for
bi-directional ioctl().  This is not safe. There are ways to
trigger write calls that result in the return structure that
is normally written to user space being shunted off to user
specified kernel memory instead.

For the immediate repair, detect and deny suspicious accesses to
the write API.

For long term, update the user space libraries and the kernel API
to something that doesn't present the same security vulnerabilities
(likely a structured ioctl() interface).

The impacted uAPI interfaces are generally only available if
hardware from drivers/infiniband is installed in the system.

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jann@thejh.net>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgunthorpe@obsidianresearch.com>
[ Expanded check to all known write() entry points ]
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Doug Ledford <dledford@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (WARN_ON_ONCE(!ib_safe_file_access(filp)))', '\t\treturn -EACCES;']}
description: The InfiniBand (aka IB) stack in the Linux kernel before 4.5.3 incorrectly relies on the write system call, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (kernel memory write operation) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a uAPI interface.

code_evidence: The write() entry point begins by only checking count and copying the header; it performs no validation that the caller's file was opened through the expected uAPI path before dispatching commands.

In the extended-command branch, a user-supplied ex_hdr.response pointer is validated with access_ok and then used as the output buffer, so command output can be written to caller-chosen kernel memory.
When ex_hdr.response is zero, the code only checks output word counts and does not reject the request, allowing command output to be sent to an unintended destination.
INIT_UDATA_BUF_OR_NULL builds ucore/uhw output buffers from ex_hdr.response, propagating the user-controlled address into the command handler.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to enforce an access-control constraint on the write() interface, letting a caller direct privileged output to memory it should not control; this improper permission enforcement fits CWE-264's scope of access-control weaknesses.

evidence_lines.code:
INIT_UDATA_BUF_OR_NULL(&ucore, buf, (unsigned long) ex_hdr.response,
hdr.in_words * 8, hdr.out_words * 8);
INIT_UDATA_BUF_OR_NULL(&uhw,
buf + ucore.inlen,
(unsigned long) ex_hdr.response + ucore.outlen,
ex_hdr.provider_in_words * 8,
ex_hdr.provider_out_words * 8);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ib_uverbs_write dispatches uAPI commands via write() without first verifying that the file access is safe, and the extended path forwards a user-controlled ex_hdr.response address as the output buffer. Trigger: a local user issues a crafted write() with the extended flag and a chosen response pointer. Supported consequence: command output is written to caller-specified kernel memory, enabling kernel memory corruption or denial of service.

description: EOSIO/eos eos version after commit f1545dd0ae2b77580c2236fdb70ae7138d2c7168 contains a stack overflow vulnerability in abi_serializer that can result in attack eos network node. This attack appear to be exploitable via network request. This vulnerability appears to have been fixed in after commit cf7209e703e6d3f7a5413e0cb1fe88a4d8e4b38d .

code_evidence: The operator looks up name in _vo and, when found, calls abi_from_variant::extract on itr->value() with no recursion-depth argument. The call recurses into nested ABI data without any bound or depth counter passed along.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-674 fits because the function performs recursion with no controlling depth condition, allowing attacker-influenced nesting to consume the program stack. It is uncontrolled recursion rather than merely excessive input size, since the missing constraint is the recursion bound itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursive extract call is invoked without a recursion-depth limit, so nested variant/ABI structures drive unbounded recursion. Trigger: a network-supplied ABI containing deeply nested data reaches this operator repeatedly. Consequence: stack exhaustion leading to a node crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: make the internal memory data base the default

Having a file backed data base has the only advantage of being capable
to dump the contents of it while Xenstore is running, and potentially
using less swap space in case the data base can't be kept in memory.

It has the major disadvantage of a huge performance overhead: switching
to keep the data base in memory only speeds up live update of xenstored
with 120000 nodes from 20 minutes to 11 seconds. A complete tree walk
of this configuration will be reduced from 7 seconds to 280 msecs
(measured by "xenstore-control check").

So make the internal memory data base the default and enhance the
"--internal-db" command line parameter to take an optional parameter
allowing to switch the internal data base back to the file based one.

This is part of XSA-419.

commit_msg:
powerpc/tm: Block signal return setting invalid MSR state

Currently we allow both the MSR T and S bits to be set by userspace on
a signal return.  Unfortunately this is a reserved configuration and
will cause a TM Bad Thing exception if attempted (via rfid).

This patch checks for this case in both the 32 and 64 bit signals
code.  If both T and S are set, we mark the context as invalid.

Found using a syscall fuzzer.

Fixes: 2b0a576d15e0 ("powerpc: Add new transactional memory state to the signal context")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v3.9+
Signed-off-by: Michael Neuling <mikey@neuling.org>
Signed-off-by: Michael Ellerman <mpe@ellerman.id.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* Get the top half of the MSR */', '\tif (__get_user(msr_hi, &tm_sr->mc_gregs[PT_MSR]))', '\t\treturn 1;', '\t/* Pull in MSR TM from user context */', '\tregs->msr = (regs->msr & ~MSR_TS_MASK) | ((msr_hi<<32) & MSR_TS_MASK);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Get the top half of the MSR from the user context */', '\tif (__get_user(msr_hi, &tm_sr->mc_gregs[PT_MSR]))', '\t\treturn 1;', '\tmsr_hi <<= 32;', "\t/* If TM bits are set to the reserved value, it's an invalid context */", '\tif (MSR_TM_RESV(msr_hi))', '\t\treturn 1;', '\t/* Pull in the MSR TM bits from the user context */', '\tregs->msr = (regs->msr & ~MSR_TS_MASK) | (msr_hi & MSR_TS_MASK);']}
description: The signal implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.3.5 on powerpc platforms does not check for an MSR with both the S and T bits set, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (TM Bad Thing exception and panic) via a crafted application.

code_evidence: restore_tm_user_regs reads the user-controlled MSR high word from tm_sr->mc_gregs[PT_MSR] into msr_hi and merges its TM bits into regs->msr without checking for the reserved T+S combination.
The merged regs->msr is then used to select transactional FP state loading, continuing the signal-return restore with an unvalidated MSR configuration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes attacker-controlled MSR metadata from the signal frame and fails to validate that it is a legal encoding before applying it, matching improper input validation (CWE-20). The patch adds the missing MSR_TM_RESV check; this is validation of input, not a bounds or pointer error.

evidence_lines.code:
if (msr & MSR_FP) {
regs->msr |= (MSR_FP | current->thread.fpexc_mode);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signal-return path accepts a user-supplied MSR whose top half may contain both the T and S bits, a reserved encoding, without validating it. Trigger: a local process crafts a signal frame with that MSR value. Consequence: the bad state reaches rfid, causing a TM Bad Thing exception and kernel panic (DoS).

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.9. There is a use-after-free in atalk_proc_exit, related to net/appletalk/atalk_proc.c, net/appletalk/ddp.c, and net/appletalk/sysctl_net_atalk.c.

code_evidence: proto_register failure is checked, but the return value of sock_register is discarded with a cast to void, so a failure is not propagated to the caller.
atalk_proc_init() is called unconditionally and its return value is ignored; no error path is taken when procfs setup fails.
atalk_register_sysctl() is likewise called unconditionally with no check, and the only branch at out simply returns rc.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked initialization leads to later access of proc_dir_entry memory after it has been freed during the exit path, directly matching CWE-416. The defect is the missing error handling that leaves dangling proc structures, not a plain null dereference or leak.

evidence_lines.code: (void)sock_register(&atalk_family_ops);

atalk_proc_init();
atalk_register_sysctl();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: initialization failures are silently ignored, so atalk_init reports success even when atalk_proc_init did not create the proc entries. Trigger: the module is then unloaded and atalk_proc_exit runs, walking/removing proc entries that were never created or were already freed. Supported consequence: a freed proc_dir_entry is referenced, yielding a use-after-free read in pde_subdir_find.

commit_msg: Fix ext2 buffer overflow in r2_sbu_grub_memmove
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (fileblock < INDIRECT_BLOCKS)', '  else if (fileblock < INDIRECT_BLOCKS + blksz / 4)'], 'added_lines': ['  if (fileblock < INDIRECT_BLOCKS) {', '  } else if (fileblock < INDIRECT_BLOCKS + blksz / 4)']}
description: The grub_memmove function in shlr/grub/kern/misc.c in radare2 1.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack-based buffer underflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted binary file, possibly related to a buffer underflow in fs/ext2.c in GNU GRUB 2.02.

code_evidence: The direct/indirect branch selects a block index from fileblock after only bounding it against INDIRECT_BLOCKS and blksz/4; fileblock is attacker-influenced from the filesystem image.

In the double-indirect branch, rblock is computed and then indir[rblock / perblock] is used as a disk address, while the outer bound at lines 69-70 uses (blksz/4 + 1) rather than perblock, so rblock can exceed the loaded block table.

The result indexes indir[rblock % perblock] at line 91 without validating that the second disk read populated the expected block, and the guard does not prevent an out-of-range index into the allocated blksz buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes/accesses an allocated buffer past its end due to a faulty range check, which matches CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. It is not merely an integer overflow because the missing bound directly permits an out-of-bounds index into indir.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an incorrect upper bound for the double-indirect range combined with unchecked index arithmetic on fileblock from a crafted ext2 image. When fileblock falls in the miscomputed range, rblock/perblock can index past the blksz-sized indir buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read/write of block addresses and a crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
ANDROID: KVM: arm64: Move addr_is_allowed_memory() check into host callback

Since host stage-2 mappings are created lazily, we cannot rely on the
pte in order to recover the target physical address when checking a
host-initiated memory transition.

Instead, move the addr_is_allowed_memory() check into the host callback
function where it is passed the physical address directly from the
walker.

description: deepin-clone before 1.1.3 uses a predictable path /tmp/.deepin-clone/mount/<block-dev-basename> in the Helper::temporaryMountDevice() function to temporarily mount a file system as root. An unprivileged user can prepare a symlink at this location to have the file system mounted in an arbitrary location. By winning a race condition, the attacker can also enter the mount point, thereby preventing a subsequent unmount of the file system.

code_evidence: The partclone command string is built with a fixed, world-predictable log path /tmp/partclone.log and passed to process->start(); the function never creates, checks ownership of, or opens that path exclusively. Any local user can pre-create or replace /tmp/partclone.log (e.g., with a symlink) before the privileged process opens it, and the same fixed name is reused for both read and restore branches.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a time-of-check/time-of-use race on a shared /tmp resource: the path is assumed exclusive but can be modified concurrently by an interfering local user before the process opens it, matching CWE-362's exclusivity/atomicity violation. It is not merely a predictable-name issue (CWE-377) because the exploitable condition is the concurrent replacement window.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function hands a predictable /tmp path to an external process that opens it for logging without exclusive creation or ownership checks. Trigger: an unprivileged user pre-creates or swaps that path before the privileged partclone invocation. Consequence: the privileged process follows the attacker-controlled file/symlink, allowing unintended file writes or denial of the logging operation.

commit_msg:
avcodec/exr: More strictly check dc_count

Fixes: out of array access
Fixes: exr/deneme

Found-by: Burak Çarıkçı <burakcarikci@crypttech.com>
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (dc_size > 0) {', '        if (dc_count > (6LL * td->xsize * td->ysize + 63) / 64)'], 'added_lines': ['    {', '        if (dc_count != dc_w * dc_h * 3)']}
description: dwa_uncompress in libavcodec/exr.c in FFmpeg 4.4 allows an out-of-bounds array access because dc_count is not strictly checked.

code_evidence: dc_count is read from the untrusted header at line 24 and only guarded by the weak bound dc_count > (6LL * td->xsize * td->ysize + 63) / 64 at line 65 before dc_data is allocated with dest_len = dc_count * 2LL (line 63).
The decode loop indexes dc[idx] at line 102, where idx = (x>>3) + (y>>3)*dc_w + dc_w*dc_h*j (line 99), bounded by dc_w*dc_h*3 elements; the guard does not enforce this exact count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-129 applies: an untrusted count is used to size and index an array without validating that the index stays within valid bounds. This is improper index validation, not merely a generic buffer overflow, since the flaw is the missing exact constraint dc_count == dc_w*dc_h*3.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: dc_count comes from the attacker-controlled EXR header and is only loosely bounded relative to image dimensions. The dc_data buffer is sized from dc_count, but the loop reads dc_w*dc_h*3 entries regardless, so a dc_count smaller than the required count leaves the read index past the allocated region, causing an out-of-bounds array access.

description: Clara Genomics Analysis before 0.2.0 has an integer overflow for cudapoa memory management in allocate_block.cpp.

code_evidence: Each offset advance multiplies sizeof(T) by max_nodes_per_window_ and max_poas_ (and constants like CUDAPOA_MAX_NODE_EDGES, max_sequences_per_poa_) inside cudautils::align<size_t, 8>. commit_msg:
Avoid crash on crash report when a bad function pointer was called (#11298)

If Redis crashes due to calling an invalid function pointer,
the `backtrace` function will try to dereference this invalid pointer
which will cause a crash inside the crash report and will kill
the processes without having all the crash report information.

Example:

```
=== REDIS BUG REPORT START: Cut & paste starting from here ===
198672:M 19 Sep 2022 18:06:12.936 # Redis 255.255.255 crashed by signal: 11, si_code: 1
198672:M 19 Sep 2022 18:06:12.936 # Accessing address: 0x1
198672:M 19 Sep 2022 18:06:12.936 # Crashed running the instruction at: 0x1
// here the processes is crashing
```

This PR tries to fix this crash be:
1. Identify the issue when it happened.
2. Replace the invalid pointer with a pointer to some dummy function
   so that `backtrace` will not crash.

I identification is done by comparing `eip` to `info->si_addr`, if they
are the same we know that the crash happened on the same address it tries to
accesses and we can conclude that it tries to call and invalid function pointer.

To replace the invalid pointer we introduce a new function, `setMcontextEip`,
which is very similar to `getMcontextEip` and it knows to set the Eip for the
different supported OS's. After printing the trace we retrieve the old `Eip` value.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    logStackTrace(getMcontextEip(uc), 1);'], 'added_lines': ['    logStackTrace(getAndSetMcontextEip(uc, NULL), 1);']}
description: ** DISPUTED ** A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in Redis up to 6.2.7/7.0.5. Affected is the function sigsegvHandler of the file debug.c of the component Crash Report. The manipulation leads to denial of service. The complexity of an attack is rather high. The exploitability is told to be difficult. The real existence of this vulnerability is still doubted at the moment. Upgrading to version 6.2.8 and 7.0.6 is able to address this issue. The patch is identified as 0bf90d944313919eb8e63d3588bf63a367f020a3. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-211962 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability. NOTE: The vendor claims that this is not a DoS because it applies to the crash logging mechanism which is triggered after a crash has occurred.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The watchdog handler only logs a backtrace via getMcontextEip and contains no resource allocation or release logic; nothing in the function supports improper resource shutdown/release (CWE-404).

commit_msg:
ofp-group: Don't assert-fail decoding bad OF1.5 group mod type or command.

When decoding a group mod, the current code validates the group type and
command after the whole group mod has been decoded.  The OF1.5 decoder,
however, tries to use the type and command earlier, when it might still be
invalid.  This caused an assertion failure (via OVS_NOT_REACHED).  This
commit fixes the problem.

ovs-vswitchd does not enable support for OpenFlow 1.5 by default.

Reported-at: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/oss-fuzz/issues/detail?id=9249
Signed-off-by: Ben Pfaff <blp@ovn.org>
Reviewed-by: Yifeng Sun <pkusunyifeng@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        OVS_NOT_REACHED();', '        OVS_NOT_REACHED();'], 'added_lines': ['        return OFPERR_OFPGMFC_BAD_TYPE;', '        return OFPERR_OFPGMFC_BAD_COMMAND;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Open vSwitch (OvS) 2.7.x through 2.7.6, affecting parse_group_prop_ntr_selection_method in lib/ofp-util.c. When decoding a group mod, it validates the group type and command after the whole group mod has been decoded. The OF1.5 decoder, however, tries to use the type and command earlier, when it might still be invalid. This causes an assertion failure (via OVS_NOT_REACHED). ovs-vswitchd does not enable support for OpenFlow 1.5 by default.

code_evidence: The switch on group_type handles known OFPGT11 values and returns OFPERR_OFPBPC_BAD_VALUE for non-select group types, but the default case calls OVS_NOT_REACHED(), an assertion macro, for any unrecognized group_type value.

The switch on group_cmd handles known OFPGC15 commands and returns OFPERR_OFPBPC_BAD_VALUE for disallowed commands, but its default case also calls OVS_NOT_REACHED() for any unrecognized group_cmd value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The default branches invoke an assertion macro that an attacker can reach via malformed group-mod input, matching CWE-617 (Reachable Assertion). The fix replaces the assertions with error returns, confirming the reachable-assertion cause rather than a memory-safety weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes group_type and group_cmd are always among the enumerated values and uses OVS_NOT_REACHED() instead of returning an error. Trigger: a decoded group mod carrying an out-of-range type or command reaches these default branches. Consequence: the assertion fires and aborts the process, causing a crash/DoS rather than a protocol error.

description: A flaw was found in upx canPack in p_lx_elf.cpp in UPX 3.96. This flaw allows attackers to cause a denial of service (SEGV or buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impacts via a crafted ELF. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to system availability.

code_evidence: canPack reads DT_RELA/DT_RELASZ values from the dynamic segment into rel_off and relsz without validating them against file_size. It then forms rp = (Elf64_Rela *)&file_image[rel_off] and last = relsz + (char *)rp, and the loop for (; rp < last; ++rp) dereferences rp->r_offset and rp->r_info. A crafted ELF with an out-of-range rel_off or oversized relsz makes rp/last point outside the allocated file_image buffer, so the loop reads (and later relocation handling writes) past the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked rel_off/relsz drive pointer arithmetic and dereferences beyond the file_image buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) for the relocation writes; the missing bounds check is the root cause. The consequence of out-of-bounds reads alone would fit CWE-125, but the relocation processing writes to the computed addresses, supporting the write classification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled DT_RELA/DT_RELASZ entries are used as an offset and size into file_image without checking them against file_size. Trigger: a crafted ELF whose dynamic table supplies rel_off beyond the image or relsz that overruns it. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/writes during relocation iteration, causing SEGV or memory corruption and crash (availability impact).

commit_msg:
genetlink: Fix a memory leak on error path

In genl_register_family(), when idr_alloc() fails,
we forget to free the memory we possibly allocate for
family->attrbuf.

Reported-by: Hulk Robot <hulkci@huawei.com>
Fixes: 2ae0f17df1cd ("genetlink: use idr to track families")
Signed-off-by: YueHaibing <yuehaibing@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Kirill Tkhai <ktkhai@virtuozzo.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto errout_locked;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tgoto errout_free;', 'errout_free:']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.6. There is a memory leak issue when idr_alloc() fails in genl_register_family() in net/netlink/genetlink.c.

code_evidence: Lines 20-27 allocate family->attrbuf via kmalloc_array when maxattr is set and parallel_ops is false; on allocation failure the code jumps to errout_locked.
Lines 30-34 call idr_alloc; if it returns a negative id, err is set and control jumps directly to errout_locked, bypassing any release of the earlier allocation.
The errout_remove path at lines 45-47 performs kfree(family->attrbuf), but it is only reached from the mc-groups validation failure at line 38, not from the idr_alloc failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because the function fails to release memory (family->attrbuf) that was allocated and is no longer reachable after the error return. This is a missing-release-on-error-path weakness, distinct from a use-after-free or double-free since the pointer is simply abandoned.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the idr_alloc failure branch (lines 32-34) jumps to errout_locked, skipping the kfree of family->attrbuf that was allocated earlier at lines 21-23. Trigger: idr_alloc returns a negative value after a successful attr buffer allocation. Consequence: the attr buffer memory is never released, leaking kernel memory on each such failure.

commit_msg:
Fix a hang with SSL_peek()

If while calling SSL_peek() we read an empty record then we go into an
infinite loop, continually trying to read data from the empty record and
never making any progress. This could be exploited by a malicious peer in
a Denial Of Service attack.

CVE-2016-6305

GitHub Issue #1563

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (!peek) {'], 'added_lines': ['            if (peek) {', '                /* Mark any zero length record as consumed CVE-2016-6305 */', '                if (SSL3_RECORD_get_length(rr) == 0)', '                    SSL3_RECORD_set_read(rr);', '            } else {']}
description: The ssl3_read_bytes function in record/rec_layer_s3.c in OpenSSL 1.1.0 before 1.1.0a allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) by triggering a zero-length record in an SSL_peek call.

code_evidence: The read loop computes n from the record length, copies n bytes, and only advances/sets the record read in the non-peek branch (116-123). In the peek case the record is advanced only when n equals the record length (125-128); for a zero-length record n is 0, so read_bytes stays 0 and line 133 jumps back to start without consuming the record.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is failure to validate a property of received input (record length of zero) before processing it, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The DoS is the consequence; the root cause is the missing zero-length check, not a memory-safety error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function does not validate/handle the zero-length record condition during peek, so a peer-supplied empty record is never marked consumed. Trigger: remote attacker sends a zero-length record and calls SSL_peek. Consequence: line 133 loops to start indefinitely, causing CPU-consuming denial of service.

commit_msg: Use break instead of continue (fixes #1072)

description: ImageMagick 7.0.7-26 Q16 has excessive iteration in the DecodeLabImage and EncodeLabImage functions (coders/tiff.c), which results in a hang (tens of minutes) with a tiny PoC file. Remote attackers could leverage this vulnerability to cause a denial of service via a crafted tiff file.

If GetCacheViewAuthenticPixels returns NULL (line 20), status is set false but continue (line 23) keeps the loop running across all rows.
SyncCacheViewAuthenticPixels failure at line 40 only sets status=MagickFalse; the loop continues to the next iteration, so the row count drives unbounded iteration with no early exit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-834 fits: the loop's iteration count is bounded only by attacker-controlled image->rows and error paths fail to terminate it early, enabling resource-consumption DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is that row-loop errors set status but use continue (or fall through) rather than break, so the loop still executes for all image->rows. A crafted TIFF with a large row count triggers excessive iteration, consuming CPU for tens of minutes (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow (CVE-2021-21309). (#8522)

On 32-bit systems, setting the proto-max-bulk-len config parameter to a high value may result with integer overflow and a subsequent heap overflow when parsing an input bulk (CVE-2021-21309).

This fix has two parts:

Set a reasonable limit to the config parameter.
Add additional checks to prevent the problem in other potential but unknown code paths.

(cherry picked from commit d32f2e9999ce003bad0bd2c3bca29f64dcce4433)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    assert(newlen > len);   /* Catch size_t overflow */', '    assert(hdrlen + newlen + 1 > len);  /* Catch size_t overflow */']}
description: Redis is an open-source, in-memory database that persists on disk. In affected versions of Redis an integer overflow bug in 32-bit Redis version 4.0 or newer could be exploited to corrupt the heap and potentially result with remote code execution. Redis 4.0 or newer uses a configurable limit for the maximum supported bulk input size. By default, it is 512MB which is a safe value for all platforms. If the limit is significantly increased, receiving a large request from a client may trigger several integer overflow scenarios, which would result with buffer overflow and heap corruption. We believe this could in certain conditions be exploited for remote code execution. By default, authenticated Redis users have access to all configuration parameters and can therefore use the “CONFIG SET proto-max-bulk-len” to change the safe default, making the system vulnerable. **This problem only affects 32-bit Redis (on a 32-bit system, or as a 32-bit executable running on a 64-bit system).** The problem is fixed in version 6.2, and the fix is back ported to 6.0.11 and 5.0.11. Make sure you use one of these versions if you are running 32-bit Redis. An additional workaround to mitigate the problem without patching the redis-server executable is to prevent clients from directly executing `CONFIG SET`: Using Redis 6.0 or newer, ACL configuration can be used to block the command. commit_msg:
GHSL-2023-013: Memory corruption decoding UTF16

Memory corruption when decoding UTF16 strings (GHSL-2023-013)

Fixes defect GHSL-2023-013 found by the GitHub Security Lab team via
oss-fuzz.

The variable outlen was not initialized and could cause writing a zero
to an arbitrary place in memory if ntlm_str_convert() were to fail,
which would leave outlen uninitialized.

This can lead to a DoS if the write hits unmapped memory or randomly
corrupting a byte in the application memory space.

Make sure to zero out only if ntlm_str_convert() succeeds, but for good
measure also initialize outlen to 0.

Fixes CVE-2023-25564

Signed-off-by: Simo Sorce <simo@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    size_t outlen;', '    /* make sure to terminate output string */', "    out[outlen] = '\\0';", ''], 'added_lines': ['    size_t outlen = 0;', '    } else {', '        /* make sure to terminate output string */', "        out[outlen] = '\\0';", '']}
description: GSS-NTLMSSP is a mechglue plugin for the GSSAPI library that implements NTLM authentication. Prior to version 1.2.0, memory corruption can be triggered when decoding UTF16 strings. The variable `outlen` was not initialized and could cause writing a zero to an arbitrary place in memory if `ntlm_str_convert()` were to fail, which would leave `outlen` uninitialized. This can lead to a denial of service if the write hits unmapped memory or randomly corrupts a byte in the application memory space. This vulnerability can trigger an out-of-bounds write, leading to memory corruption. This vulnerability can be triggered via the main `gss_accept_sec_context` entry point. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.0.

code_evidence: Line 9 declares `size_t outlen;` without initialization.

Line 23 calls ntlm_str_convert() passing &outlen; if it fails, outlen is left uninitialized. Line 24 then unconditionally executes `out[outlen] = '\0';`, using the uninitialized length as an index into the malloc'd buffer before the error check at line 26.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes a byte at an index derived from an uninitialized variable, so the store can fall outside the allocated buffer, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. This is not merely an uninitialized read (CWE-457) because the write itself, not just the value read, is the harmful operation.

evidence_lines.code: size_t outlen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: outlen is never initialized before ntlm_str_convert() is invoked, and the null-termination write at line 24 occurs regardless of the conversion result. Trigger: a crafted UTF16 field whose conversion fails leaves outlen holding an indeterminate value. Consequence: the write at out[outlen] targets an arbitrary offset, producing an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt memory or crash (DoS).

PolyFlags* pNewFlagAry = new PolyFlags[ nNewSize ];
memcpy( pNewFlagAry + nSecPos, mpFlagAry + nPos, nRest );
