commit_msg:
Input: aiptek - fix crash on detecting device without endpoints

The aiptek driver crashes in aiptek_probe() when a specially crafted USB
device without endpoints is detected. This fix adds a check that the device
has proper configuration expected by the driver. Also an error return value
is changed to more matching one in one of the error paths.

Reported-by: Ralf Spenneberg <ralf@spenneberg.net>
Signed-off-by: Vladis Dronov <vdronov@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dmitry.torokhov@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Verify that a device really has an endpoint */', '\tif (intf->altsetting[0].desc.bNumEndpoints < 1) {', '\t\tdev_err(&intf->dev,', '\t\t\t"interface has %d endpoints, but must have minimum 1\\n",', '\t\t\tintf->altsetting[0].desc.bNumEndpoints);', '\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\tgoto fail3;', '\t}', '\t\terr = -EINVAL;']}
description: The aiptek_probe function in drivers/input/tablet/aiptek.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows physically proximate attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) via a crafted USB device that lacks endpoints.

code_evidence: aiptek_probe reads intf->altsetting[0].endpoint[0] without verifying that the interface descriptor reports any endpoints; a crafted USB device with bNumEndpoints == 0 leaves this entry absent. The resulting endpoint pointer is then dereferenced for bEndpointAddress and bInterval in usb_fill_int_urb.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer it assumes valid but which can be NULL when the device has zero endpoints, matching CWE-476. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the missing endpoint yields a NULL entry that is dereferenced.

evidence_lines.code:
endpoint = &intf->altsetting[0].endpoint[0].desc;
usb_fill_int_urb(aiptek->urb,
aiptek->usbdev,
usb_rcvintpipe(aiptek->usbdev,
endpoint->bEndpointAddress),
aiptek->data, 8, aiptek_irq, aiptek,
endpoint->bInterval);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no check on the endpoint count before indexing endpoint[0]. Trigger: plugging in a malformed USB device lacking endpoints. Consequence: NULL/invalid endpoint dereference during probe, crashing the kernel (denial of service).

commit_msg:
display-store: Pass the display object rather than the id in the removed signal

By the time GdmDisplayStore emits the "display-removed" signal, the display
is no longer in the store and gdm_display_store_lookup will not work in
signal handlers.

Change the "display-removed" parameter from the display id to the GdmDisplay
object, so that signal handers can perform any cleanup they need to do

CVE-2018-14424

Closes: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gdm/issues/401
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    const char      *id,', '        GdmDisplay *display;', '        display = gdm_display_store_lookup (display_store, id);', '        if (display != NULL) {', '                g_dbus_object_manager_server_unexport (manager->priv->object_manager, id);', '                g_signal_handlers_disconnect_by_func (display, G_CALLBACK (on_display_status_changed), manager);', '                g_signal_emit (manager, signals[DISPLAY_REMOVED], 0, id);', '        }'], 'added_lines': ['                    GdmDisplay      *display,', '        char    *id;', '        gdm_display_get_id (display, &id, NULL);', '        g_dbus_object_manager_server_unexport (manager->priv->object_manager, id);', '        g_free (id);', '        g_signal_handlers_disconnect_by_func (display, G_CALLBACK (on_display_status_changed), manager);', '        g_signal_emit (manager, signals[DISPLAY_REMOVED], 0, display);']}
description: The daemon in GDM through 3.29.1 does not properly unexport display objects from its D-Bus interface when they are destroyed, which allows a local attacker to trigger a use-after-free via a specially crafted sequence of D-Bus method calls, resulting in a denial of service or potential code execution.

code_evidence: The handler receives only a display id, then re-resolves the object via gdm_display_store_lookup(display_store, id). By the time 'display-removed' fires the display has already been removed from the store, so the lookup returns NULL and the unexport, signal disconnect, and DISPLAY_REMOVED emit are all skipped. The D-Bus object is therefore never unexported.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The stale exported D-Bus object references freed display memory that is later accessed, matching CWE-416 (use after free). The defect is the missing unexport/cleanup, not a mere NULL dereference or logic error, since the consequence is reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cleanup is gated on a lookup that cannot succeed after removal, so the D-Bus object remains exported while its backing GdmDisplay is destroyed. Trigger: a local attacker issues a crafted sequence of D-Bus method calls that causes displays to be created and destroyed; subsequent calls reach the still-exported object, yielding a use-after-free and denial of service or possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Avoid some undefined pointer arithmetic

A common idiom in the codebase is:

if (p + len > limit)
{
    return; /* Too long */
}

Where "p" points to some malloc'd data of SIZE bytes and
limit == p + SIZE

"len" here could be from some externally supplied data (e.g. from a TLS
message).

The rules of C pointer arithmetic are such that "p + len" is only well
defined where len <= SIZE. Therefore the above idiom is actually
undefined behaviour.

For example this could cause problems if some malloc implementation
provides an address for "p" such that "p + len" actually overflows for
values of len that are too big and therefore p + len < limit!

Issue reported by Guido Vranken.

CVE-2016-2177

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>

code_evidence: After reading a DTLS cookie length i from attacker-influenced data, p is advanced by i and then compared with limit; the addition p += i (line 16) can wrap before the check at line 17.
Cipher-list length i from n2s is added to p at line 21, then p >= limit is checked at line 22, so the boundary test relies on undefined pointer arithmetic.
Compression-list length i is added to p at line 25 before the p > limit test at line 26, again allowing the pointer addition to overflow.
p + 2 at line 28 computes a pointer beyond the buffer before checking against limit.
The loop condition p + 4 <= limit at line 31 performs the same undefined pointer arithmetic.
p + size > limit at line 35 adds an attacker-controlled extension size to p before validating the bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because attacker-controlled length values are added to a pointer and the resulting value can overflow/wrap, defeating the boundary checks. The consequence is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) but stems from the integer wraparound in the offset computation that precedes the check.

if (p >= limit)

p += i;
if (p >= limit)

p += i;
if (p > limit)
if ((p + 2) >= limit)
while ((p + 4) <= limit) {
if (p + size > limit)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is pointer arithmetic (p + i, p + 2, p + 4, p + size) performed before validating that the offset stays within the buffer, which is undefined behavior and can wrap when the offset is large. A remote peer supplies oversized length fields in the TLS/DTLS handshake, causing the wrapped comparison to pass and the code to read past the buffer, leading to a crash or unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12897/ISO CLNS: Use ND_TTEST() for the bounds checks in isoclns_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Don't pass the remaining caplen - that's too hard to get right, and we
were getting it wrong in at least one case; just use ND_TTEST().

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tisoclns_print(ndo, p, length, length);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tisoclns_print(ndo, p, length);']}
description: The ISO CLNS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isoclns_print().

code_evidence: In the PPP_OSI case, handle_ppp forwards the packet pointer p and length to isoclns_print, passing length a second time as an additional caplen argument. The function itself performs no bounds validation before this call; it trusts the caller-supplied length and delegates all buffer access to isoclns_print. The patch removes the redundant caplen argument, which is the parameter that caused the parser's bounds checks to be computed incorrectly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an out-of-bounds read: the ISO CLNS parser accesses memory beyond the intended buffer due to incorrect length handling propagated from handle_ppp. This matches CWE-125 rather than an out-of-bounds write, since only reads occur.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: handle_ppp passes the packet length into isoclns_print as a caplen value without any verification, and the callee's manual bounds computations using that value were wrong. Trigger: a crafted ISO CLNS/PPP packet reaching the PPP_OSI branch. Consequence: isoclns_print reads past the end of the captured buffer (buffer over-read).

commit_msg:
HID: corsair: fix DMA buffers on stack

Not all platforms support DMA to the stack, and specifically since v4.9
this is no longer supported on x86 with VMAP_STACK either.

Note that the macro-mode buffer was larger than necessary.

Fixes: 6f78193ee9ea ("HID: corsair: Add Corsair Vengeance K90 driver")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hovold <johan@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Jiri Kosina <jkosina@suse.cz>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar data[8];', '\t\treturn -EIO;', '\t\treturn -EIO;', '\treturn snprintf(buf, PAGE_SIZE, "%d\\n", current_profile);'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar *data;', '', '\tdata = kmalloc(8, GFP_KERNEL);', '\tif (!data)', '\t\treturn -ENOMEM;', '\t\tret = -EIO;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\t\tret = -EIO;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\tret = snprintf(buf, PAGE_SIZE, "%d\\n", current_profile);', 'out:', '\tkfree(data);', '', '\treturn ret;']}
description: drivers/hid/hid-corsair.c in the Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.6 interacts incorrectly with the CONFIG_VMAP_STACK option, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash or memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging use of more than one virtual page for a DMA scatterlist.

code_evidence: A stack buffer 'char data[8]' is declared and its address is passed directly to usb_control_msg as the DMA/receive buffer for an 8-byte transfer. The driver places a buffer on the kernel stack and lets the USB core DMA into it, which is invalid when VMAP_STACK gives the stack more than one virtual page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The DMA writes into a stack buffer assumed to be a valid contiguous 8-byte region, but under VMAP_STACK the operation can affect memory beyond that buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root cause is the stack-DMA buffer, not a simple length miscalculation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the USB control-transfer receive buffer is a stack array whose physical pages may not be contiguous under CONFIG_VMAP_STACK, so DMA into it can cross the intended buffer/page boundary. Trigger: a local user reads the current-profile sysfs attribute, invoking usb_control_msg on the stack buffer. Consequence: system crash or memory corruption (the commit moves the buffer to kmalloc).

commit_msg:
dccp/tcp: fix routing redirect race

As Eric Dumazet pointed out this also needs to be fixed in IPv6.
v2: Contains the IPv6 tcp/Ipv6 dccp patches as well.

We have seen a few incidents lately where a dst_enty has been freed
with a dangling TCP socket reference (sk->sk_dst_cache) pointing to that
dst_entry. If the conditions/timings are right a crash then ensues when the
freed dst_entry is referenced later on. A Common crashing back trace is:

 #8 [] page_fault at ffffffff8163e648
    [exception RIP: __tcp_ack_snd_check+74]
.
.
 #9 [] tcp_rcv_established at ffffffff81580b64
#10 [] tcp_v4_do_rcv at ffffffff8158b54a
#11 [] tcp_v4_rcv at ffffffff8158cd02
#12 [] ip_local_deliver_finish at ffffffff815668f4
#13 [] ip_local_deliver at ffffffff81566bd9
#14 [] ip_rcv_finish at ffffffff8156656d
#15 [] ip_rcv at ffffffff81566f06
#16 [] __netif_receive_skb_core at ffffffff8152b3a2
#17 [] __netif_receive_skb at ffffffff8152b608
#18 [] netif_receive_skb at ffffffff8152b690
#19 [] vmxnet3_rq_rx_complete at ffffffffa015eeaf [vmxnet3]
#20 [] vmxnet3_poll_rx_only at ffffffffa015f32a [vmxnet3]
#21 [] net_rx_action at ffffffff8152bac2
#22 [] __do_softirq at ffffffff81084b4f
#23 [] call_softirq at ffffffff8164845c
#24 [] do_softirq at ffffffff81016fc5
#25 [] irq_exit at ffffffff81084ee5
#26 [] do_IRQ at ffffffff81648ff8

Of course it may happen with other NIC drivers as well.

It's found the freed dst_entry here:

 224 static bool tcp_in_quickack_mode(struct sock *sk)↩
 225 {↩
 226 ▹       const struct inet_connection_sock *icsk = inet_csk(sk);↩
 227 ▹       const struct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_get(sk);↩
 228 ↩
 229 ▹       return (dst && dst_metric(dst, RTAX_QUICKACK)) ||↩
 230 ▹       ▹       (icsk->icsk_ack.quick && !icsk->icsk_ack.pingpong);↩
 231 }↩

But there are other backtraces attributed to the same freed dst_entry in
netfilter code as well.

All the vmcores showed 2 significant clues:

- Remote hosts behind the default gateway had always been redirected to a
different gateway. A rtable/dst_entry will be added for that host. Making
more dst_entrys with lower reference counts. Making this more probable.

- All vmcores showed a postitive LockDroppedIcmps value, e.g:

LockDroppedIcmps                  267

A closer look at the tcp_v4_err() handler revealed that do_redirect() will run
regardless of whether user space has the socket locked. This can result in a
race condition where the same dst_entry cached in sk->sk_dst_entry can be
decremented twice for the same socket via:

do_redirect()->__sk_dst_check()-> dst_release().

Which leads to the dst_entry being prematurely freed with another socket
pointing to it via sk->sk_dst_cache and a subsequent crash.

To fix this skip do_redirect() if usespace has the socket locked. Instead let
the redirect take place later when user space does not have the socket
locked.

The dccp/IPv6 code is very similar in this respect, so fixing it there too.

As Eric Garver pointed out the following commit now invalidates routes. Which
can set the dst->obsolete flag so that ipv4_dst_check() returns null and
triggers the dst_release().

Fixes: ceb3320610d6 ("ipv4: Kill routes during PMTU/redirect updates.")
Cc: Eric Garver <egarver@redhat.com>
Cc: Hannes Sowa <hsowa@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Jon Maxwell <jmaxwell37@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tstruct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_check(sk, np->dst_cookie);', '\t\tif (dst)', '\t\t\tdst->ops->redirect(dst, sk, skb);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!sock_owned_by_user(sk)) {', '\t\t\tstruct dst_entry *dst = __sk_dst_check(sk, np->dst_cookie);', '\t\t\tif (dst)', '\t\t\t\tdst->ops->redirect(dst, sk, skb);', '\t\t}']}
description: Race condition in the audit_log_single_execve_arg function in kernel/auditsc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.7 allows local users to bypass intended character-set restrictions or disrupt system-call auditing by changing a certain string, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: bh_lock_sock(sk) is taken, and if sock_owned_by_user(sk) is true the code only increments LINUX_MIB_LOCKDROPPEDICMPS but still proceeds.

For NDISC_REDIRECT the code unconditionally calls __sk_dst_check(sk, np->dst_cookie) and dst->ops->redirect without checking sock_owned_by_user(sk), so the cached dst_entry can be released while userspace holds the socket lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: concurrent access to the shared dst_entry lacks the necessary exclusivity, and an interfering user-locked sequence can modify/release it during the redirect sequence. The premature free is the consequence of the race, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The redirect path mutates and releases the shared sk_dst_cache dst_entry without honoring the user lock: do_redirect()->__sk_dst_check()->dst_release() races with a concurrent userspace operation, decrementing the dst_entry reference twice. The dst_entry is freed prematurely while another socket still references it, causing later use-after-free crashes.

commit_msg:
ALSA: msnd: Optimize / harden DSP and MIDI loops

The ISA msnd drivers have loops fetching the ring-buffer head, tail
and size values inside the loops.  Such codes are inefficient and
fragile.

This patch optimizes it, and also adds the sanity check to avoid the
endless loops.

Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=196131
Bugzilla: https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=196133
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\twhile (readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wTail) !=', '\t       readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead)) {', '\t\tu16 wTmp, val;', '\t\tval = readw(pwMIDQData + 2 * readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead));', '\t\t\tif (test_bit(MSNDMIDI_MODE_BIT_INPUT_TRIGGER,', '\t\t\t\t     &mpu->mode))', '\t\t\t\tsnd_rawmidi_receive(mpu->substream_input,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t    (unsigned char *)&val, 1);', '', '\t\twTmp = readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead) + 1;', '\t\tif (wTmp > readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wSize))', '\t\t\twritew(0,  mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead);', '\t\telse', '\t\t\twritew(wTmp,  mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead);'], 'added_lines': ['\tu16 head, tail, size;', '\thead = readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead);', '\ttail = readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wTail);', '\tsize = readw(mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wSize);', '\tif (head > size || tail > size)', '\t\tgoto out;', '\twhile (head != tail) {', '\t\tunsigned char val = readw(pwMIDQData + 2 * head);', '\t\tif (test_bit(MSNDMIDI_MODE_BIT_INPUT_TRIGGER, &mpu->mode))', '\t\t\tsnd_rawmidi_receive(mpu->substream_input, &val, 1);', '\t\tif (++head > size)', '\t\t\thead = 0;', '\t\twritew(head, mpu->dev->MIDQ + JQS_wHead);', ' out:']}
description: The snd_msnd_interrupt function in sound/isa/msnd/msnd_pinnacle.c in the Linux kernel through 4.11.7 allows local users to cause a denial of service (over-boundary access) or possibly have unspecified other impact by changing the value of a message queue head pointer between two kernel reads of that value, aka a "double fetch" vulnerability.

code_evidence: The loop condition compares two separate reads of JQS_wTail and JQS_wHead; the body then performs a third independent read of JQS_wHead and uses it to index pwMIDQData at 2*head without validating head against JQS_wSize.
The new head is derived from yet another read of JQS_wHead and only compared to a fresh read of JQS_wSize, so a racing value can bypass the wraparound check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a memory read at an unvalidated offset into MIDQ_DATA_BUFF, matching CWE-125's out-of-bounds read. The double fetch is the root cause enabling the unchecked index, not a separate weakness label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The head pointer is fetched multiple times from shared DMA memory rather than cached once, so a concurrent writer can change it between reads. The index used for the readw of pwMIDQData is thus not bounded by the size value checked elsewhere, allowing an out-of-bounds read; the loop can also fail to terminate.

commit_msg:
commit b9258a2cece4ec1f020715fe3554bc2e360f6264 upstream.

struct can_frame contains some padding which is not explicitly zeroed in
slc_bump. This uninitialized data will then be transmitted if the stack
initialization hardening feature is not enabled (CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL).

This commit just zeroes the whole struct including the padding.

Signed-off-by: Richard Palethorpe <rpalethorpe@suse.com>
Fixes: a1044e36e457 ("can: add slcan driver for serial/USB-serial CAN adapters")
Reviewed-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org>
Cc: linux-can@vger.kernel.org
Cc: netdev@vger.kernel.org
Cc: security@kernel.org
Cc: wg@grandegger.com
Cc: mkl@pengutronix.de
Cc: davem@davemloft.net
Acked-by: Marc Kleine-Budde <mkl@pengutronix.de>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
Signed-off-by: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tcf.can_id = 0;', '\t*(u64 *) (&cf.data) = 0; /* clear payload */', ''], 'added_lines': ['\tmemset(&cf, 0, sizeof(cf));']}
description: An issue was discovered in slc_bump in drivers/net/can/slcan.c in the Linux kernel 3.16 through 5.6.2. It allows attackers to read uninitialized can_frame data, potentially containing sensitive information from kernel stack memory, if the configuration lacks CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL, aka CID-b9258a2cece4.

code_evidence: Local struct can_frame cf is declared at line 4 and only partially initialized: line 8 sets cf.can_id and line 35 zeroes only the data array, leaving other fields and struct padding uninitialized.
Lines 36-45 fill only cf.data[0..can_dlc-1] for non-RTR frames; remaining bytes and padding are never written.
Line 58-59 copies the entire sizeof(struct can_frame) from &cf into the skb, transmitting the uninitialized bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies a resource (struct can_frame) that has not been fully initialized, and the uninitialized padding is read and exposed, matching CWE-908. The consequence is information disclosure from uninitialized memory, not a buffer overflow or out-of-bounds access.

evidence_lines.code:
memcpy(skb_put(skb, sizeof(struct can_frame)),
&cf, sizeof(struct can_frame));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is incomplete initialization of a stack struct whose full size is later copied to a packet buffer. Trigger is a valid slcan frame; the whole can_frame including uninitialized padding is memcpy'd into the skb and sent via netif_rx_ni, leaking kernel stack memory when CONFIG_INIT_STACK_ALL is absent.

Fixed the ossl_a2ulabel() function which also contained a potential

This overflow could result in a crash (causing a denial of service).

The function also did not NUL-terminate the output in some cases.

The two issues fixed here were dentified and reported

description: A buffer overrun can be triggered in X.509 certificate verification, specifically in name constraint checking. Note that this occurs after certificate chain signature verification and requires either a CA to have signed a malicious certificate or for an application to continue certificate verification despite failure to construct a path to a trusted issuer. An attacker can craft a malicious email address in a certificate to overflow an arbitrary number of bytes containing the `.' character (decimal 46) on the stack. This buffer overflow could result in a crash (causing a denial of service). In a TLS client, this can be triggered by connecting to a malicious server. In a TLS server, this can be triggered if the server requests client authentication and a malicious client connects.

code_evidence: Declares fixed-size stack buffer a_ulabel[LABEL_BUF_SIZE] and passes its size to ossl_a2ulabel, which writes the decoded label into it. The return value is only checked for <= 0; there is no independent bound on how many bytes the decoder writes, and strcmp then reads the buffer as a NUL-terminated string.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies decoded input into an output buffer without verifying the input size is below the output size, matching CWE-120's buffer-copy-without-size-check. It is not merely an out-of-bounds read, since the write overflow is the primary defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a fixed stack buffer is handed to a decoder whose output size is not constrained to the buffer size, so a crafted input label can write past a_ulabel. Trigger: a malicious certificate name processed through ossl_a2ucompare. Supported consequence: stack memory corruption and crash (denial of service); a missing NUL terminator can also cause strcmp to read out of bounds.

Bug #700169 - unchecked type

Bug #700169 "Type confusion in setcolorspace"

In seticc() we extract "Name" from a dictionary, if it succeeds we then
use it as a string, without checking the type to see if it is in fact
a string.

Add a check on the type, and add a couple to check that 'N' is an integer
in a few places too.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-704 fits because the function treats a ref of unverified type as an integer, an incorrect type conversion/interpretation. Contrast with CWE-843 (type confusion), which is the downstream effect; the direct defect is the missing type validation before integer use.

description: The Web Animations implementation in Blink, as used in Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux, improperly relies on list iteration, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-destruction) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted web site.

code_evidence: RemovePlayer iterates players_list_ using head()/end()/next() and calls node->RemoveFromList() on the matching node inside the loop, then returns. The traversal state (node, next()) is derived from the same list being mutated, so removing the current node and advancing the iterator are not separated safely.

It is not a parsing or input-validation flaw, which is why a narrower member weakness is not selected.

commit_msg:
ksmbd: validate length in smb2_write()

The SMB2 Write packet contains data that is to be written
to a file or to a pipe. Depending on the client, there may
be padding between the header and the data field.
Currently, the length is validated only in the case padding
is present.

Since the DataOffset field always points to the beginning
of the data, there is no need to have a special case for
padding. By removing this, the length is validated in both
cases.

Signed-off-by: Marios Makassikis <mmakassikis@freebox.fr>
Acked-by: Namjae Jeon <linkinjeon@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Steve French <stfrench@microsoft.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset) ==', '\t    offsetof(struct smb2_write_req, Buffer)) {', '\t\tdata_buf = (char *)&req->Buffer[0];', '\t} else {', '\t\tif ((u64)le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset) + length >', '\t\t    get_rfc1002_len(work->request_buf)) {', '\t\t\tpr_err("invalid write data offset %u, smb_len %u\\n",', '\t\t\t       le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset),', '\t\t\t       get_rfc1002_len(work->request_buf));', '\t\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t}', '\t\tdata_buf = (char *)(((char *)&req->hdr.ProtocolId) +', '\t\t\t\tle16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset));', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif ((u64)le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset) + length >', '\t    get_rfc1002_len(work->request_buf)) {', '\t\tpr_err("invalid write data offset %u, smb_len %u\\n",', '\t\t       le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset),', '\t\t       get_rfc1002_len(work->request_buf));', '\t\terr = -EINVAL;', '\t\tgoto out;', '\t}', '\tdata_buf = (char *)(((char *)&req->hdr.ProtocolId) +', '\t\t\t   le16_to_cpu(req->DataOffset));']}
description: An issue was discovered in ksmbd in the Linux kernel 5.15 through 5.18 before 5.18.18. fs/ksmbd/smb2pdu.c lacks length validation in the non-padding case in smb2_write.

code_evidence: length comes from the client-controlled req->Length. When DataOffset equals offsetof(smb2_write_req, Buffer), the branch at lines 12-14 sets data_buf = &req->Buffer[0] and skips the bounds check, so no relationship between length and the actual request buffer size is enforced before ksmbd_rpc_write reads length bytes from data_buf at line 27.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing length validation lets a read of length bytes from a buffer whose actual size is smaller, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). It is not a write overflow because the untrusted length is consumed as a read size.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the non-padding path bypasses the DataOffset+length > get_rfc1002_len check, so a client-supplied Length is trusted. Trigger: a Write request whose DataOffset equals the Buffer offset but whose Length exceeds the remaining request data. Consequence: ksmbd_rpc_write reads past the request buffer, leaking memory or crashing.

commit_msg:
FreeBSD: Fix UNIX permissions checking

Reviewed-by: Ryan Moeller <ryan@iXsystems.com>
Reviewed-by: Brian Behlendorf <behlendorf1@llnl.gov>
Signed-off-by: Matt Macy <mmacy@FreeBSD.org>
Closes #10727
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tboolean_t owner = B_FALSE;', '\tboolean_t groupmbr = B_FALSE;', '\tuid_t uid = crgetuid(cr);', '\tmutex_enter(&zdp->z_acl_lock);', '\tif (FUID_INDEX(zdp->z_uid) != 0 || FUID_INDEX(zdp->z_gid) != 0) {', '\t\tgoto out_slow;', '\t}', '', '\tif (uid == zdp->z_uid) {', '\t\towner = B_TRUE;', '\t\tif (zdp->z_mode & S_IXUSR) {', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\tgoto out_slow;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '\tif (groupmember(zdp->z_gid, cr)) {', '\t\tgroupmbr = B_TRUE;', '\t\tif (zdp->z_mode & S_IXGRP) {', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t} else {', '\t\t\tgoto out_slow;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '\tif (!owner && !groupmbr) {', '\t\tif (zdp->z_mode & S_IXOTH) {', '\t\t\tgoto out;', '\t\t}', '\t}', 'out:', '\tmutex_exit(&zdp->z_acl_lock);', '\treturn (0);', 'out_slow:', '\tmutex_exit(&zdp->z_acl_lock);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: OpenZFS before 2.0.0-rc1, when used on FreeBSD, allows execute permissions for all directories.

code_evidence: If ZFS_NO_EXECS_DENIED is set, the function immediately returns 0 (execute allowed) without consulting z_mode permission bits.
The ACL lock is taken and FUID-indexed owners/groups fall through to out_slow, which returns 1 (denied); the remaining logic is reached only for plain numeric uid/gid.
Owner path: when uid matches z_uid, it returns 0 only if S_IXUSR is set, otherwise out_slow returns 1.
Group path: groupmember() sets groupmbr and returns 0 only if S_IXGRP is set, else out_slow returns 1.
Other path: only when neither owner nor groupmbr is set does it check S_IXOTH and return 0; otherwise it falls through to out.
out: releases the lock and returns 0, granting execute.
out_slow: releases the lock and returns 1, denying execute.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function attempts a UNIX permission authorization check but misroutes the failure case, granting access when the check should deny; this is an incorrect authorization check (CWE-863). It is not merely a missing check: the S_IXOTH test exists but its negative outcome is mishandled.

evidence_lines.code:
if (zdp->z_pflags & ZFS_NO_EXECS_DENIED)
return (0);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 'other' branch falls through to the out label (return 0) when S_IXOTH is not set, so a non-owner/non-group caller is granted execute despite lacking the other-execute bit. Trigger: a caller unrelated to the file owner/group invoking zfs_fastaccesschk_execute on a mode without S_IXOTH. Consequence: unauthorized execute permission on directories, bypassing the mode-based authorization check.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.4. The 9p filesystem did not protect i_size_write() properly, which causes an i_size_read() infinite loop and denial of service on SMP systems.

code_evidence: Line 19 unconditionally calls i_size_write(inode, stat->st_size) in the P9_STATS_BASIC branch.
Lines 49-50 call i_size_write(inode, stat->st_size) when P9_STATS_SIZE is set in the else branch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The seqcount read loop's exit condition cannot be reached under concurrent unsynchronized i_size_write() calls, matching an unreachable-exit-condition infinite loop (CWE-835). This is not merely a data race consequence: the supported impact is the non-terminating loop and CPU lockup.

evidence_lines.code: i_size_write(inode, stat->st_size);

if (stat->st_result_mask & P9_STATS_SIZE)
i_size_write(inode, stat->st_size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: i_size_write() updates i_size using a seqcount that i_size_read() spins on until a stable read is observed. Because these writes are not serialized under inode->i_lock, concurrent v9fs_vfs_getattr paths can repeatedly race the seqcount, so a reader in generic_fillattr() never reaches a stable state and loops indefinitely, causing a soft lockup/DoS.

Fixes issue #1033 reported by @ping86

bpf_adj_branches() would need to potentially adjust branch targets
which cross the patchlet boundary to accommodate for the additional
delta. Eventually that lead to the case where the target offset could
not fit into insn->off's upper 0x7fff limit anymore where then offset
wraps around becoming negative (in s16 universe), or vice versa
depending on the jump direction.

Therefore it becomes necessary to detect and reject any such occasions
in a generic way for native eBPF and cBPF to eBPF migrations. For
the latter we can simply check bounds in the bpf_convert_filter()'s
BPF_EMIT_JMP helper macro and bail out once we surpass limits. The
bpf_patch_insn_single() for native eBPF (and cBPF to eBPF in case
of subsequent hardening) is a bit more complex in that we need to
detect such truncations before hitting the bpf_prog_realloc(). Thus
the latter is split into an extra pass to probe problematic offsets
on the original program in order to fail early. With that in place
and carefully tested I no longer hit the panic and the rewrites are
rejected properly. The above example panic I've seen on bpf-next,
though the issue itself is generic in that a guard against this issue
in bpf seems more appropriate in this case.

Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Martin KaFai Lau <kafai@fb.com>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>

description: The BPF subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.17 mishandles situations with a long jump over an instruction sequence where inner instructions require substantial expansions into multiple BPF instructions, leading to an overflow. This affects kernel/bpf/core.c and net/core/filter.c.

code_evidence: The BPF_EMIT_JMP macro computes the branch offset as addrs[target] - addrs[i] - 1 and then subtracts (insn - tmp_insns), storing the result directly into insn->off, a signed 16-bit field. The only prior check is target >= len || target < 0; the computed offset is never compared against the s16 range before assignment, so a large expansion delta silently truncates/wraps the stored offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits: a computed value is placed into a fixed-size 16-bit destination without verifying it fits, so the size/range of the input (offset) is not checked against the output field, producing a memory-corrupting overflow. A pure integer-overflow label (CWE-190) is less precise because the concrete defect is the unchecked write into the bounded insn->off field.

evidence_lines.code:
#define BPF_EMIT_JMP\
do {\
if (target >= len || target < 0)\
goto err;\
insn->off = addrs ? addrs[target] - addrs[i] - 1 : 0;\
\
insn->off -= insn - tmp_insns;\
} while (0)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pc-relative jump offset computed from address deltas is written into the 16-bit insn->off without a range check. Trigger: a long jump across instructions that expand heavily (e.g., hardening rewrites), making the delta exceed S16_MAX/S16_MIN. Consequence: the offset wraps to a wrong (negative or positive) value, redirecting execution to unintended instructions, which can cause out-of-bounds access and kernel panic as in the report.

Fix arrow function this binding resolving if environment record is present

This patch fixes #4872 and fixes #4876.

After the guard, parent is assumed to be an object: ecma_get_object_from_value (line 34) and ecma_op_object_get_with_receiver (line 41) are called on it, while ecma_op_resolve_super_base (line 15) can return null/undefined for arrow functions whose this binding was not resolved.

commit_msg:
tls: clear data after a starttls acknowledgement

After a starttls acknowledgement message, clear the buffers of any
incoming data / commands.  This will ensure that all future data is
handled securely.

Co-authored-by: Pietro Cerutti <gahr@gahr.ch>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    // Clear any data after the STARTTLS acknowledgement', '    mutt_socket_empty(conn);']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

code_evidence: After sending STARTTLS and reading the acknowledgement via smtp_get_resp, the code proceeds directly to mutt_ssl_starttls without discarding any buffered data already received after the acknowledgement. Any bytes the peer (or a man-in-the-middle) placed after the STARTTLS response remain in the connection buffer and are subsequently interpreted within the TLS context.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Externally supplied protocol data is accepted and passed into a downstream TLS/command context without neutralization of the extra elements, matching improper neutralization of special elements used by a downstream component. The specific STARTTLS response-injection variant is a child weakness; CWE-74 is the appropriate class-level target here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the client does not drain the socket buffer between the STARTTLS acknowledgement and the TLS handshake. Trigger: a server or MITM appends injected data to the STARTTLS response. Consequence: the injected bytes are parsed in the TLS session, enabling response injection that can influence later SMTP exchanges.

Return a TFLite error if gather_nd will result in reading invalid memory

PiperOrigin-RevId: 463054033
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['inline void GatherNd(const RuntimeShape& params_shape,', '                     const ParamsT* params_data,', '                     const RuntimeShape& indices_shape,', '                     const IndicesT* indices_data,', '                     const RuntimeShape& output_shape, ParamsT* output_data) {', '    int from_pos = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['inline TfLiteStatus GatherNd(const RuntimeShape& params_shape,', '                             const ParamsT* params_data,', '                             const RuntimeShape& indices_shape,', '                             const IndicesT* indices_data,', '                             const RuntimeShape& output_shape,', '                             ParamsT* output_data) {', '    int64_t from_pos = 0;', '    }', '    if (from_pos < 0 || from_pos + res.slice_size > params_shape.FlatSize()) {', '      return kTfLiteError;', '  return kTfLiteOk;']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The `GatherNd` function takes arguments that determine the sizes of inputs and outputs. If the inputs given are greater than or equal to the sizes of the outputs, an out-of-bounds memory read is triggered. This issue has been patched in GitHub commit 595a65a3e224a0362d7e68c2213acfc2b499a196. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.10.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.9.1, TensorFlow 2.8.1, and TensorFlow 2.7.2, as these are also affected and still in supported range. There are no known workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: from_pos is computed from indices_data[...] times dims_to_count[j]; the original code performs no bounds check on the resulting offset.
The memcpy then reads sizeof(ParamsT)*res.slice_size bytes from params_data + from_pos, so an attacker-influenced index produces a read offset outside params_data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads from params_data at an unvalidated computed offset, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The missing check on from_pos/slice_size relative to the source buffer is the read-side weakness; a write-side overflow would instead be CWE-787.

std::memcpy(output_data + i * res.slice_size, params_data + from_pos,
sizeof(ParamsT) * res.slice_size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the gather offset from_pos is derived from untrusted index values and used directly as a source pointer without validating it against params_shape.FlatSize(). A crafted indices tensor yields a negative or oversized from_pos, and memcpy reads past the params buffer, giving an out-of-bounds read (crash or memory disclosure).

commit_msg:
Fix a double-free bug.

In the dlt_config_file_set_section function of dlt_config_file_parser.c:
  s-name is not set to null after free.
  It will be freed again in the dlt_config_file_release function.

Signed-off-by: Zhongyang.Bao <Zhongyang.Bao@zeekrlife.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        s->name = NULL;']}
description: An issue in dlt_config_file_parser.c of dlt-daemon v2.18.8 allows attackers to cause a double free via crafted TCP packets.

code_evidence: When calloc for s->keys fails, the code frees s->name at line 20 but returns without clearing the pointer, leaving s->name dangling in file->sections[section].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees the same address (s->name) and retains the pointer, enabling a second free of that address elsewhere, which matches CWE-415 Double Free. A use-after-free (CWE-416) would require a read/write through the dangling pointer, which is not shown here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on the s->keys allocation-failure path, s->name is freed but not set to NULL, so the section still holds a dangling pointer. Trigger: a later release path (dlt_config_file_release) frees s->name again, producing a double free; consequence is heap corruption/memory modification potentially leading to availability or code-execution impact.

commit_msg: Don't process empty input for cherokee_validator_parse_basic and cherokee_validator_parse_digest
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Guard empty input', '\t */', '\tif (unlikely(str == NULL || str_len == 0))', '\t\tgoto error;', '', 'error:', '\tcherokee_buffer_mrproper (&auth);', '\treturn ret_error;']}
description: Cherokee 0.4.27 to 1.2.104 is affected by a denial of service due to a NULL pointer dereferences. A remote unauthenticated attacker can crash the server by sending an HTTP request to protected resources using a malformed Authorization header that is mishandled during a cherokee_buffer_add call within cherokee_validator_parse_basic or cherokee_validator_parse_digest.

end   = auth.buf + auth.len;

entry = comma + 1;
entry = comma + 1;

commit_msg: Fixed infinite loop cauesd by invalid dns packets
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\tif (!(i & DN_COMP_BITMASK))', '\t\t\t\t\ti =- 12;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t{', '\t\t\tunsigned short lowest_pos = length;', '\t\t\t\t\tif ((i & DN_COMP_BITMASK) != DN_COMP_BITMASK)', '\t\t\t\t\ti -= 12;', '', '\t\t\t\t\tif (i >= lowest_pos)', '\t\t\t\t\t\treturn std::make_pair((unsigned char *) NULL, "Invalid decompression pointer");', '\t\t\t\t\tlowest_pos = i;', '\t\t}']}
description: InspIRCd before 2.0.7 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop).

code_evidence: The CNAME/PTR loop continues while q==0 and i<length, so termination depends entirely on i progressing; the only other bound is o+256<1023 on the buffer.

On a compressed label (payload[i]>63), i is overwritten with the 14-bit pointer from the packet and then reduced by 12; nothing forces this new i to be greater than the previous position, so a pointer can target an already-visited or earlier offset.

The non-compressed branch advances i by payload[i]+1 and q is set only when payload[i]==0, so a backward jump re-reads earlier bytes; res[o] is written each iteration but o only grows via label copies, and res[o]=0 is reached only after q becomes 1.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers improper resource management; an unbounded loop driven by attacker-controlled packet data is a resource-consumption failure. The missing monotonic-pointer check is the cause; the infinite loop and CPU exhaustion are the consequence, distinguishing it from a memory-corruption weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
res[o] = 0;
break;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decompression pointer targets are not constrained to advance monotonically, so a crafted DNS reply whose compression pointer points backward at an earlier label makes the loop repeatedly re-read the same payload bytes without q ever becoming 1. Trigger: a remote malformed CNAME/PTR answer with a self-referential or backward pointer. Consequence: the loop never terminates, consuming CPU indefinitely (denial of service).

commit_msg:
With write operation on psi files replacing old trigger with a new one,
the lifetime of its waitqueue is totally arbitrary. Overwriting an
existing trigger causes its waitqueue to be freed and pending poll()
will stumble on trigger->event_wait which was destroyed.
Fix this by disallowing to redefine an existing psi trigger. If a write
operation is used on a file descriptor with an already existing psi
trigger, the operation will fail with EBUSY error.
Also bypass a check for psi_disabled in the psi_trigger_destroy as the
flag can be flipped after the trigger is created, leading to a memory
leak.

Fixes: 0e94682b73bf ("psi: introduce psi monitor")
Reported-by: syzbot+cdb5dd11c97cc532efad@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Analyzed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Suren Baghdasaryan <surenb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Acked-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220111232309.1786347-1-surenb@google.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpsi_trigger_replace(&ctx->psi.trigger, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['\tpsi_trigger_destroy(ctx->psi.trigger);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's implementation of Pressure Stall Information. While the feature is disabled by default, it could allow an attacker to crash the system or have other memory-corruption side effects.

code_evidence: The release callback reads ctx->psi.trigger and passes it to psi_trigger_replace(&ctx->psi.trigger, NULL), which frees the existing trigger object while other users (e.g., pending poll() on trigger->event_wait) may still hold references to it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees a trigger object whose memory may still be referenced by pending poll() operations, matching CWE-416 (reusing freed memory). This is use-after-free rather than a mere leak because the freed waitqueue is later dereferenced.

evidence_lines.code:
struct cgroup_file_ctx *ctx = of->priv;
psi_trigger_replace(&ctx->psi.trigger, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the trigger's waitqueue is freed on this release path while concurrent poll() callers can still dereference trigger->event_wait. Trigger: closing/releasing the cgroup file frees the trigger; a pending poll() then accesses the freed waitqueue. Supported consequence: memory corruption/crash (use after free).

description: Stack-based buffer overflow in decoder/impeg2d_vld.c in mediaserver in Android 6.x before 2016-04-01 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 25812590.

code_evidence: u4_numCoeffs is incremented by the decoded run and then used as an index into pu1_scan and *pi4_num_coeffs; writes to pi2_outAddr[*pi4_num_coeffs] and pu1_pos[*pi4_num_coeffs] occur before any bound check on *pi4_num_coeffs.
Same pattern: u4_numCoeffs += u4_run; u4_pos = pu1_scan[u4_numCoeffs++ & 63]; then pu1_pos[*pi4_num_coeffs] and pi2_outAddr[*pi4_num_coeffs] are written with no check that *pi4_num_coeffs < 64.

In the non-intra branch, u4_run is added to u4_numCoeffs and the resulting index drives writes to pi2_outAddr[*pi4_num_coeffs]/pu1_pos[*pi4_num_coeffs]; the guard at line 315 only checks u4_numCoeffs after the write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs writes to pi2_outAddr[*pi4_num_coeffs] and pu1_pos[*pi4_num_coeffs] without restricting the index to the buffer's intended 64-element boundary, directly matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The root cause is the missing in-loop index constraint rather than a pure integer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The decoder writes coefficients into pi2_outAddr and pu1_pos indexed by *pi4_num_coeffs, which grows with attacker-controlled run lengths from the bitstream. The bound check on u4_numCoeffs is performed only after the indexed writes, so a crafted media file can advance the index past the 64-entry block and cause out-of-bounds stack writes, leading to memory corruption and possible code execution.

commit_msg:
Clean up handling of counted blobs of bytes.

Don't treat the count+blob as itself a blob of bytes; use FT_NONE.
Create it with an unknown length (-1, meaning "to end of packet, for
now"), and set its length once we've finished dissecting it.  Dissect
the raw bytes of a prefixed-bytes item regardless of whether we're
building a protocol tree or not.

This means we do a better job of handling a too-large length; instead of
overflowing the offset, we throw an exception and stop dissecting, so we
don't run the risk of looping infinitely.

Bug: 14841

(cherry picked from commit a03eacc7aabd04a6fd0db978e0d7597220ac0515)

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0 to 2.6.1, 2.4.0 to 2.4.7, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.15, the Bazaar protocol dissector could go into an infinite loop. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-bzr.c by properly handling items that are too long.

code_evidence: plen is read directly from the packet as a 32-bit value with no bound check, then used to compute the length 4 + plen passed to proto_tree_add_item.
The function returns 4 + plen as the number of bytes consumed, so a large plen produces a large offset advance (or overflow) that the caller uses to continue dissecting.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the unchecked plen propagates into the returned offset, allowing the caller's iteration to never terminate. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the supported consequence is a non-terminating dissection loop.

evidence_lines.code: return 4 + plen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The attacker-controlled plen is never validated against the remaining tvb length before being added to offset. A too-large plen makes the offset arithmetic overflow or move past the buffer while the caller keeps invoking the dissector, so the dissection loop cannot reach its exit condition, causing CPU exhaustion (DoS). The root cause is the missing length constraint; the infinite loop is the consequence.

commit_msg:
PR22200, DWARF5 .debug_line sanity check

The format_count entry can't be zero unless the count is also zero.

	PR 22200
	* dwarf2.c (read_formatted_entries): Error on format_count zero.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (format_count == 0 && data_count != 0)', '    {', '      _bfd_error_handler (_("Dwarf Error: Zero format count."));', '      bfd_set_error (bfd_error_bad_value);', '      return FALSE;', '    }', '']}
description: read_formatted_entries in dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, does not properly validate the format count, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to concat_filename.

code_evidence: format_count is read from the untrusted ELF/DWARF buffer; when it is zero the loop at 19 never runs and format_header_data points just past the count byte.
The data loop at 28 still executes data_count times even when format_count is zero, so the inner loop at 32 never initializes fe.name or any other fe field.
Because the inner loop is skipped, the DW_LNCT_path case never assigns stringp, leaving fe.name uninitialized.
read_string is the path assignment used when a DW_LNCT_path format is present; with zero formats it is never reached.
callback is invoked with fe.name even though it was never set, passing an uninitialized/NULL-derived pointer into downstream filename handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing validation lets an uninitialized (NULL-derived) filename pointer reach callback, causing a dereference of a pointer expected to be valid, matching CWE-476. The consequence is a denial-of-service crash, not merely an out-of-bounds read.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!callback (table, fe.name, fe.dir, fe.time, fe.size))
return FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function does not reject a zero format_count combined with nonzero data_count, so each data entry is processed with no format descriptors to populate fe. fe.name (and fe.dir/time/size) remain uninitialized, and callback receives that garbage pointer, leading to a NULL/invalid pointer dereference and crash when the filename is consumed. Trigger is a crafted ELF with zero format count and nonzero data count.

commit_msg:
As shown through runtime testing, the "filename" allocation is not
always freed in perf_event_parse_addr_filter().

There are three possible ways that this could happen:

 - It could be allocated twice on subsequent iterations through the loop,
 - or leaked on the success path,
 - or on the failure path.

Clean up the code flow to make it obvious that 'filename' is always
freed in the reallocation path and in the two return paths as well.

We rely on the fact that kfree(NULL) is NOP and filename is initialized
with NULL.

This fixes the leak. No other side effects expected.

[ Dan Carpenter: cleaned up the code flow & added a changelog. ]
[ Ingo Molnar: updated the changelog some more. ]

Fixes: 375637bc5249 ("perf/core: Introduce address range filtering")
Signed-off-by: "kiyin(尹亮)" <kiyin@tencent.com>
Signed-off-by: Dan Carpenter <dan.carpenter@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Ingo Molnar <mingo@kernel.org>
Cc: "Srivatsa S. Bhat" <srivatsa@csail.mit.edu>
Cc: Anthony Liguori <aliguori@amazon.com>
--
 kernel/events/core.c | 12 +++++-------
 1 file changed, 5 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\tgoto fail_free_name;', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto fail_free_name;', '', '\t\t\t\tkfree(filename);', '\t\t\t\tfilename = NULL;', 'fail_free_name:', 'fail:'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tkfree(filename);', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto fail;', '\t\t\t\t\tgoto fail;', '\tkfree(filename);', 'fail:']}
description: A flaw memory leak in the Linux kernel performance monitoring subsystem was found in the way if using PERF_EVENT_IOC_SET_FILTER. A local user could use this flaw to starve the resources causing denial of service.

code_evidence: Each loop iteration reaching IF_SRC_FILE/IF_SRC_FILEADDR overwrites filename via match_strdup without freeing any previous allocation, so a prior filename is leaked on reallocation.

On the non-kernel path, failure after assigning filename (e.g., !event->ctx->task or kern_path error) jumps to fail_free_name, which frees filename, but the success path frees filename and sets NULL; however, the error paths before this block (e.g., state checks, kstrtoul failures) go to fail, which does not free filename, leaking it.

On successful completion, kfree(orig) is executed and 0 returned, but filename is not freed if it was allocated and not yet freed (e.g., when state != IF_STATE_ACTION triggers goto fail, or when the loop exits with filename still set). The fail label frees filters and orig but not filename, so any filename allocated and not freed before reaching fail leaks.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates memory for filename and fails to release it on multiple paths, matching CWE-401 (Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime). The leak is due to insufficient tracking/release of allocated memory, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: filename is allocated with match_strdup and overwritten on subsequent iterations without freeing the previous allocation, and several error/exit paths (goto fail) do not free filename. Trigger: malformed or repeated filter input causes allocation then early exit or reallocation. Consequence: unreleased memory accumulates, leading to resource consumption/DoS.

description: RIOT 2020.04 has a buffer overflow in the base64 decoder. The decoding function base64_decode() uses an output buffer estimation function to compute the required buffer capacity and validate against the provided buffer size. The base64_estimate_decode_size() function calculates the expected decoded size with an arithmetic round-off error and does not take into account possible padding bytes. Due to this underestimation, it may be possible to craft base64 input that causes a buffer overflow.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only changes the output parameter type from unsigned char* to void* and forwards arguments to base64_encode_base; it contains no buffer-size estimation, bounds check, or memory access that could cause the described overflow.

commit_msg:
binding: Moves the check for the first access to the initial document into BindingSecurity.

Checks the access to the initial document and reports it not only at
securityCheck() in V8Window.cpp but also at every call to
BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() because V8 only calls back
securityCheck() on property lookups, and not for function invocation.

BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo() is called with every possible
cross-origin window, which means every possible new window.  Thus,
shouldAllowAccessTo() should be the right place to check the access
to the initial document.

BUG=630662
TBR=benwells@chromium.org

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2209303002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#412195}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    return canAccessFrame(isolate, accessingWindow, target->document().getSecurityOrigin(), target->document().domWindow(), exceptionState);'], 'added_lines': ['    return canAccessFrame(accessingWindow, target->document().getSecurityOrigin(), target->document().domWindow(), exceptionState);']}
description: Google Chrome before 53.0.2785.89 on Windows and OS X and before 53.0.2785.92 on Linux does not properly validate access to the initial document, which allows remote attackers to spoof the address bar via a crafted web site.

code_evidence: shouldAllowAccessTo forwards the accessing window and target's document security origin and dom window to canAccessFrame; the function itself performs no check on whether target is the initial document before granting access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-254 covers security-feature/access-control deficiencies; here the access-control check for the initial document is incomplete, directly supporting this category.

evidence_lines.code:
bool BindingSecurity::shouldAllowAccessTo(v8::Isolate* isolate, const LocalDOMWindow* accessingWindow, const Node* target, ExceptionState& exceptionState)
return canAccessFrame(isolate, accessingWindow, target->document().getSecurityOrigin(), target->document().domWindow(), exceptionState);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the access-decision function delegates origin checks to canAccessFrame without separately validating access to the initial document. Trigger: a crafted cross-origin site invokes properties/functions on a window whose target document is the initial document. Consequence: access is allowed, enabling address-bar spoofing.

commit_msg: tar: fix crash on broken tar file.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tdir = GSF_INFILE_TAR (subdir);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tdir = GSF_IS_INFILE_TAR (subdir)', '\t\t\t\t\t? GSF_INFILE_TAR (subdir)', '\t\t\t\t\t: dir;']}
description: An error within the "tar_directory_for_file()" function (gsf-infile-tar.c) in GNOME Structured File Library before 1.14.41 can be exploited to trigger a Null pointer dereference and subsequently cause a crash via a crafted TAR file.

code_evidence: gsf_infile_child_by_name() returns a GsfInput* subdir that may be non-NULL but not a GsfInfileTar instance.
When subdir is truthy, the code unrefs subdir and then blindly casts it via GSF_INFILE_TAR(subdir) without checking its actual type.

} else
dir = tar_create_dir (dir, dirname);

commit_msg:
ps_dec: sanitize iid_index before mixing

index range is supposed to be withing -7 and 7 or -15 and 15 depending on
iid_mode (see Table 8.24, ISO/IEC 14496-3:2005).

Indexes outside these boundaries are likely to be errors and should be
sanitized to avoid memory corruption. Replace any index under
-no_iid_steps (-7 or -15 depending on iid_mode) by -no_iid_steps. Replace
any index above no_iid_steps by no_iid_steps. Try to process further.

This commit addresses CVE-2019-6956 (fixes #39).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                /* index range is supposed to be -7...7 or -15...15 depending on iid_mode', '                   (Table 8.24, ISO/IEC 14496-3:2005).', '                   if it is outside these boundaries, this is most likely an error. sanitize', '                   it and try to process further. */', '                if (ps->iid_index[env][bk] < -no_iid_steps) {', '                    fprintf(stderr, "Warning: invalid iid_index: %d < %d\\n", ps->iid_index[env][bk],', '                        -no_iid_steps);', '                    ps->iid_index[env][bk] = -no_iid_steps;', '                } else if (ps->iid_index[env][bk] > no_iid_steps) {', '                    fprintf(stderr, "Warning: invalid iid_index: %d > %d\\n", ps->iid_index[env][bk],', '                        no_iid_steps);', '                    ps->iid_index[env][bk] = no_iid_steps;', '                }', '']}
description: An invalid memory address dereference was discovered in the sbr_process_channel function of libfaad/sbr_dec.c in Freeware Advanced Audio Decoder 2 (FAAD2) 2.8.8. The vulnerability causes a segmentation fault and application crash, which leads to denial of service.

code_evidence: ps->iid_index[env][bk] is used directly as an index into sf_iid via no_iid_steps + iid_index and no_iid_steps - iid_index, with no bounds check on iid_index.
For iid_mode >= 3, iid_index indexes cos_betas_fine/sin_betas_fine at [-iid_index] or [iid_index]; values beyond ±15 exceed the table bounds.
For iid_mode < 3, iid_index indexes cos_betas_normal/sin_betas_normal similarly, exceeding ±7.
In the icc_mode >= 3 branch, sincos_alphas_B_fine is indexed at no_iid_steps + iid_index and 30 - (no_iid_steps + iid_index), so an out-of-range iid_index yields an out-of-bounds table read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs reads of memory buffers (the IID coefficient tables) using an unchecked index, accessing locations outside the intended buffer boundaries. This is exactly an out-of-bounds read within the buffer-bounds restriction weakness described by CWE-119; the missing range constraint on iid_index is the specific mechanism enabling it.

evidence_lines.code:
c_1 = sf_iid[no_iid_steps + ps->iid_index[env][bk]];
c_2 = sf_iid[no_iid_steps - ps->iid_index[env][bk]];

cosb =  cos_betas_fine[-ps->iid_index[env][bk]][ps->icc_index[env][bk]];
sinb = -sin_betas_fine[-ps->iid_index[env][bk]][ps->icc_index[env][bk]];

cosb =  cos_betas_normal[-ps->iid_index[env][bk]][ps->icc_index[env][bk]];
sinb = -sin_betas_normal[-ps->iid_index[env][bk]][ps->icc_index[env][bk]];

cosa = sincos_alphas_B_fine[no_iid_steps + ps->iid_index[env][bk]][ps->icc_index[env][bk]];
sina = sincos_alphas_B_fine[30 - (no_iid_steps + ps->iid_index[env][bk])][ps->icc_index[env][bk]];

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the absence of a constraint on ps->iid_index[env][bk], which is attacker-influenced decoded bitstream data, before it is used as an array index. When iid_index falls outside the allowable ±no_iid_steps range, the table accesses (sf_iid, cos/sin betas, sincos_alphas_B) read outside their intended bounds, causing an invalid memory dereference and a crash (denial of service).

commit_msg:
Use spinlocks to deal with workers introducing a wrapper
bigben_schedule_work(), and several spinlock checks.
Otherwise, bigben_set_led() may schedule bigben->worker after the
structure has been freed, causing a use-after-free.

Fixes: 4eb1b01de5b9 ("HID: hid-bigbenff: fix race condition for scheduled work during removal")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230125-hid-unregister-leds-v4-3-7860c5763c38@diag.uniroma1.it
Signed-off-by: Benjamin Tissoires <benjamin.tissoires@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tschedule_work(&bigben->worker);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tbigben_schedule_work(bigben);']}
description: The Linux kernel through 6.1.9 has a Use-After-Free in bigben_remove in drivers/hid/hid-bigbenff.c via a crafted USB device because the LED controllers remain registered for too long.

code_evidence: The function obtains bigben from hid_get_drvdata and only guards against NULL; it does not hold a reference or otherwise prevent concurrent teardown of the device structure.
The LED state is read and updated under bigben->lock, but the lock is released before the work decision is acted upon.
When work is true, bigben->work_led is set and schedule_work(&bigben->worker) is called without revalidating bigben or holding the lock, so the worker field may already have been freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function accesses bigben->worker via schedule_work after the structure may have been freed by concurrent removal; the missing lifetime synchronization is the use-after-free, not merely a generic race condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the work is scheduled after the spinlock is dropped, so teardown can free bigben between the state check and schedule_work. Trigger: a LED brightness change racing with device removal/unregistration. Consequence: schedule_work dereferences freed bigben->worker, giving a use-after-free that may crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
Fix RCE vulnerability on feed enrichment

Currently there are a few places in the code that do not check URLs for
the presence of a command prefix, allowing malicious websites to run any
command in the local system.

Trying to run feed enrichment (i.e. after option "Extract full content
from HTML5 and Google AMP" is enabled) in a subscription that produces
this item:

    <item>
      <title>Check /tmp/bad-item-link.txt</title>
      <link>|date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt</link>
    </item>

will cause Liferea to call update_request_new on URL
"|date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt" and then blindly run the command. A
similar effect happens when running the feed enrichment in a item that
links to a document like this:

    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html>
     <head>
      <title>AMP URL RCE PoC</title>
      <link rel="amphtml" href="|date > /tmp/bad-amp-url.txt">
     </head>
     <body>
         Check the results in /tmp/bad-amp-url.txt
     </body>
    </html>

once Liferea tries to load the AMP URL.

There are other calls to update_request_* functions where URLs are
validated correctly (e.g. in feed icons and comments) and do not trigger
this vulnerability. Since the subscription update is the exception where
feed commands are supported (and welcome!) I chose to lock this feature
behind a non-persistent flag and only enable it when required. This is
safer than adding the flag in updateOptions, which is usually reused in
subordinate requests.

This failure exists since commits b8288389820a3f510ef4b21684b22439c41d95a5
and b67dbba73443ab7b36fcd3c78aa803e974c0f23e from Setember 2017.

description: A vulnerability was found in liferea. It has been rated as critical. Affected by this issue is the function update_job_run of the file src/update.c of the component Feed Enrichment. The manipulation of the argument source with the input |date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt leads to os command injection. The attack may be launched remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The name of the patch is 8d8b5b963fa64c7a2122d1bbfbb0bed46e813e59. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-222848.

code_evidence: update_job_run checks only whether the first character of job->request->source is '|'; if so, it logs the URL and calls update_exec_cmd(job) without any validation or trust check, then returns. The source string is attacker-controllable (feed item link or AMP href), so a value such as '|date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt' reaches the command executor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function passes externally influenced source data directly to a command executor without neutralizing shell metacharacters, which is exactly CWE-78 OS command injection. This is not merely SSRF or path traversal, since the '|' prefix explicitly selects local command execution.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the '|' command prefix is treated as sufficient authorization, with no check that the request originates from a trusted subscription context. Trigger: a malicious feed item or AMP URL supplies source beginning with '|'. Consequence: update_exec_cmd executes the attacker-chosen shell command under the application's privileges (RCE).

commit_msg:
The function l2cap_get_conf_opt will return L2CAP_CONF_OPT_SIZE + opt->len
as length value. The opt->len however is in control over the remote user
and can be used by an attacker to gain access beyond the bounds of the
actual packet.

To prevent any potential leak of heap memory, it is enough to check that
the resulting len calculation after calling l2cap_get_conf_opt is not
below zero. A well formed packet will always return >= 0 here and will
end with the length value being zero after the last option has been
parsed. In case of malformed packets messing with the opt->len field the
length value will become negative. If that is the case, then just abort
and ignore the option.

In case an attacker uses a too short opt->len value, then garbage will
be parsed, but that is protected by the unknown option handling and also
the option parameter size checks.

Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
Reviewed-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Johan Hedberg <johan.hedberg@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (len < 0)', '\t\t\tbreak;']}
description: A heap address information leak while using L2CAP_GET_CONF_OPT was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.1-rc1.

code_evidence: `len` is initialized from `chan->conf_len` (line 7), the length of the remote-supplied configuration request. The loop condition (line 17) only checks `len >= L2CAP_CONF_OPT_SIZE` before subtracting the value returned by `l2cap_get_conf_opt` (line 18), which is `L2CAP_CONF_OPT_SIZE + opt->len` with the attacker-controlled `opt->len`. No post-subtraction bound check exists, so `len` can become negative while the parser continues reading option data past the actual packet buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading option data beyond the intended packet buffer is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), matching the described heap address information leak. It is not CWE-787 because the primary consequence is a read leak rather than an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop trusts the length returned by `l2cap_get_conf_opt`, which incorporates the remote-controlled `opt->len`, without verifying the remaining length stays non-negative. Trigger: a malformed L2CAP configuration request with an oversized `opt->len`. Consequence: the parser advances past the packet bounds and reads heap memory, leaking information or causing a crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['#ifdef LIBRAW_LIBRARY_BUILD', '  imgdata.process_warnings |=  LIBRAW_WARN_PARSEFUJI_PROCESSED; ', '#endif']}
description: An error related to the "LibRaw::panasonic_load_raw()" function (dcraw_common.cpp) in LibRaw versions prior to 0.18.6 can be exploited to cause a heap-based buffer overflow and subsequently cause a crash via a specially crafted TIFF image.

code_evidence: Tag 0x130 sets fuji_width from a single byte: fuji_width = !(fgetc(ifp) & 8), i.e. a boolean.
After the tag loop, height <<= fuji_layout and width >>= fuji_layout apply the layout-derived shift without any bound relating the resulting dimensions to buffer sizes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unvalidated tag-derived geometry leads to out-of-bounds memory operations in subsequent processing, matching CWE-119's operation outside an intended buffer boundary.

evidence_lines.code:
fuji_width = !(fgetc(ifp) & 8);
}

height <<= fuji_layout;
width >>= fuji_layout;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The parser derives image dimensions/shift state (fuji_layout, fuji_width) directly from attacker-controlled TIFF tags without validating them against allocated buffer sizes. A crafted TIFF yields inconsistent width/height, so later raw-loading code indexes outside the intended buffer, causing a heap-based buffer overflow and crash.

commit_msg:
x86/HVM: prefill partially used variable on emulation paths

Certain handlers ignore the access size (vioapic_write() being the
example this was found with), perhaps leading to subsequent reads
seeing data that wasn't actually written by the guest. For
consistency and extra safety also do this on the read path of
hvm_process_io_intercept(), even if this doesn't directly affect what
guests get to see, as we've supposedly already dealt with read handlers
leaving data completely unitialized.

This is XSA-239.

Reported-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            data = 0;', '                data = 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 HVM guest OS users to obtain sensitive information from the host OS (or an arbitrary guest OS) because intercepted I/O operations can cause a write of data from uninitialized hypervisor stack memory.

code_evidence: Local uint64_t data is declared uninitialized; on the read path it is passed by address to ops->read(), and if a handler ignores p->size and writes fewer bytes than the full width, the untouched high bytes remain stack garbage, which are then propagated via p->data = data to the guest/hypervisor consumer.

On the write path, when p->data_is_ptr is false, data is taken from p->data; when it is true, hvm_copy_from_guest_phys() may partially fill data, and the uninitialized remainder is passed to ops->write().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect leaks hypervisor stack contents across a trust boundary to a guest, which is a confidentiality exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor. CWE-200 fits because the observable consequence is disclosure of internal memory; the underlying uninitialized-memory weakness is the cause, but the supported impact here is information exposure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stack variable data is not zero-initialized before being handed to size-parameterized read/write handlers that may only fill part of it. Trigger: an intercepted I/O operation whose handler ignores the access size, or a partial guest-physical copy. Consequence: uninitialized hypervisor stack bytes are read back or written out, disclosing host/guest memory contents.

description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. The estimator for the cost of some convolution operations can be made to execute a division by 0. The function fails to check that the stride argument is strictly positive. Hence, the fix is to add a check for the stride argument to ensure it is valid. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: OpDimensionsFromInputs is called on the input shape without validating that the stride/shape dimensions are strictly positive.
The returned dims drive arithmetic: ops = dims.iz * (dims.batch * dims.ix * dims.iy * 4 + 6 + rsqrt_cost) and ops = dims.batch * dims.ix * dims.iy * dims.iz * 2.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The description states the estimator can be made to divide by zero because the stride is not checked to be strictly positive, matching CWE-369 (Divide By Zero). The function's unchecked dimension derivation feeding the arithmetic is the relevant path; this is not merely an integer overflow.

evidence_lines.code:
ConvolutionDimensions dims = OpDimensionsFromInputs(
op_info.inputs(0).shape(), op_info, &found_unknown_shapes);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dimension derivation accepts a zero stride/dimension, and the resulting zero value flows into the cost computation. Trigger: a crafted convolution/batchnorm op_info with a zero stride leads to a division-by-zero inside dimension calculation. Supported consequence: crash/DoS of the estimator.
