commit_msg:
Commit a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars") is
checking whether maps are read-only both from BPF program side and user space
side, and then, given their content is constant, reading out their data via
map->ops->map_direct_value_addr() which is then subsequently used as known
scalar value for the register, that is, it is marked as __mark_reg_known()
with the read value at verification time. Before a23740ec43ba, the register
content was marked as an unknown scalar so the verifier could not make any
assumptions about the map content.

The current implementation however is prone to a TOCTOU race, meaning, the
value read as known scalar for the register is not guaranteed to be exactly
the same at a later point when the program is executed, and as such, the
prior made assumptions of the verifier with regards to the program will be
invalid which can cause issues such as OOB access, etc.

While the BPF_F_RDONLY_PROG map flag is always fixed and required to be
specified at map creation time, the map->frozen property is initially set to
false for the map given the map value needs to be populated, e.g. for global
data sections. Once complete, the loader "freezes" the map from user space
such that no subsequent updates/deletes are possible anymore. For the rest
of the lifetime of the map, this freeze one-time trigger cannot be undone
anymore after a successful BPF_MAP_FREEZE cmd return. Meaning, any new BPF_*
cmd calls which would update/delete map entries will be rejected with -EPERM
since map_get_sys_perms() removes the FMODE_CAN_WRITE permission. This also
means that pending update/delete map entries must still complete before this
guarantee is given. This corner case is not an issue for loaders since they
create and prepare such program private map in successive steps.

However, a malicious user is able to trigger this TOCTOU race in two different
ways: i) via userfaultfd, and ii) via batched updates. For i) userfaultfd is
used to expand the competition interval, so that map_update_elem() can modify
the contents of the map after map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load() were executed.
This works, because userfaultfd halts the parallel thread which triggered a
map_update_elem() at the time where we copy key/value from the user buffer and
this already passed the FMODE_CAN_WRITE capability test given at that time the
map was not "frozen". Then, the main thread performs the map_freeze() and
bpf_prog_load(), and once that had completed successfully, the other thread
is woken up to complete the pending map_update_elem() which then changes the
map content. For ii) the idea of the batched update is similar, meaning, when
there are a large number of updates to be processed, it can increase the
competition interval between the two. It is therefore possible in practice to
modify the contents of the map after executing map_freeze() and bpf_prog_load().

One way to fix both i) and ii) at the same time is to expand the use of the
map's map->writecnt. The latter was introduced in fc9702273e2e ("bpf: Add mmap()
support for BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY") and further refined in 1f6cb19be2e2 ("bpf:
Prevent re-mmap()'ing BPF map as writable for initially r/o mapping") with
the rationale to make a writable mmap()'ing of a map mutually exclusive with
read-only freezing. The counter indicates writable mmap() mappings and then
prevents/fails the freeze operation. Its semantics can be expanded beyond
just mmap() by generally indicating ongoing write phases. This would essentially
span any parallel regular and batched flavor of update/delete operation and
then also have map_freeze() fail with -EBUSY. For the check_mem_access() in
the verifier we expand upon the bpf_map_is_rdonly() check ensuring that all
last pending writes have completed via bpf_map_write_active() test. Once the
map->frozen is set and bpf_map_write_active() indicates a map->writecnt of 0
only then we are really guaranteed to use the map's data as known constants.
For map->frozen being set and pending writes in process of still being completed
we fall back to marking that register as unknown scalar so we don't end up
making assumptions about it. With this, both TOCTOU reproducers from i) and
ii) are fixed.

Note that the map->writecnt has been converted into a atomic64 in the fix in
order to avoid a double freeze_mutex mutex_{un,}lock() pair when updating
map->writecnt in the various map update/delete BPF_* cmd flavors. Spanning
the freeze_mutex over entire map update/delete operations in syscall side
would not be possible due to then causing everything to be serialized.
Similarly, something like synchronize_rcu() after setting map->frozen to wait
for update/deletes to complete is not possible either since it would also
have to span the user copy which can sleep. On the libbpf side, this won't
break d66562fba1ce ("libbpf: Add BPF object skeleton support") as the
anonymous mmap()-ed "map initialization image" is remapped as a BPF map-backed
mmap()-ed memory where for .rodata it's non-writable.

Fixes: a23740ec43ba ("bpf: Track contents of read-only maps as scalars")
Reported-by: w1tcher.bupt@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Acked-by: Andrii Nakryiko <andrii@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tbpf_map_write_active_inc(map);', '\tbpf_map_write_active_dec(map);']}
description: A race condition was found in the Linux kernel's ebpf verifier between bpf_map_update_elem and bpf_map_freeze due to a missing lock in kernel/bpf/syscall.c. In this flaw, a local user with a special privilege (cap_sys_admin or cap_bpf) can modify the frozen mapped address space. This flaw affects kernel versions prior to 5.16 rc2.

code_evidence: Lines 19-23 check map_get_sys_perms for FMODE_CAN_READ/WRITE and reject with -EPERM; this permission check is the state validation.
Lines 53-59 acquire rcu_read_lock and call map->ops->map_lookup_and_delete_elem, which reads and deletes map data based on the earlier permission check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits because the resource state (map permissions) is checked at lines 19-23 before being used at line 56, and the state can change in between. This is a time-of-check to time-of-use race, not simply a missing lock.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function validates map write permissions at lines 19-23 and later performs lookup-and-delete at line 56 under rcu_read_lock. The permission state can change between the check and the map operation because the check is not held against concurrent map_freeze or pending updates, so the operation may act on a map whose state no longer matches the checked permissions.

description:
Versions of the package yhirose/cpp-httplib before 0.12.4 are vulnerable to CRLF Injection when untrusted user input is used to set the content-type header in the HTTP .Patch, .Post, .Put and .Delete requests. This can lead to logical errors and other misbehaviors.

**Note:** This issue is present due to an incomplete fix for [CVE-2020-11709](https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-UNMANAGED-YHIROSECPPHTTPLIB-2366507).

code_evidence: Line 5 generates a multipart boundary via detail::make_multipart_data_boundary(). Lines 11-12 build a Content-Type header value by concatenating the literal prefix with that boundary and insert it directly into res.headers without any CR/LF validation or neutralization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-74 fits: externally influenced data is used to construct an output record (an HTTP header) without neutralizing special elements, changing interpretation by a downstream component. The CRLF-injection child weakness is the specific mechanism, but the target label is CWE-74.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Content-Type header value is assembled by string concatenation and stored via raw headers.emplace rather than a sanitizing setter, so special elements such as CR/LF in the boundary are not neutralized. Trigger: a boundary value containing CRLF reaches this header construction. Consequence: the injected sequence alters how the downstream HTTP parser interprets the response headers (header/response splitting).

commit_msg:
The syzbot fuzzer found a bug in the p54 USB wireless driver.  The
issue involves a race between disconnect and the firmware-loader
callback routine, and it has several aspects.

One big problem is that when the firmware can't be loaded, the
callback routine tries to unbind the driver from the USB _device_ (by
calling device_release_driver) instead of from the USB _interface_ to
which it is actually bound (by calling usb_driver_release_interface).

The race involves access to the private data structure.  The driver's
disconnect handler waits for a completion that is signalled by the
firmware-loader callback routine.  As soon as the completion is
signalled, you have to assume that the private data structure may have
been deallocated by the disconnect handler -- even if the firmware was
loaded without errors.  However, the callback routine does access the
private data several times after that point.

Another problem is that, in order to ensure that the USB device
structure hasn't been freed when the callback routine runs, the driver
takes a reference to it.  This isn't good enough any more, because now
that the callback routine calls usb_driver_release_interface, it has
to ensure that the interface structure hasn't been freed.

Finally, the driver takes an unnecessary reference to the USB device
structure in the probe function and drops the reference in the
disconnect handler.  This extra reference doesn't accomplish anything,
because the USB core already guarantees that a device structure won't
be deallocated while a driver is still bound to any of its interfaces.

To fix these problems, this patch makes the following changes:

	Call usb_driver_release_interface() rather than
	device_release_driver().

	Don't signal the completion until after the important
	information has been copied out of the private data structure,
	and don't refer to the private data at all thereafter.

	Lock udev (the interface's parent) before unbinding the driver
	instead of locking udev->parent.

	During the firmware loading process, take a reference to the
	USB interface instead of the USB device.

	Don't take an unnecessary reference to the device during probe
	(and then don't drop it during disconnect).

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+200d4bb11b23d929335f@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Acked-by: Christian Lamparter <chunkeey@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.1. There is a use-after-free caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/net/wireless/intersil/p54/p54usb.c driver.

code_evidence: Line 7 signals fw_wait_load before the callback finishes using priv; the disconnect handler waits on this completion and may then free priv, so lines 8-14 dereference priv (priv->fw, p54u_start_ops(priv), priv->udev) after the free can occur.
After the completion, the error path reads priv->udev->dev.parent at line 16 and uses udev (line 17, 20), continuing to touch memory reachable through the possibly-freed priv.
Line 25 releases the udev reference, but the core issue is the early completion allowing concurrent deallocation while the callback still uses priv.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The callback dereferences priv after the completion permits disconnect to free it, which is precisely CWE-416: referencing memory after it has been freed. This is a lifetime/ordering flaw, not merely a null-pointer or race-only issue.

evidence_lines.code: usb_put_dev(udev);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the firmware-load callback signals fw_wait_load at line 7 before it has finished using priv. Trigger: p54u_disconnect concurrently waits for that completion and frees the private structure, after which the callback executes lines 8-24 on freed memory. Supported consequence: use-after-free leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Use spinlocks to deal with workers introducing a wrapper
bigben_schedule_work(), and several spinlock checks.
Otherwise, bigben_set_led() may schedule bigben->worker after the
structure has been freed, causing a use-after-free.

Fixes: 4eb1b01de5b9 ("HID: hid-bigbenff: fix race condition for scheduled work during removal")
Signed-off-by: Pietro Borrello <borrello@diag.uniroma1.it>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230125-hid-unregister-leds-v4-3-7860c5763c38@diag.uniroma1.it
Signed-off-by: Benjamin Tissoires <benjamin.tissoires@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tschedule_work(&bigben->worker);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbigben_schedule_work(bigben);']}
description: The Linux kernel through 6.1.9 has a Use-After-Free in bigben_remove in drivers/hid/hid-bigbenff.c via a crafted USB device because the LED controllers remain registered for too long.

code_evidence: INIT_WORK(&bigben->worker, bigben_worker) initializes the worker and spin_lock_init(&bigben->lock) initializes the lock guarding it. At line 79, probe directly calls schedule_work(&bigben->worker) without taking bigben->lock or checking bigben->removed, so nothing coordinates this scheduling with the concurrent removal path that frees bigben.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The worker outlives the freed bigben object and dereferences it afterward, which is exactly CWE-416 (referencing memory after it is freed). The missing lock/removed check is the mechanism; the use-after-free is the resulting weakness, distinct from a mere race condition.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: probe schedules bigben->worker without the lock that removal uses to mark the structure removed and cancel work. Trigger: a crafted USB device is removed while bigben_probe is still running, so bigben_remove frees bigben and the already-queued worker later executes on freed memory. Supported consequence: use-after-free of the bigben structure.

description: lldpd before 0.8.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (assertion failure and daemon crash) via a malformed packet.

code_evidence: lldpd_alloc_mgmt is called with addr_ptr/addr_length derived from the received management-address TLV; when it returns NULL, line 178 executes assert(errno == ENOMEM). The assertion assumes allocation failure can only be ENOMEM, but errno for a malformed/oversized address may differ, so the assert aborts the daemon instead of taking the existing malformed path.

commit_msg: Bug #735 heap-overflow in get_l2len_protocol
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (datalen < l2_net_off)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (datalen <= l2_net_off)']}
description: The component tcprewrite in Tcpreplay v4.4.1 was discovered to contain a heap-based buffer overflow in get_l2len_protocol at common/get.c:344. NOTE: this is different from CVE-2022-27941.

code_evidence: Line 64 computes l2_net_off = sizeof(*eth_hdr) + *l2offset. The pre-patch check at line 65 (datalen < l2_net_off, now <=) fails to reject the case datalen == l2_net_off, so the ethernet header may end exactly at the buffer end.
After parse_metadata updates l2_net_off, line 76 only rejects datalen < l2_net_off, again allowing l2_net_off == datalen. Line 78 then sets *l2len = l2_net_off.
When ether_type <= 1500, line 82 reads pktdata[l2_net_off] with the high nibble check; if l2_net_off equals datalen this dereferences one byte past the allocated packet buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe access at line 82 indexes the packet buffer at l2_net_off without ensuring l2_net_off < datalen, an out-of-bounds memory access on a buffer whose length is datalen. This matches CWE-787's out-of-bounds write/access family; the missing <= constraint is the localized defect.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: off-by-one boundary checks (strict < instead of <=) let l2_net_off equal datalen. Trigger: an Ethernet frame whose computed L2 length exactly equals the captured datalen with ether_type <= 1500. Consequence: line 82 reads pktdata[l2_net_off] out of bounds, corrupting/inspecting memory beyond the packet buffer (heap over-read leading to the reported overflow impact).

commit_msg:
Store errors that result from leaf certificate verification.

In the case that a verification callback is installed that tells the
verifier to continue when a certificate is invalid (e.g. expired),
any error resulting from the leaf certificate verification is not stored
and made available post verification, resulting in an incorrect error being
returned.

Also perform leaf certificate verification prior to adding the chain, which
avoids a potential memory leak (as noted by tb@).

Issue reported by Ilya Shipitsin, who encountered haproxy regress failures.

ok tb@
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!x509_verify_cert_valid(ctx, leaf, NULL))', '\t\treturn 0;', '', '\tif (!x509_verify_cert_hostname(ctx, leaf, name))', '\t\treturn 0;', '', '\tctx->chains_count++;'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Verify the leaf certificate and store any resulting error. */', '\tif (!x509_verify_cert_valid(ctx, leaf, NULL))', '\t\treturn 0;', '\tif (!x509_verify_cert_hostname(ctx, leaf, name))', '\t\treturn 0;', '\tif (ctx->error_depth == 0 &&', '\t    ctx->error != X509_V_ERR_UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY)', '\t\tchain->cert_errors[0] = ctx->error;', '', '\tctx->chains_count++;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in x509/x509_verify.c in LibreSSL before 3.6.1, and in OpenBSD before 7.2 errata 001. x509_verify_ctx_add_chain does not store errors that occur during leaf certificate verification, and therefore an incorrect error is returned. This behavior occurs when there is an installed verification callback that instructs the verifier to continue upon detecting an invalid certificate.

code_evidence: Leaf certificate validity and hostname checks run via x509_verify_cert_valid and x509_verify_cert_hostname; on failure the function returns 0 without recording the specific verification error into chain->cert_errors.
After the checks, ctx->chains_count is incremented and ctx->error is unconditionally reset to X509_V_OK and error_depth to depth, discarding any leaf verification error that occurred.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs certificate validation but fails to preserve the validation result for the leaf, so an invalid certificate can be treated as valid after a callback continues. This is improper certificate validation (CWE-295); it is not merely an error-handling bug because the observable certificate-validity outcome is wrong.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a verification callback is installed that permits continuing on an invalid certificate, the leaf verification error is not stored in chain->cert_errors and ctx->error is overwritten with X509_V_OK. Post-verification callers therefore see an incorrect success/error state for the leaf certificate, rather than the actual validation failure.

commit_msg:
net: rose: fix UAF bugs caused by timer handler

There are UAF bugs in rose_heartbeat_expiry(), rose_timer_expiry()
and rose_idletimer_expiry(). The root cause is that del_timer()
could not stop the timer handler that is running and the refcount
of sock is not managed properly.

One of the UAF bugs is shown below:

    (thread 1)          |        (thread 2)
                        |  rose_bind
                        |  rose_connect
                        |    rose_start_heartbeat
rose_release            |    (wait a time)
  case ROSE_STATE_0     |
  rose_destroy_socket   |  rose_heartbeat_expiry
    rose_stop_heartbeat |
    sock_put(sk)        |    ...
  sock_put(sk) // FREE  |
                        |    bh_lock_sock(sk) // USE

The sock is deallocated by sock_put() in rose_release() and
then used by bh_lock_sock() in rose_heartbeat_expiry().

Although rose_destroy_socket() calls rose_stop_heartbeat(),
it could not stop the timer that is running.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdel_timer(&sk->sk_timer);'], 'added_lines': ['\tsk_stop_timer(sk, &sk->sk_timer);']}
description: There are use-after-free vulnerabilities caused by timer handler in net/rose/rose_timer.c of linux that allow attackers to crash linux kernel without any privileges.

code_evidence: rose_stop_heartbeat() only calls del_timer(&sk->sk_timer). del_timer() does not wait for an already-running timer handler and does not hold or release a sock reference, so it cannot prevent rose_heartbeat_expiry() from continuing to use sk after the socket is freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's timer cancellation leaves a window in which freed sock memory is subsequently accessed by the running timer handler, which is a use-after-free (CWE-416). It is not merely a resource leak: the freed object is actively dereferenced.

evidence_lines.code: del_timer(&sk->sk_timer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stop path uses del_timer(), which cannot synchronize with a concurrently executing timer handler and does not manage the sock refcount. Trigger: rose_release/rose_destroy_socket frees sk via sock_put() while rose_heartbeat_expiry() is running and later calls bh_lock_sock(sk). Consequence: use-after-free of the freed sock, causing kernel crash or memory corruption.

The size of the TransferFunction', '             * depends on 1<<bitspersample. So if we increase it, an access', '             * out of the buffer will happen at directory flushing.', '             * Another option would be to clear those targs. ', '             */', '            td->td_bitspersample = 8;', '            td->td_sampleformat = SAMPLEFORMAT_UINT;', '        }']}
description: LibTIFF 4.0.0alpha4, 4.0.0alpha5, 4.0.0alpha6, 4.0.0beta7, 4.0.0, 4.0.1, 4.0.2, 4.0.3, 4.0.4, 4.0.4beta, 4.0.5, 4.0.6 and 4.0.7 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer over-read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TIFF image, related to "READ of size 512" and libtiff/tif_unix.c:340:2.

evidence_lines.code:
td->td_bitspersample = 8;
td->td_sampleformat = SAMPLEFORMAT_UINT;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bits-per-sample value is overwritten without regard to the allocated TransferFunction size, which was sized from the original (e.g., 1-bit) value. commit_msg:
Fixed bug in 'lua_upvaluejoin'

Bug-fix: joining an upvalue with itself could cause a use-after-free
crash.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  LClosure *f1;', '  UpVal **up1 = getupvalref(L, fidx1, n1, &f1);', '  UpVal **up2 = getupvalref(L, fidx2, n2, NULL);'], 'added_lines': ['  UpVal **up1 = getupvalref(L, fidx1, n1);', '  UpVal **up2 = getupvalref(L, fidx2, n2);', '  if (*up1 == *up2)', '    return;']}
description: Lua 5.3.5 has a use-after-free in lua_upvaluejoin in lapi.c. For example, a crash outcome might be achieved by an attacker who is able to trigger a debug.upvaluejoin call in which the arguments have certain relationships.

code_evidence: getupvalref resolves up1 and up2 to pointers into the closure's upvalue slots. When both arguments reference the same upvalue, *up1 and *up2 are the same object, yet line 6 decrements its refcount via luaC_upvdeccount before line 7 overwrites the slot and line 8 increments the (possibly freed) object's refcount.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to and increments a reference-count field of an object it may have just released through luaC_upvdeccount, which is a use-after-free. This is not merely a double-free or reference-count leak: the stale pointer is dereferenced and modified after release.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: no check that the two resolved upvalues are distinct before the refcount is decremented. Trigger: a debug.upvaluejoin call whose arguments resolve to the same upvalue. The decrement can free the object while *up1 still aliases it, so the subsequent write to *up1 and refcount increment touch freed memory, yielding a crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
[lite] Update TfLiteIntArrayCreate to return size_t

PiperOrigin-RevId: 416439896
Change-Id: I847f69b68d1ddaff4b1e925a09b8b69c1756653b
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['int TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(int size) {', '  int computed_size = sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size;'], 'added_lines': ['size_t TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes(int size) {', '  size_t computed_size = sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size;']}
description: Tensorflow is an Open Source Machine Learning Framework. An attacker can craft a TFLite model that would cause an integer overflow in `TfLiteIntArrayCreate`. The `TfLiteIntArrayGetSizeInBytes` returns an `int` instead of a `size_t. An attacker can control model inputs such that `computed_size` overflows the size of `int` datatype. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.8.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.7.1, TensorFlow 2.6.3, and TensorFlow 2.5.3, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: The function computes the allocation size as `sizeof(dummy) + sizeof(dummy.data[0]) * size`, where the multiplication and addition are performed in `int` arithmetic (parameter `size` is `int`), and the result is returned as `int`. No check constrains `size` before multiplication, so a large attacker-controlled `size` can wrap `computed_size` to a small or negative value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs a size calculation whose result can exceed the range of `int`, producing a wraparound that violates the assumption the computed allocation size is larger than the input; this is CWE-190. It is not merely a signedness conversion issue, since the arithmetic itself overflows.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size computation uses signed `int` for the multiplication and the accumulator, so a large `size` overflows before the value is used for allocation. Trigger: attacker supplies a crafted TFLite model with a large array length. Consequence: the wrapped size yields an undersized buffer, leading to memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflows when parsing style records

Closes #124, #126.

According to https://download.microsoft.com/download/5/0/1/501ED102-E53F-4CE0-AA6B-B0F93629DDC6/Office/Excel97-2007BinaryFileFormat(xls)Specification.pdf
a "STYLE: Style Information (293h)" record might be 4 or 3+ bytes
long, depending on the first word.

We need to check that we've read enough bytes for the whole
record, so
- first we check that we have a word at least,
- then we check the subtype of the record.
- If it is a built-in style, then it has 4 bytes, so we check that.
- Otherwise the length of the name is in byte 3, so the whole record
  is 3 + buf[3] bytes long. So we need at least three bytes before we
  check the length in byte 3. Then we check if we have 3 + buf[3]
  bytes.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (xls_isRecordTooSmall(pWB, &bof1)) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (xls_isRecordTooSmall(pWB, &bof1, buf)) {']}
description: Buffer Overflow vulnerability in libxlsv.1.6.2 allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code and cause a denial of service via a crafted XLS file to the xls_parseWorkBook function in xls.c:1018.

code_evidence: buf is allocated to exactly bof1.size bytes (line 24) and filled with bof1.size bytes (line 29); the size check is invoked with only the BOF header and buffer, not validated against the STYLE record layout before the switch dispatches.

For XLS_RECORD_STYLE, the code reinterprets buf as a struct with idx/ident/lvl and reads styl->idx (line 158) and, when the built-in-style bit is set, styl->ident/styl->lvl (lines 160-161) without confirming bof1.size covers those fields; the get_string path at line 163 also assumes buf[2] exists.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is insufficient bounds validation of an attacker-controlled record length before indexing into the buffer. However, the observed accesses are reads (styl->idx/ident/lvl), which fits CWE-125 more closely than CWE-787; CWE-787 requires a write past the buffer, and no out-of-bounds write is shown in this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the STYLE handler reads fixed struct fields from a record buffer sized only by the attacker-controlled bof1.size, and the pre-switch size check does not enforce the STYLE-specific minimum. Trigger: a crafted XLS record with id XLS_RECORD_STYLE and a size smaller than the accessed struct fields. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of heap memory, potentially crashing or leaking data; the patch's addition of buf to xls_isRecordTooSmall targets this sizing gap.

commit_msg:
Jann Horn reported that SO_PEERCRED and SO_PEERGROUPS implementations
are racy, as af_unix can concurrently change sk_peer_pid and sk_peer_cred.

In order to fix this issue, this patch adds a new spinlock that needs
to be used whenever these fields are read or written.

fscanf() uses dynamic formatting to prevent buffer overflow

CVE: CVE-2020-29394

Signed-off-by: KHANH LUONG HONG DUY <khanh.luonghongduy@vn.bosch.com>

description: A buffer overflow in the dlt_filter_load function in dlt_common.c from dlt-daemon through 2.18.5 (GENIVI Diagnostic Log and Trace) allows arbitrary code execution because fscanf is misused (no limit on the number of characters to be read in the format argument).

code_evidence: str1 is a fixed-size stack buffer of DLT_COMMON_BUFFER_LENGTH; the loop repeatedly fills it with fscanf using the literal format "%254s", which caps input at 254 characters without regard to the actual buffer size.
The second fscanf at line 27 uses the same unbounded-by-buffer-size format, so the maximum token length is dictated by the hardcoded 254 rather than sizeof(str1).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes input into a stack buffer without a width bound tied to that buffer's size, producing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is the underlying memory-write error; the format string itself is not attacker-controlled, so it is not a format-string weakness.

str1[0] = 0;
if (fscanf(handle, "%254s", str1) != 1)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the field width in the fscanf format is a hardcoded 254 that is not derived from the destination buffer size. If DLT_COMMON_BUFFER_LENGTH is smaller than 255, a long whitespace-delimited token from an attacker-supplied filter file is written past the end of str1, corrupting adjacent stack data and enabling crash or code execution.

description: The kernel in Amazon Web Services FreeRTOS before 10.4.3 has an integer overflow in queue.c for queue creation.

code_evidence: Line 9 computes xQueueSizeInBytes as a size_t product of uxQueueLength and uxItemSize; line 11 then adds sizeof(Queue_t) to that product and passes the sum to pvPortMalloc as the allocation size.
Line 10 guards only the multiplication (length*itemSize) against overflow; no check constrains the subsequent addition sizeof(Queue_t)+xQueueSizeInBytes, so the sum can wrap to a small value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the addition assumes the result is always larger than xQueueSizeInBytes, but size_t wraparound can yield a smaller allocation size. The existing multiplication check (line 10) addresses a distinct wraparound site, not this addition.

evidence_lines.code:
xQueueSizeInBytes = ( size_t ) ( uxQueueLength * uxItemSize ); 
pxNewQueue = ( Queue_t * ) pvPortMalloc( sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes );
configASSERT( ( uxItemSize == 0 ) || ( uxQueueLength == ( xQueueSizeInBytes / uxItemSize ) ) );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the allocation size expression on line 11 adds a fixed header size to an attacker-influenced size_t without an addition-overflow check. Trigger: large uxQueueLength/uxItemSize values that pass the multiplication check but make sizeof(Queue_t)+xQueueSizeInBytes wrap. Consequence: a small buffer is allocated, and subsequent queue storage initialization (lines 14-21) can write beyond it, causing memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
With write operation on psi files replacing old trigger with a new one,
the lifetime of its waitqueue is totally arbitrary. Overwriting an
existing trigger causes its waitqueue to be freed and pending poll()
will stumble on trigger->event_wait which was destroyed.
Fix this by disallowing to redefine an existing psi trigger. If a write
operation is used on a file descriptor with an already existing psi
trigger, the operation will fail with EBUSY error.
Also bypass a check for psi_disabled in the psi_trigger_destroy as the
flag can be flipped after the trigger is created, leading to a memory
leak.

Fixes: 0e94682b73bf ("psi: introduce psi monitor")

Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

code_evidence: The function loads a trigger pointer under RCU and immediately takes a kref reference before polling [8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15]. It then calls poll_wait on &t->event_wait and touches t->event [16,17,18] before dropping the reference at [19]. The reference protects only the RCU dereference window; once kref_put runs, the waitqueue registered by poll_wait may still be referenced by the wait machinery.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code allows a pointer to freed trigger memory (specifically its embedded waitqueue) to remain reachable through the poll wait mechanism, which is exactly use-after-free (CWE-416). This is not merely a race on a live object; the object's lifetime ends while a reference remains.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function registers a waitqueue entry on t->event_wait via poll_wait but releases its kref before the poll wait is completed, so a concurrent trigger replacement can free the trigger. Trigger: a writer overwrites the psi trigger while a poll() is pending. Consequence: pending poll dereferences freed trigger->event_wait, causing a use-after-free crash or memory corruption.

description: In the Linux kernel before 4.12, Hisilicon Network Subsystem (HNS) does not consider the ETH_SS_PRIV_FLAGS case when retrieving sset_count data, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (buffer overflow and memory corruption) or possibly have unspecified other impact, as demonstrated by incompatibility between hns_get_sset_count and ethtool_get_strings.

code_evidence: hns_gmac_get_sset_count reports a nonzero string count only when stringset equals ETH_SS_STATS, returning ARRAY_SIZE(g_gmac_stats_string); for ETH_SS_PRIV_FLAGS it falls through to line 5 and returns 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The mismatch between the reported count and the strings later written causes a write outside the intended buffer, which is the out-of-bounds memory operation described by CWE-119. It is a buffer-bounds error rather than merely an incorrect return value.

evidence_lines.code:
if (stringset == ETH_SS_STATS)
return ARRAY_SIZE(g_gmac_stats_string);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The count function omits the ETH_SS_PRIV_FLAGS string set. A caller that queries the private-flag count gets 0, so the buffer sized from this count is too small; when ethtool_get_strings subsequently populates the private-flag strings, it writes beyond the allocated buffer, corrupting adjacent memory. Root cause is the missing string-set case in the count; the out-of-bounds write is the consequence.

commit_msg:
Fix RCE vulnerability on feed enrichment

Currently there are a few places in the code that do not check URLs for
the presence of a command prefix, allowing malicious websites to run any
command in the local system.

Trying to run feed enrichment (i.e. after option "Extract full content
from HTML5 and Google AMP" is enabled) in a subscription that produces
this item:

    <item>
      <title>Check /tmp/bad-item-link.txt</title>
      <link>|date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt</link>
    </item>

will cause Liferea to call update_request_new on URL
"|date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt" and then blindly run the command. A
similar effect happens when running the feed enrichment in a item that
links to a document like this:

    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html>
     <head>
      <title>AMP URL RCE PoC</title>
      <link rel="amphtml" href="|date > /tmp/bad-amp-url.txt">
     </head>
     <body>
         Check the results in /tmp/bad-amp-url.txt
     </body>
    </html>

once Liferea tries to load the AMP URL.

There are other calls to update_request_* functions where URLs are
validated correctly (e.g. in feed icons and comments) and do not trigger
this vulnerability. Since the subscription update is the exception where
feed commands are supported (and welcome!) I chose to lock this feature
behind a non-persistent flag and only enable it when required. This is
safer than adding the flag in updateOptions, which is usually reused in
subordinate requests.

This failure exists since commits b8288389820a3f510ef4b21684b22439c41d95a5
and b67dbba73443ab7b36fcd3c78aa803e974c0f23e from Setember 2017.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tupdate_request_allow_commands (request, TRUE);']}
description: A vulnerability was found in liferea. It has been rated as critical. Affected by this issue is the function update_job_run of the file src/update.c of the component Feed Enrichment. The manipulation of the argument source with the input |date >/tmp/bad-item-link.txt leads to os command injection. The attack may be launched remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The name of the patch is 8d8b5b963fa64c7a2122d1bbfbb0bed46e813e59. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-222848.

code_evidence: update_request_new builds a request from subscription_get_source(subscription), i.e. the feed/website URL, with no validation or neutralization of command-prefix characters.
The subscription filter is copied verbatim into request->filtercmd, another externally influenced command string passed downstream.

The request is then handed to update_execute_request (via prepare_update_request), which processes the source URL; the patch adds update_request_allow_commands(request, TRUE) to gate this command-capable path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-78 fits because externally controlled feed input is used to construct an OS command without neutralizing special elements like the pipe/command prefix, leading to command injection and RCE.

evidence_lines.code:
if (subscription_get_filter (subscription))
request->filtercmd = g_strdup (subscription_get_filter (subscription));

if (SUBSCRIPTION_TYPE (subscription)->prepare_update_request (subscription, request))
subscription->updateJob = update_execute_request (subscription, request, subscription_process_update_result, subscription, flags);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the subscription source URL and filter are taken from feed data and placed into an UpdateRequest without rejecting command prefixes such as '|'. Trigger: a malicious feed item whose link begins with '|date >/tmp/...' is processed during feed enrichment. Consequence: the URL reaches the command execution path, allowing arbitrary OS commands to run.

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow in malloc when tcache is enabled [BZ #22375]

When the per-thread cache is enabled, __libc_malloc uses request2size (which
does not perform an overflow check) to calculate the chunk size from the
requested allocation size. This leads to an integer overflow causing malloc
to incorrectly return the last successfully allocated block when called with
a very large size argument (close to SIZE_MAX).

This commit uses checked_request2size instead, removing the overflow.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  size_t tbytes = request2size (bytes);'], 'added_lines': ['  size_t tbytes;', '  checked_request2size (bytes, tbytes);']}
description: The malloc function in the GNU C Library (aka glibc or libc6) 2.26 could return a memory block that is too small if an attempt is made to allocate an object whose size is close to SIZE_MAX, potentially leading to a subsequent heap overflow. This occurs because the per-thread cache (aka tcache) feature enables a code path that lacks an integer overflow check.

code_evidence: Line 11 computes the tcache chunk size from the caller-controlled bytes via request2size, which (per the commit) performs no overflow check; line 12 then derives tc_idx from that potentially wrapped tbytes. The result feeds the tcache lookup at lines 15-19.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked size arithmetic that wraps on extreme input, matching CWE-190's integer overflow producing a small value used as an allocation size. It differs from a missing bounds check alone because the arithmetic itself wraps before any use.

evidence_lines.code:
size_t tbytes = request2size (bytes);
size_t tc_idx = csize2tidx (tbytes);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: request2size on an attacker-controlled size near SIZE_MAX wraps, producing a tiny tbytes/tc_idx instead of rejecting the request. Trigger: __libc_malloc called with a very large size while USE_TCACHE is enabled. Consequence: the wrapped index drives a tcache lookup that can return an undersized chunk, so the caller believes it has a large block and later writes beyond it (heap overflow).

commit_msg:
nbd/server: get rid of nbd_negotiate_read and friends

Functions nbd_negotiate_{read,write,drop_sync} were introduced in
1a6245a5b, when nbd_rwv (was nbd_wr_sync) was working through
qemu_co_sendv_recvv (the path is nbd_wr_sync -> qemu_co_{recv/send} ->
qemu_co_send_recv -> qemu_co_sendv_recvv), which just yields, without
setting any handlers. But starting from ff82911cd nbd_rwv (was
nbd_wr_syncv) works through qio_channel_yield() which sets handlers, so
watchers are redundant in nbd_negotiate_{read,write,drop_sync}, then,
let's just use nbd_{read,write,drop} functions.

Functions nbd_{read,write,drop} has errp parameter, which is unused in
this patch. This will be fixed later.

description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.1-DEV.

code_evidence: Line 4 computes val >> (nb_bits-1) and line 5 computes 1<<nb_bits; both shift amounts derive from nb_bits without an upper bound, so nb_bits >= 32 makes the shift count exceed the operand width (undefined behavior).
The same shifts recur in the non-fixed-point branch at lines 15-16, so both code paths share the unchecked shift-count dependency on nb_bits.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the shifts compute values assumed to fit the integer representation while nb_bits can exceed it, yielding wraparound/undefined results. It is not merely a bounds issue: the arithmetic on val and 1<<nb_bits is where the integer representation is exceeded.

evidence_lines.code:
if (val >> (nb_bits-1) ) {
s32 neg = (s32) val - (1<<nb_bits);

if (val >> (nb_bits-1) ) {
s32 neg = (s32) val - (1<<nb_bits);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nb_bits is used directly as a shift amount in (nb_bits-1) and 1<<nb_bits without validating it against the 32-bit operand width. Trigger: a caller supplies nb_bits >= 32 (or 0, which the patch guards). Consequence: undefined shift behavior and a corrupted neg/scale computation feeding gf_divfix, producing wrong coordinate values and potential instability.

description: In the Linux kernel before 5.2.9, there is a use-after-free bug that can be caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/usb/misc/yurex.c driver, aka CID-fc05481b2fca.

code_evidence: Line 5 drops the USB device reference via usb_put_dev(dev->udev) at the start of cleanup. Lines 10-11 and 17-18 subsequently pass dev->udev into usb_free_coherent, dereferencing the device pointer after its reference was released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses dev->udev after usb_put_dev may have freed it, matching CWE-416's reference-after-free pattern. It is not merely a double free or leak; the stale pointer is actively dereferenced in usb_free_coherent.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reference to dev->udev is dropped before the buffers associated with that device are freed. Trigger: yurex_delete runs during release; usb_put_dev may free the usb_device, then usb_free_coherent dereferences the freed device pointer, producing the KASAN use-after-free read reported in usb_free_coherent.

commit_msg: Added extra EOF check and some minor refactoring.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  SkipRGBMipmaps(image, dds_info, 3);', '', '  return MagickTrue;'], 'added_lines': ['  return(SkipRGBMipmaps(image,dds_info,3,exception));']}
description: coders/dds.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted DDS file.

code_evidence: The bit-count field from the DDS header is only checked for 8/16/32-bit paths; the 16-bit branch requires a specific bitmask, but the else branch at line 35 processes any other bitcount as 24-bit RGB.

The read loop trusts dds_info->width and dds_info->height, and only skips a fourth byte when rgb_bitcount == 32; other bitcounts are read as three bytes without validating that the header value is a supported format.
After the loop, SkipRGBMipmaps is called but its result is discarded, and the function returns MagickTrue unconditionally.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of attacker-controlled header properties (bit count, dimensions) before use, matching CWE-20's input-validation class. It is not merely a transform/filter issue, since the malformed values are accepted and used directly to drive processing.

evidence_lines.code:
SkipRGBMipmaps(image, dds_info, 3);
return MagickTrue;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the DDS pixelformat bit-count and image dimensions from the file are not validated against supported values before driving blob reads and pixel allocation. Trigger: a crafted DDS file with an unexpected rgb_bitcount (or inconsistent dimensions) reaches the else branch and is processed as 24-bit data. The mismatch between declared and consumed data can cause excessive resource use or a crash, supporting the reported denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fixed heap-use-after-free in JSON.parse().

This correctly fixes the issues addressed in 1405:9beb9ea093b5.
The initial fix wrongly assumed that the "value" pointer is still valid when
njs_is_fast_array(&state->value) is true and the pointer can be used for
the fast path.  This is not the case when the array object is resized.

Moreover, the fast path branch may be completely eliminated because
JSON.parse() with the replacer function is relatively slow by itself.

This closes #323, #324, #325 issues on GitHub.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        /*', '         * The njs_function_apply() function can convert fast array to object.', '         * After this conversion, there will be garbage in the value.', '         */', '', '        if (njs_fast_path(njs_is_fast_array(&state->value)', '            && (state->index - 1) < njs_array(&state->value)->length))', '        {', '            if (njs_is_undefined(&parse->retval)) {', '                njs_set_invalid(value);', '', '            } else {', '                *value = parse->retval;', '            }', '', '            break;', '        }', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: njs through 0.4.3, used in NGINX, has a use-after-free in njs_json_parse_iterator_call in njs_json.c.

code_evidence: Line 26 caches value = prop->value.data.u.value, a raw pointer into the array/object storage. Line 28 calls njs_function_apply with the user replacer function, which may resize or convert the fast array, invalidating that cached pointer. Lines 33-34 then test njs_is_fast_array(&state->value) and index against the array length, and lines 37/39 dereference the stale value pointer (njs_set_invalid(value) or *value = parse->retval).
When the fast-array test fails, lines 43-49 use njs_value_property_i64_delete/set with the index instead of the stale pointer, which is the safe path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits: the function retains and later writes through a pointer to array element storage after a callback may have freed/reallocated it. This is a use-after-free, not merely an out-of-bounds or uninitialized read, because the stale pointer references previously valid, subsequently freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cached value pointer from prop->value.data.u.value is used after njs_function_apply may have resized/converted the fast array and freed the backing storage. Trigger: a replacer function that mutates the array during JSON.parse. Consequence: dereferencing freed memory in njs_set_invalid(value) or *value assignment, yielding use-after-free (crash or memory corruption).

commit_msg:
Seth found that the CPU-entry-area; the piece of per-cpu data that is
mapped into the userspace page-tables for kPTI is not subject to any
randomization -- irrespective of kASLR settings.

On x86_64 a whole P4D (512 GB) of virtual address space is reserved for
this structure, which is plenty large enough to randomize things a
little.

As such, use a straight forward randomization scheme that avoids

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                                       const char **err_desc)'], 'added_lines': ['                                       int in_generator, const char **err_desc)', '    assert(!in_generator); /* this function is processing headers (before generators get assigned), not trailers */', '']}
description: h2o is an open source http server. In code prior to the `8c0eca3` commit h2o may attempt to access uninitialized memory. When receiving QUIC frames in certain order, HTTP/3 server-side implementation of h2o can be misguided to treat uninitialized memory as HTTP/3 frames that have been received. When h2o is used as a reverse proxy, an attacker can abuse this vulnerability to send internal state of h2o to backend servers controlled by the attacker or third party. Also, if there is an HTTP endpoint that reflects the traffic sent from the client, an attacker can use that reflector to obtain internal state of h2o. This internal state includes traffic of other connections in unencrypted form and TLS session tickets. This vulnerability exists in h2o server with HTTP/3 support, between commit 93af138 and d1f0f65. None of the released versions of h2o are affected by this vulnerability. There are no known workarounds. Users of unreleased versions of h2o using HTTP/3 are advised to upgrade immediately.

code_evidence: h2o_http3_read_frame populates frame and is checked only by its return code; when the return is nonzero the function returns at line 10 without inspecting frame. When the return is zero, frame.type is read at line 11, but no initialization of frame is visible in this function, so the frame structure's contents depend entirely on the parser having filled it. The switch at lines 12-17 then dispatches on frame.type and returns 0 for unrecognized types, allowing the caller to treat the stream as having received frames.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 fits because the code reads a resource (the frame structure) that was not initialized in this function and whose initialization by the parser is not guaranteed on the success path. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read, since the defect is the absence of initialization rather than indexing outside an object.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function consumes the frame structure produced by h2o_http3_read_frame without any local initialization and without verifying that the parser fully populated it. Trigger: receiving QUIC/HTTP-3 frames in an unexpected order lets the parser return success while leaving parts of frame unset; the subsequent frame.type test and switch then act on uninitialized memory. Supported consequence: the stream state machine advances based on garbage, which the description ties to disclosure of internal state to attacker-controlled backends.

commit_msg:
If the device node of dvb_ca_en50221 is open() and the
device is disconnected, a UAF may occur when calling
close() on the device node.

The root cause is that wake_up() and wait_event() for
dvbdev->wait_queue are not implemented.

So implement wait_event() function in dvb_ca_en50221_release()
and add 'remove_mutex' which prevents race condition
for 'ca->exit'.

[mchehab: fix a checkpatch warning]

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221121063308.GA33821@ubuntu
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <v4bel@theori.io>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!try_module_get(ca->pub->owner))'], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_lock(&ca->remove_mutex);', '', '\tif (ca->exit) {', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&ca->remove_mutex);', '\t\treturn -ENODEV;', '\t}', '', '\tif (!try_module_get(ca->pub->owner)) {', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&ca->remove_mutex);', '\t}', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&ca->remove_mutex);', '\tmutex_unlock(&ca->remove_mutex);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.10. In drivers/media/dvb-core/dvb_ca_en50221.c, a use-after-free can occur is there is a disconnect after an open, because of the lack of a wait_event.

code_evidence: The function derives 'ca' from file->private_data and, without any synchronization against teardown, calls try_module_get(ca->pub->owner) and returns -EIO on failure.
On success it sets ca->open, wakes the thread, and calls dvb_ca_private_get(ca), but there is no wait_event()/lock ordering ensuring the disconnect path has completed before these accesses.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing synchronization lets open() reference the dvb_ca_private structure after teardown frees it, matching CWE-416 (use after free). This is a race-induced lifetime flaw, not merely a null dereference or resource leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: open() and the disconnect/release path lack a shared wait_event/mutex, so open() can proceed while the device is being torn down and 'ca' is freed. Trigger: open() races with a disconnect; subsequent accesses to ca->pub, ca->open, or the thread wakeup touch freed memory. Consequence: use-after-free, potentially crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
Chain binding only requires the rule addition/insertion command within
the same transaction. Removal of rules from chain bindings within the
same transaction makes no sense, userspace does not utilize this
feature. Replace nft_chain_is_bound() check to nft_chain_binding() in
rule deletion commands. Replace command implies a rule deletion, reject
this command too.

Rule flush command can also safely rely on this nft_chain_binding()
check because unbound chains are not allowed since 62e1e94b246e
("netfilter: nf_tables: reject unbound chain set before commit phase").

Fixes: d0e2c7de92c7 ("netfilter: nf_tables: add NFT_CHAIN_BINDING")
Reported-by: Kevin Rich <kevinrich1337@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (nft_chain_binding(chain))', '\t\treturn -EOPNOTSUPP;', '']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's netfilter: nf_tables component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

Addition and removal of rules from chain bindings within the same transaction causes leads to use-after-free.

We recommend upgrading past commit f15f29fd4779be8a418b66e9d52979bb6d6c2325.

code_evidence: After chain lookup, the function proceeds to nft_ctx_init and rule iteration/deletion without rejecting a chain that is currently bound (nft_chain_binding). The patch adds that check after the IS_ERR handling; the pre-patch code lacks any binding guard before nft_delrule/nft_delchain.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's missing nft_chain_binding check allows rules to be freed while still referenced by a chain binding, so subsequent accesses operate on freed memory, matching CWE-416 (Use After Free). The added -EOPNOTSUPP guard directly prevents that reuse path.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nf_tables_delchain permits deletion of rules/chains that are part of a binding within the same transaction, without verifying the chain is not bound. Trigger: userspace issues a delete/flush on a bound chain in the transaction, freeing rules while the binding still references them; a later transaction step reuses the freed rule memory. Supported consequence: use-after-free leading to memory corruption or local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
index: convert `read_entry` to return entry size via an out-param

The function `read_entry` does not conform to our usual coding style of
returning stuff via the out parameter and to use the return value for
reporting errors. Due to most of our code conforming to that pattern, it
has become quite natural for us to actually return `-1` in case there is
any error, which has also slipped in with commit 5625d86b9 (index:
support index v4, 2016-05-17). As the function returns an `size_t` only,
though, the return value is wrapped around, causing the caller of
`read_tree` to continue with an invalid index entry. Ultimately, this
can lead to a double-free.

Improve code and fix the bug by converting the function to return the
index entry size via an out parameter and only using the return value to
indicate errors.

Reported-by: Krishna Ram Prakash R <krp@gtux.in>
Reported-by: Vivek Parikh <viv0411.parikh@gmail.com>

code_evidence: read_entry is declared to return size_t, so the error return 0 at line 15 is indistinguishable from a valid zero-length entry size.
Line 70 checks INDEX_FOOTER_SIZE + entry_size > buffer_size and returns 0, again an error encoded as the size_t return value rather than a distinct failure code.

Lines 72-77 free tmp_path and return 0 on index_entry_dup failure, or return entry_size on success; callers cannot tell success from failure, matching the commit message's note that -1 wraps around in size_t.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 fits because the described and committed consequence is a double-free reachable through the caller continuing with an invalid index entry after read_entry misreports failure. The function itself supplies the flawed error/size channel that enables that downstream double-free rather than performing the second free directly.

Trigger: a crafted index file drives an error branch (e.g., oversized entry at line 70). Fix a buffer-overrun in SimpleParser

Summary: In the failure case, we might have already consumed the entire string.

Reviewed By: binliu19, ottoni

Differential Revision: D19610775

description: Insufficient boundary checks when decoding JSON in TryParse reads out of bounds memory, potentially leading to DOS. This issue affects HHVM 4.45.0, 4.44.0, 4.43.0, 4.42.0, 4.41.0, 4.40.0, 4.39.0, versions between 4.33.0 and 4.38.0 (inclusive), versions between 4.9.0 and 4.32.0 (inclusive), and versions prior to 4.8.7.

code_evidence: parseValue() may consume the entire input; skipSpace() is then called unconditionally on line 6 before the bounds check on line 7. skipSpace() advances parser.p while inspecting characters, so if the pointer is already at inp+length it reads past the buffer end before parser.p != inp + length is evaluated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads memory past the intended input buffer via skipSpace() without a prior bounds check, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not a write overflow, since the fault is an over-read during whitespace scanning.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: skipSpace() runs before validating that parsing succeeded and consumed exactly the input, so a fully consumed or failed parse leaves parser.p at the buffer end and skipSpace reads beyond it. Trigger: crafted JSON that consumes all input. Consequence: out-of-bounds read, potentially crashing the process (DoS).

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12995/Check for DNS compression pointers that don't point backwards.

This is what BIND 9.11.0-P2 does; it not only detects pointers that
loop, as "point backwards" means "point before anything we've processed
so far, including what we're processing right now", so the pointer can't
point to itself (as that's what we're processing right now).

This fixes an infinite loop discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

Also, add some infinite-pointer-loop captures.

More checks should be done.  We might, for example, want to make sure
the upper 2 bits of the label length/pointer byte are 00 or 11, and that
if we encounter a pointer and jump backwards to what we think is a label
the label ends before the beginning of the last label we processed, to
make sure the pointer doesn't point backwards into the *middle* of a
label, and also make sure the entire name is <= 255 bytes long.

code_evidence: The while loop at line 21 follows DNS compression pointers by setting cp = bp + offset at line 29; the only loop-protection is chars_processed, incremented at lines 35 and 58/65, checked against data_size at line 36.

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Make VERW flushing runtime conditional

Currently, VERW flushing to mitigate MDS is boot time conditional per domain
type.  However, to provide mitigations for DRPW (CVE-2022-21166), we need to
conditionally use VERW based on the trustworthiness of the guest, and the
devices passed through.

Remove the PV/HVM alternatives and instead issue a VERW on the return-to-guest
path depending on the SCF_verw bit in cpuinfo spec_ctrl_flags.

Introduce spec_ctrl_init_domain() and d->arch.verw to calculate the VERW
disposition at domain creation time, and context switch the SCF_verw bit.

For now, VERW flushing is used and controlled exactly as before, but later
patches will add per-domain cases too.

No change in behaviour.

This is part of XSA-404.

commit_msg:
ALSA: timer: Fix double unlink of active_list

ALSA timer instance object has a couple of linked lists and they are
unlinked unconditionally at snd_timer_stop().  Meanwhile
snd_timer_interrupt() unlinks it, but it calls list_del() which leaves
the element list itself unchanged.  This ends up with unlinking twice,
and it was caught by syzkaller fuzzer.

The fix is to use list_del_init() variant properly there, too.

Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Tested-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tlist_del(&ti->active_list);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tlist_del_init(&ti->active_list);']}
description: The snd_timer_interrupt function in sound/core/timer.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4.1 does not properly maintain a certain linked list, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (race condition and system crash) via a crafted ioctl call.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over timer->active_list_head and processes instances whose RUNNING flag is set, modifying shared ti state while holding timer->lock.
When an instance is not AUTO, its RUNNING flag is cleared and, if other timers remain running, list_del(&ti->active_list) removes the entry without reinitializing it.
Later, the same instance's ack_list is added to the ack_list_head and slave instances are traversed, so the instance remains reachable via other paths after its active_list entry was deleted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper synchronization of a shared linked list across concurrent code sequences, matching CWE-362's concurrent execution with a timing window. It is not merely a logic bug: two sequences can act on the same list node, violating exclusivity.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: list_del() leaves ti->active_list in a stale, non-reinitialized state after unlinking, while the instance continues to be referenced through ack/slave handling. A concurrent snd_timer_stop()/ioctl path can then unlink the same element again, corrupting the list; the resulting double unlink causes a crash or instability (DoS).

commit_msg:
Disallow namespace nodes in XPointer ranges

Namespace nodes must be copied to avoid use-after-free errors.
But they don't necessarily have a physical representation in a
document, so simply disallow them in XPointer ranges.

Found with afl-fuzz.

Fixes CVE-2016-4658.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    ret = (xmlXPathObjectPtr) xmlMalloc(sizeof(xmlXPathObject));', '    if (ret == NULL) {', '        xmlXPtrErrMemory("allocating range");', '\treturn(NULL);', '    }', '    memset(ret, 0 , (size_t) sizeof(xmlXPathObject));', '    ret->type = XPATH_RANGE;', '    ret->user = start;', '    ret->index = startindex;', '    ret->user2 = end;', '    ret->index2 = endindex;'], 'added_lines': ['    ret = xmlXPtrNewRangeInternal(start, startindex, end, endindex);']}
description: xpointer.c in libxml2 before 2.9.5 (as used in Apple iOS before 10, OS X before 10.12, tvOS before 10, and watchOS before 3, and other products) does not forbid namespace nodes in XPointer ranges, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (use-after-free and memory corruption) via a crafted XML document.

code_evidence: The function allocates an xmlXPathObject and stores the caller-supplied start/end nodes and indices directly into ret->user, ret->index, ret->user2, ret->index2 without validating that these nodes are not namespace nodes. xmlXPtrRangeCheckOrder only reorders the range; it does not reject namespace nodes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the unchecked namespace-node endpoints cause out-of-bounds/use-after-free memory operations on internal structures. Distinguish from CWE-416 (use-after-free): the root cause here is the missing restriction on buffer/node operands, with the use-after-free being the resultant memory-safety consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the range constructor accepts arbitrary node pointers, including namespace nodes that lack a physical document representation, and stores them in the XPath range object. Trigger: a crafted XML/XPointer expression whose range endpoints are namespace nodes. Consequence: later range processing dereferences/copies these nodes, leading to use-after-free and memory corruption, which can enable code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  _contentLength = atoi(lp);', '  if (_contentLength <= 0) {', '    XmlRpcUtil::error("Error in XmlRpcClient::readHeader: Invalid Content-length specified (%d).", _contentLength);'], 'added_lines': ['  // avoid overly large or improperly formatted content-length', '  long int clength = 0;', '  clength = strtol(lp, nullptr, 10);', '  if ((clength <= 0) || (clength > __INT_MAX__)) {', '    XmlRpcUtil::error("Error in XmlRpcClient::readHeader: Invalid Content-length specified.");', '  _contentLength = int(clength);']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: The Content-length value parsed from the network header is converted with atoi() at line 39 and stored into the int member _contentLength. The only validation at line 40 rejects values <= 0, so a decimal string exceeding INT_MAX is not detected before conversion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the code performs an int conversion of an attacker-controlled length without constraining it to the int range, exactly the unchecked integer conversion/overflow pattern. A stricter strtol() with range checking (as the patch adds) would prevent the wraparound; this is not merely a parsing-format weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an untrusted Content-length header is decoded with atoi() directly into an int, with no upper-bound or conversion-failure check. Trigger: a remote peer sends a header whose numeric value exceeds INT_MAX; atoi() returns an implementation-defined/overflowed int that may be negative or wrapped. The <=0 guard only catches some wrapped results, so a large or wrapped length can pass or mislead subsequent size logic, supporting integer-overflow-driven misbehavior (e.g., incorrect allocation/read sizing or DoS).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. Due to lack of validation in `tf.raw_ops.RaggedTensorToTensor`, an attacker can exploit an undefined behavior if input arguments are empty. The implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/656e7673b14acd7835dc778867f84916c6d1cac2/tensorflow/core/kernels/ragged_tensor_to_tensor_op.cc#L356-L360) only checks that one of the tensors is not empty, but does not check for the other ones. There are multiple `DCHECK` validations to prevent heap OOB, but these are no-op in release builds, hence they don't prevent anything. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick these commits on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

Inner loops [17,18,21,22] push real_length plus (row_length - real_length) entries per row, so total appended size depends on row_split values; the only check [25,26] is a DCHECK that is a no-op in release builds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to correctly validate/calculate the buffer size (result length) against row_split-derived expectations, matching CWE-131's incorrect buffer size calculation, which enables the OOB. This is a size-computation/validation flaw, not merely an unchecked index.

In release builds an inconsistent or empty row_split lets result->size() diverge from the expected size, and downstream indexing uses these mismatched sizes, yielding heap OOB.

commit_msg:
Fixed Array.prototype.concat() when "this" is a slow array.

Previously, when the current appended element is fast array the "this"
array was expected to always be a fast array also.  This may not be the
case when the previous appended element was not fast thus converting
the "this" array to a slow form.

Previous fix introduced in 2c1382bab643 (0.7.2) was not complete, the
correct fix is to never assume "this" is fast, whereas njs_array_add()
may only be called with fast arrays.

This closes #471 issue in Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    ret = njs_array_add(vm, array, &retval);', '                    if (njs_slow_path(ret != NJS_OK)) {', '                        return NJS_ERROR;'], 'added_lines': ['                    ret = njs_value_property_i64_set(vm, &this, length,', '                                                     &retval);', '                    if (njs_slow_path(ret == NJS_ERROR)) {', '                        return ret;']}
description: nginx njs 0.7.2 is vulnerable to Buffer Overflow. Type confused in Array.prototype.concat() when a slow array appended element is fast array.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function performs no buffer copy; the concat loop appends elements via njs_array_add/njs_value_property_i64_set, and the diff only changes the append API to handle slow 'this' arrays, so CWE-120's buffer-copy-without-size-check mechanism is not evidenced.

commit_msg:
pkey: add support for PKCS #8 key serialization

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#private_to_der, #private_to_pem are added to the
generic PKey class. They serialize the private key to PKCS #8
{Encrypted,}PrivateKeyInfo format, in DER- and PEM- encoding,
respectively. For symmetry, also add #public_to_der and #public_to_pem
that serialize the public key into X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo format.

OpenSSL::PKey.read now reads DER-encoded PKCS #8 keys as well as the
"raw" private keys. PEM-encoded PKCS #8 keys have been already handled
by PEM_read_bio_PrivateKey().

description: The Ruby http gem before 0.7.3 does not verify hostnames in SSL connections, which might allow remote attackers to obtain sensitive information via a man-in-the-middle-attack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only registers PKey methods (including serialization methods) in Init_ossl_pkey; it contains no hostname verification, SSL connection handling, or information-exposure logic matching the described vulnerability, and merely defining private_to_der/private_to_pem is not itself an exposure.

commit_msg: core(persistence): added null ptr checks
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (!ptr)', '            CV_PARSE_ERROR_CPP("Invalid input");', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in OpenCV before 4.1.1. There is a NULL pointer dereference in the function cv::XMLParser::parse at modules/core/src/persistence.cpp.

code_evidence: Line 3 dereferences ptr via *ptr without first verifying that ptr is non-NULL.
Line 5 computes beg = ptr + 1 and the loop at lines 6-9 increments ptr and dereferences it through cv_isprint(*ptr), so a NULL input propagates into further dereferences.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the function dereferences a pointer it assumes is valid but which can be NULL, matching the NULL pointer dereference definition. The missing guard, not an out-of-bounds index, is the core issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: parseKey trusts the caller-supplied ptr to be valid and dereferences it immediately at line 3 (and again in the loop) with no NULL check. Trigger: a caller passing a NULL buffer pointer. Consequence: a crash/denial of service from reading through the NULL pointer.

commit_msg:
gdImageScaleTwoPass memory leak fix

Fixing memory leak in gdImageScaleTwoPass, as reported by @cmb69 and
confirmed by @vapier.  This bug actually bit me in production and I'm
very thankful that it was reported with an easy fix.

Fixes #173.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        gdFree(tmp_im);'], 'added_lines': ['        gdImageDestroy(tmp_im);']}
description: The gdImageScaleTwoPass function in gd_interpolation.c in the GD Graphics Library (aka libgd) before 2.2.0, as used in PHP before 5.6.12, uses inconsistent allocate and free approaches, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a crafted call, as demonstrated by a call to the PHP imagescale function.

code_evidence: When a horizontal pass is needed, tmp_im is allocated by gdImageCreateTrueColor at line 18, which allocates a gdImagePtr structure plus pixel buffers. The cleanup at lines 34-36 releases it with gdFree(tmp_im), which frees only the struct, not the pixel data or other members allocated by gdImageCreateTrueColor. The fix swaps gdFree for gdImageDestroy, confirming the mismatch between allocation and deallocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 covers resource management errors such as improper deallocation leading to resource exhaustion. The inconsistent allocate/free pairing here directly matches that weakness rather than a memory-safety violation like use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tmp_im, an image created via gdImageCreateTrueColor, is deallocated with gdFree, which does not release the pixel buffers owned by the image. Trigger: any call where src_width != new_width (so tmp_im is freshly allocated) and src_height != new_height. Consequence: per-call memory leak, allowing repeated crafted imagescale calls to exhaust memory and cause denial of service.

description: The yr_arena_write_data function in YARA 3.6.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (buffer over-read and application crash) or obtain sensitive information from process memory via a crafted file that is mishandled in the yr_re_fast_exec function in libyara/re.c and the _yr_scan_match_callback function in libyara/scan.c.

code_evidence: The repeat loop computes next_input = input + i * input_incr before checking bytes_matched + i against max_bytes_matched, so the pointer may be advanced beyond the buffer for large i.
The code then dereferences *next_input in the literal comparison at line 109, reading memory past the end of the input buffer.
After the loop, bytes_matched is incremented by repeat_any_args->min without clamping to max_bytes_matched, allowing the matched count to exceed the buffer bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function reads *next_input beyond the intended input buffer due to missing bound validation before the dereference. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, and the consequence is memory disclosure or DoS.
